while he himself, outside the hall,
set up another bed,
holding a bow and arrows to await the fox.
On the third night,
he suddenly said:
"Have you all slept well enough?
I have just shot the fox,
and will retrieve it tomorrow."
Everyone thought he was mad and did not believe him.
At dawn,
they saw blood on the window,
followed the trail of blood,
and entered a large pit,
where under the grass they found a female fox,
pierced by an arrow and dying.
Àn's wife burned the fox to ashes,
consumed it entirely,
and from then on, Àn recovered.
Later, he served as Deputy Magistrate of Yuánwǔ County.
While in the official hall,
he suddenly saw an old fox servant
bowing twice to Àn,
saying she was the family's
wet nurse.
"In the past, our young lady was wrongly killed by the Cuī family.
The master and mistress constantly reminisce,
never ceasing to speak of it.
Now they wish to marry their younger daughter to you, Wáng Láng, to renew the bond.
Therefore, I am sent to convey their intent,
and to select an auspicious day for the wedding."
Àn was very frightened.
He agreed,
offering generous rewards,
amounting to tens of thousands.
After making arrangements,
he hastily took out over ten bolts of silk brocade
and burned them in the main street.
The old servant then said to her mistress:
"There are countless handsome men under heaven;
why insist on taking this old Wáng gentleman as a son-in-law?"
With these words, she vanished.
Yuán Jiāzuò
Yuán Jiāzuò, Tutor to Prince Níng of the Táng dynasty,
at age fifty,
was appointed by imperial decree as Deputy Magistrate of Yuán County.
The post was vacant,
and notoriously ominous,
as all who held it died.
When Jiāzuò took office,
the deputy magistrate's residence had been uninhabited for several terms,
with buildings in ruins
and overgrown with thorns.
Jiāzuò cleared the thorns,
repaired the walls,
and sat in the official hall.
The local elders and clerks were all afraid,
advising him not to stay, but he refused.
Soon, a demon caused disturbances at night,
but Jiāzuò remained unmoved,
waiting to see where it entered.
The next day, he dug there,
and found a fox,
an old one,
along with several dozen of its offspring.
Jiāzuò cooked them all,
and when it was the old fox's turn,
it spoke:
"My spirit can reach heaven,
foreseeing fortune and misfortune.
I beg you to spare me,
for I can benefit people.
Now this residence is already peaceful;
what harm is there in letting me go?"
Jiāzuò stepped forward and spoke with it,
and it fully informed him of his official promotions.
It also said:
"I wish to be your eyes and ears,
always by your side."
So Jiāzuò spared the fox.
Later, as the fox predicted,
after his term ended, he was indeed promoted.
Within a few years, he rose to Censor.
The fox then departed.
Lǐ Línfǔ
During the Táng dynasty, when Lǐ Línfǔ was serving as chancellor,
he once returned from court
and sat in the front corridor of his hall.
He saw a black fox,
of very large build,
like an ox or horse,
with a dark, glossy coat,
emerge from the hall,
dash into the courtyard,
and look around.
Línfǔ ordered bows and arrows,
intending to shoot it,
but before he could,
it had already vanished from sight.
From then on, for several days,
whenever he sat during the day,
a black fox would appear.
That year, Línfǔ’s property was confiscated.
Sūn Zèngshēng
The Táng dynasty Daoist priest Sūn Zèngshēng originally made his living by training falcons.
Later, while releasing a falcon,
he entered a cave
and saw several dozen foxes reading books.
An old fox sat in the center,
passing them along in turn for instruction.
Zèngshēng strode right in,
seized one of the books, and left.
The next day,
over ten people came to his door with gold and silk, seeking to redeem it.
Zèngshēng refused.
They said:
"Even if you obtain this,
you won’t be able to understand or use it.
If you copy one and return it,
we will teach you the oral formulas."
Zèngshēng eventually learned their methods
and became a renowned master of esoteric arts.
The foxes initially made an agreement with Zèngshēng
not to reveal it to others.
If he violated this,
he would surely meet a violent death.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzōng persistently sought the methods from him.
Zèngshēng refused to hand them over,
and in the end, he was executed.
Wáng Xuán
Wáng Xuán, a regional inspector of Sòngzhōu during the Táng dynasty,
was exceptionally handsome in his youth
and was bewitched by a female fox.
Family members who sometimes saw her
described her as graceful and beautiful.
Even children who encountered her
would compose themselves and pay their respects.
She called herself "the new bride"
and responded to everyone with perfect propriety.
Thus, people enjoyed seeing her.
Every Duānwǔ Festival and other fine holidays,
she would send gifts,
saying:
"The new bride offers these to so-and-so young master or so-and-so lady to prolong life."
People laughed at this,
but the gifts she gave were plentiful.
Later, when Xuán’s official rank rose high,
the fox no longer came.
It is said that when one’s emolument is weighty,
such creatures cannot work their strange arts.
Lǐ □
Dōngpíng County Captain Lǐ □, upon first obtaining his official post,
traveled from the Eastern Capital to his place of duty.
One night, he stopped at Gùchéng.
At the inn, there was an old acquaintance who made a living selling húbǐng.
His wife, surnamed Zhèng, was of exceptional beauty.
Lǐ saw her and was delighted,
and thus lodged at their place.
Lingering for several days,
he then paid fifteen thousand cash to secure the Hú woman.
After arriving in Dōngpíng,
he doted on her exceedingly.
Her nature was gentle and graceful,
full of charm, cunning, and romantic allure;
in matters of women's work,
there was nothing she did not understand thoroughly;
and she especially mastered the subtleties of music.
After three years in Dōngpíng,
they had a son.
Later, Lǐ was tasked with transporting tax goods to the capital,
and he returned together with Zhèng.
Upon reaching Gùchéng,
they held a grand feast for the local villagers,
which lasted over ten days.
Lǐ urged their departure repeatedly,
but Zhèng firmly claimed illness and would not rise,
and Lǐ, pitying her, acquiesced.
After another ten-plus days,
unable to avoid it any longer,
duty required they leave.
As they reached the outer city gate,
she suddenly complained of a stomachache,
dismounted and ran off,
swift as the wind.
Lǐ and several of his servants galloped at full speed,
but could not catch up.
She entered Gùchéng,
turned into Yìshuǐ Village,
and her pace slackened slightly.
Lǐ could not bear to abandon her,
He pursued her again.
Just as he was about to reach her,
she entered a small hole.
He called out to her with all his might,
but there was only silence, no response.
Heartache and sorrow gripped him,
words failed and tears fell.
As dusk fell,
villagers stuffed grass into the mouth of the hole,
and he returned to the inn to stay the night.
At dawn,
he went again to call for her,
but saw nothing.
He then used smoke to fumigate the hole.
After a long time,
villagers dug several zhàng deep,
and saw a vixen dead in the hole,
its clothes shed like a sloughed skin,
On its feet were brocade socks.
Lǐ sighed for a long while,
then finally buried it.
Returning to the inn,
he took hunting dogs to bite his son,
but the child showed no reaction at all,
[He was] frightened and afraid.
He then took the child to the capital,
and left him with relatives to raise.
After delivering the taxes,
he returned again to the Eastern Capital,
and married a woman of the Xiāo family.
Lady Xiāo,
often called Lǐ "the fox husband,"
and at first Lǐ had no reply.
One evening,
Lǐ and Lady Xiāo, hand in hand,
returned to their chamber for intimate play,
and he spoke of the matter again.
Suddenly, they heard a voice in the front hall.
Lǐ asked:
"Who comes by night?"
The reply was:
Do you not recognize Zhèng Sìniáng?"
Lǐ had long cherished her memory,
and hearing her
words,
immediately leapt up joyfully.
He asked:
"Are you a ghost?
Or a human?"
She replied:
"I am indeed a ghost."
He wished to
approach her but could not.
Sìniáng,
then said to Lǐ:
"The ways of humans and spirits are different.
Why must your worthy wife repeatedly insult and curse me?
Moreover, the son we bore,
sent far away to be raised by others—
those people all say he is fox-born,
and do not provide him clothing or food.
Do you not care at all?
You should arrange for his care soon,
so that I may have no regrets in the Nine Springs.
If your wife continues her insults,
and the child remains uncared for,
it will surely bring calamity upon you."
Having spoken, she vanished.
Thereafter, Lady Xiāo did not dare speak of the matter again.
At the end of the Táng dynasty's Tiānbǎo era,
the child was over ten years old,
and quite unharmed.
Lǐ Kuí
The Táng Chancellor Lǐ Kuí,
in the early Qiányuán era,
served as a Zhōngshū Shèrén.
One day after returning from court,
he saw a white fox on the stone fulling block in his courtyard.
He ordered a servant boy to chase it,
but it had already disappeared.
At the time, there was a guest at Kuí's gate,
and when the matter was discussed,
the guest said:
"This is an auspicious sign,
I dare offer congratulations."
The next day,
he was indeed selected as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Sòng Pǔ
Sòng Pǔ,
during the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
served as Captain of Chángchéng.
He himself said that when he was young,
he and his companions set traps at night for wild foxes,
but caught nothing for several nights.
Later, on a moonlit night,
they were again engaged in this activity.
They saw a ghost wearing a bamboo hat, riding a fox,
singing the "Dú Pánzi" tune,
arriving at the trap site.
The fox was about to enter the trap,
but the ghost then placed its hand on the fox's cheek,
causing it to turn back.
This happened several times.
On a later night,
Pǔ again hid by the trap waiting,
and the ghost came riding the fox once more,
with two small ghosts leading the way,
going back and forth to the trap site.
Pǔ and the others caught nothing and gave up.
There was also one named Tán Zhòng who said
that when he was young and setting a trap,
he suddenly saw an old man with a cane come to the base of the tree where he was hiding.
The old man looked up and asked what sort of person was up in the tree.
Zhòng was still young at the time,
and was very frightened.
His elder brother then angrily shouted:
"Old wild fox,
how dare you act like this?"
He climbed down the tree to chase it,
and the fox then transformed and ran away.
Monk Yàntōng
In Jìnzhōu's Chángníng County, there was a monk named Yàntōng who practiced the dhūta ascetic discipline.
As night approached,
he would invariably seek lodging in the dense woods among disordered graves.
Even amid wind, rain, dew, or snow,
his discipline remained unchanged;
even when faced with demons and spirits,
his mind did not waver.
One moonlit night,
he rested to the left of a pile of bones by the roadside,
when suddenly a demon fox came staggering along.
At first, it did not anticipate Yàntōng's presence in the tree shadows,
so it picked up a skull and placed it on its head,
then shook it.
If the skull fell off,
it would not look back,
but instead choose another.
After no more than four or five attempts,
it finally found one
that sat firmly atop its head.
Then it gathered leaves and flowers,
using them to conceal its form,
and as it glanced around,
they transformed into clothing.
In an instant,
it changed into a woman
and gracefully departed.
By the roadside,
it waited for passersby.
Soon, someone came hastening south on horseback,
and upon hearing this from afar,
the demon fox began wailing by the road.
The traveler halted his horse and asked her,
to which she replied:
"I am a singer,
traveling with my husband to the capital.
This morning, my husband was killed by bandits,
who plundered all our possessions.
Alone and far from home,
I long to return north,
but have no means to do so.
If you would take me in,
I vow to offer my humble self
to serve as your maidservant."
The traveler was a soldier from Yìdìng,
and he dismounted to look closely at her.
Pleased by her beauty,
and moved by her earnest words,
he helped her onto the back of his horse to travel together.
Yàntōng suddenly emerged and said to him:
"This is a demon fox—
how can you be so careless?"
With that, he raised his monk's staff and struck the fox's head,
causing the skull to fall off immediately.
The fox then resumed its original form and fled.
Rén Shì
was a female demon.
There was a certain Gentleman Wéi,
named Yín,
the ninth son,
maternal grandson of Prince Xìn'ān Wéi Huī.
In his youth he was carefree and unrestrained,
fond of drinking wine.
His paternal cousin's brother-in-law was named Zhèng Liù,
though his given name is not recorded.
He had practiced martial arts from an early age,
and was also fond of wine and women,
but poor and without a home,
he lodged with his wife's family.
He and Yín got along well,
and were constantly together without separation.
In the summer, the sixth month of the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Yín and Zhèng were walking together on a road in Cháng'ān,
on their way to meet for drinks at Xīnchāng Lǐ.
When they reached the south of Xuānpíng,
Zhèng excused himself, saying he had some business,
and asked to leave separately,
promising to join them later at the drinking place.
Yín rode his white horse eastward,
while Zhèng rode his donkey southward,
entering through the north gate of Shēngpíng.
By chance, he encountered three women walking on the road,
among whom was one dressed in white,
of exceptionally beautiful appearance.
When Zhèng saw her, he was startled and delighted,
and urged his donkey forward,
now suddenly going ahead of her,
now suddenly falling behind,
wishing to make advances but not daring to.
The woman in white from time to time glanced sidelong at him,
her expression indicating she was receptive.
Zhèng teased her, saying:
"One so beautiful as you,
yet walking on foot—
why is that?"
The woman in white laughed and said:
"Since you have a mount but don't understand how to lend it,
what else can I do but walk?"
Zhèng said:
"This poor mount is hardly worthy to replace such a beauty's steps,
but I now offer it to you.
I shall be content to follow on foot."
They looked at each other and laughed heartily.
Their companions also bantered and flirted with each other,
and soon they grew familiar and intimate.
Zhèng followed them,
eastward to Lèyóu Yuán,
by which time it was already dark.
He saw a residence,
with an earthen wall and a carriage gate,
the buildings within quite imposing.
As the woman in white was about to enter,
she turned and said:
"Please wait a moment before coming in."
One of her maidservants
remained by the gate screen,
and asked Zhèng his surname and rank.
After Zhèng had told her,
he also asked hers,
to which she replied:
"Surname Rén,
the twentieth."
After a short while,
he was invited inside.
Zhèng tethered his donkey at the gate,
placed his hat on the saddle,
and then saw a woman over thirty years old,
who came to greet him—
this was Rén Shì's elder sister.
Candles were lit and a meal set out,
and they raised their cups and drank several rounds.
Rén Shì then reappeared after changing her attire,
and they drank merrily with great joy.
Late into the night they retired to bed,
and her lovely form and beautiful qualities,
her singing, laughter, and demeanor,
every gesture and movement was enchanting,
almost as if not of this world.
As dawn approached,
Rén Shì said:
"You should leave now.
My brothers are registered in the Imperial Music Academy,
and serve in the Southern Administration;
they will rise and go out in the morning,
so you must not linger."
So they arranged to meet again later, and he departed.
After he left,
and reached the ward gate,
the gate was still locked and not yet opened.
Beside the gate was a shop where a foreigner sold pancakes,
just then lighting his lamps and stoking his stove.
Zhèng rested beneath its curtain,
sitting and waiting for the drum signal,
and took the opportunity to speak with the shopkeeper.
Pointing in the direction from which he had come, Zhèng asked him:
"Turning east from here,
there is a gate—
whose residence is that?"
The shopkeeper said:
"That is a collapsed wall and abandoned land,
there is no residence there."
Zhèng said:
"I just passed by it,
how can you say there is none?"
He argued stubbornly with him.
The shopkeeper suddenly understood,
and said:
"Ah.
Now I know.
There is a fox spirit there,
who often lures men to spend the night with her;
I have seen it three times already.
Have you now encountered her too?"
Zhèng flushed and concealed the truth, saying:
"No."
At daybreak,
he went back to look at the place,
and saw the earthen wall and carriage gate as before.
Peering inside,
all he saw was overgrown weeds and a deserted garden.
After returning,
he met Yín.
Yín reproached him for missing their appointment,
but Zhèng did not reveal the truth,
answering with other matters.
Yet he longed for her enchanting beauty,
wishing to see her once more,
and kept her in his heart, unable to forget.
After about ten days,
while Zhèng was out walking,
he caught a glimpse of her in a clothing shop in the West Market,
with her former maidservant in attendance.
Zhèng immediately called out to her,
but Rén Shì turned sideways and moved through the crowd to avoid him.
Zhèng called repeatedly and pressed forward,
so she finally turned her back, standing,
and shielded herself with a fan, saying from behind it:
"Since you know what I am,
why do you still approach me?"
Zhèng said:
"Even though I know,
what does it matter?"
She replied:
"The affair is shameful,
and I find it hard to show my face."
Zhèng said:
"If I long for you so earnestly,
how can you bear to abandon me?"
She replied:
"How would I dare abandon you?
I only fear that you will come to despise me."
Zhèng swore an oath,
his words growing even more earnest.
Then Rén Shì turned her eyes toward him and lowered her fan,
her radiant beauty as stunning as before.
She said to Zhèng:
"In this world, there are many like me,
you just haven't recognized them,
so don't think I am unique or strange."
Zhèng asked to renew their intimacy with her.
She replied:
"Generally, those of my kind
are hated and feared by people
for no other reason
than because they harm people.
But I am not like that.
If you do not despise me,
I wish to devote myself to serving you for the rest of my life."
Zhèng agreed and discussed finding a place to live with her.
Rén Shì said:
"East from here,
there is a house for rent.
Its main room is high and spacious,
with side rooms in the courtyard.
Outside the gate it is secluded and quiet,
suitable to rent and live in.
The other day, south of Xuānpíng,
the one who rode a white horse eastward—
wasn't that your wife's brother?
His household has many utensils,
which we could borrow."
At that time, Yín's uncles were away on duties in various places,
and the utensils from their three courtyards
were all stored away.
Zhèng followed her words and found the house,
then went to Yín to borrow utensils.
When asked what they were for,
Zhèng said:
"I have recently obtained a beautiful woman,
and have already rented a house for her;
I wish to borrow some to furnish it."
Yín laughed and said:
"Judging by your appearance,
I was certain to obtain someone ugly and crude,
how could there be such an unparalleled beauty?"
Yín then lent all the curtains, beds, and mats needed,
and sent a clever and sharp-witted servant boy
to follow and spy on them.
Soon the boy came running back with his report,
panting and drenched in sweat.
Yín met him and asked:
"Is there one?"
He said:
"There is."
He asked again:
"What does she look like?"
He said:
"She is extraordinary,
I have never seen anyone like her in the world!"
Yín had many relatives and connections,
and had long indulged in carefree travels,
so he knew many beautiful women.
He then asked:
"Who is as beautiful as so-and-so?"
The servant boy said:
"She is not in the same league!"
Yín listed four or five of the most beautiful women he knew,
and each time the boy said:
"Not in the same league."
At that time, the sixth daughter of the Prince of Wú,
who was Yín's younger cousin,
was as lush and radiant as a goddess,
and was unanimously considered the foremost beauty among all their relatives.
Yín asked:
"How does she compare to the sixth daughter of the Prince of Wú?"
Again he said:
"Not in the same league."
Yín clapped his hands in great astonishment and said:
"How can there be such a person in the world?"
He immediately ordered water to be drawn to wash his neck,
wrapped his head in a cloth, applied lip balm, and went.
When he arrived,
Zhèng Zǐ happened to be out.
Yín entered the door,
and saw a young servant holding a broom sweeping,
there was a maidservant at the gate,
but he saw nothing else.
He questioned the young servant,
the young servant laughed and said:
"There is no one."
Yín looked all around the room,
and saw a red skirt peeking out from under the door.
He pressed closer to observe,
and saw Rèn shì hiding herself behind a fan.
Yín pulled her,
and brought her out,
to examine her in the light,
and she was even more beautiful than what had been described.
Yín fell madly in love with her,
and embraced and tried to force himself on her,
but she would not submit,
so Yín used his strength to overpower her.
Just as he was pressing urgently,
she then said:
"I submit.
Please allow me a little respite."
Once he complied,
she resisted as before.
This happened several times.
Yín then used all his strength to hold her tightly,
Rèn shì's strength was exhausted,
and she was sweating as if drenched by rain.
Realizing she could not avoid it,
she relaxed her body and no longer resisted,
but her expression turned sorrowful.
Yín asked:
"Why do you look so unhappy?"
Rèn shì sighed deeply and said:
"How pitiable Zhèng Liù is!"
Yín said:
"What do you mean?"
She replied:
"Zhèng shēng has a six-foot-tall body,
yet cannot protect a single woman,
how can he be considered a real man!
Moreover, you, sir, have been wealthy and extravagant since youth,
and have obtained many beautiful women,
there are many who are comparable to me.
But Zhèng shēng is poor and lowly,
the one who truly satisfies him,
is only me.
How can you bear, with your surplus,
to take away what another lacks?
Pitying his poverty and hunger, unable to stand on his own,
wearing your clothes,
eating your food,
is why I am bound to you.
If coarse food could sustain him,
it would not have come to this."
Yín was heroic and righteous,
and upon hearing her words,
he immediately released her.
He straightened his clothes and apologized:
"I dare not."
Soon Zhèng Zǐ arrived,
and he and Yín looked at each other and laughed happily.
From then on,
all of Rèn shì's firewood, grain, and livestock provisions,
were supplied by Yín.
Rèn shì would sometimes come and go,
entering and leaving by carriage, horse, sedan, or on foot,
with no fixed residence.
Yín spent his days with her,
very happily.
Whenever they were intimate and familiar,
there was nothing they did not do,
except they never crossed the line into impropriety.
Therefore Yín loved and respected her,
and spared no expense,
not a single meal or drink
passed without him thinking of her.
Rèn shì knew he loved her,
and thus spoke to thank him:
"I am ashamed by the depth of your affection for me.
But with my humble qualities,
I am not worthy of repaying your great kindness;
moreover, I cannot betray Zhèng shēng,
so I cannot fulfill your desires.
I,
am from Qín.
I grew up in the city of Qín,
my family originally were entertainers,
my cousins and relatives
were mostly taken as concubines by others,
therefore, in the pleasure quarters of Cháng'ān,
I am familiar with all of them.
If there are any extraordinary beauties,
whom you desire but cannot obtain,
I can secure them for you.
I wish to use this to repay your kindness."
Yín said:
"That would be wonderful!"
In the market, there was a clothes-selling woman named Zhāng Shíwǔniáng,
whose skin was pure and white,
and Yín had long fancied her.
He thus asked Rèn shì if she knew her,
she replied:
"She is my younger cousin,
securing her is easy."
After more than ten days,
she indeed secured her.
After a few months, he grew tired and ended it.
Rèn shì said:
"Market women are easy to obtain,
and are not enough to demonstrate my effectiveness.
If there are secluded and unparalleled ones difficult to scheme for,
try mentioning them,
and I wish to exert all my intelligence and effort."
Yín said:
"On the recent Cold Food Festival,
I went with two or three friends to Qiānfú Temple,
and saw General Diāo Miǎn hosting a musical performance in the hall,
there was one skilled at playing the shēng,
sixteen years old,
with twin hair buns hanging by her ears,
her delicate appearance was stunningly beautiful.
Do you know her?"
Rèn shì said:
"That is Chǒngnú.
Her mother is my elder cousin,
I can seek her out."
Yín bowed before her seat.
Rèn shì agreed,
and then went in and out of the Diāo household.
After over a month,
Yín urged and asked about her plan,
Rèn shì wished to have two rolls of fine silk as a bribe,
and Yín provided them as requested.
Two days later,
while Rèn shì and Yín were eating,
Miǎn sent an old servant leading a black horse to fetch Rèn shì,
Rèn shì, hearing the summons,
smiled and said to Yín:
"It is done."
Initially, Rèn shì had caused Chǒngnú to fall ill,
and neither acupuncture nor medicine reduced it.
Her mother and Miǎn were extremely worried,
and were about to consult shamans.
Rèn shì secretly bribed a shaman,
pointing out her own residence,
and made the shaman say that moving there would be auspicious.
When they came to examine the illness,
the shaman said:
"It is unfavorable to stay at home,
she should go out and reside in a certain place to the southeast,
to obtain vital energy."
Miǎn and her mother examined the location,
and it was Rèn shì's residence.
Miǎn then requested to stay there.
Rèn shì falsely declined, saying it was too cramped,
After earnest entreaty, she finally consented.
He then transported clothing, ornaments, and playthings,
and together with her mother, sent them to Rén Shì’s residence.
Upon arrival, her illness was cured.
Within a few days,
Rén Shì secretly arranged for Wéi Yín to have relations with her,
and after a month, she became pregnant.
Her mother grew fearful,
and hastily returned to be with Wéi Miǎn,
after which contact ceased.
Another day,
Rén Shì said to Master Zhèng:
“Can you obtain five or six thousand coins?
I intend to make a profit.”
Master Zhèng said:
“Yes.”
He then borrowed from others,
and obtained six thousand coins.
Rén Shì said:
“In the market, there is a horse for sale;
on its thigh there is a blemish.
You should buy it and keep it.”
Master Zhèng went to the market,
and indeed saw a man leading a horse seeking to sell it,
with a black mark on its left thigh.
Master Zhèng bought it and returned.
His wife and brothers all mocked him, saying:
“This is a worthless thing;
what purpose does buying it serve?”
Not long after,
Rén Shì said:
“The horse can now be sold.
You should get thirty thousand for it.”
Master Zhèng then went to sell it.
Someone offered twenty thousand,
but Master Zhèng refused.
The whole market said:
“Why is he so stubborn to pay a high price,
and why are you so attached that you won’t sell?”
Master Zhèng rode it home,
and the buyer followed him to his gate,
repeatedly increasing his offer,
until it reached twenty-five thousand.
Still, he refused,
saying:
“I won’t sell for less than thirty thousand.”
His wife and brothers gathered and berated him.
Master Zhèng, having no other choice,
finally sold it,
but in the end, it did not
reach thirty thousand.
Afterwards, he secretly inquired about the buyer,
asking the reason,
and learned that he was a groom from Zhāoyìng County whose horse with a blemished thigh
had died three years earlier.
This official had not yet removed it from the register,
and the government was demanding its assessed value,
amounting to sixty thousand coins.
If he could buy a replacement for half that,
the profit would still be considerable.
If he had a horse to make up the number,
then the assessed value of three years’ fodder and grain,
would all go to the official,
and moreover, the compensation would be minimal,
hence the purchase.
Rén Shì also, because her clothes were worn and tattered,
begged Yín for clothing.
Yín was about to buy whole bolts of silk for her,
but Rén Shì did not want that,
saying:
“I wish to have ready-made garments.”
Yín summoned the merchant Zhāng Dà to buy them for her,
and had him see Rén Shì,
to ask what she desired.
When Zhāng Dà saw her,
he exclaimed in astonishment to Yín:
“This must be a celestial being or noble relative,
whom you, sir, have secretly taken,
and she is not one who should exist in the mortal world.
I urge you to return her quickly,
lest disaster befall you.”
Such was the captivating beauty of her appearance.
In the end, she bought ready-made clothes,
but did not sew them herself,
and no one understood her intention.
More than a year later,
Master Zhèng was transferred for military service,
and appointed as Guǒyì Captain of the Huáilǐ garrison,
located in Jīnchéng County.
At that time, Master Zhèng already had a wife;
although he spent his days outside,
he slept indoors at night,
often regretting that he could not spend his evenings exclusively with her.
When about to take up his post,
he invited Rén Shì to go with him,
but Rén Shì did not wish to go,
saying:
“Traveling together for ten days or a month
would not suffice for joy.
I ask that you calculate and provide provisions for me,
and I will stay quietly here awaiting your return.”
Master Zhèng earnestly pleaded,
but Rén Shì became even more unwilling.
Master Zhèng then sought Yín’s assistance,
and Yín joined in urging and persuading her,
also questioning her reason.
After a long while, Rén Shì said:
“There is a shaman who said
that this year it is inauspicious for me to travel west,
hence I do not wish to go.”
Master Zhèng was greatly puzzled,
and without considering other possibilities,
he and Yín laughed heartily, saying:
“One so intelligent as you,
yet believing in such demonic superstitions—
why?”
They insisted on their request,
and Rén Shì said:
“If the shaman’s words prove true,
I would merely die for you,
what good would that be?”
The two men said:
“How could such a thing be?”
They pleaded as earnestly as before.
Rén Shì, having no alternative,
finally set out.
Yín lent her a horse,
and they saw her off at Língāo,
waving their sleeves in farewell.
After two nights’ journey,
they reached Mǎwéi.
Rén Shì rode on horseback ahead,
while Master Zhèng followed on a donkey behind.
A maidservant rode separately,
further behind.
At that time, the keeper of the west gate was training hunting dogs in Luòchuān,
and had been doing so for ten days.
They happened to meet on the road,
when a gray dog leapt out from the grass.
Master Zhèng saw Rén Shì suddenly fall to the ground,
revert to her original form, and flee southward.
The gray dog pursued her,
and Master Zhèng ran after, shouting and calling,
but could not stop it.
After more than a li,
she was caught by the dog.
Master Zhèng, with tears in his eyes,
took money from his pouch to redeem her body and bury it,
carving a wooden marker.
Looking back at her horse,
he saw it grazing by the roadside;
her clothes were all laid upon the saddle,
her shoes and stockings still hung from the stirrups,
like a cicada’s shed skin.
Only her hair ornaments had fallen to the ground,
nothing else remained,
and the maidservant had also vanished.
More than ten days later,
Master Zhèng returned to the city.
Yín, seeing him, was delighted,
and greeted him, asking:
“Is Rén Shì well?”
Master Zhèng replied with tears:
“She is dead!”
Hearing this, Yín also grieved deeply,
and they embraced in the room,
expressing their sorrow fully.
Gradually, Yín asked the cause of her death,
and he answered:
“She was killed by a dog.”
Yín said:
“Though dogs are fierce,
how could they harm a person?”
He replied:
“She was not human.”
Yín exclaimed in shock:
“Not human?
Then what was she?”
Master Zhèng then recounted the whole story from beginning to end,
and Yín was astonished, sighing endlessly.
The next day,
Yín ordered a carriage and went with Master Zhèng to Mǎwéi,
opened the grave to look,
and after a long lament, returned.
Reflecting on past events,
they realized that only her clothes were not made by herself,
which was rather unusual.
Later, Master Zhèng became a Chief Inspector,
his household grew very wealthy,
with more than ten horses in the stable.
He died at the age of sixty-five.
During the Dàlì era,
Shěn Jìjì resided in Zhōnglíng,
and once traveled with Yín,
who often spoke of these events,
hence they are known in greatest detail.
Later, Yín became a Palace Censor,
and concurrently Prefect of Lǒngzhōu,
and thus passed away without returning.
Alas!
Even among strange creatures,
there are those who embody human virtues.
Indeed!
Facing violence without losing integrity,
sacrificing oneself for another unto death—
even among women today, there are none who can compare.
It is regrettable that Mr. Zhèng was not a discerning man,
merely delighting in her beauty without inquiring into her true nature.
Had there been a man of profound insight,
he would surely have been able to grasp the principles of transformation,
discern the boundary between spirit and human,
compose writings of great beauty,
and convey the essence of subtle emotions,
not stopping at mere admiration of her graceful demeanor.
What a pity!
In the second year of the Jiànzhōng era (781 AD),
Jìjì, from the position of Left Reminder, along with the Imperial Guard
General Péi Jì, Assistant Governor of the Capital Sūn Chéng, Director of the Ministry of Revenue Cuī Xū, and Right Reminder Lù Chún,
were all demoted
Residing in the southeast,
traveling from Qín to Wú,
we journeyed together by water and land.
At that time, former Reminder Zhū Fàng,
joined us while traveling.
We sailed the Yǐng River and crossed the Huái,
our boats following the current.
By day we feasted, by night we conversed,
each recounting strange tales.
When the gentlemen heard the story of Rènshì,
they were all deeply astonished and sighed,
and thus requested Jìjì to record it,
to document the extraordinary.
Written by Shěn Jìjì.
Lǐ Cháng
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Cháng served as Registrar of Jiàngzhōu,
acting concurrently as Director of Household Registration.
It was long rumored that this office was inauspicious;
if a small hole appeared in the main hall,
the Director of Household Registration would surely die,
and it was widely known as the "Director's Hole."
When Cháng took up his concurrent duties,
he resided in this hall.
After more than ten days,
his son, over ten years old,
went to the toilet,
where a woman in a white skirt grabbed his head and tried to lift him onto the wall.
He was rescued and escaped harm,
and she suddenly vanished.
Cháng angrily cursed,
and a tile thrown from mid-air struck his hand.
His cousin, of the Cuī family,
served as Adjutant of the prefecture,
That day, he came to Cháng's place
and said it was a wild fox spirit.
Qūwò was abundant with hawks and hounds,
and they should be gathered in large numbers.
Soon, dung was thrown into Cuī's cup.
A few days later,
the hounds arrived,
and Cháng went on a great hunt,
capturing several cunning foxes,
which he hung from the eaves.
That night,
he heard a voice from the eaves calling, "Registrar Lǐ!"
"It was the fox matron causing trouble;
why wrongfully kill my mother?
I wish to drink with the Registrar,
tomorrow you may prepare wine to receive me."
Cháng replied,
"I already have wine ready,
come tomorrow morning."
At dawn,
wine was prepared and the fox arrived,
though its form was invisible,
its words were clearly heard.
Cháng then exchanged cups with it,
and when it came to the fox's turn,
the wine vanished in an instant.
The fox drank about three dǒu in total,
while Cháng only drank two shēng.
Suddenly, it said,
"Today I am drunk,
fear I may breach etiquette.
The Registrar may cease;
the fox matron is not worth worrying about!
Tomorrow I shall send a method to exorcise it."
The next day,
as Cháng was about to enter the office,
he suddenly heard from the eaves,
"Receive the method."
Soon, a ball of paper fell,
which Cháng opened and examined,
finding inside a slip.
It instructed to place a lamp on
a mat,
and behind the mat, write a talisman,
the method of which was very detailed.
Cháng followed the instructions,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
Wáng Shēng
In Hángzhōu, there was a man named Wáng Shēng.
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
he bid farewell to his family and journeyed to the capital.
He gathered his modest assets,
intending to rely on relatives and acquaintances,
hoping to secure an official post.
When he reached Pútián,
he left the main road
to seek out an old estate belonging to his maternal relatives.
As evening fell,
he saw two wild foxes leaning against a tree in a cypress grove, standing like humans,
each holding a yellow paper document,
chatting and laughing face to face,
as if no one else were around.
Wáng Shēng shouted at them,
but they did not react.
He then took his slingshot,
drew it to full stretch and shot,
hitting the eye of the fox holding the document.
The two foxes dropped the document and fled.
Wáng Shēng hurried over,
retrieved the document,
which was only a sheet or two,
written in characters resembling Sanskrit script that he could not decipher.
He then sealed it in his book bag and left.
That evening,
he lodged at an inn ahead,
and spoke of the incident to the innkeeper.
Just as they were marveling at the event,
suddenly a man arrived with luggage to stay the night,
suffering from a severe eye ailment,
as if unbearable,
yet his speech was clear.
Hearing Wáng Shēng's words, he said:
"This is truly strange.
How may I see that document?"
Just as Wáng Shēng was about to produce it,
the innkeeper noticed a tail hanging down from the bed of the man with the eye ailment,
and said to Wáng Shēng:
"This is a fox."
Wáng Shēng hastily tucked the document into his robe,
grabbed his knife and chased the man,
who transformed into a fox and fled.
After the first watch,
someone knocked on the door again.
Wáng Shēng, his heart stirred, said:
"If you come again this time,
I will face you with knife and arrows."
The person outside the door said:
"If you do not return my document,
do not regret it later!"
From then on, there was no further news.
Wáng Shēng kept the document secret,
securely sealed and hidden.
Arriving in the capital,
he sought official posts and paid visits,
but the waiting period stretched long.
He then mortgaged his old family fields and gardens,
settled near the city wards,
to plan for his livelihood.
Over a month later,
a servant boy arrived from Hángzhōu,
entered the gate,
holding a mourning announcement. Wáng Shēng met him and inquired,
only to learn that his mother had passed away.
The family's misfortune had occurred.
After several days,
he heard the news and wept bitterly.
Wáng Shēng then looked at the letter,
which bore his mother's handwriting, saying:
"My family's roots are in Qín,
I do not wish to be buried in a foreign land.
The properties and lands in Jiāngdōng must not be diminished in the slightest.
However, the assets in the capital
can all be disposed of
to fund the funeral arrangements.
Once everything is prepared,
then come personally to escort me."
Wáng Shēng then sold off all his fields and houses,
not waiting for favorable prices,
obtained the funds,
prepared all the funeral rites and supplies,
leaving nothing lacking.
Afterward, he traveled east by sedan chair,
to meet the funeral carriage.
Upon reaching Yángzhōu,
he saw a boat in the distance,
with several people aboard,
all laughing joyfully and singing.
As he drew closer to look,
they were all members of Wáng Shēng's family.
He thought they had sold the family property,
and now it belonged to others.
In a moment,
his younger siblings lifted the curtain and came out,
all dressed in colorful clothes, chatting and laughing.
In his astonishment,
his family on the boat cried out in surprise,
saying:
"The young master has arrived!
Why is he dressed so strangely?"
Wáng Shēng secretly sent someone to inquire,
and then appeared himself.
His mother came out in shock.
Wáng Shēng hastily removed his mourning garments,
approached and bowed.
His mother came forward and asked him,
exclaiming in alarm:
"How can this be?"
Wáng Shēng then produced the letter his mother had sent,
but it was merely a blank sheet of paper.
His mother also said:
"The reason I came here is that last month I received your letter saying
you had recently obtained an official post,
instructing me to sell all the property in Jiāngdōng
to prepare for moving to the capital.
Now we have nowhere to return to."
When his mother produced the letter Wáng Shēng had sent,
it too was a blank sheet of paper.
Wáng Shēng then sent messengers to the capital,
disposing of all the funeral items.
Gathering the remaining funds,
he escorted his mother from Huái,
and proceeded to Jiāngdōng.
Of their former possessions, less than one or two-tenths remained,
only a few rooms,
barely enough to shelter them from wind and rain.
He had a younger brother,
separated for several years,
who suddenly arrived one day.
Seeing the family's decline,
he inquired about the cause.
Wáng Shēng recounted the whole story in detail,
and also described the incident with the demon fox,
saying:
"It must have been this that brought the disaster."
His brother sighed in amazement,
and Wáng Shēng took out the demon fox's document to show him.
As soon as his brother took the document,
he stepped back, placed it in his robe, and said:
"Today, return my celestial document."
With these words,
he transformed into a fox and departed.
Lǐ Zìliáng
In the Táng Dynasty, Lǐ Zìliáng in his youth lived between the two rivers,
unrestrained and not engaging in productive work.
He was fond of hawks and falcons,
often exhausting his purse and goods
for the use of falconry gear and leashes.
When Mǎ Suì was stationed in Tàiyuán,
he recruited those skilled with hawks and hounds for hunting.
Zìliáng then went to the military headquarters,
presenting himself.
Zìliáng’s physique was robust and valiant,
and Suì was pleased with him at first sight,
placing him by his side.
Whenever they called the hawks to chase game,
it never failed to satisfy and delight him.
Within a few years,
he accumulated positions up to the rank of Yámén Dàjiàng.
Once while hunting and releasing a hawk to chase a fox,
the fox darted into an ancient tomb,
and the hawk followed it.
Zìliáng immediately dismounted,
and taking advantage of the momentum, leaped into the tomb.
It was about three zhàng deep,
and inside it was as bright as if lit by candles.
He saw a damaged coffin on a brick platform,
and also a dàoshi about a chǐ tall,
holding two paper documents standing on the coffin.
Zìliáng then snatched the documents,
and there were no other objects,
so he carried the hawk on his arm and left.
The dàoshi followed, calling out:
"Please leave the documents,
and I shall offer a generous reward."
Zìliáng did not respond,
but looked at them;
the characters were all ancient seal script,
and no one could recognize them.
The next morning,
a dàoshi,
elegant in demeanor and appearance,
came to visit Zìliáng.
Zìliáng said:
"Where is the immortal master from?"
The dàoshi said:
"I am not of this mortal world.
It is because General yesterday forcibly seized the celestial talisman.
This is not something the General should possess.
If you return it,
I will surely offer a substantial reward."
Zìliáng firmly refused to give it,
so the dàoshi dismissed the attendants and said:
"The General is only a subordinate commander.
I can, within three years,
make you the commander of this army.
Would that not fulfill your utmost desire?"
Zìliáng said:
"If it truly were as you wish,
it is still not credible.
What then?"
The dàoshi then leaped up spiritedly,
ascending into the air.
Soon there were immortals with crimson scepters,
jade boys and white cranes,
hovering in the sky,
to welcome him.
After a short while, he descended again,
and said to Zìliáng:
"Can you not see?
Is this the talk of a liar?"
Zìliáng then bowed twice,
and returned the documents to him.
The dàoshi joyfully said:
"The General indeed has fortune and blessings.
In the ninth month two years from now,
it shall be as promised."
This was in the second year of the Zhēnyuán era.
By the autumn of the fourth year,
Mǎ Suì went to the imperial court for an audience.
The senior and meritorious generals of Tàiyuán,
those with high official ranks,
more than ten followed him,
and Zìliáng’s position was the lowest.
The Emperor asked:
"Tàiyuán is an important northern stronghold.
Who can replace you?"
Suì was dazed and unclear,
only remembering Zìliáng’s name,
so he reported:
"Lǐ Zìliáng can."
The Emperor said:
"Among Tàiyuán’s officers,
there should be senior ones with merit and seniority.
Zìliáng is a junior,
and I have never heard of him.
Please reconsider."
Suì, in haste, did not know how to reply,
and said again:
"From what I have observed,
no one but Zìliáng is suitable."
This repeated several times,
and the Emperor still did not consent.
Suì went out and saw the generals,
sweating with shame down his back.
He secretly vowed in his heart
that later he must recommend the one with the most seniority and virtue.
The next day, the Emperor asked again:
"After all, who can replace you?"
Suì, as before, was confused,
only remembering to recommend Zìliáng.
The Emperor said:
"We shall await discussion and decision by the宰相."
Another day, when the宰相 entered for an audience,
the Emperor asked which of Mǎ Suì’s generals was worthy.
The宰相 was startled,
unable to know the others,
and also replied with Zìliáng.
Thus he was appointed Gōngbù Shàngshū
and Jiédùshǐ of Tàiyuán.
Lǐ Lìngxù
Lǐ Lìngxù was the elder cousin of Vice Minister of War Lǐ Shū.
His uncle was appointed as the Deputy Magistrate of Jiāngxià County,
so Lìngxù went to visit him.
After he had been seated for a long time,
the gatekeeper reported:
"A young lady has sent a servant to relay a message."
The servant was called in,
and Lìngxù saw a maid of quite graceful appearance,
who said:
"My lady pays her respects to her elder brother and sister-in-law."
She added that she was glad Lìngxù had come from afar.
The Deputy Magistrate's wife also sent a message:
"Can your lady come here to see her nephews?"
She also said:
"If your lady has any delicacies,
she may send them over."
After the maid left,
his uncle said to Lìngxù:
"Do you know?
I have been acquainted with a fox for over a year now."
Shortly after,
someone arrived carrying large food containers.
A servant in a yellow robe carried them,
along with the maid who had delivered the message earlier.
They arrived together,
saying:
"My lady will come shortly."
In a moment,
she arrived at the gate in a carriage adorned with four golden rings,
accompanied by over twenty attendants.
The Deputy Magistrate's wife went out to welcome her.
They saw a woman,
about thirty years old,
with her hair styled in double cloud-like buns,
shining and lustrous.
Her maids were all dressed in fine silks,
and a rare fragrance filled the residence.
Lìngxù retreated inside,
but after the woman entered the hall and took her seat,
she said to the Deputy Magistrate's wife:
"Since Lìngxù is my nephew,
why doesn't he come out?"
Hearing this,
Lìngxù came out and bowed.
She said to him:
"My nephew truly has the demeanor of a scholar and gentleman."
After sitting for a long while,
she said to Lìngxù:
"I see you are very sincere and honest,
and you must have urgent difficulties troubling your heart."
Lìngxù also understood the reason for her words.
They conversed all day before she took her leave.
She visited several times afterward,
each time bringing rare delicacies.
After half a year,
Lìngxù planned to return to Dōngluò.
His aunt then said:
"This time, Auntie has truly won Lìngxù's heart.
Auntie is facing a calamity,
and plans to follow Lìngxù to Dōngluò.
Is that acceptable?"
Lìngxù was startled and said:
"My travel provisions are meager,
and arranging for a carriage
seems impossible."
She replied:
"Just agree,
and Auntie's family will
borrow a carriage themselves.
I will only bring two female attendants
and the maid Jīnhuā, who has served me before.
As for Auntie's affairs,
Lìngxù should understand,
and there is no need to say more.
Just prepare an empty clothes chest,
and have the servant leading the camel
open it slightly at each checkpoint, inn, or shop.
Auntie will rest inside for a while,
and when the chest is opened,
she will naturally come out.
Isn't that easy?"
Lìngxù agreed.
When they set off,
he opened the chest.
He saw three or four dark shadows enter the chest,
and their movements adhered to the previous agreement.
When they reached the Eastern Capital,
just before arriving at his residence,
Lìngxù asked:
"Where can we settle you?"
Jīnhuā replied:
"My lady would find the granary very convenient."
Lìngxù immediately cleaned and swept the granary,
secretly arranging everything for her.
Only the servant leading the camel knew about it,
and none of the other family members were aware.
Whenever she needed anything,
Jīnhuā would come to fetch it herself,
and Auntie would occasionally appear.
Several months later, she said:
"The calamity has passed,
and I plan to leave."
Lìngxù asked:
"Where do you intend to go?"
Auntie replied:
"Hú Xuán has been appointed as the Prefect of Yùzhōu.
Since his two daughters have grown up,
they need to be matched in marriage,
and I am now arranging matters for him."
The following year, Lìngxù was eligible for official selection,
but as the selection approached,
his family was poor and he had no plan,
so he went to Yùzhōu.
Upon entering the region,
he saw a notice that read:
"I come from a humble family and stand alone,
with no relatives or connections.
I fear some may falsely claim kinship or acquaintance
and recklessly demand provisions.
If such cases are reported promptly,
they will certainly be punished according to the law."
Traveling merchants
all praised Prefect Hú's integrity,
and those seeking favors had completely ceased.
Lìngxù was frightened by this,
hesitating for a long time,
but he had no choice.
So he secretly entered Yùzhōu,
and though he saw others paying visits,
none gained anything.
Lìngxù then presented his name card,
and the Prefect immediately invited him in.
Upon seeing him, the Prefect was extremely pleased,
as if meeting an old friend.
He said:
"Although we have not met before,
I knew you were in urgent difficulty,
and I have long awaited your esteemed presence.
Why have you come so late!"
He then provided lodging for him,
offering generous provisions.
Throughout the entire prefecture, people said:
"Since the Prefect arrived,
nothing like this has ever happened."
Every day, Lìngxù entered the residence for joyful banquets,
but they only discussed current affairs,
and nothing else was mentioned.
After more than a month,
Lìngxù bid farewell.
Xuán said:
"I will arrange travel provisions for you,
to cover the expenses for the selection."
He then gathered the county magistrates and said:
"Since I arrived in this prefecture,
I have never been troubled by relatives or acquaintances.
Lǐ Lìngxù is an outstanding talent in the land,
someone I have long admired all my life,
and after meeting him yesterday,
I know he is a true gentleman,
which is why I hold him in high regard.
You gentlemen should meet him as well.
Now he is going to attend the selection,
and each of you must provide him with provisions,
ensuring they are not meager."
The officials had always feared his authority,
so from the county magistrates downward,
none gave less than several dozen bolts of silk as gifts.
Lìngxù received a thousand bolts of silk,
and his travel preparations were fully arranged.
A farewell banquet was also held for him.
As Lìngxù was leaving through the halberd gate,
he saw another gate,
and Jīnhuā came out from inside, saying:
"My lady wishes to see you in the mountain pavilion courtyard."
When he entered,
Auntie had already come out,
her face beaming with joy.
She said:
"Couldn't you wait for the two girls to be married?"
She added:
"Lìngxù bought some citrus fruits,
but didn't give any to Auntie.
How stingy!"
Lìngxù was startled and said:
"I did buy some,
but I didn't dare to send them specially."
She laughed and said:
"I was only joking.
The ones you bought are not good enough.
Auntie has superior ones of her own."
She gave them to Lìngxù to take with him,
and ordered them to be fetched.
Each one was as large as a fist.
After they parted,
she called Lìngxù back and said:
"These are difficult times,
"The silk and luggage I'm carrying,
I fear encountering bandits;
what should I do about it?"
Then she said:
"I'll lend you Jīnhuā to go with you.
But if any urgent matter arises,
just think of Jīnhuā,
and there will be no trouble."
Lìngxù traveled for several days,
and indeed encountered over fifty bandits.
Lìngxù, terrified, fell from his horse.
Suddenly he thought of Jīnhuā,
and immediately saw over three hundred elite cavalry
coming from the mountains,
their military appearance extremely imposing,
the weapons they held
gleaming so brightly they could reflect light.
They killed nearly all the bandits,
then Jīnhuā ordered the knights to withdraw and gallop away,
still commanding the troops to depart safely.
As they were about to reach the capital,
they stayed overnight at a roadside inn.
The innkeeper's daughter was ill,
said to be caused by a demon.
Lìngxù asked the innkeeper:
"What kind of illness is this?"
He replied:
"It seems like a demonic affliction;
we've tried many doctors and methods,
but none could cure it even temporarily."
Lìngxù said:
"How about treating it?"
The innkeeper earnestly declined and thanked him,
begging for help:
"If only it could be slightly reduced,
my repayment will not be light."
So Lìngxù thought of Jīnhuā,
and in a moment she arrived,
fully explaining the situation.
After briefly seeing the girl's illness,
she said:
"Easy."
Then she set up an altar,
burned incense and chanted incantations.
Shortly after,
a fox, severely afflicted with mange,
was bound and brought to the altar.
Jīnhuā sentenced it to one hundred lashes,
blood flowing all over the ground.
Then she drove it away,
and the girl recovered.
Upon reaching the capital,
Jīnhuā bid farewell to Lìngxù.
Lìngxù said:
"You've toiled far to accompany me,
but I have nothing to give as a parting gift."
So he prepared wine and food.
After drinking merrily, he said:
"Since there are no formalities,
I have one question—
would it be difficult to answer?"
Jīnhuā said:
"If there's something, just speak."
Lìngxù said:
"I wish to hear about your lady's family background and origins."
She replied:
"The lady was originally the daughter of a certain prefect.
Her uncles and brothers
are not far removed from Lìngxù.
She married as the wife of a man surnamed Sū,
fell ill, and passed away.
Jīnhuā was her accompanying maid;
several months later, she also died,
hence she is able to be by the lady's side.
The Heavenly Emperor assigned the lady as the wife of General Tiānláng,
so she possesses divine powers.
Jīnhuā also benefits from the master's residual grace.
Hú Xuán is the master's own nephew.
The innkeeper's daughter treated yesterday—
that fox was a servant at the master's gate;
there are many like them,
and Jīnhuā can control them."
As for the elite cavalry that came to rescue,
they were heavenly soldiers.
Jīnhuā can summon them,
regardless of number.
Lìngxù thanked her and said:
"When will we meet again?"
Jīnhuā said:
"Originally, it was due to the convergence of marital fate,
lasting only until today.
From now on, the marital ties are severed,
and we must bid farewell forever."
Lìngxù was melancholy for a long time,
conveying his thanks to the lady,
urging her to take utmost care.
He generously offered gifts to Jīnhuā,
but she refused to accept any and departed.
Hú Xuán later served as prefect of several provinces and then passed away.
Péi Shǎoyǐn
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a Deputy Prefect of Jiānglíng named Péi,
whose personal name is lost.
He had a son over ten years old,
intelligent and quick-witted,
well-versed in literature,
with a bright and handsome appearance,
and Péi cherished him deeply.
Later, the boy fell ill,
and after ten days, his condition worsened severely,
with medicine proving ineffective.
Péi then sought out Daoist practitioners
to perform incantations and exorcisms,
hoping to alleviate his suffering.
Someone knocked at the door,
claiming to be a man named Gāo,
who practiced talismanic arts.
Péi immediately invited him in
and asked him to examine his son.
The man said:
"This boy's illness is not an ordinary one;
it is caused by a demon fox.
However, I have the skill to cure him."
Péi thanked him and pleaded for his help.
The man then performed talismanic rituals to summon and interrogate the spirits.
After nearly the time it takes to eat a meal,
the boy suddenly rose and said:
"My illness is now cured."
Péi was overjoyed,
believing Gāo to be a genuine practitioner.
He prepared food and drink,
and afterward, generously rewarded him with silk and money,
thanking and sending him off.
The man said:
"From now on, I will come daily to check on him."
He then left.
Although the boy's other ailments were cured,
his spirit was still unsettled,
often speaking deliriously,
or laughing and crying uncontrollably.
Whenever Gāo came,
Péi would mention this and plead for his help.
Gāo said:
"This boy's spirit
has been captured by the demon,
and has not yet returned.
Within ten days, it should recover,
so please do not worry."
Péi believed him.
After a few days,
another man named Wáng arrived,
claiming to possess divine talismans
capable of exorcising demonic illnesses through incantations,
and requested an audience.
Péi spoke with him,
and Wáng said:
"I have heard that your beloved son is ill
and has not yet recovered;
I wish to see him."
Péi immediately led him to see his son.
Wáng exclaimed in shock:
"This young master is afflicted by a fox demon!
If not treated promptly,
his condition will worsen."
Péi then mentioned Gāo.
Wáng laughed and said:
"How do you know Gāo is not a fox?"
He then sat down
and began setting up for an exorcism ritual.
Suddenly, Gāo arrived,
and upon entering, he shouted angrily:
"How could you, now that this boy is recovering,
invite a fox into the room?
He is the one causing the illness!"
Seeing Gāo arrive,
Wáng also shouted:
"Indeed, a demon fox!
Now you have finally come.
Why pretend to perform exorcisms with other arts?"
The two argued fiercely,
insulting and cursing each other endlessly.
The Péi household was greatly alarmed and bewildered.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest arrived at the door,
privately telling a servant:
"I have heard that Lord Péi's son is afflicted by a fox demon.
I am skilled at seeing ghosts.
Just inform him
and request an audience."
The servant hurriedly reported to Péi,
who came out and explained the situation.
The Daoist priest said:
"This is easy to handle."
He entered and saw the two men,
who again shouted:
"This is also a fox demon!
How dare he pose as a Daoist priest to deceive people?"
The Daoist priest also cursed them:
"Foxes should return to the wilds and ancient tombs;
why disturb humans?"
Soon after, they closed the door and fought,
for the duration of several meals.
Péi grew even more fearful,
and his servants were panicked and confused,
with no plan of action.
By evening,
it fell silent, with no sound heard.
When they opened the door to look,
three foxes lay on the ground, panting,
unable to move.
Péi whipped them all to death,
and his son recovered fully after another ten days or so.
Zhāng Jiǎnxī
Zhāng Jiǎnxī of Nányáng,
in the late Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
made a living by hunting with falcons in the Xú-Sì region.
On that day, the sky had just cleared,
and his falcon missed its prey,
soaring high into the clouds.
Jiǎnxī followed its trail,
splitting up with his companions to search.
Soon, night fell,
around the first watch,
and he unknowingly arrived at an ancient ruin.
Suddenly, he saw the light of a candle,
and as he approached,
he realized it was glowing from inside a tomb.
Peering inside,
he saw a fox leaning on a table,
reading a booklet.
Beside it were a group of rats,
serving tea,
offering fruits and chestnuts,
all behaving like humans with clasped hands.
Jiǎnxī angrily shouted at them,
startling the fox, which fled,
gathering its booklets
and hiding in a deep, dark hole.
Jiǎnxī used his falcon pole to fish out one booklet
and returned home.
By the fourth watch,
he heard someone outside his house calling for the booklet,
but when he went out to look, he saw nothing.
By dawn,
everything had vanished.
From then on, the calls came every night without end.
Jiǎnxī found this deeply strange,
so he took the booklet into the city,
intending to show it to others.
When he was about three or four lǐ from the city,
he suddenly met an acquaintance,
who greeted him
and asked where he was going.
Jiǎnxī then took out the booklet
and described the fox incident.
The man also laughed in surprise,
took the booklet,
and whipped his horse to gallop away.
Looking back at Jiǎnxī, he said:
"Thank you for returning the booklet."
Jiǎnxī chased him urgently,
but the man transformed into a fox,
and the horse into a river deer,
making them impossible to catch.
Jiǎnxī turned his cart back into the city,
visited the acquaintance's house,
only to find the man had never left home,
and realized it was a fox that had come to reclaim the booklet.
The booklet was bound
just like a human's,
with similar paper and ink,
but the writing was fox script,
illegible to humans.
Jiǎnxī managed to copy a few lines from the beginning
to show others.
Xuē Kuí
In the final years of the Zhēnyuán era,
General Xiāo Wèi Xuē Kuí was residing north of the Yǒngníng Lóngxīng Temple.
There were many demon foxes,
roaming freely at night,
and showing no fear of people.
Xuē Kuí and his entire household were terrified,
not knowing what to do.
Someone suggested:
"Demon foxes fear hunting dogs the most.
In the mansion of Grand Marshal Lǐ to the west,
there are quite a few falcons and hounds.
Why not borrow some of the finest ones
and wait for the foxes at dusk?"
Xuē Kuí thought this was an excellent idea.
He immediately went to the Lǐ family's younger generation and explained the situation.
The Lǐ family was pleased to hear it
and leashed three dogs to lend him.
That evening, the moon was bright.
Xuē Kuí released the dogs
and secretly observed them with his family.
They saw the three dogs, all leashed,
with three foxes riding on them,
running around the courtyard,
east, west, north, and south,
doing as they pleased.
By dawn,
the three dogs were exhausted,
lying down and refusing to eat.
As soon as dusk fell,
they were ridden again,
kicking balls across the wide courtyard.
If the dogs slowed down even slightly,
they were whipped thoroughly.
Xuē Kuí had no choice
and eventually moved away,
indeed.
Jì Zhēn
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Jì Zhēn whose family was residing in the Qīng-Qí region.
He once traveled west to Cháng'ān,
and upon reaching Shǎn,
since Zhēn was on good terms with a local official there,
on that day, as he was about to bid farewell and depart,
the official insisted on keeping him for a drink.
They drank until dusk before finally parting ways.
Zhēn had not traveled ten lǐ from the city
when he suddenly fell from his horse in a stupor,
while his two servants drove ahead with his luggage and clothes.
By the time Zhēn awoke from his drunken state,
it was already twilight.
His horse had also gone ahead,
so noticing horse urine beside a small path to the left of the road,
he went to search along it.
Unconsciously, he walked several lǐ,
when suddenly he saw a towering vermilion gate,
shaded by dense locust and willow trees.
Having lost both his servants and horse,
Zhēn felt disheartened.
He then knocked on the gate,
which was already locked.
A young servant boy came out to look,
and Zhēn immediately asked:
"Whose residence is this?"
The boy replied:
"It is the country villa of Vice Director Lǐ."
Zhēn requested an audience,
and the boy hurriedly went to report.
After a short while,
someone came to invite the guest inside,
asking him to rest in the guest quarters.
He was then led through the gate,
where to the left was a very clean and spacious guest area.
The screens and partitions set up there
were all adorned with ancient landscapes, famous paintings, and classical texts.
The cushions, beds, and such furnishings
were generally clean and unadorned.
Zhēn sat for a long time
before the young servant came out and said:
"My master will be here shortly."
Soon, a gentleman appeared,
around fifty years old,
wearing a crimson sash and silver insignia,
of very imposing stature.
He met with Zhēn,
and after exchanging courtesies, they sat down.
Zhēn then recounted in detail how his old friend, the official,
had kept him for a drink,
and how he had become deeply intoxicated on the road,
not realizing it had grown dark.
Having lost both his servants and horse,
he wished to lodge there for one night—would that be possible?
Lǐ said:
"I only worry that this humble and narrow place
is unfit for a distinguished guest;
how could there be any objection?"
Zhēn thanked him, feeling ashamed.
Lǐ then said:
"I once served as an official in Shǔ,
but soon resigned due to illness.
Now I have retired and settled here."
As they conversed,
his speech proved very sharp and erudite,
and Zhēn greatly admired him.
Lǐ also ordered a servant to inquire after Zhēn's servants and horse,
and soon both arrived,
whereupon they were settled.
Afterwards, a meal was set out and they dined together.
After eating,
they drank several cups of wine before retiring to sleep.
The next day,
Zhēn rose early to bid farewell and depart,
but Lǐ said:
"I wish I could have one more day to enjoy your delightful company."
Moved by his sentiment,
Zhēn stayed,
and departed the following day.
When he reached the capital,
after residing there for over a month,
someone knocked at his door,
introducing himself as the presented scholar Dúgū Zhǎo.
Zhēn invited him in to sit and converse;
he was very intelligent and eloquent.
Moreover, he said:
"My home is in Shǎn.
Traveling west yesterday,
I passed by Vice Director Lǐ's place,
and he could not stop praising your excellence.
He also wishes to form a marital alliance with you,
so he sent me to pay my respects
and convey this intention.
What do you think?"
Delighted, Zhēn agreed.
Zhǎo said:
"I am now returning to Shǎn.
When you travel east back home,
you should visit Vice Director Lǐ again
and thank him for his kindness."
Then he bid farewell and left.
A month or so later,
Zhēn returned to visit Vice Director Lǐ's country villa.
When Lǐ saw Zhēn arrive,
he was overjoyed.
Zhēn then relayed Dúgū Zhǎo's words
and thanked him.
Lǐ then kept Zhēn there,
selected an auspicious date,
and
proceeded with the wedding ceremony on the appointed day.
His wife was exceptionally beautiful,
and also intelligent, gentle, and graceful.
Zhēn stayed for about a month
before taking his wife and children back to Qīng-Qí.
From then on, news from Mr. Lǐ never ceased.
Zhēn was devoted to Dàoist practices;
every morning upon rising,
he would read the *Huángtíng Nèijǐng Jīng*.
Lady Lǐ often stopped him, saying:
"You are fond of the Dào,
but are you comparable to Qín Shǐhuáng or Hàn Wǔdì?
In terms of effort devoted to seeking immortality,
who could match Qín Shǐhuáng or Hàn Wǔdì?
Those two were honored as Sons of Heaven,
possessing all the wealth under heaven.
They exhausted the empire's resources to study the ways of immortality,
yet still died at Shāqiū
and were buried at Màolíng.
Moreover, you are but a commoner;
how can you be deluded by the pursuit of immortality?"
Zhēn scolded her,
then finished reading the scroll.
Considering her someone who understood the Dào,
he never suspected she might be of another kind.
Over a year later,
Zhēn took his family to the capital for official reassignment.
When they reached the outskirts of Shǎn,
Mr. Lǐ kept his daughter with him
and sent Zhēn ahead to the capital.
The following autumn,
Zhēn was appointed as an aide in Yǎnzhōu,
and Lady Lǐ joined him at his post.
Several years later, his term ended,
and they returned to Qí-Lǔ.
More than ten years later,
Lady Lǐ had borne seven sons and two daughters.
Their talents, qualities, appearances, and bearing
all surpassed those of ordinary people.
Moreover, Lady Lǐ's countenance remained dignified and beautiful,
no different from when she was young.
Zhēn cherished her even more.
Not long after,
she fell gravely ill.
Zhēn rushed about seeking physicians and shamans,
leaving no stone unturned,
but she never recovered.
One day, dismissing the attendants, she grasped Zhēn's hand,
and with sobs and streaming tears, said:
"I know my death is near,
yet I endure the shame to confess my innermost feelings to you.
I beg you to be lenient and forgive my faults,
allowing me to speak my fill."
Already, she was choked with sobs, unable to continue.
Zhēn also wept for her,
firmly comforting her.
Then she said:
"One word—I truly know I will be blamed by you for this,
but considering our nine young children are still here,
and will be a burden to you,
I still feel compelled to speak.
Moreover, I am not a human of this world.
By heavenly decree, I was destined to be your mate.
With this lowly fox spirit's humble substance,
I have served you with broom and dustpan for twenty years,
never committing the slightest offense,
yet
I have brought you worry because of my otherkind nature.
With a woman's sincere blood-bound heart,
I believe I have given my all.
Today, as I prepare to depart,
I dare not entrust my remaining demonic aura to you.
Thinking of the tender young ones before your eyes—
they are all humans of this world, your heirs—
when my breath is exhausted,
I beg you to remember your affection for these weak children.
Do not hold a grudge against my dry bones;
allow my whole body to remain intact,
and bury it in the earth.
That would be a gift for a hundred lifetimes."
When she finished speaking, she was again overcome with grief,
tears streaming down in a hundred lines.
Zhēn was shocked and bewildered,
heartbroken and sorrowful,
choked and unable to speak.
They wept facing each other for a long time.
Then she covered her head with the quilt,
turned to face the wall and lay down,
and for the time of a meal, there was no sound.
Shēng then lifted the quilt,
and saw a dead fox beneath it.
Shēng was deeply moved and mourned for it,
arranging its burial with all due rites,
just as one would for a human.
Shēng then went straight to Shǎn,
to visit the residence of the Lǐ family,
but found only ruins, graves, and overgrown thorns,
deserted with nothing to be seen,
and returned home in melancholy.
After living there for over a year,
his seven sons and two daughters,
passed away one after another.
Looking at their remains,
they were all human,
and to the end, he harbored no ill will.
Liú Yuándǐng
once recounted an old tale:
wild foxes are called purple foxes;
at night, they strike their tails to produce fire,
and when they intend to cause mischief,
they must don a skull and bow to the Northern Dipper.
If the skull does not fall,
they transform into humans.
When Liú Yuándǐng governed Càizhōu,
Càizhōu had just been ravaged,
and the foxes in the food market were rampant.
Liú dispatched officials to oversee
the capture,
and daily at the polo grounds, they set dogs loose,
chasing them for sport.
Over the course of a year, hundreds were killed.
Later, they caught a mangy fox.
They released five or six dogs,
but none dared to chase it,
and the fox did not flee either.
Liú found this most strange,
and ordered inquiries for hunting dogs from the households of great generals; the army supervisor also boasted of his own.
When the huge dogs arrived,
they all stood in a circle guarding it.
After a long while, the fox slowly moved,
went straight up to the main hall,
passed through the platform,
exited behind the hall,
reached the city wall,
and in a moment, vanished without a trace.
From then on, Liú no longer ordered captures.
In Daoist arts, there is a separate method concerning celestial foxes,
which says celestial foxes have nine tails,
are golden in color,
and serve in the palaces of the sun and moon;
they have talismans and days for rituals,
through which they can thoroughly comprehend the workings of yīn and yáng.
Zhāng Lìběn
During the Táng dynasty, when Chancellor Niú Sēngrú was in the Secretariat,
the grassland official Zhāng Lìběn had a daughter
who was bewitched by a demonic creature.
When the demon came,
the girl would put on heavy makeup and splendid attire,
and in her chamber,
she would seem to converse and laugh with someone.
When it left,
she would wail and weep uncontrollably.
For a long time, she called herself Vice-Minister Gāo.
One day,
she suddenly recited a poem:
"With tall hat and wide sleeves, in Chǔ palace attire,
Alone I stroll the quiet hall, chasing the night's cool.
I tap the bamboo by the steps with a jade hairpin,
Singing a clear song under the frosty moon."
Lìběn then casually copied it down.
Lìběn was friends with the monk Fǎzhōu,
and when he went to his residence,
he showed him the poem, saying:
My daughter is young and has never studied books,
I don't know how she could do this.
Zhōu then gave Lìběn two pills,
and told him to have his daughter take them.
Within ten days, her illness cured itself.
The girl said that
behind the house there was a bamboo grove,
close to the tomb of Vice-Minister Gāo Kǎi,
and within it was a den of wild foxes,
which was why she had been bewitched.
After taking the pills,
the illness was never heard to recur.
Yáo Kūn
During the Tàihé era,
there was a retired scholar named Yáo Kūn who did not seek glory or advancement,
often finding contentment in fishing.
He lived south of Wàn'ān Mountain in the Eastern Capital Luòyáng,
finding joy in his qín and wine.
Nearby lived a hunter,
who made his living by trapping foxes and hares with nets.
Yáo Kūn, being kind-hearted,
often bought them and set them free,
thus saving hundreds of lives.
Yáo Kūn had an old estate,
which he had mortgaged to the Bodhi Temple on Sōng Ridge.
He took the money and went to redeem it.
The monk in charge of the estate, Huì Zhǎo, was a vicious man.
He often dug a well several zhàng deep in a secluded spot,
threw in several hundred jīn of huángjīng (a medicinal herb),
and sought people to test it by consuming it,
to observe the changes.
He then got Yáo Kūn drunk,
and threw him into the well.
He covered the well with a millstone.
When Yáo Kūn awoke,
he had no way to jump out,
and could only satisfy his hunger by eating the huángjīng.
After several days and nights like this,
suddenly someone at the mouth of the well called Yáo Kūn's name,
and said to him:
"I am a fox,
grateful that you have saved many of my descendants,
so I have come to teach you.
I am a fox who has attained communion with heaven.
Initially, I burrowed into a tomb,
and through an opening above,
I glimpsed the Milky Way and the stars,
and felt a longing for them.
Regretting that my body could not soar,
I concentrated my gaze and focused my spirit.
Suddenly, without realizing it, I flew out,
treading on emptiness and riding the clouds,
ascended to the Milky Way,
and paid respects to the celestial officials.
If you can purify your spirit and eliminate distractions,
focus your gaze on the profound void,
with such precise concentration,
in less than thirty days you will naturally fly out.
Even the tiniest opening
will pose no obstacle."
Yáo Kūn asked:
"What evidence do you have for this?"
The fox said:
"Have you not heard what the *Xīshēng Jīng* says:
'The spirit can make the body fly,
and can also move mountains.'
Strive hard."
Having said this, it left.
Yáo Kūn believed its words,
and acted accordingly.
After about a month,
he suddenly was able to jump out through the hole in the millstone.
He then went to see the monk,
who was greatly shocked,
and saw that the well remained as before.
The monk bowed to Yáo Kūn and questioned him about the matter.
Yáo Kūn told him:
"I merely consumed huángjīng inside for a month,
my body became as light as a spirit,
and I was able to fly out on my own,
with no obstruction from the opening."
The monk believed him,
sent a disciple down
with a rope,
and told the disciple to come check in a month.
The disciple did as instructed,
and came to check after over a month.
The monk had already died in the well.
Yáo Kūn returned home, and after about ten days,
a woman calling herself Yāotáo
came to see Yáo Kūn.
She claimed to be the daughter of a wealthy family,
who had been lured away by a young man,
gone missing and unable to return,
and wished to serve him.
Yáo Kūn saw her,
She was enchantingly beautiful and alluring.
As for poetry and letters,
she was also exceptionally skilled.
Yáo Kūn grew fond of her.
Later, Yáo Kūn responded to an imperial summons,
and took Yāotáo with him to the capital.
When they reached the Pándòu Lodge,
Yāotáo became unhappy.
She took a brush and wrote on a bamboo slip,
composing a poem that said:
"Long adorned with lead powder among mortals,
wishing to shed this adornment brings a sorrowful face.
Even though the moon shines over Qīngqiū tonight,
it cannot again illuminate my former cloud-like hair."
She recited it for a long time,
and Yáo Kūn also became startled.
Suddenly, a local official sent someone with a fine hound,
intending to present it to Péi Dù.
Entering the lodge,
the hound saw Yāotáo,
glared angrily, broke its leash,
and crouched as it ascended the steps.
Yāotáo then transformed into a fox,
leapt onto the hound's back and gouged out its eyes.
Greatly frightened,
the hound howled and fled the lodge,
dashing toward Jīng Mountain.
Yáo Kūn was greatly alarmed,
chased after them for several lǐ,
but the hound was already dead,
and the fox had disappeared without a trace.
Yáo Kūn was filled with melancholy and sorrowful regret,
unable to proceed for the entire day.
When night fell,
an old man came to Yáo Kūn with fine wine,
saying they were old acquaintances.
After drinking,
Yáo Kūn still could not recall how they knew each other.
When the old man finished drinking,
he bowed deeply and left,
saying:
"I have repaid you sufficiently,
and my granddaughter is also safe."
He then vanished.
Only then did Yáo Kūn realize it was the fox.
After that, there was no further news.
Yǐn Yuàn
Yǐn Yuàn was a man who
once took the imperial examination but did not pass.
He served as the
sheriff of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
After his term ended,
he retired to the countryside,
finding solace in writing.
Suddenly, one day,
a man dressed in white came to visit him,
introducing himself as the son of the Zhū family from Wúxīng,
saying, "From a young age, I have been devoted to learning.
I have secretly heard that you, sir, take pride in your literary accomplishments.
I wish to seek your guidance,
and hope you will not refuse me."
Yuàn immediately invited him in to converse,
and inquired about his background.
The man said:
"My family resides in Lánchuān.
In my early years, I and Censor Wáng both served at the northern gate.
Now, I have been staying at Wáng's villa for many years."
From then on, he would come every four days.
He was exceptionally eloquent and insightful,
with elegant and refined expressions.
Yuàn grew very fond of him.
Yuàn then said to him:
"Your wit and profound insights
