could allow you to travel among the commanderies and kingdoms,
becoming a distinguished guest of nobles and lords.
Why do you choose to remain obscure,
hiding your traces in the wilderness?"
The man replied:
"It is not that I do not wish to visit nobles and lords,
but I fear that unexpected disaster may befall me at any moment."
Yuàn asked:
"Why do you speak such ominous words?"
Zhū said:
"Since the beginning of this year,
my dreams and divinations have shown signs of impending doom."
Yuàn tried to console him with words,
and the man appeared rather ashamed.
Later, on the Double Ninth Festival,
someone gifted Yuàn a bottle of strong wine.
Zhū also arrived,
so Yuàn offered him the wine to drink.
At first, he declined, citing illness,
and dared not drink.
But then he said:
"Meeting on such a fine festival,
how could I not partake in the host's joy?"
He then filled his cup and drank.
After a short while,
he became heavily intoxicated and bid farewell.
Before he had walked even a few dozen steps,
he suddenly collapsed to the ground,
transforming into an old fox,
so drunk it could not move.
Yuàn immediately killed it.
He then went to inquire about Censor Wáng's villa.
An old farmer told Yuàn:
"Censor Wáng was originally a deputy general.
Years ago, he was stationed in Lánchuān,
where he fell ill due to being bewitched by a fox and died.
It has been many years now.
His grave is a few dozen steps north of the village."
Yuàn ordered his servant to search for Censor Wáng's grave,
and indeed, there was a burrow.
Yuàn later became a censor himself,
and secretly spoke of this incident.
This occurred in the early years of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty.
The Wéi Family Son
The son of the Wéi family from Dùlíng resided in Hánchéng,
with a villa located over ten lǐ north of the town.
In the autumn of the tenth year of the Kāichéng era, he went there from the town.
As dusk fell,
he saw a woman dressed in plain white clothes,
carrying a gourd,
approaching from the north.
She said to Wéi:
"I have lived in the northern part of the town for many years.
My family is very poor.
Now, I have been insulted by the local official.
I intend to bring a lawsuit against him.
I hope you can write down the details for me,
so I can take it to the town authorities,
hoping to clear my shame."
Wéi agreed.
The woman then bowed to Wéi and sat in the field,
taking a wine cup from her clothes and saying:
"There is wine in the gourd.
I wish to drink to our hearts' content with you."
She then poured wine and offered it to Wéi.
Just as Wéi was about to raise the cup,
a group of hunters on horseback arrived from the west,
leading several dogs.
The woman saw them,
immediately ran eastward a few dozen steps,
and transformed into a fox.
Wéi was greatly frightened.
Looking at the cup in his hand,
he saw it was a skull,
and the wine resembled the appearance of cow urine.
Wéi fell ill with a fever,
and it took over a month for him to recover.
Zhāng Zhífāng
In the gēngyín year of the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhāng Zhífāng, Military Commissioner of the Lúlóng Army, Acting Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
submitted a memorial requesting permission to come to the capital to pay homage to the emperor.
An imperial edict graciously granted his request.
Previously, the Zhāng family had governed the land of Yān for generations,
and the people of Yān had long submitted to their grace.
They treated guests at the Yāntái with courtesy,
and comforted the brave warriors of the Yìshuǐ.
The land was fertile and the soldiers numerous.
The imperial court often indulged them.
When Zhífāng succeeded to his post,
emerging from among silken-clad youths,
and occupying a position as a regional overlord,
he never paid any heed to the joys and sorrows of the common people.
Instead, he indulged in wine within his chambers,
and wantonly hunted beasts across the plains.
He bestowed lavish rewards upon hunters,
and showered great favor on his attendants.
In his later years, the entire army grew deeply resentful,
and Zhífāng began to feel somewhat uneasy.
Some among his attendants devised a plan for him,
and so he moved his entire household westward to the capital.
Emperor Yìzōng appointed him General of the Left Martial Guard,
but Zhífāng, obsessed with falconry and hunting,
paid no attention to the duties of his office.
He often set traps and nets across the main roads,
so that not a single dog or pig was spared,
and if any of his servants displeased him,
he would kill them on the spot.
Someone said:
"Beneath the imperial carriage wheels,
one cannot arbitrarily execute people."
His mother said:
"Is there anyone more exalted than my son?"
His arrogance and transgressions can thus be known.
Thereupon, the censors submitted a joint memorial,
requesting that he be arrested and handed over to the Chamberlain for Law Enforcement.
The Son of Heaven could not bear to punish him according to the law,
so he demoted him to Military Advisor to the Prince of Yān,
ordering him to take up duties in the eastern capital, Luòyáng.
When Zhífāng arrived in the Eastern Capital,
not only did he fail to reform himself,
but his idle wandering became even more extreme.
All around Luòyáng,
the flying creatures and the beasts of prey,
upon seeing him, would recognize him,
and would surely raise a clamorous howl and flee.
There was a man named Wáng Zhīgǔ,
a tribute scholar from the eastern feudal lords.
Although he had dabbled slightly in Confucian studies,
he repeatedly failed the selection examinations of the Ministry of Rites,
so he withdrew to wander among mountains and rivers,
occupying himself with polo and drinking games,
roaming about the southern and northern neighborhoods.
At this time, someone introduced him to Zhífāng,
and Zhífāng invited him in.
Seeing his sharp tongue and eloquent speech,
Zhífāng unconsciously drew closer on his mat,
and from then on, they grew intimate day by day.
In the winter, the eleventh month of the rénchén year,
Zhīgǔ once rose early in the morning.
His rented lodging had no fire,
gloomy clouds filled the sky,
and he felt quietly unhappy,
so he walked to Zhífāng's residence.
Upon arrival, he found Zhífāng hastily preparing,
about to go hunting.
He said to Zhīgǔ:
"Can you come along?"
Zhīgǔ showed a reluctant expression due to the severe cold,
so Zhífāng turned to a young page and said:
"Fetch the short black robe."
He asked Zhīgǔ to put it on.
Zhīgǔ then added his hempen garment over it,
and they rode off together.
Once out the Chángxià Gate, a light sleet began to fall;
passing through the Quēsài Pass, the dense snow poured down like a torrent.
They crossed the Yīshuǐ and headed southeast,
treading the northern foothills of the Wàn'ān Mountain,
and their hunting gains were very plentiful.
They emptied their feathered cups,
roasted rabbit haunches,
scarcely feeling the harshness of winter.
When the sleet cleared and the snow stopped,
the sun was about to set,
when suddenly a large fox sprang up before Zhīgǔ's horse.
Spurred by wine, he gave chase,
but after several li could not catch up,
and also became separated from the hunting party.
In a short while,
sparrows chattered in the smoky dusk,
and he no longer knew where to go.
Faintly, he heard the evening bell from Luòchéng,
but could only wander lost on woodcutters' paths and ancient trails.
Soon, the mountains and rivers grew dark,
as if the first watch was nearly half past.
Gazing into the distance,
he saw a torch burning very brightly,
so he followed the light of the accumulated snow towards it.
After what seemed like over ten li more,
he arrived at a place where tall trees intertwined their branches,
and a vermilion gate stood open in the middle,
with a gleaming white wall stretching across—
truly a first-class mansion fit for the northern palace gates.
Zhīgǔ dismounted at the gate,
intending to linger until dawn.
Not long after,
as his small horse shifted and jingled its bridle,
the gatekeeper noticed him,
and asked from behind the door, "Who is there?"
Zhīgǔ replied:
"I am Wáng Zhīgǔ of Tàiyuán, a tribute scholar from Chéngzhōu.
This morning, a friend who is returning to his old retreat in Kōngtóng Mountain,
I bid him farewell by the banks of the Yīshuǐ,
and could not resist the parting cup.
After we parted with a sleeve-grasp,
my horse bolted,
and again I could not stop it,
losing my way until I arrived here.
At daybreak I shall depart;
I beg you not to reproach me."
The gatekeeper said:
"This is the estate of Vice Commissioner Cuī of the Nánhǎi Circuit.
The master recently received an imperial summons and has gone to the capital,
and the young master has also followed the reporting officials westward on his journey.
Only the women of the inner chambers remain here.
How can you stay long?
I dare not decide on my own to let you stay or go;
I must report this inside."
Although Zhīgǔ was apprehensive and uneasy,
he reckoned it was already midnight;
where could he go?
So he stood with folded hands and waited.
After a little while,
someone came from inside holding a honey-coated torch,
who shook the tube, opened the door,
and led out a matron.
Zhīgǔ stepped forward and bowed,
then recounted his circumstances.
The matron said:
"The mistress conveys this message:
The master and the young master are both not at home.
According to propriety, there is no way to entertain a guest,
however, our dwelling is remote, bordering the mountains and marshes,
where jackals and wolves howl.
If we firmly refuse you,
it would be like seeing someone drowning and not offering aid.
Please lodge in the outer hall;
tomorrow you may leave."
Zhīgǔ expressed his thanks,
and followed the matron inside.
They passed through multiple gates.
The side rooms where one could eavesdrop,
the pillars and brackets were grand and spacious,
the curtains and drapes fresh and splendid.
Silver lamps were lit,
an ornate mat was spread,
and Zhīgǔ was invited to sit.
After three rounds of wine,
a feast covering a square zhàng was presented again;
leopard fetus and bream belly,
exhausting the finest delicacies of land and water.
The matron also came from time to time to encourage him.
After the meal,
the matron further inquired about Zhīgǔ's family lineage, official clan,
and his relatives on both the paternal and maternal sides.
Zhīgǔ told her everything.
Then she said:
"Young scholar, you are a descendant of a noble family with carriages and robes,
a rare jewel of gold and jade.
You are both in the prime of youth,
and pure in conduct.
This truly makes you a worthy husband for a virtuous lady.
My mistress, out of deep love for her young daughter who is approaching the hair-pinning age,
has long entrusted matchmakers,
seeking a fine match for a long time.
What night is this night,
that we encounter a fine gentleman!
The harmony of Pān and Yáng can be followed,
the omen of the phoenix is present here.
I wonder what your noble sentiments are on this?"
Zhīgǔ composed his expression and said:
"I am ashamed that my writing lacks the resonance of metal,
my talent is not the polish of jade.
How could I dare hope for a family?
I only worry about wallowing in the mud.
I never expected such favor to reach this lost traveler,
such joy to meet in the depth of night;
to hear a pure voice in the Lǔ mansion,
to approach auspicious airs at the Qín terrace.
The two guests wandering in spirit,
compared to this, are nothing to consider;
the three stars shining down,
I only fear I may not rise to meet them.
If I could be entrusted to your powerful clan,
and favored with a fine match,
then the aspirations of my entire life,
would all be fulfilled herein."
The nursemaid was delighted,
and entered with playful banter to report.
Coming out again, she conveyed her mistress's message:
"Since my daughter moved to the Cuī family,
she has truly upheld virtuous conduct;
serving with the reverence due to ancestral rites,
she understands the harmony of marital life.
Her only concern is for her young daughter,
hoping to find a match with a gentleman.
Since you have graciously accepted this honorable proposal,
it fulfills her long-held wish.
Sending a swift letter to the capital,
the journey is not far;
preparing the full array of wedding gifts,
the matter is not presumptuous.
Her joy and comfort are immense,
and she looks upon you with great anticipation."
Zhīgǔ bowed deeply and replied:
"I am but a lowly creature of dust,
destined for obscurity,
yet your noble family of high standing
has suddenly deigned to select me.
I pledge by the clear waters
to serve you with utmost devotion;
like a crane yearning or a duck hastening,
I await only your gracious command."
Zhīgǔ bowed again.
The nursemaid teased:
"On the day when the brocade pheasant robe is to be removed,
and the blue phoenix case fully opened;
her beauty like the halo of the moon,
the chamber as if veiled in mist—
will you remember this moment then?"
Zhīgǔ thanked her and said:
"For a mortal to approach an immortal,
to rise from the earth to the heavens—
without such a recommendation,
who could act as his own matchmaker?
I shall engrave this kindness upon my heart,
inscribe it upon my girdle;
vowing for a lifetime,
to carry it with me wherever I go."
He bowed once more.
By then, the moon had sunk into the courtyard,
making it a truly fine night.
The nursemaid invited Zhīgǔ to remove his outer garments and rest.
When he took off his hemp robe, a black gown was revealed underneath.
The nursemaid chided him:
"How can a scholar in broad-sleeved robes
wear a short-backed garment like this?"
Zhīgǔ apologized:
"This was borrowed from an acquaintance I often visit,
it is not my own."
She asked from whom,
and he replied:
"It was lent by Vice-Director Zhāng Zhífāng of Lúlóng."
Suddenly, the nursemaid shrieked and fell to the ground,
her face ashen as death.
Once she rose,
she turned and fled into the house without a backward glance.
From afar, a loud shout was heard:
"Madam has made a grave error—
the guest staying overnight is one of Zhāng Zhífāng's lot!"
Then the madam's voice was heard shouting:
"Drive him out at once,
do not invite calamity!"
Thereupon, maids and young servants rushed forth in a crowd,
holding blazing torches,
dragging white clubs as they ascended the steps.
Zhīgǔ, terrified and flustered,
stumbled
into the courtyard,
looking around and pleading for mercy,
but curses and insults rained down upon him,
and he barely managed to escape through the gate.
No sooner had he left
than the gate was barred and bolted shut,
and the clamor within showed no sign of ceasing.
Zhīgǔ stood dumbfounded by the roadside,
sighing to himself for a long while.
About to hide by a crumbling wall,
he found his horse tethered beneath it,
and so he galloped away.
In the distance, he saw what looked like a great fire blazing across the plains,
and he spurred his horse toward it.
Upon arrival, it turned out to be a rent-collecting cart where oxen were being fed by a fire.
Inquiring about the location,
he learned it was east of the Yī River,
south of the Grass Inn.
He then rested his head on the reins and dozed off.
After the time it takes to eat a meal, the eastern sky grew bright,
and his mind settled somewhat,
so he whipped his horse onto the main road.
By the time he reached the city gates,
several of Zhífāng's horsemen had already come searching for him.
They escorted him back to Zhífāng's residence from afar.
Upon seeing Zhífāng,
Zhīgǔ was so overwhelmed with indignation he could not speak.
Zhífāng comforted him,
and once seated,
Zhīgǔ recounted the strange events of the night.
Zhífāng stood up and slapped his thigh, saying:
"Do mountain sprites and tree demons
also know that there is a Zhāng Zhífāng in the human world?"
He then had Zhīgǔ stay put.
Gathering several dozen more of his men,
all skilled archers who could pierce hides with their arrows,
he treated them to wine and pork shoulders,
and set out southward again with Zhīgǔ.
Once they reached north of Wàn'ān,
with Zhīgǔ leading the way,
hoofprints were still visible in the lingering snow.
They went straight to a grove of cypress trees,
where they found stone tablets discarded in wild pits,
and firewood gatherers' traces remaining in the dense woods.
In the middle stood over ten large burial mounds,
all dens of foxes and hares,
with paths worn beneath them.
Thereupon, Zhífāng ordered nets to be spread all around,
and bows drawn ready;
inside, they bundled straw and shouldered spades,
digging and smoking them out.
Shortly after,
a horde of foxes burst forth,
some scorched and battered,
others entangled in the nets,
and still others struck by arrows—
in all, over a hundred foxes, large and small, were captured and taken back.
Zhāng Jǐn
There was a Daoist priest named Zhāng Jǐn,
who was fond of talismanic arts,
but despite diligent study, he achieved no success.
Once, while traveling as a guest, he arrived at the market of Huàyīn,
where he saw a melon seller,
bought some melons, and ate them.
Beside him was an old man,
and Jǐn noticed his hungry appearance,
so he took some melons and gave them to him.
After eating over a hundred melons,
Jǐn realized the old man was extraordinary,
and treated him with even greater respect.
As the old man was about to leave,
he said to Jǐn:
"I am the god of the land here,
moved by your kindness,
I have something to repay you."
Then he took out a book and said:
"This contains techniques for suppressing fox spirits,
you should diligently practice them."
Jǐn accepted it,
and the old man vanished.
That day,
Jǐn stayed overnight in a village near the county,
where he heard a woman in the household crying and shouting,
behaving as if insane.
He asked the host about it,
who replied:
"There is a woman in my family,
who recently became afflicted with madness.
Every day at dusk,
she dresses up in fine clothes and makeup,
saying she is summoning Lord Hú to come.
We have tried to treat her,
but nothing works."
Jǐn immediately wrote a talisman,
and placed it on the eaves and door.
That evening,
someone on the eaves wept and cursed, saying:
"What kind of Daoist priest is this,
meddling in other people's affairs!
You should leave quickly!"
Jǐn angrily rebuked it,
and after a long while, a loud voice said:
"I will leave as a slave."
Then all fell silent.
Jǐn wrote several more talismans,
and the illness was completely cured.
The host gave him several dozen bolts of silk as thanks.
Jǐn once traveled alone,
and since he had heavy luggage,
he needed servants to help.
After staying a few days,
suddenly two slaves came to see him,
Jǐn,
they introduced themselves as "Dé'ér" and "Guībǎo."
They had once served the Cuī family,
but when Cuī took up an official post elsewhere,
they were abandoned,
and now had nowhere to go,
so they wished to serve by his side.
Jǐn accepted them,
and both slaves were diligent, clever, and sharp,
especially trustworthy.
When Jǐn traveled east,
all his books, talismanic arts,
luggage, and clothes
were entrusted to Guībǎo to carry.
As they approached the pass,
Guībǎo suddenly cursed loudly, saying:
"Treating me as a slave,
as if you were ordering your own father around."
Then he ran off at full speed.
Jǐn, shocked and angry, chased after him,
but he ran like the wind,
and vanished in an instant.
Soon after, Dé'ér also disappeared,
and all the luggage
was lost.
At that time, there was military conflict in Qín and Lǒng,
and the pass was strictly guarded,
travelers without proper documents
were all executed.
Since he dared not cross east,
he returned to his host.
He told him everything,
and the host angrily said:
"How could such a thing happen?
This is insatiable,
and now you come to trouble me again!"
So he stayed at a farmer's house,
but received no provisions at all.
He was then invited by the farmer to work alongside him,
plowing by day and resting at night,
enduring extreme fatigue and hardship.
While resting under a large tree,
he looked up and saw two boys, who said:
"We are Dé'ér and Guībǎo.
How does it feel to be a slave?"
They also said:
"These talismanic arts are our book,
lost long ago.
Now we are glad to have it back,
but are we heartless toward you?"
Then they threw the luggage back to him, saying:
"Hurry back,
your fellow villagers are waiting for you to write talismans."
Then they laughed loudly and left.
Jǐn retrieved his luggage,
and went back to his host,
who was now amazed.
He gave him several more bolts of silk,
and only then could Jǐn leave.
From then on, he never wrote talismans again.
Zǎn Guī
In the Táng dynasty, a man named Zǎn Guī from Cháng'ān lost his mother,
and then suffered a fire,
which burned all his family property,
leaving him in extreme poverty.
He had six young children,
and Guī had no means to support them.
His wife said to Guī:
"We are so poor now,
staying together means suffering hunger and cold,
and there is no way to survive.
I wish to sell myself to someone,
to get money to help you and our children,
what do you think?"
Guī said:
"I have lost my property by chance,
and now I am destitute and helpless.
To let you do this,
I truly cannot bear it."
His wife said again:
"If we do not do this,
we will all starve or freeze to death."
Only then did Guī agree.
A few days later,
an old man came to their door,
and Guī invited him in.
When they spoke of the children's hunger and cold,
and his wife's wish to sell herself,
the old man felt sorrow for a long while,
then said to Guī:
"My family has been wealthy for generations,
I live below Lántián.
I just heard people talk about your wife's intention,
and now I hear you say it too.
I now wish to buy your wife,
and will offer one hundred thousand coins."
Guī and his wife both agreed.
The next day, the old man
brought one hundred thousand coins,
and took Guī's wife away.
He also said to Guī:
"If your children miss their mother,
just bring them to the foot of the mountain to visit me,
and I will let them meet."
Three years later,
all the children had died,
and Guī was again destitute,
so he begged for food in Cháng'ān.
Suddenly one day,
he remembered the old man's words,
and went to the foot of Lántián to visit him.
Soon he saw a wild temple,
with magnificent gates and buildings,
looking like a nobleman's mansion.
The gatekeeper questioned him,
and the old man ordered Guī to enter.
Food was served,
and his wife was brought out,
to meet Guī.
When his wife heard that all the children had died,
she wailed loudly,
and then stopped breathing.
The old man, startled, rushed inside,
and became very angry,
intending to harm Guī.
Guī, frightened, ran out,
and when he looked back, the mansion was gone,
and he saw his wife dead before an ancient tomb,
with a cave beside the tomb.
Guī and others from the foot of the mountain dug up the tomb together,
and saw an old fox run out,
then he knew his wife had been bought by the old fox.
Fox Dragon
At the foot of Líshān Mountain, there was a white fox,
which startled and harassed the people below the mountain,
and they could not get rid of it.
During the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
one day it suddenly bathed itself in a hot spring.
In a short while,
clouds steamed and mist surged,
a fierce wind arose,
and it transformed into a white dragon,
ascending to the heavens and departing.
Later, when it was overcast or dark,
people often saw the white dragon soaring by the mountain.
After three years of this,
suddenly an old man appeared,
who every night
would weep in front of the mountain.
After several days,
people waited and asked him the reason.
The old man said:
"My fox-dragon has died,
so I weep."
People asked him:
"Why is it called a fox-dragon?
And why do you weep?"
The old man said:
"The fox-dragon
transformed from a fox into a dragon,
and died after three years.
I am the son of the fox-dragon."
People asked again:
"How can a fox transform into a dragon?"
The old man said:
"This fox
was born endowed with the righteous energy of the west,
hence its white color.
It did not roam with others,
nor did it dwell near them.
The fox resided at the foot of Líshān Mountain for over a thousand years,
and later by chance mated with a female dragon.
Heaven above learned of this,
and thus commanded it to become a dragon.
It is just like a mortal in the human world becoming a sage!"
Having spoken, he vanished.
The people of Cāngzhǔ
In Jiāngnán there are no wild foxes,
in Jiāngběi there are no partridges—
so goes the old saying.
In the year Jiǎchén of the Jìn Tiānfú era,
in the village of Cāngzhǔ, Gōng'ān County, a family named Xīn
had a dog chase a woman,
who climbed a tree and fell,
and was bitten to death by the dog.
It turned out to be an old fox,
with a tail seven or eight feet long.
Thus it is correct
As for the demon of the fox,
it cannot be said that Jiāngnán has none,
but they are rare.
In Shǔ, Péng, Hàn, Qióng, and Shǔ, they are absolutely absent;
only in mountainous commanderies are they often found,
where locals call them wild dogs.
There is also the huángyāo,
with a long tail and black head,
and a scorched yellow waist.
If it cries in a village,
then an inauspicious event will occur.
A Villager's Wife
As the Shì Shuō states,
foxes can bewitch people—
this is likely not untrue.
There was a villager who lived near a mountain forest,
and his wife once went alone into the woods.
Then a fox appeared,
happily wagging its tail,
and approached amiably,
walking and following closely,
staying by the woman's side,
sometimes in front, sometimes behind,
and she could not drive it away.
This became a regular occurrence;
if it heard her husband coming, it would stay far away,
and a bow and arrow could not reach it.
Suddenly one day,
the woman and her mother-in-law went together into the mountains to gather vegetables,
and the fox secretly followed them.
When the woman and her mother-in-law became slightly separated among the thickets,
the fox emerged from the grass,
wagging its tail as it approached,
joyfully like a household dog.
The woman then lured it forward,
wrapped it in her skirt,
called her mother-in-law to help beat it,
and carried it back home.
Neighbors came to see it,
and it closed its eyes,
as if ashamed and blushing.
They then killed it.
Although this one had the peculiarity of bewitching people,
it could not transform.
The tale of Rènshì—
how could it be false!
Shuàirán
In the western mountains, there is a snake
with a head and tail of differing sizes,
and colors of five hues.
If a person or creature touches it,
strike its head and the tail arrives,
strike its tail and the head arrives,
strike its waist and both head and tail arrive.
It is named "Shuàirán."
In Chángshān, Kuàijī,
this snake is most abundant.
Sūnzǐ's Art of War says:
"Commanding the three armies,
their momentum should be like Shuàirán."
Shéqiū
In the Eastern Sea, there is Shéqiū,
a perilous place,
with much damp marshland,
where many snakes dwell.
There are no people,
and some snakes have human heads and serpent bodies.
The Mountain Northwest of Kūnlún
Northwest of Kūnlún, there is a mountain
with a circumference of thirty thousand lǐ,
encircled by a giant snake
that goes around it three times.
The snake is ninety thousand lǐ long.
The snake often resides on this mountain,
drinking and feeding from the vast sea.
Green Snake
In the □ stone cave of Gùzhǔ Mountain,
there is a green snake about three chǐ long,
roughly the size of a little finger.
It likes to perch on treetops;
looking at it, it resembles a girdle
wrapped among the branches and leaves.
It is not venomous,
and upon seeing people, it flies through the air.
Bàoyuān Snake
In Lǐngnán, there is the Bàoyuān snake.
If a person touches it,
it will follow them for three to five lǐ.
If one kills a snake,
then a hundred snakes will gather.
Using a centipede for self-defense
can avert this.
Venomous Snakes
In the Wǔxī and Qiánzhōng regions south of the mountains,
there are venomous snakes,
black with upturned snouts,
coiled in the grass.
Their fangs are inverted hooks;
from several paces away,
they come straight at you,
swift as a shot arrow.
Their bite causes instant death;
if it strikes a hand, the hand is severed;
if it strikes a foot, the foot is severed.
Otherwise, the whole body swells and rots,
and not one in a hundred survives.
These are called fù snakes.
There is the huánghóu snake,
which likes to be on rooftops.
It is non-venomous
and does not harm people,
but is adept at eating venomous snakes.
When full,
it hangs its head straight down,
dripping saliva.
Where it hits the ground, it spurts up
and turns into sand lice,
which cause illness in people.
On its forehead is the character for "king,"
marking it as the leader of snakes.
It often eats fù snakes.
Planting millet attracts snakes,
but burning antelope horns and human hair
will prevent snakes from daring to come.
The rán snake
can grow as large as fifty or sixty zhǎng,
with a girth of five or six chǐ.
Even the smaller ones are no less than thirty or forty zhǎng,
with a girth proportionate to their length.
Its body is mottled,
with patterns like brocade.
Local people say
that in spring and summer, it often waits in the mountains and forests for deer.
When a deer passes by, it seizes it.
It swallows the deer starting from the tail,
but the head and antlers get stuck outside its mouth.
It then goes deep into the forest,
props its head against a tree,
and waits for the deer to decompose.
Once the head and antlers fall to the ground,
it swallows the deer's body into its belly.
After this,
the snake becomes extremely weak,
but once the deer is digested,
it becomes robust, sleek,
and even stronger than before it ate the deer.
Some say
it eats one deer a year.
Another account states
that the rán snake often swallows deer,
and after digesting them completely,
it coils around a tree to expel the bones.
When it is nursing its sores,
its fat is exceptionally delicious.
If women's clothing is thrown at it,
it coils up and does not rise.
Its gallbladder is near the head in the first ten days of the month,
and near the tail in the middle ten days.
Rán Snake Gallbladder
In Quánjiàn Prefecture, rán snake gallbladders are presented as tribute.
They are harvested on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Two pillars are set up five or six chǐ apart,
and the snake's head and tail are struck.
A stick is then used to tap back and forth under its belly,
causing the gallbladder to gather.
It is then cut out with a knife.
The wound is sealed with medicine,
and the snake does not die.
If harvested again,
and marks are seen under its ribs,
it is released.
The rooster-crowned snake
has a head like a rooster with a crown.
Its body is over a chǐ long,
with a girth of several cùn.
Anyone bitten by it will surely die.
It is found at the foot of Kuàijī Mountain.
The explosive-bodied snake
is one or two chǐ long,
and its shape is like gray.
When it hears the sound of people walking,
it flies out from the forest,
looking like a dry branch.
It strikes people horizontally,
and those hit all die.
The yellow-collared snake
is one or two chǐ long,
and its color is like gold.
It dwells in rock crevices.
When rain is about to fall,
it makes a sound like an ox roaring.
Those bitten also die.
It is found on Sìmíng Mountain.
The blue snake
has a highly poisonous head,
but its tail can detoxify poison.
It is found in Chénjiā Cave in Wúzhōu.
Southerners use its head to make poison,
called "blue medicine,"
which kills people instantly.
If the tail is taken and consumed,
it counteracts the poison.
Bā Snake
The bā snake eats elephants,
and after three years, it expels the bones.
Eating it cures diseases of the heart and abdomen.
Mánjiāng Snake
In Nán'ān, the Mánjiāng snake
reaches its peak in the fifth and sixth months.
A giant snake emerges from the river and climbs ashore,
its head like an open hat.
Countless snakes follow it
into Yuèwáng City.
Two-Headed Snake
Sháozhōu has many two-headed snakes,
which build ant mounds to avoid water.
Ant mounds are
piles of earth made by ants to form platforms.
Cāngwú also has many two-headed snakes,
no longer than one or two chǐ.
Some say
they are transformed from earthworms.
Yán Huí
Yán Huí and Zǐlù were sitting together at the gate of the Master's residence
when a ghostly creature sought to see Confucius.
Its eyes were like the sun,
and its appearance
was very imposing.
Zǐlù lost his spirit,
and his mouth was too paralyzed to speak.
Yán Yuān then put on his shoes, took up his sword, and stepped forward,
grabbed it by the waist,
whereupon it transformed into a snake,
and he immediately beheaded it.
Confucius came out to see,
and sighed, saying:
"The brave do not fear,
the wise do not doubt;
the wise may not be brave,
the brave need not be wise."
Shǔ's Five Dīng
In the thirty-second year of King Xiǎn of Zhōu,
Shǔ sent an envoy to pay homage to Qín.
King Huì of Qín had repeatedly presented beautiful women to the King of Shǔ,
who was moved and thus paid homage.
King Huì knew the King of Shǔ was fond of women,
so he promised to marry five daughters to Shǔ.
Shǔ sent the Five Dīng to escort them.
On their way back to Zǐtóng,
they saw a snake entering a cave.
One of them grabbed its tail,
but could not pull it out.
When all five helped,
they shouted and pulled the snake,
causing the mountain to collapse.
The Five Dīng and the five Qín women were all crushed to death,
and the mountain split into five ridges,
with a flat stone at the top.
The King of Shǔ grieved deeply,
He then climbed it,
and named it "Five Maidens' Tomb Mountain."
On the flat stone, he built the "Gazing at Wives' Tower"
and the "Longing for Wives' Terrace."
Today, the mountain is also called "Five Dīng's Tomb."
Lady Zhāolíng
Xiǎohuáng County
was the Huángxiāng area of the Sòng region.
When Duke Pèi raised troops and fought in the wild,
he lost his mother in Huángxiāng.
After the land was pacified,
he sent an envoy with a catalpa coffin to summon her spirit from the wilderness.
At that time, a red snake appeared in the water,
bathed itself,
and entered the catalpa coffin.
At the place where it bathed, some hair was left behind,
so she was posthumously honored as Lady Zhāolíng.
Zhāng Kuān
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Zhāng Kuān was the Governor of Yángzhōu.
Before this, two old men were disputing over mountain land,
and they came to the prefecture to argue over the boundaries,
with no resolution for years.
When Kuān took office, they came again.
Kuān observed that the two old men were not human,
so he ordered soldiers with halberds to escort them in.
He asked:
"What kind of spirits are you?"
The old men fled,
but Kuān shouted and struck them,
and they transformed into two snakes.
Dòu Wǔ
In the Later Hàn, Dòu Wǔ's mother gave birth to Wǔ and simultaneously gave birth to a snake.
They sent it into the wilderness.
Later, his mother passed away.
When it came time for the burial, before the coffin was lowered into the grave,
a large snake emerged holding grass in its mouth.
It went straight to the place of mourning,
struck the coffin with its head,
tears and blood flowing together.
It bowed and stretched, twisting and turning,
as if with a grieving, weeping expression.
After a while, it left.
People at the time knew it was an auspicious sign for the Dòu family.
Chǔ King Yīng's Daughter
Lǔ Shàoqiān possessed an immortal's talisman.
The young daughter of the King of Chǔ, Yīng, was afflicted by a demon,
and they summoned Shàoqiān.
Before Shàoqiān had traveled several dozen lǐ, he stopped to lodge for the night.
At night, there came one riding in a turtle-shell carriage,
followed by several thousand cavalry.
He called himself Bó Jìng
and came to visit Shàoqiān.
He then presented several kegs of wine
and several trays of delicacies.
As they parted, he said:
"The illness of the King of Chǔ's daughter
is my doing.
If you, sir, will turn back for me,
I will thank you with two hundred thousand cash."
Shàoqiān took the money
and immediately turned back.
He went to Chǔ by another route
to treat her.
In front of the girl's chamber,
there was one who pushed open the door,
and they only heard it say:
"Shàoqiān has deceived your father."
Then there was the sound of wind going northwest.
Looking at the spot, there was a basin full of blood.
The girl then lost consciousness
and did not revive until midnight.
The master sent people to follow the wind.
Northwest of the city, they found a dead snake,
several zhàng long,
with hundreds of small snakes
lying dead beside it.
Later, an imperial edict was sent down to the commanderies and counties.
On that very day,
the Grand Minister of Agriculture had lost two hundred thousand cash,
and the Office of the Imperial Household had lost several trays.
Shàoqiān carried the money and submitted a memorial,
fully explaining the circumstances.
The Son of Heaven found it extraordinary.
Zhāng Chéng's Mother
When Zhāng Chéng's mother, Sūn shì, was pregnant with Chéng,
she was riding in a light boat, enjoying herself on the riverbank,
when suddenly a white snake, three zhàng long,
leapt into the boat.
The mother incanted:
"If you are an auspicious sign,
do not poison or bite me."
She then placed it in a box and brought it back,
putting it inside her room.
After one night, she looked at it.
The snake was no longer to be seen.
She sighed with regret.
Neighbors said to each other:
"Yesterday we saw a white crane at the Zhāng household,
spreading its wings and soaring into the clouds."
They told Chéng's mother,
who had a divination performed.
The diviner said:
"This is auspicious.
Snake and crane are creatures of longevity.
From the chamber into the clouds
is an image of rising from lowliness to height.
In the past, King Héliǘ of Wú buried his sister,
sacrificing beautiful women,
famous swords, and precious objects,
exhausting the wealth of Jiāngnán.
Before seventeen years had passed,
carved clouds covered the valleys,
beautiful women roamed the streets,
white cranes soared in the woods,
white tigers roared on the mountainsides.
All were the essence-spirits of the past.
Now that they have emerged into the world,
they should cause your descendants to attain positions surpassing the highest ministers
and gain renown throughout Jiāngbiǎo.
If you bear a son,
you can name him after this."
When Chéng was born,
he was named Báihè (White Crane).
Chéng begot Zhāo,
who reached the position of Chancellor
and served as General Assisting Wú.
He lived past ninety years of age,
a testament to the auspicious sign of the snake and crane.
Féng Gǔn
When Chariot and Horse General Féng Gǔn of Bà Commandery was an Imperial Counselor,
he opened his seal-ribbon case.
Inside were two red snakes, about three chǐ long,
which fled, one north, one south.
Greatly worried and frightened,
he consulted a diviner, who said:
"This is auspicious.
You, sir, will later become a border general,
with 'east' in your title."
Five years later,
he indeed became a Senior General.
Soon after, he was appointed as Governor of Liáodōng.
Wèi Shū
During the Xiánníng era of the Jìn,
Wèi Shū served as Minister over the Masses.
In his ministry, there were two snakes.
They were ten zhàng long.
They resided on the flat ridge of the main hall's roof.
They stayed there for several years,
and people did not know.
They only wondered why the ministry repeatedly lost children, chickens, dogs, and the like.
Later, one snake came out at night.
Passing by a pillar,
it was injured by a blade.
Wounded, it could not climb back up.
Only then was it discovered.
They mobilized several hundred laborers
and attacked it together for some time
before finally managing to kill it.
Looking at its dwelling place,
they found bones and skeletons filling the space under the eaves.
Thereupon, they demolished the ministry buildings
and rebuilt them.
Dù Yù
When Dù Yù was Governor of Jīng Province,
stationed in Xiāngyáng,
there was a banquet gathering.
He became heavily drunk
and shut himself in his studio to sleep alone,
not allowing anyone to approach.
Later, he was drunk again.
From outside, they heard
vomiting in the studio.
The sounds were very distressing,
causing everyone to tremble with fear.
There was a minor clerk
who secretly opened the door to look.
He saw a large snake on the bed,
hanging its head over the bedside, vomiting.
There was no sign of a person at all.
He went out and secretly reported this.
Wú Měng
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
in Yùzhāng, there was a large snake,
over ten zhàng long.
It blocked the road.
Travelers who passed by
were invariably sucked in by the snake
and devoured; the count had already reached hundreds.
The Daoist priest Wú Měng and his disciples went to kill the snake.
Měng said:
"This is the essence of Shǔ.
When the snake dies, the Shǔ rebels will be pacified."
Soon after, indeed, Dù Tāo was destroyed.
Yán Hán
During the Jìn, Yán Hán's sister-in-law was ill.
She needed the gallbladder of a bearded snake,
but they could not obtain it.
Hán worried and sighed for days.
A youth appeared holding a blue bag and gave it to Hán.
Hán looked inside.
It was a snake's gallbladder.
The youth transformed into a blue bird and flew away.
Sīmǎ Guǐzhī
Sīmǎ Guǐzhī, whose courtesy name was Dàoyuán,
was skilled at shooting pheasants.
During the Tàiyuán era,
as he was about to set up a decoy and hide,
the decoy pheasant called,
and a wild pheasant responded.
He tried to find the one that had responded,
and found its head and wings had already become those of a pheasant,
but half its body was still a snake.
In the imperial armory of the Jin dynasty court,
a pheasant suddenly appeared,
and people at the time considered it an anomaly.
Minister Zhāng said:
"This is a transformation from a snake."
He immediately ordered a search of the armory,
and indeed found a snake's shed skin.
Also during the Tàiyuán era,
a man from Rǔnán entered the mountains
and saw a bamboo,
inside which a snake's form had already taken shape,
while the upper branches and leaves remained as before.
In Tónglú, Wújùn,
people once cut down some leftover bamboo.
Overnight,
they saw the bamboo pole had turned into a pheasant,
with its head and neck fully formed,
but its body not yet transformed—
this too was a transformation from bamboo to snake.
Zhāng Gǒu
Zhāng Gǒu of Wúxīng was plowing in the fields,
and placed his meal among the wild rice plants.
Every evening when he went to retrieve it to eat,
the food was already gone.
This happened not just once.
Later he lay in wait,
and saw a large snake stealing the food.
Gǒu chased it and stabbed it with a □ fork.
The snake fled,
and Gǒu pursued it
to a burrow,
where he only heard a crying voice saying:
"You've wounded me!"
Someone said, "Hand it over to Léigōng,
and have him strike it dead with a thunderbolt."
In a moment,
thunder and rain came,
and a thunderbolt struck down over Gǒu.
Gǒu then leapt about and shouted angrily:
"Heaven made me poor,
so I labor hard plowing and cultivating.
The snake came to steal my food—
the fault lies with the snake.
How dare you instead strike me with a thunderbolt?
This Léigōng is utterly ignorant!
If Léigōng comes,
I will use a □ to chop open your belly!"
In a moment,
the clouds and rain gradually dispersed,
and the thunderbolt turned to strike the snake's burrow instead,
killing several tens of snakes.
A Scholar of the Tàiyuán Era
During the Tàiyuán era of Jin,
there was a scholar who married his daughter to someone in a nearby village.
When the time came,
the groom's family sent people to fetch her.
The bride's family prepared a fine send-off,
and also had the bride's younger sister accompany her.
Upon arrival,
they saw multiple gates and layered pavilions,
comparable to those of princes and marquises.
Under the corridor pillars were lamps,
and a maidservant, solemnly dressed, stood watch.
The inner chamber had very beautiful curtains and canopies.
When night fell,
the bride hugged her wet nurse and wept,
but could not speak.
The wet nurse secretly felt around inside the canopy
with her hand,
and found a snake,
as thick as a pillar several arm-spans around,
coiled around the girl
from her feet to her head.
The wet nurse fled in terror.
The maidservants guarding the lamps under the pillars
were all small snakes,
and the lamps were the snakes' eyes.
Mùróng Xī
At the end of the Western Jin dynasty,
in the third year of the Guāngshǐ era of Mùróng Xī,
as Xī was returning from an excursion,
a willow tree south of the city called out like a person, saying:
"Great King, stop."
Xī detested this,
and had the tree cut down.
Beneath it was a snake,
ten feet long.
By the sixth year,
Xī was overthrown by Féng Bá,
and was destroyed.
The Old Woman of Qióngdū
In Qióngdū County of Yìzhōu, there was an old woman who was poor and alone.
Whenever she ate,
a small snake,
with horns on its head,
would appear among her dishes.
The old woman took pity on it and fed it,
and later it gradually grew to over ten feet long.
The county magistrate had a horse
that was suddenly sucked in by a snake.
The magistrate, greatly enraged,
arrested the old woman.
The old woman said:
"It's under the bed."
He then ordered people to dig,
but the deeper they dug, the less they found.
The county magistrate then killed the old woman.
The snake then appeared in the magistrate's dream, saying:
"Why did you kill my mother?
I shall take revenge!"
From then on, the sound of wind and rain was often heard.
After thirty days,
that evening,
the common people were all startled and said to each other:
"Why is there a fish on your head?"
Everyone they met said the same thing.
That night,
an area of forty li square,
the entire city sank all at once into a lake.
The locals call it Qiónghé,
also Qióngchí.
Only the foundation of the old woman's former house did not sink,
and it remains to this day.
When fishermen go to catch fish,
they always lodge there.
It is also said this water is clear,
and at the bottom one can still distinctly see the city walls, towers, and railings.
Tiānmén Mountain,
its peaks are mostly steep and beautiful,
with winding cliffs and valleys.
There is a great cliff wall rising straight up for thousands of ren,
where plants and trees intertwine,
and clouds and mist envelop and obscure it.
Below it lies a narrow, faint path.
When travelers pass by,
they suddenly soar upward and emerge above the forest,
as if ascending to immortality,
and thus leave the mortal world.
Such occurrences gradually became too many to record.
People traveling north and south
called it the Immortal Valley.
At that time, there were those who delighted in the Dao,
who came from thousands of li away,
bathed by the cliffside,
hoping to ascend to immortality.
Those who were present
beneath this forest
all flew away without exception.
One evening,
a wise man said to others:
"This must be a demonic creature,
not the path of immortals."
So he tied a stone to himself
and led a dog into the valley.
The dog also flew away,
and thus he knew it was an evil aura that sucked them in.
He then summoned the nearby mountain villages,
recruiting several hundred young men,
armed with weapons
and carrying large clubs.
First, they set fire to burn the grass,
and then they cut down the bamboo and trees.
When they reached the mountainside to observe,
they saw from afar a creature
tens of zhang long,
looming high and low,
hanging its head and looking down.
As they gradually approached,
it turned out to be a giant python.
Thereupon, he ordered the young men to beat drums, leap, shoot arrows,
and then hack and stab.
Its mouth gaped over a chi wide,
still trying to harm people,
but its strength was no match for the crowd.
After a long time, it finally died.
The human bones and remains of other animals it had swallowed
piled up
on either side like mounds.
There was also a man traveling
who fell into a deep mountain stream
with no way out.
Starving and near death,
he saw many turtles and snakes around him,
stretching their necks toward the east morning and evening.
The man then prostrated himself and imitated them,
and he no longer felt hunger.
His body became lighter and more agile,
able to climb the rocky banks.
After several years,
he tried stretching his body and raising his arms,
and suddenly he soared above the stream,
immediately able to return home.
His complexion was joyful and radiant,
and he became noticeably more clever and wise than before.
When he returned to eating grains
and tasting flavors,
within a hundred or so days,
he returned to his original nature.
The Prefect of Xīnzhōu
The Prefect of Xīnzhōu in Táng was a position plagued by misfortune,
with many successive officeholders dying.
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng,
a Jīnwú Guards officer came to try this post.
Upon arriving,
he slept alone in the main hall at night.
After the second watch,
he saw something black outside the eaves,
shaped like a large boat,
with eyes several zhang apart.
The Prefect asked what deity it was,
and it replied:
"I am a great snake."
The Prefect ordered it to change its appearance to speak with him,
and the snake then transformed into human form,
coming into the hall.
The Prefect then asked why it killed people,
and the snake said:
"I never had any intent to kill;
the guests simply died of fear themselves."
The Prefect asked again:
"If you had no intent to kill,
why did you repeatedly appear in physical form?"
It said:
"I have grievances and stagnation,
and I need the Prefect to help me."
Asked what grievances it had,
it said:
"In my youth,
I once entered an ancient tomb,
and since then my body gradually grew larger,
unable to find a way out.
Foxes, rabbits, raccoon dogs, and the like
sometimes entered the tomb,
and only then could I eat them.
Now I remain trapped in the earth,
unable to die,
so I sought Your Excellency."
The Prefect asked:
"If that is the case,
should we dig you out?
What do you think?"
The snake said:
"I am coiled for over ten li;
if you try to excavate,
the entire city will collapse.
Now, east of the city is Wáng Village,
and west of the village is a catalpa tree.
Your Excellency may hold a fasting ritual,
and have people dig two zhang deep by the tree.
Inside, there is an iron case.
Open the case and look inside,
and I will be able to emerge."
With these words, it took its leave.
At dawn,
they went to dig as instructed,
found the case,
brought it back to the hall, and opened it.
A blue dragon flew out of the case into the sky,
went straight to kill the snake,
splitting it in half from head to tail.
The snake was thus killed.
The strange occurrences ceased.
The Magistrate of Yúgān County
In Póyáng Commandery, the magistrate of Yúgān County,
would die just days after assuming office.
Afterward, no one would take up the post,
and the residence fell into ruin.
During the Xiāntiān era,
there was a scholar from a poor family
who came to serve as magistrate.
Upon arrival,
the clerks requested that the magistrate reside in a separate office.
The magistrate then ordered the old residence to be restored,
clearing away the brambles and weeds,
and repairing the walls and buildings.
He stayed alone in the main hall,
lighting candles at night to keep watch.
After the second watch,
a creature resembling a white sack three dǒu in size
came hopping and rolling to the front of the bed,
then leaped directly onto the table.
The magistrate showed no fear.
Slowly, he reached out to touch it with his hand—
it truly was a leather sack filled with water.
He then said to it:
"Move the lamp for me to the southwestern corner."
As soon as he finished speaking, the lamp was already in the southwestern corner.
He then said:
"You can give me a massage."
The sack rolled onto his body,
and it felt quite comfortable and soothing.
He then teased it:
"Can you make my bed float in the air?"
In a moment,
it was already in the air.
Everything he said was fulfilled as he wished.
As dawn approached,
it leaped away.
The magistrate searched for it
and found it vanish beside the pond in the compound.
The next day,
he examined the spot where it had disappeared
and saw a hole,
only as large as an ant's burrow.
He dug it up,
and after about a zhang, the hole grew larger,
measuring over three chǐ in circumference,
with unfathomable depth.
The magistrate then ordered many cauldrons, firewood, and kindling to be prepared,
and had all the pond water drawn to boil,
pouring it into the hole.
After about a hundred hú,
thunderous sounds came from the hole,
and the ground shook.
Another hundred hú were poured in,
and then it fell silent.
They then dug with combined efforts,
and after several zhàng,
they found a giant snake,
over a hundred chǐ long.
Countless smaller snakes surrounded it,
all perishing in the hole.
The magistrate had the large snake dried into jerky,
and distributed it as rewards throughout the county.
Afterward, peace and auspiciousness returned.
Wáng Zhēn's Wife
Wáng Zhēn, the magistrate of Huàyīn County, had a wife named Zhào,
the daughter of a wealthy family from Yānzhōng.
She was beautiful in appearance
and married Wáng Zhēn at a young age.
After accompanying him to his post,
about half a year later,
suddenly a young man
would wait for Wáng Zhēn to leave
and then visit Zhào's bedroom.
As he came and went frequently,
he teased and seduced Zhào into an affair.
One day,
Wáng Zhēn returned from outside
and saw this young man sharing a mat with Zhào,
drinking, laughing, and enjoying themselves,
which greatly shocked him.
Zhào suddenly collapsed, breathless,
and the young man transformed into a giant snake,
fleeing in a rush.
Wáng Zhēn ordered the maids to help Zhào up,
and soon Zhào also transformed into a snake,
rushing away together.
Wáng Zhēn pursued them
and saw them both enter Huàshān Mountain,
disappearing after a while.
Zhū Jìn
Zhū Jìn was
a wandering knight from Chén and Cài.
While traveling in Rǔnán,
he stayed at an inn.
At the time, the innkeeper Dèng Quánbīn had a daughter
with dignified and beautiful features,
but she was often deluded by ghostly apparitions.
Despite all attempts at treatment,
none could cure her.
Once, Zhū Jìn was drinking at a friend's place
and returned late at night.
He rested in the courtyard.
By the second watch,
he saw a person dressed in white,
with very bright and clean clothes,
enter Dèng Quánbīn's daughter's room.
After a while,
he heard lively conversation and laughter from the room,
and unable to sleep,
he took his bow and arrows and hid in the dark,
waiting for the person to emerge.
He waited until rooster crow,
when he saw the girl escorting a young man out.
Zhū Jìn shot at him,
hitting him as he fled.
Zhū Jìn shot again,
but lost his trail.
At dawn, he informed Dèng Quánbīn,
and together they followed the blood trail.
About five lǐ from the residence,
the trail led into a large hollow in a withered tree.
They ordered people to cut down the tree,
and indeed found a snake,
snow-white in color,
over a zhàng long,
with two arrows in its body, dead.
The girl recovered from then on,
and Dèng Quánbīn married his daughter to Zhū Jìn.
Méngshān Mountain
On Méngshān Mountain in Fèi County of the State of Lǔ, there was a long-abandoned temple.
Whenever people tried to build a hall there,
a snake several dozen zhàng long
would emerge and frighten them,
so no one could settle there peacefully.
Qín Zhān
Qín Zhān lived in Qūhé.
While traveling in the wilderness of Péngxīng,
suddenly a creature like a snake
burst into his brain.
When the snake came,
a foul odor was first detected,
then it entered through the nose,
coiling inside his head.
He felt a cold, watery sensation,
and heard within his brain
the sound of chewing and slurping.
After a few days, it left.
Soon it returned,
but he took a towel
and tightly bound his nose and mouth,
so it could not enter.
For years, nothing else happened,
except he suffered from a heavy head.
Guǎngzhōu People
People from Guǎngzhōu were cutting wood in the mountains together
when they suddenly saw three eggs in a stone nest,
as large as a shēng measure.
They took them and boiled them.
Just as the water began to heat,
they heard sounds like wind and rain from the forest.
In a moment,
a snake ten arm-spans thick,
four or five zhàng long,
came straight over,
took the eggs from the boiling water with its mouth, and left.
Soon after, all three men died.
Yuán Xuányīng
The Grand Administrator of Wúxīng,
Yuán Xuányīng was about to take up his post.
He consulted a fortune-teller about his fortune,
who said:
"According to the method,
upon taking office, there will be a red snake causing mischief,
but you must not kill it."
When he arrived,
indeed, a red snake was coiled on the stone case containing the bronze tiger tally.
Yuán Xuányīng ordered it killed.
Later, he was indeed harmed by the rebel Xú Fù.
Xuē Zhòng
In Kuàijī Commandery, a clerk from Yín County named Xuē Zhòng obtained leave to return home.
He arrived home at night,
found the door closed,
and heard the sound of a man sleeping on his wife's bed.
He called his wife,
and after a long while, she came out from the bed.
She opened the door.
Grasping a knife, he immediately confronted his wife and asked:
"Who is that drunk person on the bed?"
His wife was greatly shocked and alarmed,
and thus bitterly pleaded her innocence,
insisting there was truly no one.
Zhòng's home had only one door;
once he entered,
he closed it and searched his wife.
He found absolutely nothing.
He saw a snake hidden by the bed's foot,
smelling of wine and foul,
so Zhòng chopped the snake into inch-long pieces,
and threw them into the ditch behind.
After a day, his wife died.
A few days later,
Zhòng also died,
but then suddenly revived.
He recounted that upon first dying,
someone shackled him.
He was taken to a place
where an official asked:
"Why did you kill someone?"
Zhòng replied:
"I truly committed no murder."
The official said:
"You claim you didn't kill,
yet recently you chopped something into inch-long pieces and threw it into the back ditch.
What was that?"
Zhòng said:
"I merely killed a snake."
The prefectural lord was startled and, having realized something, said:
"I intended to employ him as a deity,
yet he dared to debauch another's wife,
and even lodge a complaint against someone."
He ordered his attendants to bring him.
A clerk led in a man
wearing a plain headscarf and cap,
and thoroughly interrogated him about his crime of debauchery and falsehood.
He was ordered to be delivered to prison.
Zhòng was then promptly sent out by the authorities,
and suddenly returned [to life].
Gù Kǎi
During the Chén period, Gù Kǎi from Wúxīng was in the fields, climbing a tree to pick mulberry leaves,
when he saw a large, multi-colored snake enter a small hole.
Following it, snakes came one after another,
some three chi, some five chi, following in succession,
roughly numbering in the hundreds.
Kǎi hurriedly descended the tree,
and looked at the place where they entered,
but saw no hole at all.
At dusk, he returned home.
Kǎi fell ill, became mute,
and could no longer speak.
The Shùtí Family
In the Suí dynasty, in Xià County, Jiàng Prefecture, the Shùtí family
had newly built a residence.
As they were about to move in,
suddenly countless snakes
flowed from the rooms out the door.
Their density was like silkworms on a tray,
covering the ground completely.
At the time, a passing traveler said:
"I know how to use talismans for suppression."
He took four peach branches, wrote talismans on them,
and nailed them around the four sides of the residence.
The snakes gradually retreated,
and the talismans were also moved accordingly.
The snakes entered the center of the hall,
where there was a hole
as large as a basin's mouth.
The snakes all entered it completely.
He ordered a hundred hú of boiling water to be poured in.
After one night,
they dug with shovels,
several chi deep.
They found two hundred thousand strings of ancient copper coins.
Thus, they broke and melted them down,
cast new coins,
and became immensely wealthy.
The snakes were the essence of the ancient copper.
Emperor Suí Yáng
The "Sōu Shén Jì" states:
"A snake of a thousand years can sever and rejoin itself."
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"A divine snake can sever its own body and rejoin itself."
Emperor Suí Yáng dispatched people to Lǐngnán,
to remote mountains by the sea,
seeking this snake several times,
and it reached Luòxià.
The ones obtained
were about three chi long,
with yellow-black coloration,
their heads patterned like brocade,
entirely resembling gold in color.
They could not poison people,
and understood how to eat meat.
If one wanted to make it sever its own body,
one would first provoke it to anger,
causing it to be unable to bear its furious venom,
and it would sever itself into three or four pieces.
The severed places
were as if cut by a knife.
One could see the patterns of its skin and bones,
and there was also blood.
However, after the prolonged anger subsided,
the three or four severed pieces would gradually rejoin and reconnect,
the body restored as before,
also as if it had never been severed.
Suí dynasty Editorial Director Dèng Lóng said
this is a type of spiritual snake
that severs itself;
it does not necessarily require a thousand years.
Xìngfú Temple
In Cháng'ān's Xìngfú Temple, there was a Ten Lights Buddha Hall.
Its building was extremely magnificent,
said to have been constructed during the Suí dynasty.
During the Zhēnguàn period,
the temple monks, considering its age was long and distant,
feared it might collapse,
so they calculated the expenses and labor,
intending to renew its structure,
and were about to demolish it.
Once they opened the door,
they saw tens of thousands of snakes
linked together on the ground,
coiled and piled up like a mass,
shaking their heads and gaping their mouths,
as if ready to devour.
The temple monks were greatly terrified,
believing Heaven pitied the heavy labor,
and thus manifested this spiritual transformation.
Thereupon, they dared not remove or destroy it.
Zhāng, the Cavalry Officer
There was a man named Zhāng Qíshì,
who himself said
that when he was young, he followed Duke Yīng, Lǐ Jì, across the sea.
They encountered a storm that lasted over ten days,
and they had no idea how many tens of thousands of miles they had traveled.
When the wind calmed and the waves stilled,
they suddenly saw two black creatures.
Their heads resembled snakes,
and they were as large as giant ships,
their length so great it seemed endless.
In an instant,
they reached the ship.
Both wrapped their heads around the vessel and pushed it sideways,
moving as swiftly as the wind.
The sailors were terrified,
unsure how to resist,
and already resigned to being devoured,
they could only chant the Buddha’s name, praying for a quick death.
After a long while,
they arrived at a mountain,
where wrecked ships lay piled up like debris.
Each of them thought to themselves,
“Those people must have all been eaten by these creatures.”
Suddenly,
the wind picked up fiercely again.
Looking back behind the ship,
they saw three more snakes,
chasing after them and catching up,
seemingly intent on fighting over their prey.
The two snakes released the ship
and turned back to battle the three snakes on the sand,
all coiling and wrestling on a solitary island.
The sailors took advantage of this to hoist the sails and ride the wind,
thus escaping the danger.
Several days later,
they reached another mountain,
where they saw smoke in the distance,
assuming it was inhabited.
They lowered the sails and went ashore,
Two men went ahead together,
and they came upon a very large gate.
They stepped forward and knocked.
A person several zhang tall appeared,
covered entirely in white hair.
He came out, saw the two men,
and ate them.
One man immediately fled back to the ship.
He had just boarded
and had not yet cast off
when the white-haired being came running, trying to pull the ship back.
The sailors each took up bows and knives, hacking and shooting at him.
They struck him with several blows,
and only then did he release them.
When they were about a li from the shore,
they saw dozens of these beings on the bank,
shaking their fists and shouting loudly.
They then drifted with the wind for another five or six days,
until they saw an island in the distance.
They moored the boat and asked the people there,
who said it was within the boundaries of Qīngyuǎn County,
part of Nánhǎi.
Lǐ Chóngzhēn
During the Guāngzhái era of Emperor Gāozōng,
Lǐ Chóngzhēn served as the Chief Administrator of Yìzhōu.
In front of his hall, there was a mandarin orange tree bearing a single fruit the size of a chicken egg.
It ripened late,
and had a tiny hole like a needle prick.
All the officials found it strange.
Just as they were about to present it,
they delayed for a long time and eventually stopped.
When they cut it open,
they found a red-spotted snake inside,
over a chǐ long.
Later, Chóngzhēn was eventually executed for his crimes.
Also, in Liánzhōu, there was a mandarin orange tree
that in the fourth month
bore a fruit as large as a fist.
When cut open,
it contained a two-headed snake.
Mǎlǐng Mountain
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Kāiyuán era,
at the side of Mǎlǐng Mountain in Chēnzhōu, there was a white snake,
six or seven chǐ long,
and a black snake over a zhàng long.
Suddenly,
the two snakes fought.
The white snake swallowed the black snake,
but when it reached the thicker part,
the corners of its mouth split open,
and blood gushed out profusely.
The black snake’s head went in,
but it bit a hole in the white snake’s side,
and its head emerged over two chǐ out.
Soon after, both snakes died.
More than ten days later,
heavy rain fell,
and mountain floods surged violently,
washing away over five hundred households
and causing more than three hundred people to go missing.
The Virtuous One of Zhìxiàng Temple
At Zhìxiàng Temple in Cháng’ān, there was a virtuous one
who, from the age of over ten,
had been cultivating the Way in the Western Chán Hall.
Under the seat in the Buddha hall of the temple,
there was always a snake.
When the virtuous one first began cultivating the Way,
the snake was as thick as one arm-span.
After more than forty years,
it had grown as large as a hall pillar.
People,
Although the snake and the people saw each other,
they did not harbor any animosity.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the virtuous one went to the Buddha hall at night to pay respects.
There was no lamp in the hall,
yet it was filled with brilliant light.
He found this very strange.
Then, from where the snake emerged,
he obtained a pearl about a cùn in diameter.
He took it to the market and set a high price,
hoping to find someone who recognized its value.
After several days,
a foreign merchant came to trade,
offering a fixed price of a million coins.
The virtuous one said:
“This is a luminous pearl,
surely priceless.
How can you offer such a price?”
The foreigner replied:
“Pearls from clams are indeed precious,
but this is a snake pearl,
and its value rarely exceeds a thousand strings of cash.”
The virtuous one sighed in admiration and acceptance,
and sold it to him.
Lǐ Línfǔ
The residence of Lǐ Línfǔ
was originally the residence of Lǐ Jìng.
There was a Master Hóng, renowned for his Daoist arts during the time of Emperor Ruìzōng,
who once passed by this residence
and said to people:
“Whoever lives here in the future
will attain untold nobility.”
Afterward, the place remained uninhabited for a long time.
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Línfǔ held the position of Fèngyù,
and he subsequently moved in and lived there.
Someone reported this to Master Hóng,
who said:
“How extraordinary!
My words have indeed come true.
This person will hold the position of Chancellor for nineteen years,
becoming the most powerful and noble in the land.
This
is the man.
However,
I fear that if he alters the central gate,
disaster will befall him.”
Lǐ Línfǔ indeed became Chancellor under Emperor Xuánzōng,
wielding his power arrogantly,
and for a long time, people resented him.
In his later years,
someone presented him with an excellent horse,
very tall,
but the gate of his residence was slightly too low,
making it impossible to ride the horse through.
So he decided to alter and rebuild it.
Just as they began dismantling the eaves,
suddenly, tens of thousands of snakes
appeared among the roof tiles.
Lǐ Línfǔ was disgusted by this,
and immediately halted the work, unable to proceed with the demolition.
Not long after,
Lǐ Línfǔ’s property was confiscated.
From the beginning of his chancellorship to the confiscation,
it was indeed nineteen years.
Wéi Zǐchūn
In Línhuái Commandery, there was a lodge pavilion,
situated by the Sì River.
In the pavilion stood a great tree,
its circumference spanning several dozen arm spans,
It rose abruptly, robust and towering,
its shade covering a hundred paces.
Often, fierce winds and swift thunder
would arise there in the evening.
People would see two lights in the pavilion,
facing each other, moving up and down,
glaring like lightning.
Once the wind ceased,
the lights would also vanish.
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a man named Wéi Zǐchūn, renowned for his courage and strength.
It happened that Zǐchūn was a guest in Línhuái,
and someone told him of this matter.
Zǐchūn said:
"I can lie in wait for it."
So, carrying his clothes and provisions, he settled in the pavilion to watch.
One evening later,
a great wind and thunder indeed shook the ground,
the pavilion's buildings trembled,
and sure enough, two lights were seen illuminating the pavilion.
Zǐchūn then gathered his clothes and descended,
when suddenly he felt something coiling around his body,
cold as frozen water,
binding him inextricably.
Turning to look,
he saw two old men behind him.
Zǐchūn immediately exerted himself, swinging his arms,
and with a sudden sound,
his bonds also loosened.
He then returned to the pavilion.
Before long, the wind and rain cleared,
and a stench like a salted fish market was smelled in the pavilion.
The next day, looking around,
they saw a giant snake, severed in the middle and dead,
its blood covering the ground.
The villagers gathered to look,
thinking Zǐchūn must have died.
But when they saw him,
they were greatly astonished.
From then on, the pavilion was free from the calamity of wind and thunder.
Xuānzhōu River
In Xuānzhōu's Quètóu Town,
in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the river water rose greatly, flooding thirty lǐ.
The Wú people were skilled swimmers,
and they all entered the water to gather firewood and timber.
In the middle of the river, a piece of timber floated down,
over ten zhàng long.
The swimmers went to look at it,
and it turned out to be a giant snake.
Its color was yellow,
buoyed by the water,
it drifted down the middle of the river.
The swimmers, frightened, turned back,
but the snake opened its mouth and seized one of them.
The swimmer was held sideways in the snake's mouth,
which raised its head,
lifting him several chǐ out of the water.
The swimmer still cried out loudly for rescue,
but none of the onlookers dared to save him.
Lǐ Qíwù
Lǐ Qíwù, Governor of Hénán,
during the Tiānbǎo era,
was demoted to Prefect of Jìnglíng.
In the southern tower of the commandery city, white smoke appeared;
it was said that if the Prefect did not change his ways, he would die,
and the locals regarded this as a constant omen.
Qíwù, having been dismissed,
felt deeply resentful.
When white smoke suddenly emerged from the tower,
he became angry and said:
"I do not fear death,
what can the spirits do to me?"
He ordered someone to find the source of the smoke,
and it was reported:
"The white smoke is all white insects,
likely a giant snake."
Qíwù ordered it to be dug up.
The hole gradually enlarged,
and inside was a giant snake,
its body like a huge vat.
He ordered several tens of hú of oil to be boiled in a cauldron,
and when it was boiling, they poured it on the snake.
The snake initially roared like thunder,
shaking the city walls,
and it took a full day before it died.
Then he had people fill the trench and block it up.
Qíwù also suffered no further mishaps.
Yán Tǐngzhī
Yán Tǐngzhī served as Prefect of Wèizhōu.
When he first took office,
he was attending to official business in the hall.
A small snake entered through the door,
went to the desk,
and rested its head on the desk.
Tǐngzhī, not understanding at first,
quickly took his ivory tablet
and pressed its head down to the ground.
Standing upright, he pondered intently.
After a short while,
the snake transformed into a talisman.
Tǐngzhī thought it was the work of a sorcerer,
but after searching without finding anything, he let the matter drop.
Tiānbǎo Woodcutter
During the Tiānbǎo era,
a woodcutter entered the mountains, got drunk, and lay down,
where he was swallowed by a snake.
The man, slightly awake,
felt strange movements of his body,
and opening his eyes, he could not see,
only then realizing he had been swallowed by a creature.
So, using his woodcutter's knife, he cut open the belly,
and managed to get out.
Dizzy and confused,
it took a long time before he came to his senses.
From then on, half of the man's body shed its skin,
as if afflicted with leprosy.
Master Wúwèi
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Master Wúwèi was in Luòyáng.
At that time, there was a giant,
snake,
of very strange appearance,
over a zhàng tall,
fifty chǐ in girth,
massive and imposing.
It coiled and emerged from the foot of the mountain,
and all the people of Luò saw it.
Then Wúwèi said:
"Later, this snake will breach the waters and flood Luò City."
He then expounded Buddhist scriptures with great profundity.
The snake, by evening,
would come riding the wind and dew,
as if listening attentively.
Wúwèi then rebuked,
it, saying:
"You are a snake,
dwelling deep in the mountains,
secure in your own place.
Why do you intend to unleash poison upon the world?
Leave quickly,
and do not harm living people."
Upon hearing this, the snake
bowed its head to the ground,
as if with a look of shame,
and in a moment, it died.
Later, when Ān Lùshān occupied Luòyáng,
destroying all the palaces and temples,
it indeed corresponded to Wúwèi's prediction of breaching the Luò River to flood the city.
Zhāng Hào
After Hóngzhōu City was established by Mǎ Yuàn,
it was never repaired or renovated again.
A legend circulated:
"Anyone who repairs it will surely die."
During the Yǒngtài era,
Governor Zhāng Hào repaired it without hesitation.
Suddenly, at the northwest corner of the city, a large pit was encountered,
and inside the pit, two snakes were seen,
one white and one black,
with heads resembling oxen,
bodies as large as giant jars,
over sixty feet long,
coiled in the pit,
with countless smaller snakes.
They immediately reported it to Zhāng Hào,
who ordered them to drive the snakes out.
They used bamboo strips to bind the snakes' heads
and pulled them.
The snakes initially did not open their eyes,
but followed as they were pulled out.
There were many small snakes,
and some soldiers injured over ten of the smaller ones,
which were still as large as drinking bowls.
The two snakes followed each other into the release pond beneath the Xúrú Pavilion.
The pond was several fathoms deep,
and all the turtles crawled out onto the shore,
where they were caught by people.
The fish also puffed their gills and emerged from the water,
and soon all died.
Seven days later,
Zhāng Hào passed away.
His assistant Zhèng Cóng and the magistrate of Nánchāng, Mǎ Jiǎo,
both died one after the other.
Bì Qiántài
Bì Qiántài, a Left Reminder of the Táng Dynasty,
was from Rénqiū, Yíngzhōu.
When his parents turned fifty,
he prepared their burial site in advance.
By the time his father was eighty-five,
he also made a coffin himself,
slightly larger and taller,
but found the burial site too small,
so he added twenty thousand bricks.
When he opened the burial site to renovate it,
there were countless snakes.
It was still cold in the first month,
and the snakes were hibernating and unable to move.
He took the snakes and threw them into an empty well,
but still could not remove all of them.
The snakes were golden in color.
Bì Qiántài personally opened the site with his servant,
and soon fell ill and died.
Over a month later,
both his parents passed away.
This was because he opened the burial site at an inopportune time.
Dù Wěi
Palace Censor Dù Wěi once traveled beyond the Líng region,
arriving at Kāngzhōu.
The post-horse stopped,
It said:
"Please avoid the poisonous creature."
Then they saw a large snake crossing the road from the south,
several fathoms long,
with a black tortoise chasing it from behind.
South of the road was a large pine tree,
and the snake climbed to a high branch and coiled around it,
lowering its head to look down at the black tortoise.
The black tortoise looked up from beneath the tree with its nose,
and two streams of green smoke emerged from its nostrils,
directly striking the snake's head.
The snake then split apart and died,
falling beneath the tree.
They also saw a centipede as large as a kite.
Niú Sù once asked Sīmǎ Dí of Kāngzhōu about this matter,
and Dí said:
"In the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
due to the sea tide in Guǎngfǔ,
a centipede drifted ashore,
dead.
When one of its claws was dissected,
it yielded one hundred and twenty catties of meat.
In the market of Guǎngzhōu,
someone had a cage containing a two-headed snake.
He gathered a crowd and said:
'Do you know the two-headed snake?
If you see a two-headed snake,
both heads emerge together.
What I have now is different from that—
each head of the snake is separate,
would you like to see it?'
The market-goers asked to see it,
so he took out the snake.
The snake was two feet long,
with heads at both ends.
There was an entertainer in the market
who often made a living by handling snakes,
and whenever he held snakes,
he did not avoid poisonous ones.
When he saw the two-headed snake,
he picked it up with his hand.
The snake bit his hand,
and the entertainer cried out in pain,
dropping the snake to the ground.
He applied medicine to it,
but it did not heal.
The bitten area swelled,
and gradually spread,
soon covering his entire body.
The entertainer died,
and his body swelled greatly,
with his flesh and bones turning into water,
his body like a water-filled sack.
After a while, the water burst forth,
and he completely dissolved.
Both the man and the two-headed snake disappeared."
Hǎizhōu Hunter
The people of Hǎizhōu made hunting their livelihood,
and once, a hunter shot a deer in the mountains of the Eastern Sea.
Suddenly, he saw a snake,
black in color,
as large as a continuous mountain range,
nearly ten fathoms long,
with eyes like the sun.
It emerged from the sea,
and the man, terrified upon seeing the snake,
knew,
he could not escape death.
So he prostrated himself.
reciting Buddha's name.
The snake reached the man's location,
picked up the man and his bow and arrows with its mouth,
and crossed the sea with him.
They traveled far to a mountain,
where the snake placed the man on a high cliff.
Soon, another snake came from the south,
arriving at the mountain,
similar in appearance to the first snake but twice as large.
The two snakes fought each other at the foot of the mountain.
At first, they coiled around each other with their bodies,
and after a long time,
they began biting each other with their mouths.
The archer realized they were seeking his help.
So he prepared a poisoned arrow,
intending to shoot.
The larger snake had already lost one eye,
so the man shot its other eye,
hitting it with several arrows in succession.
After a long time,
the larger snake finally died,
collapsing to the ground.
The smaller snake was also severely injured from head to tail,
so it carried several pecks of large pearls, turquoise, and other treasures,
and sent the man back to his original location.
Lǐ Zhōu's Younger Brother
Lǐ Zhōu's younger brother suffered from a wind ailment,
and someone said snake wine could cure it,
so he sought a black snake.
He placed it alive in a covered jar,
adding yeast and malt.
After several days,
the snake's sounds never ceased,
and when it was fully fermented,
the aroma was intensely strong.
He filled a cup and drank it.
In a moment,
his body completely turned into water,
with only his hair remaining.
