Yánshēng
Once there was a scholar who,
on the road, encountered a small snake
and thus took it in to raise.
After several months, it gradually grew large.
The scholar often carried it on his shoulder,
and named it Jiānshēng.
Later, when it could no longer be carried,
he released it into the great marsh east of Fàn Xiàn.
After more than forty years,
the snake had grown as large as an overturned boat.
It was called the divine python,
and anyone who went into the marsh
would surely be devoured.
By then, the scholar had grown old and frail.
While passing by the edge of this marsh,
he was told by people:
"There is a great snake inside that eats people;
you should not go there."
It was the height of winter and bitterly cold.
The scholar reasoned that snakes hibernate in winter,
so this could not be true,
and thus he crossed the great marsh.
After traveling more than twenty lǐ,
suddenly a snake pursued him.
The scholar still recognized its shape and color,
and from afar said to it:
"Are you not my Jiānshēng?"
The snake then lowered its head,
and after a long while, finally left.
Returning to Fàn Xiàn,
the county magistrate, hearing that he had seen the snake and not died,
considered it strange,
and had him imprisoned,
sentencing him to death.
The scholar privately lamented:
"Jiānshēng,
raising you has instead caused my death—
is this not too cruel!"
That night,
the snake attacked and sank the entire county into a lake,
only the prison did not sink,
and the scholar was spared.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a man named Dúgū Yǐ,
whose maternal uncle was the magistrate of Fàn Xiàn.
On the third day of the third month,
he went boating on the lake with his family,
and for no reason, they capsized and drowned.
Several members of the family nearly died.
The Guests of Sōng Shān
At the beginning of the Yuánhé era,
there were five or six guests on Sōng Shān,
all of whom were staying in the mountains to study.
In early autumn,
they sought refuge from the heat beneath the Two Emperors Pagoda.
As the day grew late,
they saw beneath the pagoda a great snake, several zhàng long,
coiled around the pagoda's core,
raised off the ground.
more than ten zhàng high.
Everyone watched in terror,
and one guest said:
"This could supply the kitchen with dried meat."
All agreed,
and among them was one guest skilled in archery.
Someone said:
"Large creatures may be dragon spirits;
killing it might bring disaster.
Is a meal of dried meat
really worth it here?
Better not to do it."
But the other guests were determined,
and could not be dissuaded.
The skilled archer shot one arrow,
and it struck;
with a second arrow,
the snake uncoiled and fell to the ground,
and everyone together killed it.
The guests each attended to kitchen duties:
some wielded knives to slice and carve,
while others went into the temple to fetch firewood, charcoal, salt, and vinegar.
The one who had advised against killing it
looked unhappy,
and so took his leave and returned.
After he had gone several lǐ from the temple,
the sky had already darkened,
when suddenly thunder arose.
Among them, some had also returned separately,
but several guests still remained beneath the pagoda.
In an instant,
clouds and mist gathered heavily,
darkening everything near and far,
hail fell like a torrent,
a fierce wind swept from all directions,
breaking trees and hurling stones,
thunder and hail raged furiously,
shaking the mountains and rivers.
Several men were struck dead beneath the pagoda;
those who had returned earlier
also died on the road.
The one guest who had not wanted to kill it,
before reaching his mountain dwelling,
took shelter in an empty temple.
He closed the door,
but lightning and thunder followed him inside.
Terrified,
he reflected that he had not been part of the conspiracy,
and should not be harmed for it.
So he declared loudly:
"I did not join the others in killing this snake;
divine justice is clear-sighted,
and should not punish the innocent indiscriminately!
I beg you to examine this carefully."
When he finished speaking,
the thunder and lightning ceased together,
and the wind and rain subsided.
This guest alone survived.
Dèng Jiǎ
During the Bǎolì era,
there was a man named Dèng Jiǎ,
who served the Mǎoshān Daoist priest Qiào Yán.
Qiào Yán
was truly a man of the Way,
able to transform tiles and stones into medicine,
and summon ghosts and spirits with talismans.
Dèng Jiǎ was diligent, sincere, and devout,
never feeling the toil or hardship;
he scarcely closed his eyes at night,
and did not rest in bed by day.
Qiào Yán also took note of him,
but when he taught him the art of medicine,
Dèng Jiǎ ultimately could not master it;
when he received the talismans,
they produced no effect.
The Daoist said:
"You have no affinity for these two arts,
you cannot force yourself to learn them."
Instead, he taught him the art of subduing the snakes of heaven and earth,
an art that within the entire realm,
he alone possessed.
Dèng Jiǎ acquired it and returned home.
When he reached Wūjiāng,
he suddenly encountered the magistrate of Kuàijī who had been bitten on the foot by a venomous snake.
The sounds of his agonized cries
shook the entire neighborhood.
All those who possessed arts
were unable to subdue it,
so Dèng Jiǎ proceeded to treat him.
First, he used a talisman to protect his heart,
and the pain immediately stopped.
Dèng Jiǎ said:
"I must summon the snake of its original kind,
to have it draw out its venom.
Otherwise,
the foot will have to be amputated."
Suspecting that someone was subduing it, the snake
had fled several li away.
So he set up an altar in a mulberry grove,
four zhang wide,
surrounded it with red silk,
and then flew talismanic characters,
summoning all snakes within ten li.
In no time, they arrived,
piling up on the altar,
over a zhang high,
who knows how many tens of thousands there were.
Behind them were four large snakes,
each three zhang long,
as thick as a well-bucket,
coiled atop the pile.
At that time, all vegetation within over a hundred paces,
even in midsummer, withered and turned yellow.
Dèng Jiǎ then went barefoot and climbed,
ascending to the top of the snake pile.
He struck the heads of the four large snakes with a green branch, saying:
"I appoint you as the five rulers,
to govern the snakes within your boundaries.
How dare you allow venom to harm people?
If it was you, stay;
if not, leave!"
Dèng Jiǎ then descended,
and the snake pile collapsed.
The large snakes left first,
the smaller ones followed,
until they were all gone.
Only one small snake remained,
earth-colored, resembling a chopstick,
just over a chi long,
dazed and unwilling to leave.
Dèng Jiǎ had the magistrate carried over,
let his foot hang down,
and commanded the snake to draw out the venom.
At first, the snake stretched and contracted, finding it difficult,
but Dèng Jiǎ commanded it again,
and as if something were urging it on,
it could only extend a few cun.
A greasy substance flowed from its back,
and with no other choice, it opened its mouth
and sucked at the wound.
The magistrate felt within his brain
something like a needle moving downward.
The snake then split its skin and turned into water,
leaving only its spine on the ground.
The magistrate was then free of suffering,
and richly rewarded Dèng Jiǎ with gold and silk.
At that time, in Wéiyáng, there was a certain Mr. Bì,
who often played with a thousand snakes,
performing daily in the marketplace,
and thus amassed great wealth,
building a large mansion.
After his death,
his son wanted to sell the mansion,
but could do nothing about the snakes,
so he summoned Dèng Jiǎ with gold and silk.
Dèng Jiǎ arrived,
gave him a talisman,
and flew the snakes over the city walls,
only then was he able to sell the house.
Dèng Jiǎ later went to Fúliáng County,
as spring was approaching.
At that time,
in the tea gardens,
there had long been venomous snakes,
and people dared not pick the tea leaves,
dozens having already died.
The locals, knowing of Dèng Jiǎ's divine arts,
pooled gold and silk,
asking him to remove the menace.
Dèng Jiǎ set up an altar
and summoned the snake king.
There was a large snake as thick as a thigh,
over a zhang long,
resplendent with brocade-like colors,
followed by ten thousand others.
The large one alone ascended the altar
to contend with Dèng Jiǎ in a contest of arts.
The snake gradually rose,
its head lifting several chi,
trying to surpass Dèng Jiǎ's head.
Dèng Jiǎ used his staff to prop up his hat, making it higher,
and the snake's head ultimately strained,
unable to surpass Dèng Jiǎ's hat.
The snake then collapsed into water,
and the remaining snakes all died.
If the snake's head had surpassed Dèng Jiǎ's,
then Dèng Jiǎ would have turned into water.
From then on, the tea gardens were rid of their venomous serpents.
Dèng Jiǎ later lived at Mǎoshān to study the Dao,
and is still there to this day.
Sū Rùn
Folklore tells of an old woman
who, during the time of the Qín dynasty,
once caught a strange fish
and released it into the Yuèchéng River in Kāngzhōu.
Later, it grew somewhat larger, like a dragon.
Whenever the old woman drew water or washed clothes in the river,
the dragon would always come to her side,
and this became customary.
One day,
while the old woman was preparing fish,
the dragon came again.
She playfully poked it with a knife,
accidentally cutting off its tail,
and the old woman died.
The dragon piled up sand and stones
to form a mound over her grave.
People called it the "Stub-tailed Dragon"
and built a temple for it that lasted over a thousand years.
At the end of the Tàihé era,
the temple keeper,
wishing to deify the matter
to deceive people,
took a group of small snakes,
used arts to subdue them,
and hid them beneath the temple,
calling them dragon offspring,
and ordered them to drink wine.
He placed them in a handkerchief box
and carried them to the city markets.
The Yuè people were fond of ghosts and strange things,
and vied to make offerings,
of which the temple keeper always took half.
At the beginning of the Kāichéng era,
Sū Rùn, a former general of Cāngzhōu, became the prefectural governor.
Knowing full well it was false,
yet coveting the wealth,
he further deified it.
He used the gold and silk obtained
to repair Buddhist temples and official buildings.
One day, a military officer was bitten by a snake,
and Sū Rùn did not allow treatment,
but instead straightened his official cap and tablet,
and ordered someone to go speak to the old woman.
The bitten person died shortly after,
and he then claimed
it was punishment for disrespecting the deity.
The ignorant people quickly spread the story,
and belief grew even firmer.
Once, someone killed one of the snakes,
dried it by fire,
and hid it,
yet afterward, the snakes in the temple multiplied.
To this day, it remains so.
Lìzhōu's Clerk Lǐ
During the Kāichéng era,
there was a gentleman named Lǐ from Lǒngxī,
who served as the recorder and military advisor of Lìzhōu.
He resided in the official residence,
and once, upon rising early in the morning,
he saw several hundred snakes in the courtyard.
Greatly frightened,
he ordered them all to be discarded in the wilderness outside the city.
The next morning,
the snakes gathered again in the courtyard.
Lǐ became even more fearful,
and found it strange as well,
so he again ordered them to be removed.
One day later,
the snakes returned once more.
Lǐ exclaimed in alarm:
"Could it be that Heaven is about to bring disaster upon me?"
His face remained sorrowful for a long time.
More than ten days later,
Lǐ was reported to the prefect for corruption.
Officials were dispatched to his door,
intending to investigate his crimes
and report them to the emperor.
Panicked and terrified,
with no way to find peace,
he hanged himself from a tree in the courtyard,
breaking his neck and dying.
Lǐ had a wife,
who, grieving that her husband had met such an unjust death,
also hanged herself.
Thereupon, the household servants were struck with terror,
and several of them threw themselves into a well.
Indeed, the omen of the snakes' appearance foretold the disaster.
The prefect was none other than Lǐ Xíngshū.
Zǎn Lǎo
The elderly monk Lóngyán of Chángshòu Temple said that
once, while in Héngshān,
a villager was bitten by a venomous snake,
and died shortly after.
When the body was examined,
the swelling had risen over a foot high.
His son said:
"If Zǎn Lǎo were here,
we would have nothing to worry about."
So they invited Zǎn Lǎo to come.
He then surrounded the corpse with ashes,
opening four gates.
First, he said:
"If it enters from the feet,
then there will be no saving him."
He then stepped firmly and held his ground.
After a long time, the snake still had not come.
Zǎn Lǎo grew furious,
so he took several shēng of rice,
and molded it into the shape of a snake to curse it.
Suddenly, it wriggled and moved out the door.
After a while,
the rice snake led another snake to enter from the deceased's head,
going straight to the wound.
The corpse gradually lowered,
and the snake shrank and died.
The villager then came back to life.
Féng Dàn
There was a man named Féng Dàn,
who often suffered from illness.
A doctor instructed him to soak snakes in wine and drink it.
After drinking one jar initially,
his illness was reduced by half.
He then ordered his family to catch a snake in the garden,
throw it into the jar,
and seal it for seven days.
When opened,
the snake leaped out,
raising its head over a foot high,
went out the door,
and thus disappeared without a trace.
Where it passed,
the ground swelled up several inches.
Lù Shào
The court official Lù Shào said that
he once remembered a man who soaked snakes in wine,
having killed several dozen snakes before and after.
One day,
as he leaned over the jar to inspect the wine,
something jumped out
and bit his nose, nearly severing it.
Looking at it,
it turned out to be a snake's skull.
Due to the wound and scarring,
his nose appeared as if it had been sliced off.
Zhèng Huī
The presented scholar Zhèng Huī recounted that
his family lived in Gāoyóu,
and his relative's Lú family estate was near the water.
Several neighboring families together killed a white snake.
Not long after,
suddenly there was a great thunderstorm with heavy rain,
causing a flood.
Several families were swept away and drowned without exception,
only the Lú residence in the middle remained unharmed.
Zhāng Èzi
The deity Zhāng Èzi of Zǐtóng County
is located at the place where the Five Giants pulled out the snake.
Some say
it was a snake raised by a man named Zhāng from Juànzhōu,
and thus a shrine was established.
People of the time called it Zhāng Èzi,
and the deity was very efficacious.
During the pseudo-Shǔ regime, Wáng Jiàn's heir, named Yuányīng,
was intelligent and knowledgeable,
excelling in horsemanship and archery.
His teeth were always exposed,
so he often covered his mouth with his sleeve,
and those around him dared not look up at him.
He had snake-like eyes and was dark-skinned,
appearing fierce and vulgar.
He stayed awake all night,
and eventually was executed for treason.
On the night of his execution,
the temple priest of Zǐtóng Temple
was urgently reprimanded by Èzi,
who said:
"I have long been in the river,
and have only just returned now.
How could the temple have become so desolate and filthy?"
From this, the people of Shǔ knew that Yuányīng was the essence of the temple snake.
Xuǎnxiān Chǎng
In the southern regions, there is a Xuǎnxiān Chǎng (Immortal Selection Ground),
located beneath a steep cliff.
At its summit, there is a cave,
traditionally said to be the dwelling of immortals.
Every year on the Zhōngyuán Festival,
one person is selected to ascend.
Taoist practitioners build an altar below,
and when the time comes,
people from near and far, wearing ceremonial caps and robes,
gather there.
They prepare rituals,
set up fasting and offerings,
burn incense, and pray.
After seven days,
the crowd selects the one with the highest virtue and morality,
pure and sincere,
who stands solemnly on the altar with a tablet.
The others bid farewell with clasped sleeves and withdraw,
gazing from afar and bowing in reverence.
At that time, five-colored auspicious clouds
slowly descend from the cave entrance
to the altar ground.
The one of high virtue,
with robes and hat unmoving,
clasps both palms together,
and steps onto the five-colored clouds to ascend.
The onlookers all weep with envy and admiration,
bowing toward the cave entrance.
In this way, one or two people are selected each year.
The following year, a highly virtuous person was chosen,
when suddenly a cousin who was a bhikkhu,
coming from Wǔdū Mountain, went to bid him farewell.
The bhikkhu carried about a jīn of realgar,
and gave it to him, saying:
"On the path, this medicine is highly valued.
Please secretly place it between your waist and abdomen.
Be careful not to
lose it."
The highly virtuous one was very pleased,
and carried it with him as he ascended the altar.
When the time came,
he indeed stepped onto the clouds and ascended.
More than ten days later,
a foul stench was noticed from the mountain cliff.
Several days later,
a hunter,
climbing along the cliff, reached the cave,
and saw a large python
rotting inside.
The bones of those who had ascended before
were piled like a mountain within the giant cave.
It turned out that the five-colored clouds
were the python's poisonous breath,
which regularly inhaled these ignorant Taoists to fill its belly.
How tragic!
Gǒuxiān Shān
In the land of Bā Cóng,
the terrain is full of cliffs and precipices,
with water spirits and tree spirits
found everywhere.
The people live among streams and ravines,
making hunting their livelihood.
In a hollowed-out place,
there is a cave,
and the residents cannot fathom where it leads.
When hunters release their dogs here,
they often call but the dogs do not return,
instead staring wide-eyed and wagging their tails,
gazing at the cliffside cave.
At such times, colorful clouds descend,
welcoming the hunting dogs and lifting them into the cave.
This happens year after year,
and those fond of the Dao call it Gǒuxiān Shān, the Mountain of the Dog Immortals.
Once, a wise man,
alone in his disbelief,
tied a dog,
took his bow and arrows, and went there.
Upon arrival, he fastened a thick rope around the dog’s waist,
tying it to a large tree,
then stepped back to observe.
When the colorful clouds descended,
the dog, entangled, could not follow,
and howled repeatedly.
Soon, something appeared,
with a head as large as a jar,
eyes like lightning,
Its scales shone brightly,
casting a cold light over the stream valley,
and gradually it lowered itself from the cave to look at the dog.
The hunter, with a poisoned arrow, shot it.
Once struck,
it was never seen again.
After about ten days,
a foul stench filled the mountain.
The hunter then descended from the mountaintop,
lowering himself by rope to investigate,
and saw a giant python,
rotting among the rocks.
Thus, the tales of the Mountain of the Dog Immortals
came to an end forever.
Lǐ Huáng
In the second year of the Yuánhé era,
Lǐ Huáng of Lǒngxī,
was the nephew of the Salt and Iron Commissioner Lǐ Xùn.
While awaiting his official appointment,
he took advantage of his free time to visit the Eastern Market in Cháng'ān,
and caught a glimpse,
He saw a calf-drawn carriage,
with several maidservants inside conducting trade.
Lǐ Huáng peered into the carriage,
and saw a young lady dressed in white,
graceful and possessing a beauty unmatched in her generation.
Lǐ Huáng inquired about her,
and a servant replied:
"The young lady is a widow,
the daughter of the Yuán family.
She was previously married into the Lǐ family,
and now wears mourning garments for her Lǐ husband.
She has just completed the mourning period,
That is why she is here to purchase these items."
He further asked if she might remarry,
to which the servant smiled and said:
"I do not know."
Lǐ Huáng then took out money,
and silk,
to purchase various embroidered goods,
and the maidservants relayed the message:
"We will borrow the money to buy these,
please follow us to the residence to the left of Zhuāngyán Temple,
and we will repay you without fail."
Lǐ Huáng was pleased.
At that time,
it was already late,
so he followed the calf-drawn carriage.
It was nightfall when they reached their destination.
The calf-drawn carriage entered the middle gate,
and the young lady in white alighted from the carriage,
with servants surrounding her with curtains as she entered.
Lǐ Huáng dismounted from his horse,
and soon saw a servant bring out a couch,
saying:
"Please sit for a while."
After he sat down,
the servant said:
"Is the young gentleman free to receive the money tonight?
If not,
does he have a host here?
He may return to his host,
and tomorrow morning would not be too late."
Lǐ Huáng replied:
"I have no intention of collecting the money now,
but I also have no host here,
why are you keeping me at such a distance?"
The servant went inside,
and came out again, saying:
"If you have no host,
then why not stay here,
but please do not mock our humble accommodations."
Soon, the servant said:
"Please come in, young gentleman."
Lǐ Huáng straightened his clothes and entered,
and saw an elderly lady dressed in blue standing in the courtyard.
Upon meeting, she said:
"I am the aunt of the young lady in white."
They sat in the central courtyard,
and after a short while,
the young lady in white came out.
Her plain skirt was radiant,
her pure complexion was as bright as jade,
her speech was elegant and composed,
no different from an immortal.
After a brief exchange of pleasantries,
she turned and went back inside.
The aunt sat and apologized:
"You have shown such kindness in lending us money to purchase these colorful fabrics,
none of the buyers who have come recently
can compare to you.
But what about the borrowed items?
What?
I am deeply worried and ashamed."
Lǐ Huáng said:
"The fabrics are coarse and plain,
hardly worthy of adorning a beauty,
how dare I
mention the price?"
She replied:
"She is simple and unrefined,
unworthy of serving as your wife.
However, in our humble home, we have a debt of thirty thousand coins.
If you, young gentleman, do not disdain her,
she is willing to serve by your side."
Lǐ Huáng was pleased.
He bowed beside her,
and bent down to consider it.
Lǐ Huáng had a trading post,
which was nearby,
so he ordered his servant to fetch thirty thousand coins.
In a short while, they arrived.
The door to the western room
opened with a creak.
The meal was fully prepared,
all laid out in the western room.
The aunt then invited Lǐ Huáng to sit,
and the surroundings dazzled with brilliance.
The young lady soon arrived,
was asked to sit,
bowed to her aunt and sat down,
and six or seven people shared the meal.
After eating,
wine was served, and they drank joyfully.
He stayed for three days,
enjoying all manner of pleasures.
On the fourth day,
the aunt said:
"Young gentleman Lǐ, you should return now,
lest the Minister find it strange that you are delayed.
Will it not be difficult to visit again later?"
Lǐ Huáng also felt the desire to return,
so he accepted her words, bowed, and took his leave.
He mounted his horse,
and his servant noticed that Lǐ Huáng had an unusually foul, fishy odor.
Upon returning home,
he was asked where he had been for so many days,
and he replied with evasive words.
He then began to feel heavy in body and dizzy in head,
and asked for a blanket to lie down.
Previously, he had married a daughter of the Zhèng family,
who was by his side and said:
"Your official appointment has been settled.
Yesterday, when the appointment was processed,
they could not find you,
so I,
had my two brothers handle the appointment on your behalf,
and it is already done."
Lǐ Huáng replied with words of gratitude and shame.
Soon, his Zhèng brother-in-law arrived,
and questioned him about his whereabouts.
Lǐ Huáng was already beginning to feel dazed,
his responses disordered and incoherent.
He said to his wife:
"I will not rise again."
Though he spoke,
he only felt his body beneath the blanket gradually dissolving away.
When the blanket was lifted to look,
there was only a pool of water,
with only his head remaining.
His family was greatly shocked and terrified,
and called the servant who had accompanied him to question him,
who recounted the whole story.
When they went to search for the old residence,
it was an empty garden.
There was a honey locust tree,
with fifteen thousand coins hanging on the tree,
and fifteen thousand coins beneath the tree,
but nothing else was seen.
When they asked the people of that area,
they said:
"Often, there is a huge white snake under the tree,
and nothing else.
As for the surname Yuán,
it was likely taken from the empty garden as a surname."
There is another account:
During the Yuánhé era,
Lǐ Tīng, the military governor of Fèngxiáng,
had a nephew named Lǐ Guǎn,
who served as a military officer in the Imperial Guards.
He went out for an excursion from Yǒngníng Ward,
and when he reached outside Ānhuà Gate,
he encountered a carriage,
decorated with silver,
extremely bright and beautiful.
It was drawn by a white ox,
followed by two maidservants,
both riding white horses,
dressed entirely in white,
with graceful and charming appearances.
Lǐ Guǎn, being a son of a noble family,
did not restrain himself,
and immediately followed them.
As dusk approached,
the two maidservants said:
"Young gentleman, you are a noble person,
the women you see are all beauties.
We are of lowly status,
and coarse and plain,
unworthy of your generous affection.
However, there is fortunately a beautiful lady in the carriage,
truly worthy of your attention."
Lǐ Guǎn then asked the maidservants,
and galloped his horse alongside the carriage.
They smiled and turned back, saying:
"Young gentleman, just follow along,
I have already spoken. "
Guǎn then followed them,
and smelled an extraordinary fragrance filling the road.
At dusk,
they reached the Fèngchéng Garden,
and two maidservants said:
"Our lady lives east of here,
and has now gone ahead.
Please, sir, linger here for a while,
and I will come out to welcome you shortly."
Once the carriage entered,
Guǎn halted his horse by the roadside.
After a long while,
he saw a maid come out and beckon.
Guǎn then dismounted.
Entering, he sat in the hall,
and only smelled a renowned fragrance entering his nose,
unlike anything of the mortal world.
Guǎn then had his men and horses enter Ānyì Ward to lodge.
After dusk,
he finally saw a young woman,
dressed in plain white,
sixteen or seventeen years old,
beautiful as an immortal.
The joy in Guǎn's heart
was beyond description.
When he emerged,
he already saw his men and horses waiting outside the gate.
He then bid farewell and returned.
Just upon reaching home,
he felt a pain in his head,
which soon grew worse.
By the Chén-Sì hours (7-11 AM),
his head split open and he died.
His family questioned the servants
about the places they had been the previous night.
The attendants fully recounted the events,
saying:
"Our master smelled a rather strange fragrance,
but what we smelled
was merely a snake stench, unbearable to approach."
The whole family was shocked and aggrieved.
They immediately ordered servants
to re-examine the place where they had stopped the previous night.
They only saw within a withered pagoda tree
traces of a large coiled snake.
They then felled the tree
and dug it up.
The large snake was already gone,
but there were several small snakes,
all white.
They killed them all and returned.
The Monk Lìngyīn
The Monk Lìngyīn
was crossing the mountains via the Zǐwǔ Valley,
heading to Jīnzhōu.
He saw a bamboo sedan chair ahead,
with maidservants in mourning attire following it.
For several days,
he never saw a person inside.
Lìngyīn then hurriedly lifted the curtain to peek.
There was a woman,
with a human head but a very large snake body.
Lìngyīn was greatly startled.
The woman said:
"Unfortunately, my karma is heavy,
and my body suddenly transformed.
Why does the venerable one peek at me?"
He asked her servant,
who said: "We wish to send her to the top of the Qínlǐng Mountains."
Lìngyīn then recited meritorious verses for her,
and escorted them to the Qínlǐng Mountains.
He no longer saw the woman's head,
as she entered the forest.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Wèi's Elder Sister
Vice Censor-in-Chief Duke Wèi had an elder sister
whose nature was harsh, cruel, and malicious.
Many maids and servants died from her whippings and beatings.
Suddenly, she contracted a feverish illness for six or seven days,
and said herself:
"I will no longer see people."
She often shut herself alone in her room,
and those who wished to approach
would inevitably be met with her angry shouts and rebukes.
After more than ten days,
they suddenly heard rustling sounds from the room.
Stealthily coming to peek,
upon entering the hall,
they immediately felt a foul, fishy, poisonous odor.
Opening the window,
they saw she had transformed into a large snake,
over ten feet long,
of a reddish, mottled color.
Her clothes, claws, and hair
were scattered on the bed and mattress.
The snake glared angrily and chased people,
terrifying the whole household.
Everyone together sent it into the wilderness.
This was likely caused by her violent and cruel nature.
A Man from Púzhōu
A man from Púzhōu was digging the ground to make a well.
The pit was over ten feet deep,
when he encountered a square stone and could not reach water.
Wanting to remove the stone and dig further,
he suddenly fell into a deep pit.
Hibernating snakes were there, one as large as an overturned boat,
the smaller ones like ordinary snakes.
The man was initially very frightened,
but over time became somewhat accustomed.
He was hungry with nothing to eat.
The snakes inhaled air,
so he imitated them,
and then was no longer hungry.
After many months,
he heard the sound of thunder.
At the first clap,
the snakes raised their heads.
In a moment, they all moved,
and soon scattered.
The large one went ahead,
and they exited and re-entered in succession.
Knowing they would not harm him,
he went forward and embraced its neck.
The snake then went straight ahead.
Following a white path,
as if traveling ten li,
ahead there was a beacon fire.
It then placed the man on the ground and left.
The man went to ask the beacon keeper,
who said it was Píngzhōu.
A Poor Man from Xiàngwèi
In Xiàngwèi, there was a poor man
who was hoeing wasteland in a garden
when he saw a large snake.
He struck and killed it.
Soon he saw a large burrow,
with over ten small snakes inside.
He again killed and buried them,
and after finishing, returned home.
The next day,
someone came holding a petition to accuse him, saying:
"My entire family, young and old, was killed
and buried in the garden."
Officials arrested this man and interrogated him.
He clearly did not confess.
Inspecting the garden,
they found a pit
containing over ten people.
He only said he had beaten to death over ten snakes the previous day
and buried them there,
and had not killed any people.
He did not know where this calamity
came from.
If he were to be sentenced and executed,
it would be a great injustice.
The officials were suspicious.
They investigated the original accuser,
but found no one.
They then ordered a return to the garden
to re-examine the place where he had buried the snakes the previous day.
They only saw over ten dead snakes,
and no longer saw any people.
He was thus exonerated.
The Shūnyú Scholar
A scholar traveled to Pānyú,
passing through various commanderies.
While traversing the mountains,
he saw a vapor over ten feet high,
resembling smoke.
A local villager said:
"This is the Gāngzǐ snake swallowing an elephant."
They then informed the village,
beat drums and shouted loudly,
and the snake retreated into a rocky valley.
After a night had passed,
the villagers each took earthen jars and went there,
seeing an elephant still standing,
but its flesh and bones had all turned to water.
They then pierced it with needles,
and collected the water.
The villagers said,
that if one carries this across the sea in a boat,
it repels flood dragons.
Also, an official in the south saw a large snake,
several zhang long,
with a diameter of about one chi and five cun.
Inside its belly was something,
like a wooden stake or peg,
as it moved along a tree eating its leaves,
the object in its belly
gradually dissolved until nothing remained.
The villagers then said:
"This snake swallowed a deer,
and this tree's leaves can dissolve it."
He then ordered his attendants to pick and collect the leaves.
After returning,
if someone suffered from indigestion,
or abdominal bloating,
they would take the leaves to make a decoction and drink it.
After a night,
and by noon there was no report.
When they removed the blanket to look,
only dried bones remained,
the rest had turned to water.
A Commoner of Pí Xiàn
In Pí Xiàn, a commoner obtained a small snake by the canal outside the southern wall,
over a chi long.
He gutted its five viscera,
coiled and skewered it,
placed it over a fire,
and roasted it for several days.
The commoner's child, a few years old,
suddenly developed red swelling all over the body,
with skin blistering and breaking.
The child then spoke, saying:
"Your family unjustly killed me,
gutted the stomach from my belly,
and placed me over a fire.
Now I will make your child know this pain."
The family heard this in shock and amazement,
took the snake and removed the bamboo skewer,
sprinkled water on it,
burned incense and prayed in apology,
then returned it to its original place.
After a long while,
it slithered away,
and the child also recovered fully.
Yóu Shào
The seat of Lǔshān Xiàn in Rǔzhōu
was the Western Guǎngzhōu during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Now, southeast of the inner city, there is a shrine to a demonic deity.
Its front courtyard spans several hundred paces,
and the elders say
it was once a large polo field.
On either side of the main gate are twin locust trees, each twenty arm-spans around,
with branches and trunks luxuriant and spreading.
It is also said they were planted at that time.
By the beginning of the Zhōnghé era,
turmoil arose in the eastern Xia region,
and commanderies and cities were in chaos.
The prefectural governor, Yóu Shào,
was a general from Xǔ.
He ordered subordinate counties to cut trees to build palisades for self-defense,
and even mulberry, paper mulberry, catalpa, and maple trees
were not spared.
When they were about to fell the twin locust trees,
that evening,
a giant python coiled upon them,
its sound like rumbling thunder,
its eyes like shooting stars.
The garrison commander Lǐ Fán was in charge of the matter.
Fán was a military man,
and hearing this, he deemed it a demon.
He then led his men personally to cut it down.
As the axe fell, blood rained and splattered,
the腥气 overwhelming people.
His heart was shaken, and he stopped.
The twin locust trees survive to this day.
Chéng Ruì
The Jīngzhōu military governor Chéng Ruì, leading Càizhōu troops,
garrisoned Jiānglíng.
As the military governor Zhāng Guī plotted against him,
he abandoned his headquarters
and fled to Zǐguī.
One night, a giant snake coiled around his body,
nearly causing his death.
He then said:
"If I have wronged you,
my life or death is at your will."
After a short while,
the snake also vanished and left.
Thereafter, he recruited households,
trained soldiers,
and moved his garrison to Zhǔgōng.
Soon he received the commander's tally and banner,
pacified the devastated region,
and diligently governed.
In the first year,
the residents numbered only seventeen households.
By the final year, there were ten thousand households.
He served the king diligently and upheld the state,
promoted commerce and agriculture,
earning considerable praise.
The court called it "Northern Hán, Southern Guō."
Sūn Guāngxiàn
Sūn Guāngxiàn once traveled to Jiǎogǔ
and stayed overnight at Shénshān.
He saw on the ridge, in a plank hut,
a large wooden root carved into a giant python,
with incense and lamps arranged before it.
He then asked the old innkeeper:
"What deity is that?"
The old man said:
"During the Guānghuà era,
when Yáng Shǒuliàng governed Bāo,
a snake lay across this ridge path,
seven or eight chi tall,
its head and tail unseen.
Countless small snakes flanked it on all sides.
Each time it dragged its body,
trees and woods were crushed and broken.
It took nearly half a month to pass completely,
blocking travelers.
They then gathered grass and burned it at the roadside,
fearing its lingering poison,
before proceeding."
The following year,
Yáng was executed.
Zhū Hànbīn
During the Zhēnmíng era of the Liáng dynasty,
when Zhū Hànbīn first governed Ānlù,
suddenly one day,
as dawn light first appeared,
a large snake was seen southwest of the city.
Its head rested on the great city wall,
its tail dragged into the local earth god temple on the southern bank of the moat.
Its head was as large as a five-dǒu vessel,
its eyes like lightning,
its huge mouth gaping,
gazing upon the city.
Its body was no less than a hundred chi long,
several arm-spans thick,
straddling the rampart for sheep and horses,
and spanning above the moat.
The rest of it still coiled within the temple walls.
A city guard on night duty,
suddenly encountering it,
let out a great shout,
lost his soul and died.
The entire prefecture was alarmed and fearful,
not knowing the reason.
The following year,
Huái bandits arrived unexpectedly,
besieged the city and attacked,
but after several days failed to capture it and retreated.
Was this perhaps a forewarning from the deities?
Niú Cúnjié
Liáng Niú Cúnjié was stationed in Yùnzhōu,
and he built a grand mansion at the southwest corner of the inner city.
While constructing the earthen walls and digging the ground,
they discovered a snake den,
with countless snakes of all sizes.
Cúnjié ordered them killed,
and they were transported to the wilderness,
requiring over ten cartloads to remove them all.
At the time, someone said:
"This is a snake lair."
That year,
Cúnjié died from a carbuncle on his back.
Shuǐ Qīng Chí
In Tàiyuán's subordinate county, there is a place called Shuǐ Qīng Chí,
which was used by the prefecture for praying for rain and performing dragon-offering rituals.
At the end of Hòu Táng Zhuāngzōng's reign,
when crossing the Hé River to the south,
he arrived at the commandery,
went hunting,
and set up tents by the pool,
using it as a resting place.
Suddenly, several giant snakes emerged from a cave,
all entering the pool.
After a long while,
one snake, red and white in color,
could be seen from a distance, measuring about four feet in girth,
with length to match.
The hunters all drew their crossbows and fired continuously,
shooting it dead.
Flames appeared on the four mountains.
The fish and turtles in the pool all died,
floating on the water.
The hunters butchered and ate them,
and the meat was very delicious.
Zhuāngzōng soon learned of this,
and at the time, flatterers
considered it an omen of conquering Liáng,
but a Wǔtái monk said:
"Our king should quickly cross the river and engage in decisive battle;
as for the future of the Liáng dynasty,
how can it last long?"
This is also similar to the story of cutting the white snake.
Wáng Sītóng
During the reign of Hòu Táng's Shàodì,
when the Prince of Qīngtài rose in Qíyáng,
the court ordered the Western Capital's garrison commander Wáng Sītóng to lead the imperial army to suppress him.
After the royal army marched west,
news of the encampment soon arrived,
and officials in Yōngjīng daily ascended the western tower,
hoping for news of victory.
Suddenly one day,
as officials leaned against the railing facing west,
they saw two large snakes on the sheep-and-horse city wall,
facing each other east and west,
and attendants from afar threw pellets to scare them.
At that moment, one person hit the eastern snake's head,
and it writhed and fell below the wall,
lying stiff and motionless.
Someone was sent to look,
and it was already dead.
The western snake slowly retreated into its nest.
Those with insight secretly discussed it, saying:
"The Prince of Lù was born in the yǐsì year,
and Commander Wáng was also born in the yǐsì year,
both having the snake as their zodiac sign.
Now the eastern snake was hit in the head and died,
is this not an ill omen for the royal army?"
Not ten days later,
the generals rebelled and defected to the Prince of Lù,
and Sītóng's trusted generals, starting with Wáng Yànhuī,
all surrendered to the city of Qí.
Sītóng fled alone on horseback,
and ultimately perished in service to the king.
The omen of the snake's death,
could it not be clear?
Xú Tǎn
At the end of the Qīngtài era,
there was a man named Xú Tǎn who took the imperial examination,
failed,
traveled south to Zhǔgōng,
and then went to Xiázhōu,
seeking old friends,
and lodged at the foot of Fùduī Mountain.
There was an old inn,
and that night, after resting with his qin and books,
he suddenly saw a woodcutter with a gaunt appearance,
who seemed to have a sorrowful expression.
Tǎn then asked him the reason,
and the woodcutter, with tearful eyes, replied:
"I am a resident of this mountain,
named Lǐ Gūzhú.
My wife had long suffered from a chronic illness,
which did not heal for years.
Yesterday, I went into the mountain to gather wood,
and after two nights had not returned,
my wife's body suddenly changed.
Fearing it would startle people,
she said to a neighboring old woman:
'My body has already transformed,
please inform my husband.'
When I returned, she told me:
'I can no longer endure,
only my corpse remains,
please ask the neighbors to carry me,
and place me at the mountain pass as a favor.'
As she said,
they moved her there.
Shortly after,
they suddenly heard what sounded like a great storm,
and everyone was frightened.
She also said:
'When the time comes, return quickly,
and be careful not to look back.'
Then she expressed the sorrow of parting.
Soon they saw in the mountains,
countless large snakes,
all gathering around his wife.
His wife then got out of bed,
stretched and then curled,
transformed into a python,
and joined the snakes as they left.
Then on a large rock, she dashed her head,
shattering it on the ground."
To this day, there are still descendants of the snake clan named Lǐ there.
Zhāng Shì
During the Wáng Shǔ period,
the wife of Dù the judge, named Zhāng Shì,
was from a scholarly family.
She lived with Dù for several decades,
gave birth to a son,
and died after passing sixty.
After being encoffined at home,
several weeks later,
when she was to be buried outside,
at the moment of opening the coffin,
they felt the coffin shaking,
thinking she had revived.
They opened it to look,
and saw she had transformed into a large snake,
coiled and winding,
with flesh and bones scattering,
and shortly after,
it slowly went into the forest and disappeared.
Also, a nun named Wáng Sāngū from Jìngmíng Temple in Xīngyuán,
also transformed into a large snake in her coffin.
As for Dù's wife,
in her later years, she did not respect her husband,
who was old, ill, with failing sight, hearing, and unable to walk steadily,
and Zhāng Shì treated him like a dog or pig,
and he died from cold and hunger.
People believed transforming into a snake was the retribution.
Gù Suì
The court official Gù Suì once privately recounted
that his ancestor once served as magistrate of Gōng'ān,
and after his term ended,
he temporarily resided by the Jīng River bank near the county.
The area was surrounded by many trees and reeds,
and one moonlit night when he had not yet slept,
he slowly stepped outside,
and saw a long object,
as thick as a rafter,
lying on the ground.
Thinking it was a door bolt,
he lifted his foot to kick it,
and the object rose with his kick,
winding around him from chest and back down to below the waist,
coiling dozens of times,
and he fell to the ground,
unconscious and unaware.
His family wondered why he had not returned late at night,
and sent someone to look,
seeing something gleaming brightly around his waist.
It was writhing on the ground.
Approaching to look,
they saw a large snake coiled around him,
and it could not be untangled.
So they took a sharp blade and cut the snake,
placing it on the ground in segments,
but it remained coiled and did not straighten,
and the constriction caused suffocation,
leading to loss of speech,
and he died within ten days.
Qútáng Gorge
Someone was traveling through the Qútáng Gorge,
during the winter months,
when the plants and trees were withered and dry.
A wildfire swept across the peaks and ridges,
stretching over mountains and spanning valleys,
its red flames illuminating the sky.
Suddenly, from between the cliffs and crags,
came a sound like a massive rock collapsing and falling,
a crashing, rumbling noise.
He stopped and waited,
and saw an object as round as a large granary,
rolling down to level ground.
He had no idea what it could be.
Upon closer inspection,
it turned out to be a snake.
He then cut it open to examine it,
and found that the snake had swallowed a deer,
which was still inside its belly.
The wildfire had burned fiercely,
causing it to fall down the mountain.
This is what is meant by the saying, "The Bā snake swallows an elephant"—
it is indeed credible.
Old Jìn
In the long valley northwest of Fēnglóng Mountain in Jǐngxíng County, Héngzhōu,
there was a venomous snake occupying the area,
capable of harming people,
so none of the villagers dared to go there.
A herb gatherer named Jìn Sìwēng entered the northern mountains,
when suddenly he heard the sound of wind and rain.
He climbed onto a solitary rock to look,
and saw a white snake, about thirty feet long,
coming from the east.
It quickly climbed a tree,
coiled itself on a southwest-facing branch,
and hung its head to rest.
After a short while,
a creature about the size of a plate,
resembling a toad,
with a color like smoke-stained,
brown earth,
and four legs, came hopping along.
It reached the tree where the snake was coiled,
looked up,
and the snake hung its head and died.
From then on, the snake demon ceased its activities.
Previously, in Lǐzhōu, there was a young cuckoo
that was swallowed by a snake.
A creature resembling a toad
spat out a white vapor directly at it,
causing it to fall and die.
Could this not be the same creature that Old Jìn saw?
All venomous creatures must have something that can subdue them—
this is likely the will of Heaven.
Jǐng Huàn
Jǐng Huàn served as the magistrate of Báishí County in Bìzhōu.
While traveling and ascending the Bā Ridge,
which was perilously steep and thousands of feet high,
after about seven or eight stages of the journey,
he reached the Jade Maiden Temple.
There, a giant serpent lay across the path ahead,
with a diameter of about seven or eight feet,
its scales no smaller than an open fan,
its head and tail hanging down the mountainside.
Only the sound of snapping trees could be heard,
echoing through the mountain valleys.
The servants and attendants trembled with fear,
unable to proceed.
So they stayed overnight in a mountain cave,
and from a high vantage point,
they finally saw its tail by the end of the day.
They thought it might be a dragon,
but a dragon's movements
are always accompanied by wind and rain.
That day was clear and bright,
so they realized it was a snake.
Thus, they understood that fish large enough to swallow boats,
birds vast enough to obscure the sky,
and creatures of extraordinary size among insects and birds
truly exist.
A Person from Shūzhōu
A person from Shūzhōu entered
Qián Mountain,
saw a large snake,
and killed it.
Upon inspection, it had legs,
which he found very strange,
so he carried it out.
He intended to show it to others,
and on the road, he encountered several county officials.
He told them:
"I killed this snake, and it has four legs."
The officials could not see it,
and said:
"Where is it?"
He replied:
"Right in front of you,
why can't you see it?"
He then threw the snake on the ground,
and they finally saw it.
But then, the person carrying the snake became invisible,
which people found bizarre,
so they abandoned the snake.
It seems this snake could not hide its own form while alive,
but after death, it could hide the form of a person.
This principle is unfathomable.
Jiǎ Tán
Jiǎ Tán, Minister of War of the false Wú regime,
said that someone he knew, serving as the military governor of Lǐngnán,
obtained an orange,
as large as a liter measure.
He intended to present it to the emperor,
but the supervising eunuch considered it an extraordinary object
and advised against presenting it lightly.
So he took a needle and pricked it slightly under the stem,
whereupon it wriggled and moved.
He ordered it to be cut open,
and inside was a small red snake several inches long.
Yáo Jǐng
Yáo Jǐng, military governor of Shòuzhōu under the false Wú regime,
in his childhood,
served Liú Jīn, the military governor of Háozhōu,
working in the stables.
Liú Jīn once walked to the stables,
and saw Yáo Jǐng sleeping,
with two small red snakes playing on his face,
going in and out of his nostrils.
After a long while, Yáo Jǐng woke up,
and the snakes disappeared.
From then on, Liú Jīn rapidly promoted and favored him,
marrying his daughter to him,
and Yáo Jǐng eventually rose to high office.
Wáng Rěn
Wáng Rěn, military governor of Shòuzhōu under the false Wú regime,
returned to Yángdū after leaving his post,
and served as a commanding general.
While sitting in the official hall,
talking with guests,
suddenly a small red snake fell from the roof to the ground,
and coiled toward Wáng Rěn.
Wáng Rěn ordered it to be covered with a vessel,
and after a long while, when they lifted the cover to look,
only a bat flew away.
That year,
Wáng Rěn was promoted to the rank of Píngzhāng Shì.
A Person from Ānlù
A person from Ānlù surnamed Máo
was skilled at eating venomous snakes,
swallowing them with wine.
He once traveled to Qí'ān,
and then went to Yùzhāng.
He often performed with snakes in the market,
making a living by begging.
After more than ten years,
a firewood seller
came from Póyáng,
and stayed overnight at the foot of Huángbèi Mountain.
He dreamed of an old man who said:
"Deliver a snake for me to the snake-handler Máo Shēng in Jiāngxī."
When he reached Guānbù Gate in Yùzhāng, his firewood nearly sold out,
and he found a pale white snake
coiled in his boat,
motionless when touched.
The firewood seller then remembered his earlier dream,
so he took it to the market,
searched for Máo Shēng,
and gave it to him.
As Máo was about to handle it,
the snake bit his breast in response,
and Máo cried out and fell to the ground,
dying shortly after.
After some time, the body decayed,
and the snake was nowhere to be found.
Zhāntú Country
During the Zhōu dynasty,
the state of Zhāntú presented a phoenix chick,
which was transported in a carriage adorned with jasper flowers,
decorated with five-colored jade,
and drawn by a red elephant.
Upon reaching the capital,
it was raised in the Garden of Divine Birds,
fed with jade nectar,
and nourished with yúnshí.
Both of these items are recorded in the "Shàngyuán Jīngfāng."
When the phoenix first arrived,
its feathers had not yet fully displayed their splendor.
By the time King Chéng performed the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài
and the shàn sacrifice at Shèshǒu,
its patterns and colors had become radiant and dazzling.
All the flying and running creatures of the Central Plains
ceased their clamor and cries,
submitting in awe to the arrival of this divine bird from afar.
When King Chéng passed away,
the phoenix soared into the sky and departed.
Fènghuáng Tái
The bones of the phoenix are black,
and the male and female cry differently in the morning and evening.
The emperor ordered Líng Lún to create twelve yuè pipes to imitate their calls,
one for the male's voice,
and one for the female's sound.
This gave rise to the music piece "Fènghuáng Tái."
Beneath the feet of this phoenix are objects resembling white stones.
When the phoenix occasionally descends,
if one waits for the spot where it alights
and digs three chǐ deep,
a round stone resembling an egg
and pure white in color can be found.
Ingesting it calms the mind and spirit.
Yuán Tíngjiān
Yuán Tíngjiān, a scholar of the Táng Imperial Academy and a friend of Prince Chén,
once resigned from his post as military advisor in Suìzhōu
and retired to the mountains within the prefecture to study.
Suddenly, a being with a human body and a bird's head
came to visit Tíngjiān.
Its attire and cap were magnificent,
and it was followed by thousands of birds.
It spoke, saying:
"I am the king of all birds.
Having heard of your fondness for music,
I have come to meet you."
It then stayed for several nights,
teaching Tíngjiān the subtleties of musical tones,
the sounds and meanings of written characters,
and even the languages of a hundred birds.
It visited in this manner for over a year.
As a result, Tíngjiān became proficient in music,
excelling in written language,
surpassing all others of his time.
He also mastered yīn-yang arts and numerology,
leaving no subject unexplored.
While serving in the Imperial Academy,
he compiled the ten-volume "Yùnyīng,"
but before it could be disseminated,
the Western Capital fell to the Hú forces,
and Tíngjiān also passed away.
Suīyáng Phoenix
In the autumn of the fourteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
an unusual bird,
blue in color
and resembling a turtledove or magpie,
soared over the outskirts of Suīyáng
and alighted in a thicket.
Thousands of birds of various kinds
gathered their flocks
and arrayed themselves to its left, right, front, and back.
Moreover, morning and evening, each brought insects and grains to offer it.
Whenever this bird flew,
all the birds would clamor and lead the way before it,
flank it on both sides,
and crowd behind it,
as if performing escort and guard duties.
When it rested, they would encircle it, facing inward.
Even the rituals of ministers attending the Son of Heaven
could not surpass this.
The people of Suīyáng all flocked to the countryside to witness the spectacle,
believing it to be a spiritual being among feathered creatures.
Yet its appearance did not resemble that of a luán or phoenix,
making it all the more extraordinary.
At the time, Lǐ Áo was a guest in Suīyáng.
Áo declared:
"This is a true phoenix."
He then composed a chapter titled "Zhī Fèng,"
recording the event in detail.
Luán
During Yáo's seventh year of reign,
luán and hú birds came to gather year after year,
qílín roamed the marshes and lakes,
while owls fled to the remote deserts.
The state of Zhézhī
presented the Chóngmíng bird,
also known as the "double-pupiled" bird.
It was said to have double pupils in each eye,
resembled a chicken in appearance,
and cried like a phoenix.
Occasionally, it shed its feathers
and flew using its fleshy wings.
It could fight and drive away fierce tigers,
preventing evil disasters from causing harm.
It was fed with jade paste.
Sometimes it came several times a year,
other times it did not come for years.
The people of the state would sweep and clean their doorways,
hoping to welcome the Chóngmíng bird's visit.
Some carved wood,
others cast metal,
to create likenesses of this bird
and place them between their doors and windows.
Then, evil spirits and monstrous beings
would naturally retreat and submit.
To this day, on the first day of each year,
people carve or paint chickens on their doors and windows—
this is a surviving tradition of that image.
Crane Xú Shì
During the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái of Jìn,
Xú Shì was out inspecting the fields
when he saw a woman
of radiant and fair complexion,
who approached him with flirtatious words.
The woman then chanted:
"Long have I listened for your pleasing voice,
day and night, my heart waited in anticipation.
How fortunate to meet this fine man,
yet my innermost feelings remain distant and unsettled."
Shì, captivated by her,
happily invited her to a cottage.
The woman prepared food and drink, mostly fish,
and Shì did not return for days.
His brothers went searching for him
and found him by the lakeside,
sitting opposite the woman.
One brother struck the woman with a rattan staff,
whereupon she transformed into a white crane
and soared high into the sky.
Shì remained in a daze for over a year before recovering.
The Feather Gatherer of Wúchéng
In the third year of the Dàyè era of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
when imperial feather regalia were first being made,
most of the feather cloaks came from Jiāngnán,
depleting the supply almost entirely.
At that time, a man from Wúchéng County, Húzhōu,
covered in coarse hair, entered the mountains to gather feathers.
He saw a great tree a hundred chǐ tall,
with a crane's nest atop it, nurturing its young.
The man wanted to take the chicks,
but there were no branches below,
and it was too high to climb.
So he took an axe to fell the tree.
The crane, knowing the man intended to take its young
and fearing they would be killed,
used its beak to pluck its own feathers and drop them down.
The man gathered them
and found them perfectly suitable for the task at hand.
Thus, he spared the tree.
The Wife of the Ministry of Revenue Clerk
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the wife of a Bureau of Revenue clerk was beautiful,
but had fallen ill due to a demonic possession,
though no one knew it.
The family owned a fine horse,
which was always fed double the usual fodder,
yet grew increasingly emaciated and weak.
He asked his neighbor, a foreigner, about this,
who was also a sorcerer.
The foreigner laughed and said:
"A horse grows weary traveling a hundred lǐ,
yet now it travels over a thousand lǐ instead,
how could it not grow thin?"
The clerk said:
"It never goes out,
and there is no one else in the household,
how could this happen?"
The foreigner said:
"Whenever you are on night duty,
your wife goes out at night,
and you simply do not know it.
If you do not believe me,
the next time you are on duty,
try returning to observe,
and you will surely know."
The clerk followed his advice,
returned at night,
and hid in another place.
At the first watch,
his wife rose and adorned herself,
ordered the maid to saddle the horse,
and mounted it at the steps.
The maid rode a broom behind her,
and they rose gently into the air,
disappearing from sight.
The clerk was greatly alarmed,
and the next day went to see the foreigner,
saying in fear:
"The demonic possession is indeed true,
what should I do about it?"
The foreigner told him to wait and observe again the following night.
That night,
the clerk returned and hid behind a curtain in the hall,
but his wife soon returned,
asking the maid why there was a human scent,
and ordered the maid,
to use the broom
as a torch,
lighting up the entire hall and corridors,
forcing the clerk to scramble into a large jar in the hall.
After a short while,
they mounted the horse and left again,
but since the broom had already been burned,
there was nothing else to ride,
so the wife said:
"Ride whatever is available,
why must it be a broom?"
In a hurry,
the maid rode the large jar and followed.
The clerk inside the jar,
was too afraid to move.
After a short while,
they arrived at a place,
which was atop a mountain in a forest,
where tents and curtains were set up,
and a lavish feast was prepared.
There were seven or eight people drinking together,
each with a partner,
feasting and drinking at their seats,
being intimate and affectionate to the fullest,
and they did not disperse until several watches later.
The women mounted their horses,
and the wife ordered the maid to ride the jar,
but the maid exclaimed in alarm:
"There is someone inside the jar."
The wife, drunk,
ordered him pushed down the mountain,
and the maid, also drunk,
pushed the clerk out,
who dared not speak,
and then rode the jar away.
By dawn,
the clerk saw no one around,
only the remaining ashes and embers,
so he searched for a path,
and after traversing dozens of lǐ of rugged terrain, finally reached the mountain pass.
He asked about the location,
and was told it was Làngzhōu,
over a thousand lǐ from the capital.
Begging his way with great hardship,
after more than a month,
he barely managed to return home.
His wife, surprised, asked where he had been for so long,
and where he had come from,
but the clerk answered with an excuse.
He went again to ask the foreigner,
seeking his help to deal with the matter,
and the foreigner said:
"The demon has fully taken form,
wait for her to leave again,
then quickly capture and bind her,
and burn her with fire."
They heard a voice in the air begging for mercy,
and after a short while,
a gray crane fell into the fire,
burned to death,
and his wife's illness was thus cured.
Péi Hàng
Tóngzhōu Sīmǎ Péi Hàng once recounted that
his second cousin once removed was traveling from Luòzhōng
to Zhèngzhōu.
After several days on the road,
he dismounted early one morning during his journey
and heard the sound of groaning from the left side of the path.
He parted the thickets to search
and found a sick crane beneath the brambles,
its wings drooping and beak lowered,
with festering sores under its wings, devoid of feathers.
He was startled by the sound,
when suddenly an old man in white clothes, dragging a staff,
arrived within a few dozen paces
and said to him:
"Young master,
do you understand how to pity this crane?
If it could be smeared with human blood,
it would be able to fly again."
Péi was quite knowledgeable in the Way,
and his nature was lofty and detached.
He promptly replied:
"I am willing to draw blood from my arm;
it is no difficulty."
The old man laughed and said:
"Your resolve is strong indeed,
but the blood must come from a person who has been human for three lifetimes
to be effective.
You, young master, were not human in your previous life.
Only Hú Lúshēng in Luòzhōng
has been human for three lifetimes.
Your journey this time,
unless it is urgent,
how could you go to Luòzhōng
to seek out Hú Lúshēng?"
Péi joyfully turned back,
and before two nights had passed,
he reached Luòzhōng,
where he sought out Hú Lúshēng,
fully recounting the matter
and bowing in supplication.
Hú Lúshēng showed no sign of difficulty or ease.
He opened a bundle,
took out a stone box
about the size of two fingers,
pricked his arm with a needle,
and let the blood drip until the box was full.
He handed it to Péi and said:
"Say no more."
When Péi returned to the crane's location,
the old man was already there.
He said happily:
"You are indeed a man of your word."
He then instructed Péi to smear all of it on the crane.
He also invited Péi, saying:
"My dwelling is not far from here;
you may stay a while."
Péi sensed he was no ordinary person
and addressed him as "elder."
He then followed him.
After only a few li,
they came to a manor
with bamboo fences and thatched huts,
the courtyard overgrown and in disarray.
Péi was very thirsty
and asked for something to drink.
The old man pointed to an earthen niche:
"There is a little drink inside;
you may go and take it."
Péi looked inside the niche
and saw an apricot kernel
and a fan like a bamboo hat,
filled with a liquid
that was pure white in color.
He lifted it with effort and drank,
and was no longer hungry or thirsty.
The taste was like apricot curd.
Péi realized he was a recluse
and bowed, requesting to become his servant.
The old man said:
"You have worldly fortune and rank;
even if you stayed, you would not fulfill your ambition.
Your esteemed uncle has truly attained something;
I have long associated with him,
though you yourself are unaware.
Now I have a message
that you must deliver for me."
He then wrapped an object in a bundle,
about the size of a box,
and warned him not to open it secretly.
He then led Péi to see the crane again.
The crane's injured spots had already grown feathers.
He also said to Péi:
"Having drunk the apricot liquid,
you will mourn the affections of your nine clans,
and moreover, be warned against wine and lust."
Péi returned to Luòzhōng.
On the way, he examined what he was carrying
and was about to open it
when red snakes poked their heads out from each of the four corners of the bundle.
Péi then stopped.
When his uncle received the message,
he opened it immediately.
Inside was something like dried barley rice, more than a shēng in volume.
His uncle later traveled to Wángwū
and his end is unknown.
Péi lived to be ninety-seven.
Also,
Chancellor Lǐ,
while traveling on Sōngshān,
saw a sick crane
that also said it needed human blood.
Chancellor Lǐ
removed his robe and immediately pricked his blood.
The crane said:
"There are very few true humans in the world;
you are not one."
It then instructed him to pluck an eyelash
and take it to the Eastern Capital,
saying that if he looked through it,
he would know.
Chancellor Lǐ looked at himself midway
and saw a horse's head.
When he reached the Eastern Luò,
he encountered many people,
but none were fully human—
all were dogs, pigs, donkeys, or horses.
Only one old man was human.
Chancellor Lǐ explained the sick crane's intent,
and the old man laughed,
dismounted from his donkey, bared his arm, and pricked his blood.
Chancellor Lǐ obtained it
and smeared it on the crane.
It recovered immediately,
and the crane thanked him, saying:
"You will become a chancellor in an enlightened era,
and moreover, you will ascend to immortality.
Our meeting again is not far off;
be diligent and do not slacken."
Chancellor Lǐ thanked it,
and the crane then soared into the sky and departed.
Cranes
become red after a hundred years,
yellow after five hundred years,
then blue-green after another five hundred years,
and white after yet another five hundred years,
living for three thousand years.
Sū Qióng
During the Yuánxīng era of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
there was a man just over twenty years old
who was not yet married,
yet his eyes did not covet beauty,
and he had never engaged in lewd behavior.
Once, while walking in the fields,
he saw a very beautiful woman
who said to the young man:
"I have heard that you consider yourself a man of integrity like Liǔ Xiàhuì;
do you also indulge in secret liaisons?"
The woman then sang.
The young man showed slight signs of being moved.
Later, he saw her again,
and the young man asked her name.
She replied:
"My surname is Sū, given name Qióng,
and my home is along the way."
He then invited her back and they enjoyed themselves fully.
Suddenly, his younger cousin burst in
and struck the woman with a staff,
whereupon she transformed into a female white crane.
Parrots can fly;
most birds have toes
arranged three in front and one behind,
but only parrots have four toes evenly divided.
In most birds, the lower eyelid moves upward,
but this bird alone moves both eyelids,
resembling human eyes.
Zhāng Huà
Zhāng Huà had a white parrot.
When Huà went out and returned,
the bird would report on the good and bad behavior of the servants.
Later, it fell silent and said nothing.
Huà asked the reason,
and the bird said:
"I have been hidden in a jar,
how could I know anything?"
When the master was away,
he ordered the parrot to be summoned.
The parrot said:
"Last night I had a bad dream,
it is not suitable for me to go out."
They forced it to come to the courtyard,
where it was seized by a hawk.
It was taught to peck at the hawk's beak,
and barely managed to escape.
The Parrot Putting Out a Fire
A parrot flew and perched on another mountain,
where the birds and beasts of the mountain all treated it with great respect.
The parrot thought to itself,
although this is pleasant, it cannot last long,
and so it left.
A few days later,
a great fire broke out on the mountain.
Seeing it from afar,
the parrot dipped its feathers in water,
flew over, and sprinkled it.
A heavenly deity said:
"Although you have the will,
your effort is negligible.
What is there to speak of?"
It replied:
"Although I know it is of no use,
I once lived as a guest on this mountain.
The neighboring beasts acted kindly,
all were like brothers to me,
I cannot bear to see it."
The heavenly deity was moved and praised it,
and immediately extinguished the fire.
Xuěyīnǚ
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐngnán presented a white parrot,
which was kept in the palace.
After many years,
it became quite intelligent and perceptive,
thoroughly understanding speech.
The Emperor and the Guìfēi
both called it Xuěyīnǚ (Snowy Maiden).
Its nature was tame and docile;
it was often allowed to drink, peck, fly, and sing freely,
yet it never strayed beyond the screens and curtains.
The Emperor ordered that poems by recent literary officials be taught to it,
and after a few repetitions, it could recite them.
Whenever the Emperor played board games with his consorts and princes,
if the Emperor began to lose,
the attendants would call for Xuěyīnǚ,
and it would surely fly onto the game board,
flapping its wings to disrupt the game.
Sometimes it would peck the hands of the consorts and princes,
preventing them from making moves.
One day,
it flew onto the Guìfēi's dressing table
and said:
"Xuěyīnǚ dreamed last night of being seized by a bird of prey;
will my life end here?"
The Emperor ordered the Guìfēi to teach it the "Heart Sutra",
and from then on, it memorized it diligently and thoroughly,
reciting it day and night without rest,
as if fearing disaster,
like one praying for deliverance.
When the Emperor and the Guìfēi went to a separate palace for an excursion,
the Guìfēi placed the parrot on her palanquin
and went together with it.
Upon arrival,
the Emperor ordered the accompanying officials to conduct a hunt in front.
The parrot was playing on the palace railings
when suddenly a hawk appeared,
seized it, and killed it.
The Emperor and the Guìfēi
sighed for a long time,
then ordered it buried in the garden,
erecting a parrot mound.
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a five-colored parrot in the palace,
able to speak and very clever.
When the Emperor ordered attendants to try pulling his royal robe,
it would glare and scold them.
Xióng Yánjǐng, an official of the Qí Prince's literary staff,
presented a "Parrot Ode",
which the Emperor showed to all his ministers.
Liú Qián's Daughter
A commoner named Liú Qián in Lǒngyòu was very wealthy,
but had only one daughter,
just of hair-pinning age,
beautiful in appearance.
Successive suitors came seeking her hand,
but her father did not consent.
The family kept a parrot,
unparalleled in its ability to speak,
and this girl talked with it daily.
Later, she obtained a volume of Buddhist sutras,
and the parrot would recite them.
If there were any mistakes,
the girl would certainly correct it.
Every time it recited this sutra,
the girl would burn incense.
Suddenly one day,
the parrot said to the girl:
"Open my cage,
you stay inside it,
I shall fly away."
The girl, surprised, asked it:
"Why do you say this?"
The parrot said:
"You and I are originally of the same kind.
By chance, you were born into Liú Qián's family.
Now you must return to your original clan;
do not find my words strange.
Others do not recognize you,
but I certainly recognize you."
The girl was alarmed
and told her parents.
Her parents then opened the cage
and released the parrot to fly away,
keeping watch over their daughter day and night.
Three days later,
the girl died without cause.
Her parents wept in shock without end.
Just as they were about to bury her,
her corpse suddenly turned into a white parrot and flew away,
no one knew where.
Hawk of King Wén of Chǔ
King Wén of Chǔ was fond of hunting.
Someone presented him with a hawk.
The king saw it was extraordinary,
so he went hunting at Yúnmèng.
Furred and feathered creatures
fought and bit each other,
but this hawk stared intently,
gazing far into the clouds.
Suddenly there appeared a bright white object,
its form indistinguishable.
The hawk then raised its feathers and soared,
shooting up like a flying bolt of lightning.
In a moment,
feathers fell like snow,
blood rained down like rain,
and a great bird fell to the ground.
Measuring its wingspan,
it was several tens of lǐ wide.
A knowledgeable gentleman of the time said:
"This is a young great roc."
Liú Yù
During the Yǒnghuī era of the Táng,
a man from Láizhōu named Liú Yù was very fond of hawks.
He went to the cliffs of Zhīfú Mountain
and lowered himself by rope to fetch hawk chicks.
Just as he was about to reach the nest, the rope broke,
and he fell onto a tree branch.
Above and below were sheer cliffs,
with no way to advance or retreat.
The parent hawk saw the man
and, carrying meat, dared not go to the nest.
It dropped the meat from afar.
Yù caught the meat and fed the hawk chicks,
eating the leftovers himself.
After fifty or sixty days,
the chicks could fly.
He then tore his clothes to tie to the hawks' feet,
tying three loops on each arm.
He passed his body through them and descended.
The hawks flew,
pulling his two arms.
By the time he reached the bottom of the ravine,
he was completely unharmed.
He then tied up the hawks and returned.
A man from Yèjùn
When Xuē Sōng was governing Wèi,
there was a man in Yèjùn who enjoyed raising hawks and falcons.
One day,
someone brought a hawk to offer to the man of Yè,
and the man bought it.
This hawk was exceptionally divine and handsome;
the man of Yè had raised many hawks and falcons at home,
but none could compare to it.
He often carried it on his arm for amusement,
never letting it leave his hand.
Later, an Eastern Barbarian saw it
and offered over a hundred bolts of silk as payment,
saying:
"I have been thinking of this,
but do not know its use."
The man said:
"This is a sea eagle,
excellent at warding off the calamity of flood dragons and hornless dragons.
You should release it south of Yè city,
and you will see its use."
Previously, flood dragons in the pond south of Yè city had often been a calamity for people,
and the people of the commandery had suffered from it for years.
The man of Yè then took it there,
and the sea eagle suddenly plunged into the water of the pond.
After a while, it emerged,
having caught a small flood dragon.
Once out,
it ate it almost entirely.
From then on, the people of Yè were spared this calamity.
Someone reported this to Xuē Sōng,
who then ordered the man of Yè to be questioned about the matter.
The man of Yè then offered the sea eagle to him.
Eagle of Wèi Gōngzǐ
Wèi Gōngzǐ Wújì was once in his chamber
while reading,
when a turtledove flew under his desk,
and an eagle chased and killed it.
Wújì was angered by its fierce cruelty,
He thus ordered the capture of eagles throughout the state,
and over two hundred were caught.
Wújì approached the cage with his sword and said:
"The one that killed
the turtledove yesterday
should bow its head and admit guilt;
those that did not
may flap their wings."
One eagle lowered its head and remained motionless.
Falcon of Bǎoguàn Temple
At Bǎoguàn Temple in Dōngguāng County, Cāngzhōu,
there were often gray falcons gathering on the multi-storied pavilion,
along with several thousand pigeons.
In winter, each evening,
the falcon would take a pigeon to warm its feet,
and by dawn,
it would release it without killing it.
Other eagles and falcons
did not dare to invade.
Luòyàn Hall
Emperor Táng Tàizōng kept a white falcon,
named General,
which would catch birds
by driving them to the front of the hall,
then strike and kill them,
hence the hall was named Luòyàn Hall.
The emperor often had it deliver letters,
from the capital to Luòyáng for Prince Wèi,
and also fetch replies,
making several round trips a day.
Was it not akin to Lù Jī's Huáng'ěr?
Jiāozhǐ
Many people in Jiāozhǐ Commandery raise peacocks,
some giving them as gifts for food,
or killing them to make dried meat.
People also raise their chicks as decoys,
setting up nets nearby,
to catch wild peacocks.
When they see one flying down,
they pull the net to cover it sideways,
pluck its golden-green feathers,
and adorn them as fans or dusters.
Some take the whole bird,
cutting off its tail while alive,
to use as local tribute.
It is said
that if taken alive, the golden-green color does not fade.
Luózhōu
In the mountains of Luózhōu, there are many peacocks,
flying in flocks of several tens as pairs.
Females have short tails,
without golden-green feathers.
Males at three years old
have small tails,
and by five years, they grow large tails.
They begin to grow in early spring,
and after the third or fourth month, they shed again,
flourishing and fading along with the flowers.
However, they are very fond of their tails and quite jealous.
Whenever they wish to roost in the mountains,
they must first choose a place to place their tails,
then settle there.
Southerners who capture them alive
wait for heavy rain,
then go to seize them.
Their tails become wet and heavy,
unable to soar high,
and even if people approach,
they love their tails so much,
fearing they might be injured,
that they no longer fly away.
Even if tamed for quite some time,
upon seeing beautiful women in fine clothes or children in silk garments,
they will chase and peck them.
In fragrant times and charming scenes,
upon hearing pipes, strings, reed instruments, and songs,
they will spread their wings and tails,
gaze about and dance,
as if with intent.
Mountain valley barbarians cook and eat them,
their taste like goose,
and they counteract a hundred poisons.
If people eat their meat,
drinking medicine will not cure illness.
Their blood and heads
counteract great poisons.
Southerners obtain their eggs,
having chickens incubate them, and they hatch.
Their feet are slightly curved,
and their call sounds like "dūhù."
Locals who take their tails
hold knives in hidden places among dense bamboo to conceal themselves,
waiting for them to pass,
then swiftly cut off their tails.
If not cut immediately,
upon looking back once,
the golden-green color loses its luster.
Wáng Xuān
Lú Zhào lived in Jīnghǎi,
and saw Attendant Wáng Xuān had a peacock.
One day, a servant came to report:
"A snake has coiled around the peacock,
and it will soon be poisoned to death."
Wáng Xuān ordered it to be rescued,
but his attendant laughed and did not rescue it.
Wáng Xuān was angry,
and the attendant said:
"The snake and the peacock are mating."
Hàn Swallow
Those that gather mud to build nests,
with slightly smaller calls, are Hàn swallows.
Táo Shènglì annotated the Běncǎo, stating
that those with purple chests, light and small, are Yuè swallows,
while those with mottled black chests and loud calls are Hú swallows.
They prefer to build long nests,
and Yuè swallows are not used in medicine.
Yuè and Hàn
also have slight differences.
Hú Swallow
Whenever there are things like fox white or marten fur,
swallows seeing them will shed their feathers,
or swallows may hibernate underwater.
An old saying goes: if swallows do not enter the house,
take paulownia wood and carve male and female figures,
throw them into a well,
and swallows will surely come.
Those with mottled black chests and loud calls,
named Hú swallows,
have nests that can hold a bolt of plain silk.
Thousand-Year Swallow
Between Qí and Lǔ,
swallows are called yǐ,
and they build nests avoiding the days of wù and jǐ.
The Xuánzhōng Jì states
that thousand-year swallows have their nest entrances facing north.
The Shùyì Yào states
that five-hundred-year swallows grow barbarian beards.
Jìn Omen
In the year when the Wei dynasty yielded to the Jin,
a white light resembling the shape of birds and sparrows appeared below the northern palace gate,
sometimes flying about and coming and going.
The officials immediately reported it,
and the emperor ordered hunters to set nets,
capturing a white swallow.
Considering it a divine creature,
they made a golden cage
and placed it within the palace.
After ten days, it was nowhere to be found.
Commentators said:
"It is an auspicious sign of the virtue of metal."
In the time of Shī Kuàng,
white swallows came to nest,
and upon examining the charts of auspicious responses,
it indeed matched the discussion.
Shī Kuàng
was a man of Jin,
and the discussions from ancient to modern times correspond.
Yuán Dàokāng
Yuán Dàokāng of the Later Wei, styled Jǐngyí,
dwelt in the Línlǜ Mountains,
