living in secluded valleys,
quietly secluded in his humble cottage,
not descending to the human world
for over twenty years.
He consumed medicinal herbs and fungi
to delight his spirit.
When Gāo Huān was chancellor,
he summoned him three times, but Dàokāng did not accept.
Dàokāng, because the times were chaotic,
did not wish to respond.
When it came to Gāo Yáng,
he was summoned again,
but still did not rise to the occasion.
In Dàokāng's study, a pair of swallows always nested,
never failing to come year after year.
Dàokāng, because he repeatedly refused summons,
and also,
fearing calamity,
unconsciously sighed in distress.
That evening,
the autumn moon shone brightly,
and a clear breeze rustled forth.
Dàokāng gazed at the moon in quiet contemplation,
when suddenly he heard a swallow call his style name, saying:
"Jǐngyí,
you originally found joy in tranquility;
why now such deep sorrow and thought?"
Dàokāng was astonished,
and then realized it was the swallow.
It spoke again:
"Jǐngyí, Jǐngyí,
find joy for a lifetime."
Dàokāng said:
"You are a bird yet speak;
why do you nest in my house?"
The swallow said:
"I am punished by the Supreme God,
temporarily in bird form.
Because of your abundant virtue,
I have come to rely on you."
Dàokāng said:
"I forget profit,
do not sell myself in the human world,
therefore I shut my door and cultivate the Way,
wishing to prosper my virtue—
is this what you speak of?"
The swallow said:
"Those who dwell in seclusion within the realm
all seek fame and reputation.
Only you understand the Way,
standing aloof from the clamor,
therefore the spirits respect and entrust you,
and myriad numinous beings submit to your virtue."
The swallow said:
"Tomorrow at daytime,
I will meet you at the front stream."
Dàokāng then took his staff to the southern stream,
awaiting their arrival.
When daytime came,
he saw two swallows fly from the northern ridge and descend into the ravine,
one transforming into a youth in black garments,
the other into a maiden in black garments.
They came forward and said to Dàokāng:
"Now we shall return;
because you summoned us,
we came here to transform.
Yet we have nothing to leave as farewell;
you have a hidden ambition,
the dark and unseen admire you,
your lifespan shall be extended by forty years,
this we give in return."
Having spoken,
they again became a pair of swallows and flew away,
to an unknown destination.
At that time, Dàokāng was already forty years old,
and indeed he later lived to eighty-one.
Fàn Zhì
Fàn Zhì, Vice Minister of Revenue of the Han, said
that once swallows nested under his house,
raising several chicks,
and were already feeding them.
The female was seized and eaten by a cat,
the male chirped mournfully,
and after a long while, flew away.
Immediately, it returned with another swallow as its mate,
and fed the chicks as before.
Within a few days,
the chicks fell to the ground one after another,
writhing and stiffening.
Children cut open their bellies to look,
and found caltrop seeds in their crops;
it was likely harmed by the new mate.
Flight Count
The partridge's flight count follows the months;
for example, in the first month,
it flies once and then stops in its nest,
not rising again.
In the twelfth month, it rises twelve times,
and is most difficult to catch;
southerners set nets to capture it.
Flies Southward
The partridge resembles a female pheasant,
and flies only southward,
never northward.
Yáng Fú's *Record of Strange Things in Jiāozhōu* states:
"A bird resembling a female pheasant,
named partridge;
its heart yearns for the south,
with no thought of going north."
Wú-Chǔ Partridge
The partridge
is found everywhere in the lands of Wú and Chǔ.
South of the mountains, this bird is especially numerous.
Its meat is white and tender,
far superior to chicken and pheasant.
It can counteract the poison of wild aconite and mushrooms.
On its breast are white round spots,
and its back is interspersed with purple-red feathers.
It is as large as a wild pheasant,
and often calls in pairs.
*The Records of Nányuè* states:
"Although the partridge flies back and forth east and west,
when it begins to spread its wings,
it must first soar southward.
Its call sounds like 'shè bó zhōu.'"
Also, *Materia Medica* states:
"Its call sounds like 'gōu zhōu gé zhé.'"
Lǐ Qúnyù's poem "Hearing Partridges While Traveling in the Mountains" says:
"Just as I pass through winding, rugged paths,
again I hear the 'gōu zhōu gé zhé' sound."
Magpies Know Tàisuì
Magpies know the location of Tàisuì.
*Records of the Investigation of Things* states:
"Magpie nests face away from Tàisuì."
This is not due to intelligence,
but follows nature.
*Huáinánzǐ* says:
"Magpies know that when the year is windy,
they depart.
Tall trees,
nest on side branches."
Also, when magpies build nests,
they take branches from the treetops,
not those that have fallen to the ground;
moreover, they entwine branches to hold their eggs.
At noon on the Dragon Boat Festival,
burn their nest,
and apply moxibustion to the sick person;
the illness will be cured immediately.
Zhāng Hào
Zhāng Hào of Chángshān served as Chancellor of Liáng.
After a recent rain,
a bird resembling a mountain magpie
gradually descended and fell to the ground.
A commoner picked it up,
and it immediately transformed into a round stone.
Hào broke it open with a hammer,
and obtained a gold seal,
inscribed with the words "Seal of the Marquis of Loyalty and Filial Piety."
Hào reported this to the emperor.
It was stored in the imperial archives.
Hào later rose to the position of Grand Commandant.
Later, Fán Xíngyí, a Court Gentleman for Consultation from Rǔnán, collated texts at the Eastern Library,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"During the times of Yáo and Shùn,
there once existed such an office.
Now that Heaven has bestowed this seal,
it should be reinstated."
The Country of Tiáozhī
In the first year of the Yǒngníng era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
the country of Tiáozhī came to present a rare auspicious sign:
a bird named zhīquè,
standing seven chǐ tall,
that understood human speech.
When that country was at peace,
flocks of zhīquè would soar.
In the past, during the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
when the four barbarian tribes were submissive,
some presented this kind of què,
which was tame and gentle.
When auspicious or joyful events occurred,
it would flap its wings, soar, and sing.
According to Zhuāng Zhōu:
"The què of Diāolíng
are probably of this kind."
Lí Jǐngyì
At the end of the Zhēnguān era of the Táng dynasty,
Lí Jǐngyì of Nánkāng lived near Kōngqīng Mountain.
A magpie often nested beside his dwelling,
and he would regularly feed it.
Later, a neighbor who had lost some cloth
falsely accused Jǐngyì of stealing it,
and he was imprisoned in the Nánkāng jail.
After more than a month,
he still refused to confess under interrogation.
Just as they were about to interrogate him further,
the magpie alighted on the prison tower,
facing Jǐngyì with apparent joy,
as if conveying a message.
That very day, news arrived of an imperial pardon.
The officials questioned how he had learned of it,
and he said:
"I met a man dressed in black with a plain collar who told me."
Three days later, the pardon indeed arrived.
When Jǐngyì returned to the mountain,
he realized that the man in black with the plain collar
was the magpie's messenger.
Zhāng Chāngqī
Zhāng Chāngqī, Governor of Rǔ Prefecture,
was the brother of Zhāng Yìzhī.
Relying on imperial favor, he was arrogant and haughty,
and brutally oppressive toward his subordinates.
Someone from Liáng County reported
that a white magpie had been sighted.
Chāngqī ordered his Registrar, Yáng Chǔyù, to capture it.
Chǔyù had about seventy cages of sparrowhawks,
and coated their talons with wax.
Upon reaching the woods where the white magpie was seen,
a flock of magpies followed it.
Upon seeing the sparrowhawks, they scattered in flight,
leaving only the white one behind.
A sparrowhawk stretched itself to seize it,
causing no injury whatsoever,
and delivered it caged.
Chāngqī laughed and said:
"This magpie has redeemed your life."
Chǔyù kowtowed and said:
"Heaven has spared Yù.
Otherwise,
I would have thrown myself into the river or sea,
not daring to face you, my lord."
He bowed in gratitude and departed.
Cuī Yuán's Wife
It is said that a magpie's nest always contains a ridgepole.
When the wife of Minister Cuī Yuán was still at her parental home,
she and her sisters saw a magpie building a nest in the rear garden.
Together, they carried a piece of wood,
as thick as a writing brush handle
and over a chǐ long,
and placed it in the nest.
The others all failed to see it.
Common saying holds that seeing a magpie on a roof beam foretells future nobility.
Qiánlíng
In the eighth year of the Dàlì era,
on the main hall of the Shàngxiān Temple at the Qiánlíng mausoleum,
a pair of magpies carried twigs and mud
to repair fifteen damaged gaps.
The chief ministers submitted a memorial congratulating the emperor on this auspicious sign.
Pigeon Messengers
Chéng Fùlǐ, a Secretary of the Dàlǐ Court, reported that
Persian ships often kept pigeons.
Pigeons could fly several thousand lǐ,
and they would release one to fly home
as a message of safe arrival.
The Treasure Pheasant of Chéncāng
During the time of Duke Mù of Qín,
a man from Chéncāng dug in the earth and found a creature
that resembled a sheep but was not a sheep,
resembled a pig but was not a pig.
He led it to present to Duke Mù.
On the way, he met two boys who said:
"This is the wǎngliàng.
It often dwells underground,
feeding on the brains of the dead.
If you wish to kill it,
thrust a cypress branch into its head."
The creature then said:
"These two boys are called Jībǎo (Treasure Pheasants).
He who obtains the male will become king;
he who obtains the female will become a feudal lord."
The man from Chéncāng then released the creature
and chased the two boys.
The two boys transformed into pheasants
and flew into the forest.
The man from Chéncāng reported this to Duke Mù.
The duke dispatched men for a large hunt,
and indeed captured the female,
which then turned into stone.
It was placed between the Qiān and Wèi rivers.
Later, Duke Wén established a shrine there,
naming it Chénbǎo.
The male flew south and settled there.
The present-day Zhìfēi County in Nányáng
is that very place.
The Chǔ Pheasant
A man from Chǔ was carrying a mountain pheasant.
A passerby asked him:
"What bird is that?"
The carrier deceived him, saying:
"It is a fènghuáng."
The passerby said:
"I have long heard of the fènghuáng,
and now I truly see one.
Will you sell it?"
The carrier said:
"Yes."
The passerby then offered a thousand pieces of gold,
but the carrier refused.
He requested to double the price,
and only then did the carrier agree.
Just as he was about to present it to the King of Chǔ,
the bird died overnight.
The passerby did not regret the loss of his gold,
but only regretted not being able to present it.
The story spread among the people of the state,
and all believed it was a true fènghuáng and thus precious,
and that he rightly wished to present it.
The matter eventually reached the ears of the King of Chǔ.
The king was moved by his desire to present it to him,
summoned him, and bestowed generous rewards upon him,
exceeding ten times the price paid for the "fènghuáng."
The Woman of Wèi
The composition "Pheasants Fly at Dawn" was created by
the governess of a woman from Wèi.
The daughter of the Marquis of Wèi was to marry the Crown Prince of Qí,
but on the journey, she heard that the Crown Prince had died.
She asked her governess:
"What should I do?"
The governess replied:
"Let us proceed to attend
the funeral."
After the funeral rites were completed,
she refused to return home,
and in the end, she died.
The governess regretted this deeply.
She took the zither that the young lady had played herself,
and played it atop the grave mound.
Suddenly, two pheasants emerged together from the tomb.
The governess stroked the female pheasant and said:
"Have you truly become a pheasant?"
Before she finished speaking,
they both took flight and rose up,
suddenly vanishing from sight.
The governess, grief-stricken,
took up the zither and composed this piece,
hence it is called "Pheasants Fly at Dawn."
The Long-Crowing Rooster
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
Jiāozhǐ and Yuèxī presented long-crowing roosters, watch-crowing roosters.
They were tested against the water clock,
and not a moment was off.
Their long crowing lasted for the duration of a meal without ceasing,
and they had long spurs and were skilled at fighting.
The Subterranean-Singing Rooster
In the third year of the Jiàn'ān era,
Xūtú presented a subterranean-singing stone rooster.
Its color was like cinnabar,
and it was as large as a swallow.
It often stayed underground,
singing at the proper times,
its sound able to carry far and wide.
When that state heard its song,
they would slaughter animals to sacrifice to it.
They dug at the place where the sound came from,
and obtained this rooster.
If the world was at peace,
it would soar and fly, rising and dipping,
considered an auspicious sign,
also called the Treasure Rooster.
That state had no ordinary chickens;
people listened underground
to mark the passage of time.
A Daoist master said:
"In the past, an immortal minister gathered stones,
entered a cave for several miles,
and obtained a cinnabar stone rooster.
He pounded it into powder for medicine.
Those who consumed it gained a strong voice and vitality,
dying only after reaching an advanced age."
Formerly, in the first year of the Bǎodǐng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
from all directions they presented rare and strange treasures,
including an amber swallow.
Placed in a quiet room,
it would naturally sing and fly about,
being of this same category.
The "Luòshū" states:
"The treasure of Xūtú,
is an omen of Earth's virtue.
A glorious auspicious sign for the great Wèi."
Sūn Xiū
Sūn Xiū was fond of pheasant hunting.
When the season arrived,
he would go out at dawn and return only at dusk.
None of his ministers failed to remonstrate with him, saying:
"This is a trivial creature,
why indulge in it so excessively?"
He replied:
"Although it is a small creature,
its integrity surpasses that of men,
which is why I am fond of it."
Wú Qīng
A commoner from Xúzhōu named Wú Qīng,
in the fifth year of the Tàiyuán era, was conscripted for a campaign.
The people killed a chicken to pray for good fortune.
The cooked chicken head was placed on a plate,
when suddenly it crowed,
its sound very prolonged.
Later, they defeated the rebel commander Shào Bǎo,
and Bǎo died in battle on the front lines.
At that time, corpses lay scattered in disarray,
and none could be identified.
Wú Qīng saw a man wearing a white robe,
suspected it was the enemy commander,
and thus took the head to report.
Upon investigation,
it was indeed Bǎo's head.
For his merit, Wú Qīng was appointed Governor of Qīnghé,
rising suddenly from the ranks of common soldiers,
swiftly ascending to a position of honor.
The omen of the chicken
thus turned into an auspicious sign.
The Governor of Guǎngzhōu
When the Governor of Guǎngzhōu's coffin was returned for burial,
his eldest son Ānjí,
died of illness in the third year of Yuánjiā.
His second son
also died of illness in the fourth year.
Someone advised placing a rooster in the coffin.
This rooster, every time just before dawn,
would crow three times inside the coffin,
its sound profoundly sorrowful and piercing,
no different from when it crowed on its perch.
After a month or so,
its sound was heard no more.
Zhù Jīgōng
Zhù Jīgōng
was a man from Luòyáng.
He lived north of Shīxiāng at the foot of the mountain,
raising chickens for over a hundred years.
All his chickens had names,
numbering over a thousand.
At dusk they roosted under trees,
by day they were let loose to roam.
If he wanted to catch one, he would call its name,
and it would come according to its breed.
He sold chickens and their chicks,
earning over ten million cash,
which he would then set aside and leave.
He went to Wú,
and there raised pond fish.
Later, he ascended Mount Wú,
and hundreds of chickens and sparrows
often appeared by his side.
Zhū Zōng
Zhū Zōng of Línhuái was in mourning for his mother,
and constantly stayed in an outer residence.
His wife at home fell ill,
and he saw his former wife appear.
The woman said:
"The mourning rites are solemn,
there is no need for you to return frequently."
Zhū Zōng said:
"Since this tragedy began,
when have I ever come inside?"
The woman said:
"You have come many times."
Zhū Zōng realized it was a demon,
and instructed his wife's maid
to wait for its arrival,
then immediately shut the door and seize it.
When it came,
he rushed over to look,
and the creature, unable to escape,
swiftly transformed into an old white rooster.
Upon inquiry, it was found to be a domestic chicken;
they killed it, and the hauntings ceased.
The Dàijùn Post Station
Within the borders of Dàijùn, there was a post station
haunted by disturbances that could not be stopped.
There was a brave and strong scholar
traveling at dusk,
who wished to stop and lodge at the station.
The station officer tried to dissuade him.
The scholar said:
"I can handle this myself."
So he stayed and had a meal.
At night, as the scholar sat in front,
a hand appeared,
playing a five-holed flute.
The scholar laughed and said to the ghost:
"Stop right there.
You only have one hand,
how can you cover all the holes?
Let me play it for you."
The ghost said:
"Do you think I have too few fingers?"
Then it extended its hand again,
and immediately dozens of fingers appeared.
The scholar, knowing it could be attacked,
drew his sword and struck it,
obtaining an old rooster.
Gāo Yí
In the Táng dynasty, Gāo Yí of Bóhǎi was immensely wealthy.
Suddenly, he fell ill for over a month,
passed away peacefully,
but his chest remained warm.
After a full day, he revived.
He said
that a man in white clothes,
blind in one eye,
had brought a petition to the underworld court,
accusing him of killing his wife and children.
Gāo Yí replied that he had never met this old man.
The underworld official said:
"Your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
so we shall release you for now."
Then he realized the man in white was actually the old blind spotted hen in his home.
He ordered it shot and killed,
and the haunting ceased.
Empress Tiānhòu
After the Wénmíng era of the Táng dynasty,
many prefectures across the land
presented hens that had transformed into roosters.
Some were half-transformed,
half not yet changed.
This was an omen of Wǔ Zétiān ascending to the throne.
Wèi Hào
Wèi Hào, serving as a county official,
traveled to a subordinate county.
Arriving at the home of a villager named Wáng Xìngzài,
he was just dozing off
when he dreamed of a woman in black clothes leading over ten children,
all dressed in yellow.
They all pleaded for their lives,
kowtowing repeatedly.
Shortly after, they appeared again.
Wèi Hào was greatly disturbed by this matter,
so he urged for the meal to be served so he could proceed.
Just then, someone close to Wèi Hào reported:
"Wáng Xìngzài's family is poor;
they have nothing to prepare a feast.
There is one hen
that is currently brooding chicks
and has been for over ten days.
They intend to kill it."
Only then did Wèi Hào understand:
the woman in black clothes was indeed a black hen.
He then ordered it released.
That night, he dreamed again,
and they departed gratefully and joyfully.
The Wealthy Man of Héféi
In Héféi, there was a wealthy man named Liú,
who loved eating chicken.
Whenever he killed a chicken,
he would always first cut off both feet,
place them in a wooden cabinet,
let the blood drain completely,
and then cook it,
believing this removed the foul odor.
Later, Liú fell ill,
developing a sore on his temple.
After it healed,
small chicken feet grew within the scar.
Every time he used a towel or combed his hair,
he would inevitably injure those feet.
When injured, they would bleed profusely over his face,
causing pain all day long.
This continued for years;
not a day passed without injury,
and he eventually died from this.
Shǐ Kuī
During the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
Shǐ Kuī of Zhāng'ān Commandery had a dappled rooster at home,
skilled at crowing.
Shǐ Kuī's daughter often fed and cared for it.
The rooster would not eat unless fed by the girl.
Xún Qiān persistently requested it,
but the rooster refused to eat,
so it was returned to Shǐ Kuī.
A few days later,
in the morning,
the girl and the rooster went missing.
Neighbors heard the rooster heading west.
They pursued it to a body of water,
where they found only the girl's clothes and rooster feathers by the shore.
This water is now called É Xī (Goose Creek).
Yáo Lüè
During the Yìxī era,
the Qiāng chieftain Yáo Lüè demolished a ditch in Luòyáng
to obtain bricks.
He found a pair of golden-colored roosters,
necks entwined, crowing loudly.
Their cries were heard from afar.
He kept them in this ditch.
É Gōu (Goose Ditch)
Northwest of Zhānggōngchéng in Jǐnán Commandery lies É Gōu.
During the Southern Yān period,
a fisherman lived by the water.
He often heard the sound of geese.
Among the many geese, one had a particularly clear and bright bell sound.
Waiting for it,
he saw a goose with an extremely long neck.
He caught it with a net.
Around its neck was a bronze bell,
attached with a silver chain.
Inscribed faintly were the characters for the first year of Yuándǐng.
Clerk Zǔ
During the Jiǔshì era,
in Yuèzhōu, there was a clerk named Zǔ
(his given name is unknown).
One morning, going out early,
he saw someone carrying geese toward the market.
A goose, upon seeing Clerk Zǔ,
repeatedly looked back and cried out.
Zǔ then paid money to redeem it.
He went to a Buddhist temple,
intending to release it for a long life.
However, the goose refused to enter the temple.
Instead, it followed closely behind Zǔ,
passing through workshops and markets,
through crowded and populous places,
not leaving his side for a single step.
Zǔ took it in and cared for it.
Left Assistant Secretary Zhāng Xī personally witnessed and recounted this.
The Zhōu Family's Son
There was a man surnamed Zhōu from Rǔnán,
a native of Wújùn,
whose name has been lost.
His family resided in Kūnshān County.
During the Yuánhé era,
he passed the imperial examination with distinction in the míngjīng category,
was selected for appointment,
and obtained the post of sheriff of Kūnshān.
After taking up his official duties,
before reaching the county town by several tens of lǐ,
he lodged at an inn.
At night, he dreamed of a gentleman,
dressed in white robes, of very elegant appearance,
but with blood soaking his lapel,
as if wounded in his chest.
After bowing, he wept and said to Zhōu Shēng:
"I am one who dwells amidst woods and springs,
and because I do not favor the dusty world,
I have been able to live in peace for many years.
Now, having chanced to walk through the fields,
I unfortunately encountered your servant,
who bound me.
I am by nature a free spirit;
once bound,
my heart was greatly displeased.
Moreover, he set a mad dog upon me to bite my chest,
and I could not bear the indignation.
I beg you, sir, to take pity and release me.
Otherwise,
I will die within days."
Zhōu Shēng said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction,
and dare not forget it."
Having spoken, he suddenly awoke,
and secretly found it strange.
The next day,
he arrived at his home.
That evening,
he again dreamed the man in white came and said:
"I previously pleaded my case to you,
and fortunately you took pity and promised.
Yet I am still bound.
I hope you will not change your benevolent heart,
but quickly untie my bonds for me,
so that I may not remain a prisoner in your home.
That would be my good fortune."
Zhōu then asked:
"Then, your name and surname—
may I hear them?"
The man said:
"I am a bird."
Having spoken, he then left.
The next day again,
Zhōu Shēng then told his servant about the dream,
and questioned him about the matter.
It turned out the servant, while out in the wilds,
had caught a goose,
and caged it to bring home.
The night before last,
a dog had wounded its chest.
Zhōu Shēng immediately ordered it released.
That evening,
he again dreamed the man in white came to bid farewell and give thanks, then left.
A man from Pínggù,
a man from Pínggù in Chùzhōu visited his relatives by marriage,
and stayed overnight.
At midnight,
he heard voices speaking in the bedroom.
He slowly rose to listen,
and it was a flock of geese saying:
"Tomorrow morning our master will kill me.
Take good care of all the children."
They spoke in great detail.
At dawn,
the guest prepared to leave.
The host said:
"I have a very fat goose,
and will prepare it for you to eat."
The guest told him everything.
Thereupon, the host and his entire household ceased eating goose.
Soon after,
the whole village no longer ate it.
Fighting Geese in Hǎilíng.
In the year yǐmǎo,
in the western village of Hǎilíng Commandery, two geese fought in the air.
After a long time, they fell to the ground.
Their size was about five or six chǐ,
with feet like donkey hooves.
All the villagers who killed and ate them died.
The following year,
troops captured Hǎilíng.
Duck.
When Jìn's Zhōu Fǎng was young, he traveled upriver with merchants.
In the evening, they stopped below the Gōngtíng Temple.
His companions said to each other:
"Who dares to spend the night inside the temple?"
Fǎng was bold and decisive by nature,
so he went up and stayed in the temple.
The whole night passed peacefully.
In the morning, upon rising,
he saw a white-haired old man in the temple.
Fǎng then seized him,
and he transformed into a drake.
Fǎng carried it back to the boat,
intending to cook it,
but it then flew away.
Afterward, nothing else unusual happened.
Féng Fǎ.
During the Jiànwǔ era of Jìn,
Féng Fǎ from Shàn County was traveling on business.
One evening he lodged at Dí Táng.
He saw a woman,
dressed in mourning clothes,
fair-skinned,
short in stature,
who asked for passage.
The next morning,
as the boat was about to depart,
she said:
"I'll go ashore briefly to fetch my travel funds."
After she left,
Fǎ discovered he was missing one bó of silk.
The woman placed two bundles of fodder in the boat.
This happened ten times she went ashore,
and ten bó of silk were lost.
Fǎ suspected she was not human,
so he bound her feet.
The woman said:
"Your silk is in the grass ahead."
She transformed into a large white egret.
He cooked and ate it,
but the meat was not very tasty.
A Scholar from Qiántáng.
A scholar from Qiántáng, surnamed Dù,
was traveling by boat.
It was snowing heavily at dusk,
when a woman in plain clothes approached.
Dù said:
"Why not come into the boat?"
They then flirted with each other.
Dù closed the boat and took her aboard.
Later, she transformed into a white egret and flew away.
Dù was disgusted by this,
and soon fell ill and died.
White Egrets of Lízhōu.
In Tōngwàng County of Lízhōu,
every year in early summer,
a pair of white egret chicks falls to the ground.
Ancient lore says
the birds flee the miasma.
Before departing,
they leave one egret as an offering to the mountain god.
Also, whenever the commandery governor or military commander is about to be replaced,
one day prior,
there will invariably be a pair of white egret chicks
that fly from the Dàdù River to the commandery city,
circle and alight,
and after three to five days return.
The military and administrative authorities call them the "Herald Birds."
They then welcome the new and send off the old,
and never make a mistake.
Southerners Catching Wild Geese
Wild geese roost on the shores of rivers and lakes,
among sandy islets,
often in flocks of hundreds or thousands.
The largest among them stays in the center,
ordering the sentinel geese to surround and keep watch.
Southerners who gather and hunt them
wait for overcast weather
or moonless nights.
Hiding a candle inside an earthenware jar,
several men carrying clubs
hold their breath and sneak forward.
Just as they are about to reach the flock,
they briefly raise the candle,
then immediately hide it again.
The sentinel geese cry out in alarm,
and the large geese are also startled,
but after a moment, they settle down again.
When the men prepare to advance and raise the candle once more,
the sentinel geese are alarmed again.
After this happens several times,
the large geese angrily peck the sentinel geese.
The candle-bearers then slowly press closer,
and raise the candle again.
Now, fearing the pecking,
the sentinel geese no longer move.
Then, raising the candle high,
the club-wielders rush together into the flock,
striking wildly,
and capture a great many.
Long ago, a man from Huáinán named Zhāng Níng, who held the position of Píngshì, told this story;
this man had personally engaged in such hunting.
In Hǎilíng,
east of Hǎilíng County,
many people make their living by hunting wild geese.
They often keep one goose,
removing the six main flight feathers to use as a decoy.
One day, when a flock of geese was returning to their northern habitat,
the decoy goose suddenly spoke in human language to its owner, saying:
"I have repaid your debt in full,
release me to go back."
Thereupon it soared into the sky and departed,
and from then on, this man never hunted geese again.
Interlocking Feet
When mynah birds mate,
they interlock their feet,
chirping rapidly and flapping their wings as if fighting,
often falling to the ground.
It is customary to take their interlocked feet to make an aphrodisiac potion.
Talking Ability
Mynah birds,
it was said in ancient times, could be made to fetch fire,
and their mimicry of human speech surpasses that of parrots.
Taking the essence from their eyes,
grinding it with human milk,
and dripping it into the eyes
enables one to see things beyond the clouds and sky.
Huán Huō
When Huán Huō, the Minister of Works of the Jìn dynasty, was in Jīngzhōu,
he had an aide-de-camp who,
on the fifth day of the fifth month,
trimmed a mynah bird's tongue to teach it to speak,
and it could name everything.
Later, at a large gathering,
it imitated all kinds of human voices,
each one remarkably similar.
At the time, there was an assistant with a stuffy nose,
so the bird stuck its head into a jar to mimic him.
There was also a steward who stole beef,
so the aide-de-camp reported to Huán Huō:
"He hid it wrapped in fresh lotus leaves behind the screen."
A search was conducted,
and the thief was caught and punished.
Youth of Guǎnglíng
In Guǎnglíng, there was a youth who kept a mynah bird,
and he loved it dearly.
After eighty days in its cage, it died.
He placed it in a small coffin
and was about to bury it in the wilderness.
Upon reaching the city gate,
the gatekeeper opened it to inspect,
and it turned out to be a human hand.
He seized the youth and detained him with the authorities.
After eighty days in custody,
it reverted to being a dead mynah bird,
and he was then released.
Sparrow Blindness at Dusk
Sparrows all lose their sight at dusk and cannot see.
There are people who cannot see at dusk either;
this is what is called sparrow blindness.
Owls can detect the finest details at night,
but during the day, they close their eyes and cannot see hills or mountains—
such is their unique nature.
Diàowū Mountain
At Diàowū Mountain in Shǔ,
pheasants and sparrows come to mourn,
which is most sorrowful.
The local people light fires at night,
lying in wait to catch them.
Those without a crop, who do not eat,
seem to be especially grieving.
Considering them righteous, the people do not kill them.
Yáng Xuān
When Yáng Xuān was the governor of Hénèi,
while touring the county,
he saw a flock of sparrows chirping in a mulberry tree.
Xuān said to his clerks:
"Ahead, there is spilled grain from an overturned cart."
Wūtái of Yuè
When the King of Yuè entered the state,
red crows flew flanking the king;
thus, Gōu Jiàn was able to enter the state.
He built the Wūtái (Crow Terrace),
speaking of the crows' extraordinary nature.
Hé Qiánzhī
During the Jìn dynasty, Hé Qiánzhī, the magistrate of Yíngdào County, obtained a crow within the county's borders.
It was as large as an egret,
and from its knee to its thigh,
there was naturally a bronze ring piercing through.
Wūjūn Mountain
Mount Wūjūn,
is a famous mountain in Jiàn'ān,
located one hundred li west of the county seat.
In recent times, there was a Daoist priest named Xú Zhòngshān,
who from a young age sought to become an immortal,
devoting himself single-mindedly to this ambition.
He lived in poverty and maintained rigorous discipline,
growing even more diligent as the years passed.
When he met people on the road,
he would observe propriety,
yielding to all, regardless of age.
If fruits or grains were newly ripe,
he would make offerings,
first presenting them to the empty void,
then distributing them equally among the elders.
A villager who had stolen something was found guilty and
sentenced to death.
Zhòngshān went to the authorities,
taking the blame for the theft upon himself,
stating that the thief should not die,
and that executing an innocent person
was something his conscience could not bear.
He then removed his cap and loosened his belt,
submitting to the severe law.
The officials in charge, suspicious, pardoned him.
Zhòngshān was once traveling in the mountains
when he encountered a torrential downpour,
buffeted by fierce wind and thunder,
and lost his way.
Suddenly, in a flash of lightning,
he saw a house,
resembling a prefectural or provincial office,
and went there to take shelter from the rain.
Upon reaching the gate,
he saw a man in brocade robes,
who looked at Zhòngshān.
Zhòngshān then announced himself, saying, "This humble Daoist priest from the countryside, Xú Zhòngshān, pays his respects."
The man in brocade robes identified himself as the Gatekeeper Envoy, Xiāo Héng,
and also bowed.
They then discussed the reason for the storm,
and Xiāo Héng warmly invited him inside.
Zhòngshān asked:
"I have always lived in this area,
but have never seen this mansion before."
The Gatekeeper said:
"This is the dwelling place of immortals,
and I am the gatekeeper official."
Soon, a young woman appeared,
her hair arranged in double buns,
wearing a crimson skirt and a blue-patterned gauze blouse,
holding in her left hand a golden-handled yak-tail banner.
She called out:
"Envoy, with whom are you communicating outside,
without reporting it?"
He replied:
"This is the countryside Daoist priest, Xú Zhòngshān."
A moment later,
another call came:
"The Immortal Official summons Xú Zhòngshān to enter."
The young woman he had seen earlier
led Zhòngshān in through the corridor.
They reached a small courtyard south of the hall,
where he saw a man,
around fifty years of age,
with skin, body, beard, and hair all white,
wearing a gauze head-wrap cap,
and a white gauze silver-embroidered cape.
He said to Zhòngshān:
"I know you have cultivated diligently for many years,
transcending the ordinary world.
I have a young daughter who is quite familiar with the Daoist teachings.
Due to her past karma,
she is destined to be your wife,
and today is an auspicious time."
Zhòngshān descended the steps, expressing his thanks with a bow,
and rose.
He then requested to pay his respects to the lady of the house,
but was stopped:
"I have been widowed for seven years.
I have nine children,
three sons and six daughters.
The one who will be your wife
is my youngest daughter."
He then ordered the rear hall to prepare for the auspicious ceremony.
Soon, wine and food were laid out,
and after he and Zhòngshān finished eating together,
as night deepened, the sound of jade pendants was heard,
along with an extraordinary, rich fragrance,
and the glow of bright lamps and candles,
leading him away to another chamber.
Three days after the wedding,
Zhòngshān, pleased with his dwelling,
wandered through the rooms.
In a west-facing shed,
he saw fourteen feathered skins hanging on a clothes pole.
One was kingfisher-blue skin,
the rest were all crow skin.
Among the crow skins,
one was a white crow skin.
Going further southwest,
there was another shed,
where on a clothes pole,
he saw forty-nine feathered skins,
all of owls.
Zhòngshān privately found this strange.
Returning to his room,
his wife asked him:
"You were just walking around;
what did you see
that has made you so downcast?"
Zhòngshān did not answer.
His wife said:
"When immortals ascend lightly,
they all borrow wings.
If not,
how could they traverse thousands of li in an instant?"
She then asked:
"Whose are the crow skin feathers?"
He said:
"Those are my father-in-law's garments."
He asked further:
"Whose are the kingfisher-blue skin feathers?"
She said:
"Those are the garments of the maids who regularly serve as messengers and guides."
"And whose are the other crow skin feathers?"
She said:
"They are the garments of my brothers and sisters."
He asked again:
"Whose are the owl skin feathers?"
She said:
"They are the garments of those who keep watch and patrol at night,
like the gatekeeper Xiāo Héng and his kind."
Before the conversation ended,
suddenly the entire household was alarmed.
Asked the reason,
his wife told him:
"The villagers are about to hunt,
setting fire to the mountain."
Soon, everyone said:
"We haven't yet managed to make clothes for Gentleman Xú.
Today's parting
can truly be called a hasty encounter."
They then took all the feathered skins
and flew away in their respective directions.
The mansion he had seen earlier
was nowhere to be found.
Hence, the place was named Mount Wūjūn.
Wèi Líng
In the Táng dynasty, Wèi Líng served as Assistant of the West Market.
He kept a red-beaked crow,
which would beg for coins among crowds of people.
When someone gave a coin,
it would carry it in its beak to Wèi Líng's place.
It collected several hundred coins daily,
and people of the time called it Assistant Wèi's Crow.
Three-legged Crow
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
someone presented a three-legged crow.
Those around her remarked:
"One leg is fake."
Empress Wǔ laughed and said:
"Just have the history books record it;
why bother investigating its authenticity?"
The *Táng Shū* states:
"In the first year of the Tiānshòu era,
someone presented a three-legged crow,
which Empress Wǔ considered an auspicious sign for the Zhōu dynasty."
Emperor Ruìzōng said:
"The crow's front leg is fake."
Empress Wǔ was displeased.
A moment later,
one leg fell off.
Lǐ Nà
In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
flocks of crows from Zhèng and Biàn prefectures flew into the territories of Tián Xù and Lǐ Nà,
carrying wood to build a wall.
It reached a height of two to three chǐ,
covering over ten square lǐ.
Xù and Nà, disgusted, ordered it burned,
but after a couple of nights, it was restored as before,
and the crows' beaks were all bleeding.
Lǚ Shēng's Wife
Lǚ Shēng of Dōngpíng,
a man of the State of Lǔ,
made his home in Zhèng.
His wife, née Huáng, was gravely ill and near death.
She told her mother-in-law:
"I am ill and about to die,
yet I have heard that when a person dies, they become a ghost.
I have always regretted that the living and ghosts cannot communicate,
causing the survivors even greater sorrow.
Now, since you care for me so deeply,
when I die,
I will surely be able to inform you through dreams."
After her death,
the mother-in-law dreamed that Huáng came to her,
weeping and saying:
"In my lifetime, I was without merit;
now I have become a different creature.
I was born in the thick woods of the eastern wilds of Zhèng.
The one with black wings,
crying out with its call—
that is me.
Seven days from now,
I will come to pay my respects to you.
I hope you will remember my lifetime
and not reject me because I am a different creature."
Having said this, she departed.
Seven days later,
sure enough, a bird came from the east,
arrived at the Lǚ family home,
perched on a tree in the courtyard,
and cried mournfully for a long time.
Her mother-in-law wept and said:
"It truly is as in my dream.
Do not forget our past bond;
come directly to my dwelling."
The bird then flew into the main hall,
circled and cried plaintively.
After only about the time it takes to eat a meal,
it finally flew away toward the east.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng personally led a campaign against Yùnzhōu,
and the army encamped at Wèinán.
At that time, the construction of a new fortification had just been completed.
He thus climbed up to survey the area from atop it,
and saw a bird alight between the high planks and caw,
its cry very harsh.
Deputy Commander Lǐ Fán said:
"This bird's cry—
does it portend misfortune?"
His vanguard, Zhū Yǒuyù, had been ambushed by Zhū Xuān,
and withdrew his troops southward.
Our main army was unaware of this,
and thus advanced northward,
marching.
They encountered Zhū Xuān's forces arriving.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng whipped his horse and fled south,
entering a village,
and was pursued by the enemy.
Ahead was a ditch,
quite deep and wide.
In the urgent moment,
he suddenly saw that within the ditch, sorghum stalks had piled up to form a path,
right before his horse.
He then leaped over it.
Deputy Commander Lǐ Fán and the commandery general Gāo Xíngsī were killed by the enemy.
Zhāng Guīyǔ served as the rear-guard cavalry,
wielding his spear and fighting fiercely,
and barely managed to survive and return,
his body pierced by fifteen arrows.
Only then did they realize that the bird at Wèinán
was an omen foreshadowing these events.
The Crying Owl
At the summer solstice, the yīn energy stirs, leading to slaughter and harm.
This is the season of plunder and injury.
Therefore, when a vicious bird cries at someone's home,
it is an omen of death.
It is also said:
"The owl eats its mother's eyes
before it can fly."
Guō Pú stated:
"It lies concealed in the earth as an owl."
The "Treatise on Sacrifices" in the Book of Hàn records:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven
would in spring offer sacrifices to the Yellow Emperor,
using one owl and one pòjìng beast."
The Kite
The kite,
according to tradition, is born when a falcon has three offspring, one of which becomes a kite.
When Empress Zhāng of Emperor Sùzōng monopolized power,
whenever wine was served,
she often mixed kite brains with the wine,
causing people to stay drunk long and become forgetful.
Also, common folklore says
the kite does not drink from springs or wells,
but only when rain moistens its wings
does it get water to drink.
The Scops Owl Sees at Night
The scops owl is a type of owl.
When made into a decoy,
it can attract other birds.
The scops owl during the day
cannot see anything.
At night, it flies to catch mosquitoes and gnats.
The scops owl belongs to the same category as the ghost carriage.
They all fly at night and hide by day.
Some are fond of eating people's fingernails,
and thus know good and bad fortune.
When misfortune is imminent, they cry on the roof,
indicating there will be calamity.
Therefore, people bury their trimmed nails
inside the doorway,
likely to avoid this.
It is also called the night-roaming woman,
fond
of haunting infants.
Thus, infants' clothes
must not be left under the stars and dew,
for fear of its haunting.
Also named ghost carriage,
in spring and summer,
whenever it is slightly overcast,
it flies by crying.
They are especially numerous beyond the mountains,
and love to enter people's homes,
diminishing their spirit energy.
Some say
it has nine heads,
and one was once bitten off by a dog.
It constantly drips blood,
and the household where its blood drips
will suffer misfortune.
The "Record of the Seasons of Jīngchǔ" states:
"Upon hearing it,
one should call the dog."
It also says:
"The owl is as large as a zhèn bird,
has an evil cry,
and its flying into a house is inauspicious."
Its meat is delicious,
suitable for roasting.
Thus, Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Seeing the pellet, one thinks of roasted owl."
It also says:
"The ancients prized roasted owl."
They valued its rich flavor.
The Shuōwén explains:
"The owl is an unfilial bird;
it eats its mother before it can fly."
The Book of Hàn states:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month, owl soup is made
to be bestowed upon all officials."
Because it is a vicious bird,
they eat it on the fifth day.
The ancients prized roasted owl and owl soup,
likely wishing to exterminate its kind.
Also, some say
the scops owl eats people's discarded nails.
This is incorrect.
Rather, the scops owl can pick up fleas and lice at night.
The words for 'nail' (zhǎo) and 'flea' (zǎo) sound similar,
hence the mistaken saying.
The Night-Roaming Woman
It is also said
the night-roaming woman,
also called the Heavenly Emperor's daughter,
also named the hook star,
flies at night and hides by day,
like a ghost or spirit.
Clad in feathers, she is a flying bird;
shedding her feathers, she becomes a woman.
She has no children,
and delights in stealing people's children.
She has breasts on her chest.
When people give treats to children,
they must not be left exposed.
Children's clothes also must not be sun-dried exposed,
for if her feathers fall on the clothes,
it will cause bird hauntings.
Some say she marks the clothes with blood spots,
or that she is transformed from women who died in childbirth.
Warding Off Owls
Cháng Qiān performed an exorcism for Duke Jǐng of Qí using the methods of the Zhōu rituals to expel an owl,
and the owl then spread its wings, fell to the ground, and died.
Zhāng Lǜgēng
had an owl that crowed in the morning in the courtyard tree of Zhāng Lǜgēng,
his wife considered it an ill omen,
and repeatedly spat at it.
Zhāng said:
"Quickly sweep and clean,
I am about to receive a promotion."
Before he finished speaking,
congratulatory guests were already at the door.
A Person from Yōngzhōu
In the early years of Zhēnguān,
a person from Yōngzhōu was walking at night,
when he heard an owl hooting urgently,
and it kept flying back and forth brushing against his head.
This man was disgusted,
He
struck it with his whip,
the owl died,
and he covered it with soil before leaving.
After walking several li,
he encountered some thieves,
who saw blood on his clothes,
and asked him what blood it was.
He then told them everything.
The men did not believe him,
and took him to the place where he had buried the owl.
Earlier, there had been a thief who killed someone,
cut off the head,
buried it, and left,
but later could not find it.
When they brushed away the soil to retrieve the owl,
they found a human head.
They all thought he was the thief,
seized him and interrogated him,
causing him great suffering.
Wéi Zhuān
In the Dàzhōng era,
Wéi Zhuān took the imperial examination,
his literary talent was abundant but his poverty grew increasingly severe.
At the end of the year, hungry and cold,
he had no means to support himself.
There was a man named Wéi Guāng,
who treated him as a clansman,
and vacated an outer room of his residence to lodge him.
On the night the results were posted,
the wind and snow were bitterly cold,
messengers reporting Wéi Guāng's success
came one after another,
but Zhuān had no news of passing the examination.
Guāng invited him to a small pavilion at the edge of the hall,
prepared wine and food to comfort him.
He saw maids counting clothes and luggage,
and servants arranging carriages and horses.
Zhuān returned to his quarters at midnight,
sat huddled by the stove, sighing sorrowfully.
Awaiting Guāng's success,
he intended to prepare congratulatory gifts,
but Zhuān sat pressed against a broken window,
using a horizontal bamboo pole to hang a mat to cover it.
Suddenly, an owl hooted at the eaves,
and soon perched on the bamboo pole.
Zhuān was terrified,
took a whip and went out to chase it away,
it flew up and returned again,
and only after a long time did it leave.
He said,
to the attendant:
"Even if I fail,
I have no regrets,
but such a monstrous bird causing trouble,
I fear I may also suffer unexpected disaster."
Soon after, the palace drum suddenly sounded,
the results were posted,
and Zhuān had passed the examination.
Guāng's clothes, utensils, carriages, and horses
were all given to him.
The Flying Saliva Bird
Nánhǎi is three thousand li from Kuàijī,
there is a Dog Country,
in the country there is a flying saliva bird resembling a rat,
with wings like a bird and red feet.
Every dawn,
before the various roosting birds have dispersed,
each occupies a tree,
with saliva in its mouth like glue,
flies around the tree,
saliva falling like rain,
spraying over the branches and leaves.
When other birds arrive, it is like a net,
and then it eats them.
If by noon it has not caught anything,
it chases them through the air and ensnares them with saliva,
never missing.
If a person catches and dries it,
it can cure thirst.
Its saliva, after being spread, dries within half a day,
falls off by itself,
and then it spreads it again.
Jīngwèi
There is a bird like a crow,
with a patterned head, white beak, and red feet,
named Jīngwèi.
In the past, the daughter of the Red Emperor, named Nǚ Wá,
went to play in the Eastern Sea,
drowned and did not return,
her spirit transformed into Jīngwèi.
Therefore, Jīngwèi often takes wood and stones from the Western Mountains,
to fill the Eastern Sea.
The Benevolent Bird
Duke Wén of Jìn burned the forest to seek Jiè Tuī,
a white crow circled the smoke and cawed,
or perched beside Jièzǐ,
and the fire could not burn him.
The people of Jìn praised it,
built a high platform,
named it the Sīyāntái (Thinking of Smoke Terrace).
They planted trees of benevolence and longevity,
the trees resemble cypress but have long, soft branches,
and their flowers are edible.
Therefore, the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says:
"Among beautiful trees,
there are the flowers of the longevity tree."
This is it.
Some say,
this crow was perceptive,
on the mountain where Jiè was burned,
for hundreds of li, no more nets were set.
They called it the benevolent bird.
Common people also call the benevolent bird with a white breast the compassionate crow,
which is this type.
Dì
In the ruins of Yōuzhōu,
north of Yǔshān,
there is a bird skilled in singing.
It has a human face and a bird's beak,
eight wings and one foot,
feathers like a pheasant,
walks without treading the ground,
named Dì,
its voice resembles bells, chimes, sheng, and yú.
"Shìyǔ" says:
"When the green Dì sings,
the times are peaceful."
In prosperous and enlightened eras,
it soars and sings in marshes,
its notes match the pitch pipes,
it flies but does not walk.
When Yǔ pacified the waters and land,
it perched on rivers and mountains,
where it gathered,
a sage was sure to emerge.
Since ancient times, when casting various tripods and vessels,
its image was always depicted.
Inscriptions and praises continue to this day.
Hán Péng
The Hán Péng bird
belongs to the category of waterfowl like ducks and grebes.
This bird flies in pairs,
floating on streams and shores.
Among waterfowl, species such as mandarin ducks, grebes, and others
are all found north of the mountain ranges,
but the Hán Péng bird has never been seen there.
According to Gān Bǎo's Records of Searching for the Supernatural:
"Minister Hán Péng
had a beautiful wife,
whom King Kāng of Sòng seized.
Hán Péng resented this,
so the king imprisoned him,
and Hán Péng eventually committed suicide.
His wife secretly rotted her clothes,
and when the king ascended a tower with her,
she threw herself from it.
Those around her tried to catch her by her clothes,
but the clothes could not withstand their grip.
She left a note on her sash, saying:
'I wish for my body to be returned to the Hán family for a joint burial.'
The king was furious,
ordering them to be buried
facing each other.
After one night,
suddenly, a catalpa tree was seen growing above the two graves,
with roots intertwined below
and branches connected above.
There were also birds like mandarin ducks
that constantly perched on the tree,
crying mournfully morning and evening."
Southerners believe this bird is the essence of Hán Péng and his wife,
hence naming it after the Hán family.
The Arrow-Tailed Bird
The arrow-tailed bird
sings like a wild magpie,
with wings and feathers mottled yellow and green.
Its tail grows two branches,
over two feet long,
straight and not drooping.
Only the tip of the tail has feathers,
resembling arrow fletching,
hence it is called the arrow-tailed bird.
The Tiny Bird
In the fifth year of the Yuánfēng era of the Hàn dynasty,
the state of Lèbì presented tiny birds as tribute.
Hundreds of them were contained in a jade cage measuring one square foot,
each as large as a fly.
They resembled parrots in shape,
and their calls could be heard for several miles,
sounding like the cry of a yellow swan.
The people of that state often used these birds to tell time,
hence they were also called "time-keeping insects."
The emperor obtained them
and released them within the palace.
Within ten days,
they disappeared without a trace.
Greatly regretting this,
he sought them but could not find them again.
The following year,
these birds returned and gathered on the palace curtains,
sometimes even entering sleeves.
Thus, they were renamed "cicada birds."
Palace ladies and concubines such as Jiéyú delighted in them,
and anyone on whose clothes these birds alighted
would receive favor and affection.
By the end of Emperor Wǔ's reign,
they gradually died off on their own.
People especially cherished their skins,
and those who wore them
often became charming to men.
The Queen Mother's Messenger
In Hán Mountain of Qí Commandery, there is a bird with green feet and a red beak,
white wings and a crimson forehead,
named the Queen Mother's Messenger.
Long ago, when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn climbed this mountain,
he obtained a jade box
five inches long.
As the emperor descended the mountain,
the jade box suddenly transformed into a white bird and flew away.
It is said that on the mountain lies the Queen Mother's medicine box,
often guarded by this bird.
Mandarin Ducks
During the Hàn dynasty,
the two leaves of the southern gate in Yān County
suddenly made sounds—one saying "yuān,"
the other saying "yāng."
Morning and evening, as the gate opened and closed,
the sounds were heard in the capital.
By the end of the Hàn dynasty, people found this ominous,
so they ordered the gate destroyed.
The two leaves transformed into mandarin ducks
and flew away together.
Later, Yān was renamed Yànchéng County.
The Five-Colored Bird
When Yáng Zhèn died,
before his burial,
a large five-colored bird over ten feet tall
flew down from the sky
to the front of Yáng Zhèn's coffin,
lifting its head and crying mournfully,
its tears wetting the ground.
On the day of the burial,
it soared upward into the sky.
The Man from Xīnyù
A man from Xīnyù County in Yùzhāng saw six or seven women in the fields,
all wearing feather garments.
Not realizing they were birds,
he crept forward
and obtained the feather garment one of them had removed,
hiding it away.
He then approached the other birds,
which all flew away,
leaving one bird unable to depart.
The man took her as his wife,
and they had three daughters.
Later, the mother had her daughters ask their father
and learned the garment was under a pile of rice.
Retrieving it,
she put it on and flew away.
Later, she returned with garments for her three daughters,
who also flew away.
The Zhāng Family
In the capital, a woman of the Zhāng family lived alone in a room.
A turtledove entered from outside
and perched on her bed.
The Zhāng woman prayed:
"If the dove brings misfortune,
fly up to the ceiling;
if it brings fortune,
enter my bosom."
Reaching out with her hand,
she obtained a golden hook.
From then on, her descendants gradually prospered,
and their wealth multiplied ten-thousandfold.
A merchant from Shǔ arrived in Cháng'ān
and, hearing of this,
bribed a maidservant heavily.
The maidservant stole the hook and gave it to the merchant.
After the Zhāng family lost the hook,
they gradually declined and grew poor.
The Shǔ merchant also fell into poverty and hardship.
He then returned the hook to the Zhāng family,
and the Zhāng family prospered again.
The Gold-Washing Bird
During the Wei period,
the Kingdom of Kūnmíng presented a gold-spitting bird as tribute.
The people of that kingdom said:
"Our land is nine thousand lǐ from Ránzhōu.
This bird originates from there,
its shape resembling a sparrow,
its color yellow,
its feathers soft and dense.
It often soars over the sea.
Those who catch it with nets
consider it an utmost auspicious sign.
Hearing of the virtue of Great Wei,
which extends to remote wilderness,
we crossed mountains and sailed seas
to come and present it to the great kingdom."
The emperor obtained this bird
and kept it in the garden of spiritual fowl,
feeding it pearls
and giving it turtle brain to drink.
The bird often spat out gold dust like millet grains,
which could be smelted to make vessels.
In the past, during Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's time,
there was a tribute of a large sparrow—
this is of the same kind.
This bird feared frost and snow,
so a small chamber was built to house it,
named the Cold-Repelling Terrace.
All its windows and doors were made of crystal,
allowing light to pass through inside and out,
while always shielding it from wind, rain, dust, and mist.
Palace women vied to use the gold it spat out to adorn their hairpins and pendants,
calling it Cold-Repelling Gold.
Thus, palace women teased each other, saying:
"If you don't wear Cold-Repelling Gold,
how can you win the monarch's heart?
If you don't wear Cold-Repelling Ornaments,
how can you gain the monarch's favor?"
Thereupon, those seeking to charm and seduce vied to use these treasures as personal adornments,
and even when walking or sleeping, they carried them to curry favor.
When the Wei dynasty perished,
its precious treasures, ponds, and terraces
became overgrown with weeds,
and the gold-spitting bird
also soared away on high.
Qiū
In the second year of Yǒngjiā of Jìn,
a qiū bird gathered in Shǐ'ān County.
A wooden arrow pierced it,
with an iron arrowhead,
its length six and a half cùn.
Judging by the arrow,
the archer must have been fifteen or sixteen chǐ tall.
The Magistrate of Yíngdào
During the Tàiyuán era of Jìn,
the magistrate of Yíngdào, Hé Xiézhī, left his post
and obtained a bird in the mountains within the county borders,
as large as an egret,
blue in color with red eyes.
On its knees and thighs,
there naturally were bronze ring patterns,
with sizes and carvings turning and shifting like
lǎnzi,
exquisitely crafted as if by human skill.
Thereupon, it was passed around for viewing in the capital.
Yíngdào is now part of Dàozhōu.
Paper Kite Transforming into a Bird
In the third year of Tàiqīng of Liáng Wǔ,
when Hóu Jǐng besieged Táichéng,
cutting off distant communication,
Jiǎnwén made a paper kite to fly in the air,
to urgently seek help from outside.
Hóu Jǐng's strategist Wáng Wěi,
said to Hóu Jǐng:
"Where this paper kite reaches,
the matter will be communicated outside."
He ordered skilled archers among his attendants to shoot it,
and when it fell,
it transformed into a bird,
flying into the clouds,
and no one knew where it went.
Chún
When Āndìng's original earthen walls were built,
sacrifices were offered with
gū wine vessels.
Suddenly, a chún bird flew onto a gū vessel,
hence the place was named Chúngū City.
Later, during the Dàtǒng era of Wén Dì of Wèi,
it was established as Chúngū County.
Dài Wénmóu
There was a man named Dài Wénmóu
who lived in seclusion in the Yángchéng Mountains.
Once, while eating in the guest hall,
he suddenly heard a voice calling:
"I am an envoy of the Heavenly Emperor,
wishing to descend and rely on you.
May I?"
Wénmóu heard this and was greatly startled.
The voice spoke again:
"Do you doubt me?"
Wénmóu then knelt and said:
"I live in poverty,
fearing it is insufficient for your descent."
Thereafter, he cleaned and swept, set up a seat,
and diligently offered food morning and evening.
Later, Wénmóu secretly discussed this indoors,
and his wife said:
"This is likely a fox spirit seeking to rely on you."
Wénmóu said:
"I suspect so too."
Then, during the sacrificial offering,
the spirit spoke:
"I have accompanied you,
intending to benefit you,
yet unexpectedly you harbor doubts and dissent."
While Wénmóu was apologizing,
suddenly, sounds like dozens of people shouting came from the hall.
Going out to look,
he saw a large bird,
multicolored,
with dozens of white doves following it,
flying northeast into the clouds and disappearing.
Auspicious Bird
When Emperor Yáng returned from campaigning against Liáo,
he stationed at Wànghǎi Town in Liǔchéng Commandery.
Stepping out to observe,
there were two large birds,
with white feathers and red beaks,
resembling cranes or egrets.
They emerged from the heavens,
soaring and descending in pairs,
standing fifteen or sixteen chǐ tall,
eight or nine chǐ long.
They hovered tamely and peacefully,
soaring and dancing above the imperial camp.
The emperor ordered Assistant Editor Yú Chuò to compose an "Inscription on the Auspicious Bird" and present it.
The emperor commanded it to be engraved on the spot,
and also ordered Palace Attendant Yán Pí to paint their likeness.
Secretary Yú Shìnán presented a "Eulogy on the Auspicious Bird,"
and the emperor ordered it to be written at the beginning of the painting.
Spring-Announcing Bird
In the Gùzhǔ Mountains, there is a bird resembling a myna but smaller,
bluish-yellow in color.
Every year in the first and second months,
it calls out:
"Spring has arrived!"
In the third and fourth months,
it calls out:
"Spring is departing!"
Tea pickers call it the Spring-Announcing Bird.
Crowned Duck
The shíshǒu fish
transforms into a crowned duck in autumn.
The crowned duck has a stone in its head.
Qín Jíliǎo
Róng, Guǎn, Lián, and Bái prefectures produce this bird.
It roughly resembles a parrot,
with red beak and feet.
Behind its two eyes, near the brain,
there is a yellow fleshy crest.
It excels at imitating human speech,
its voice loud and clear,
more distinct than a parrot's.
It is fed with cooked egg yolk and rice, shaped like dates.
Some say
that in Róngzhōu, there are purely red and purely white ones,
but none have been seen.
Wéi's Son
In Yángyáng Commandery, there was a temple to the Zhāng Nǚláng.
During the Shàngyuán era,
a man named Wéi was traveling in Yángyáng
and passed by the temple.
He thus loosened his saddle to rest.
Suddenly, he saw a pair of clogs inside the temple, lying on the ground.
The gentleman looked at them
and saw they were woven from straw,
with a very fine texture,
white in color and of exquisite craftsmanship.
Wéi then stored them in his bag
and soon departed.
When he reached the commandery seat,
the commandery governor lodged Wéi in a guesthouse pavilion.
That night,
Wéi placed the clogs he had obtained
in front of him and went to sleep.
By the next day, they had vanished from their place,
and no one could find where they were.
After only about the time it takes to eat a meal,
they were found on the tiled roof of the guesthouse pavilion.
The servants were astonished
and reported it to Wéi.
Wéi immediately ordered them to climb onto the roof and retrieve them.
Once they were obtained,
he placed them before him again.
The next day they disappeared once more,
and again were found on the tiled roof.
This happened three times.
Wéi secretly said to his servant:
"Isn't this strange?
We should secretly watch them."
That night,
his servant secretly watched through a crack.
As midnight approached,
the clogs suddenly transformed into a white bird
and flew onto the roof.
Wéi ordered them to be captured and burned,
and it then flew away.
Bird Bandit
Lǐ Jìng's younger brother, Kèshī, held the office of General of the Right Martial Guard.
He hunted in all four seasons,
never pausing or resting.
In the southwest outskirts of the capital, near the Lǐshuǐ River,
all the birds and beasts recognized him.
Every time he went out,
magpies and crows would compete to chase and clamor at him.
People called him the Bird Bandit.
Bird Ministry
Féng Yǎn, a Jǐshì official,
had a residence in the Qīnrén ward.
To the south was a hilltop pavilion garden,
where he kept an extremely large number of geese, ducks, and various other fowl.
He often dispatched a household servant to manage them.
People of the time called it the Bird Ministry.
Liú Jǐngyáng
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's time,
the Left Guard Military Officer Liú Jǐngyáng was sent on a mission to Lǐngnán.
He obtained a pair of Jíliǎo birds,
one male and one female,
which understood human speech.
Upon reaching the capital, he presented them.
He kept the female
while the male, distressed and resentful, refused to eat.
Wǔ Zétiān asked:
"Why are you so listless?"
The bird spoke, saying:
"My mate was taken by the envoy,
and now I miss her greatly."
She then summoned Liú Jǐngyáng and said:
"Why have you concealed one bird and not presented it?"
Liú Jǐngyáng kowtowed and apologized.
He then presented it,
and Wǔ Zétiān did not punish him.
Locust-Eating Birds
During the Kāiyuán era,
in Bèizhōu, locusts were devouring the grain.
Several thousand large white birds
and tens of thousands of small white birds appeared
and ate all the insects.
Lú Róng
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
Lú Róng of Fànyáng lay ill and alone in bed.
Suddenly, he saw a large bird flying from afar.
In a moment, it alighted on a tree in the courtyard,
standing four or five feet tall,
its shape resembling an owl,
with eyes as large as cups
and a beak over a foot long.
It descended to the ground and mounted the steps.
After a short while,
it entered the room and climbed onto the bed.
It raised its two wings;
on the wings were hands,
holding a small spear,
intending to strike Lú Róng.
Lú Róng lay prostrate, terrified and sweating.
Suddenly, someone else entered through the back door
and said to the bird:
"This is a good man;
take care not to harm him."
The bird then flew away,
and the person also followed it out.
Lú Róng's illness was cured from then on.
Lady Zhāng
Lady Zhāng, wife of Lǐ Quánzhāng, the Prefect of Púzhōu,
was the aunt of Niú Sù.
In the twenty-fifth year of the Kāiyuán era,
she died at the Yīquē estate.
While Lady Zhāng lay ill,
a bird perched on a tree in the courtyard.
It had a white head, red feet,
a yellow belly, and vermilion wings.
Its cry only said:
"Regretful, oh mother!"
It continued like this day and night without ceasing.
After more than ten days,
Lady Zhāng passed away,
and the bird then vanished.
Wáng Xù
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Wáng Xù, the Registrar of Tāizhōu, fell ill and was near death.
A large bird flew into Wáng Xù's room,
walked to the bedside,
pointed its beak toward Wáng Xù, and cried out:
"Take, take."
Wáng Xù then died.
The Great Bird of Wǔgōng
In the eighth year of the Dàlì era,
a great bird appeared in Wǔgōng,
and a flock clamored at it.
The Camp Commander Zhāng Rìfēn shot and captured it.
It had fleshy wings and a fox-like head,
with four feet,
each foot having claws.
Its wingspan was four feet wide,
and its shape resembled a bat.
Huàn □,
also named Duò Yì,
has a shape similar to a magpie.
If a person shoots at it,
it catches the arrow in its beak and shoots it back at the person.
Ribbon-Spitting Bird
On the southern mountain of Yúfù County, there is a bird as large as a myna.
Its plumage is mostly black,
mixed with yellow and white,
and its head somewhat resembles a pheasant.
Sometimes it spits out an object several inches long,
brilliantly colored in red,
its shape and color resembling a ribbon,
hence it is named the Ribbon-Spitting Bird.
Also, when it eats, it always stores food in its crop,
which swells before its breast as large as a peck measure.
Fearing to bump its crop,
it always keeps far from plants and trees when walking,
so it is also called the Tree-Avoiding Bird.
Cuckoo
At the beginning of spring, they urge each other to sing.
The first to sing coughs up blood and dies.
Once, a person was traveling
and saw a flock sitting silently.
He casually imitated their call,
and died immediately.
Hearing its first call
foretells separation for the listener.
Hearing its call from a latrine
is inauspicious.
The method to ward it off
is to respond with the bark of a dog.
The Mosquito Mother Bird,
resembles a grebe in shape,
with a large and long beak,
and catches fish in ponds to eat.
Each time it calls,
mosquitoes and gnats fly out from its mouth.
Common folklore says
that if its feathers are gathered to make a fan,
it can repel mosquitoes.
It is also called the Mosquito-Spitting Bird.
The Paulownia Flower Bird:
In the Jiànnán, Péng, and Shǔ regions,
there is a bird as large as a finger,
displaying all five colors,
with a crest resembling a phoenix.
It feeds on paulownia flowers;
whenever the paulownia trees bloom, it arrives,
and when the paulownia flowers fall, it departs,
no one knows where it goes.
Commonly called the Paulownia Flower Bird,
it is extremely tame and gentle,
perching on women's hairpins,
and does not fly away throughout the entire banquet.
People love it,
and it causes no harm.
The Great Bird of Zhēnlà Country:
In Zhēnlà Country, there is Mount Gélàng,
ten thousand zhàng high,
with a cave halfway up its slope.
Previously, there was a Làng Bird,
resembling an old owl in appearance,
as large as a camel.
When people passed by,
it would seize and devour them,
then soar into the sky and fly away,
causing great suffering among the people.
The king of Zhēnlà took a large piece of beef,
inserted a small, sharp sword inside it,
with both ends pointed and sharp,
and had someone carry it along the path.
The bird seized and swallowed it,
and thus died,
and the species vanished thereafter.
The Bǎishé Bird:
The Bǎishé sings in spring,
and by the summer solstice, it only eats earthworms.
After the first lunar month, when the ground thaws,
earthworms emerge, and the bird arrives.
After the tenth lunar month,
when earthworms hide, the bird departs.
This is an example of the mutual responsiveness of creatures.
The Stork:
In the Jiāng-Huái region, a flock of storks circling in flight is called a "stork well."
Storks also enjoy flying in circles,
and this always heralds wind and rain.
If people raid nests to take stork chicks,
a sixty-mile drought will ensue.
They can fly in flocks,
brushing against the clouds and stirring up rain,
causing the rain to disperse.
Furthermore, in the south, there are storks that eat snakes.
Whenever they encounter a large rock,
knowing a snake lies beneath it,
they stand before the rock,
performing steps like a Dàoshi's Yǔ steps,
causing the rock to turn over with a rumble,
and thus they capture and devour the snake.
Villagers who learned this method
waited for the storks to raise their young,
climbed the tree,
and bound the nest with a bamboo rope.
The stork would inevitably perform its method to undo it,
so they spread sand beneath the tree,
to copy the footprints left behind and imitate the steps.
The Gānchóng Bird:
In the late Dàzhōng era,
Shūzhōu reported that flocks of birds had built a nest,
seven chǐ wide,
and one zhàng high,
where swallows, sparrows, eagles, and kites,
waterfowl and mountain birds,
all mingled as tame and friendly as one.
There was also a bird
with a human face and green feathers,
its beak and claws all dark reddish-purple.
Its call sounded like "gān chóng,"
so it was called the Gānchóng Bird.
At that time, people painted pictures of it
and sold them in the markets.
The Hoopoe:
During the Wáng Shǔ period, Vice Minister of Justice Lǐ Rénbiǎo was residing in Xǔzhōu
and intended to present himself for the imperial examinations.
At that time, Minister Xuē Néng was the regional commander.
Lǐ first compiled fifty of his own poems as a gift,
dipped his brush and completed the scroll,
and was reading it leaning on a table in a small pavilion.
Before finishing three or five poems,
a hoopoe flew in from the eaves,
landed on the table,
tame and friendly.
After a long while,
it stretched its neck, drooped its wings, and danced,
facing the person as if about to speak.
After another long while,
it turned and danced again.
This happened three times,
before it soared away.
Lǐ found this strange,
but did not tell anyone.
The next day, he presented his poems,
and Xuē treated him with great courtesy.
After a few days,
Xuē married his daughter to him.
The Great Bird of the Northern Sea:
In the Northern Sea, there is a great bird,
a thousand lǐ tall.
On its head is the character "tiān,"
on its chest, the character "hòu,"
on its left wing, the character "yī,"
and on its right wing, the character "lè."
Its head faces due east,
and it catches fish in the center of the sea.
Sometimes it raises its wings to fly,
and its feathers brush against each other,
creating sounds like thunder and wind.
The Crow:
Wēn Zhāng served as the Governor of the Capital,
ruthless in executions,
and the capital feared him.
One day,
he heard the bell rope being pulled but saw no one,
and this happened three times—
it turned out to be a crow.
The Governor said:
"This must be someone who has taken its chicks, and it has come to plead."
He ordered an officer to follow the crow and arrest the person.
The crow circled around,
leading the officer to a tree outside the city walls,
where indeed someone had taken its chicks
and was still resting under the tree.
The officer arrested and delivered him.
The Governor, considering the matter unusual,
had the chick-catcher executed.
The Strange Birds of Xiānjū Mountain:
In the second year of the Yǒngpíng era of Wáng Shǔ,
auspicious writings left by Zhāng Hóngdào of Běimáng Mountain were discovered at Xiānjū Mountain in Shífāng.
Thus, funds were allocated,
entrusted to Zhàozhōu Cavalry Commander Zhào Hóngyuē,
to construct a temple.
When building the Hall of the Heavenly Venerable,
the materials and stones were vast,
and the labor required was immense.
On that day,
as they were about to raise the great beam,
over three hundred skilled workers and laborers tied ropes, shouted, and pulled,
the noise shaking the surroundings.
Suddenly, three strange birds appeared:
one red and crimson,
the other two pure white,
with tails like trailing silk,
each over two chǐ long.
They perched on the beam,
moving up and down along the ropes,
among the crowd,
showing no fear at all.
The workers stroked, held, and played with them,
as if they were tame and raised.
Once the beam was raised into place,
the birds flew away.
The Oriole
In recent years,
someone captured a fledgling oriole
and kept it in a bamboo cage.
Its parents, male and female, fluttered their wings together,
crying mournfully day and night outside the cage,
refusing to eat or drink at all.
So the fledgling was placed outside the cage,
Then the parents came to feed it again.
Even if people were nearby,
they showed no fear whatsoever.
Suddenly one day,
when the fledgling was not released from the cage,
the male and female circled around, flying and crying,
unable to get inside.
One threw itself into the fire,
the other dashed against the cage and died.
When their bellies were cut open for examination,
their intestines were found broken into pieces.
The Great Fish of the Eastern Sea
Among the great creatures of the East,
there is a fish in the Eastern Sea.
Those who travel the sea
may encounter its head on the first day,
and its tail on the seventh day.
When this fish gives birth, the water for a hundred lǐ turns to blood.
The Tuó Fish
The Bówùzhì states:
"In the Southern Sea, there is a tuó fish.
If its head is cut off,
dried,
and its teeth knocked out,
it can regenerate,
but only up to three times, after which it ceases."
The Nánzhōuzhì also says the same.
Moreover, it is said by people of Guǎngzhōu
that crocodiles can chase oxen and horses on land,
overturn boats and kill people in water,
yet when encountering a net, they dare not touch it—
such is their caution.
When one becomes pregnant,
it lays hundreds of eggs on land.
When they take form,
some become snakes,
some turtles,
some soft-shelled turtles,
some fish,
some tuó,
and some become jiāo—
altogether more than ten kinds.
When captured and slaughtered by people,
its spirit can summon thunder, lightning, wind, and rain.
This is likely a divine creature akin to dragons.
The Great Fish of the Southern Sea
Hé Lǚguāng, the military governor of Lǐngnán,
was a native of Zhūyá.
He lived by the great sea
and said
that he personally witnessed three extraordinary things:
The first:
There were two mountains in the sea,
separated by six or seven hundred lǐ.
On clear mornings, looking from afar,
their green-blue color appeared close.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
there was a great thunderstorm in the sea,
raining mud,
resembling blown foam,
and heaven and earth were dark for seven days.
People coming from the mountain area said
that a huge fish,
carried by the current into the space between the two mountains,
could neither advance nor retreat.
After a long time,
its gills caught on a cliff,
and after seven days, the mountain split,
allowing the fish to leave.
The thunder
was the sound of the fish;
the muddy rain
was foam blown from its mouth;
the darkness of heaven and earth
was its exhaled breath.
The second:
There is an island in the sea,
spanning several thousand lǐ in breadth.
On the island are creatures
resembling several toads.
The larger ones measure four to five hundred lǐ in circumference,
the smaller ones about a hundred lǐ or more.
Every full-moon night,
they spew white vapor from their mouths,
which rises to the moon,
vying with its light.
The third:
There is a mountain in the sea,
several tens of lǐ in circumference.
Every early summer,
a great snake appears, like a mountain a hundred rèn high,
its length unknown but spanning several hundred lǐ.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
the snake drank from the sea,
causing the water level to drop for over ten days.
As if extremely thirsty,
it coiled itself around a mountain dozens of times,
then lowered its head to drink water.
After a long time,
it was swallowed by a huge creature in the sea.
About half a day later,
the mountain,
then split apart,
and both the snake and the mountain were completely swallowed—
it remains unknown what creature did the swallowing.
The Whale
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
in Léizhōu, a thunder god fought with a whale.
The whale emerged from the water,
while dozens of thunder gods darted up and down in the sky,
some unleashing fire,
others hurling curses and strikes.
The battle lasted seven days before ceasing.
Coastal residents went to watch,
unable to tell which side prevailed,
but they saw the sea turn crimson.
The Carp
During the Kāiyuán era,
in Tāizhōu, by the sea,
a great snake fought with a carp.
The snake was as large as a house,
coiling several times around a solitary island,
stretching its head toward the water.
The fish was like a small hill,
with red fins and eyes,
moving back and forth over five or six lǐ,
posturing for mutual attacks.
The fish used its scales and fins to strike the snake from above,
while the snake bit at the fish from below with its mouth.
They fought like this for three days,
and in the end, the snake was struck dead by the fish.
The Mermaid
They exist in the Eastern Sea.
The larger ones are five or six chǐ long,
shaped like humans,
with eyebrows, eyes, mouth, nose, hands, claws, and head all resembling beautiful women—
nothing is lacking.
Their skin and flesh are white as jade,
without scales,
but with fine hair,
multicolored, light, and soft,
one or two cùn long.
Their hair is like a horse’s tail,
five or six chǐ long.
Their genitalia are no different from those of men and women.
Widowers and widows along the coast often capture them
and raise them in ponds or marshes.
During mating,
they are no different from humans,
and they do not harm people.
The Great Crab of the Southern Sea
In recent times, there was a Persian who often said that
he had sailed by ship across the sea,
traveling to the land of India six or seven times already.
On his final voyage,
the ship drifted into the great ocean,
not knowing how many thousands of miles it went,
until it reached a sea island.
On the island, he saw a foreigner dressed in grass and leaves,
and, frightened, asked him about it.
