The foreigner said
that in the past, he and several dozen companions had been shipwrecked and drowned,
and only he himself had followed the current
and managed to reach this place.
Thus, he gathered tree fruits and grass roots to eat,
which allowed him to survive.
The crew pitied him,
so they took him aboard the ship.
The foreigner then explained
that the great mountains on the island were all made of chariot-axle jade, agate, glass, and other various treasures,
too numerous to count.
The sailors all abandoned their own cheap goods to gather them.
Once the ship was full,
the foreigner urged them to depart quickly,
saying that if the mountain spirit arrived,
it would certainly regret the loss.
So they hoisted the sails with the wind,
and sailed about forty-some miles,
when from afar they saw a red object on the peak, shaped like a snake,
which gradually grew larger over time.
The foreigner said:
"This is the mountain spirit regretting the loss of its treasures,
coming to pursue us.
What shall we do about it?"
The sailors were all trembling with fear.
Suddenly, they saw two mountains emerge from the sea,
hundreds of zhang high.
The foreigner joyfully said:
"These two mountains
are the great crab's claws.
This crab often likes to fight with the mountain spirit,
and the spirit mostly cannot defeat it,
and fears it greatly.
Now that its claws have emerged,
we have nothing to worry about."
The great snake soon reached the crab's location,
and they coiled and fought for a long time.
The crab clamped the snake's head,
and it died on the water,
looking like a chain of mountains.
The ship's crew thereby managed to escape.
Sea manta ray
The sea manta ray fish
is the mightiest creature on the sea;
even the smaller ones are over a thousand chi long.
The saying that it can swallow boats
is certainly not false.
Every year,
Guǎngzhōu regularly dispatches copper ships.
When the ships pass Nán'ān for trade,
northerners occasionally seek to join this voyage.
After a round trip of one year,
their hair becomes streaked with white.
It is said that
along the route, passing Tiáolí,
In the deep and broad areas,
they also see more than ten mountains,
sometimes emerging, sometimes submerging,
which initially caused great astonishment.
The polemen said:
"Those are not mountains,
but sea
They are the backs of manta ray fish."
Indeed, they saw two eyes flashing,
and fins like winnowing baskets.
At this critical and perilous moment,
in the middle of the day, a sudden drizzle fell.
The boatmen said:
"This is the manta ray fish spraying water;
the water disperses in the air,
and the wind blows it over like rain."
When they approached the fish,
they immediately drummed on the boat and shouted,
and in an instant, it submerged and left.
Returning from Jiāozhǐ,
they then abandoned the boat,
took the route along the coast of Léizhōu to return,
not fearing hardship and toil,
all to avoid the danger of the sea manta ray.
Then, calmly reflecting, they said:
"If the old manta ray were to glare and open its mouth,
our boat would be like a leaf falling into a dry well.
How could one not grow white-haired from this?"
Crocodile,
its body is earth-yellow in color,
has four legs,
a long tail,
and its shape resembles that of a Chinese alligator,
but its movements are agile and swift.
Its mouth is densely lined with saw-like teeth,
and it often harms people.
In the southern regions, deer are numerous,
and they fear this creature the most.
When deer run on the cliffs and banks above,
groups of crocodiles roar below them,
and the deer inevitably become terrified and fall off the cliffs,
often caught by the crocodiles.
This is also an example of one creature subduing another.
Therefore, when Grand Tutor and Chancellor Lǐ Déyù was demoted to Cháozhōu,
passing through Crocodile Shoal,
his boat was damaged,
and all his lifelong precious curios,
ancient books and paintings,
were lost to the depths at once.
He then summoned the Kunlun slaves from the ship to retrieve them,
but they saw an extreme number of crocodiles,
and did not dare to approach casually.
This was indeed the lair of the crocodiles.
Wúyú kuài fish
King Sūn Quán of Wú once traveled on the river,
and after eating sliced fish, there were leftovers,
so he threw them into the midstream,
and they transformed into fish.
Today, there is a fish still called the Wúyú kuài,
several cun long,
as large as a chopstick,
still resembling the shape of sliced fish.
Stone-head fish,
shaped like a manta ray fish.
Regardless of its size,
there are two stone-like objects in its brain,
resembling buckwheat grains.
They are lustrous and white like jade.
There are curious people
who often buy smaller specimens of this fish,
store them in bamboo containers,
and let them rot.
Then they wash them,
take the stone-like objects from the fish's brain,
and use them to plant wine tallies,
which is considered quite refined.
Yellow wax fish,
also known as the horizontal fish of rivers and lakes.
Its head and mouth are long,
its scales are all golden in color.
When sliced and roasted,
it is delicious but poisonous.
Sometimes it is fried and dried,
and at night it emits light like a lantern candle.
There was a northerner residing in the South Sea
who bought this fish to eat,
and discarded its head into a waste basket.
After midnight,
there was suddenly a glow,
and upon closer inspection,
he became even more frightened.
When he illuminated it with a candle,
it was only the fish head,
but when the candle was removed, it glowed again.
Thinking it ominous,
they each opened their food boxes,
and looked at the remaining slices,
which also glowed like fireflies.
At dawn,
they inquired extensively among the locals,
and learned that this was normal for this fish,
so their worries and doubts were immediately dispelled.
Cuttlefish
The cuttlefish,
was formerly called Hé Bó Cóng Shì (River Earl's Assistant).
When a small one encounters a large fish,
it immediately releases ink covering an area of several square feet to conceal itself.
Some people from Jiāngdōng take its ink to write contracts,
in order to swindle others of their property.
The writing appears like faint ink,
and after a year the characters vanish,
leaving only blank paper.
Seafaring people say,
that in the past, the Qín Emperor traveled east,
and discarded his counting bag into the sea,
which transformed into this fish.
Its shape resembles a counting bag,
with two extremely long straps.
Another account says,
the cuttlefish has an anchor,
and when it encounters wind, one of its tentacles lowers the anchor.
Héng Gōng Fish
In the northern wilderness, there is a Stone Lake,
a thousand *li* square,
with banks over five *zhàng* deep.
It is perpetually frozen,
thawing only for about fifty or sixty days around the summer solstice.
There is a Héng Gōng fish,
seven or eight *chǐ* long,
shaped like a carp but red in color.
By day it stays in the water,
at night it transforms into a human.
It cannot be pierced,
and will not die if boiled.
If boiled with two black plums, it will die.
Eating it can stop evil illnesses.
Gǔ Léi
The country of Fúnán produces crocodiles,
the large ones being twenty or thirty *zhàng* long,
with four legs,
resembling a gecko in appearance.
They often swallow people alive.
The King of Fúnán ordered people to catch these fish,
and placed them in a moat,
throwing criminals into it.
If they deserved death,
the crocodile would eat them;
if they were innocent,
the crocodile would sniff but not eat them.
The crocodile has another name, Hū Léi.
Bears can subdue them.
They grab their snouts and drag them to shore,
tearing them apart to eat.
It is also called Gǔ Léi.
In autumn, it transforms into a tiger,
with three claws.
It appears in Sīléi and other prefectures of the Southern Sea,
and is common in the Yīng Pān village by the sea.
Péng Kuò
A type of crab is named Péng Kuò.
It uses its pincers to take mud and make pellets,
from when the tide comes in until it goes out,
sometimes making three hundred pellets,
hence it is also called the Three Hundred Pellet Great Péng Kuò.
Líng Fish
The Líng fish sticks out its tongue,
ants cling to it,
and it then swallows them.
It also opens its scales,
letting ants enter inside,
then suddenly shakes vigorously,
and then licks them up.
Ní Fish
Southwest of Jīnyì Ridge,
there is Pánlóng Mountain.
The mountain has a stalactite cave,
slantingly traversed by a stream,
named the Líng Shuǐ Stream.
Within the stream are fish,
all with long tails and four feet,
red bellies,
swimming calmly.
Fishermen dare not catch them.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"The Ní resembles a catfish,
has four feet,
and its cry is like a small child's."
Jīnshāng
Prefecture's streams also have this fish,
where it is called the Nà fish.
Flatfish,
Southerners call it the shoe-sole fish,
in Jiāng-Huái it is called the sand-dragging fish.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"In the east there is the flatfish,
which cannot move unless paired,
its name is called Dié."
Its shape resembles an ox spleen,
with fine purple scales,
one side, one eye,
two pieces must join together to move.
Lùzǐ Fish,
□ color,
its tail and fins all have deer-like spots,
reddish-yellow.
The *Luózhōu Tújīng* says:
"In the sea south of the prefecture, there is an islet.
Every spring and summer,
this fish jumps onto the islet,
and transforms into a deer."
Someone once picked up a fish,
its head had already turned into a deer,
but its tail was still a fish's.
Southerners say:
"When a fish transforms into a deer,
the meat is rank,
and cannot be eaten."
Zǐ Guī Mǔ (Offspring Return to Mother)
Yáng Fú's *Jiāozhōu Yìwù Zhì* says:
"Regarding the shark as a fish,
once its offspring are reared,
if frightened they must return to the mother,
going back into her belly.
When small they do this,
when large they no longer do."
The *Pānzhōu Jì* says:
"The Yúxī fish is two *zhàng* long,
several arm-spans in girth.
When it first gives birth,
the offspring are small,
and follow the mother to seek food.
If frightened at dusk, they return into the mother's belly."
The *Wú Lù* says:
"The offspring of the Yúxī fish
go out in the morning to seek food,
and return to the mother's belly at dusk."
The *Nányuè Zhì* says:
"At dusk they enter from the navel,
at dawn they exit from the mouth."
The crucian carp,
has markings like a tiger.
It is commonly said,
if it is not cooked thoroughly,
those who eat it will surely die.
This has been passed down as a constant truth.
In Ráozhōu, there was a man named Wú,
whose family was very prosperous,
and his wife's family was also wealthy.
The couple lived in harmony,
never having any discord,
Once,
one day,
Wú returned home drunk,
threw himself onto the bed,
and his wife straightened his clothes and removed his shoes,
lifting his feet.
The drunk man moved about,
accidentally hitting his wife in the chest,
and his wife suddenly fell dead,
but the drunk man did not know.
He was immediately seized and abused by his wife's family,
who said,
He had beaten her to death.
The lawsuit dragged on for years,
and the prefectural authorities could not resolve it,
so the matter was reported to the emperor.
Wú's relatives,
fearing that when the imperial decree arrived, he would surely face severe punishment,
which would bring shame upon the entire clan,
fed him raw crucian carp in prison.
After doing this several times,
it ultimately did not harm him,
and he became even more robust and cheerful.
Soon after, he was pardoned and released.
After returning home,
his descendants flourished,
and he lived to the age of eighty,
eventually dying of old age.
Moreover, if it is not cooked thoroughly,
it can still kill people,
yet he ate it raw several times,
and it did not harm him.
Was this his fate?
Jìyú
In the southeastern sea, there is a place called Zǔzhōu,
where the jìyú fish is found.
It is eight feet long,
and eating it is suitable for relieving summer heat and avoiding wind.
The appearance of this fish
is similar to the small jìyú found in rivers and lakes.
In Xúnyáng, there is Qīnglín Lake,
where the larger jìyú are over two feet long,
and the smaller ones are a full foot long.
They are delicious to eat,
and can also relieve chills and fever.
□ fish,
Northeast of Jǐnán Commandery, there is a □ pit.
It is said that
during the Jǐngmíng era of the Wèi dynasty,
someone dug a well and found a fish,
as large as a mirror.
That night,
river water flooded into this pit,
and the people living in the pit
all turned into □ fish.
Huánghóng fish
The huánghóng fish,
is yellow in color and has no scales.
Its head is pointed,
and its body resembles a large oak leaf.
Its mouth is under its jaw,
and behind its eyes are ears,
with openings connected to the brain.
Its tail is one foot long,
ending in three spines,
which are very poisonous.
□ chóng juàn
The □ chóng juàn,
commonly called Zīyí,
is a giant among mountain turtles.
A person can stand on its back,
and it can carry them as it walks.
It is found in the mountains of Cháoxún,
where locals capture it,
and take its shell to sell.
To keep the shell intact,
they must use wooden wedges to remove the flesh.
The turtle roars like an ox,
and its sound echoes through the valleys.
In Guǎngzhōu, there are skilled craftsmen
who take its shell, which is yellow, translucent, and free of sunspots,
boil and flatten it,
and inlay it with black tortoiseshell patterns,
to make combs, cups, and other utensils,
which are very beautiful.
Hǎiyàn
In Shípǔ of Qíjiānguān County, there is a sea fish,
that rides the tides to and fro,
over thirty zhang long,
black and scaleless,
and its sound is like that of an ox.
The locals call it hǎiyàn.
Jiāoyú
The jiāoyú is found in Hépǔ,
three zhang long,
with armor on its back,
and pearls.
Its patterns are hard and strong,
and can be used to decorate knife blades,
or to file objects.
Fēngzhōu fish
In Fēngzhōu, there is a waterway
that flows from Tǔbō,
cold as ice and snow in summer.
There are fish one or two cun long,
that come and go at certain times,
covering the water like porridge.
People catch and cook them to eat,
and even if thousands of households take them, they cannot be exhausted.
It is unknown where they come from.
Sea shrimp
A man named Liú Xún once boarded a sea vessel,
entered the helm cabin,
and suddenly saw two giant shrimp shells hanging on the window board.
Their heads, tails, pincers, and legs were all intact,
each seven or eight feet long.
The head accounted for one part,
the mouth was sharp as a blade,
and above the mouth were whiskers like red chopsticks,
each two or three feet long.
The legs had pincers,
as thick as a person's thumb,
over two feet long,
with thorns like rose branches,
red, sharp, and hard,
untouchable by hand.
The brain shell was hollowed out,
curved over a foot long,
far more than just a cup or bowl.
The "Běi Hù Lù" states:
"When Téng Xún was the governor of Guǎngzhōu,
a guest told Xún:
'There are shrimp whiskers as long as one zhang,
suitable for use as walking sticks.'
Xún did not believe it,
so the guest went to the Eastern Sea,
brought back a four-foot-long whisker to show Xún,
and only then did Xún acknowledge its extraordinariness."
Wǎ wūzi,
are a type of clam or mussel,
formerly called hānzi in the southern regions.
Recently, because Shàngshū Lú Jūn governed the area,
they were renamed wǎ wūzi,
as their shells have ridges like roof tiles,
hence the name.
Inside the shell is flesh,
purple and filling the belly,
still highly valued by the people of Guǎng,
often roasted to accompany wine,
commonly called tiān luán zhì.
Eating too much causes bloating,
and pain in the back and shoulders,
but its nature is not fully understood.
Yìnyú,
one foot three cun long,
with a square mark on its forehead like a seal,
bearing characters.
When large fish are destined to die,
it first stamps them with this seal.
Stone Grouper
Sēng Xíngrú said,
In Jiànzhōu there is a stone grouper,
which likes to mate with snakes.
In the southern regions there are many wasp nests,
the nests are as large as pots,
and they often swarm to sting people.
The locals take stone groupers and roast them beside the wasp nests,
then tie them to poles,
facing the sun,
so that the fish's shadow falls on the nest.
In a short while,
hundreds of birds as large as swallows
attack the nest in turn,
shattering it into pieces like leaves,
and the wasps are completely wiped out.
Well Fish
Duàn Chéngshì of the Táng dynasty said,
The well fish has a cavity in its brain.
Whenever it inhales water,
it spurts it out from the brain cavity,
like a flying spring,
scattering into the sea.
Boatmen compete to collect it with empty vessels.
Seawater is salty and bitter,
but after passing through the fish's brain cavity,
it becomes as fresh as spring water.
Chéngshì heard this from the Indian monk Shàntíshèng.
Strange Fish
People of the Eastern Sea often catch a fish
five or six feet long,
with stomach and intestines shaped like Hu-style knives and spears.
Some call it the Qínhuáng fish.
Pángpī
A large fish by the sea,
with twelve stones on its back marking the hours.
Also called Lítóunì,
or Pángpī.
Its urine is very poisonous.
Eel
A certain Mr. Hóu from Píxiàn
caught an eel in a hemp-soaking pond.
It was about a foot in girth.
He cooked and ate it,
and his white hair turned black again,
his lost teeth regrew,
and from then on he felt light and vigorous.
Hawksbill Turtle
The hawksbill turtle resembles a tortoise in shape,
but its belly and back shells have speckled patterns.
The *Běncǎo* says:
"The hawksbill detoxifies.
The larger ones are called Pósuō stones,
and are also said to ward off evil."
In Guǎngnán, a Lútíng man
captured a live hawksbill turtle and presented it to Regional Commander Sì Xuēwáng.
The prince ordered two small pieces to be taken from its back shell while alive,
and wore them on his left arm to ward off poison.
The turtle suffered greatly
from having its shell peeled off alive.
Later, it was kept in the northern pond behind the commander's residence,
waiting for the peeled area to gradually regenerate,
and then the Lútíng man was sent to return it to the seashore.
Some say
that if the hawksbill is alive,
wearing its shell is effective:
if there is poison in the food or drink,
the hawksbill shell will shake on its own;
if it is dead,
this effect is lost.
Hǎishù
In the Southern Sea there is a sea creature
with a long left front limb
and a short right front limb.
Its mouth is on its side near the back.
It often uses its left limb to grasp things,
places them in its right limb,
where teeth in the right limb chew them,
before putting them into its mouth.
It is over three feet in size,
and makes a "shù shù" sound,
so southerners call it Hǎishù.
Sea Mirror
People of Guǎng call it Gāoyè.
It consists of two plates
that join to form its shape.
The shell is round,
and very smooth and translucent inside.
When the sun
shines on it, it glows like mica.
Inside there is a little flesh like a clam's embryo,
and in its belly there is a small red crab,
as small as a soybean,
but with fully formed pincers.
When the sea mirror is hungry,
the crab comes out to gather food.
When the crab is full and returns to the belly,
the sea mirror is also full.
If pressured by fire,
the little crab will come out,
and once it leaves the gut, the sea mirror dies immediately.
If cut open alive,
with the crab still alive in its belly,
it too will die shortly after.
Jellyfish
In Guǎngzhōu it is called shuǐmǔ,
in Mǐn it is called tuō.
Its form is a congealed mass,
some pale purple,
some white.
Large ones are like overturned hats,
small ones like bowls.
Below its gut are things like hanging floss,
commonly called feet,
but it has no mouth or eyes.
Often several dozen shrimp dwell beneath it,
sucking its fluids.
It floats on the water.
When encountered by hunters,
it suddenly sinks and disappears,
which is actually the shrimp sensing something.
In the southern regions people like to eat it,
saying it is warming in nature,
and cures illnesses from river fish.
But it is very fishy,
and must be washed repeatedly with plant ash and raw oil
until clean and translucent like crystal or purple jade.
The flesh can be up to two inches thick,
with thinner parts also over an inch.
First boil pepper, cassia, or nutmeg,
shred ginger and fry it,
or use five-spice meat vinegar,
or shrimp vinegar,
and eat it like sliced raw fish.
Shrimp vinegar is best,
as things of the same kind attract each other.
Jellyfish is originally a congealed substance from the yin sea,
yet eating it is warming and tonic.
The reason for this is unclear.
Crab
In the eighth month, crabs have awns inside their bellies.
The awns are truly like rice awns,
about an inch long.
They are offered eastward to the sea god.
Before offering the awns,
they cannot be eaten.
Centipede Crab
The land of Shànyuàn produces the centipede crab,
nine feet long,
with four pincers.
Boiled into glue,
it is called pincer glue,
superior to phoenix beak glue.
Táng Crab
The commandery of Píngyuán offered Táng crab as tribute,
collected from the Héjiān region,
presented annually.
They cut ice and use torchlight,
hang old dog meat,
and when crabs sense the dog meat they surface,
and are thus caught.
One is worth a hundred coins.
Wrapped tightly in felt and tied to a post horse,
they are rushed to the capital.
The 𝌖 fish is produced in Zhāng'ān County.
The 𝌖 fry go out in the morning to seek food,
and return in the evening into their mother's belly,
which can accommodate four fry.
Their cheeks are red like gold,
and they are very vigorous;
nets cannot restrain them.
Commonly they are called "Hé Bó's sturdy children."
The parrot conch:
its spiraled, pointed end is curved like a beak,
resembling a parrot's mouth,
hence it is named thus.
Its shell has blue-green patterns;
the larger ones can hold two shēng.
The inside of the shell is glossy and translucent like mica.
Made into wine cups,
they are exotic and delightful.
The red conch:
its size is also similar to the parrot conch.
The shell is thin and red,
and can also be used as a wine vessel.
Carving small conches to serve as feet,
and attaching them with glue and lacquer,
makes them especially fine and esteemed.
Mandarin duck turtle:
In the villages of Chūníng County, there are many mandarin duck turtles.
Their shells are thin, narrow, and dry;
their heads resemble geese,
different from ordinary turtles,
and they can bite dogs.
Salamander fish:
The salamander fish is like a catfish,
with four legs and a long tail;
it can climb trees.
During droughts,
it carries water up the mountain,
covers itself with grass and leaves,
opens its mouth,
and when birds come to drink the water,
it sucks them in and eats them.
Its cry is like that of a small child.
People in the gorges eat it,
first tying it to a tree and whipping it
until a white fluid comes out from its body,
like gou juice;
only after removing this can it be eaten,
otherwise it is poisonous.
Horseshoe crab:
The female horseshoe crab often carries the male on her back when moving.
Fishermen always catch them in pairs.
Southerners display them in shops for sale;
the males have little meat.
An old account says
that when crossing the sea, they pile up on each other's backs,
reaching a height of one chǐ,
like a sail,
riding the wind to travel.
Nowadays, on horseshoe crab shells there is a growth,
seven or eight cùn high,
like stone coral,
commonly called "horseshoe crab sail."
To this day, in Mǐn and Lǐng regions, horseshoe crab paste is highly valued.
They have twelve legs;
their shells can be made into hats,
second only to white horn.
Southerners take their tails to make small rúyì scepters.
Flying fish:
In Lǎng Mountain and Lǎng River there are flying fish.
The fish are one chǐ long and can fly;
when active they soar into the clouds and sky,
when resting they return to the pool bottom.
Tiger crab:
Its shell has tiger-like stripes;
it can be fashioned into wine vessels.
Along with the red crab, both are produced along the shores of Qióngyá.
Although not rare treasures,
they are also not easily gathered.
Oyster:
The oyster is the oyster.
When first growing on seashore islands,
it is like a fist-sized stone,
gradually expanding on all sides.
Some grow as high as one or two zhàng,
jagged like mountains.
Inside each chamber,
there is one piece of oyster meat,
varying in size depending on its growth stage.
Every time the tide comes in,
all the oysters open their chambers,
waiting for insects and ants to enter,
then close them.
The coastal barbarians known as Lútíng use axes and wedges to pry open the shells,
burn them with fierce fire,
and the oysters then open their chambers.
They pick out the meat,
store it in small bamboo baskets,
and go to the market
to exchange for xīgǔ rice.
Larger oyster meat is salted and roasted,
smaller ones are stir-fried;
the meat has a flavorful taste.
Eating too much of it
blocks the intestines and bones.
Red grass carp lord:
Along the carp's spine there is a row of scales;
each scale has a black dot.
All, large and small, have thirty-six scales.
According to Táng dynasty law,
if one catches a carp,
one should release it immediately,
and still must not eat it.
It is said that for selling the red grass carp lord,
the seller is sentenced to sixty strokes.
Thunder cave fish:
In Xīng Prefecture there is a place called Thunder Cave.
The water usually fills half the cave.
Whenever there is thunder,
water blocks the cave and flows out,
and fish follow the current out.
The common people often wait for the thunder,
spread nets around the trees,
and catch unlimited numbers of fish.
If there is no thunder,
fishermen gather and beat drums at the cave mouth,
and fish also come out,
but the catch is half that during thunder.
When Wéi Xíngguī was governor of Xīng Prefecture,
he wrote to relatives and old friends,
relating this matter.
Dragon tail:
In the Eastern Sea there is a fish
with a dragon tail resembling a hawk;
when it stirs the waves, rain falls.
Thus its image is placed on roof ridges.
Ox fish:
Ox fish skin is taken from the sea and hung up;
when the sea tide comes,
its hair stands on end.
Stone crab:
The larger ones are over one chǐ long;
their two claws are extremely strong.
In the eighth month they can fight tigers,
and the tigers are no match.
They molt with the high tide,
shedding once and growing once.
Bēn fú:
Also called jì,
it is neither fish nor flood dragon.
As large as a boat,
two or three zhàng long,
resembling a catfish,
it has two teats on its underside;
male and female, yīn and yáng, are like humans.
If you take its young and place them on shore,
they cry like infants.
There is a hole on its neck
that connects to the head;
air comes out with a hissing sound.
This surely means strong winds;
travelers use it as an omen.
Legend says it is transformed from a lazy woman.
Killing one yields
three or four hú of oil.
Taking it to burn in lamps,
it dims when used for reading or spinning,
but shines brightly in places of joy and pleasure.
Arm-binding fish.
The turtle-like creature,
when going into the sea to catch it,
one must first make offerings.
Then, by stating the number to be taken,
they will emerge on their own,
and thus can be captured.
If one does not keep faith,
then wind and waves will capsize the boat.
The Rooster-Beaked Fish
When Lǐ Déyù was young,
he often saw an aquatic creature in Míngzhōu,
which had two legs,
a beak like a rooster,
and a body like a fish.
The Sword Fish
A sea fish that lives a thousand years becomes a sword fish,
also called the pipa fish,
shaped like a pipa and fond of singing,
hence the name.
The tiger fish, when old, becomes a jiāo;
small fish in rivers,
which transform into locusts and devour the five grains,
after a hundred years become rats.
The Lazy Woman Fish
In Huáinán, there is a lazy woman fish.
Folklore says
that in the past, a woman of the Yáng family,
angered by her mother-in-law,
drowned and became a fish.
Its fat can be used to light lamps and candles.
If used to illuminate drumming, playing the qín or sè, or board games,
it shines brilliantly,
but if used to illuminate spinning and weaving,
it does not glow again.
Yellow Sparrows Transforming into Clams
In the Huái River,
yellow sparrows transform into clams in autumn,
and in spring, they become yellow sparrows again.
Sparrows, after five hundred years, transform into giant clams.
The Tiānniú Fish,
three zhàng in length and width,
eyes as large as dou measures,
mouth under the ribs,
exposing teeth without lips,
two fleshy horns like arms,
two wings six chǐ long,
tail five chǐ long.
Xià Gǔn
Yáo commanded Xià Gǔn to control the floods,
but after nine years, there was no success.
Gǔn drowned himself in the Yǔyuān,
transforming into a black fish.
At times, raising its head and shaking its scales, it swam across the waves.
Those who saw it called it the river spirit,
for the Yǔyuān connects to the sources of rivers and seas.
People of antiquity built a temple for Gǔn at the foot of Yǔshān,
offering sacrifices in all four seasons.
Often, this black fish was seen emerging with jiāolóng, frolicking in the water.
Onlookers were startled and awed.
When Shùn commanded Yǔ,
to dredge rivers and stabilize mountains,
he traveled everywhere under the sun and moon,
only avoiding the land of Yǔshān.
When crossing vast seas, giant turtles served as bridges;
when traversing steep mountains, divine dragons carried him on their backs.
All were moved by his sage virtue.
As for Gǔn's transformation,
accounts vary,
though the divine transformation is consistent,
the color and form differ.
Black fish, yellow bear—
the four sounds are easily confused,
errors arose in transmission and transcription,
so it is briefly recorded here.
The Man from the Eastern Sea
In the past, a man traveled the Eastern Sea.
When fierce winds wrecked his boat,
he could not repair it in time,
and adrift with wind and waves,
he knew not where he was headed.
After a day and a night,
he reached a solitary islet,
and his companions rejoiced.
They dropped anchor and moored,
went ashore to cook food,
but before the food was done, the islet sank.
Those on the boat cut the mooring ropes,
and the boat drifted again.
The former solitary islet
was actually a giant fish.
It inhaled and exhaled waves,
moving swiftly as the wind.
Over ten people died on that islet.
The Kūnmíng Pond,
had a stone-carved whale.
Whenever thunder and rain came,
the fish would often roar,
its head and tail moving.
In the Hàn dynasty, sacrifices were made to it to pray for rain,
often with results.
Xú Jǐngshān
Emperor Míng of Wèi was touring the Luò River,
where several white otters were in the water,
beautiful, clean, and adorable,
but they fled at the sight of people.
The emperor wished to catch them,
but could not succeed.
Attendant Xú Jǐngshān memorialized:
"I have heard that otters are fond of zīyú,
and will not avoid death for them.
We can use this to deceive them."
He then painted two zīyú on a board,
and hung it on the shore.
Thereupon, the otters competed to chase them,
and were caught all at once.
The emperor greatly praised him,
saying:
"I have heard you are skilled at painting,
how is it so marvelous?"
He replied:
"I have never held a brush,
but what others create,
I can approximate!"
The emperor said:
"This is making good use of one's strengths."
Pān Huìyán
East of Gāoyuàn City in Píngyuán, there was a fish ford.
Legend says
that at the end of the Wèi dynasty,
Pān Fǔjūn of Píngyuán, styled Huìyán,
boarded a boat from Báimǎ to take up his post,
when his counting pouch
fell into the water.
The pouch originally contained one liǎng of stalactite.
After three years in the commandery,
the Jì River flooded,
and a fish was caught,
three zhàng long,
five chǐ wide.
When its belly was cut open,
the pouch that had fallen into the water earlier was found inside.
The golden needles were still there,
but the stalactite had completely dissolved.
From the fish, several tens of hú of fat were obtained,
and people of the time found it extraordinary.
Gě Xuán
Gě Xuán saw someone presenting a large fish.
Xuán said:
"I shall trouble this fish to go to the River Earl's place for a moment."
He then placed a cinnabar-inscribed paper into the fish's mouth
and threw it into the water.
After a while,
the fish returned, leaping onto the shore,
and spat out ink writing,
blue-black in color,
like wooden leaves, flying about.
Another time, Xuán was sitting in a tower with the King of Wú,
and saw people making clay figures to pray for rain.
Xuán said:
"Rain is easy to obtain."
He then wrote a talisman and placed it in the shrine.
In a short time,
heavy rain poured and flooded.
The emperor said:
"Are there fish in the water?"
Xuán wrote another talisman and threw it into the water.
In a moment,
hundreds of large fish appeared,
and he had people catch them to eat.
Jiè Xiàng
Jiè Xiàng and the King of Wú were discussing the deliciousness of mullet,
so they dug a pit in the palace courtyard,
filled it with water drawn from a well,
and requested a fishing rod.
Jiè Xiàng rose, baited the hook,
and in a moment,
caught a mullet.
The Emperor was amazed and delighted,
and ordered a cook to slice it for eating.
Lóngmén
Lóngmén Mountain is in the Hé dōng region.
Yǔ cut through the mountain to create a gateway,
which is wide.
Over a lǐ in breadth,
the Yellow River flows down through its center.
Carriages and horses cannot pass along its two banks.
Every year in late spring,
yellow carp swim upstream against the current,
and those that succeed transform into dragons.
Furthermore, Lín Dēng states,
that below Lóngmén,
every year in the last month of spring, yellow carp
come rushing from the sea and various rivers to gather there.
In a single year,
those that ascend Lóngmén
number no more than seventy-two.
Upon first ascending Lóngmén,
rain clouds immediately follow them,
and heavenly fire burns their tails from behind,
whereupon they transform into dragons.
The waters of Lóngmén are deep and surge like arrows,
flowing downstream for seven lǐ,
with a depth of three lǐ.
Fish in the Pond
The *Fēngsú Tōng* states:
"When the city gate catches fire,
disaster reaches the fish in the pond."
An old explanation says:
"Chí Zhòngyú is a person's name.
He lived by the Sòng city gate.
When the city gate caught fire,
the flames spread to his home,
and Chí Zhòngyú was burned to death."
Another account says,
when the Sòng city gate caught fire,
people drew water from the pond
to douse the flames,
emptying the pond completely.
The fish were all exposed and died.
This metaphor illustrates how the spread of evil
also harms the good and cautious.
Tōngchuān River
Within the boundaries of Tōngchuān there are many otters,
each owned and raised by someone,
all kept along the riverbanks.
If an otter enters its burrow,
inserting a pheasant tail feather in front of the otter hole
will prevent the otter from coming out.
Remove the tail feather, and it emerges.
After catching a fish,
it must come ashore,
whereupon people seize the fish from it.
It catches many fish,
and only then eats some itself.
Once full,
people clap a board to drive it back,
and reinsert the pheasant tail feather,
so it dares not come out again.
The Sea Voyager
Once, a man voyaging at sea came upon an island,
with very lush trees,
so he moored his boat and went ashore.
He made a fire by the water's edge,
but halfway through cooking, the forest sank into the water.
He hastily cut the mooring rope,
and thus managed to get away.
Upon closer inspection,
it was a giant crab.
Yin Fire
Fish and clams born in the sea,
when placed in a dark place, emit light.
Upon first seeing this,
one considers it strange and unusual.
Local people often deduce the reason,
which is that they are born of salt water.
When the sea is overcast and gloomy,
The waves appear as if aflame across the sea.
If you strike them with an object,
they scatter like sparks.
When there is moonlight, they are no longer visible.
Mù Xuánxū's "Rhapsody on the Sea" states:
"The yin fire flickers dimly."
Could this be what it refers to?
Péi Zhòu
Péi Zhòu of the Táng dynasty,
in the seventh year of the Kāiyuán era,
was appointed Military Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
During mid-autumn,
while the night water-clock had not yet run its course,
suddenly, dawn broke.
The stars and moon vanished,
and birds flew about chirping.
The entire commandery was astonished by this,
unable to explain it.
However, it was already daytime,
so Lord Péi dressed in his official robes and went out.
The military and administrative officers
had already gathered at his gate.
He hastily summoned his aides and guests.
When they arrived, they all found it strange,
but thought it a mass delusion,
insisting it could not truly be midnight turning to dawn.
He then inquired with the timekeeper,
who said:
"It is normally not yet the third watch of the night."
Lord Péi could not fathom the reason,
so he kept his guests in the main hall,
waiting together for the sun to rise.
After a long while,
the sky darkened again,
and the night scene returned as before.
The officials then returned home carrying candles.
The next morning,
Lord Péi convened a large assembly of the military and administrative staff,
seeking an explanation,
but no one could clarify it.
Péi then ordered messengers to inquire in all directions,
and the entire region reported the same phenomenon.
He then sent messengers north to inquire beyond the Xiāng Mountains.
North of the Xiāng Mountains,
there was no such event.
Several months later,
a merchant ship arrived from the distant south,
and its crew told the locals:
"On the night of the eleventh day of the eighth month,
while our ship was sailing,
we suddenly encountered a giant sea turtle emerging from the ocean.
It raised its head facing north,
and its two eyes were like suns,
illuminating a thousand lǐ.
The finest details were visible.
After a long time, it submerged again,
and the night darkness returned."
Checking the time,
it matched the night Lord Péi had gathered his guests and staff.
Wáng Mínzhī
When Táng Wáng Mín was at Láoshān,
he sent someone to inform Xǔ Chényán, the governor of Lángyá, saying:
"In the Shā Village of Línyí County in your jurisdiction,
there is a fish with reversed scales,
which is needed to prepare medicine.
I wish to meet with you, Governor, there."
Chényán agreed to this,
and then ordered Shā Village to prepare supplies
to await the arrival of the Great Harmony Master.
When the master met Chényán,
Chényán ordered fishermen to catch what was sought.
To the west of Shā Village there was a body of water,
several hundred paces from north to south,
and ten zhang from east to west,
its color was extremely deep black,
and on the shore stood a shrine.
The village elders told Chényán:
"Ten years ago,
a youth from the village hooked something in the water while fishing,
which was very large in appearance.
He could not pull it out,
so he cast dozens of fishing lines,
and only then managed to pull its head out.
It looked like a fierce beast,
with closed eyes,
as large as a carriage wheel.
The villagers thought it was dead,
so they bound it with ropes,
wrapped it around a tree,
and ten people pulled it together.
Suddenly, the fierce beast opened its eyes and gave a great shake,
its roar like thunder.
More than ten people near it were shaken to death,
and twenty others were terrified out of their wits and became afflicted,
after which the fierce beast returned to the water.
So we built this shrine to pray to it,
and it always responds to prayers for rain or drought.
As for a fish with reversed scales,
there has never been such a thing."
Chényán then stopped.
Hán Yù
Hán Wéngōng Yù, Vice Minister of Personnel of the Táng,
was demoted from Vice Minister of Justice to be the prefect of Cháoyáng.
Previously, to the west of the prefecture there was a large deep pool,
in which lived a crocodile,
about a hundred or so feet long.
Whenever it became angry, the water of the pool would surge and churn,
and the forests and hills would shake as if in an earthquake.
Whenever the people's horses or cattle approached the water,
it would suck them in and devour them,
and in the blink of an eye, all would be harmed,
with casualties too numerous to count,
and the people had suffered from this for years.
When Yù arrived to govern the prefecture,
on the third day after his arrival,
he asked the people about their grievances,
and they all said:
"It is the crocodile in the pool to the west of the prefecture."
Yù said:
"I have heard that utmost sincerity can move the gods.
In the past, when Lǔ Gōng governed Zhōngmóu,
pheasants became tame and locusts avoided the area;
when Huáng Bà governed Jiǔjiāng,
tigers all fled.
This shows that the influence of good governance
can indeed transform wild beasts."
He then ordered his court officer
to place sacrificial animals and wine beside the pool,
and prayed, saying:
"You are a creature of the water,
do not bring harm to the living."
Afterwards, he poured wine into the water.
That evening,
there was wind and thunder to the west of the prefecture,
the sound shaking the mountains and fields,
and by midnight it cleared.
The next day,
the villagers went to look at the pool,
and found the water had dried up.
Yù ordered someone to trace its path,
and sixty li to the west of the pool,
the land had changed to form a new pool,
and the giant crocodile had also moved there.
From then on, the people of the prefecture were spared this calamity.
Thus, Huángfǔ Shí, a former Vice Director of the Ministry of Works, wrote in his "Epitaph for Yù":
"When he served as prefect of Cháoyáng from the Ministry of Justice,
it is said that the cave-dwelling tribes and coastal barbarians
were all happily transformed;
crocodiles and rice crabs
no longer harmed the people or their property."
This refers to this event.
Yúnxiāng Villager
At the end of the Yuánhé era of the Táng,
there was a commoner in Yúnxiāng County, Jūnzhōu,
seventy years old,
who kept more than ten otters,
and made his living by catching fish.
He would release them every other day,
and before releasing them,
he would first confine them in a deep sluice gate,
making them hungry,
and then release them.
Without the labor of nets,
he gained substantial profit.
When he clapped his hands and called them,
the otters would all come.
They would climb onto his lap and knees,
as tame as guard dogs.
Lǐ Fú, Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue,
witnessed this personally.
Chìlǐng Stream
Below Chìlǐng in Shèzhōu, there is a large stream.
Folklore says that in the past, someone built a fish weir across the stream,
and the fish could not pass downstream,
so at midnight they flew over this ridge.
That person then set up nets on the ridge to catch them.
Some fish flew over the nets,
while others, unable to fly over, turned into stone.
Now, whenever it rains,
these stones turn red,
hence the name Chìlǐng (Red Ridge),
and Fúliáng County derived its name from this.
According to the "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú," it says:
"The patterned flying fish flies at night and touches the net."
This is likely the same kind of phenomenon.
Gǔn
Yáo sent Gǔn to control the floodwaters,
but he could not fulfill his duty,
so he was executed.
Gǔn at Yǔshān
transformed into a huángnéng,
and entered Yǔquán.
Nowadays, when people in Kuàijī sacrifice at the temple of Yǔ,
they do not use néng.
Those dwelling in water are called néng,
while those dwelling on land are called xióng.
Huán Chōng
When Jìn's Huán Chōng was the governor of Jiāngzhōu,
he sent someone to travel around Lúshān,
hoping to witness something miraculous.
After climbing a high peak,
they found a lake,
surrounded by mulberry trees.
In the lake was a wrecked boat and red-scaled fish.
The envoy was extremely thirsty
and wanted to go drink the water,
but the red-scaled fish raised their fins toward him,
and the envoy did not dare to drink.
Lǐ Tāng
In the dīngchǒu year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Gōngzuǒ of Lǒngxī was sailing on the Xiāo and Xiāng rivers and Cāngwú,
when he happened to meet Yáng Héng of Hóngnóng, an official on the southern expedition, who had moored his boat by an ancient shore.
They lingered at a Buddhist temple;
the river was empty, the moon floated,
and they spoke of strange and wondrous tales.
Yáng told Gōngzuǒ:
"During the Yǒngtài era,
when Lǐ Tāng served as prefect of Chǔ Prefecture,
there was a fisherman
who fished at night at the foot of Guī Mountain.
His fishing line became entangled with something,
and would not come out.
The fisherman, being a strong swimmer,
quickly dove down fifty zhàng.
He saw a great iron chain,
coiled around the mountain's base,
its end impossible to find.
He then reported it to Tāng.
Tāng ordered several dozen fishermen and skilled divers
to pull up the chain,
but their strength was insufficient to control it.
Adding over fifty oxen,
the chain finally began to move,
gradually coming toward the shore.
At that time, there was no wind or waves,
yet startling waves churned and surged,
terrifying the onlookers.
At the end of the chain,
a beast appeared,
shaped like an ape,
with a white head and long mane,
snowy fangs and golden claws.
It suddenly came ashore,
standing about five zhàng tall.
Its crouching posture was like that of an ape,
but its two eyes could not open,
dull as if in a daze.
Water flowed from its eyes and nose like springs,
its drool and foam were foul and stinking,
so that people could not approach.
After a long while, it stretched its neck and yawned;
its eyes suddenly opened,
their brilliance like lightning.
It looked around at the people,
as if about to burst into furious rage.
The onlookers fled.
The beast then slowly pulled the chain, dragging the oxen,
and went back into the water,
never to appear again.
At that time, Chǔ had many renowned scholars;
they and Tāng looked at each other in shock and fear,
not knowing the reason.
At that time,
Only the fisherman knew where the chain was,
but the beast was never seen again."
In the winter of the eighth year of the Yuánhé era, Gōngzuǒ,
while seeing off the court official Mèng □ from Chángzhōu to Zhūfāng,
was hosted with full courtesy by Provincial Inspector Xuē Píng.
At that time, Mǎ Zhí of Fúfēng, Lú Jiǎnnéng of Fànyáng, and Péi Qú of Hédōng were all staying at the same lodge;
they gathered around the stove and talked throughout the night.
Gōngzuǒ again recounted the earlier event,
just as Yáng had described.
In the spring of the ninth year,
Gōngzuǒ visited ancient sites in Eastern Wú,
sailing on Dòngtíng Lake with Prefect Yuán Xī,
ascending Bāo Mountain,
and lodging at the hermitage of the Daoist Zhōu Jiāo.
Entering a spiritual cave,
they searched for immortal texts,
and among the stone crevices found the eighth volume of the ancient "Classic of Mountains and Waterways."
The writing was ancient and strange,
the binding moth-eaten and damaged,
and they could not understand it.
Gōngzuǒ and Master Jiāo studied it carefully together:
"When Yǔ regulated the waters,
he came three times to Tóngbǎi Mountain.
Fierce winds raced and thunder roared;
stones howled and trees cried out.
The Five Earls held back the rivers,
the Celestial Elders marshaled troops,
but they could not proceed.
Yǔ grew angry,
summoned all the spirits,
and ordered a search for Kuí and Lóng.
The many lords of Tóngbǎi bowed and begged for their lives.
Yǔ then imprisoned Hóngméngshì, Zhāngshāngshì, Dōulúshì, and Lílóushì.
He then captured the water deity of the Huái and Guō rivers,
named Wúzhīqí,
who was skilled in speech and response,
and knew the depths of the Jiāng and Huái,
and the distances of plains and marshes.
Its form was like an ape,
with a contracted nose and high forehead,
a blue body and white head,
golden eyes and snowy fangs.
Its neck stretched a hundred chǐ,
its strength surpassed nine elephants.
It fought, leaped, and ran swiftly,
light and agile in an instant,
so that one could not gaze at it for long.
Yǔ gave it the Zhānglǜ,
but could not control it;
he gave it the Wūmùyóu,
but could not control it;
he gave it to Gēngchén,
who could control it.
Owls, spleen-demons, tree-spirits, water-nymphs, mountain-goblins, and stone-monsters
gathered and swarmed for several decades,
but Gēngchén fought and drove them away.
He locked its neck with a great rope,
pierced its nose with a golden bell,
and moved it to the foot of Guī Mountain in Huáiyīn,
so that the Huái River would forever flow peacefully into the sea.
After Gēngchén,
all who depicted this form
were spared from the calamities of Huái's waves, wind, and rain."
Thus, what Lǐ Tāng saw,
and what Yáng Héng recounted,
matched the "Classic of Mountains and Waterways."
Qí Huàn
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Qí Huàn, the investigative commissioner of Hénán and prefect of Biànzhōu, due to the perilous urgency of Xúchéng,
petitioned to dig an eighteen-lǐ canal,
reaching to the Qīng River.
The canal was dug section by section by each prefecture and county.
Cuī Yánhuī, the assistant magistrate of Zhēnyuán County in Bózhōu, supervised the laborers of his county,
and after digging several thousand steps,
they discovered a dragon hall.
At first, they thought it was an empty cave,
but it appeared newly built,
clean and spacious all around.
Under the north wall lay a five-colored hibernating dragon,
over one zhàng long,
with five or six carp,
each a chǐ long.
There were also two-headed spirit turtles,
one chǐ two cùn long,
with eyes nine fēn long.
Huī reported this to Wū Yuánchāng, the inspector of the canal project,
who submitted a report to Qí Huàn.
Huàn ordered the dragon moved into the Huái River,
and the turtles released into the Biàn River.
Huī moved the dragon and fish over two hundred lǐ,
to the banks of the Huái,
where millions of fish
leaped toward the dragon,
causing the water to boil.
The dragon entered the Huái, spouting water,
and clouds and mist grew dark and obscure;
it was never seen again.
When they were about to move it,
Inspector Yuán Xī plucked one of its whiskers.
Yuánchāng sent someone to deliver the turtles to Sòng,
but when they encountered a body of water,
they temporarily released the turtles into the water.
The water was only a few chǐ wide,
and no more than five cùn deep,
yet the large turtle disappeared.
They drained the water to search for it,
but could not find it,
only retrieving a small turtle.
Zǐ Yīngchūn
Zǐ Yīngchūn
was a man of Shūxiāng,
skilled in entering water.
He caught a red carp,
and admiring its color,
took it home,
and raised it in a pond.
He fed it rice and grain repeatedly;
after a year,
it grew over a zhàng long,
and grew horns and wings.
Zǐ Yīng was frightened,
and bowed in apology.
The fish said:
"I have come to welcome you.
Climb onto my back,
and I will ascend with you."
Each year, he returned to see his wife and children,
and the fish would welcome him again.
Thus, in Wú, households made shrines to the spirit fish Zǐ Yīng.
The Boy of Luò River
Someone saw a stable boy washing horses in the Luòshuǐ River.
After a short while,
he saw a creature like a white silk ribbon,
extremely bright and glistening,
wrap around the stable boy’s neck two or three times,
and the boy immediately fell into the water and died.
Such creatures are found everywhere in water and near bays and moorings.
People who die while bathing or washing horses
are all said to be dragged away by yuán (soft-shelled turtles),
but that is not true.
This creature is called báitè,
and one should be careful to guard against it—
it is a type of jiāo (flood dragon).
CH0F01A0 & - ;Ghost
The guì fish resembles the lǐ fish,
with red-spotted patterns,
and can grow over a foot long.
It is found in the Yùzhāng region.
They often dwell in muddy ponds,
sometimes numbering in the hundreds.
CH0F01A0 They can create ghostly illusions and strange phenomena,
and can also bewitch people.
Near their muddy ponds,
the surrounding fields
are not dared to be cultivated by people.
If someone is informed and makes offerings to them,
and pays a high rent,
the fields will become exceptionally fertile,
but one must conceal their own name when leasing them.
After three years, they must leave,
and only then can they avoid harm.
If someone is afflicted by them,
they can twist a person’s face
and reverse their hands and feet.
Only after praying and making offerings can one be spared.
They can also travel on land at night,
leaving muddy footprints along the paths they take,
and wherever they go,
a rustling sound can be heard.
The Great General of the Twenty-Five Northern Divisions
CH0F01A0 possesses a broken spring talisman script.
If it is inscribed
on bricks or stones
and thrown into their pond,
or written on wooden boards and stakes
and nailed by the pond’s edge,
they will inevitably move elsewhere during wind, rain, thunder, and lightning.
Only those skilled in this art can perform it.
Red Turtles of Luózhōu
In the boundaries of Luózhōu and Biànzhōu in Lǐngnán,
the waters are filled with red turtles,
as large as spoons
and bright red in color.
Whether birds, beasts, or water buffalo,
once they enter the water, they are dragged into deep pools,
sucked of their blood, and die.
Some say
that jiāolóng (flood dragons) make them do it,
but the reason is unknown.
Hán Xún
In the Táng dynasty, at Hán Xún’s estate in Fùyáng County, Hángzhōu, a well was dug.
When it reached a depth of only five or six feet,
thousands of fish were found in the soil,
which was slightly moist.
Fēng Lìngzhēn
In the Táng dynasty, Fēng Lìngzhēn served as the prefect of Chángzhōu.
He transported timber upstream from Jiāngnán
to Luòyáng to build a temple.
When the craftsmen cut the wood,
they found a crucian carp several inches long inside,
as if carved and placed there.
Níngzhēn Temple
In the Táng dynasty, at the eastern corridor pillar of Níngzhēn Temple in Huáizhōu,
which had stood for over fifty years,
the Daoist priests often heard the sound of a frog from within the pillar,
but they did not know the exact location.
Later, when the pillar decayed and was replaced,
the kitchen staff chopped it for firewood,
and inside the pillar, they found a frog.
The pillar originally had no holes.
Shǔjiāng Villager
In the Táng dynasty, a villager from Shǔ
caught a giant turtle in the river,
larger than usual,
over a foot long,
with a crimson fringe.
After boiling it overnight,
it remained lively as before.
After another day of heating,
the water dried up, but it still did not die.
The whole family was terrified,
thinking it was a dragon,
so they threw it into the river.
It floated away
and was never seen again.
Zhāng Húzi
In the Táng dynasty, a fisherman named Zhāng Húzi from Wújùn once caught a giant fish in Tàihú Lake.
On its belly were written characters in red:
"Nine times ascending Lóngmén Mountain,
three times drinking Tàihú’s water.
After all, I did not become a dragon,
my fate burdened by Zhāng Húzi."
Bǎi Jūn
In the Táng dynasty, a commoner named Bǎi Jūnhuái from Shuǐnán Township, Xúnyáng County, Jīnzhōu,
caught a fish several feet long
while fishing at Lèmò Pool in the Hànjiāng River.
On its body were written characters:
"Three times crossing the sea,
twice ascending the Hàn.
Arriving at Lèmò,
my fate belongs to Bǎi Jūn."
Yè Lǎngzhī
In the first year of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Yè Lǎngzhī, a man from Nánkāng County, sent his slave Dāngguī to guard the fields.
Downstream from the fields was a marsh called Niǎobēi,
where suddenly a creature began calling,
its voice like a goose but louder.
The slave entered the water to investigate
and found a large creature,
slippery and writhing,
with its head buried in the marsh’s depths.
The slave took a knife, entered the water,
and cut off a section over six feet in circumference
and about two zhang in length.
He dragged it ashore
and skinned and gutted it.
Dozens of neighbors roasted and ate it together.
The meat was tender, fatty, and delicious,
surpassing all other flavors.
On its back was a white tendon as thick as a shinbone,
resembling a sturgeon’s nose,
and it tasted especially delicious.
The rest was made into dried meat.
On the night the creature died,
Yè Lǎngzhī dreamed of a person,
tall, large, and dark-skinned,
who said:
"I am the messenger of Zhāngchuān.
While drunk and wandering alone,
I accidentally fell into the marsh
and was killed by your slave.
Not only have I failed in my royal duty,
but I have also suffered dismemberment and humiliation.
My flesh was carved, my organs gutted,
and I was salted, roasted, and eaten.
The pain of this injustice
is unmatched in all of history.
I have no prior grievance with you,
but if you kill the slave,
I will consider the debt repaid,
and the blame will rest solely on the perpetrator.
Otherwise, according to divine law,
I fear your household will suffer calamity."
Yè Lǎngzhī woke in fright
but could not bring himself to kill the slave.
The following year,
the slave died when a bamboo tip pierced his abdomen.
That summer,
Yè Lǎngzhī’s entire family fell ill,
and eight people died.
Liǔ Zōngyuán
Liǔ Zōngyuán, the Prefect of Liǔzhōu in the Táng dynasty, a native of Hédōng,
was once demoted from a court official to the position of Marshal of Yǒngzhōu.
On his way, he reached Jīngmén
and stayed at a courier station.
That night,
he dreamed of a woman dressed in yellow clothes,
who bowed twice and wept, saying:
"I am a resident of the Chǔ River.
Now, unfortunately,
I am about to die at any moment.
Only you can save me.
If I am spared,
not only will I be eternally grateful,
but I will also be able to increase your official salary and benefits.
You will become a general and a minister,
and it will not be difficult.
I hope you, a wise gentleman, will consider this."
Liǔ Zōngyuán thanked her and agreed.
After waking up,
he silently found it strange.
When he fell asleep again,
he dreamed of the woman once more,
both pleading and thanking him,
and she left only after a long while.
The next morning,
an official arrived,
announcing that the commander of Jīngmén had ordered
a banquet in honor of Liǔ Zōngyuán.
Liǔ Zōngyuán had already ordered his carriage prepared,
but since it was still early,
he took a nap.
Once again, he dreamed of the woman,
her face filled with distress,
anxious and hurried,
turning to Liǔ Zōngyuán and saying:
"My life
now hangs by a thread in a fierce wind,
dangerously close to snapping and drifting away.
Can you not consider the urgency of this matter?
Please quickly devise a plan.
Otherwise,
I will be severed along with the broken thread.
I hope you, sir, will agree."
After speaking,
she bowed and pleaded again,
then took her leave.
Still not fully understanding,
he lowered his head and pondered:
"I have dreamed of this woman three times in one night,
her words so earnest.
Could it be that one of my officials has wronged someone?
Or perhaps the banquet host intends to serve fish as my meal?
If I can save it,
that would be my duty."
He immediately ordered his carriage to go to the prefectural banquet.
There, he recounted his dream to the commander of Jīngmén
and summoned the officials for questioning.
An official said:
"The day before yesterday,
a fisherman caught a huge yellow-scaled fish in his net,
intending to serve it as a meal.
Its head has already been cut off."
Liǔ Zōngyuán exclaimed in shock:
"So it was indeed the dream from that night!"
He immediately ordered the fish to be taken and thrown into the river,
but the fish was already dead.
That night,
he dreamed of the woman again,
this time without her head.
Liǔ Zōngyuán found it even more strange.
Wáng Yáo
During the Huìcháng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Wáng Yáo who served as the Chief Military Officer of Héngzhōu.
He was once appointed
as the Magistrate of Yì County.
As Wáng Yáo was about to depart for his post,
he dreamed at night of a person
clad in armor,
with a dignified and imposing appearance.
The person claimed to be a descendant of Féng Yí,
on his way to the seashore,
when he was suddenly caught in a net,
captured by a fisherman from Zhāngchuān.
He was about to be placed on the cutting board
to be served as a meal for the magistrate.
His life would end the next morning,
so he came to inform him,
hoping for rescue and mercy,
and promising generous repayment."
After Wáng Yáo woke up,
he said to his attendants:
"This must be the county officials welcoming me
by catching fish for the feast."
He urgently sent someone to the county,
where the cook was indeed about to prepare the fresh fish,
preparing
the ingredients
for sliced fish.
When informed of Wáng Yáo's order,
they threw the fish into the water.
The fish immediately flapped its fins and raised its dorsal fin,
swimming away proudly.
That night,
Wáng Yáo dreamed again of the same person, who wept with gratitude, saying:
"I was spared from being cooked in a cauldron,
and allowed to return to the waves of the rivers.
I now know the benevolence of the magistrate,
which far surpasses the kindness of Liǔ Zōngyuán!"
He then knelt for a long time before leaving.
Liǔ Yí
During the Táng dynasty, a man named Liǔ Yí from Hédōng was living in Luòyáng.
One spring day, he went fishing in the Yī River
and caught a huge fish,
which he brought home
and placed in a basin of water.
Earlier, Liǔ Yí had an infant son,
just six or seven years old.
That night,
Liǔ Yí dreamed that the fish bit his son's chest with its beak.
Startled, he woke up.
Sure enough, he heard his son crying and saying:
"I just dreamed of a big fish biting my chest,
and the pain was unbearable,
so I cried."
This matched Liǔ Yí's dream,
and he found it strange.
He then examined his son's chest,
and indeed, there was a wound with blood.
Liǔ Yí grew even more fearful.
The next morning,
he threw the fish back into the Yī River.
He also asked monks to chant sutras and draw images.
In just over ten days,
his son's wound healed.
From then on, Liǔ Yí never went fishing again.
Cuī Tuò
When Cuī Tuò, the Minister of Sacrifices of the Jìn dynasty, was still a student,
he once visited his aunt's home.
At night, he stayed in the study hall with his cousins.
The next morning,
his aunt's family was hosting guests.
That night, he dreamed of nineteen people, all dressed in green,
bowing in a circle,
pleading for their lives,
their words filled with sorrow and urgency.
Cuī Tuò said:
"I am merely living in seclusion
and have no official duties.
Why are you telling me this?"
They all replied:
"If you just agree,
we will be saved!"
Cuī Tuò said:
"If there is an opportunity,
I will certainly not hesitate to help."
They all rejoiced, leaped with joy, bowed twice, and left.
After waking up,
he washed, combed his hair, dressed properly,
and went to the main hall to see his aunt.
He saw a jar of water with turtles floating in it.
Counting them,
there were exactly nineteen, large and small.
Their colors
also roughly matched those in his dream.
He then told his aunt,
recounting his dream in detail,
and bowed twice, pleading for them.
His aunt did not object,
and immediately ordered a servant to place them in a container.
She personally went to the waterside to release them.
The Dyer
In Guǎnglíng, there was a dyer who lived south of the Jiǔqǔ Pond.
He dreamed of a young man dressed in white asking to stay with him.
The dyer replied:
"My home is cramped and humble,
and cannot accommodate you."
The young man then entered the kitchen.
That night,
the entire family dreamed of him.
The next day, they found a white turtle in the kitchen,
over a foot wide,
with eyes like gold.
The dyer sent it to Lǐ Qīyī, a Taoist priest at the Zǐjí Palace.
When placed in water,
its color turned golden, and its eyes became red.
When taken out of the water, it turned white again.
Lǐ Qīyī could not understand this,
so he returned it to the pond,
and it was never seen again.
The Man from the Sea
Recently, a man from the coast found something in a fish trap,
which was a human hand,
with a face on its palm,
complete with all seven orifices,
capable of moving but unable to speak.
It was passed around and examined for a long time,
and someone said:
"This is a divine creature,
and it should not be killed."
The man then placed it on the water,
and the creature floated away,
for several dozen paces,
when it suddenly laughed loudly several times,
leaped, and disappeared into the water.
The Monk of Fǎjù Temple
Inside Fǎjù Temple, there was a monk
who was initially in his room.
When night fell,
he suddenly said to his disciples:
"Outside, there are tens of thousands of people,
wearing hats on their heads,
begging this poor monk to save their lives."
He hurriedly opened the door to look,
and saw over ten people carrying turtles,
so he ransomed and released them.
Lǐ Yánfú
Lǐ Yánfú, the commissioner of the Fēngzī Court in the pseudo-Shǔ state, was napping in the official hall during the day
when he dreamed of thirty people in black hats kneeling at the foot of the steps,
only saying, "We beg for our lives."
Startled awake,
his servant reported
that outside the gate, villagers had offered thirty turtles.
Realizing it was the dream,
he released them.
Zǐlù
When Confucius was trapped in Chén,
he played the zither and sang in the guesthouse.
At night, there was a person,
over nine chǐ tall,
dressed in black with a tall hat,
whose shouts shook those around.
Zǐlù led him out,
fought with him in the courtyard,
and subdued him.
On the ground.
It turned out to be a large anchovy,
over nine chǐ long.
Confucius sighed and said:
"This creature,
why has it come here?
I have heard that when things grow old, spirits gather around them,
arriving in times of decline.
Its coming here
must be because I am trapped and out of food,
and my followers are ill?
Creatures of the six domestic animals,
as well as turtles, snakes, fish, turtles, plants, and trees,
can all become monsters when imbued with spirit,
hence they are called the 'five yǒu.'
In the five directions of the five elements,
each has its creatures.
Yǒu means old,
so when creatures grow old, they become monsters.
Killing them ends it,
so what is there to worry about?"
Chángshuǐ County
During the Qín dynasty,
there was a nursery rhyme in Chángshuǐ County that said:
"When blood appears at the city gate,
it will sink and become a lake."
An old woman heard this,
grew worried and fearful,
and went to spy on it every morning.
The gate guard wanted to tie her up,
but the woman explained her reason.
After the woman left,
the gate guard killed a dog
and smeared its blood on the gate.
When the woman went again,
she saw the blood and ran away,
not daring to look back.
Suddenly, a great flood arose,
threatening to submerge the county.
The registrar Hé Gàn went in to report to the magistrate,
and the magistrate, seeing Gàn, said:
"Why have you suddenly turned into a fish?"
Gàn replied:
"Your honor has also turned into a fish!"
And so it sank and became a valley.
The Gūsū Man
During the Later Hàn dynasty,
in Gūsū, there was a man
dressed in white clothes,
wearing a headscarf,
with a majestic appearance,
standing seven chǐ tall,
with well-defined eyebrows and eyes.
Accompanied by six or seven followers,
he visited households everywhere,
seducing women,
and showed no fear of people day or night.
When people tried to ambush and capture him,
wind and rain would immediately arise,
and even though the commandery had soldiers,
they dared not confront him.
Anyone who offended him
was inevitably harmed.
After over a month,
the magician Zhào Gǎo, who was in Zhào,
heard of the trouble in Wú,
and hurriedly came by boat.
Gǎo had just disembarked and walked to the northern embankment of Gūsū
when he saw this monster from afar,
with passersby fleeing left and right, having nowhere to hide.
Gǎo said:
"This is what troubles the people of Wú."
At that time, the governor of Kuàijī was escorting an imperial envoy,
and they met,
also taking refuge in a guesthouse.
Gǎo then paid them a visit.
The governor knew Gǎo had magical skills,
and was very pleased.
Gǎo said to the commandery governor:
"Do you wish to see it?"
He then requested water and lit incense,
let out several long whistles,
and a sudden wind from the heavens arrived,
with the sound of dozens of people responding in the air.
Gǎo threw the talisman in his hand,
and the talisman flew away like the wind.
In an instant,
they saw the monster as if someone had brought it,
looking very frightened.
Gǎo said to it:
"How dare you deceive and show no fear?"
Then, pressing his sword, he said:
"Execute it."
Immediately, a whirlwind carried it out.
Gǎo said to the governor:
"You may look at it now."
Before the envoy had even left the gate,
it was reported that a hundred paces away,
there was a large white flood dragon,
three zhàng long,
beheaded by the roadside,
and the remaining six or seven,
all had their bodies and heads separated,
also creatures like giant turtles and alligators.
Over ten thousand onlookers gathered around,
all exclaiming that from then on, there would be no more trouble.
The Person from Yǒngkāng
During the time of Sūn Quán of Wú,
a man from Yǒngkāng entered the mountains and encountered a large turtle,
so he chased it.
The turtle then spoke, saying:
"I wandered out at an inopportune time,
and thus was caught by you."
The man found this very strange.
He loaded it onto his cart to take out
and present to the King of Wú.
At night, they moored at Yuèlǐ,
tying the boat to a large mulberry tree.
In the middle of the night,
the tree called out to the turtle, saying:
"How weary you must be, Yuánxù!
What has brought you to this?"
The turtle said:
"I have been captured and bound,
and am about to be boiled for stew.
Even if they used all the firewood from the southern mountains,
they could not cook me through."
The tree said:
"Zhūgě Yuánxùn is widely learned;
he will surely cause you suffering.
If he seeks someone like me,
what plan could you devise?"
The turtle said:
"Zǐmíng, say no more,
or disaster will befall you as well."
The tree fell silent and ceased.
Upon arrival,
Sūn Quán ordered the turtle boiled.
They burned a hundred cartloads of firewood,
but the turtle's words remained as before.
Zhūgě Kè said:
"Then use old mulberry wood to cook it properly."
The man who presented it also recounted the conversation between the turtle and the tree.
Sūn Quán immediately sent men to fell the tree and fetch it.
Using it, the turtle was boiled and promptly fell apart.
To this day, mulberry wood is still often used to cook turtles,
and country folk therefore call turtles "Yuánxù."
Wáng Sù
In the fourth month of the first year of the Wǔfèng era of the young emperor of Wú,
a commoner named Wáng Sù from Yúyáo County in Kuàijī
had an unmarried daughter,
aged fourteen,
of beautiful appearance.
Many young men from the neighborhood sought to marry her,
but her parents, cherishing her, did not wed her off.
One day,
a young man,
with jade-pure features and demeanor,
over twenty years old,
calling himself Jiāng Láng,
expressed his wish to marry this girl.
Her parents, fond of his looks and character,
thus consented.
When asked about his family,
he said:
"We reside in Kuàijī."
Several days later,
he brought three or four women,
some old, some young,
and two young men,
all to their home.
Thereupon, they presented wealth as betrothal gifts,
and the marriage was completed.
After a year had passed,
the girl became pregnant.
By the twelfth month,
she gave birth to something like a silk sack,
as large as a shēng measure,
lying motionless on the ground.
Her mother found it very strange and eerie.
She cut it open with a knife,
and it was entirely filled with white fish roe.
Wáng Sù then asked Jiāng Láng:
"What was born is all fish roe;
I don't know the reason for this?"
Wáng Sù still did not realize,
but Jiāng Láng said:
"It is my misfortune,
that such a strange thing was produced."
The mother alone suspected Jiāng Láng was not human.
She therefore told Wáng Sù.
Wáng Sù secretly ordered a servant
to wait until Jiāng Láng undressed for bed,
then take the clothes he had worn and examine them.
They all had patterns like scales and armor.
Seeing this, Wáng Sù was greatly alarmed.
He ordered a large stone to press down on them.
By dawn,
they heard Jiāng Láng, unable to find his clothes,
cursing and shouting unusually fiercely.
Soon they heard something heavy collapse,
its sound shaking from outside.
The servants hurriedly opened the door to look,
and saw under the bed a white fish,
six or seven chǐ long,
not yet dead,
flapping on the ground.
Wáng Sù chopped it to pieces,
threw it into the river,
and the girl later married someone else.
Fèi Chángfáng
In Rǔnán there was a demon
that often dressed in a governor's robes,
went to the prefectural office gate and beat the drum,
plaguing the commandery.
When Fèi Chángfáng arrived,
he knew it was a monster,
and thus rebuked it.
It immediately removed its robes and cap, kowtowed,
begging to reform itself,
and transformed into an old turtle,
as large as a carriage wheel.
Fèi Chángfáng ordered it to put on the governor's robes again,
wrote a document,
addressed to the Lord of Gě Bēi,
and it kowtowed, streaming tears,
and took the document away.
Watching it,
they saw it stand the document by the bank of Gě Bēi,
then wrap its neck around it and die.
Zhāng Fú
A man from Póyáng named Zhāng Fú
was returning by boat
when by the wild waters he suddenly saw a woman,
quite beautiful,
riding in a small boat alone.
Zhāng Fú said:
"What is your surname?
Why are you traveling so lightly,
without a rain hat in the rain?
You may come aboard to take shelter from the rain."
They then bantered with each other,
and she entered to sleep with Zhāng Fú.
She tied the small boat she came in
to the side of Zhāng Fú's boat.
Around the third watch,
the rain cleared and the moon was bright.
Zhāng Fú looked at the woman—
she was actually a large softshell turtle.
He tried to seize her,
but she swiftly ran into the water.
Looking at the small boat,
it was actually a section of a tree trunk,
over a zhàng long.
Dīng Chū
In Wújùn's Wúxī there was a large reservoir called Shànghú Bēi.
The reservoir officer, Dīng Chū,
whenever heavy rain fell,
would patrol the dikes.
During the spring rains,
Dīng Chū went out to inspect the embankment.
At dusk,
he glanced back and saw a young woman behind him,
dressed entirely in dark blue clothes,
holding a dark blue umbrella.
She called from behind, chasing him:
"Officer Dīng, wait for me!"
Dīng Chū was momentarily bewildered,
thinking to stop and wait for her,
but then doubted he had ever seen her before.
Now suddenly a woman was walking in the gloomy rain;
he feared she must be a ghostly creature.
Dīng Chū then walked quickly.
Looking back, he saw the woman
chasing him just as swiftly.
Dīng Chū therefore ran urgently,
increasing the distance from her.
Looking back at the woman,
he saw her throw herself into the reservoir,
with a splashing sound,
her clothes and umbrella flying apart.
Looking closely, it was a large gray otter,
and the clothes and umbrella were all lotus leaves.
This otter transformed into human form
to seduce young men on multiple occasions.
Xiè Fēi
The Daoist priest Xiè Fēi from Dānyáng went to Shíchéng to buy a cauldron and was on his way back,
when dusk fell,
and he could not reach home.
There was a temple in the mountains,
situated by a stream,
so he entered to stay overnight.
He loudly declared:
"I am an envoy of the Heavenly Emperor,
stopping here to rest."
Still, he feared that someone might rob him of his gold,
and his mind was troubled and uneasy.
In the middle of the night, around the second watch,
someone came to the temple gate,
calling out:
"Hé Tóng."
Tóng responded.
"There is a human presence in the temple—who is it?"
Tóng said:
"Someone who claims to be an envoy of the Heavenly Emperor,
he will leave shortly."
After a while,
another arrived,
called Tóng,
and asked the same as before.
Tóng answered as before,
and the visitor sighed and left again.
Xiè Fēi, disturbed and unable to sleep,
got up.
He called Tóng and asked:
"Who was the one who came first?"
Tóng replied:
"That was the white alligator from the hole by the water."
"And what are you?"
"I am the turtle from the crevice in the cliff north of the temple."
Xiè Fēi secretly memorized all this.
At daybreak, he informed the local residents,
saying:
"There are no gods in this temple,
only creatures like turtles and alligators.
It is a waste to offer them wine and meat in sacrifice.
Quickly bring spades,
and let us go together to exterminate them."
The people were also quite suspicious,
so they gathered and went to dig them out,
killed them all,
then destroyed the temple and ended the sacrifices.
After that, peace and quiet returned.
Gù Bǎozōng
Gù Bǎozōng, styled Shìsì,
was a man of Jiāngxià,
who often fished in the river.
Once on a summer night, by his thatched hall facing the moon before retiring,
suddenly there appeared a man with white hair and beard,
who called himself an old man,
resembling a fisherman.
He came straight to the foot of the hall,
then bowed to Bǎozōng,
sat cross-legged,
and only wept.
Bǎozōng said:
"Where has the old man come from?"
He did not speak,
but after a long while said to Bǎozōng:
"The journey overland was very tiring,
so I cannot speak quickly."
Bǎozōng said:
"Where did the old man just come from?
And where are you going now?"
He replied:
"I come from Jiāngzhōu,
and return to Jiāngxià."
Having said this, he wept again.
Bǎozōng said:
"Is the old man not a supernatural being?"
He answered:
"I am indeed not human.
Because you live in seclusion,
I came to speak with you."
Bǎozōng said:
"I am but a rustic who fishes,
to relieve the toils of life—
what seclusion is there?"
He replied:
"The world is on the brink of war and chaos,
how can you speak of seclusion?"
Bǎozōng said:
"The world today is peaceful and orderly,
what chaos could there be?"
He replied:
"Have you not seen the ambitions of Huán Xuán?"
Bǎozōng then asked:
"If there is to be war,
can you tell the time?"
The old man said:
"Is this not the fifth year of Lóng'ān?"
Bǎozōng said:
"It is."
He counted on his fingers and wept again,
saying to Bǎozōng:
"The year after next, the era name will change.
One more year,
Huán Xuán will usurp the state.
Not long after usurping,
he will be defeated by 'Mǎo Jīn'."
Bǎozōng said:
"Who is 'Mǎo Jīn'?"
He replied:
"You will know later."
Having said this,
he added to Bǎozōng:
"Within twenty years,
you will witness a great change in the Mandate."
Bǎozōng said:
"The old man has come from afar,
what will you eat?"
He replied:
"I ask for your usual fare."
Bǎozōng then ordered food to be served,
him.
After the old man finished eating,
he said to Bǎozōng:
"Tonight I am on a mission,
I must go to the river ahead.
At dawn tomorrow,
I hope you will watch."
He also said:
"Within a hundred li,
I alone am different,
thus I foretell calamities and auspices—
we are such beings."
Bǎozōng said:
"I do not understand these words,
how can they be verified?"
He replied:
"They are omens of war and arms."
Having said this, he went out.
Bǎozōng saw him off outside the door,
and they parted.
At dawn,
Bǎozōng went to the river to watch,
and heard the wind and water gradually grow fierce,
fish emerged in waves,
countless as far as the eye could see.
Those watching passed on the word,
the line stretched over a hundred li from head to tail,
among them was a great white fish,
over a hundred zhang long,
raising its head to look around,
and after a while, it submerged.
This was the sixteenth day of the sixth month in the fifth year of Lóng'ān.
Bǎozōng was greatly astonished.
Two years later,
the seventh year of Lóng'ān was changed to Yuánxīng.
In the second year of Yuánxīng,
on the Rénwǔ day of the eleventh month,
Huán Xuán indeed usurped the throne.
In the third year, in the second month,
General Jiànwǔ Liú Yù raised a righteous army and destroyed Huán Xuán,
restoring Emperor Ān of Jìn to the throne.
Seventeen years later,
Liú Yù received the abdication of Jìn.
All was exactly as the fish had foretold.
The people of Wǔchāng
During the Yongchū era of Emperor Gāo of Sòng,
Zhāng Chūn served as the governor of Wǔchāng.
At that time, someone was marrying off their daughter.
Before she could board the carriage,
