the girl suddenly became possessed,
rushed out and attacked people,
saying:
"I do not wish to marry."
A shaman said:
"This is an evil spirit."
He took the girl to the riverbank,
then beat a drum,
using spells and incantations to treat her.
The next day,
a green snake came to where they were seated.
They immediately drove a large nail through its head.
By noon,
they saw a large turtle come from the river,
prostrating itself before the shaman.
The shaman wrote a talisman in vermilion on the turtle's back,
and sent it back into the river.
By evening,
a large white alligator emerged from the river,
now sinking, now floating.
The turtle followed behind, urging it on.
The alligator, knowing it was doomed,
bravely came forward.
It first entered the curtained area,
bid farewell to the girl,
and wept bitterly, saying:
"I have lost my beloved."
After this, the girl gradually recovered.
Someone asked: "If the possessing spirit belongs to one creature,
how could there be three now?"
The shaman said:
"The snake was the messenger,
the turtle was the matchmaker,
and the alligator was her intended match."
The three creatures that were captured
were all killed.
The Widow Yán
In the Dàxià camp of Jiànkāng, there was a widow named Yán.
In the early Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
someone named Huá Dū claimed to have formed a relationship with Yán.
A night watchman saw a man walking toward the Protectorate Army office,
which was located inside the Jiànyáng Gate.
The watchman shouted and questioned him.
He replied:
"I am Huá Dū, returning to the office."
He headed straight along the western wall, intending to enter.
The watchman, because he was violating the night curfew,
intercepted and attacked him.
He then transformed into an alligator.
Inspecting the place where he entered and exited,
it was very smooth and slippery,
leading to a pond inside the office grounds.
There had previously been an alligator den in the pond.
After many years, it had gained the power to bewitch people.
It was killed, and the hauntings ceased.
Yín Ér
A commoner named Yín Ér from Ānchéng,
during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
was left to guard the house while his father was briefly away.
He was ordered to watch the house.
Suddenly, he saw a person,
about twenty years old,
riding a horse and holding an umbrella,
with four attendants,
all dressed in yellow,
coming from the east.
At the gate, he called out to Yín Ér,
asking for a temporary place to rest.
They then entered the courtyard of the house,
sat on a folding chair,
with one attendant holding the umbrella over him.
Yín Ér noticed that his clothes had no seams,
were multicolored and patterned,
resembling scales rather than fur.
After a while,
rain was about to come.
This person mounted his horse to leave,
turned back and said to Yín Ér:
"I will come again tomorrow."
He then headed west,
stepping into the air and ascending.
In a moment,
clouds and mist gathered from all sides,
turning the bright day into darkness.
The next day,
a great flood suddenly arrived,
rivers and valleys boiled and surged,
hills and gullies were submerged in vast waters.
Just as it was about to drown Yín's house,
suddenly a huge fish appeared,
over three zhàng long,
coiled itself directly in the path of the water.
Thus, the Yín family was spared from being swept away.
The Daughter of the Prince of Guǎnglíng
The Buddhist monk Sēng Yáo possessed divine incantations,
and was especially skilled at curing possessions.
The daughter of the Prince of Guǎnglíng fell ill due to possession,
and Yáo treated her.
Upon entering,
he closed his eyes and cursed:
"Old demon, you do not think to keep to the Way but dare to violate a person!"
The girl then wailed loudly, saying:
"They have killed my husband!"
The spirit beside her said:
"My life ends today!"
It then sighed mournfully,
and said again:
"This divine one cannot be dealt with."
It then transformed into an old alligator,
ran out into the courtyard,
and Yáo ordered his servant to kill it.
Yáng Chǒunú
Yáng Chǒunú from Hénán often went to Zhāng'ān Lake to gather cattails.
As dusk approached,
he saw a woman.
Her clothes were not very clean,
but her appearance was beautiful.
She came by boat carrying vegetables,
and approached Chǒunú.
She said her home was by the lake,
and as it was nearly dark, she could not return,
so,
she moored her boat to stay over.
She borrowed eating utensils to share a meal,
on the plate were dried fish and raw vegetables.
After eating,
they began to joke and laugh.
Chǒunú sang teasingly to her.
The woman replied:
"My home is by West Lake's side,
As dusk falls, the sunlight fades.
Finding shelter with a good host,
Unwittingly, my heart feels at ease."
Soon, they put out the light and slept together.
He noticed a fishy smell,
and her fingers were very short.
He then suspected she was a demon.
This creature sensed his thoughts,
hurriedly left the room,
transformed into an otter,
and ran straight into the water.
Xiè Zōng
Xiè Zōng, an official of the Principality of Kuàijī, was returning from leave.
Passing by Wúgāo Bridge,
his fellow boatmen went to the market,
leaving Zōng alone on the boat.
A woman appeared,
graceful and gentle in demeanor,
who came to the boat
and they began to amuse themselves together.
The woman stayed overnight for merry feasting,
then asked to travel with them.
Zōng agreed.
From then on, the boatmen heard laughter and talk every night.
After more than a year,
their comings and goings became even more frequent.
His cabin mate secretly watched,
but saw no one.
Knowing it was a demon,
they together threw a cover over it.
After a long while,
they caught one creature,
as large as a pillow.
Soon after,
they caught two more,
both as small as fists.
Looking at them,
they were three turtles.
Zōng, grieving and longing,
after several days finally understood.
He recounted the past, saying:
"This woman bore two sons in one year,
the elder named Dàomǐn,
the younger named Dàoxīng."
Zōng also said:
"This woman and the two boys,
when first captured, were terrified,
their forms all shrank,
and they said to Zōng:
'You can take our pillow and throw it away.'"
At that time, his clan uncle Dàomíng was a Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat.
He kept the three turtles in a cage to show them.
Zhāng Fāng
At the Xiàshì Temple in Guǎnglíng,
in the eighteenth year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty (441 CE),
Zhāng Fāng's daughter Dàoxiāng was seeing her husband off on his journey north.
As dusk fell,
she took shelter for the night beneath the temple gate.
During the night, a creature
impersonated her husband and came to her, saying:
"The sorrow of parting is unbearable;
I cannot bring myself to leave."
Dàoxiāng soon became dazed and lost her senses.
At that time, there was a man named Wáng Zuǎn who could cure evil afflictions.
Suspecting Dàoxiāng was possessed by a demon,
he was asked to treat her.
Just as he began to insert the acupuncture needles,
an otter ran out from under the woman's quilt and fled into a nearby stream.
Dàoxiāng's illness was then cured.
Zhōng Dào
Zhōng Dào, a clerk of Yǒngxīng County in the Sòng dynasty, had just recovered from a severe illness.
His amorous desires became twice as strong as usual.
He had previously been fond of a woman from the Báihèxū area,
and even now he still yearned for her.
Suddenly, he saw this woman shaking out her clothes as she approached,
and he immediately became intimate with her.
After this, she came to him several times.
Zhōng Dào said:
"I very much desire some clove fragrance."
The woman said:
"What's so difficult about that?"
She then scooped up a handful of the fragrant substance
and gave it to Zhōng Dào.
Zhōng Dào invited the woman to chew on it with him,
but the woman said:
"My breath is naturally fragrant;
I have no need for this."
When the woman went out the door,
a dog suddenly saw her,
chased her, and bit her to death.
She turned out to be an old otter.
The so-called fragrant substance in her mouth was actually otter dung.
Zhōng Dào immediately felt it was foul and filthy.
A Man from Jìn'ān
A man from Jìn'ān Commandery was damming a stream to catch fish
when suddenly a man wearing a white cap
and a yellow silk unlined robe
came to visit him,
and they ate and drank together.
After the meal,
the visitor said to him:
"Tomorrow when you catch fish,
there will be a very strange, large fish.
It will be at the very front.
Be careful not to kill it."
The next day,
sure enough, there was a huge fish,
seventy or eighty feet long,
that came straight toward the net.
The man immediately struck and killed it.
When he cut open its belly,
he saw inside all the food they had eaten.
After that, the man's household nearly all died out.
Liú Wànnián
In the third year of the Yuánhuī era of Emperor Hòufèi of the Sòng dynasty (475 CE),
the garrison commander of Jīngkǒu, Liú Wànnián, was patrolling at night west of Běigù Mountain.
He saw two men
whose demeanor was dignified and handsome,
and whose skin was as white as jade.
From a distance, they called to Wànnián and said:
"How closely related are you, by surname and clan, to the current emperor?"
Wànnián replied:
"We look to different surnames, but they are the same."
One of them said:
"Although your clans are different,
I fear disaster will reach you."
Wànnián said:
"What fault have I committed?"
They replied:
"If you leave your post,
disaster will not reach you."
Hearing what the two men said,
Wànnián found it even more strange.
Wànnián said to the two men:
"I deeply thank you for this forewarning.
How can I repay you?"
Wànnián wanted to invite them back to his garrison,
but the two men said:
"We are not of this world,
and do not eat the food of this world."
While Wànnián was still speaking with them,
they transformed into fish
and flew into the river.
The next day, Wànnián pleaded illness,
and thus resigned from his position.
Later events indeed turned out as the fish had said.
Wēishēng Liàng
In the Míngyuè Gorge, there were two streams flowing east and west.
In the second year of the Shēngpíng era of Emperor Shùn of the Sòng dynasty (478 CE),
a man from the streams, Wēishēng Liàng, caught a white fish three feet long.
He placed it in his boat
and covered it with grass.
When he returned and went to prepare it,
he saw a beautiful woman beneath the grass,
fair and dignified,
about sixteen or seventeen years old.
She said of herself:
"I am a daughter of Gāotáng.
By chance, I transformed into a fish to swim about,
and was caught by you."
Liàng asked her:
"Since you are human,
can you become my wife?"
The woman said:
"A hidden destiny makes it so;
why would it not be possible?"
For the next three years, she was Liàng's wife.
Then she suddenly said:
"My allotted time here is fulfilled;
I request to return to Gāotáng."
Liàng said:
"When will you come again?"
She replied:
"When feelings cannot be forgotten,
thoughts will bring me back."
After that, she came and went three or four times a year,
and her final whereabouts were unknown.
The Reed Pond
Northeast of Lěiyáng County was a Reed Pond, eight or nine qǐng in area.
Its depth was unfathomable.
There was a huge fish in it.
Every fifth day,
it would leap vigorously out of the water.
It could be three arm-spans around,
and its appearance was most unusual.
Whenever it emerged from the water,
small fish would scatter and flee,
following the water up onto the shore,
too many to count.
It is also said
that in this pond there was a jiāo fish.
Every fifth day it would transform:
sometimes into a beautiful woman,
sometimes into a handsome man.
Moreover, it caused many disturbances and troubles.
The people of the commandery warned each other,
so no one dared harbor harmful intentions toward it.
Later, it was struck by lightning,
and this pond then dried up.
A Man from Péngchéng
In Péngchéng, there was a man who married a wife but was not pleased with her,
and stayed outside for over a month.
The wife said:
"Why do you not come back in?"
The man said:
"You go out every night,
so I do not come in."
The wife said:
"I have never gone out."
The husband was startled.
The wife said:
"You yourself have other intentions,
and must have been bewitched by something else.
When she comes again later,
you should seize and hold her,
then get a torch to look at her—
what kind of creature is she?"
Later, the one he desired returned,
pretending to be his wife.
As she hesitated and had not yet entered,
someone pushed her from behind, making her go forward.
She then got onto the bed.
The husband grabbed her and said:
"Why do you go out every night?"
The woman said:
"You have been having an affair with the girl from the eastern house,
and now, startled, you want to blame it on ghosts and spirits,
using our previous agreement to cover it up."
The husband released her
and lay with her.
In the middle of the night, his mind cleared.
He then thought:
"A demon bewitches people—
this is not my wife."
He then went forward to seize and hold her,
shouting loudly for a torch.
She gradually shrank,
and when he uncovered her to look,
he found a carp two feet long.
Zhū Fǎgōng
Zhū Fǎgōng from Shānyīn
once went on a journey
and rested under a tangerine tree east of Táichéng.
Suddenly, a young woman,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a very graceful and beautiful appearance,
as dusk approached,
sent a maidservant to speak with Fǎgōng.
That evening,
she intended to come stay with him.
After everyone had settled down for the night,
she arrived,
claiming her surname was Tán
and that she lived by the city wall.
They then slept together.
At dawn, she said:
"I will come again tomorrow."
This went on for several nights.
Every morning when she left,
the maidservant would come to fetch her.
There was also a boy,
about six or seven years old,
graceful and lovely,
whom the woman said was her younger brother.
Later, one morning as she was leaving,
the woman's skirt opened,
revealing a turtle's tail and turtle feet.
Fǎgōng then realized she was a demon
and wanted to seize her.
When she came again that evening,
he immediately lit a torch to search for her,
but soon lost track of where she was.
Wáng Huàn
Wáng Huàn of Qí was traveling from Jiànyè to Zhǔgōng
and reached Jiāngzhōu,
where he moored his boat by the shore.
Late at night,
the wind rose and the moon shone brightly.
Suddenly, he heard more than ten people clamoring on the sandbar ahead,
all with women's voices.
Huàn found it strange
and said to the others:
"How could there be such people in the middle of the river?"
He then rowed a small boat alone,
taking cover in the shade of the reeds,
and followed the northern bank of the sandbar.
Among the thick reeds, he saw more than ten women,
some dressed in green,
some in blue-green,
half sitting and half standing.
One of the sitting women wept and said:
"I originally lived with my sisters in a hidden dwelling,
always by the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
I never expected, sisters,
that I would vainly be taken as a wife by a boy from up the gorge,
leading to this separation."
One of the standing women sighed and said:
"The tide has its return,
but as for me, once I leave,
I fear there will be no day of return."
Before she finished speaking,
a north wind gently rose.
The standing woman said:
"The tide is coming,
we can go home."
Huàn quickly rushed out from the reeds to capture them,
but they all transformed into turtles
and entered the water, leaving.
Cài Xīng
A commoner from Jìnlíng, Cài Xīng, suddenly fell into a mad illness.
He would sing and chant irregularly
and often laughed and talked with several people in the air.
Sometimes he said:
"Whose daughter should I take next!"
Another person said:
"We already have many at home."
Later one night,
he suddenly heard more than ten people bringing something into the home of Liú Yúzhī, a fellow villager.
Yúzhī drew his knife and went out the back door,
where he saw a black figure,
who shouted angrily:
"I am the lake chief,
coming to visit you,
and you want to kill me!"
He then called to his companions:
"Why don't you help me?"
Yúzhī then fiercely swung his knife, cutting wildly,
and struck a large softshell turtle and a wildcat.
Lǐ Zēng
Lǐ Zēng from Yǒngyáng was traveling past a large stream
when he saw two flood dragons floating on the water.
He shot an arrow at them,
and one of the flood dragons was hit.
Zēng returned home,
and later went out to the market again.
There, a woman,
dressed in plain clothes with tears in her eyes,
was holding the arrow he had shot.
Zēng, finding it strange, asked her about it.
The woman replied:
"What is the use of asking?
You have acted with such violence!"
She then returned it to him,
handed over the arrow, and vanished.
Zēng, horrified, hurried away,
but before reaching home,
he died suddenly on the road.
Xiāo Téng
East of the road outside the south gate of Jīnchéng in Xiāngyáng,
there was an official residence for aides,
which was traditionally said to be extremely haunted.
Those who lived there would either die or fall ill.
When Crown Prince Zhāomíng of the Liáng dynasty was governing the region,
he assigned the residence to his official Lǚ Xiūqiàn.
Xiūqiàn often slept at the northern end of the hall.
A ghost pulled Xiūqiàn,
and he fell to the ground.
After a long time, he came to his senses.
Soon after, Xiūqiàn was found guilty and ordered to commit suicide.
Later, when Xiāo Téng first took up his post,
upon reaching Yángkǒu Bank,
suddenly a man wearing a tall white gauze hat,
black cloth trousers,
and a draped robe approached Téng.
Suspicious of his unusual attire,
Téng refused him.
After traveling several li, the man appeared again,
asking for a ride.
Téng grew even more suspicious.
This happened several times.
Téng had several concubines,
whose behavior and actions
gradually became abnormal.
They would sing, laugh, weep, and wail,
no longer adhering to their usual demeanor.
When Téng arrived in Xiāngyáng,
this man also came once a day,
and later stayed for days without leaving.
He liked to wear draped robes and tied trousers,
riding a dog as he moved about.
Sometimes he would transform in an instant,
reciting poems and songs,
talking and laughing as if nothing were amiss,
claiming to be Zhōu Yú.
He constantly stayed at Téng’s residence.
Téng tried various exorcism rituals to drive him away,
and sometimes he would leave temporarily,
but soon return.
Téng then led twenty of his disciples,
drawing swords to attack him.
The man either leaped onto the roof beam
or fled into the woods,
moving with such speed
that they could not capture him.
He then entered the screen behind Téng’s concubines
and sang a song:
“Meeting joy at Yángkǒu Bank,
forming love at Táolín Ferry.
The walnut is thrown away, leaving only the flesh,
surprised you do not recognize a person.”
Shortly after,
a Daoist priest named Zhào Tányì set up an altar for Téng,
performing rituals and incantations.
As soon as the Daoist entered the gate,
all the concubines began wailing sorrowfully,
as if bidding farewell forever.
Soon, a turtle over a foot in diameter
came to the altar and died.
The concubines also recovered.
Téng’s concubines’ voices and appearances were mostly unchanged.
The advisory military officer Wéi Yánbiàn, who was fond of jesting,
remarked during a banquet:
“I have often heard people say ‘cunning as a ghost,’
but now I see that this ghost must be a foolish ghost.
If it were cunning,
it would not have haunted Xiāo Téng’s concubines.
Judging from this,
it is clear that ghosts are foolish.”
Liǔ Zhèn
Liǔ Zhèn of Hédōng, styled Zǐyuán,
enjoyed quiet and leisure from a young age,
and did not seek glory or wealth.
During the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty,
he traveled from Sīzhōu to Shàngyuán,
and fell in love with its scenery.
West of Zhōngshān, in Jiànyè Village,
he bought land and built a thatched hut,
dug springs and planted trees,
living a reclusive life like a farmer.
The nearby residents
all called him “Father Liǔ.”
His residence overlooked the river,
and once, while leaning on his staff and gazing into the distance,
he suddenly saw three or four small children on the sandbar ahead,
each about a foot tall,
playing back and forth.
From afar, he heard them calling to each other, asking for food.
Zhèn found this strange.
Shortly after,
the wind and waves surged violently,
and a large fish leaped in fright,
accidentally landing on the sandbar.
The children rushed forward to eat it.
Then he heard the children calling out:
“Even if we cannot finish it,
leave some for Father Liǔ.”
Zhèn was even more astonished.
He then took a small boat
and went straight to capture them.
Before reaching the shore,
all the children transformed into otters
and entered the water, disappearing.
Zhèn took the large fish and shared it with the villagers.
Not long after,
he returned north to Luòyáng.
On a pillar in his study,
he inscribed a poem:
“The rivers and mountains are not a long-term plan,
but to satisfy the heart for a while.
Moreover, I think of the scholars of Luòyáng,
now returning to my old forest.”
This was in the seventh year of Tiānjiàn.
Emperor Wén of Suí
During the Kāihuáng era of Emperor Wén of Suí,
someone often came to the inner palace to harass the palace women.
The palace supervisor reported this,
and the emperor said:
“The gate guards are very strict;
how could anyone enter!
It must be a demon.”
He then warned the palace women:
“If it comes again,
just strike it with a sword.”
Later, it came at night and climbed onto the bed.
A palace woman drew a sword and struck it,
as if hitting dry bones.
The creature fled and fell,
and the palace woman chased it.
It then entered a pond and disappeared.
The next day,
the emperor ordered the pond drained.
They found a turtle over a foot long,
with sword marks on its shell.
They killed it, and the disturbances ceased.
Dàxīng Village
At the end of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
villagers in the southwest of Dàxīng City held a Buddhist gathering.
An old man with white hair, wearing a white robe and skirt,
came to ask for food and then left.
No one recognized him,
so they followed to observe him.
After walking about two li,
he suddenly disappeared.
There was only a pond,
in which a white fish over ten feet long swam,
followed by countless smaller fish.
People competed to shoot it with arrows,
but some broke their bows or snapped their strings.
Eventually, someone hit it.
They cut open its belly
and found cooked rice inside.
A few days later,
the canal suddenly flooded,
and the families of those who shot the fish all drowned.
Wànqǐng Pond
In the Táng dynasty, there was a Wànqǐng Pond in Qízhōu,
teeming with fish, turtles, and all kinds of aquatic creatures.
Nothing was lacking.
During the Xiánhēng era,
suddenly a monk came holding an alms bowl to beg for food.
An elder in the village offered him vegetarian food,
which he ate before leaving.
Soon after, a fisherman caught a fish
six or seven feet long,
with scales like embroidery and armor-like markings,
its body adorned with patterns like brocade and precious designs,
exceptionally different from ordinary fish.
They planned to send it to the prefecture as a gift,
but it died upon reaching the village.
So they cut it open and divided it among themselves.
Inside its belly, they found the vegetarian food the elder had offered,
still intact and clearly recognizable.
The villagers then held a Buddhist ceremony by the pond to pray for its soul,
and from then on, there were no more aquatic creatures in the pond.
To this day, it remains barren.
Chángxū Country
During the Dàzú era of the Táng dynasty,
Initially,
a scholar accompanied an envoy from Xīnluó,
but a wind blew them to a certain place.
The people there all had long beards,
and their language was mutually intelligible with that of the Táng,
so it was called the Land of Long Beards.
The population was very prosperous,
and their buildings, clothing, and caps
were slightly different from those of the Central Kingdom.
The land was called Fúsāngzhōu.
Their official titles
included Zhèng, Zhǎng, Jí, Bō, Rì, Mò, Dǎo, and Luó, among others.
The scholar visited several places,
and the people of that country all respected him.
Suddenly, one day,
several dozen carriages and horses arrived,
saying the king was summoning the guest.
They traveled for two days
before reaching a large city,
where armored soldiers guarded the gates.
The envoy led the scholar inside,
and he prostrated himself in audience.
The palace halls were lofty and spacious,
and the ceremonial guards were like those of a king.
Seeing the scholar bowing and prostrating,
the king rose slightly,
then appointed the scholar as the Chief of Winds,
and also as his son-in-law.
The princess was very beautiful,
but had several dozen strands of beard.
The scholar's power and influence were illustrious,
and he was rich in pearls and jade,
yet whenever he returned home,
seeing his wife displeased him.
The king often held grand gatherings on nights of the full moon.
On one such occasion,
the scholar saw that all the consorts and concubines had beards,
and thus composed a poem:
"Flowers without leaves are not lovely,
women with beards are also ugly.
If, father-in-law, you tried making them all beardless,
it might not be worse than them all having beards."
The king laughed heartily and said:
"So my son-in-law still cannot forget about the beards on my daughter's chin and cheeks?"
After more than ten years,
the scholar had one son and two daughters.
Suddenly, one day,
the king and his ministers appeared worried and distressed.
The scholar, finding it strange, asked about it.
The king wept and said:
"Our country faces a calamity,
a disaster is imminent,
and only you, my son-in-law, can save us."
The scholar said in alarm:
"If the calamity can be averted,
I will not spare even my life."
The king then ordered a boat prepared,
and sent two envoys to accompany the scholar,
saying:
"We trouble you, son-in-law, to visit the Dragon King of the Sea.
Just say that the Land of Long Beards, on the seventh island of the third shoal in the Eastern Sea,
faces calamity and seeks rescue.
Our country is extremely small,
so you must repeat it several times."
Then, weeping, they clasped hands and parted.
The scholar boarded the boat,
and in an instant reached the shore.
The shore's sand was all of the seven treasures,
and the people were all tall, wearing caps and robes.
The scholar then stepped forward,
requesting an audience with the Dragon King.
The dragon palace resembled the depictions of the heavenly palace in Buddhist temples,
its brilliance dazzling and overwhelming,
making it hard to look directly.
The Dragon King descended the steps to welcome him,
and the scholar ascended the hall step by step with him.
Asked about his purpose for coming,
the scholar explained.
The Dragon King immediately ordered a swift investigation.
After a long while,
someone from outside reported:
"Within our realm, there is no such country."
The scholar again pleaded sorrowfully,
detailing that the Land of Long Beards was on the seventh island of the third shoal in the Eastern Sea.
The Dragon King again scolded the envoy to search carefully,
and report quickly.
After about the time of a meal,
the envoy returned and said:
"The shrimp on that island are collectively designated as Your Majesty's food supply for this month,
and they were rounded up the day before yesterday."
The Dragon King laughed and said:
"So our guest was beguiled by shrimp.
Although I am king,
all that I eat is mandated by celestial decree,
and I cannot eat arbitrarily.
Now, for our guest's sake, I will reduce my consumption."
He then ordered someone to lead the guest to see,
where they saw several dozen iron cauldrons as large as houses,
filled with shrimp.
Among them were five or six
that were red in color,
as large as arms,
and upon seeing the guest, they jumped and leaped,
as if pleading for rescue.
The guide said:
"This is the shrimp king."
The scholar could not help but weep with sorrow.
The Dragon King ordered the release of one cauldron of shrimp, including the shrimp king.
He then ordered two envoys to escort the guest back to the Central Kingdom.
In one night, they reached Dēngzhōu.
Looking back at the two envoys,
they were giant dragons.
Lǐ Yù
Lǐ Yù of Dūnhuáng in the Táng dynasty,
during the Kāiyuán era,
was appointed Prefect of Shàozhōu.
He took his family to assume his post,
sailing across Dòngtíng Lake.
The weather was clear at the time,
so they went ashore.
There, he had a nosebleed onto the sand,
which was licked by a river demon (tuó).
Suddenly, another Lǐ Yù appeared,
whose form, body, clothing, and speech
were no different from his own self.
Lǐ Yù's original self
was subdued by the demon's magic,
and bound in the water.
His wife, children, and family
welcomed and served the demon impostor as he took up his post,
and the people of the prefecture were also unaware.
He served as prefect for several years,
when a great drought struck the land,
and the western river became shallow enough to wade across.
The Dàoshi Yè Jìngnéng, responding to an urgent summons from Emperor Xuánzōng, was traveling from Luófú Shān,
and passed by Dòngtíng Lake.
Suddenly, he saw a man bound and facedown in the sand,
and asked:
"Who are you?"
Lǐ Yù explained his situation.
Jìngnéng wrote a talisman and pasted it on a large rock,
and the rock immediately flew up into the air.
The demon impostor was just holding court at his desk in the morning,
when he was struck by the flying rock,
and reverted to his original form.
At that time, Zhāng Yuè was the Prefect of Yuèzhōu,
and he submitted a detailed memorial,
and also provided a boat to send Lǐ Yù to his prefecture.
Only then did his family and wife believe him.
To this day, those traveling by boat
warn each other not to shed blood into the waves,
because of this incident.
Xiè Èr
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a scholar from the Eastern Capital, due to insufficient travel funds,
journeyed south to the Jiāng-Huái region,
seeking help from understanding friends.
He was in distress and gained nothing,
lingering in Yángzhōu for a long time.
In the same lodge was a man named Xiè Èr,
who pitied his disappointment,
and constantly wished to assist him,
saying to the scholar:
"Do not grieve so.
If you wish to return north,
I shall present you with three hundred thousand coins."
Upon parting,
he gave him a letter, saying:
"My residence lies east of the Wèiwáng Pond.
When you reach the pond,
knock on the large willow tree.
If a family member comes out,
you should hand over this letter,
and then take the money."
The scholar did as instructed,
went straight and knocked on the large tree.
After a long while,
a young maidservant emerged,
asked the reason,
and he said:
"Xiè Èr ordered me to deliver a letter."
Suddenly, he saw vermilion gates and white walls.
The maidservant went in and came back out,
leading him inside.
He saw an elderly woman, robust and strong,
sitting in the main hall,
who said to the scholar:
"My son's letter has troubled you to deliver.
He instructed to give you three hundred thousand coins,
and now I shall not go against his wish."
When the man came out,
he already saw three hundred thousand coins on the bank,
all were official stamped coins,
but their color was somewhat tarnished.
The scholar suspected they were from spirits or monsters,
not knowing from where they were obtained.
He feared using them might not be in accordance with natural principles,
so he reported it to the authorities,
recounting the whole story from beginning to end.
The Governor of Hénán reported the matter,
and everyone said:
"In the Wèiwáng Pond there is a soft-shelled turtle den,
it is likely from there."
An imperial decree was issued,
ordering them to shoot into it.
They obtained several dozen Kūnlún slaves,
all holding knives and spears,
and sank into the den.
They captured several dozen soft-shelled turtles, large and small.
Finally, they caught one turtle,
as large as a joined bed.
The officials killed them all,
and obtained several thousand items of coins and silks.
Five years later,
the scholar was selected for a minor official post in Jiāngnán.
On his way to assume the post,
when he reached the eastern shopfront in the Yángzhōu market,
he suddenly saw Xiè Èr,
who angrily said:
"I treated you not unkindly,
why then did you betray me,
to such an extent?
My old mother and family members
all met with violent deaths,
and it is because of you."
Having said this, he took his leave and departed.
The scholar was greatly frightened,
and for over ten days did not proceed to his post.
Urged by his companions,
he finally set off.
After traveling over a hundred lǐ,
they encountered a storm,
and the entire family perished.
People of the time said:
"It is believed to have been caused by Xiè Èr's vengeance."
A Fisherman from Jīngzhōu
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
a fisherman from Jīngzhōu caught a green fish while angling,
ten chǐ in length,
with five-colored circular patterns on its scales,
exceptionally beautiful and elegant.
The fisherman did not recognize it,
and because it differed from ordinary fish,
he did not take it to the market,
but cooked and ate it himself.
It was tasteless,
which he found quite strange.
Five days later,
suddenly several dozen chariots and horsemen arrived at the fisherman's place.
The fisherman, startled and fearful, came out and bowed.
He heard an angry voice from a chariot say:
"My prince,
on his way to pay respects to the Eastern Sea,
why did you kill him?
I sent a general to search for the prince,
and you killed him as well.
I shall now make your body crumble and disintegrate,
suffering pain like the prince and the general!"
Having said this,
he shouted at the fisherman,
and the fisherman collapsed,
breaking into a profuse, terrified sweat.
After a long while, he regained consciousness.
His family helped him back,
and he then contracted leprosy.
Over ten days later,
his body, mouth, nose, hands, and feet ulcerated and festered,
his flesh disintegrating and scattering,
and after several months, he died.
Liú Chéng
Among the commoners of Dāngtú in Xuānchéng commandery,
there were Liú Chéng and Lǐ Huī,
both unfamiliar with agricultural work.
They once used a large boat to transport fish and crabs,
selling them in the Wú-Yuè region.
In the spring, the third month of the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
they loaded their goods from the Xīn'ān River to transport to Dānyáng commandery.
When they reached Xiàzhā Pǔ,
forty lǐ from Xuānchéng,
as dusk fell,
they moored the boat,
and both went ashore.
At that time, Lǐ Huī went to a village house on the shore of the pǔ,
leaving Liú Chéng alone on the river.
Looking around at the cloudy islands,
utterly devoid of human traces,
he suddenly heard from the boat continuous cries of "Āmítuófó,"
the voices extremely fierce.
Startled, Chéng looked,
and saw a large fish in the boat shaking its whiskers and nodding its head,
calling out "Āmítuófó" in a human voice.
Chéng was both afraid and horrified,
his hair standing completely on end.
He immediately hid in the reeds to observe.
Soon, ten thousand fish in the boat
all leaped and called out "Buddha,"
their voices shaking the earth.
Chéng was greatly terrified,
hurriedly boarded the boat,
and threw all the fish into the river.
After a while, Lǐ Huī arrived.
Chéng told Huī everything in detail.
Huī angrily said:
"How can you, a brat, engage in such demonic falsehoods?"
He spat and cursed for a long time.
Chéng had no way to justify himself,
so he used his clothing and funds to compensate for their value.
Afterwards, with the remaining hundred coins,
he exchanged for over ten bundles of reed grass,
and placed them on the shore.
The next day,
when moving them onto the boat,
he suddenly felt they were heavy and could not be lifted.
Unpacking and looking,
he found fifteen thousand strings of cash,
with a label that read:
"Returning the price of your fish."
Chéng found this even more extraordinary.
That day,
at Guāzhōu, he met with a group of monks for a meal,
and gave all the cash strings as alms.
At that time, there was a man named Wàn Zhuāng,
who had retired from his post as magistrate of Jīngyáng to reside in Guāzhōu,
learned of this matter in detail,
and passed it on for recording.
Xuè Èrniáng
In the Táng dynasty, in Báitián of Chǔzhōu,
there was a shamaness named Xuè Èrniáng,
who claimed to serve the Great King Jīntiān,
and could expel evil spirits and malevolent forces.
The local people revered her.
Among the villagers was a certain Shěn,
whose daughter was afflicted by a demon, becoming deranged,
sometimes mutilating her own body,
stepping into fire or throwing herself into water.
Moreover, her belly gradually swelled,
as if she were pregnant.
Her parents were deeply troubled by this,
and invited Shamaness Xuè to discern the cause.
Upon her arrival,
she set up an altar inside the house,
laid the afflicted girl within the altar,
and placed a large fire pit beside it,
with an iron cauldron heated until it glowed red.
The shamaness then donned full ceremonial attire, played music,
danced and drummed to invoke the deity.
After a short while, the deity descended,
and the onlookers bowed repeatedly.
The shamaness offered wine and prayed:
"Summon the demon swiftly."
After these words,
the shamaness entered the fire pit and sat down,
her complexion remaining calm as usual.
After a long while,
she shook her garments and stood up,
placed the heated cauldron over her head while dancing and drumming,
and when the music ended, removed it,
then sat upon a folding chair.
She commanded the afflicted girl to bind herself,
and the girl's hands twisted behind her back as if bound.
She ordered her to confess.
At first, the girl wept and would not speak.
The shamaness grew greatly angered,
seized a knife and struck her,
but the blade passed through as if slicing air, leaving her body unharmed.
The afflicted girl then said:
"I submit!"
And confessed, saying:
"I am an old otter from the Huái River,
who fell for this girl while she was washing yarn.
I did not expect to encounter a holy master.
I beg to vanish from now on.
Only, it pains me that the child in her womb is not yet born.
If, after its birth, you do not kill it,
but return it to me,
that would be an unexpected boon."
After speaking, she sobbed,
and everyone pitied her.
She then took up a brush and composed a farewell poem:
"With the tide I came, with the tide I rise,
When the tide recedes, on empty shores I lie.
What comes must eventually go,
Passion easily kindled, passion hard to satisfy.
My heart breaks for the child within,
Under the cold autumn moon on the river, I sigh."
The afflicted girl had never known how to write,
yet now she put brush to paper,
her words and calligraphy both exquisite.
Shortly after,
the girl fell into a deep sleep,
and the next day she was completely recovered.
Only then did she explain:
When she first went to wash yarn,
a handsome young man had seduced her,
and thus they began their liaison,
though she herself was unaware of it all.
Over a month later,
she gave birth to three otter pups.
She intended to kill them.
But someone said:
"That demon kept its word;
we are humans, yet we act recklessly.
It would be better to release them."
So the person took them to the lake,
where a giant otter leaped up to meet them,
and vanished with them into the depths.
Zhào Píngyuán
In the early Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man from Tiānshuǐ named Zhào Píngyuán,
who had a country estate south of the Hàn River.
Once, he went with the scholars Liú Jiǎncí from Péngchéng and Duàn Qízhēn from Wǔwēi to the Wúmíng Lake,
to catch fish and make sliced fish.
In a short while,
they caught several dozen fish.
Among them was a white fish over three chǐ long,
its scales like plain brocade,
dazzling to the eyes,
its fins and gill covers variegated with five colors,
vivid and lovely.
Liú and Duàn said:
"This fish's appearance is extraordinary;
we must not kill it."
Píngyuán said:
"You fellows are too pedantic to eat it,
but I can certainly eat it!"
Before he finished speaking,
they suddenly saw a group of children in the lake,
all wearing half-sleeved jackets and white trousers,
running swiftly over the water,
shouting and playing back and forth,
showing not the slightest fear.
The two guests grew even more afraid,
and again pleaded for the white fish's life.
Píngyuán would not allow it,
and shouted to the cook:
"Quickly, slice the fish and bring it here."
In a short while,
the sliced fish arrived.
As Píngyuán and his two guests were halfway through eating,
a violent storm of wind and thunder suddenly arose.
With a clap of thunder,
white smoke rose from the feet of the children on the lake's surface,
and a great wind followed.
The two guests sensed the ominous change in the atmosphere,
and looking around, saw a temple within three lǐ,
so they rushed toward it for shelter.
Píngyuán merely gave a slight smile,
and was just picking up his chopsticks again
when flying sand broke trees,
rain and fire mingled as they fell,
lightning flashed and thunder roared,
as if heaven were collapsing and earth splitting open.
The two guests were terrified,
looking at each other, their faces pale,
thinking Píngyuán must have been reduced to dust.
After a while, the rain cleared.
The two guests ran back to where they had eaten the fish,
and saw Píngyuán sitting on the ground,
unconscious and unaware.
The two guests supported him,
calling out and questioning him.
After a long while, he opened his eyes and said:
"A terrible affair,
a terrible affair!
After all the trouble of eating the sliced fish,
a man in a blue robe
pulled it out from my throat
and threw it into the lake.
My stomach feels utterly empty now!"
The servant who had wielded the knife
had vanished without a trace,
and only returned after several months.
Píngyuán questioned him about what had happened.
He said:
"At first, I saw the blue-robed man in the lightning, angrily cursing,
and then I was taken under his command,
ordered to carry his clothing bundle.
We traveled for over ten days,
until we reached a place
densely populated and bustling,
with markets crowded and diverse.
The blue-clad man said:
'This is Yìzhōu.'
After walking another five or six days,
we reached another prosperous gathering place.
The blue-robed man said:
'This is Tánzhōu.'
That evening,
he led me into a wilderness and said:
'You have followed me for a long time;
surely you have suffered hardships?
Now I bid you farewell.'
Then he took a stick of dried meat from his bosom and gave it to me,
saying:
'When you are hungry, eat this,
and you can reach home.'
He also said:
'Convey my meaning to Zhào Píngyuán:
do not prematurely take life.
Wasting the gifts of heaven
is detested by the divine way.
If he offends again,
there will certainly be no pardon.'"
From then on, Píngyuán never fished again for the rest of his life.
Gāo Yù
During the Yuánhé era,
there was a recluse named Gāo Yù who made his living by fishing.
Once he moored his boat at Zhāo Tán,
and late at night, around the third watch, he was still awake.
Suddenly, he saw three large lotus flowers on the lake,
their red blossoms unusually splendid.
Three beautiful women were each sitting atop one,
all of them
They wore white robes,
as pure and bright as snow,
their faces radiant and enchanting,
gleaming like immortals.
Together they spoke:
"Tonight the waters are calm and clear,
the sky is high and the moon bright.
With hearts at ease, we admire the scenery—
a perfect time to speak of mysteries."
One of them said:
"There is a small boat nearby—
could they be listening to our words?"
Another replied:
"Even if there is,
they are not men who wash their hat-strings,
so there is no need to fear."
They said to each other:
"Zhāo Tán has no bottom, and Júzhōu floats—
truly no empty saying."
Then one said:
"Let each of us speak of the Way we follow."
The next said:
"My nature inclines to Buddhism."
The next said:
"I follow Daoism."
The next said:
"I follow Confucianism."
Each discussed the principles of their own teaching,
their reasoning extremely profound.
One said:
"Last night I had an inauspicious dream."
The other two asked:
"What dream?"
She replied:
"I dreamed my descendants were in panic,
our dwelling was uprooted,
we were driven out by people,
the whole clan forced to flee—
this is inauspicious."
The other two said:
"Wandering souls are fickle—
not worth believing."
The third said:
"Let each calculate what food we will obtain tomorrow morning."
After a long while, she said:
"According to our preferences—
a Buddhist monk, a Daoist priest, and a Confucian scholar.
Alas!
What we just discussed
has become an omen,
and it may well bring disaster."
Having spoken,
they vanished in an instant.
Yù heard their words clearly
and remembered them in detail.
At dawn,
sure enough, a Buddhist monk came to cross the lake,
and when he reached midstream, he drowned.
Yù was greatly alarmed and said:
"Last night's words were not false!"
Immediately after,
a Daoist priest moored his boat to cross.
Yù urgently tried to stop him,
but the priest said:
"You are deluded by demons—
the monk's death was mere chance.
I am summoned by a wise man;
even if I die, I will not regret it,
for I cannot break my promise."
He scolded the boatman and crossed,
and when he reached midstream, he too drowned.
Next came a Confucian scholar,
carrying a book bag, heading straight to cross.
Yù pleaded:
"The monk and priest ahead have already drowned!"
The scholar said sternly:
"Life and death are fate.
Today my clan holds an auspicious fast—
I cannot neglect the mourning rites."
As he was about to row,
Yù grabbed the scholar's sleeve and said:
"My arm may be severed,
but you must not cross."
The scholar cried out by the shore,
when suddenly something like a white silk ribbon
flew out from the lake,
wrapped around the scholar, and pulled him in.
Yù and others on the shore rushed to grab his clothes,
but a slippery, slimy fluid flowed forth,
making it impossible to hold on.
Yù sighed deeply:
"It is fate!"
In moments, all three were gone.
Soon after, two travelers arrived in a leaf-like boat—
one old man and one youth.
Yù approached the old man
and asked his name.
The old man said:
"I am Táng Gōubiē from Qíyáng Mountain.
I am now heading to Chángshā
to visit the ritual master Zhāng Fǎmíng."
Yù had long heard of his lofty Daoist arts
and divine skills,
so he paid him great respect.
Suddenly, they heard weeping from the shore—
the relatives of the three drowned men.
The old man inquired,
and Yù recounted the whole story.
The old man angrily said:
"How dare they harm people like this!"
He opened his case,
took out a cinnabar brush and wrote a seal script charm,
then ordered his disciple on the same boat:
"Take this talisman into the lake
and command the water monsters
to depart immediately!"
The disciple then held the talisman and entered the water
as if walking on flat ground.
Following the mountain foot for several hundred zhang,
he saw a large, bright, gleaming cave
like a human dwelling.
Three white pigs were sleeping on a stone couch,
with several dozen piglets
playing beside them.
When the disciple brought the talisman,
the three pigs suddenly startled awake,
transforming into white-robed beauties,
and the piglets also turned into young girls.
Holding the talisman, they wept:
"Our inauspicious dream has indeed come true!"
They said:
"Please inform our former master for us—
we have lived here a long time;
how could we not feel attachment?
Allow us three days to return to the Eastern Sea,
and we will each offer a bright pearl."
The disciple said:
"I have no use for them."
He refused and returned,
reporting everything to the old man.
The old man angrily said:
"Go back and tell these beasts:
they must leave this place by tomorrow morning.
Otherwise,
I will send the Six Dīng deities to their cave to slay them."
The disciple went again,
and the three beauties wailed:
"We respectfully obey your command."
The disciple returned.
The next morning,
black qi rose from the lake surface,
and in moments,
fierce winds and swift thunder arose,
stirring waves as high as mountains.
Three huge fish, several zhang long,
with countless smaller fish circling them,
swam away along the current.
The old man said:
"This journey of mine has been very fruitful.
If not for you,
how could I have rid Zhāo Tán of this scourge?"
He then traveled east and west by boat with Yù.
The monk Fǎzhì
The monk Fǎzhì from Táishān traveled to Huáiyīn,
where he saw a fisherman who bowed respectfully and invited him.
Fǎzhì followed him to a thatched hut,
and the fisherman served him food with great care.
Fǎzhì found this rather strange,
so he asked:
"As a disciple who makes a living by fishing,
I am naturally a sinner.
Why do you show such reverence upon seeing a monk?"
The fisherman replied:
"In the past, at Kuàijī Mountain, I encountered the venerable Yúnyuǎn preaching the Dharma to the crowd.
I briefly joined in the rejoicing,
and gained insight into the holy teachings.
Since then, whenever I see a monk,
I feel immeasurable joy."
The monk was astonished,
and urged him to change his occupation.
The fisherman said:
"Although I have heard the good path,
I am still trapped in nets and snares,
just as you, a monk,
have not fully devoted yourself to the precepts.
Our sins are the same,
so why doubt this?"
The monk, ashamed, withdrew.
Looking back,
he saw the fisherman transform into a large softshell turtle,
which entered the Huái River,
and the thatched hut also vanished.
Dèng Yuánzuǒ
Dèng Yuánzuǒ
was a man from Yǐngchuān
who traveled to Wú for study.
He loved exploring mountains and rivers,
and wherever there was a scenic spot,
he visited them all.
While paying respects to the elder,
the magistrate of Chángchéng,
they exchanged pleasantries about old times,
drank heartily, and parted.
As he approached Gūsū,
he mistakenly entered a path,
rugged and winding,
for over ten miles,
without encountering any houses,
seeing only overgrown weeds.
As dusk fell,
Dèng Yuánzuǒ strained his eyes forward,
and suddenly saw a light,
thinking it must be a household,
he sought it out and headed there.
Upon arrival,
he saw a snail-shell-like hut,
with only one woman,
about twenty years old.
Dèng Yuánzuǒ then pleaded:
"I visited Chángchéng today and parted,
returning drunk,
and mistakenly took this path.
Now night has fallen,
and if I continue forward,
I fear being harmed by wild beasts.
I beg you, madam, to allow me to stay for one night.
How could I dare forget your kindness?"
The woman said:
"My father is not home,
what should I do?
Moreover, the family is poor,
with no fine bedding or proper service.
If you, sir, do not mind,
then I shall comply."
Dèng Yuánzuǒ was hungry,
so he stayed.
The woman prepared an earthen bed,
spread soft grass on it,
and after he sat down,
she served food.
Dèng Yuánzuǒ, hungry, ate it,
finding it extremely delicious.
The woman then slept beside Dèng Yuánzuǒ.
At dawn,
Dèng Yuánzuǒ suddenly realized he was lying in a field,
with a snail beside him,
as large as a liter measure.
Recalling the food he had eaten the previous night,
he felt very uneasy,
and vomited,
seeing that
it was all blue mud.
Dèng Yuánzuǒ sighed in astonishment for a long time,
but did not harm the snail.
From then on, Dèng Yuánzuǒ devoted his heart to the Daoist path,
and never traveled again.
Yáo Clan
The Yáo clan of the Jìnghǎi Army in Dōngzhōu led their followers to catch sea fish,
to fulfill the annual tribute.
It was already late,
and they had caught very few fish,
just as they were worrying,
they suddenly caught a person in their net,
black in color,
covered in long hair all over,
standing with hands clasped.
When questioned, he did not respond.
The sea captain said:
"This is what is called a sea person.
Seeing one surely brings disaster.
Please kill him,
to avert the calamity."
Yáo said:
"This is a divine being.
Killing him would be inauspicious."
So he released him and prayed:
"If you can bring me a school of fish,
to spare me the crime of failing my duty,
then I will believe you are divine."
The hairy man walked backward on the water,
and disappeared after several dozen steps.
The next day,
they caught a great haul of fish,
double the usual annual amount.
Sòng Clan
The military official Sòng from Jiāngxī once went to Xīngzǐ to buy timber,
and saw a noisy crowd by the water,
where fishermen had caught a large softshell turtle.
The turtle repeatedly looked at Sòng,
so Sòng paid a thousand coins to redeem it,
and released it into the river.
Several years later,
while mooring his boat at Lóngshā,
suddenly a servant arrived,
saying, "Chief Clerk Yuán summons you."
Sòng was puzzled.
"I don’t know any Chief Clerk."
Nevertheless, he went,
and suddenly arrived at a mansion,
where an official came out to greet him.
Sitting with him, the official said:
"Do you still recognize me?"
Sòng thought about it,
but truly did not recognize him.
The official continued:
"Do you remember releasing a softshell turtle in the river at Xīngzǐ?"
Sòng said:
"Yes."
The official said:
"I am that turtle.
I once committed a crime,
and the Emperor ordered me to be exiled as an aquatic creature.
I was captured by fishermen,
and without your kindness,
my bones would have rotted by now.
Now I have become the Chief of Jiǔjiāng.
The reason for summoning you
is to repay you.
Your son is fated to drown,
and his name is on the register here.
In a few days,
the Míngshān deity will visit the envoy of Lúshān,
and his journey will bring violent wind and rain.
Your son is destined to die at that time.
Now there is another person with exactly the same name,
also fated to drown,
but his time is slightly earlier.
I will take him as a substitute.
Your son should quickly go ashore and hide,
otherwise he cannot escape."
Sòng expressed his thanks and left,
and before he knew it, he was back at his boat.
A few days later,
there was indeed a storm disaster,
and many died,
but Sòng’s son was spared.
Shǐ Clan’s Daughter
A woman of the Shǐ family from Wǔtán Village in Lìshuǐ,
having grown weary from planting rice,
lay down to rest beneath a tree.
She saw a creature,
terrifying with its scales, horns, claws, and spurs,
come and settle upon her.
Later she became pregnant,
and gave birth to a carp,
which she raised in a basin.
As it grew larger day by day,
she eventually placed it into the Tóujīnlài stream.
Soon after,
a villager cutting grass
accidentally severed its tail.
The fish immediately leaped up and swam away,
with wind and rain following it,
until it entered Tài Lake and stopped.
Her family gradually became wealthy.
Later, when the woman died,
every Cold Food Festival,
the fish would come with a school of fish to her grave.
To this day,
it only comes once every leap year.
Also, a fisherman named Lǐ Hēitǎ always set his nets in the river.
Suddenly he caught an infant,
about three chǐ tall.
The net was entangled by a mess of slime,
and for ten days it could not be undone.
A Daoist priest saw it and said:
"You can pour molten iron on it."
They did as he said,
and it came undone.
Looking at the infant,
its mouth, nose, eyebrows, and hair were as if painted,
but it had no eyes.
Its mouth still had the smell of wine.
Everyone was afraid,
and they threw it back into the river.
Fishermen
Recently, a fisherman moored his boat at the foot of Mǎdāng Mountain.
The moon was bright and the wind was calm.
He saw a large soft-shelled turtle emerge from the water,
climb straight to the mountaintop,
and crane its neck to look around in all directions.
After a while,
a brightly colored boat surged out from the river water,
with over ten people gathered drinking wine,
and courtesans, music, and lavish furnishings.
They toasted and feasted for a long time.
Then a large warship came downstream from upstream,
the sound of its oars shaking the gathering.
The colored boat then sank.
The earlier turtle also descended,
but before reaching the water,
it suddenly died on the riverbank.
The idea is that the water deity had sent this turtle as a lookout,
but it did not know the warship was coming,
so it was executed.
Mother of the Huáng Family
During the reign of Emperor Líng of the Later Hàn,
the mother of the Huáng family in Jiāngxià bathed and transformed into a soft-shelled turtle,
entering a deep abyss.
Afterwards, she would appear from time to time.
When she first bathed, she wore a silver hairpin.
When she appeared,
it was still on her head.
Mother of Sòng Shìzōng
The mother of Sòng Shìzōng from Qīnghé in the Wèi dynasty,
during the Huángchū era,
bathed in the bathroom in summer,
instructing the children of the household to close the door.
The family members, through a hole in the wall,
peeked and saw a large soft-shelled turtle in the water of the bathing basin.
They then opened the door,
and everyone, young and old, entered,
but it paid no attention to them at all.
She had previously worn a silver hairpin,
which was still on her head.
They all watched over her, weeping,
but there was nothing they could do.
She went outside,
moving away very swiftly.
They chased her but could not catch up.
She then entered the water.
A few days later, she suddenly returned,
walked around the house as in her lifetime,
said absolutely nothing, and left.
People at the time said Shìzōng should hold a funeral,
but Shìzōng believed that although his mother's form had changed,
her vitality still existed,
so he ultimately did not hold a funeral.
This is similar to the mother of the Huáng family in Jiāngxià.
Mother of Xuān Qiān
In the first year of the Bǎodǐng era of Sūn Hào of Wú,
the mother of Xuān Qiān from Dānyáng,
eighty years old,
transformed into a soft-shelled turtle while bathing.
Qiān and his brothers closed the door to guard her.
They dug a large pit in the main hall,
filled it with water,
and the turtle entered the pit to play.
After several days,
it suddenly stretched its neck to look outside.
When the door was slightly ajar,
it immediately leaped out on its own,
went to a distant pond,
and was never seen again.
A Person from Jiāngzhōu
At the end of the Jìn dynasty,
a person from Jiāngzhōu, over a hundred years old,
grew a horn on his head.
Later, after entering the river in front of his house,
he transformed into a carp,
with the horn still on his head.
Afterwards, he would return briefly from time to time,
his appearance as in his lifetime,
drinking with his descendants,
and leaving after a few days.
Since the end of the Jìn dynasty,
he has never been seen again.
Dújiǎo
Dújiǎo [The One-Horned] was
a person from Bàjùn.
He was probably several hundred years old.
Common folk had lost his name,
but he grew a single horn on his head,
so they called him Dújiǎo.
Sometimes he would suddenly leave for many years,
or remain silent for dozens of days.
But when he spoke,
the meaning and essence were subtle and profound,
and no one could fathom them.
Where he lived, he transformed others solely through virtue,
and also provided considerable instruction.
One day, he bid farewell to his family,
entered the river in front of his house,
and transformed into a carp,
with the horn still on his head.
Later, he would return briefly from time to time,
his appearance as in his lifetime,
feasting and drinking with his descendants.
After a few days, he would leave.
Xuē Wěi
Xuē Wěi,
in the first year of the Qiányuán era of the Táng dynasty,
served as the registrar of Qīngchéng County in Shǔ Prefecture,
serving concurrently with Assistant Magistrate Zōu Pāng, Sheriff Léi Jì, and Péi Liáo.
That autumn,
Wěi fell ill for seven days,
when suddenly he appeared lifeless as if having passed away,
unresponsive to repeated calls,
yet his chest remained faintly warm.
His family could not bear to prepare him for burial immediately,
so they gathered around and kept watch over him.
After twenty days had passed,
he suddenly let out a long sigh and sat up,
addressing his household,
saying:
"I do not know how many days have passed in the mortal world!"
They replied:
"Twenty days."
He said:
"Quickly,
go and see if the officials are just now eating sliced fish.
Tell them I have already revived,
and that there is a most extraordinary tale,
asking the gentlemen to put down their chopsticks and come listen."
The servant hurried to see the officials,
who indeed were about to eat sliced fish,
and so he relayed the message.
They all stopped their meal and came.
Wěi said:
"Did you gentlemen order the household servant Zhāng Bì to seek fish?"
They replied:
"Yes."
He then asked Bì:
"Did the fisherman Zhào Gān hide a huge carp,
offering a small one in response to the order,
and you, finding the hidden one among the reeds,
brought it here?
Just as you entered the county office,
the household clerk was sitting east of the gate,
the correction clerk was sitting west of the gate,
both playing chess.
Upon entering,
and reaching the steps,
Zōu and Léi were playing a board game,
while Péi was eating a peach.
Bì reported that Gān had hidden a large fish,
and Péi the fifth ordered him whipped.
Then it was handed over to the cook Wáng Shìliáng—
did he happily kill it?"
They asked each other in turn,
and it was indeed so.
The crowd said:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"The carp that was just killed—
that was me."
The crowd exclaimed in astonishment:
"We wish to hear the story."
He said:
"When I first fell gravely ill,
oppressed by fever,
it was almost unbearable.
Suddenly, in my distress, I forgot my illness,
detesting the heat and seeking coolness,
I took up my staff and left,
unaware it was a dream.
Once outside the city walls,
my heart felt joyful and free,
like a caged bird or confined beast gaining its liberty.
No one knew of me.
Gradually entering the mountains,
the mountain walk grew increasingly stifling,
so I descended to roam by the riverbank.
I saw the river pool deep and clear,
the autumn scenery delightful;
gentle ripples undisturbed,
the water like a mirror reflecting the distant sky.
Suddenly, I felt the desire to bathe,
so I removed my clothes on the bank
and leaped right in.
Since childhood, I have been fond of water,
but since reaching adulthood,
I had never played in it again.
Encountering this chance to indulge freely,
it truly fulfilled a long-held wish.
And I thought:
'Humans floating cannot compare to the swiftness of fish;
how can I take on the form of a fish and swim vigorously?'
A fish beside me said:
'It is only that you, sir, do not wish it.
To be granted a true form is also easy,
let alone seeking to take one on?
I shall make arrangements for you, sir.'
And decisively it left.
Not long after,
a fish-headed figure several feet tall,
riding a giant salamander to guide the way,
followed by several dozen fish,
proclaimed the River Earl's decree:
'Dwelling in cities or swimming in waters,
floating and sinking follow different paths;
if it is not one's preference,
then one remains ignorant of the flowing waves.
Registrar Xuē's heart yearns for the depths,
his spirit longs for idle vastness,
delighting in the boundless realm,
releasing his heart to the clear river;
weary of the sentiments of steep cliffs,
he casts aside his official cap for an illusory world.
Temporarily following the transformation into scales,
it is not an abrupt change of body.
He may provisionally serve as the red carp of the eastern pool.
Alas!
Relying on long waves to capsize boats,
one offends the obscure;
ignorant of the fine hook while coveting bait,
one is harmed by the obvious.
Let none lose themselves,
to bring shame upon their kind;
you must strive diligently.'
Listening, I looked at myself—
and already I was clad in fish form.
Thereupon, I released myself to swim,
wherever my thoughts went, there I arrived;
upon the waves or at the pool's bottom,
nowhere did I not move with ease;
the Three Rivers and Five Lakes,
I leaped and traversed nearly all.
However, assigned to remain in the eastern pool,
each evening I must return.
Soon, I grew extremely hungry,
and could find no food.
Following along a boat,
I suddenly saw Zhào Gān lowering his hook,
its bait fragrant and sweet.
In my heart, I knew to be cautious,
yet unconsciously I drew near to take it.
I thought:
'I am
a human,
temporarily a fish;
unable to seek food,
how can I swallow his hook?'
And so I left it and went away.
After a while,
my hunger grew even more severe.
I thought:
'I am an official,
playing at fish form.
Even if I swallow the hook,
would Zhào Gān dare kill me?
Surely he would send me back to the county office.'
And so I swallowed it.
Zhào Gān reeled in his line and pulled me out.
As Gān's hand was about to reach me,
Wěi called out to him repeatedly,
but Gān paid no heed.
Instead, he threaded a rope through my gills
and tied me among the reeds.
Soon after, Zhāng Bì came and said:
'Deputy Magistrate Péi wishes to buy fish,
and it must be a large one.'
Gān said:
'I have not caught any big fish,
but there is a small one over ten catties.'
Bì said:
'I am ordered to fetch a large fish;
why would I want a small one?'
Then he himself searched among the reeds, found Wěi, and lifted him out.
Wěi also said to Bì:
'I am the registrar of your county,
transformed into a fish swimming in the river.
Why do you not bow to me?'
Bì paid no attention,
carrying him along as he went.
Though Wěi cursed incessantly,
Bì,
never looked back.
Entering the county gate,
he saw the county clerks sitting and playing chess.
Wěi called out to them loudly,
but none responded at all.
They only laughed and said:
'Fearsome—
this fish
is worth over three or four catties.'
Then, upon reaching the steps,
Zōu and Léi were playing a board game,
Péi was eating a peach.
They were all pleased the fish was large
and urged that it be handed over to the kitchen.
Bì reported that Gān had hidden a huge fish,
offering a small one in response to the order.
Péi grew angry
and had him whipped.
I called out to you gentlemen, saying:
'I am the Duke,
We served together as officials,
yet now you see me being killed,
and you do not even try to save me,
urging instead to hasten my death—
is this humane?'
He cried out loudly and wept,
but the three gentlemen paid no heed,
handing him over to the butcher.
A man named Wáng Shìliáng,
just then sharpening his blade,
gleefully threw me onto the table.
I cried out again:
'Wáng Shìliáng,
you are the butcher I often employ,
why are you killing me?
Why not seize me and report to the officials?'
Shìliáng acted as if he did not hear,
pressing my neck against the chopping block and beheading me.
As that head fell,
I too awoke from the dream,
and thus received the summons.'
All the gentlemen were greatly astonished,
their hearts filled with pity and compassion.
However, Zhào Gān's capture,
Zhāng Bì's seizure,
the county clerk's game of chess,
the three gentlemen's arrival at the steps,
and Wáng Shìliáng's impending slaughter—
all had seen the fish's mouth move,
but in truth, none had heard anything.
Thereupon, the three gentlemen all gave up eating minced fish,
abstaining for the rest of their lives.
Wěi recovered fully from then on,
later rising repeatedly in office to become Deputy Magistrate of Huáyáng,
and eventually passed away.
Táotángshì
In the era of Táotáng,
the state of Zhàoshāng presented a thousand-year-old divine turtle,
over three feet square,
with inscriptions on its back,
all in tadpole script,
recording events since the creation of the world.
The emperor ordered it transcribed as the Turtle Chronicle.
Fú Tāo, in recounting the emperor's merits and virtues in an inscription, said:
'Written in vermilion, the text of the Turtle Chronicle.'
Yǔ
Yǔ exhausted his efforts in digging channels and ditches,
dredging rivers and leveling mountains.
A yellow dragon dragged its tail ahead,
while a black turtle carried blue clay behind.
The black turtle
was an envoy of the river essence.
Under the turtle's chin were seal characters,
all in ancient script,
forming words for the mountains and rivers of the Nine Provinces.
Wherever Yǔ excavated,
he sealed and marked the sites with blue clay,
having the black turtle imprint them.
The modern practice of piling earth to mark boundaries
is a legacy of this.
Gě Hóng
Gě Hóng said:
'The thousand-year-old numinous turtle
possesses all five colors.
The male
has two bones protruding on its forehead,
resembling horns.
Bathe it with vermilion ink,
then carve off its shell,
roast it over fire,
pound it, and ingest it.
Take a square-inch dose three times a day for seven days,
finishing one whole shell,
and you will live a thousand years.'
Zhāng Guǎngdìng
Chén Zhònggōng's *Records of Strange Tales* states:
Zhāng Guǎngdìng, fleeing chaos to avoid disaster,
had a four-year-old daughter
who could not walk.
Unable to bear abandoning her,
he suspended a basket in an ancient tomb,
hoping to retrieve her bones someday.
After three years,
he returned to fetch them,
only to find her still alive.
When questioned,
the girl replied:
'When the food ran out, I grew hungry.
Seeing a creature beside me,
stretching its neck to breathe,
I imitated it,
and thus survived.'
Guǎngdìng entered the tomb to look,
and it was a turtle.
Chén Shí's words
are indeed not false.
Gànxiàn Clerk
During the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
Fàn Yín served as Governor of Nánkāng Commandery.
At that time, a clerk from Gànxiàn recounted
that he had previously gone into the mountains to gather firewood
and caught two turtles,
each as large as a two-foot platter.
Not having gathered enough firewood,
he came upon two trees growing side by side.
The clerk placed the turtles sideways between the trees
and went back to gathering.
Having gone somewhat far from where the turtles were left,
it began to rain,
and he was too lazy to retrieve them.
Twelve years later,
he reentered the mountains
and saw the earlier turtles.
One's shell had already dried up,
while the other was still alive,
extremely elongated.
The trees had grown around it,
at that spot,
it was about four inches thick,
with both ends over a foot thick,
shaped like a saddle.
Xī Shìliǎo
Xī Shìliǎo was constructing a tomb in Kuàijī,
where the ground was rocky.
Later, when breaking a large rock,
he found a turtle inside,
about 1.2 feet long,
within the rock.
The rock had no holes at all,
could it be that the turtle and the rock were born together?
Once broken out,
the turtle moved about no differently from an ordinary turtle.
The rock accommodated the turtle
as if carved and placed there by a person.
Mèng Yànhuī
In the third year of Wǔchéng, gēngwǔ,
on the fifth day of the sixth month, guǐhài,
Mèng Yànhuī, Governor of Guǎnghàn, reported
that in the West Lake, there was a golden turtle an inch in diameter,
swimming atop lotus leaves.
A painting was made and presented to the emperor.
Yínglíng
In Yínglíng, Dàozhōu, there is a tuó,
with a shell eight feet long.
Naturally, there are characters underneath,
and its four feet, front and back,
each tread upon a turtle.
When it treads on the turtles, it sometimes travels,
crossing mountains and fording waters.
Common folk dare not offend it.
Xīngyè Temple
The Nine-Bend Spirit Turtle Pond,
located three li northeast of Xiāngyáng County east of Biànxué Temple.
The old city originally had Xīngyè Temple,
now merged into Biànxué Temple.
In the first year of the Táng Jǐnglóng era, a person from Chénliú surnamed Ruǎn,
residing in Xiāngyáng,
donated wealth,
at the east courtyard of this temple.
Constructed halls and buildings,
at that time there was a drought and the pond dried up,
so they excavated to widen and deepen it,
suddenly heavy rain caused the pond to overflow,
and there was a large turtle,
several feet tall,
as large as half a bed,
walking along the bank.
The crowd exclaimed in surprise,
and the turtle then leaped into the pond.
Temple monk Líng Xiù said,
in the courtyard there is a broken stele,
which says it is the Xīngyè Temple stele.
The stele inscription was composed by Liáng Dynasty Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Yǔ Yuánwēi,
the text that can be transmitted says,
this temple had a spirit turtle,
three chi five cun long,
hibernating in winter and appearing in spring,
for many years;
it followed the crowd into the hall,
and ate at the appropriate times.
Inspector Ānlù Prince Zhào frequently encountered this turtle,
the broken stele was therefore erected,
now located in the east courtyard of Biànxué Temple.
The temple hall repaired by the Ruǎn family,
in front of the stūpa in the courtyard,
the pond is still present,
five chi deep,
twenty paces square.
Táng Tàizōng
At the end of Táng Wǔdé era,
Tàizōng wanted to quell internal troubles,
in the garden pond there was a white turtle,
swimming on a lotus leaf.
Tàizōng took it,
it transformed into white stone,
sparkling and pure like jade,
after ascending the throne,
he issued an edict saying:
"The August Heaven shows favor and protection,
bestowing a precious turtle."
Liú Yànhuí
In the Táng Dynasty, Liú Yànhuí's father was the prefect of Húzhōu,
a subordinate obtained a turtle from a silver mine,
one chi long,
and presented it to the prefect.
All the officials congratulated saying:
"If you eat this turtle,
you will live a thousand years."
The prefect declined, saying he was not the right person,
so he personally rode a horse,
and returned the turtle to the mine site.
More than ten years later,
the prefect died.
Yànhuí became a Sīshì official in Fángzhōu,
taking his family to assume the post,
encountering mountain floodwaters overflowing,
submerging all flat land,
the whole family was terrified,
not knowing where to go.
Suddenly a large turtle came to lead the way,
Yànhuí discussed with his family:
"The turtle is a spiritual creature,
now coming to guide us,
it seems like a deity."
Over thirty people followed the turtle,
all walking in shallow areas,
traveling over ten li,
until they reached flat land,
escaping the flood disaster,
the whole family was surprised and delighted,
not knowing the reason.
That night,
Yànhuí dreamed the turtle said:
"I was formerly at the silver mine,
received kindness from your late father the prefect,
therefore I repay the favor now."
Wúxīng Fisherman
During the Táng Kāiyuán era,
a fisherman from Wúxīng,
often saw a large turtle on the Tiáo River,
each of its four feet stepping on a turtle as it walked.
The fisherman knew it was a spirit turtle,
threw a stone at it,
hit and captured it.
After some time,
he presented it to the prefectural assistant Péi.
Péi summoned a turtle diviner,
the turtle diviner said:
"This is a kingly turtle,
cannot be used to divine minor matters,
whatever is divined will surely die."
Péi was always arrogant and reckless,
at that time there was a magpie in the courtyard,
its chicks still young,
so to test this,
he ordered the diviner to drill the turtle.
Several days later,
strong wind damaged the magpie nest,
the magpie chicks all died.
Then he ordered to divine his maid,
whether her pregnancy was a boy or girl,
the omen indicated:
"Will give birth to a son."
The son was born,
but soon died as well.
Péi later eventually presented this turtle.
Táng Míng Huáng Emperor
Táng Míng Huáng Emperor once had a fangshi present a small turtle,
one cun in diameter and golden-colored, very lovely,
saying:
"This turtle is divine and does not eat,
can be placed inside a pillow case,
to ward off the poison of giant snakes."
The emperor often kept it in a handkerchief box,
a young eunuch deeply favored,
but implicated by relatives,
was to be exiled to the southern border,
not wishing to bend the law to exempt him,
secretly gave him this turtle saying:
"The southern wilderness has many giant pythons,
always keep this turtle by your side,
then you can avoid suffering."
The eunuch bowed and received it.
When he reached a county under Xiàng Prefecture,
the village market and guest houses,
were completely empty without a single person,
so he lodged at an inn.
That night,
the moon was bright as day,
but there were sounds of wind and rain,
gradually approaching.
So he took out this turtle,
placed it on the steps,
after a long while,
the divine turtle stretched its neck and exhaled breath,
like a thread of fire,
straight up three to four chi high,
slowly dispersing.
Afterward the turtle swam and rested as usual,
the previous wind and rain sounds,
had also ceased.
By dawn,
the post station officials gradually arrived,
bowing in rows in the courtyard saying:
"Yesterday we knew an imperial envoy was coming,
and should have prepared to welcome you,
but it happened that a traveler mistakenly killed a snake.
Everyone knew the vengeful snake would surely cause harm this night,
nearby residents,
all went out thirty to fifty li away,
to avoid its poison.
We did not dare go far,
only hid in nearby mountain caves,
crouching until dawn.
Now the imperial envoy is unharmed,
this is due to divine protection,
not human power."
After some time,
travelers gradually arrived,
saying on the road were over ten giant snakes,
all already rotten.
From then on there were no more vengeful creatures,
people could not fathom the reason.
Over a year later,
the eunuch was recalled to Cháng'ān,
and again presented the golden turtle to the emperor,
weeping and thanking him:
"Not only was my life,
preserved by this,
but also the people of the south,
permanently rid of poisonous creatures.
The lives saved,
are beyond count.
Truly due to the imperial virtue,
and the power of the divine turtle."
Níngjìn Commoner
In the fourth year of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
north of the Shā River in Níngjìn County, Zhàozhōu,
there was a large pear tree,
which the common people often prayed to.
Suddenly, several thousand snakes,
coming from the southeast,
crossed the northern bank,
gathered under the pear tree into two piles,
while those remaining on the southern bank formed one pile.
Soon, three turtles, each about an inch in diameter,
circled around,
and all the piled-up snakes died.
They then climbed onto the piles,
and saw that the snakes' bellies all had sores,
as if struck by arrows.
The Prefect Kāng Rìzhī depicted the pear tree and the three turtles and presented them as tribute.
Historical Commentary
The Táng historical commentary states that when he was a general,
he suddenly noticed a light in his wife's room,
found it strange,
and thus searched the room with his wife,
but found nothing.
One day,
his wife opened her dressing case while doing her morning makeup,
and suddenly inside the case was a golden turtle,
the size of a coin,
emitting five-colored vapor,
filling the entire room.
They later kept and raised it.
Xú Zhòng
In Fúzhōu,
in the late Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a villager was selling a cage of turtles,
thirteen in total.
The medicine peddler Xú Zhòng bought them for five huán.
The villager said:
"These are sacred turtles,
they must not be killed."
Xú placed them in the courtyard,
one turtle used the others as a base to walk,
with eight turtles leading the way,
all about six inches in size.
Xú then released them into the woods behind the Qiányuán Temple,
and they disappeared overnight.
Gāo Chóngwén
Lǐ Déyù, the Duke of Zànhuáng of the Táng dynasty, said:
"In Shǔ, it is said that when Zhāng Yí built the Chéngdū city walls,
they repeatedly collapsed.
At that time, a turtle circled and walked around,
and following the path of one turtle, they built the walls,
and soon the city was completed.
Before I arrived at the commandery,
I had heard that the turtle shell was still within the city walls.
Recently, I inquired among the elders,
and an official of the military supplies treasury named Yǔwén Yù
said it had always been kept in the treasury.
In the early Yuánhé era,
the military governor Gāo Chóngwén learned of it,
and ordered craftsmen to cut it into belt ornaments and waist accessories."
From Zhāng Yí to Gāo Chóngwén, over a thousand years had passed,
and the turtle shell was still preserved,
yet a military officer destroyed it,
which is deeply regrettable.
Merchant on the Biàn River
In the Táng dynasty, a merchant moored his boat on the Biàn River,
caught a huge turtle,
and roasted it in the stove fire.
That night,
he forgot to take it out,
