and the next day when he retrieved it to look,
the shell was already charred.
He brushed off the ashes,
placed it on the dining table,
intending to eat it.
After a long while,
it stretched out its neck and moved its limbs,
slowly walking on the table,
alive as usual.
Everyone found it strange,
and threw it into the water,
where it swam away.
Southerners
Southerners collect turtle urine,
as they are jealous by nature and mate with snakes.
Sometimes when a female snake arrives,
they chase, fight, and bite each other,
and the weaker one may die.
When collecting it,
they take a male turtle and place it in a porcelain bowl or small plate,
behind the turtle,
use a mirror to reflect it.
Once the turtle sees itself in the mirror,
it becomes aroused and loses urine.
Alternatively, they use a paper wick heated in the fire,
touch its rear,
which also causes it to lose urine,
but this is not as effective as using the mirror.
This method was obtained from the Taoist priest Chén Zhāo.
Also, people by the sea say,
dragons lay three eggs,
one of which becomes a jídiào.
The jídiào comes ashore and mates with deer,
or leaves its essence by the water's edge.
When drifting wood encounters it,
it sticks to the branches,
like grapes.
It is slightly bluish-yellow in color,
also resembling gray,
and is called zǐshāohuā,
which benefits male vitality.
There are other methods described elsewhere.
Yán Jūjìng
Yán Jūjìng, a man from Xīn'ān,
lived in a place flooded by mountain waters,
and fearing his house would collapse,
he moved his bed outside the door to sleep.
He dreamed of a dark-skinned person saying:
"You are avoiding the water here,
I am also avoiding the water and came here.
What harm am I to you?
Yet you oppress me like this,
is it not very displeasing?"
Yán Jūjìng woke up,
unable to understand the reason.
That night he dreamed three times,
and Yán Jūjìng said:
"Could it be that I should not stay here?"
He then ordered the bed to be moved,
and found that one bed leg was slanting and pressing on a turtle outside the threshold.
He released it, and it left.
Resident of Chízhōu
A resident of Chízhōu named Yáng made a living selling pickled fish.
Once, he cooked ten carp,
and had his son watch over them.
When they were almost done,
he suddenly heard pleas for mercy from the pot several times,
and the son, frightened,
ran to tell his parents.
They went together to look,
and there was not a single fish left in the pot;
they searched but could not find them.
A year later,
the family dog kept barking at the area under the threshold.
After several days,
a family member said:
"Could it be that last year's carp
are here?"
They immediately removed the threshold to look,
and found ten turtles,
which they released into the water.
The family was then unharmed.
Lǐ Zōng
Lǐ Zōng was the Prefect of Chǔzhōu.
In the commandery, a nun was walking in the market,
when she suddenly sat down on the ground,
unable to be pushed or pulled,
and for days did not eat or speak.
The local authorities reported this to Lǐ Zōng,
who ordered soldiers to lift her up.
They dug the ground beneath her,
and found a large turtle several feet long.
They released it into the water,
and the nun then recovered.
Yù Shooting
"Records of the Mysterious Middle" states:
"The yù shoots people with its breath.
From thirty paces away,
it can shoot their shadow.
If it hits a person,
six or seven out of ten die."
"The Bamboo Annals" states:
"In the second year of spring of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
King Huì of Zhōu resided in Zhèng.
People of Zhèng entered the king's palace to take a jade horse,
and the jade transformed into a yù,
which shot people."
Transforming into a Cicada
The Queen of Qí, resentful of the King's anger, died in fury.
Her corpse transformed into a cicada,
which then ascended a tree in the courtyard,
chirping and singing.
Later, the King regretted and grieved.
Hearing the cicada's song,
he would sigh in sorrow.
Saluting the Angry Frog
After King Gōujiàn of Yuè was humiliated by Wú,
he always treated scholars with utmost courtesy,
planning to subdue Wú.
One day while traveling,
he saw an angry frog.
Gōujiàn saluted it.
His attendants asked:
"Why does Your Majesty salute an angry frog?"
He replied:
"If the frog can be so angry,
how dare I not salute it?"
Upon hearing this, brave warriors
all came to Yuè,
and they subdued Wú.
Guàizāi
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn visited Gānquán.
On the imperial road, there was an insect,
red in color,
with a complete head, teeth, ears, and nose.
No one who saw it could identify it.
The Emperor then sent Dōngfāng Shuò to examine it.
Upon returning, he reported:
"This insect is named Guàizāi.
In the past, when innocent people were imprisoned,
the masses were filled with sorrow and resentment.
They all looked up and sighed, saying:
'Guàizāi, guàizāi!'
This moved Heaven above,
and it was born from their indignation,
hence the name Guàizāi.
This place must have been a prison site of Qín."
Checking the map,
it was indeed as he said.
The Emperor further asked:
"How can we get rid of this insect?"
Shuò said:
"All worries
can be dissolved with wine.
Pouring wine on it should make it vanish."
So they had someone fetch the insect and place it in wine.
In a moment, it disintegrated.
Little Insects
In the sixth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
in Shānyáng, there were small insects all resembling human forms,
very numerous.
The next day,
they were all found hanging dead from tree branches.
The Jiǎng Insect
Jiǎng Zǐwén
was a man from Guǎngyáng.
He was fond of wine and women,
frivolous and unrestrained.
He often said:
"When I die, I shall become a god."
In the late Hàn dynasty,
he served as the Commandant of Mòlíng.
While pursuing bandits to the foot of a mountain,
he was struck on the forehead by a bandit.
He then untied his official seal ribbon to bind the wound,
and shortly after died.
At the beginning of the reign of the founding ruler of Wú,
a former subordinate saw Zǐwén on the road,
riding a white horse,
holding a white feather fan,
with attendants as in his lifetime.
The witness fled in fright,
but Zǐwén pursued him,
saying:
"I am to be the local god here.
I will bring blessings
to you, the people below.
Inform the commoners
to establish a shrine for me.
If not,
there will be great calamity."
That summer,
a great epidemic broke out.
The people grew fearful and agitated,
and many secretly began to worship him.
Not long after,
he again spoke through a shaman:
"I shall greatly assist
the Sūn family.
The authorities should establish a shrine for me.
If not,
I will send insects into people's ears as a disaster."
Soon, there indeed were gadflies
that entered people's ears and caused death,
untreatable by physicians.
The people grew even more terrified.
Lord Sūn still did not believe it.
Then again, through a shaman, he said:
"If you do not sacrifice to me,
I will bring a great fire disaster."
That year,
hundreds of major fires broke out.
The fires gradually spread to the official palaces.
Lord Sūn became concerned.
Advisors at the time argued that if the god had a proper place,
he would cease to be malevolent,
and they should offer sacrifices to appease him.
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to enfeoff Zǐwén as Zhōngdū Hóu,
and his son Xù as Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
both granted official seals and ribbons.
A temple was built to manifest his divinity.
This is present-day Jiǎng Shān northeast of Jiànkāng.
From then on, epidemics and calamities ceased.
The people then greatly worshipped him.
The *Yōumíng Lù* also records this.
Yuán Kè
Yuán Kè
was a man from Jìyīn.
He was handsome and virtuous,
and many in the district wished to give him their daughters in marriage,
but he never married.
He often cultivated five-colored fragrant herbs,
for several decades,
and consumed their fruits.
One day, a five-colored moth alighted beside him.
Kè collected it and placed it on a mat.
When it was time for silkworms,
a woman arrived at midnight,
claiming to be Kè's wife,
and explained the silkworm situation.
Kè and she reared silkworms together,
obtaining one hundred and twenty cocoons,
each as large as a jar.
Reeling the silk from one cocoon
took sixty days to finish.
When done, they both departed,
and none knew where they went.
The people of Jìyīn established a shrine to worship them.
The Man in Black
In Fùyáng County of Wú, there was a man named Dǒng Zhāozhī,
who once crossed the Qiántáng River by boat.
On the river, he saw an ant on a short reed,
frightened and fearing death.
He then tied the reed to the boat with a rope.
When the boat reached shore,
the ant was able to get out.
That night,
he dreamed of a man in black clothes thanking him, saying:
"I am the king of the ants.
I am grateful for your lifesaving kindness.
If you later face urgent danger,
I will inform you."
More than ten years later,
during a time of widespread banditry,
Zhāozhī was wrongly accused as the leader of the bandits
and imprisoned in Yúyáo.
Zhāozhī suddenly remembered the ant king's dream.
As he was dwelling on it,
a fellow prisoner asked him about it.
Zhāozhī told him the whole truth.
That person said:
"Just take two or three ants in your palm and speak to them."
Zhāozhī did as told.
That night, he indeed dreamed of the man in black saying:
"Quickly flee to the mountains in Yúháng.
The world is already in chaos,
and a pardon decree will be issued soon,
indeed."
Upon waking,
the ants had gnawed through his shackles completely.
Thus, he was able to escape prison,
cross the river,
and flee to the Yúháng mountains.
Soon, he encountered the pardon,
and thus came to no harm.
Zhū Dàn, the Attendant
In Huáinán,
the historian Zhū Dàn, styled Yǒngcháng,
during the era of Sūn Hào of Wú,
served as the prefect of Jiàn'ān.
Zhū Dàn's servant's wife suffered from a ghostly illness,
and her husband suspected her of adultery.
Later, when he went out,
he secretly drilled a hole in the wall to spy on her.
He saw his wife weaving at the loom,
gazing into the distance at a mulberry tree,
laughing and speaking toward it.
The servant looked up
and saw a young man in the tree,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
wearing green lapels and sleeves,
with a green headscarf.
The servant, thinking it was a real person,
drew his crossbow and shot at him.
The young man transformed into a chirping cicada,
as large as a winnowing basket,
and flew away soaring.
His wife also cried out in shock:
"Ah!
Someone shot you!"
The servant was puzzled by this.
Some time later,
the servant saw two children talking together on the path.
One said:
"Why haven't we seen you again?"
The other was the child from the tree,
who replied:
"I was careless before,
Someone shot me,
and the wound has been festering for a long time."
The other child said:
"How are you now?"
He replied:
"Thanks to the ointment from Prefect Zhū's roof beam, which I applied,
I have recovered."
The servant reported to Zhū Dàn:
"Someone stole your ointment,
do you know about it?"
Zhū Dàn said:
"My ointment has long been placed on the roof beam.
How could anyone steal it?"
The servant said:
"That's not the case,
please take a look, Prefect."
Zhū Dàn was highly skeptical,
but went to inspect it.
The seal and label appeared unchanged.
Zhū Dàn said:
"You lowly fellow are making up stories,
the ointment is as it was."
The servant said:
"Try opening it."
Upon opening, half the ointment was gone,
and there were traces of scraping with toes.
Zhū Dàn was shocked,
and questioned him in detail.
The servant recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
Gě Huīfū
Gě Huīfū of Wūshāng in the Jìn dynasty,
during the Yìxī era,
was staying at his wife's family home.
At the third watch,
two people holding torches came to the front of the steps.
Suspecting they were villains,
he went to strike them.
As he was about to bring down his staff,
they all transformed into butterflies,
scattering and flying away in confusion.
One rushed under Gě Huīfū's armpit,
and he immediately fell to the ground,
dying shortly after.
Shǒugōng
The *Bówùzhì* states:
"If you raise a shǒugōng in a container,
feed it cinnabar,
its body will turn completely red.
When it weighs a full seven catties,
pound it ten thousand times,
and apply it to a woman's limbs.
The mark will never fade."
The *Huáinán Wàn Bì Shù* says:
"Take a shǒugōng,
newly mated,
and keep the male and female separately in jars.
After drying in the shade for a hundred days,
apply it to a woman's arm.
It will produce patterns,
but if she has intercourse with a man,
they will immediately disappear."
Flesh Fungus
The flesh fungus
refers to the ten-thousand-year-old toad,
which has horns on its head,
and under its chin, a red script of eight characters written twice.
If captured at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
dried in the shade for a hundred days,
and its foot used to draw on the ground,
water will immediately flow.
Carrying it
on the left side of the body
wards off the five weapons.
If an enemy shoots at you,
the arrows and bolts will turn back toward the shooter.
The thousand-year-old bat,
white as snow,
hangs upside down when resting,
because its brain is heavy.
If this creature is obtained and dried in the shade,
ground into powder and consumed,
it can extend a person's life to forty thousand years.
Fly Touching the Curtain
Emperor Míng of Jìn often wished to issue an amnesty,
keeping it secret and undisclosed.
He secluded himself in a private chamber,
dismissed his attendants,
and drew the curtains to draft the edict.
A large blue fly touched the curtain and entered,
gathering on the tip of his brush.
Shortly after, it flew away,
and the emperor found this strange.
He sent someone to check where the fly had gathered,
and news of the amnesty had already spread,
becoming widely known everywhere.
Cāngwú Insects
The *Bówùzhì* states:
"When someone in Cāngwú dies,
flying insects appear,
as large as wheat grains,
with shells.
Sometimes over a shí in quantity,
or three to five dǒu,
they come to feed on the corpse,
like wind and rain arriving,
and finish it in an instant.
People consider them a plague,
impossible to eradicate.
They only fear catalpa wood,
so thereafter, catalpa wood was used for coffins,
and they no longer come."
Zhàměng
Huán Qiān, courtesy name Jìngzǔ.
During the Tàiyuán era,
in the middle,
suddenly there appeared people all about an inch tall,
all clad in armor and holding spears,
riding fully equipped horses,
emerging from holes in the ground.
Their gleaming radiance dazzled the sun,
as they roamed about the residence,
in groups of several hundred.
Forming ranks and directing commands,
they clashed and stabbed at each other,
the horses being swift and agile,
the men also quite capable.
They climbed along tables and onto stoves,
searching for places of food and drink.
Wherever there was sliced meat,
they would gather in crowds,
and whatever they could manage with their strength,
they would spear and take away,
heading straight into their holes,
silently not emerging again,
or coming out and returning to their holes.
The Jiǎngshān Daoist priest Zhū Yìngzǐ ordered boiling water to be made,
and poured it into the places they entered.
Upon digging there,
they found about a hu-large ant dead in the hole.
Huán Qiān was later executed and his family exterminated.
Qīngtíng
Sīmǎ Biāo’s “Commentary on Zhuāngzǐ”
says that a child buried the head of a qīngtíng,
and without eating, danced, saying,
“This will become a pearl,”
and people laughed at him.
The “Records of the Investigation of Things” states,
“If you bury the head of a qīngtíng beneath a westward-facing door,
it will transform into a blue-green pearl.”
Zhū Dàn
In the early Sòng,
in Huáinán Commandery, there was a creature that took people’s hair buns.
The commandery governor Zhū Dàn said:
“I know what it is.”
He bought much sticky paste to smear on the walls.
In the evening, there was a bat as large as a chicken,
that alighted upon it,
and could not get away,
and killing it ended the matter.
Upon inspection,
beneath the curtain hooks there were already several hundred human hair buns.
White Earthworms
The nephew of Liú Déyuàn’s elder brother,
Tàizǎi Cóngshì Zhōngláng Dàocún,
in the first year of the Jǐnghé era,
suddenly several dozen white earthworms climbed onto the stone steps in front of his study,
their entire bodies white,
something people had never seen before.
The earthworms all opened their mouths and stuck out their tongues,
A great red color.
In the eighth month of that year,
he and Déyuàn were both executed.
Wáng Shuāng
Wáng Shuāng of Mèngzhōu,
in the early Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of the Sòng,
suddenly did not wish to see light.
He often fetched water to wet the ground,
and covered it with wild rice stalks,
sleeping, resting, eating, and drinking,
all within it.
He said,
there was always a woman,
wearing a blue skirt and white headscarf,
who came to sleep with him.
Each time he heard beneath the matting,
there were clear, distinct sounds.
Upon uncovering it,
he saw one blue-bodied, white-necked,
earthworm,
about two feet long.
He said,
this woman often gave him a box of incense as a gift,
its fragrance very refined and aromatic.
The box was actually a snail shell,
the incense was the root of the grass pú.
At that time, everyone thought Wáng Shuāng had temporarily become like a grasshopper.
Hú Chōng
Hú Chōng of Yùzhāng in the Sòng,
on an autumn evening in the fifth year of Yuánjiā,
a large centipede two feet long,
fell before Hú Chōng’s wife and younger sister,
and he ordered a maid to pick it up and throw it away.
As soon as the maid went out the door,
she suddenly saw an old woman,
her clothes foul and decayed,
her two eyes lifeless.
By the third month of the sixth year,
the entire household fell ill at that time,
and deaths followed one after another.
Lú Fén
The “Records of the Strange and Uncanny” says:
Lú Fén of Xiàyáng, courtesy name Shìjì,
from youth was fond of learning,
diligent day and night without weariness.
On the twentieth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Yǒng’ān era of Emperor Zhuāng of the Later Wèi,
as he was about to depart for Luòyáng,
friends held a feast in his study.
Late at night after the moon had risen,
suddenly from within the air of the locust tree in front of the hall,
they heard the sounds of talking and laughter,
along with the melodies of string and wind instruments.
Several friends all heard it,
and were astonished.
Soon they saw a woman dressed in black and blue clothes,
emerge from the locust tree,
and say to Fén:
“This place is not where you, sir, should come,
why have you come here?”
Fén said:
“I have just finished feasting,
and my friends heard the sound of this music,
so we came to request an audience.”
The woman laughed and said:
“You, sir, truly are surnamed Lú.”
Then she entered the hole.
Soon a gentle breeze stirred the forest,
Fén sighed in wonder,
and it was as if he grew dim and confused.
When he raised his eyes,
he saw palace buildings open wide,
gates and doors distinctly visible.
There was a woman dressed in blue clothes,
who came out and said to Fén:
“The lady commands you, sir, and the other gentlemen to meet.”
Fén entered with his three friends,
and saw several dozen people, each about over twenty years old,
standing within a great hall,
its plaque inscribed “Hall of Rain Deliberation.”
Fén and his three friends ascended the steps,
and met a woman in purple clothes.
She said to Fén:
“Just now, together with the various ladies of the palace,
during our singing and feasting,
we heard that you gentlemen had graciously descended,
and did not dare refuse,
therefore we invited you,
to meet.”
The one in purple then ordered Fén and the others to join the feast.
Afterwards, there were those dressed in white, blue, and yellow,
all about over twenty years old,
emerging from the eastern and western chambers of the hall,
about seven or eight people,
all bewitchingly beautiful, peerless in the world.
After exchanging bows,
before the joyous feast had deepened,
there was already great affection and delight.
Suddenly they heard a great wind arrive,
the beam of the Hall of Rain Deliberation broke and collapsed,
and everyone scattered at once.
Fén and his three friends all ran,
and then awoke.
Then they saw in the courtyard the ancient locust tree,
a large branch broken by the wind,
fallen with its roots.
So they took torches to illuminate the broken place,
and found a large ant nest,
three or four mole crickets,
one or two earthworms,
all dead in the nest.
Fén said to his three friends:
“How strange!
All creatures have spirits,
and moreover we just feasted with them,
not knowing by what cause we,
entered.”
Thereupon, by dawn,
they cut down this tree,
and there was nothing else unusual.
Lái Jūnchuò
When Emperor Yáng of Suí launched his campaign against Liáo,
all twelve armies were utterly destroyed.
Commander Lái Hù was executed for violating military law,
and Emperor Yáng intended to exterminate all his descendants.
Lái Jūnchuò, filled with anxiety and fear,
joined forces for several days with scholars Luó Xún, Luó Dì, and Lǐ Wànjìn,
forming a band of fugitives,
and together they fled to Hǎizhōu.
One night, lost in the darkness,
they saw a light by the roadside,
so they decided to stop there.
After knocking on the door several times,
an old servant came out to greet them.
Lái Jūnchuò then asked
whose house this was.
The servant replied:
"This is the residence of Master Kēdǒu, surnamed Wēi,
who is a xiùcai of this prefecture."
He then opened the gate,
which
closed by itself.
He knocked on the inner door and said:
"Wō'ér, today
we have four or five guests."
Wō'ér was another old servant.
He then opened the door,
lit a candle to guide the guests inside,
and led them to the guest quarters,
where beds, couches, and cushions were all well prepared.
Soon, a young boy holding a candle came out from the inner quarters
and said:
"The sixth young master is coming out."
Lái Jūnchuò and the others descended the steps to meet their host.
The host was eloquent and articulate,
engaging in sophisticated and intricate debate.
He introduced himself as:
"Wēi Wūhuò."
After exchanging pleasantries,
he invited the guests to ascend the eastern steps,
and once seated, he said:
"Wūhuò is humbled to have passed the provincial examination in this prefecture,
and thus shares a common scholarly bond with you all.
This splendid gathering under the azure sky
is truly a joyous occasion."
He then ordered wine to be served to the guests,
and as they gradually became intoxicated and merry,
conversation and banter flowed freely,
leaving everyone else unable to keep up.
Lái Jūnchuò felt somewhat indignant
and wanted to defeat him with reason,
but had no plan.
So he raised his cup and said:
"Jūnchuò proposes to start a drinking game:
if anyone's name in this gathering contains alliteration,
they shall be penalized according to the rules."
Lái Jūnchuò then said:
"Wēi Wūhuò."
This was actually a mockery of his surname.
Everyone clapped and laughed heartily,
thinking he had scored a point.
When it was Wūhuò's turn,
he changed the rule and said:
"Let us use the surnames of those present to create rhyming chants,
from two characters to three characters."
He then chanted:
"Luó Lǐ,
Luó Lái Lǐ."
Everyone was ashamed of his wit and quickness.
Luó Xún then asked:
"You are a man of refinement and elegance,
You could very well compare yourself to
a dragon,
so why choose a name that demeans you like jade?"
Wūhuò replied:
"I have long participated in the imperial examinations,
but have often been unfairly treated by the examiners.
Since I am placed behind the other scholars,
how am I different from an inchworm in a filthy pond?"
Luó Xún then asked:
"Your honorable clan,
why is it not recorded in the genealogies?"
Wūhuò replied:
"I originally belong to the Tián
clan,
descended from King Wēi of Qí,
much like the Huán and Dīng clans,
how could you be so unlearned?"
Soon after, Wō'ér brought in a feast on a large tray,
filled with delicacies from land and water,
overflowing in abundance.
Lái Jūnchuò and his servants
all ate their fill.
At night, the candles were extinguished,
and they slept side by side on couches.
At dawn, they bid farewell,
filled with regret and sorrow.
After traveling several miles,
Lái Jūnchuò still thought of Wūhuò.
They returned
to the place where they had met the previous night,
but found no trace of human habitation.
Only by the filthy pond was a large earthworm,
several feet long,
and also snails and tadpoles,
all several times larger than usual.
Only then did they realize that Wūhuò and the two servants
were all these creatures.
Disgusted by what they had eaten the previous night,
they each vomited several sheng of green mud and filthy water.
Chuánshī Disease
In the final years of the Dàyè era of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
a household in Luòyáng was afflicted with chuánshī disease,
and several brothers
died one after another.
Later, when one of them died,
his breath had not yet ceased,
and the family was weeping together.
His younger brother suddenly saw something emerge from the dead man's mouth
and leap into his own mouth.
From then on, he fell ill
and died a little over a year later.
On his deathbed,
he said to his wife:
"My illness was caused by the thing I saw.
After I die,
you must open my brain and throat
to see what is inside,
so we can understand its origin."
After saying this, he died.
His younger brother followed his instructions and opened him up,
finding an object in his brain
shaped like a fish,
with two heads,
and covered entirely with fleshy scales.
He placed it in a bowl,
where it jumped about incessantly.
When they tried feeding it various foods,
though it did not appear to eat,
everything turned into water in an instant,
and even poisons dissolved along with it.
At the time, it was midsummer, and the indigo plants were ripe,
so the monks at the temple were making indigo dye by the water.
One of them went there
and placed a small amount of indigo dye in the bowl.
The creature immediately began to dash about frantically.
In a moment,
it had turned into water.
Thus, indigo dye was used to treat choking.
Téng Tíngjùn
In the first year of the Wénmíng era,
Téng Tíngjùn of Pílíng suffered from a heat illness for many years.
Each time it flared up,
his body felt as if on fire,
and it would take several days to subside.
Famous physicians could not cure him.
Later, he went to Luòyáng for an official assignment,
and when he reached a spot fourteen or fifteen lǐ west of Yíngshuǐ,
it was nearing dusk,
and he had not yet reached his destination,
so he sought lodging at a farmhouse by the roadside.
The host had stepped out temporarily,
and had not yet returned.
Tíngjùn felt bored and restless,
so he sighed and said:
"A traveler's lot is full of hardship,
at dusk, no host in sight."
Immediately, an old man appeared,
with sparse, thinning hair,
and worn-out clothes,
emerging from the west side of the hall.
He bowed and said:
"Although this old man understands little,
I have a fondness for literary compositions.
I did not know you had arrived, sir,
and was just composing linked verses with Hé Qiěyé.
Hearing you recite 'A traveler's lot is full of hardship,
at dusk, no host in sight,'
even Cáo Pī's gate
guests,
Zǐcháng,
fear,
people,
could not surpass it.
This old man and Hé Qiěyé,
are both guests in the Hún family's household,
though poor, we still have a measure of wine,
to share with you for a refined conversation."
Tíngjùn found this very strange,
and asked:
"Where does the old man reside?"
The old man angrily said:
"I am but a humble guest who sweeps the gate for the Hún family,
my surname is Má, given name Láihé,
and I am the eldest.
Why don't you call me Má Dà."
Tíngjùn immediately apologized for his lack of discernment,
and went with him.
Circling around the western corner of the hall,
they came upon two gates,
the gates opened,
revealing a magnificent hall and layered pavilions, exceptionally elegant.
Inside the lodge were wine vessels and trays of food,
Má Dà courteously invited Tíngjùn to sit together.
After a long while,
another guest emerged from the middle gate,
Má Dà said:
"Hé has arrived."
He then descended the steps and courteously invited him to sit.
Qiěyé said to Má Dà:
"Just now I was about to compose linked verses with you,
have you finished the poem's theme?"
Má Dà then wrote down the title:
"A Linked Verse Composed Together at the Hún Family's Plains Gate Lodge," one piece,
I have already,
completed four lines.
Má Dà's poem said:
"Since I became the Hún family's neighbor,
fragrance has filled my body.
Unintentionally fond of purity and quiet,
people use me to remove dust and grime.
I have finished my four lines."
Qiěyé said:
"Mine is in seven-character lines,
and the rhyme is also different,
what should we do?"
Má Dà said:
"Just compose your own stanza,
that would not be bad either."
Qiěyé pondered for a long while and then recited:
"In winter,
each morning I go relying on smoke and fire,
when spring comes I return to nurture my offspring.
Once I sat at Fú Wáng's brush tip,
since then I seek food at the Hún family's gate."
Tíngjùn still did not realize,
seeing the lodge was splendid and grand,
he considered staying and resting there.
He composed a poem:
"Tián Wén was known for loving guests,
how many people did he actually support?
If Féng Xuān were still lacking,
now I hope to be a guest among the lowest."
Qiěyé and Má Dà,
looked at each other and laughed:
"How can you mock us?
If you were at the Hún family's gate,
you would be satiated in a single day."
Thereupon, they served a feast of fine dishes,
and drank toasts many rounds.
The host returned,
and could not find Tíngjùn,
so he had someone call for him,
Tíngjùn responded with a "yes."
But the lodge and Má and Hé, the two men,
vanished in an instant,
and he found himself sitting in the outhouse,
beside him only a large fly and a bald broom.
Tíngjùn originally had a heat illness,
but from then on it suddenly healed,
and never flared up again.
Zhāng Sīgōng
During the Táng dynasty, in the era of Empress Tiānhòu,
the Imperial Food Attendant Zhāng Sīgōng presented beef stew with a centipede on top,
as large as a chopstick,
Empress Tiānhòu stored it in a jade box.
Summoning Sīgōng, she showed it to him and said:
"Yesterday, on the stew, there was this,
an extremely poisonous creature.
Recently, there was a chicken,
that ate a black centipede and suddenly died,
upon opening its belly,
there was a handful of centipedes inside,
all other insects were completely consumed,
but this creature does not digest.
Since yesterday, I,
have felt nauseous and unable to eat."
Sīgōng kowtowed and begged for death,
but was pardoned,
and exiled to Lǐngnán along with the cook.
Locusts
In the fourth year of the Táng Kāiyuán era,
a locust plague struck north of the Hé River,
when they flew, they blotted out the sun,
as large as a finger,
they devoured seedlings, grass, tree leaves,
even the roots were completely consumed.
An imperial decree ordered officials to coordinate with prefectures and counties to drive them away,
for every one shí collected,
they would be given one shí of millet,
for every one dǒu,
millet would be given accordingly.
They dug pits to bury them,
but burying one shí caused ten shí to be born,
their eggs were as large as millet grains,
half an inch thick,
covering the ground.
Fúxiūzǐ said:
"In the past, during the time of the civil and martial sage emperor,
locusts swarmed around the capital city,
the emperor ordered them caught for observation,
and in front of the ceremonial guards, selected a large one,
prayed to it, saying:
'If my governance and punishments are perverse,
and benevolence and trust are not yet believed,
then eat my heart,
do not harm the crops.'
He then swallowed it.
In a short while,
birds like storks,
in flocks of millions,
gathered and ate the locusts completely in one day.
This was achieved through sincere feeling.
If Heaven acts by chance,
then it is as if they were never born,
if Heaven sends calamity,
burying them only makes it worse.
One should cultivate virtue and be cautious with punishments,
to respond to Heaven's reproach,
why not cultivate blessings to avert disaster,
instead of seeking to kill to eliminate misfortune.
This is the Prime Minister Yáo
Chóng's failure in the way of harmonious governance."
Cold Snake
Prince Shēn suffered from a flesh ailment,
his abdomen sagging down to his shins.
Whenever he went out,
he would bind it with white silk.
During the hot months,
his breathing became unbearably labored.
Emperor Xuánzōng decreed that two cold snakes be fetched from the south and bestowed upon him.
The snakes were several feet long,
white in color,
and did not sting people.
When held,
they were cold to the touch,
like ice.
Prince Shēn had several folds in his abdomen;
in the summer months, he would place the snakes within these folds,
and no longer felt the oppressive heat.
Lǐ Kuí
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Kuí,
during the Qiántiān era,
served as Vice Minister of Rites.
One day,
while sitting in the front corridor of the hall during the day,
he suddenly heard an extremely loud noise from within the hall,
as if a wall had collapsed.
Startled, Kuí went inside to look,
and saw a toad,
crouched on the ground,
several feet tall,
with a monstrous and peculiar appearance.
Kuí was both alarmed and astonished,
unable to fathom where it had come from.
He immediately ordered a servant
to cover it with a large earthen jar.
Someone explained:
"The toad is a creature of the moon,
and also a celestial messenger.
Now that a celestial messenger has come to your hall,
could it not be that the Supreme Deity is entrusting you with a secret mission?"
The next morning, when he opened it to look,
it had already vanished without a trace.
Several days later,
he was indeed appointed Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters.
The Registrar's Insect
In Jīntán County, Rùn Prefecture,
during the Dàlì era,
a northerner served as registrar.
He placed over ten scorpions in a bamboo tube
and set it on a tree in the office courtyard.
Later, they multiplied to over a hundred,
but due to being steamed by the local soil's energy,
they could not sting people.
The southerners did not recognize them,
and called them the 'registrar's insect'.
Zhū Yázhī
Zhū Yázhī, the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng,
during the Yuánxīng era,
suddenly had an old man
emerge from under the bed of his concubine Dǒng,
wearing a yellow robe and cap.
The hole from which he emerged
was smooth and moist, with a spring.
He then became intimate with Dǒng.
Whenever there was good or bad fortune,
he would inform her.
When Yázhī's son fell ill with malaria,
the old man said:
"For this, he should obtain a tiger's testicle and consume it."
Taking a halberd, he went toward the eastern mountains,
obtained a tiger's penis,
still retaining some warmth,
had the son roast and eat it,
and the malaria was immediately cured.
The old man often had Dǒng comb his hair,
which was like that of a wild boar.
Later, Yázhī had several Daoist masters submit petitions to the gods,
and after that, the old man disappeared.
They boiled water
and tried pouring it into that hole,
digging out several hu of large ants.
Not long after,
a villager, carrying a large knife while traveling in the wild,
encountered a man.
Upon seeing the knife,
the man took out a cake of yellow gold,
requesting to exchange it for the knife.
After handing over the knife,
the man suddenly vanished without a trace.
Upon re-examining the gold,
it turned out to be cow dung.
It was reckoned that this was the ghost from the Zhū household.
Tree Earthworms
At the residence of Hún Jiān in the capital,
outside the halberd gate, there was a small locust tree,
with a hole in it as large as a coin.
Every summer after the rain cleared,
an earthworm as thick as a large arm,
over two feet long,
with a white neck and red spots,
would lead hundreds of earthworms,
like ropes,
climbing along the tree's branches and trunk.
By dawn,
they would all retreat into the hole.
Sometimes, when startled,
they would often curl up.
Academician Zhāng Chéng said that
during Hún Jiān's time,
a tree suddenly appeared in front of the hall,
sprouting from the ground,
with earthworms hanging all over it.
There is already a source for this,
but I have forgotten the title of the book.
Mù Shīgǔ
Yóuzǐ Mù Shīgǔ,
in the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
was traveling through the villages in the Jīnlíng region.
As dusk fell,
he sought lodging at an ancient temple,
where he met the resident monk.
The monk then led him to a crude room to settle in.
The main guest hall
was sealed and not opened.
Shīgǔ grew angry
and questioned the monk.
The monk said:
"It is not out of stinginess
or to belittle you,
but because every guest who has stayed here before
has inevitably fallen gravely ill in this place.
Since I arrived here,
over thirty years ago,
nearly thirty people have been harmed.
It has been closed off
for a full year now,
and I no longer dare to let anyone stay overnight."
Shīgǔ refused to accept this,
and his words grew increasingly suspicious and accusatory.
The monk had no choice
but to have the door opened and the room swept clean.
It was indeed an old, decaying room.
Shīgǔ believed this in his heart,
but his expression remained angry.
When he went to sleep,
he could not help but prepare for danger,
so he took a handy knife from his case
and placed it under the mat at the head of the bed
to bolster his courage.
When he slept until the second watch,
he suddenly felt a chill,
startled awake,
and felt a cold, swirling wind,
as if fanned by something.
After a long while,
the fanning came again.
Shīgǔ secretly drew the knife from under the covers
and swung it once,
as if hitting something.
He then heard it fall to the left of the bed,
and nothing else happened.
Shīgǔ returned the knife to its original place
and slept peacefully.
Around the fourth watch,
the fanning came again.
Shīgǔ followed the same method as before,
swung the knife and hit something,
and again heard it fall to the ground.
He gripped the knife and waited further,
but nothing else occurred.
Soon, daybreak came.
The temple monks and nearby people
came together to knock on the door.
Shīgǔ loudly asked who it was,
and the monks were all astonished that Shīgǔ was still alive.
When asked about the reason,
Shīgǔ recounted the events in detail.
He slowly brushed his clothes and rose,
and the others then saw to the right of the bed
two bats,
both struck by the knife and lying dead in disarray.
Each wing was one chi and eight cun long,
their pearl-like eyes round and large as melons,
and silver in color.
According to the "Shényì Mìjīng Fǎ,"
a hundred-year-old bat
positions itself above a person's mouth
to absorb their vital energy,
seeking longevity.
By three hundred years old,
it can transform into human form
and fly through the heavens.
Based on this, these bats had not yet reached three hundred years,
so their supernatural power was still weak,
which is why Shīgǔ was able to subdue them.
Shīgǔ, because of this, realized he had a talent for cultivation
and the practice of arts.
He then entered Chìchéng Mountain
and was never heard from again.
For those who stay in ancient lodgings,
this is also a cautionary tale.
Chúnyú Fén
Chúnyú Fén of Dōngpíng,
a knight-errant from Wú and Chǔ,
was fond of wine and given to outbursts of temper,
careless in minor matters of conduct.
He had amassed great wealth
and kept a retinue of bold followers.
Once, on account of his martial skills, he was appointed a deputy general in the Huáinán army,
but because he offended his commander while drunk,
he was dismissed and fell into destitution,
indulging recklessly in drink as his sole occupation.
His home was ten lǐ east of Guǎnglíng Commandery.
South of his dwelling stood an ancient, massive locust tree,
its branches and trunk tall and dense,
casting clear shade over several acres.
Daily, Chúnyú would drink heavily beneath it with his band of followers.
In the ninth month of the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
he fell ill from deep intoxication.
At the time, two friends seated with him helped him home
and laid him to rest in the eastern corridor of the main hall.
The two friends said to him:
"You should sleep now.
We will tend to the horses and wash our feet,
and wait until you are slightly better before leaving."
Chúnyú removed his headcloth and lay upon the pillow,
sinking into a dazed, hazy state,
as if drifting into a dream.
He saw two envoys in purple robes,
who knelt and bowed to him, saying:
"The king of the Huái'ān Kingdom has sent his humble servants to deliver his invitation."
Without thinking, Chúnyú rose from his couch, adjusted his clothes,
and followed the two envoys to the gate.
There he saw a small carriage painted blue,
drawn by four stallions,
with seven or eight attendants on either side.
They helped Chúnyú into the carriage,
which then passed through the main gate,
headed toward the hollow of the ancient locust tree, and departed,
the driver urging the horses straight into the hollow.
Chúnyú felt this was exceedingly strange,
but dared not ask questions.
Suddenly, he beheld mountains, rivers, climate,
plants, trees, and roads
that were vastly different from the human world.
After proceeding several tens of lǐ,
there appeared outer walls and city battlements.
Carriages and people
thronged the roads without cease.
Chúnyú's attendants on either side called out strict warnings,
and pedestrians scrambled to make way on both sides.
They then entered a great city,
with vermilion gates and multi-storied towers.
On a tower was written in gold characters
the inscription: "The Great Huái'ān Kingdom."
The gatekeepers hurried forward, bowing and scurrying about.
Soon, a rider called out:
"The king, in light of the royal son-in-law's distant arrival,
commands that he rest for now at the Dōnghuá Lodge."
Thus, they led the way forward.
In a moment, a gate swung wide open,
and Chúnyú descended from the carriage and entered.
Painted balustrades and carved pillars,
along with splendid trees and rare fruits,
were arrayed in the courtyard below;
tables, mats, and cushions,
curtains, canopies, and sumptuous feasts
were laid out in the hall above.
Chúnyú felt great delight in his heart.
Then another call came:
"The Right Minister is about to arrive."
Chúnyú descended the steps to receive him with reverence.
A man in purple robes, holding an ivory tablet, hurried forward,
and the courtesies between host and guest were fully observed.
The Right Minister said:
"Our humble ruler, despite the remoteness and obscurity of our poor kingdom,
has welcomed you, noble sir,
to entrust you with a marital alliance."
Chúnyú said:
"With my lowly and unworthy person,
how could I dare aspire to such an honor?"
The Right Minister then invited Chúnyú to accompany him to the palace.
After walking about a hundred paces,
they entered a vermilion gate.
Spears, halberds, axes, and battle-axes
were arrayed on both sides,
with several hundred military officers
standing respectfully by the roadside.
Among them was Zhōu Biàn, a lifelong drinking companion of Chúnyú's,
who also hurried forward in the crowd.
Chúnyú felt a secret joy at seeing him,
but dared not step forward to ask.
The Right Minister led Chúnyú up into a vast hall,
where the imperial guards were stern and solemn,
as if in the presence of the supreme ruler.
He saw a man, tall and imposing, dignified and grave,
seated in the central position,
wearing plain white silk robes
and a crimson flower-adorned crown.
Chúnyú trembled with fear,
not daring to look up.
Attendants on either side ordered Chúnyú to bow.
The king said:
"Previously, following your honored father's command,
and not disdaining our small kingdom,
we agreed to allow our second daughter, Yáofāng, to serve you, noble sir."
Chúnyú could only prostrate himself,
not daring to utter a word.
The king said:
"For now, retire to the guest quarters,
and the ceremonies will follow in due course."
By decree,
the Right Minister also accompanied Chúnyú back to the lodge.
Chúnyú pondered this,
thinking that his father was a general stationed at the border,
who had been lost
among the barbarians,
and whose survival was unknown.
He wondered whether his father had communicated with the northern tribes
and thus brought about this affair.
His mind was greatly bewildered,
unable to discern the reason.
That evening,
lambs, geese, silks, and satins,
along with majestic demeanor and ceremonial grandeur,
music from courtesans, strings, and pipes,
feasts, lamps, and candles,
carriages, horses, and ritual gifts—
all were abundantly prepared.
There was a group of women,
some called Huáyáng Gū,
some called Qīngxī Gū,
some called Shàngxiānzǐ,
some called Xiàxiānzǐ.
There were several such groups,
each attended by several thousand followers.
They wore crowns adorned with kingfisher feathers and phoenixes,
robes of golden cloud-patterned capes,
and dazzling hairpins of jade and gold,
too brilliant to behold.
They frolicked and played,
coming and going at the gate,
vying to tease and jest with young master Chúnyú.
Their demeanor was enchanting and beautiful,
their words clever and charming,
leaving Chúnyú unable to respond.
Then one of the women said to him:
"On the last Shàngsì Festival,
I accompanied Lady Língzhī past Chánzhì Temple,
and watched the Yòuyán dance of the Brahman
in the Tiānzhú Courtyard.
I sat with the other maidens on the stone couch by the northern window.
At that time, you were young,
and also came on horseback to watch.
You alone boldly approached to be intimate,
speaking flirtatiously and jesting.
I, together with sister Qióngyīng, tied a crimson silk scarf
and hung it on a bamboo branch.
Do you not remember this?
Also, on the sixteenth day of the seventh month,
I attended
Shàngzhēnzǐ
at Xiàogǎn Temple, listening to Master Qìxuán expound the Guānyīn Sūtra.
I donated two golden phoenix hairpins during the lecture,
and Shàngzhēnzǐ donated a rhinoceros-horn box.
At that time, you were also in the lecture hall.
You asked the master for the hairpins and box to examine them,
admiring them repeatedly,
sighing in wonder for a long while.
You turned to us and said:
'These people and objects,
none are of this world.'
You asked about my people,
or inquired about my village,
but I did not answer.
Your affection was lingering,
your gaze reluctant to part.
How could you not remember this?"
Chúnyú said:
"I hold it in my heart,
never forgetting it for a day."
The group of women said:
"We never imagined that today we would become your kin."
Then three men appeared,
grandly attired with caps and sashes.
They stepped forward and bowed to Chúnyú, saying:
"We have been commanded to serve as the royal son-in-law's attendants."
One among them
was an old acquaintance of Chúnyú's.
Chúnyú pointed and said:
"Are you not Tián Zǐhuá of Féngyì?"
Tián said:
"Indeed."
Chúnyú stepped forward
and clasped his hand, reminiscing about old times for a long while.
Chúnyú asked him:
"How do you come to be here?"
Zǐhuá said:
"I wandered freely and
had the fortune to be recognized by the Right Minister, Marquis Wǔchéng, Lord Duàn,
and thus found a place to rely on."
Chún Yú Fēn asked further:
"Zhōu Biàn is here—
do you know of him?"
Tián Zǐhuá said:
"Master Zhōu is a noble man,
holding the position of Sīlì,
his power and influence are immense,
and I have often received his protection."
Their conversation and laughter were very joyful.
Soon a voice announced:
"The Royal Son-in-Law may now enter."
The three men took up their swords, pendants, ceremonial caps, and robes and changed into them.
Tián Zǐhuá said:
"I never expected to witness such a grand ceremony today,
I will never forget it."
There were several dozen fairy maidens
playing various exotic music,
melodious and clear,
the tunes sorrowful and mournful,
unlike anything heard in the mortal world.
There were also several dozen holding candles to guide the way,
and on both sides were seen golden and emerald silk screens,
colorful, jade-like, and exquisite,
stretching unbroken for several miles.
Chún Yú Fēn sat upright in the carriage,
his mind in a daze,
feeling very uneasy.
Tián Zǐhuá spoke and laughed several times to ease his mind.
The group of female relatives from earlier,
each riding phoenix-winged carriages,
also moved back and forth among them.
They arrived at a gate,
named the Palace of Cultivated Grace,
where the crowd of fairy aunts and sisters
were also gathered in great numbers on either side.
They ordered Chún Yú Fēn to descend from his carriage and bow,
with the courtesies of yielding and ascending and descending,
exactly as in the human world.
The screens and fans were removed,
and he saw a maiden,
said to be named Princess Jīnzhī,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
dignified as if a divine immortal.
The rituals of the wedding
were also quite elaborate.
From then on, Chún Yú Fēn's affection grew daily more harmonious,
his glory and splendor increased day by day,
his carriages and attire when going out or coming in,
his travels, feasts, guests, and attendants,
were second only to those of a king.
The king ordered Chún Yú Fēn, along with a group of officials, to prepare guards and
conduct a great hunt at Língguī Mountain in the west of the kingdom.
The mountains were lofty and beautiful,
the rivers and marshes broad and distant,
the forests and trees lush and abundant,
and all kinds of
birds and beasts were gathered there.
The hunting party had a great catch,
and returned only by nightfall.
On another day, Chún Yú Fēn took the opportunity to address the king:
"On the day Your Majesty recently arranged my marriage,
you said it was in accordance with my father's command.
My father was recently assisting a border general,
but the military campaign met with failure,
and he fell among the Hú tribes.
Since then, for seventeen or eighteen years, letters have ceased.
Since Your Majesty knows his whereabouts,
I beg to go and pay him a visit."
The king hastily said to him:
"Your father-in-law is stationed in the northern territories,
and correspondence continues without interruption.
You need only prepare a letter to inform him,
there is no need to go there now."
He then ordered his wife to prepare gifts of congratulation,
and sent them all at once.
After several nights, a reply came.
Chún Yú Fēn examined the letter's intent,
and it all matched his father's lifelong manner.
In the letter, there were reminiscences and teachings,
the sentiments were detailed and heartfelt,
just as in former years.
He also inquired about the survival of Chún Yú Fēn's relatives,
and the rise and fall of his hometown.
He further mentioned that the roads were distant and divergent,
and that wind and mist blocked the way,
the wording was sorrowful and bitter,
the language full of grief,
and he also did not allow Chún Yú Fēn to come for a visit.
He said that in the year Dīngchǒu,
they would meet.
Chún Yú Fēn held the letter, weeping in sorrow,
unable to contain his emotions.
Another day,
his wife said to him:
"Do you not wish to engage in governance?"
Chún Yú Fēn said:
"I am unrestrained
and unaccustomed to administrative affairs."
His wife said:
"You just take it on,
and I will assist you."
His wife then reported this to the king.
After several days,
he said to Chún Yú Fēn:
"The administration of Nánkē is in disorder,
the Grand Administrator has been dismissed,
and I wish to rely on your talent.
May I trouble you to take this post,
and go together with my young daughter?"
Chún Yú Fēn respectfully accepted the command.
The king then ordered the officials to prepare the Grand Administrator's luggage,
and brought out gold, jade, brocades, and embroideries,
with chests, dowry cases, servants, concubines, carriages, and horses arrayed along the broad avenue,
to bid farewell to the princess on her journey.
Chún Yú Fēn had been a wandering knight in his youth,
and had never dared to aspire to such things,
so at this he was greatly pleased.
He then submitted a memorial saying:
"I am but the son of a military family,
with no particular skills or arts.
To rashly assume such a great responsibility
will surely bring disgrace to the court's regulations.
I grieve that I may prove unworthy of my position,
and thus cause ruin to the state's affairs.
Now I wish to broadly seek wise and virtuous men
to assist where I fall short.
I humbly observe that Sīlì Yǐngchuān Zhōu Biàn is loyal, upright, and steadfast,
upholding the law without deviation,
possessing the capacity to assist in governance.
The retired scholar Féngyì Tián Zǐhuá is pure, cautious, adaptable,
and understands the sources of governance and transformation.
These two men have been my friends for ten years,
and I am fully aware of their talents and abilities,
so they may be entrusted with administrative affairs.
I request that Zhōu be appointed as Sīxiàn of Nánkē,
and Tián be appointed as Sīnóng,
so that my governance may achieve renown,
and the laws and regulations may not fall into disorder."
The king approved the memorial in full and sent them accordingly.
That evening,
the king and the queen consort held a farewell feast south of the kingdom.
The king said to Chún Yú Fēn:
"Nánkē is a great commandery of the kingdom,
with fertile land,
and a prosperous population.
Without benevolent governance, it cannot be well ruled.
Moreover, with the assistance of Zhōu and Tián,
you must strive diligently,
to live up to the kingdom's expectations."
The queen consort admonished the princess:
"Chún Yú-lang has a firm nature and is fond of wine,
and being young besides,
the way of a wife
values gentleness and compliance.
You must serve him well,
and then I will have no worries."
Although the borders of Nánkē are not far,
the times of morning and evening will be separate,
and today we part,
how can we not shed tears?
Chún Yú Fēn and his wife bowed and headed south,
mounting their carriages and surrounded by riders,
talking and laughing very joyfully.
After several nights, they reached the commandery.
The commandery had officials, clerks, monks, Taoists, and elders,
with music, carriages, and processions,
guards, imperial bells, and jingles,
all vying to come and welcome them.
The crowd was dense and bustling,
with the clamor of bells and drums unceasing.
After more than ten miles,
they saw battlements, towers, and pavilions,
with an auspicious air thick and dense.
They entered the great city gate.
On the gate was also a large placard,
inscribed in golden characters,
saying "Nánkē Commandery City."
Inside were vermilion balconies and halberd-guarded gates,
imposing and deep.
Chún Yú Fēn descended from the carriage,
observed the local customs,
treated illnesses and sufferings,
entrusted administrative affairs to Zhōu and Tián,
and the commandery was greatly well-governed.
From the time he governed the commandery for twenty years,
his influence and teachings spread widely,
the common people sang his praises,
erected merit and virtue steles,
and built a shrine in his honor.
The king held him in high esteem,
bestowed upon him estates and noble titles,
and his rank reached that of a chief minister.
Both Zhōu and Tián became famous for their governance.
He was promoted to a high position.
He had five sons and two daughters,
the sons were granted official posts due to their family's influence,
and the daughters were married into royal families.
His glory and prominence
reached its peak at that time,
unmatched by any generation.
That year,
the state of Tánluó
invaded this commandery.
The king ordered Chún Yúfēn to train generals and drill troops to campaign against them,
so he recommended Zhōu Biàn to lead thirty thousand soldiers
to resist the enemy forces at Yáotái City.
Biàn was brave but reckless in advancing,
His troops suffered a major defeat,
and Biàn fled alone on horseback, stripped of his armor,
returning to the city at night.
The enemy also collected their supplies and armor and withdrew.
Chún Yúfēn then imprisoned Biàn to await punishment,
but the king pardoned them both.
That month,
the Director of Justice, Zhōu Biàn, died from a carbuncle on his back.
Chún Yúfēn's wife, the princess, fell ill,
and passed away ten days later.
Chún Yúfēn then requested to be relieved of his commandery duties,
to escort the funeral procession back to the capital,
and the king permitted it,
appointing the Minister of Agriculture, Tián Zǐhuá, to act as the Governor of Nánkē.
Chún Yúfēn, in deep sorrow, led the funeral procession,
with solemn ceremonies along the way.
Men and women cried out,
officials and commoners offered sacrifices,
and those clinging to the carriage or blocking the road
were too numerous to count,
until they reached the capital.
The king and his consort, dressed in plain white, wept in the suburbs,
awaiting the arrival of the funeral carriage.
The princess was posthumously titled Princess Shùnyí,
and with full ceremonial regalia, feather canopies, and music,
she was buried at Pánlóng Gǎng, ten lǐ east of the capital.
That month,
the son of the late Director of Justice, Róng Xìn, also escorted the funeral to the capital.
Chún Yúfēn had long governed the outer territories,
forming alliances with the central state,
and the noble families and powerful clans
were all on friendly terms with him.
After leaving his commandery and returning to the capital,
his comings and goings became irregular,
and his circle of friends and followers
grew increasingly influential and powerful,
arousing the king's suspicion and fear.
At that time, a citizen submitted a memorial stating,
"Celestial omens indicate warnings,
the state faces great terror,
the capital will be relocated,
and the ancestral temples will collapse.
The trouble arises from another clan,
and the matter lies within the palace walls."
Public opinion at the time attributed this to Chún Yúfēn's extravagance and presumption,
so his guards were stripped away,
his social interactions were restricted,
and he was confined to his private residence.
Chún Yúfēn, relying on his many years of governing the commandery
without any failures in administration,
felt resentful and aggrieved by the rumors,
and became deeply unhappy.
The king also knew this,
and thus said to Chún Yúfēn:
"We have been relatives for over twenty years,
but unfortunately, my young daughter died prematurely,
unable to grow old with you,
which is truly heartbreaking.
My consort will stay to raise the grandchildren herself."
He then said to Chún Yúfēn:
"You have been away from home for a long time;
you may temporarily return to your hometown,
to see your relatives.
Your grandchildren will remain here,
so do not worry about them.
After three years,
I will send someone to fetch you."
Chún Yúfēn said:
"This is my home;
why should I return elsewhere?"
The king smiled and said:
"You are originally from the human world;
your home is not here."
Chún Yúfēn suddenly felt as if in a daze,
remaining bewildered for a long time,
before finally recalling the events of the past,
and tearfully requested to return.
The king ordered his attendants to escort Chún Yúfēn,
and Chún Yúfēn bowed twice before leaving.
He saw the two purple-robed envoys from before following him again.
Upon reaching the main gate,
he saw the carriage he was to ride in was very shabby,
and none of his former attendants or drivers
were present,
which he found deeply strange and lamentable.
He boarded the carriage and traveled several lǐ,
then exited the great city,
finding himself on the same road he had taken from the east years ago.
The mountains, rivers, plains, and fields
were exactly as they had been.
The two envoys escorting him
lacked any imposing presence,
and Chún Yúfēn grew increasingly discontented.
He asked the envoys:
"When will we reach Guǎnglíng Commandery?"
The two envoys continued singing as if nothing were amiss.
After a long while,
they finally replied:
"We will arrive shortly."
Soon, they emerged from a hole,
and he saw the lanes of his hometown,
unchanged from the past.
Overcome with sadness,
he could not hold back his tears.
The two envoys led him out of the carriage,
entered his gate,
ascended the steps,
and he found himself lying beneath the eastern corridor of the hall.
He was greatly startled and afraid,
not daring to approach.
The two envoys then loudly called his name several times,
and Chún Yúfēn awoke as if from the beginning,
seeing the servants of his household
sweeping the courtyard with brooms,
his two guests washing their feet on the couch,
the setting sun not yet hidden behind the western wall,
and the leftover wine still clear in the cup by the eastern window.
In the fleeting moments of the dream,
it felt as if a lifetime had passed.
Chún Yúfēn, filled with emotion and sighs,
called his two guests and told them everything.
They were astonished,
and went outside with Chún Yúfēn
to search for the hole beneath the locust tree.
Chún Yúfēn pointed and said:
"This is the place where I entered in my dream."
The two guests suspected it was the work of foxes or tree spirits causing mischief,
so they ordered servants to bring axes,
cut away the overgrowth,
break off the tangled roots,
and trace the hole to its source.
About a zhàng wide to the side,
there was a large hole,
with roots forming a clear, bright cavity
large enough to hold a bed.
Above it was accumulated soil,
shaped like city walls, towers, and palaces.
There were several hú of ants
hidden and gathered within.
Among them was a small platform,
colored as if cinnabar-red,
where two large ants resided,
with white wings and red heads,
about three cùn long.
Dozens of large ants flanked them as attendants,
and the other ants did not dare approach.
These were the king and queen,
and this was the capital of Huái'ān Kingdom.
They explored another hole,
straight up the southern branch about four zhàng,
winding and turning into a central space,
where there was also a small earthen city with towers,
and a group of ants resided within.
This was the Nánkē Commandery that Chún Yúfēn had governed.
Another hole,
two zhàng to the west,
was vast, hollow, and decayed,
with strange, sunken shapes.
Inside was a rotten turtle shell,
as large as a dǒu measure,
soaked by accumulated rainwater,
with small grasses growing densely,
lush and overgrown,
shading and covering the shell.
This was Língguī Shān, where Chún Yúfēn had hunted.
They explored yet another hole,
about a zhàng to the east,
where ancient roots coiled and twisted
like dragons or serpents.
Inside was a small mound of soil,
over a chǐ high,
which was the tomb at Pánlóng Gǎng where Chún Yúfēn had buried his wife.
Recalling the past events,
he felt deeply moved and sighed.
Examining and tracing all these traces,
they all matched his dream.
Not wanting his two guests to destroy them,
he quickly ordered the holes to be covered and restored as before.
That night,
a storm suddenly arose.
In the morning, they looked at the holes
and found the ants had all disappeared,
with no one knowing where they had gone.
Therefore, it was first said that the state had great fear,
and the capital city was relocated.
This is the proof of it.
He then recalled the events of the Tánluó campaign,
and again asked his two guests to investigate the traces outside.
One li east of the residence,
there was an ancient dry stream,
beside which stood a large tán tree,
covered and intertwined with vines,
blocking the sun above,
and beside it was a small hole,
where a colony of ants also gathered in hiding.
Could this not be the kingdom of Tánluó?
Alas!
The spiritual wonders of ants
are still unfathomable,
let alone the transformations of larger creatures hidden in mountains and woods?
At that time, his drinking companions Zhōu Biàn and Tián Zǐhuá
both resided in Liùhé County,
and had not visited Shēng for over ten days.
Shēng immediately sent a servant to hasten and inquire after them.
Zhōu Shēng had died suddenly from a violent illness,
and Tián Zǐhuá was also bedridden with illness.
Shēng, moved by the fleeting emptiness of Nánkē,
awakened to the transience of human life,
and thus devoted his heart to the Daoist path,
abandoning wine and women entirely.
Three years later,
in the year Dīngchǒu,
he also passed away at home,
at the age of forty-seven,
fulfilling the limit of his prior destiny.
Gōng Zuǒ, in the autumn eighth month of the eighteenth year of Zhēnyuán,
traveled from Wú to Luò,
and temporarily moored at Huáipǔ,
where he happened to meet Chúnyú Shēng Fén,
and inquired about the remnants of these events.
Repeatedly verifying the details,
he found them all to be based on facts,
and thus compiled and recorded them into a biography,
to provide material for those fond of such tales.
Although it involves spirits and speaks of marvels,
and the matters border on the unorthodox,
yet those who cling to their positions and cling to life
may take this as a warning.
May later gentlemen
take Nánkē as a mere accident,
and not let fame and status make them arrogant in this world.
Lǐ Zhào, former Military Advisor of Huázhōu, praised thus:
"Noble to the utmost in rank and position,
power overwhelming the capital.
The enlightened see this:
how different is it from a gathering of ants?"
Red-Waisted Ants
Duàn Chéngshì,
during the Yuánhé era,
lived temporarily in Chángxīng Lǐ.
In the courtyard was a colony of ants,
shaped like large reddish ants,
but colored pitch black,
with slightly red waists and segments,
pointed heads and high legs,
running most lightly and swiftly.
Whenever they captured inchworms and small insects and brought them into the nest,
they would break the mound and block the hole,
to prevent their escape.
Afterward, he moved residences several times,
and never saw them again.
Sū Zhàn
In the Yuánhé era of the Táng,
Sū Zhàn traveled to Péngquè Mountain,
carrying provisions and drilling for fire,
but found no traces of habitation in the area.
Suddenly he said to his wife:
"As I walked in the mountains,
I saw,
On the inverted cliff there was a light like a mirror;
it must be a spiritual realm.
Tomorrow I will go there,
and now I bid you farewell."
His wife and children wept and wailed,
but could not stop him.
At dawn he departed.
His wife led the servants to secretly follow him.
Entering the mountains for several tens of lǐ,
from afar they saw a white light on the cliff,
round and bright, a zhàng in diameter.
Sū then approached it.
As soon as he reached the light,
he let out a long cry.
His wife and children rushed forward to rescue him,
but his body was like a cocoon.
There was a black spider,
as large as a cooking pot,
that scurried and gathered on the cliff.
A servant used a sharp knife to cut its web,
and just as it broke,
Sū had already sunk into the brain and died.
His wife then piled firewood and burned the cliff,
and the stench filled the entire mountain.
Shí Xiàn
There was a man named Shí Xiàn,
registered in Tàiyuán,
who made his living as a merchant,
often trading in the area north of Dài.
In the midsummer of the second year of Chángqìng,
while traveling on the road near Yànmén Pass,
the heat was at its peak,
so he rested under a large tree.
Suddenly he dreamed of a monk,
with bee-like eyes, wearing a brown robe,
his appearance strange and unusual,
who came before Xiàn
and said to him:
"I dwell in a hut south of Wǔtái Mountain,
where there is a secluded forest and accumulated water,
far removed from the mundane world,
truly a place for monks to escape the summer heat.
Would the benefactor care to accompany me on a visit?
If not,
I see the benefactor suffering from the heat and near death;
would you not regret it in your heart?"
Xiàn, because the summer heat was at its peak,
and the monk had spoken to move him with talk of fortune and misfortune,
thus said to the monk:
"I wish to go with the master."
Thereupon the monk led Xiàn westward,
and after several lǐ,
indeed there was a secluded forest and accumulated water.
He saw a group of monks in the water,
and Xiàn, finding it strange, asked about it.
The monk said:
"This is the Xuányīn Pond,
so we disciples bathe in it
to wash away the scorching heat."
Then he led Xiàn to walk around the pond.
Xiàn alone found it strange that the monks were in the water,
and moreover, their appearances were all identical.
After a while, as dusk fell,
one monk said:
"Benefactor, may you listen to the chanting of our disciples."
So Xiàn stood by the pond,
and the monks in the water joined their voices and chanted.
After only about the time of a meal,
one monk took his hand and said:
"Benefactor, bathe with us in the Xuányīn Pond;
do not fear."
Xiàn then followed the monk into the pond,
and suddenly felt his whole body grow cold, shivering and trembling,
whereupon he awoke with a start.
He found himself lying under the large tree,
his clothes completely soaked,
and shivering intensely from the cold.
It was already dusk,
so he went to a village house.
By the next day,
his illness had slightly improved,
and as he walked on the road,
he heard the croaking of frogs along the way,
very much like the chanting of the monks.
So he went straight to seek it out.
After walking several lǐ,
there was a secluded forest and accumulated water,
with many frogs.
The water was indeed called Xuányīn Pond,
and the monks were actually a group of frogs.
And Xiàn said:
"These frogs can change form to affect humans;
are they not particularly strange creatures?"
Thereupon he killed them all.
Old Man Wáng
In the early years of the Bǎolì era,
in Chángshā, there was an old man named Wáng Sǒu,
whose family was poor,
and he made his living by farming.
One day, while plowing in the fields,
he was stung on the arm by an earthworm,
and the pain was severe,
so he hurried home.
The pain became increasingly unbearable,
groaning at night until dawn,
moaning during the day until evening,
and this went on for over ninety days.
A physician said,
"This is an extremely severe poison.
At the onset of the illness,
perhaps medicine could have helped.
But now the condition is deep-seated,
so I cannot know what to do."
A few days later,
the illness worsened further.
Suddenly, he heard a sound from his arm,
faint and subtle,
like that of an earthworm.
After a few more days,
the sound grew louder,
as if merging with countless other sounds,
and the pain increased accordingly.
That evening, he died.
The Walking Earthworm
Duàn Chéngshì's third cousin's paternal uncle,
in the third year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
served as an official in Lúzhōu.
Suddenly, an earthworm emerged in his courtyard,
as thick as an index finger,
and growing in length,
reaching two or three zhàng,
with a white neck,
and two feet beneath the neck,
exactly like sparrow feet,
walking along the base of the wall,
and it took several days before it died.
The House Gecko
At the end of the Tàihé era,
south of Sōngzī County, there was a scholar
who stayed at a relative's estate to study.
On the first night of his arrival,
after the second watch,
just as he had lit the lamp and sat at his desk,
suddenly a half-cùn-tall小人
wearing a géjīn hat,
and leaning on a cane, entered the door,
and said to the scholar:
"You've just arrived and have no host,
so you must be lonely."
His voice was as loud as a fly's.
The scholar, being bold by nature,
at first pretended not to see him.
The小人 then climbed onto the bed and scolded him:
"How dare you disregard the etiquette between host and guest?"
He then climbed onto the desk to peek at the books,
cursing incessantly.
He even spat on the books,
and the scholar, unable to bear it,
struck him with a brush, knocking him to the ground,
where he cried out several times
before disappearing out the door.
After a while,
four or five women appeared,
some old, some young,
all one cùn tall,
shouting loudly:
"Zhēn Guān, seeing that you are studying alone,
sent his son to converse with you
and discuss profound matters.
How could you, foolish and reckless,
cause harm to him?
Now you must face Zhēn Guān."
They swarmed like ants,
resembling attendants,
and climbed all over the scholar.
The scholar felt as if in a dream,
and they bit his limbs,
causing great pain.
They said again:
"If you don't leave,
we will damage your eyes."
Four or five of them then climbed onto his face.
The scholar, terrified,
followed them out the door.
Reaching the east side of the hall,
he saw in the distance a door,
extremely small,
like the gate of a military commander's office.
The scholar shouted:
"What kind of monstrous creature dares to bully people like this?"
He was bitten again by the crowd.
In a daze,
he found himself inside the small door.
He saw a person,
wearing a tall crown, seated in the hall,
with thousands of guards on the steps below,
all just over a cùn tall.
The person scolded the scholar:
"I pitied you for being alone,
so I sent my son to visit.
Why did you harm him?
Your crime warrants being cut in half at the waist."
Then he saw dozens of people, all holding blades and rolling up their sleeves, closing in on him.
The scholar, terrified,
apologized:
"I am foolish and ignorant,
and with my mortal eyes, I did not recognize Zhēn Guān.
I beg for my life to be spared."
After a long time, the person said:
"For now, I see you know regret."
He ordered him to be dragged out.
Before he knew it, he was outside the small door.
When he returned to the study,
it was already the fifth watch,
and the lamp was still flickering.
At dawn,
he searched for traces.
Under the ancient steps on the east wall,
there was a small hole the size of a chestnut,
where house geckos came and went.
The scholar immediately hired several workers to excavate it.
They dug several zhàng deep
and found over ten dàn of house geckos.
The largest ones were red,
about a chǐ long,
likely their king.
The soil was arranged like a building.
The scholar gathered firewood and burned them,
and afterward, nothing unusual happened.
Rǎn Duān
Rǎn Duān, an official in Diànjiāng County of Zhōngzhōu,
in the early years of the Kāichéng era of the Táng dynasty,
lost his father.
A geomancer named Yán, skilled in assessing terrain,
was hired to select a burial site.
He said:
"This place should have a gathering of creatures with royal aura."
They dug over a zhàng deep
and encountered an ant city,
several zhàng in size,
with outer walls and battlements fully formed,
and inner city gates and watchtowers,
crafted as if carved.
Inside the city, there were streets and paths,
with small mounds arranged in order,
each mound housing thousands of ants,
bustling endlessly,
and the paths were very clean and smooth.
In the tower were two ants:
one purple,
over a cùn long,
with golden feet;
the other had wings,
a slender waist and slightly smaller,
with white wings,
and veins on the wings,
likely the female.
The ants numbered approximately several hú.
A corner of the city was slightly damaged,
covered with hard soil as a lid,
so the central tower remained intact.
Once exposed by digging,
the ants were greatly disturbed,
as if pleading for help.
The county official immediately reported to the county magistrate, Lǐ Xuánzhī.
After seeing it,
he advised the official to choose another site.
The geomancer Yán performed a divination for him,
confirming the site was auspicious,
so the official requested to relocate the ants to the side of a rock,
replicating their original setup,
and scattering stone-like grains,
covering it with a board.
After ten days,
the geomancer Yán suddenly fell ill as if mad,
sometimes hitting himself,
cursing and shouting loudly,
and this continued for several days.
Lǐ Xuánzhī had always been close to the geomancer Yán,
so he prayed to the ants on his behalf
and treated him with realgar pills, curing him.
Earthworm Teeth
Duàn Chéngshì's niece's wet nurse Āshǐ,
originally from Jīngzhōu,
once said that
when she was young, she saw a neighbor's nephew named Kǒng Qiān.
Under the fence, there was an earthworm
with two teeth protruding from its mouth,
and legs like a millipede on its belly.
It was one and a half feet long
and moved faster than ordinary earthworms.
Qiān found it repulsive
and immediately killed it.
That year,
Qiān lost his mother, elder brother, and uncle,
and thus could not survive.
Wéi Jūn
There was a Censor Wéi Jūn who once served in Jiāngxià.
Later, he was sent on a mission to the capital.
On his way back,
he passed through Shāngyú
and stayed at a pavilion inn.
Suddenly, he saw a white spider descending from a pavilion pillar,
its appearance very small.
Wéi Jūn said:
"This is a pest to humans.
I've heard that even if it is small,
if it bites someone,
no good medicine can save them."
So he killed it with his finger.
Soon, another white one descended,
and he killed it as before.
Looking up,
he saw a web serving as its nest.
Wéi then ordered his attendants to take a broom
and sweep it all away.
He added:
"The pest to humans
has been eliminated by me."
The next day, as he was about to leave,
he touched the pillar with his hand.
Suddenly, he felt a sharp pain in his finger,
unbearable,
and realized a white spider had bitten him there.
Wéi Jūn was alarmed
and immediately brushed it away.
Soon, the swelling spread,
and within a few days, it covered his entire arm.
He was carried on a shoulder-borne litter to Jiāngxià,
but no medicine could help.
Eventually, his left arm festered and turned to blood,
and when the blood was exhausted, he died.
Earlier, Wéi Jūn's late mother was in Jiāngxià
and dreamed of a person in white clothes saying to her:
"We are three brothers.
Two of them were killed by your son.
I appealed to the Heavenly Emperor,
who took pity on our grievance
and granted my request."
After speaking,
the mother woke up in fright,
finding it very strange,
but could not speak of the ominous feeling.
More than ten days later, Wéi Jūn arrived,
and she learned the full story.
Only then did she understand her dream.
The day she had the dream
was indeed when he was at the pavilion inn.
The mother wept and said:
"How can he live long?"
A few days later, Wéi Jūn passed away.
Lù Yóng
Lù Yǒng of Wújùn,
resided in Chángchéng.
His family had for generations served as officials through mastery of the classics.
From childhood, Yǒng was excessively fond of eating noodles;
the more he ate, the thinner his constitution became.
When he grew up,
he was sent by his commandery
to the Ministry of Rites as a tribute candidate.
Having failed the examination,
he then became a student at the National University.
Several months later,
several Hu men
arrived at his gate with wine and food.
Once seated,
they looked at Yǒng and said:
"We are men from Nányuè,
raised among the southern barbarians.
We heard that the Son of Heaven of Táng
gathers all the talented men of the realm
and wishes to use culture and refinement to influence and move the Four Barbarians.
Therefore, we crossed seas and scaled mountains to come to Zhōnghuá,
desiring to witness the brilliance of the culture and refinement of the National University.
Only you, sir, with your lofty cap,
flowing robes,
dignified countenance,
and solemn demeanor,
are truly a Confucian scholar of the Táng dynasty.
Therefore, we
wish to form a joyful friendship with you."
Yǒng declined, saying:
"I am fortunate to be registered at the National University,
but I possess no other talents or abilities.
How is it that you gentlemen hold me in such deep affection!"
Thereupon, they feasted together merrily,
enjoying themselves to the utmost before departing.
Yǒng was a man of trust,
and believed the group of Hu men would not deceive him.
After a little over ten days,
the group of Hu men came again,
bringing silk and gold as gifts for Yǒng's longevity.
Yǒng grew suspicious that they had ulterior motives,
and firmly refused them.
The Hu men said:
"You, sir, live in Cháng'ān,
looking anxious and showing signs of hunger and cold.
Therefore, we bring this silk and gold
to cover the expenses for your servant and horse for a single day,
simply to foster our friendship with you.
How could
there be any other motive?
Please do not doubt us."
Yǒng, having no alternative,
