accepted the silk and gold.
After the Hu men left,
the other students at the National University heard of this,
and came together to tell Yǒng:
"Those Hu people generally love profit and disregard their own safety.
They will fight over trifles like salt and rice,
even to the point of killing each other.
How could they possibly abandon silk and gold to wish a friend longevity?
Moreover, there are many students at the National University.
Why do they favor you alone?
You should hide yourself in the countryside
to avoid their return."
Yǒng then moved to dwell by the Wèi River,
shutting his door and not going out.
Barely a month later,
the group of Hu men again arrived at his gate.
Yǒng was greatly alarmed.
The Hu men said joyfully:
"When you were at the National University,
we could not speak fully.
Now that you have retired to the countryside,
it is indeed as we wished."
Once seated,
the Hu men took Yǒng's hand and said:
"Our coming
is no accident.
We have a request of you,
and hope you will grant it.
Moreover, what we ask
will certainly cause you no harm.
For us, however, it would be a great boon."
Yǒng said:
"I respectfully await your instruction."
The Hu men said:
"Are you, sir, fond of eating noodles?"
He replied:
"Yes."
They said again:
"The one who eats the noodles
is not you, sir,
but a worm in your belly.
Now we wish to offer you a single pill of medicine.
If you take it,
you should vomit out the worm.
Then we will purchase it from you at a high price.
Would that be acceptable?"
Yǒng said:
"If such a thing truly exists,
how could it be unacceptable?"
Then the Hu men produced a single pill of medicine,
its color bright and purple.
They instructed him to take it.
After a short while,
he vomited out a worm,
about two cùn long,
green in color,
shaped like a frog.
The Hu men said:
"This is called the Noodle-Consuming Worm,
truly a rare treasure of the world."
Yǒng asked:
"How did you know of it?"
The Hu men said:
"Every morning we see a treasure-aura reaching across the sky,
located at the National University.
Therefore, we specifically sought you out
to obtain it.
However, for over a month now,
looking at dawn,
we saw the aura shift to the Wèi River,
and indeed you had moved there.
Furthermore, this worm coalesced from the harmonious qì of heaven and earth,
hence its fondness for eating noodles.
For wheat is sown in autumn,
and only by the following summer
does it finally bear grain,
receiving the complete qì of heaven and earth through the four seasons.
Therefore, it craves its flavor.
You should feed it with noodles,
and you will see."
Yǒng then placed over a dǒu of noodles
before it,
and the worm ate them up instantly.
Yǒng asked further:
"What is the use of this worm?"
The Hu men said:
"All the rare treasures of the world
partake of the harmonious qì.
This worm is the pure essence of that harmony.
Grasping the root to obtain the branches—
is that far-fetched!"
Then they placed the worm in a tube,
sealed it inside a golden casket,
and instructed Yǒng to place it in his bedchamber.
They told Yǒng:
"Tomorrow we shall come again."
The next morning,
the Hu men brought a heavy carriage carrying ten liǎng,
and gold, jade, silks, and brocades worth tens of thousands,
which they presented to Yǒng.
Together, they took the golden casket and left.
From then on, Yǒng became immensely wealthy.
He acquired gardens and houses,
procured the means for managing a livelihood,
daily ate fine grains and meat,
wore elegant clothes,
moved about in Cháng'ān,
and was known as a wealthy gentleman.
Barely a year later,
the group of Hu men came again.
They said to Yǒng:
"Can you, sir, accompany us on a journey across the sea?
We wish to seek the rare treasures of the ocean
to amaze the world.
And are you not, sir, a man fond of marvels?"
Since Yǒng was now very wealthy,
and had always enjoyed leisure and freedom,
he went with the group of Hu men to the seashore.
The Hu men built a dwelling and settled there.
Then they placed oil in a silver cauldron,
lit a fire beneath it,
threw the worm into the cauldron to refine it,
and for seven days the flames did not cease.
Suddenly, a youth appeared,
with hair parted and wearing a green jacket,
emerging from the sea water.
He held a moon-platter,
on which were many pearls an inch in diameter.
He came to offer them to the Hu men.
The Hu men shouted at him loudly,
and the youth looked frightened.
Holding the platter, he departed.
After the youth left,
in the time it takes to eat a meal,
a jade maiden appeared,
her appearance exceedingly alluring,
wearing clothes of misty gauze,
adorned with jade pendants and pearl earrings,
Gracefully emerging from the sea,
she held a purple jade tray,
on which were several dozen pearls,
and offered them to the foreigner.
The foreigner scolded her,
and the jade maiden left with her tray.
Soon there was an immortal,
wearing a crown of jasper,
robed in rosy clouds,
holding a crimson silk-wrapped book,
within which was a pearl,
three
inches in diameter,
its wondrous light illuminating the air,
shining for dozens of paces.
The immortal offered the pearl to the foreigner,
who smiled and accepted it.
Joyfully, he said to Yǒng:
"The ultimate treasure has arrived."
He immediately ordered the fire extinguished,
retrieved the insect from the cauldron,
and placed it in a golden box.
Though the insect had been refined for a long time,
it still leaped about as before.
The foreigner swallowed the pearl,
and said to Yǒng:
"Follow me into the sea,
and do not be afraid."
Yǒng then grasped the foreigner's belt,
and followed him in.
The seawater parted for dozens of paces,
and all the scaly and shelled creatures
fled in retreat.
They toured the dragon palace,
entered the serpent's chamber,
and among the pearls and strange treasures,
chose whatever they wished,
acquiring a great many in just one night.
The foreigner said to Yǒng:
"This can bring wealth worth hundreds of millions."
Later, he also gave Yǒng several kinds of precious shells,
which Yǒng sold in Nányuè,
earning a thousand yì of gold,
and thus became even richer.
Afterward, he never took office,
but grew old in Mǐnyuè.
Zhāng Jǐng
Zhāng Jǐng of Píngyáng,
skilled in archery,
served as a deputy general in his commandery.
Jǐng had a daughter,
just sixteen or seventeen years old,
very clever and kind,
and her parents loved her,
housing her in a side chamber.
One night,
the girl was alone in her room,
asleep,
not yet deeply,
when she suddenly heard the door creak open.
Soon she saw a man enter,
dressed in white,
plump and full-faced,
who leaned over her bed.
Fearing he was a thief,
she silently dared not look.
The man in white pressed closer with a smile,
and the girl grew even more afraid,
suspecting he might be a monster.
So she shouted:
"Are you not a thief?
If not,
then you are something else."
The man in white laughed and said:
"To suspect me of being a thief
is a mistake.
To call me something else
is even more off the mark!
I am originally the son of the Cáo family from Qí,
and they say I am handsome and graceful—
do you not know this?
Though you reject me,
I will still stay in your room."
Having said this,
he lay down on the bed
and slept,
there.
The girl loathed him,
but dared not peek,
and he did not leave until nearly dawn.
The next night he came again,
and the girl grew even more terrified.
The following day,
she told her father everything.
Her father said:
"It must be a monster."
He then took a golden awl,
threaded a string through its end,
sharpened its point,
and gave it to his daughter.
Instructing her:
"When the creature comes,
stab him with this."
That night he came again,
and the girl forced herself to converse with him;
the creature indeed spoke well.
As midnight approached,
the girl secretly stabbed the awl into his neck.
The creature leaped up with a loud cry,
dragging the string away.
The next day,
the girl told her father,
who ordered a servant to follow the trail.
A few dozen paces from the house,
under an ancient tree,
they found a hole with the string going into it.
They dug it out,
and though not deep—only a few feet—
they indeed found a grub,
about a foot long,
crouching inside,
with the awl stuck in its neck—
this was the so-called Cáo family son from Qí.
Jǐng immediately killed it,
and from then on, the hauntings ceased.
Snake Doctor
In the second year of Wáng Yànwēi's governorship of Biàn,
there was a summer drought.
At that time, the imperial tutor Lǐ □ passed through Biàn,
and a banquet was held.
Wáng expressed concern about the drought,
and Lǐ, drunk, said:
"Making rain is very easy.
Find four snake doctors,
two ten-dàn jars,
fill each with water,
float two snake doctors inside,
cover with wooden lids,
seal them tightly with mud,
and place them in busy areas.
Set up mats in front of the jars and burn incense,
select over ten children under ten years old,
give them small green bamboo sticks,
and have them take turns striking the jars day and night,
without stopping even briefly."
Wáng followed his advice and tried it,
and it rained twice in one day,
pouring heavily for several hundred lǐ.
According to old tales,
dragons and snake masters are in-laws.
Mountain Spider
It is said that Péi Mín was traveling in the mountains
when a mountain spider
lowered a silk thread like a bolt of cloth,
nearly reaching Mín.
Mín drew his bow and shot it back,
and it was as large as a cartwheel.
He then cut off several feet of its silk
and kept it.
When a subordinate had a metal-inflicted wound,
he cut a square inch of the silk and applied it,
and the bleeding stopped immediately.
Insect Transformation
Wéi Xuàn, the junior governor of Hénán,
in his youth,
once saw a strange insect on the riverbank of Kuízhōu.
At first, he thought it was a thorn,
but his attendant exclaimed in alarm:
"This insect is spiritual—
do not disturb it,
or it may cause wind and rain."
Wéi tested by stomping the ground to startle it,
and the insect flew up,
then fell to the ground as if vanishing.
Looking closely at the ground,
it seemed like a stone vein.
After a long while, it gradually rose as before,
with a claw on each thorn.
Suddenly, it entered the grass,
darting away like an arrow,
and no one ever knew what it was.
Scorpion Transformation
The large centipede-carrying insects
often transform into centipedes.
Centipedes are often carried on their backs;
Duàn Chéngshì once saw a centipede carrying over ten offspring,
the offspring still white in color,
as small as rice grains.
He also once heard Zhāng Xīfù say
that in an ancient granary in Chénzhōu, there were centipedes,
shaped like coins,
whose sting would certainly kill a person,
which were previously absent in Jiāngnán.
Louse-Expelling Herb
According to old accounts,
for louse infestations,
drinking water in which a red dragon has bathed will cure it.
Lice detest mercury;
if a person suffers from lice,
even fragrant clothes and bathing cannot stop it,
only mercury can remove them.
Dàoshi Cuī Bái said
that the scholar Zhāng Gào from Jīngzhōu
once caught a two-headed louse.
There is also a herb that grows at the damp base of mountains,
with leaves like lilies,
opposite leaves on a single stem,
the stem slightly red,
one or two chǐ tall,
named the louse-expelling herb,
capable of removing lice and nits.
Fǎtōng
In Jīngzhōu, there was a monk named Fǎtōng,
originally from Ānxī,
who became a monk in his youth in Eastern India.
He said that locusts have Sanskrit characters on their bellies,
some descending from the heavens.
They come from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the Brahma heaven.
In the Western Regions, they verify these characters
and perform rituals at their original heavenly altars to ward them off.
Nowadays, locusts have the character for "king" on their heads,
which naturally makes sense.
Some say they transform from fish eggs,
which is close to the truth.
It was previously said that insects that eat grain
are caused by corrupt officials,
who exploit the common people,
leading to insects eating the grain.
If the insect's body is black and its head red,
it represents a military official;
if its head is black and body red,
it represents a scholarly official.
Scholar from Dēngfēng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a scholar who traveled as a guest for over ten years
and returned to his estate,
which was in Dēngfēng County.
Late at night,
the scholar had not yet fallen asleep.
Suddenly, a spark of light appeared from under the wall,
initially like a firefly,
gradually growing brighter,
as large as a pellet,
flying and illuminating the four corners,
gradually lowering,
circling back and forth.
It came within just over a chǐ of the scholar's face.
Looking closely into the light,
there was a woman,
wearing a hairpin,
in a red top and green skirt,
shaking her head and swinging her arms,
Her form was delicate and lovely.
The scholar then spread his hands to catch it,
and upon lighting a candle to look,
it turned out to be rat droppings,
as large as a chicken roosting pellet.
Breaking it open to examine,
there was an insect with a red head and blue body,
which he killed.
Lice Omen
It is said that when a person is about to die,
lice leave the body.
Some say,
if you take lice from a sick person and place them before the bed,
you can divine the illness.
If the person is about to recover,
the lice will crawl toward the sick person;
if they turn their backs, death will follow.
Wall Spider
One day,
at a gathering at Jiāngfēng Pavilion,
everyone discussed folk remedies.
Duàn Chéngshì recorded a cure for wall spider bites
using alum.
Revisiting Xǔ Jūn,
he used mulberry wood ash solution,
boiled three times,
took the liquid,
mixed alum into a paste,
applied it to the wound, and it would heal,
also effective against snake venom.
From Shāng, Dèng, to Xiāngzhōu,
there are many wall spiders,
whose poison can certainly kill.
A guest at the gathering said,
in the year of the snake, it is not suitable to kill snakes.
Large Centipede
At the north gate of Ānyì County,
the locals say
there is a centipede as large as a pipa,
each time it emerges,
it does not poison people,
yet people still fear it.
Its spirit has accumulated over the years.
Red Bat
Liú Jūn said,
when the red banana flowers bloom in the south,
red bats gather among the flowers,
southerners call them red bats.
Qīngfú
The qīngfú resembles a cicada but is slightly larger in shape,
its taste is pungent,
and it is edible.
Whenever it lays eggs,
they always cling to grass leaves,
as large as silkworm eggs.
If a person takes the eggs home,
the mother will also fly there,
regardless of distance,
the mother will always know the location.
Then, each places a small coin,
in a cloth,
bury it under a shaded wall facing east,
open it after three days,
and then smear it with the mother's blood as before.
Whenever buying goods,
if you use the offspring coin first,
the offspring coin will return to the mother;
if you use the mother coin,
the mother coin will return to the offspring.
Circulating in this way,
they never cease.
If buying gold, silver, or treasures,
the coins will not return.
The qīngfú,
also known as yúbó.
Prince Téng's Painting
One day,
at a gathering at Zǐjí Palace.
Scholar Liǔ Lǔfēng said,
he once saw Prince Téng's "Painting of Bees and Butterflies."
Named Jiāngxià spots,
large sea eye,
small sea eye,
village arrival,
and cabbage flower seeds.
Strange Bee
There is a bee that looks like a wax bee,
slightly larger,
flying swiftly and vigorously.
It likes to neatly cut tree leaves,
rolling them into wood holes and wall cracks to make nests.
Duàn Chéngshì once opened a wall to search for them,
in each rolled leaf,
it was filled with filth.
Some say,
it will transform into honey.
Hermit Crab
The hermit crab,
like a snail but with legs,
resembles a spider in shape.
Originally shell-less,
it enters empty snail shells,
carrying them as it moves.
When touched, it retracts its legs,
like a snail closing its door.
If heated with fire,
it then emerges and flees,
revealing its parasitic nature.
Strange Insect
Wēn Huì was in Jiāngzhōu,
watching fishermen with guests.
One fisherman suddenly ran ashore frantically,
Wēn asked him,
but he only pointed backward at his back,
unable to speak.
The fisherman's skin was dark;
upon closer inspection,
there was something like a yellow leaf,
over a foot in size,
covered with eyes all over,
biting and impossible to remove.
Wēn ordered it burned,
and only then did it fall off.
Beneath each pair of eyes,
there was a mouth like a nail.
The fisherman bled several liters and died.
No one could identify it.
Flies
In Cháng'ān, autumn brings many flies.
Duàn Chéngshì once read five volumes of various schools daily,
greatly disturbed by them,
they brushed against his eyelashes and obscured the text,
unable to be driven away.
By chance, he swatted and killed one,
and upon close inspection,
its wings resembled those of a cicada,
its crown resembled that of a bee.
Its nature is to seek out decay,
and crave wine and meat.
According to reason, its head and wings.
Among its kind, the gray ones have a robust sound,
the gold-bearing ones have a clear sound,
listening to their sound comes from their wings.
The green ones can spoil things,
the large ones have heads like fire.
Some say,
the hemp fly,
transforms from taro roots.
Silverfish
Bǔquē Zhāng Zhōufēng said,
he once saw white melon seeds on a wall turn into white fish.
Thus understanding the meaning in Lièzǐ's words about rotten melons becoming fish.
Longhorn Beetle
It is a black-armored insect.
In midsummer Cháng'ān,
this insect sometimes appears between fences and walls,
and rain is sure to follow.
Duàn Chéngshì tested this seven times,
and each time it proved true.
White Wasp Nest
At Duàn Chéngshì's private residence in Xiūxíng Lǐ,
there was an orchard of several acres.
In the year Rénxū,
there were wasps like sesame seeds,
the wasps gathered soil to build a nest,
under the eaves in front of the courtyard,
as large as a chicken egg,
pure white and lovely.
His younger brother disliked it and destroyed it.
That winter,
he indeed suffered injuries to his hands and feet.
The *History of the Southern Dynasties* says Emperor Míng of Sòng disliked hearing about white.
The *Jīn Lóu Zǐ* says on the day of his son's wedding,
a fierce wind brought snow,
the curtains turned white,
which was considered inauspicious.
Thus it is known that the taboo against white has long existed in custom.
Poisonous Wasps
In Lǐngnán, there is a poisonous fungus,
luminous at night,
which rots after rain,
and transforms into a giant wasp.
Black in color,
with a beak like a saw,
over three fen in length.
At night, it enters people's ears and noses,
severing the heart's connections.
Bamboo Bee
In Shǔ, there are bamboo honey bees,
fond of building nests on wild bamboo.
The nest is as large as a chicken egg,
with a stem,
about a foot long.
Both the nest and honey are a lovely dark blue,
twice as sweet as ordinary honey.
Water Maggot
In southern streams and brooks, these insects are numerous,
over an inch long,
black in color.
In late summer,
they transform into horseflies,
whose sting is very poisonous.
Water Insect
In Xiàngpǔ,
its rivers and islets have water insects,
that gather on wood and eat ships,
destroying them in several tens of days.
The insects are very minute.
Bào Qiǎng
A water insect shaped like a dung beetle,
with a large belly and spines below,
and thorn-like needles,
whose sting is poisonous.
Chameleon
In the south, there is an insect called the chameleon,
corresponding to the twelve two-hour periods of the day.
This insect resembles a gecko,
with long legs,
greenish-red in color,
and fleshy crests.
In the summer months, it is often seen between fences and walls,
and custom holds that seeing it often brings desired outcomes.
Its head suddenly changes,
taking the form of the twelve earthly branches.
Duàn Chéngshì's elder cousin once saw it.
Dūn Yú
The dūn yú is shaped like a cicada,
its young like insects,
attached,
to grass leaves.
If you obtain its young, the mother flies to them,
fried and eaten,
it is pungent and delicious.
Camel Cricket
The camel cricket resembles a cricket,
slightly larger,
with long legs,
fond of burrowing by the stove.
Common saying holds that if the stove has a "horse,"
it is an omen of ample food.
Xiè Bào
In Guózhōu, there is an insect called the xiè bào,
often dwelling deep in the soil.
Sīmǎ Péi Shěnzǐ once dug a hole and captured one.
Small, resembling a toad,
but round like a ball.
Upon seeing people,
it covers its head with its front two feet crossed,
as if shy.
It can burrow into the ground like a zokor,
digging several feet deep in moments.
If it emerges above ground,
and hears the call of the xiè bào bird,
its head splits and it dies,
hence the common name.
Chariot-Shattering Insect
The chariot-shattering insect resembles a jī liáo,
gray in color,
fond of perching on tall trees,
its sound like a person chanting or whistling.
It is found in the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Dùgǔ
The dùgǔ resembles a book ribbon,
with distinct colors,
about two chǐ in length,
its head like a shovel,
with black and yellow stripes on its back,
which break off easily upon slight contact.
It often chases earthworms,
and once the earthworm ceases to move,
it climbs onto the earthworm and covers it.
After a long while, the earthworm dissolves,
leaving only muddy slime in its abdomen.
It is poisonous;
chickens die if they eat it.
It is commonly called tǔzhōng.
Léiqí
The léiqí is as large as an earthworm.
When touched with an object,
it contracts and shrinks,
rolling into a ball like a pellet.
After a long while, it extends its head,
and the ball shape gradually shrinks,
returning to its earthworm-like form.
Some say
its bite is highly venomous.
Fùyù
Before cicadas shed their skin, they are called fùyù.
It is traditionally said they transform from dung beetles.
Scholar Wéi Xuānzhuāng, residing in Dùqū,
once dug up tree roots in winter
and saw a fùyù attached to a decayed spot,
finding it strange.
Villagers said cicadas indeed transform from rotten wood.
Xuān thus dissected one to examine it,
and its abdomen was still filled with rotten wood.
Jiádié
Butterflies transform from inchworm cocoons.
Scholar Gù Fēixióng, when young,
once saw a piece of a green skirt rotting in a manure pile,
which then transformed into a butterfly.
Ministry of Works Vice-Director Zhāng Zhōufēng said
that if lily flowers are closed
and their gaps sealed with mud,
after one night,
they transform into large butterflies.
Ants
In Qínzhōng, there are many large black ants,
fond of fighting,
commonly called mǎyǐ.
Next are reddish-colored small ants,
among which are black, sluggish ones
capable of lifting iron equal to their body weight.
There are also yellowish ones,
most skilled at exploiting the weak.
When Duàn Chéngshì was a child playing,
he often placed thorny branches to block flies,
straight in their path.
These ants, upon touching them, would turn back.
Sometimes, one or several chǐ from the nest,
those entering the nest
would emerge as if pulled by a rope,
suggesting they summoned each other with sounds.
When moving, every six or seven ants,
a larger-headed one would be among them,
orderly as if in formation.
When relocating flies,
the larger-headed ones would either flank or guard the rear,
as if protecting against other ants.
Ant Mounds
Chéng Zhígōng, in the wilderness of Yìdìng,
saw
an
ant mound
over two chǐ high.
Rice Transformation
Dàoshi Xǔ Xiàngzhī said
that if cold food festival rice is covered with a basin in a dark room on the ground,
by summer,
it all transforms into red spiders.
Centipede Breath
Suíxiàn has many centipedes.
Larger ones
can suck in rabbits with their breath,
smaller ones suck in lizards.
From a distance of three or four chǐ,
flesh and bones dissolve on their own.
Yēwēng
Duàn Chéngshì’s study had many of these insects,
as they like to nest in book scrolls
or inside brush holders.
Their chirping sounds are pleasant to hear.
Sometimes, upon opening a scroll to look,
they are all small spiders,
as large as jumping spiders,
quickly sealing themselves off with mud.
Only then does one realize they do not solely carry mulberry insects.
Diāndāng
In front of Duàn Chéngshì’s study,
after each rain, there were many diāndāng nests,
deep like earthworm burrows.
They weave webs inside,
and spit
The cover is level with the ground,
as large as an elm seed.
It often lifts its lid upward,
waiting for flies or inchworms to pass by,
then flips the lid to catch them.
Once inside, it closes again,
blending with the ground in color,
with no trace of silk gaps to be found.
Its shape resembles a spider.
The "Ěryǎ" calls it "wángzhūyì",
and the "Guǐgǔzǐ" calls it "diēmǔ".
Children in Qínzhōng playfully chant:
"Diāndāng, guard your door firmly,
or the yēwēng will invade, leaving you nowhere to flee."
Guǒluǒ
Guǒluǒ,
now called yēwēng,
is a creature purely male without females,
neither mating nor reproducing.
It takes the offspring of mulberry insects and chants over them,
and they all transform into its own offspring.
Bees are also like this.
Shāshī
In Tán, Yuán, Chù, Jí, and other prefectures, there are shāshī,
which are lice from the scales of venomous snakes,
too tiny to be seen.
In summer,
snakes suffer from these lice
and hang themselves upside down over fast-flowing riverbanks,
letting the water wash off the lice.
Or they lie in the sand,
grinding the lice into the sand.
If a passerby is infected,
the bitten spot resembles a needle prick or millet grain,
surrounded by five-colored patterns,
which indicate the poison.
If treated by a shùshì with incantations,
a small portion is cut away,
and then treated with flesh-regenerating ointment,
leading to recovery.
Otherwise,
death occurs within two or three days.
Shuǐnǔ
The shuǐnǔ insect
resembles a dung beetle.
It is black,
with eight legs,
and drags its tail with pincers,
three to four chǐ long.
The tail is the crossbow.
Usually, from the first day of the fourth month, it raises its crossbow,
until the eighth month, it lowers it.
At times, it bends its tail,
from its back up to the front of its head,
holding it with its pincers.
Upon seeing a human shadow, it shoots,
and where the shadow is hit,
the person’s body swells accordingly,
similar in severity to the poison of shāshī.
One must quickly use controlled breathing to counteract it,
cut away the poisoned flesh,
to secure survival.
Otherwise,
death occurs within a day or two.
Additionally, there are many gǔdú,
so travelers must be especially cautious.
When entering a household with gǔdú,
carefully warn the host:
"Your household has gǔdú,
do not easily harm me."
Doing so will prevent the poison from taking effect.
Xú Xuánzhī
There was a man named Xú Xuánzhī,
who moved from eastern Zhèjiāng to Wú,
and resided in Lìyì Lǐ.
His residence had long been known as inauspicious,
but Xuánzhī, attracted by its flowers, trees, and rare plants,
decided to settle there.
After more than a month,
while reading at night,
he saw several hundred armored horsemen ascending from the southwestern corner of his bed,
placing silk nets on a flower-patterned carpet,
and unleashing their troops for a great hunt.
Flying birds and running beasts
were too numerous to count.
After the hunt concluded,
There were banners and leopard-tail standards,
along with several hundred outriders,
who also entered from outside,
arriving at the northwestern corner.
There were those wearing swords and carrying axes,
holding bows and hammers,
numbering several hundred in total.
Those carrying tents, curtains, and couches,
plates, dishes, cauldrons, and pots,
also numbered several hundred.
Those bearing vessels filled with delicacies from land and sea,
also numbered several hundred.
Those coming and going along the roads,
running about and serving as attendants,
also numbered several hundred.
Xuánzhī stared intently, and the scene gradually became clearer.
Reaching the central army,
there was a colorful signal flag,
and a man wearing a red turban and purple robes,
attended by several thousand followers,
arrived to the right of the table.
There was a large,
iron crown,
holding an iron tablet,
He declared:
"His Highness intends to observe fishing at Zǐshí Tán.
The vanguard, rear guard, and all armored soldiers carrying spears and halberds
shall not follow."
Thereupon, the man in the red turban dismounted,
and with several hundred attendants,
ascended onto Xuánzhī's inkstone.
Red-curtained tents were set up to the north,
and soon couches, tents, and curtains,
as well as banquet mats and dance platforms, were fully prepared.
Dozens of guests,
dressed in crimson, purple, red, and green,
and those holding shēng, yú, xiāo, and guǎn instruments,
also numbered several dozen.
They sang and danced in turns,
with jesters and entertainers,
Too many to fully record.
After several rounds of wine,
when the distinguished guests showed signs of intoxication,
the man in the red turban looked at his attendants and said:
"Fetch the fishing gear."
There were also old nets, cages, and the like, numbering several hundred in total,
all entering the inkstone together.
Not long after,
they caught several hundred thousand small fish.
The man in the red turban said to the distinguished guests:
"I have deeply mastered the art of Rèngōng,
and I shall entertain the guests with it."
He then took a fishing rod to the southern bank of the inkstone.
The musicians played "Chūnbō Yǐn,"
and before the tune ended,
he had caught over a hundred bream, carp, perch, and mandarin fish.
He immediately ordered them to be sliced and prepared for a feast,
with several dozen dishes in total,
all indescribably fragrant.
Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments
played in harmonious unison.
When the wine reached the man in the red turban,
he raised his cup, looked at Xuánzhī, and said to the guests:
"I have not studied the rites of Zhōugōng,
nor have I read the books of Master Kǒng,
yet I hold the noble position of a king.
Now this scholar,
with scorched and balding hair,
and a sallow complexion,
though he toils diligently,
what does he achieve?
If he were willing to humble himself and serve as my junior minister,
he could also join today's banquet."
Xuánzhī then covered the scene with a book,
and holding a candle to look,
saw nothing at all.
Xuánzhī set aside the book and went to sleep.
Just as he was falling asleep,
he saw several thousand armored horsemen,
descending from the western window, forming ranks and columns,
arriving with shouts and commands.
Xuánzhī cried out in alarm to his servants,
but several horsemen had already reached his bedside,
and declared:
"The Pífú Prince hunted in the lush fields of Yánglín
and fished in the deep pool of Zǐshí.
Xuánzhī, the slave at the window,
suddenly caused distress and intimidation,
scattering the soldiers into chaos,
and alarming the royal carriage.
Since he lacks the heart to face danger with nobility,
he must face the punishment of Jìnwén's return to the state.
Hand him over to General Mángdīng for pursuit and punishment."
After the proclamation,
they tied a white silk cord around Xuánzhī's neck,
and several dozen armored soldiers
dragged him away in formation.
Their movement was swift,
and in an instant, it was as if they had entered a city gate,
with onlookers packed shoulder to shoulder and piled foot upon foot,
stretching for five or six lǐ.
After traveling several more lǐ,
they saw the inner city,
where a man in red robes and headgear announced:
"The Pífú King is greatly angered, saying:
'He wears scholar's robes,
reads scholar's books,
yet does not cultivate the words and deeds of the ancients,
but instead acts recklessly and dares to offend his superiors.
Hand him over to the Three Ministers and below for deliberation.'"
They then released his bonds,
and led him into the council hall.
He saw ten men in purple robes and headgear,
and Xuánzhī bowed to each in turn,
but they all glared and sat arrogantly as they received his bows.
They listened to the accusations against him,
Especially brilliant and radiant in the human world.
At that time, the Prince, with fear and shock having entered his heart,
his illness grew increasingly severe.
The Three Ministers and below deliberated,
and requested the imposition of corporal punishment.
Before the verdict was issued,
the Grand Astrologer Mǎ Zhīxuán submitted a memorial arguing:
"I humbly submit that the Prince does not follow the classics,
and the laws,
indulging in excessive excursions and amusements,
treating danger as level ground,
bringing shock upon himself.
Xú Xuánzhī's nature is unwavering,
his broad knowledge is not shallow,
and moreover, he cultivates heavenly virtue,
making it difficult to falsely accuse him with sorcery.
Now, the Great King, unable to reflect on himself,
instead gives free rein to his whims,
trusting those many sycophants,
seeks to harm a wise man.
I have secretly observed that ominous clouds and portents frequently arise,
strange calamities repeatedly occur,
rumors and false prophecies spread in the markets,
and the people are alarmed and suspicious.
In the past, Qín shot a giant fish and declined,
and Yīn fought fierce beasts and perished.
Now, if the Great King seeks to harm those not of his kind,
he treads the path of Yīn and Qín,
and I fear that the beginning of a declining age
will start from this."
The King read the memorial and flew into a rage,
beheading Grand Astrologer Mǎ Zhīxuán at the city gate,
to warn those who spread ominous words.
At that time, a heavy rain suddenly fell,
and a minister from the marshes, □ Fēi, submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that those who indulge in excessive excursions and amusements,
and give free rein to fishing and hunting,
will surely lose their position;
those who blame worthy ministers,
and kill loyal and outspoken men,
will surely bring ruin to their state.
I humbly submit that the Prince hunted disaster in a remote place,
and fished calamity from a dark spring,
trusting illusionists,
and deluding scholars.
The sorrow of losing one's footing
is what is called bringing it upon oneself.
Now, the Great King does not investigate the wrongs of these excursions,
but instead listens to deceitful and fawning advice.
Moreover, Zhīxuán was a senior statesman of the kingdom,
truly a hereditary minister of the great court,
and it would be fitting to adopt his counsel,
to correct this collapse.
Preserving one's life might require only three remonstrations,
yet offending the superior did not harm him with a single word.
His loyalty and sincerity were just about to be fully presented,
when, to everyone's shock, his head and body were suddenly parted.
Your servant has secretly read in military texts that
rain without clouds is the sky weeping.
Now, a forthright minister has been executed,
And Heaven wept for him.
I fear that Bǐ Gàn did not die with regret in his time,
but I know that Mǎ Zhīxuán died with regret today.
Your Majesty still does not pardon Zhīxuán with lenient laws,
but seeks to justify his name through corporal punishment.
This is like gouging out my eyes to watch the Yuè army,
and it is happening again today.
In the past, the state of Yú considered Gōngzhī Qí’s words to be false,
and was eventually annexed by Duke Xiàn of Jìn;
the state of Wú regarded Wǔ Zǐxū’s advice as wrong,
and was indeed destroyed by Gōu Jiàn.
I dare not enumerate all examples from the Zhōu and Qín dynasties,
lest I burden Your Majesty’s wisdom.
I merely venture, like dust and dirt,
to add a little to the lofty Mount Sōng.
The king read the memorial,
and immediately appointed □ Fēi as Remonstrance Counselor,
posthumously honored Grand Astrologer Mǎ Zhīxuán as Grand General Who Pacifies the State,
appointed his son Mǎ Chí as Grand Astrologer,
bestowed five hundred bolts of cloth and silk as funeral gifts,
and three hundred dàn of rice each.
As for Xú Xuánzhī,
he awaited later imperial decree.
Thereupon, Chí submitted a memorial,
moving the market gate and presenting an official petition, saying:
“I have received the gracious decree stating:
‘Mǎ Zhīxuán possessed the loyalty and integrity of Prince Bǐ Gàn of Yīn,
and the remonstrance of Xīn Pí, Palace Attendant of Wèi,
yet I repeatedly acted on my own,
and was blind in recognizing talent.
I burned the beams and pillars on the morning when the great hall was to be built,
and shattered the boat and oars on the day when the great river was to be crossed.
Due to my lack of virtue,
you suffered unjustly.
Thus, it is fitting to honor the deceased with praise,
and extend rewards to his descendants.’
The imperial brush suddenly arrived,
filling me with shock and fear.
I kowtowed until my breath was exhausted,
wailed until my tears turned to blood.
I humbly submit that my late father, Zhīxuán,
studied exhaustively the ways of Heaven and humanity,
and mastered the arts of calendrics and astrology.
Through profound insight, he gained a place in this sagely court.
At the time when Your Majesty gathered the advice of humble grass-cutters,
it was the day my father displayed his excellent plans.
Harsh words are difficult to hear,
and startling advice is easily punished.
Now, blessed by the sagely wisdom that has come to light,
this injustice has been illuminated.
The vast grace showers down,
yet it still startles his already scattered spirit;
noble titles may mend the gap,
but they cannot restore his severed neck.
How can I now, because of my late father’s execution,
seek,
the honors and glory of the state?
I cannot repay King Píng,
nor can I bear to emulate Bó Yǔ.
Moreover, the celestial signs are about to change,
and the mandate of Heaven is cause for concern.
I humbly beg to be banished to a distant land,
to avoid encountering calamity and chaos.”
The king read the memorial and was displeased,
so he retired to the Awaiting Rain Hall.
After waking,
he feasted all officials at the Reaching Clouds Terrace, saying:
“I just had an auspicious dream.
Whoever can interpret it,
and cleanse my heart to make it clear,
will be granted one rank of nobility.”
All the ministers and officials
bowed their heads and listened respectfully.
He said:
“I dreamed that the Supreme Deity said,
‘I will aid you with metal,
open your state,
expand your territory,
from south to north,
red jade and stones,
to repay your virtue.’
What do you all think of this?”
The ministers all bowed and danced in congratulations, saying:
“This is a celebration from a neighboring state.”
□ Fēi said:
“This is greatly inauspicious.
What is there to celebrate?”
The king said:
“Why do you say that?”
□ Fēi said:
“Your Majesty coerces the living,
detains them in dark caverns,
and thus this ominous dream is bestowed,
arising from Heaven’s wrath.
‘Aid with metal’ means a hoe,
‘open the state’ means to cleave apart,
‘expand the territory’ means to split asunder,
‘red jade and stones’
means to burn together with fire.
Is it not that Xuánzhī will hoe our land,
attack our state,
set fires north and south,
to repay the humiliation of the severed neck?”
The king then pardoned Xuánzhī’s crime,
executed the practitioners of occult arts,
destroyed his own palace,
to avert the dream’s omen.
He then sent Xuánzhī back in a comfortable carriage.
As soon as he reached his couch,
Xuánzhī awoke.
When it was fully light,
he summoned his household servants,
and dug more than five feet deep by the western window,
finding an ant nest as large as three dàn jars.
He then set fire to burn it,
leaving none alive.
From then on, the house was no longer haunted.
Short Fox
The Sōu Shén Jì and the Hóng Fàn Wǔ Xíng Zhuàn say:
The yù (a mythical creature) shoots and is born in the south,
and is called the ‘short fox.’
Among the southern Yuè barbarians,
men and women bathe together in the same river,
and licentiousness is centered on women,
hence there are many yù.
The yù is born from the chaotic energy of licentious women.
Spider’s Grudge
Recently, in front of a temple monk’s dwelling,
there was a spider spinning a web,
of an extremely large size.
Whenever this monk saw the spider,
he would playfully strike it with something.
When the spider saw the monk coming,
it would hide and conceal itself.
This went on for several years.
One day,
it was suddenly very hot,
and the monk was alone in his room,
so he took a daytime nap.
The spider then descended onto the bed,
bit through the monk’s throat, making a wound,
and he died shortly after.
Wasps and scorpions possess venom—
these are not empty words.
Lizard
Cáo Shūyǎ’s Yì Wù Zhì says:
When fish jump and leap,
then lizards come down from the grass.
They gradually draw close to each other,
then float together on the water and mate.
After the act is finished,
the fish returns to the water’s depths,
and the lizard returns to the grass.
Yīn Láng
The Yīn family of Chénjùn had an adopted son named Láng,
who was involved with a maidservant for years.
After the maidservant died,
he still visited her incessantly,
and his mind became confused and disordered.
His mother observed this closely.
Later one evening, she saw a large spider,
shaped like a dipper,
climbing onto the bed toward Láng,
and then they happily pleasured each other.
The mother caught and killed it,
and Láng’s mind and disposition then returned to normal.
Maidservant of Yùzhāng
There was a household in Yùzhāng,
with a maidservant working by the stove.
Suddenly, there were people several inches tall,
coming into the stove area.
The maidservant accidentally stepped on and killed one with her shoe,
and then several hundred people appeared,
dressed in mourning hemp,
carrying a coffin to welcome the deceased,
with all funeral rituals prepared.
They went out the east gate,
and entered under an overturned boat in the garden.
Upon closer inspection, they were all pillbugs.
Boiling water was poured to kill them,
and they were then eradicated.
Southern Sea Poisonous Insects
In the South Sea there is a poisonous insect,
like a large lizard,
with particularly bright and clear eyes.
The locals call it the "twelve-hour insect."
Within a day and a night,
it changes its color according to the twelve hours,
now red, now yellow.
It is also called the "fence-head insect."
Legend has it that
if it injures a person, death is immediate.
After secretly biting someone,
it quickly runs atop fences,
watching the mourning of the victim's relatives.
In the various commanderies southwest of Xīnzhōu,
there are absolutely no snakes, mosquitoes, or flies.
I was exiled to the south for ten years,
and never once saw a snake.
Even lying outdoors in the height of summer,
I suffered no bites on my skin.
People here say there are few snakes in the south,
believing they are eaten by the Yílǎo tribes.
There is another type called water snake,
slightly shorter in shape,
not dwelling on land,
and not one that spits venom or bites people.
Nuòlóng
In the Nánhǎi Commandery, there are bees
that live on olive trees.
Though they have limbs,
they closely resemble tree leaves,
clinging to branches,
indistinguishable from leaves.
Southerners who gather them
first cut down the tree,
wait for the leaves to wither and fall,
and then collect them.
There is a water insect called Nuòlóng,
shaped like a lizard,
with a slight resemblance to a dragon.
Common lore says
when this insect wants to eat,
it emerges from the water and perches on a rock.
Any aquatic creature swimming by
that reaches the rock it occupies
will leap and place itself before it,
whereupon it is taken and eaten.
Those who catch it always find it in pairs.
If the male dies,
the female immediately comes,
and likewise if the female dies.
It is said that if both male and female are placed in bamboo,
separated by a node,
after a short while,
the bamboo node will open by itself.
Villagers sell the dead ones,
and illusionists use them along with bees
in arts to bewitch men for women.
Ants
In the south, ants are especially numerous.
All pillars, lintels, doors, and windows swarm with ants.
They follow paths in bustling movement,
each dwelling engaged in its tasks,
their mounds connected one after another,
with no end to their comings and goings.
Frogs and Toads
In the south, there is also an aquatic creature,
shaped like a frog,
but especially ugly in appearance.
The locals call it "há."
When made into dried meat,
and eaten,
its flavor is as delicious as partridge.
It also treats men's fatigue and debility.
Golden Tortoise Beetle,
a type of armored insect,
born on plants and trees in spring and summer,
as large as a small fingernail.
When flying, it appears different.
Perched on grass vines,
upon close inspection,
it truly resembles a little golden tortoise.
They always move in pairs.
Southerners gather them and dry them in the shade,
adorn them with gold and jadeite,
and use them as hair ornaments.
They are also similar to the green insects produced in Qiánzhōng.
Sea Mountains
Also, the people of Zhūyá
often on clear, bright days
see distant mountains arrayed in the sea,
all like emerald screens,
shifting east and west,
all of which are centipedes.
Their feelers are forty to fifty feet long.
This creature is not so strange.
Centipede,
the "Nányuè Zhì" records:
Large ones have skin that can be used to cover drums.
Taking their meat,
drying it into jerky,
it tastes better than beef.
It also says:
Large ones can devour cattle.
If villagers encounter them,
they beat drums and light torches
to drive them away.
Mosquito Wing
Under the wings of southern mosquitoes there are tiny flying insects.
Those with sharp eyes can see them.
Each lays nine eggs,
CH0F02C8 复未嘗曾有& - ; ,
which hatch into nine offspring,
fly away together,
and the mosquito remains unaware.
They also bite humans and all kinds of beasts,
and those bitten know it.
It is said these small insects bite and do not leave.
This insect is both fine and small,
hence called "xì miè,"
as in Chén Zhāng's reply to Duke Huán of Qí about the small insect.
This insect is often born in spring,
and by late summer hides in deer ears for the winter,
named "yīng ní."
Yīng ní is also very small.
Bedbug
Wall ticks are a type of earth insect
that metamorphose and live in wall crevices.
During the summer months, they bite people,
and although the wounds may heal,
they inevitably flare up again each year at the same time.
Only after several years
does their venom finally dissipate.
Their appearance is no different from cattle ticks.
In the northern capital, horses in the stables
suddenly began to grow thin and weak in succession, eventually dying,
and the losses grew worse by the day.
Although the commanding officer diligently supervised and inspected the fodder supply,
he was ultimately unable to determine the cause.
The condition of the dead horses was similar,
yet no one knew the origin of the illness.
Several stable managers had already been punished for this,
all of them bankrupting their families
to purchase horses as compensation,
after which they were executed.
There was a deputy general who was capable, astute, and knowledgeable;
in every task he undertook,
he achieved merit.
Recommended by the masses,
he was appointed to manage the stable horses.
This man diligently cared for and fed them,
personally attending to them day and night.
After a month or so,
the horses continued to die
as before.
Suspecting something else was at play,
he lit a bright torch and kept watch.
After the second watch,
the horses all stood without eating,
the black ones turning white,
and the white ones turning black.
Holding the torch to look,
he saw countless creatures
clinging to the horses,
which were wall ticks biting them.
After the fifth watch,
the wall ticks all departed,
forming a continuous line like a rope,
stretching unbroken.
The next day,
he reported the matter to the commanding officer
and traced their path of departure.
In the loft, they found a large hole,
which they flushed with boiling water.
They dismantled the loft
and excavated the hole,
finding dozens of hu of dead wall ticks.
In the hole was one large one,
several chi long,
shaped like a pipa,
golden in color,
which they burned and killed.
They filled and sealed the spot,
and the harm ceased.
White Insects
There was a man who suddenly developed sores on his face,
which worsened in the summer months,
leaving almost no intact skin,
causing extraordinary pain.
He had tried applying ointments and taking medicine,
but to no effect.
One day,
after he had gone to bed,
with the remaining candle still burning,
his roommate saw something like a string or thread
attaching to his face.
Grabbing the candle to look,
they saw white insects like lice
emerging from holes in the porcelain pillow,
biting his face.
At daybreak,
they recounted the incident,
cut open the pillow to examine it,
and found countless white insects.
They killed them all,
and the facial sores then healed.
Cán Nǚ
Cán Nǚ lived during the time of Emperor Gāoxīn,
when the Shǔ region had no established ruler or chief
and lacked any unified governance.
The people lived in clan groups,
constantly invading and preying on each other.
The former site of Cán Nǚ
is now in Guǎnghàn,
though her surname is unknown.
Her father was captured by a neighboring state
and had been gone for over a year,
with only the horse he rode still remaining.
The daughter, missing her father and separated from him,
sometimes neglected food and drink,
and her mother comforted her.
She then made a vow to the crowd, saying,
"Whoever can bring my father back
will marry this daughter."
Among the subordinates,
though they heard the vow,
none could bring her father back.
The horse, hearing these words,
startled, leaped, and shook vigorously,
broke free from its restraints, and left.
Several days later,
the father returned riding the horse.
From then on, the horse neighed
and refused to eat or drink.
The father asked the reason,
and the mother told him of the vow she had made to the crowd.
The father said:
"The vow was made to people,
not to a horse.
How can a human be matched with a non-human?
That it could rescue me from danger
is already a great merit.
The vow that was made
cannot be carried out."
The horse grew even more agitated,
and the father, angered,
shot and killed it,
then laid its skin out in the courtyard.
As the daughter passed by its side,
the horse skin suddenly sprang up,
wrapped around the girl, and flew away.
Ten days later,
the skin again rested on a mulberry tree.
The girl transformed into a silkworm,
ate mulberry leaves,
spun silk to form a cocoon,
and provided clothing for the people of the world.
Her parents, filled with regret and sorrow,
missed her incessantly.
Suddenly, they saw Cán Nǚ
riding flowing clouds,
driving this horse,
with several dozen attendants,
descending from the heavens.
She said to her parents:
"The Supreme Deity, because of my filial piety and dedication,
and my heart that does not forget righteousness,
has appointed me to the position of Immortal of the Nine Palaces,
granting me eternal life in heaven.
Do not remember me with longing anymore."
Then she soared into the void and departed.
Today, her home lies at the borders of Shífāng, Miánzhú, and Déyáng counties.
Each year, those praying for silkworms
gather from all directions like clouds,
and all receive divine responses.
In temples and monasteries,
statues of a young woman
draped in horse skin
are called Mǎtóu Niáng
and are prayed to for silkworms and mulberries.
The "Ode to Investigating the Sage" says:
"How could there be a woman
moved by that dead horse,
transforming into a silkworm,
clothing the world? This is she."
Shā Fú Effect
Chén Cángqì's *Běncǎo* states,
"Shāfú,
also called dàoxínggōuzi,
is known by the people of Shǔ as Fúyù.
It spins dry earth to make holes,
often sleeping motionless.
If taken and placed under a pillow,
it can make husband and wife fond of each other."
I have a close relative
who once obtained this creature,
but never tested it.
When I first traveled to Chéngdū,
I stayed at an inn
and became acquainted with a herbalist named Lǐ Shānrén.
I saw young men of Shǔchéng
often visiting Lǐ Shānrén with delight,
and paying him a handsome price.
I inquired about this,
and he said:
"Aphrodisiac."
Upon investigating its use,
it turned out to be shāfú.
Compared to what Chén described,
it truly was no empty talk.
Lǐ Shānrén also kept his method of preparation secret,
so others could not obtain it.
In the mountains and rivers of Wǔlíng, there is a charming herb.
Unscrupulous people exchange silver for it.
Some, due to its use, have driven men and women to madness,
suffering no small calamity.
Shědú
Shědú refers to
creatures like mosquitoes and gnats.
They exist in the Jiāng-Lǐng region,
especially around the Chēn-Lián border.
If bitten by them,
be careful not to scratch with your hand.
Instead, spread salt on the bite,
cover it with something,
and within half a day,
the poison will dissipate.
If scratched by hand,
the itching becomes unbearable,
breaking the skin and creating holes in the flesh,
and the poison worsens significantly.
In the area north of Xiāng-Héng,
the poison is somewhat milder.
From the Xiájiāng to Shǔ,
there are mázi,
black in color,
which can also bite people,
but their poison is not very severe.
Observing their habitat,
they are found on the backs of fūyán tree leaves.
They emerge in spring,
curling leaves into nests,
as large as peaches or plums,
called wǔbèizǐ,
which can treat all kinds of sores and toxins.
Collectors dry them in the sun to kill them,
preventing them from transforming.
Otherwise,
they will inevitably bore holes and emerge,
flying away as mázi.
In the Qiánnán region, there are fine dust-like creatures,
white in color and extremely small,
invisible to the eye.
They can harm people day and night,
and even deep, dense bed nets
cannot block them entirely.
Burning coarse tea,
with smoke like that of incense,
can keep them away.
Alternatively, using oiled mats or curtains as barriers
can somewhat reduce them.
Old Spider
In Tài
at the foot of Mount Tài, there is the Dàiyuè Temple,
with towers and halls all in ancient style,
dating back to distant times.
One night, a great wind arose,
with a roaring sound,
echoing through the valleys.
By morning,
it was discovered that the scripture tower had collapsed.
Amid the wreckage of the tower,
were cartfuls of miscellaneous bones.
An old spider was found there,
shaped like a short-bellied tea cauldron holding five shēng,
with legs spanning several feet when extended.
Previously, in nearby temples
or among common households,
countless young children had gone missing,
their numbers beyond reckoning.
It seems they all fell victim to being devoured.
Many were ensnared in its webs above,
or became stuck and entangled,
unable to free themselves and escape,
thus inevitably meeting their doom.
Thereupon, the temple abbot ordered firewood to burn it,
and the stench was smelled for over ten lǐ.
Lǐ Chán,
the youngest son of Chéngsì, the governor of Chǔ Prefecture,
lived in a grand mansion on Xuānpíng Lane in Guǎnglíng.
One day, while napping in the courtyard,
suddenly a white bat
flew circling around the courtyard.
The household servants vied to swat it with brooms,
but none could hit it.
After a long while,
it flew out of the courtyard gate,
and attempts to swat it there also failed.
It then flew out the main gate,
beyond the outer gate,
and vanished.
That year,
Lǐ Chán's wife passed away,
and the route taken by the hearse
was precisely where the white bat had flown.
Locust Transformation
In the final years of the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
locusts were born in burrows in the ground.
After birth,
other locusts would immediately grab their legs and wings and pull them out.
The emperor addressed the locusts, saying:
"What crime have I committed,
that you devour my seedlings?"
They then transformed into dragonflies,
an event witnessed throughout Luòyáng.
That year,
flocks of sparrows also transformed into swallows.
Water Frog
In the eastern region of Xú,
bordering Yíchuān,
there is a ditch named
Pánchē,
traditionally said to be where Xī Zhòng tested his chariots.
The ditch contains water,
and in the water lives a frog,
as large as a five-dàn urn,
with eyes like bowls.
In the past, someone
obtained medicine from its neck,
and upon taking it, transcended the mortal world.
Earthworm Sores
During the Tiānyòu era,
the Cíhé Temple in Zhèxī was rebuilt.
After the ground was prepared,
it was constantly tunneled through by earthworms,
troubling those in charge.
A monk advised covering it with lime,
which stabilized the ground,
but killed countless earthworms.
Soon after,
that monk fell ill and suffered,
his entire body itching constantly.
He constantly
needed someone with long fingernails to scratch him,
until sores formed.
From each sore, a dead earthworm emerged,
amounting to nearly hundreds of thousands.
His flesh was consumed down to the bone, and he died.
Bee Remains
A man from Lúlíng was traveling to take the imperial examinations.
When night fell on the journey,
he went to a village house to ask for lodging.
An old man came out to meet the guest and said:
"My house is cramped and has many people;
I can only accommodate you with a single bed."
Thus, he stayed at his home.
The house had over a hundred rooms,
but they were extremely narrow and small.
After a while, he mentioned he was hungry.
The old man said:
"Our household is poor;
all we eat are wild vegetables."
He then served them,
and the guest ate them,
finding them very sweet and delicious,
unlike ordinary vegetables.
When he went to sleep,
he only heard a buzzing sound.
At dawn, he awoke
to find himself lying in a field,
with a large beehive beside him.
The guest had suffered from rheumatism,
but it was cured because of this,
likely from eating the bees' leftovers.
Xióng Nǎi
In Xìnzhōu, there is Bǎn Mountain,
with deep valleys and remote gorges.
It is a place where timber is harvested,
hence the name.
A man from the prefecture named Xióng Nǎi
once went into the mountains with his companions to cut wood.
His younger brother followed to catch up with him,
but as evening fell,
he had not yet reached his elder brother.
Suddenly, he saw armored soldiers clearing the road,
coming from the east,
with loud shouts and commands.
Xiong Nai's younger brother was terrified
and hid in the grass.
Soon, banners, spears, and armor
arrived in an endless stream.
There were also pedestrians by the roadside;
those who violated the cleared path
were immediately killed.
In the midst of the army,
they escorted someone who seemed like a great general,
galloping westward and disappearing.
Only after estimating they were far away
did he dare to get up and continue.
By daybreak,
he finally saw his elder brother
and recounted everything he had witnessed.
Everyone said:
"This is not a patrol area,
and to the west, the streams and rapids are perilous and impassable;
there is nowhere to go.
How could there be such people?"
They then searched together
for about over ten li,
across a stream and rapids,
and still saw banners fluttering densely,
arranged as if for a hunting encirclement.
One brave among their group
shouted at them from afar,
and suddenly, they all vanished.
Approaching to look,
the people were all leaves,
and the horses were all large ants.
They picked them up and crushed them,
and it was said they all bled.
Zhōngsī
Locusts as a calamity
are born from malign vapors.
They have a foul, fishy smell;
some say
they transform from fish eggs.
Each year, they reproduce
three or four times.
Each time they reproduce,
their eggs number in the hundreds.
From egg to wings,
it takes about a month for them to fly.
Thus, the Book of Songs mentions that Zhōngsī have numerous offspring.
Zhōngsī are a type of locust.
When their wings are not yet formed,
they move by hopping,
and are called nymphs.
At the end of the Tiānfú era of the Jìn dynasty,
a great locust plague struck the land,
lasting for years without respite.
When they moved, they covered the ground;
when they took flight, they blotted out the sky.
Crops, plants, and trees
were left barren, with nothing remaining.
When the nymphs were at their peak,
they flowed in countless numbers,
even floating across rivers and climbing over mountains,
crossing ponds and moats
as if walking on flat ground.
Entering people's homes,
they could not be controlled or restrained.
They bored through doors and windows,
filling wells and latrines to the brim,
fouling beds and curtains with their stench,
gnawing and damaging books and clothing.
For days and nights on end,
people could not bear the suffering.
In Yùnchéng County, there was a farming family
that raised over ten pigs.
Once, by a marshland,
they encountered a massive swarm of nymphs.
The group of pigs leaped up and devoured them,
soon becoming full and satiated,
unable to move.
The nymphs, still hungry,
then nibbled at the pigs.
They piled up like mounds,
and the pigs eventually grew exhausted,
unable to fend them off,
and were all killed by the nymphs.
In the Guǐmǎo year,
the locusts all clung to plants and trees, withering and dying—
this is what is meant by the natural cycle of life and death.
Nymph Transformation
In the Jǐyǒu year,
General Xǔ Jìngqiān was ordered to inspect the summer crops in Dōngzhōu.
He reported to the throne,
saying that in the marshlands and wilds,
he saw nymphs covering over ten li.
Just as they were about to beat and capture them,
the insects transformed into white butterflies
and flew away.
The Barbarians of the Four Directions
People of the east have large noses,
with orifices connected to the eyes,
and their sinews and strength belong there;
people of the south have large mouths,
with orifices connected to the ears;
people of the west have large faces,
with orifices connected to the nose;
people of the north
have orifices connected to the genitals,
and are short;
people of the central regions
have orifices connected to the mouth.
Wúqǐ People
The Wúqǐ people live in caves and eat earth.
When one of them dies,
they are buried,
and their heart does not decay.
After a hundred years, it transforms into a person.
The Lù people's knees do not decay;
when buried, after a hundred and twenty years, they transform into a person.
The Xì people's livers do not decay;
after eight years, they transform into a person.
Imperial Daughter Zǐzé
Imperial Daughter Zǐzé had a jealous nature.
Her attendant maids were scattered and driven to the four mountains,
with nowhere to rely.
In the east, they mated with foxes,
giving birth to sons called Yāng;
in the south, they coupled with monkeys,
and had sons called Xī;
in the north, they mated with jué jiā,
and the offspring were called Cāng.
Hairy People
Within the Eight Wastelands,
there are hairy people.
They are seven or eight chǐ tall,
all like,
human in form,
with hair covering their bodies and heads,
like macaques.
The hair is over a chǐ long,
short like yak hair.
When they see people, they stare with wide eyes,
They open their mouths and stick out their tongues,
their upper lips covering their faces,
their lower lips covering their chests.
They enjoy eating humans,
pulling at tongues and noses to play together,
and if not given, they leave.
They are called Rángōng,
commonly known as Ránlì,
also named Ránxiá.
The hair of children is fearsome.
Xuānyuán Country
The country of Xuānyuán,
lies at the edge of Qióng Mountain,
where even the short-lived live eight hundred years.
In the fields of the heavens,
harmonious luán birds dance.
The people eat phoenix eggs,
and drink sweet dew.
Báimín Country
The country of Báimín,
has Chénghuáng,
which resemble foxes,
with horns on their backs.
If one rides them,
they live three thousand years.
Ōusī
In the wilds of Ōusī,
women kneel,
leaning against trees and spitting silk.
Gàimù Country
East of Yuè is the country of Gàimù,
where when the eldest son is born,
they dismember and eat him,
calling it "beneficial for younger brothers."
When the father dies,
they carry their mother on their backs and abandon her,
saying a ghost wife
cannot be lived with.
South of Chǔ,
in the country of Yánrén,
when their relatives die,
they carve off the flesh and discard it,
then bury the bones,
and thus become filial sons.
West of Qín is the country of Yìqú,
where when their relatives die,
they gather firewood and burn them,
letting the smoke rise upward,
calling it "ascending mist and clouds,"
and then become filial.
Those above consider this governance,
those below consider it custom,
and it is not necessarily wrong.
See Mòzǐ.
Nízá Country
In the third year of King Chéng's reign,
the country of Nízá came to court.
Its people claimed to have set out from their own country,
often traveling amidst the clouds,
hearing the rumble of thunder below.
Sometimes entering hidden caves,
they again heard the sound of waves above.
Sometimes crossing vast waters,
they observed the sun and moon,
to know the directions.
Counting cold and heat,
they knew the years and months.
Examined by the Chinese calendar,
their sequence matched.
The king received them with the rites for foreign guests.
Ránqiū
In the sixth year of King Chéng's reign,
the country of Ránqiū
presented Bǐchì birds,
one male and one female,
enclosed in jade cages.
The envoys from that country,
all had clenched fists and flared nostrils,
wearing cloth of clouds and mist,
like today's xiá cloth.
They passed through over a hundred countries,
before reaching the capital.
Crossing Tiěwù,
sailing the boiling sea,
there were snake isles and bee peaks.
Tiěwù was steep and harsh,
with wheels rimmed with diamond,
yet by the time they reached the capital,
they were nearly worn to nothing.
The boiling sea surged and swelled,
like cut fish, fish, turtles, skin, and bones,
hard as stone,
usable for armor.
When sailing the boiling sea,
they lined the boat bottoms with thin copper,
so dragons, snakes, and jiǎo could not approach.
Passing through snake isles,
they used leopard skins as shelters,
pushing carts inside.
Passing bee peaks,
they burned the tips of Húsū wood,
as the smoke of this wood could kill all insects.
The journey took over fifty years,
before they reached Luòyì.
King Chéng fēnged Mount Tài,
and shàned at Shèshǒu.
When they departed their country,
the people were still children,
but by the time they reached the capital,
their hair had turned white.
Upon returning to Ránqiū,
their appearances restored to youth.
The Bǐyì birds were strong,
resembling swans,
carrying,
cinnabar from the southern sea,
mud,
nested in the xuán trees of Kūnlún,
and reaching within them,
they encounter sages and come to gather,
manifesting the divine power of Duke Zhōu's assistance to the sage.
Lúfú Country,
came to court during King Zhāo of Yān's time.
Crossing the Jade River for ten thousand lǐ,
they reached that country.
The country had no evil,
birds or beasts,
waters did not raise waves,
wind did not break branches.
People all lived three hundred years,
weaving grass for clothing,
called huìfú.
They never aged until death,
all harmonious, filial, and yielding.
Those reaching over a hundred years of age,
were revered with the rites due to closest kin.
Buried in the wild,
with fragrant wood and spiritual grass,
covering the corpse.
Neighborhoods mourned and escorted,
the sounds of wailing and weeping,
shook forests and valleys.
Streams and plains ceased flowing for them,
spring trees changed color for them.
During mourning,
they took neither water nor food,
until the bones of the deceased turned to dust,
and only then did they eat.
In ancient times, when Great Yǔ followed mountains to channel rivers,
he marked,
that land as the country of no aging and pure filiality.
Fúzhé Country
In the first year of the Yuánfēng era,
Fúzhé ceased the annual tribute of lánjīn clay.
This golden soup abyss,
during the height of summer,
the water often boils and surges,
as if it were scalding hot water,
so that even flying birds cannot pass over it.
People traveling through the country
often see figures by the water's edge,
smelting this gold into vessels.
It is mixed like clay,
with a color like purple-polished gold,
but after a hundred smeltings,
its color turns white,
shining like silver,
and it is named "silver candle."
It was often used as clay
to seal various boxes and palace gates,
so that ghosts and demons dared not interfere.
During the Hàn dynasty,
when generals went on expeditions,
or envoys were sent to distant lands,
they often used this clay to seal their seals.
The missions of Wèi Qīng, Zhāng Qiān, Sū Wǔ, and Fù Jièzǐ
all received imperial seals sealed with this golden clay.
After the emperor's death, this practice ceased.
Pínsī
In the year when the Wèi emperor was the Prince of Chénliú,
envoys from the country of Pínsī came to court,
wearing garments made of five-colored jade,
like armor of today.
They did not consume the flavors of the Central Plains,
but had their own golden pot,
containing divine nectar,
congealed like fat,
of which a single taste could extend life by a thousand years.
Their country had forests of great wind trees,
sixty to seventy lǐ tall,
and skilled calculators measured them in lǐ,
with lightning and thunder often emerging from halfway up the trees.
Their branches intertwined, casting shadows above and blocking out
the light of the sun and moon.
Below, the ground was level, clean, and swept,
so that rain and dew could not penetrate.
To the east of the trees was a great stone chamber,
capable of seating ten thousand people.
On its walls were carved images of the Three Sovereigns:
the Heavenly Sovereign with twelve heads,
the Earthly Sovereign with eleven heads,
and the Human Sovereign with nine heads,
all with dragon bodies.
There were also places for膏燭.
Stones were woven together to form a bed,
on which were knee impressions two or three cùn deep,
and before the bed were bamboo slips two cùn long,
inscribed with characters like large seal script,
all recording events since the creation of the world,
which no one could decipher.
It is said that these writings existed when Fúxī drew the trigrams,
or that this was the place where Cāngjié created writing.
Nearby was a cinnabar stone well,
not dug by human effort,
reaching down to漏泉,
with water that constantly boiled and surged.
When the various immortals wished to drink,
they drew water with long ropes.
The people of Pínsī were all strong and curly-haired,
They did not eat the five grains,
cast no shadow under the moon,
and consumed cassia nectar.
Their hair,
when pulled, would lengthen,
but when released, would shrink back like a snail.
This hair was spun into ropes,
used to reach the cinnabar well,
and in the depths of winter, they could obtain a shēng or hé of water.
In the water were white frogs,
with two wings,
often coming and going above the well,
and travelers would eat them.
When Prince Jìn of Zhōu approached the well and peered in,
a blue sparrow spat out a ladle,
offering it to Zǐ Jìn,
who took it and drank,
whereupon clouds arose and snow flew.
Zǐ Jìn used his sleeve to brush away the snow,
and the clouds cleared and the snow stopped.
The white frogs transformed into white geese,
entering the clouds and swaying until they vanished.
This is what the people of Pínsī recorded,
for their years are immeasurable.
They were asked to depict their mountains, rivers, terrain, and wondrous sights,
to show to Zhāng Huá.
Huá said:
"This is a divine and extraordinary country,
difficult to verify or believe."
They were provided with carriages, horses, and precious garments,
and escorted out of the pass.
Wúmíng Country
In the eighth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
the Wúmíng Country offered tribute of an ever-burning tripod and luánfeng honey.
It is said
that their country is tens of thousands of lǐ from the Eastern Sea,
passing through countries such as Jílóu and Wòjū.
Their land is suitable for the five grains,
abundant in precious jade,
and they practice ritual, music, benevolence, and righteousness,
with no robbery or plunder,
and people live to two hundred years of age.
Their customs revere the arts of immortals,
and within a year,
there are often those who ride clouds or驾鹤.
They often observed yellow vapors like a carriage canopy,
knew that the Central Plains was ruled by the virtue of earth,
and thus wished to offer tribute.
The ever-burning tripod,
with a capacity of three dǒu,
is smooth and clean like jade,
purple in color,
and whenever food is prepared,
without lighting a fire, it cooks itself in moments,
with a fragrance and purity surpassing the ordinary.
Consuming it over time
reverses aging to youth,
and prevents all ailments.
Luánfeng honey,
it is said that the bees' humming
resembles that of luán and phoenixes,
and their bodies are adorned with five colors.
The larger ones can weigh over ten jīn,
and they build hives among deep cliffs and steep ridges,
with the largest covering two or three mǔ.
The people of the country collect their honey,
never exceeding two or three gé,
for if they overstep,
strange winds and thunder arise.
If stung, causing sores,
applying calamus root from the stones
heals them.
The honey is green in color,
stored in white jade bowls,
transparent inside and out,
like green glass.
Long-term consumption leads to longevity,
a complexion like a child's,
and white hair turning black in due time.
Even severe illnesses, blindness, or lameness
are all cured.
Nǚmán Country
In the early Dàzhōng era,
the Nǚmán Country offered tribute of double-dragon rhinoceros horn,
with two dragons,
complete with scales, manes, claws, and horns.
And míngxiá brocade,
said to be dyed with炼水香麻,
glowing and shimmering,
fragrant and clinging to people,
interwoven with five colors,
more beautiful than Central Plains brocade.
The people of that country wear high chignons and golden crowns,
with tassels,
and netted garments covering their bodies,
hence called "Púsàmán."
At that time, performers
composed the tune "Púsàmán,"
and literati often set lyrics to it.
The Queen's Country further offered dragon-oil silk and fish-oil brocade,
with extraordinarily diverse patterns,
not wetting in water,
said to contain dragon oil and fish oil.
Performers further composed the tune "Queen's Country,"
melodious and流畅,
passed down among音乐部.
Dūbō
The country of Dūbō,
a branch of the Tiělè people,
is divided into three tribes,
governing themselves.
Their custom is to build huts from grass,
with no cattle or sheep,
and they know not farming.
They have abundant lilies,
which they take as food.
They wear pelts of sable and deer,
and the poor also weave bird feathers into clothing.
The country has no punishments;
thieves are required to repay double the stolen goods.
Gǔlì
The Gǔlì state is located north of the Huíhé,
north of the Vast Sea.
It has four thousand capable soldiers.
The land produces famous horses.
The days are long and the nights short;
when the sky is just dusky,
if one boils a sheep shoulder blade until it is just cooked,
the east is already dawning.
This is likely because it is near the place where the sun sets.
Tūjué
The Tūjué worship the Zoroastrian deity.
They have no temples;
they carve felt into its image,
place it in a fur bag,
and wherever they go,
they smear it with fat or butter,
or tie it to a pole,
offering sacrifices to it throughout the four seasons.
The Jiānkūn tribe
is not descended from wolves.
The cave where their ancestors were born
is north of the Qūmàn Mountain.
They themselves say that in ancient times, a deity
mated with a cow in this cave.
These people have yellow hair and green eyes,
with red beards and mustaches.
Those whose beards and mustaches are all black
are descendants of the Hàn general Lǐ Líng and his soldiers.
The Xītú
customarily dye their teeth black.
Also, the ancestor of the Tūjué was named Shèmó.
There is a Shèlì Sea,
and a deity
west of Āshǐdémì.
Shèmó possessed divine powers.
Every evening, the sea deity’s daughter
would welcome Shèmó into the sea on a white deer,
and send him out at dawn,
continuing for several decades.
Later, the tribe was about to hold a great hunt.
In the middle of the night,
the sea deity said to Shèmó:
“During the hunt tomorrow,
from the cave where your ancestors were born,
a white deer with golden antlers will emerge.
If you shoot this deer,
our relationship will be complete and we can continue our来往;
if you fail to shoot it,
our缘分 will be severed.”
At dawn, they entered the hunting grounds,
and indeed, from the ancestral cave,
a white deer with golden antlers emerged.
Shèmó ordered his attendants to secure the encirclement,
but just as it was about to leap out of the ring,
they killed it.
Enraged,
Shèmó personally beheaded the Ā’ér chieftain,
and then swore an oath:
“From now on,
we must use
human sacrifices to worship heaven.
We shall always take them from the Ā’ér.”
Thus, they took the descendants of the tribe and beheaded them for sacrifice.
To this day, the Tūjué use human sacrifices for their banners,
a practice employed by the tribe.
After Shèmó beheaded the Ā’ér,
he returned at dusk.
The sea deity’s daughter seized Shèmó and said:
“You have killed with your own hands;
the血腥 and污秽
have severed our缘分!”
Tǔbō
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the imperial army heavily defeated the Tǔbō at Qīnghǎi.
On the battlefield,
they killed the Tǔbō Grand Military Commander Qìzàngzhē,
Zhē and others.
Some say
he was Shàngjiézàn’s son.
The Tǔbō then collected the尸体 and returned to camp.
Over a hundred people
followed the corpse, weeping as they walked,
with exceptionally solemn仪式.
They had one person stand beside the corpse to speak on its behalf,
and another person ask,
“Does the wound hurt?”
The代言者 replied:
“It hurts.”
They then applied ointment to it.
They asked again:
“Are you hungry?”
The代言者 said:
“Yes.”
They then prepared food for it.
They asked again:
“Are you cold?”
The代言者 said:
“Yes.”
They then ordered fur clothes to be put on it.
They asked again:
“Shall we return?”
The代言者 said:
“Yes.”
They then prepared a carriage and horses,
loaded the corpse, and departed.
This was relayed by an interpreter.
Such extraordinary rites
surely indicate a noble minister of their state.
Northwest Wasteland
In the Northwest Wasteland,
there is a wine called Jade-Fed Wine,
with a wine spring flowing into it.
It is ten feet wide,
and thirty feet deep.
The wine is as delicious as meat,
and as clear and澄澈 as a mirror.
There are jade goblets and jade baskets;
if one takes a goblet,
another is再生,
enduring as long as heaven,
never drying up.
Beside the stones, there is dried meat,
tasting like roe deer jerky.
Drinking this wine,
people do not experience生 or死.
The people between these wells
are born with heaven,
and though there are men and women, they do not become husband and wife,
hence it is said they do not experience生 or死.
Hèmín
In the region corresponding to the戌亥方位 northwest of the sea,
there is the Hèmín state.
The people are three inches tall,
travel a thousand lǐ in a day,
and walk swiftly as if flying,
often being swallowed by sea cranes.
Among them, there are also gentlemen and petty men.
If they are gentlemen,
they are naturally clever and skillful,
often causing trouble for the cranes.
They常 carve wood
into their own likeness,
sometimes hundreds of them,
and gather them by the荒野 waterside,
making the cranes think they are小人,
so that when swallowed, they cause harm.
After hundreds or thousands of such instances,
later, when the cranes see the real ones passing by,
they cannot eat them either.
The people mostly dwell by mountain streams and riverbanks,
digging洞穴 to form states,
with each state spanning thirty or fifty paces,
amounting to not just thousands or tens of thousands.
In spring and summer, they eat wild grass seeds,
and in autumn and winter, they eat grass roots.
In hot weather, they go naked,
and when cold, they weave fine grass into clothing.
They also understand breath control.
Another account says:
Beyond the Four Seas,
there is a state of swans.
Both men and women are seven inches tall,
naturally courteous and well-mannered,
fond of discussing and practicing跪拜.
These people all live to three hundred years old,
travel a thousand lǐ,
and no creature dares to harm them.
Though they fear sea cranes,
