as Chén Zhāng told Duke Huán of Qí,
if a crane encounters and swallows them,
they also live three hundred years.
These people do not die inside the crane,
and the crane can also fly a thousand lǐ in one go.
What Chén Zhāng told Duke Huán of Qí were小人.
Lú Wénjìn of the Qìdān,
was a man of Yōuzhōu.
Having come south,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Fànyáng.
He once said that while trapped among the Qìdān,
he often went hunting on the remote frontier
to supply the army with food.
Once, while hunting in broad daylight,
the sky suddenly turned dark,
and the stars shone brightly.
Everyone was terrified
and captured a local tribesman to question him.
He said it was the so-called "eclipse of the sun,"
which was common in that place,
and it would soon pass.
After a short while, it became bright again,
and the sun was still at noon.
He also said
that he once saw a human chest bone
by the Wúdìng River,
as large as a pillar,
about seven feet long.
Wòjū
Wǔqiū Jiǎn sent Wáng Qīng to pursue the king of Gāolí's officials,
reaching the eastern border of Wòjū.
He asked the elders,
"Are there people east of the sea?"
The elders said,
"Our people once went out in boats to fish,
encountered a storm,
and were blown for several dozen days
until they reached an island to the east.
There were people on it,
but their language was unintelligible.
Their custom was to take a young girl every seventh month
and sink her into the sea."
They also said there was another country,
also in the sea,
consisting entirely of women with no men.
They also spoke of finding a cloth garment
floating up from the sea,
its body like the clothing of a middle-sized person,
but its two sleeves were two zhang long."
They also found a broken boat
that emerged with the waves
near the seashore.
There was a person on it
with another face on the back of their neck.
They captured them,
but could not communicate,
and they refused to eat and died.
These places were all in the great sea east of Wòjū.
Jiāoyáo
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ had a human figure made of wax, over three inches tall,
with head, thighs, and ribs fully formed,
and eyebrows and eyes clearly defined.
It was said to be a person from the country of Jiāoyáo.
Xīnluó
The Kingdom of Sīnlúo,
borders Japan to the southeast,
and adjoins the Land of the Tall People to the east.
The Tall People are three zhàng in height,
with saw-like teeth and hook-like claws.
They do not eat cooked food,
but chase and eat wild beasts,
and sometimes also eat humans.
Their bodies are naked,
covered with black hair.
Their territory is bounded by a continuous mountain range stretching thousands of lǐ,
within which lies a mountain gorge,
fortified with an iron gate,
called the Iron Pass.
They constantly station several thousand archers and crossbowmen to guard it,
and because of this, no one passes through.
Also, in the Kingdom of Sīnlúo, there was a foremost nobleman named Jīn Gē.
His distant ancestor was named Páng Chí.
He had a younger brother,
who possessed considerable family wealth.
His elder brother, Páng Chí,
due to the division of the household,
begged for clothing and food.
A fellow countryman gave him a single mǔ of vacant land.
He then asked his younger brother for silkworm eggs and grain seeds.
The younger brother steamed them before giving them to him,
which Páng Chí did not know.
When it was time for the silkworms,
only one hatched.
It grew over an inch per day,
and after ten days, it was as large as an ox,
and the leaves of several trees were insufficient to feed it.
His younger brother learned of this,
lay in wait,
found an opportunity,
and killed the silkworm.
After a day,
all the silkworms from within a hundred lǐ in all directions
flew and gathered at his house.
The countrymen called it the Giant Silkworm,
thinking it was the king of silkworms.
The neighbors from all around came together to reel its silk,
but could not keep up with the supply.
Of the grain, only a single stalk grew.
Its ear was over a chǐ long.
Páng Chí constantly guarded it.
Suddenly, it was broken off by a bird,
which carried it away.
Páng Chí chased after it,
going up the mountain for five or six lǐ.
The bird entered a stone crevice.
The sun set and the path grew dark,
so Páng Chí stopped beside the rock.
At midnight, when the moon was bright,
he saw a group of little children,
dressed in red, playing together.
One little child said:
"What do you want?"
One said:
"I want wine."
The little child took out a small golden awl,
struck the rock,
and wine along with a wine vessel all appeared.
One said:
"I want food,"
and he struck it again.
Cakes, pastries, soup, and roasted meat
were spread upon the rock.
After a long while,
they finished eating and drinking and left,
inserting the golden awl into the stone crevice.
Páng Chí was overjoyed,
took the awl, and returned.
Whatever he desired, he would strike and it would be provided.
Because of this, his wealth rivaled that of the state.
He often gave pearls and jades to support his younger brother.
The younger brother said:
"Perhaps I, like my elder brother, can obtain a golden awl."
Páng Chí knew his foolishness,
and seeing that persuasion was useless,
he did as his brother said.
His brother raised the silkworms,
but obtained only ordinary ones as usual.
He planted the grain seeds,
and again only a single stalk grew.
When it was nearly ripe,
it too was carried off by a bird.
His younger brother was greatly pleased,
followed it into the mountain,
and reached the place where the bird entered.
He encountered a group of ghosts.
They angrily said,
"This is the one who stole our awl."
Then they seized him.
They said to him:
"Do you want to build three planks of sugar for me?
Or do you want your nose to grow one zhàng long?"
His younger brother chose to build three planks of sugar.
After three days,
hungry and exhausted, he could not complete it,
and begged the ghosts for mercy.
The ghosts then pulled his nose,
and his nose became like an elephant's as he returned.
The countrymen, astonished, gathered to look at him.
Ashamed and enraged, he died.
Later, his descendants played with the awl to ask for wolf dung,
and because of a thunderclap,
the awl disappeared to an unknown place.
Also, a merchant from Dēngzhōu named Mǎ Xíngyú was sailing across the sea,
intending to take the route to Kūnlún and proceed to Tónglú,
when he encountered a west wind,
which blew him to the Kingdom of Sīnlúo.
The ruler of Sīnlúo, hearing that Xíngyú had come from China,
received him with the etiquette due a guest.
Then he said:
"Although ours is a land of barbarians,
every year there are those who study the Confucian classics,
and are presented at the imperial examinations.
Those who pass with honors and return,
I invariably reward them with generous emoluments.
Thus I know that the Way of Confucius
extends even to this remote land."
Then, discussing classics and texts with Xíngyú,
Xíngyú stepped aside from his seat and said:
"I am but a vulgar and ignorant merchant.
Although I was born and raised in the Central Plains,
I have only heard of what the land is suited for,
and have not studied the meaning of the Book of Songs and Book of Documents.
To be well-versed in the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
and to understand ritual and righteousness—
surely that is the domain of the scholar-officials!
It is not the business of a lowly person."
He then declined.
The ruler of Sīnlúo exclaimed in surprise:
"I thought that all people of China
were fully acquainted with the canonical teachings.
I did not expect there still existed such ignorant customs!"
Xíngyú returned to his hometown,
ashamed that, due to greed and stinginess for clothing and food,
he was ignorant and did not know to study the Way,
and was ridiculed by barbarians—
let alone by the wise and outstanding.
Also, in the early Tiānbǎo era,
the court sent the Grand Master of Admonition, Wèi Yào, as an envoy to Sīnlúo,
to confer recognition upon the young ruler.
Yào was old in years,
and deeply dreaded the journey.
There was a traveler who had been to Sīnlúo,
so he inquired about the route.
The traveler said:
During the Yǒnghuī era,
Sīnlúo and Japan were both on friendly terms,
and envoys were dispatched to both.
The envoy, having reached Sīnlúo,
was about to proceed to Japan,
when he encountered a storm at sea.
Great waves arose,
and did not cease for several tens of days.
Drifting with the waves,
they did not know where they would reach.
Suddenly, the wind ceased and the waves calmed,
and they came to the seashore.
The sun was just about to set.
At that time, several ships of their company,
moored their boats and went ashore,
numbering over a hundred people in all.
The shore was twenty or thirty zhàng high.
Seeing dwellings,
they rushed towards them.
A tall person came out,
two zhàng in height,
fully clothed,
but they could not understand his speech.
Seeing that men from Táng had arrived,
he was greatly pleased.
Then he blocked and herded them, making them enter the house,
filled the doorway with stones,
and they all went out.
Soon, over a hundred of their kind
followed and arrived.
Then they selected from among the Táng men those with plump and full skin and bodies,
obtaining over fifty people,
cooked them all,
and ate them together.
They also brought out strong wine,
and together held a feast and revelry.
Late at night, they were all drunk.
The men thus managed to reach the various courtyards.
In the rear courtyard were thirty women,
all of whom had been blown by the wind at various times,
and had been captured.
They said that all the men had been eaten,
only the women were kept,
to make clothing.
"Now that they are drunk,
why don't you leave?
We will show you the way."
The crowd was pleased.
The women took out several hundred bolts of white silk and carried them,
Then he took a knife,
and cut off the heads of all the drunken men.
They then proceeded to the seashore,
where the shore was high,
and in the darkness they could not descend.
They all tied cloth around their bodies,
and lowered themselves down by rope,
taking turns to descend one after another.
Reaching the water's edge,
they all managed to board the ship.
By the time dawn broke and the ship set sail,
they heard cries from the mountaintop.
Looking back at the place they had come from,
there were already over a thousand of them.
They descended the mountain in a continuous stream,
and in a moment reached the shore.
Since they could not catch up with the ship,
they roared and leaped in fury.
The envoy and the woman both managed to return.
Also, recently there was a seafarer who went to Xīnlúo,
and stopped at an island,
where the ground was covered entirely with black lacquered spoons and chopsticks.
The place had many large trees,
and the traveler looked up to see the spoons and chopsticks,
which turned out to be the flowers and tendrils of the trees.
So he gathered over a hundred pairs and brought them back.
When he tried to use them,
they were too fat and could not be used.
By chance, he took them to stir tea,
and as he stirred, they dissolved away.
Also, the Six Armies Commissioner Xīmén Sīgōng,
was once sent on a mission to Xīnlúo.
Due to unfavorable winds and waters,
he drifted on the vast sea for months,
unaware of any boundaries.
Suddenly, he reached a shore to the south,
where there were fields and scenery,
so he disembarked and looked around in all directions.
Soon, a giant appeared,
whose body was five or six zhàng tall,
wearing strange clothing,
with a voice like thunder.
He looked down at Xīmén,
as if in surprise and admiration.
At that moment, he picked him up with five fingers and carried him over a hundred lǐ,
into a cave among the rocks.
There, he saw a group of elders and youngsters gathered together,
calling each other and assembling,
all competing to come and look at him as a curiosity.
Their language was incomprehensible,
but they all had joyful expressions,
as if they had obtained something extraordinary.
Then they dug a pit and placed him in it,
and came to watch over him.
After staying for two nights,
he climbed out of the pit,
and fled straight along the old path.
Just as he jumped into the ship,
the giant had already caught up with him.
The giant then used his huge hand to grab the side of the ship,
so Xīmén swung his sword,
and cut off three of his fingers.
The fingers were thicker than today's cloth-beating sticks.
The giant, having lost his fingers, retreated,
and they untied the moorings and set sail.
The water and provisions in the ship were exhausted,
and for a month they had no food.
They chewed and ate
the clothes on their bodies.
Later, they reached the northern shore,
and he presented the three fingers,
which were lacquered and stored in the imperial treasury.
After being appointed as the commander of the army,
he would rather give gold and jade to others,
but never in his life did he host guests with lavish feasts,
because he remembered the hardship of running out of food.
The Dōngnǚguó,
a branch of the Western Qiāng,
has the custom of having a woman as king.
It borders Màozhōu,
and has over eighty cities.
The place where they reside is called Kāngyánzhōu.
Within it flows the Ruòshuǐ River,
which runs southward,
and they use boats made of cowhide to cross it.
The population and soldiers number ten thousand,
scattered across valleys and mountains,
and are called Bīnjiù.
There are female officials,
called Gāobà,
who deliberate on state affairs.
The officials outside the court
are all men,
and they hold court once every five days.
The king is attended by several hundred women.
When the king dies,
the state collects many goods,
amounting to tens of thousands.
Then, from among the royal clan,
they seek out two virtuous women and establish them,
with the elder as the great king,
and the younger as the little king.
When the great king dies,
the little king succeeds to the position,
or when an aunt dies, a niece succeeds.
There are no tombs.
Their dwellings are all multi-storied houses,
with the king having nine stories,
and the common people having six stories.
The king wears a green woolen skirt,
flat,
a collarless shirt,
with sleeves that drag on the ground.
She ties her hair in a small bun with patterned brocade,
and adorns it with gold ear pendants.
She wears plain boots on her feet.
They value women and belittle men,
and their writing is the same as that of Tiānzhú.
They take the eleventh month as the beginning of the year.
Every tenth month,
they order shamans to bring wine and food,
go into the mountains,
scatter dregs and wheat into the air,
and loudly chant to summon birds.
Soon, a bird like a pheasant
flies into the shaman's bosom.
They then cut open its belly to examine it.
If there is grain inside,
the coming year's harvest will be abundant.
If there is frost or snow,
there will be a great disaster.
This custom is called bird divination,
When a person dies, they place the bones and flesh into a golden vase,
mix them with gold dust,
and bury them.
Lǐnjūn
Lǐ Shí,
styled Xuánxiū,
was a descendant of Línjūn.
Long ago, when the Wǔluò Zhōnglí Mountain collapsed,
there appeared a stone cave,
one part red as cinnabar,
the other black as lacquer.
From the red cave emerged a person
named Wùxiāng,
of the Bā surname,
clan;
from the black cave emerged others,
totaling four clans:
the Shěn clan,
the Fán clan,
the Bǎi clan,
and the Zhèng clan.
The five clans emerged and contended with one another,
so Wùxiāng thrust a spear into the cave.
Whoever could lodge it would become Línjūn.
None of the four clans could lodge it,
while Wùxiāng’s spear stuck fast.
Then they made boats from clay,
carved and painted them,
and set them afloat on water.
It was said:
“Whose boat floats shall become Línjūn.”
Only Wùxiāng’s boat floated,
so he was then proclaimed Línjūn.
Riding his clay boat,
leading his followers and soldiers,
he sailed down the Yí River,
reaching Yányáng.
The water goddess stopped Línjūn, saying:
“This place abounds in fish and salt,
the land is vast,
I shall live together with you,
you need not go further.”
Línjūn said:
“I am destined to be lord,
seeking land for my people,
I cannot stop here.”
The salt goddess stayed with Línjūn at night,
but at dawn she would leave, turning into flying insects,
and all the other spirits followed her,
their flight blotting out the sun.
Línjūn wished to kill her,
but could not distinguish her,
nor could he tell east from west in heaven and earth.
This went on for ten days,
so Línjūn gave the salt goddess a blue thread, saying:
“If you wear this, it suits you,
and I shall live with you;
if it does not suit,
I shall leave you.”
The salt goddess accepted it and wore it.
Línjūn went atop a rocky cliff,
and seeing one with a blue thread around the waist,
he knelt and shot her.
He hit the salt goddess,
and she died.
All the spirits who flew with her departed,
and the sky cleared.
Línjūn again boarded his clay boat,
sailed down,
and reached Yíchéng.
The stone banks were winding,
the spring water also curved,
looking like a cave entrance.
Línjūn sighed, saying:
“I have just emerged from a cave,
and now enter this again—
what shall I do?”
The bank then collapsed,
opening a space over three zhang wide,
with terraced steps ascending.
Línjūn climbed them,
and on the bank was a flat stone,
five chǐ long,
one zhàng square.
Línjūn rested upon it,
casting divining stalks and making calculations,
and all landed on the stone.
Thus he built a city beside it,
and settled there to dwell.
Thereafter, his descendants multiplied.
When Qín unified the realm,
it made this area the Qiánzhōng Commandery,
levying light taxes,
requiring four hundred thousand coins annually.
The Bā people called the tax cóng,
hence they were called the Cóng people.
The Dàshí Kingdom
Two thousand lǐ southwest of Dàshí is a kingdom,
in the mountain valleys,
where flowers grow on tree branches like human heads,
but they do not speak;
if people ask them questions,
they only laugh,
and after frequent laughter, they fall.
The Sī’āxiū Kingdom
In the Jīnliáo Mountain temple of the Sī’āxiū Kingdom,
there is a stone alligator.
When the monks’ food and drink are nearly exhausted,
they bow to the stone alligator,
and then food and drink are fully provided.
The Jùzhèntí Kingdom
The Jùzhèntí Kingdom reveres ghosts and spirits.
Twenty lǐ north of the city, across the Zhēnzhū River,
there is a spirit.
During the spring and autumn seasons,
whatever utensils, gold, or silver vessels the king requires
naturally appear in the spirit’s kitchen,
and vanish after the sacrifice ends.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān sent people to verify this,
and it was found true.
Zāngkē
The Lǎo people in Zāngkē
have women who give birth in the seventh month;
when they die, they are buried in upright coffins.
The Mù’ěr Yí people,
west of Jiùláo,
use deer antlers as vessels.
When they die, they are flexed and burned,
and their bones are buried.
The Mù’ěr Yí people
are black as lacquer.
When it is slightly cold, they warm themselves with heated sand,
exposing only their faces.
Qiūcí
In ancient times, there was a king of the state of Qiūcí named Āzhǔér,
who possessed divine and extraordinary powers,
capable of subduing venomous snakes and dragons.
At that time, some people bought gold, silver, and precious goods in the market,
but by midnight,
the money would all turn into charcoal.
Hundreds of households within the kingdom
lost their gold and treasures.
The king had a son who had previously left home to become a monk
and attained the fruit of an arhat.
The king asked him about it,
and the arhat said:
"This is the work of a dragon,
who dwells in the northern mountains.
Its head resembles that of a tiger,
and it is now sleeping in a certain place."
The king then changed his clothes and took up his sword,
silently making his way to the dragon's lair.
Seeing the dragon lying asleep,
he was about to strike it down.
But he thought to himself:
"If I slay a sleeping dragon,
who will know of my divine power?"
So he shouted at the dragon,
startling it awake.
The dragon transformed into a lion,
and the king immediately mounted it.
Enraged,
the dragon roared like thunder,
soared into the sky,
and flew twenty li north of the city.
The king said to the dragon:
"If you do not submit,
I will cut off your head."
Fearing the king's divine power,
the dragon spoke in human language:
"Do not kill me,
I will serve as your mount.
Wherever you wish to go,
I will take you there as you desire."
The king agreed,
and thereafter rode the dragon wherever he went.
East of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
people were fond of lewd and depraved practices,
so Qiūcí and Yútián established women's markets
to collect money.
In Qiūcí,
on the first day of the year, they would pit sheep, horses, and camels against each other,
holding games for seven days,
observing the outcomes
to predict whether the flocks and herds would decrease or multiply in the coming year.
During the Póluózhē festival,
people wore dog-headed and monkey-faced masks,
and men and women sang and danced day and night.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
they would parade statues of the Buddha and play games with ropes.
In Yānqí,
on the first day of the year and the eighth day of the second month, they celebrated the Pómózhē festival.
For three days, they held wild sacrifices,
and on the fifteenth day of the fourth month, they would roam the forests.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, they commemorated the descent of Maitreya.
On the seventh day of the seventh month, they sacrificed to their ancestors.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, they held the Másǎ festival.
On the tenth day of the tenth month,
the king performed a ritual of aversion,
leaving the palace with his household,
while a chieftain acted in his place,
for one day and one night,
handling the king's affairs.
From the fourteenth day of the tenth month onward,
they made merry every day
until the end of the year.
In Báhánnà,
during the twelfth month and on the first day of the year,
the king and the chieftains
would divide into two teams,
each selecting one man
to don armor.
The crowd would wield tiles, stones, clubs, and sticks,
attacking each other from east and west,
and the fight would only stop when the armored man died first,
using this to predict whether the year would be abundant or lean.
In the state of Qiántuó,
there was once a king, a divine man of great cunning,
named Jiādāng.
He attacked and conquered various states,
subduing all in his path.
When he reached the Five Indias,
he obtained two fine silk garments,
keeping one for himself
and giving the other to his consort.
The consort wore the garment to visit the king.
On the garment, over her breast,
was the handprint mark of turmeric,
which startled and alarmed the king.
He said to his consort:
"Why are you suddenly wearing this garment with a handprint?"
The consort replied that it was the garment the king had given her.
The king grew angry
and questioned the treasurer,
who said:
"The garment originally had this mark;
it is not my fault."
The king summoned the merchant and questioned him.
The merchant said that King Suōtuópóhèn of India
had a long-standing vow.
Every year, the fine silk he collected
was stacked in layers,
and he would dye his hands with turmeric,
pressing them onto the silk,
so that the handprint would penetrate through thousands of layers.
When a man wore it,
the handprint would appear on his back;
when a woman wore it,
the handprint would appear on her breast.
The king ordered his attendants to put on the garments,
and it was just as the merchant had said.
The king then struck his sword and declared:
"If I do not use this sword to cut off the hands and feet of King Suōtuópóhèn,
I will have no peace in eating or sleeping."
He then sent an envoy to Southern India
to demand the hands and feet of King Suōtuópóhèn.
When the envoy arrived in that country,
King Suōtuópóhèn and his ministers deceitfully replied:
"Although our country has a king named Suōtuópóhèn,
there is actually no king;
we only have a golden statue as king,
placed in the hall.
All governance and instruction
are carried out by the ministers."
The king then mobilized his elephant and cavalry forces
to campaign south against that country.
The country hid its king in an underground chamber
and cast a golden statue
to welcome King Jiā.
King Jiā knew it was a trick,
but relying on his divine power,
he cut off the hands and feet of the golden statue.
In the underground chamber,
the hands and feet of King Suōtuópóhèn all fell off by themselves.
In the state of Qiántuó,
the granary of King Shīpí
was burned by fire.
The scorched grains of rice from within
still exist to this day.
If one consumes a single grain,
they will never suffer from malaria again.
The Miáo people
In the western wilderness, there are people
whose faces, hands, and feet are all human in form,
but who have wings under their armpits,
though they cannot fly.
They are called the Miáo people.
The Book of Documents says:
"The Sānmiáo were banished to Sānwēi,"
to the four borders,
for they were gluttonous,
lewd, and without principle,
and Shùn banished them there.
The Jīgōng people
In the state of Jīgōng,
the people are skilled in crafting ingenious devices
to kill all kinds of birds.
They can make flying chariots
that travel far with the wind.
During the time of Tāng,
when the west wind blew for a long time,
the chariots of the Jīgōng people reached the borders of Yùzhōu.
Tāng destroyed their chariots
and did not show them to the people.
Ten years later,
when the east wind blew again,
he had them ride the chariots and sent them back.
Their country is ten thousand li west of Yùmén.
The tiny people of the northwest wilderness
In the northwest wilderness, there are tiny people one inch tall.
Their ruler wears red robes and a black crown,
riding in a carriage
drawn by horses,
maintaining an air of dignity wherever he resides.
If a person encounters their carriage,
they can catch and eat them,
and their taste is pungent.
They are never bitten by any creature throughout the year,
and they know the names of all things.
Moreover, they can kill the three worms in the stomach;
once the three worms are dead,
one can then consume the elixir of immortality.
Yútián
In the Later Wei Dynasty,
Sòng Yún was sent as an envoy to the Western Regions,
and traveled to the kingdom of Yútián.
The king wore a golden crown,
adorned with a chicken crest,
with two-foot-long raw silk hanging from his head,
five inches wide,
as decoration.
His regalia included drums, horns, and golden bells,
a set of bow and arrows,
two halberds,
and five lances.
Those bearing swords on his left and right
numbered no more than a hundred.
The custom there was for women to wear trousers and robes tied with belts,
riding horses at full gallop,
no different from men.
The dead were cremated,
their bones collected and buried,
with a stupa erected above.
Those in mourning cut their hair,
leaving it four inches long,
and then returned to normal life.
Only when the king died was he not cremated;
instead, he was placed in a coffin,
and buried far away in the wilderness.
Wūcháng
In the kingdom of Wūcháng,
rice ripened four times a year,
the seedlings so tall they could cover a camel,
and the grains as large as a child's finger.
Also, among the people of Wūcháng,
those guilty of capital crimes
were not executed.
Instead, they were exiled to an empty mountain,
left to fend for themselves.
In cases of suspicion or doubt,
they were given a drug to drink,
and the truth was determined by whether the outcome was clear or murky;
depending on the severity of the matter,
a judgment was made on the spot.
Hànpántuó Kingdom
The Hànpántuó Kingdom was situated right on a mountaintop,
West of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
all rivers flowed westward.
People said
this was the center of heaven and earth,
and its inhabitants
diverted water for farming.
When they heard that in the Central Plains people waited for rain to plant crops,
they laughed and said:
"How can one rely on heaven?"
Sūdūshínì Kingdom
In the Sūdūshínì Kingdom, there was a Yěchā City,
where yěchā demons once lived,
and their cave still exists.
More than five hundred families lived near the cave,
and a house was built at its entrance,
equipped with locks and keys,
with sacrifices offered twice a year.
If anyone approached the cave entrance,
smoke would emerge,
and the first to be touched by it would die,
after which the corpse was thrown into the cave.
The depth of the cave is unknown.
Mǎliú
Mǎ Fúbō had over ten families of remaining soldiers
who did not return,
but settled in Shòuqià
County,
intermarrying among themselves,
forming a community of two hundred households.
Because they lived away from their homeland,
they were called Mǎliú,
and their diet was the same as that of the Huá people.
Mountains and rivers shifted, and the bronze pillar sank into the sea,
so these people served as markers.
Wǔníng Barbarians
In the gorges, customs
remained unchanged, retaining their barbarian ways.
The Wǔníng barbarians liked to wear heart-shaped straw hats,
called tíngsuí.
They used rice to mark the years and months of burials,
pointing a hairpin toward the sky,
calling it "piercing the Northern Dipper."
Legend has it that when Pánhù first died,
he was placed in a tree,
and a hairpin was used to pierce him,
after which he transformed
into an elephant.
In Línyì County, there were goose-winged defenders,
Xuándù Kingdom
West of Wūhào was the Xuándù Kingdom,
where mountains and streams were impassable,
so people crossed by ropes,
with old ropes stretching for two thousand lǐ.
The locals farmed among the rocks,
building stone houses,
and drank by cupping their hands,
which was called "ape drinking."
Flying-Head Liáo
East of Shànshàn
and southwest of Lóngchéng,
the land stretched for a thousand lǐ,
all covered in salt fields.
Travelers passing through
would lay felt for their cattle and horses to rest on.
In the ravines south of the Lǐng Mountains,
there were often those with flying heads,
hence the name "Flying-Head Liáozi."
One day before the head flew,
a mark would appear on the neck,
encircling it like a red thread,
and the wife and children would keep watch.
When night fell,
the person would appear as if ill,
and the head would suddenly detach and fly away.
It would then search the muddy banks
for crabs and earthworms to eat,
and at dawn, it would fly back,
as if waking from a dream,
with a full stomach.
The Indian monk Púsà Shèng also said
that in the kingdom of Shépó, there were flying-head people,
whose eyes had no pupils.
In settlements,
there was one person recorded in folk tales of the strange.
The southern Luò people
could make their heads fly,
and the deity they worshipped
was named Chóngluò,
hence they were called Luò people.
In the past, Zhū Huán had a maidservant
whose head flew at night.
The *Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí* records
that during the Hàn Emperor Wǔ's time,
in the kingdom of Yīnchí, there were people in the south who could dismember themselves,
first making their heads fly to the Southern Sea,
their left hands to the Eastern Sea,
and their right hands to the Western Sea.
By evening,
the head would return to the shoulders,
but the hands, caught in a strong wind,
would be blown overseas.
Also, in the south, there were Luòtóu people,
whose heads could fly,
using their ears as wings,
and at dawn,
they would reattach to their bodies.
During the Wú period, such people were often encountered.
Tíqiāng
In the kingdom of Tíqiāng,
its people had hair
below the knees,
like that of a horse's
hooves.
They often whipped their own shins
and could travel a hundred lǐ in a day.
Fúlóu
In the seventh year of King Chéng of Zhōu,
in the southern frontier there was the country of Fúlóu.
Its people were skilled in ingenious transformations,
able to alter their forms and change their attire.
In great feats, they could summon clouds and raise mists;
in small ones, they could shrink into the space of a hair's breadth.
They adorned their garments with gold, jade, feathers, and fur.
They could spew clouds and breathe fire,
and drumming their bellies produced sounds like thunder.
Sometimes they transformed into the shapes of giant elephants, lions, dragons, snakes, dogs, or horses;
sometimes they turned into tigers.
Sometimes they spat people out from their mouths into their palms,
performing the music of all beasts,
twisting and bending between their fingers.
When appearing in human form,
they were sometimes only a few tenths of an inch tall,
or again several inches tall.
Their divine and monstrous transformations were swift and sudden,
dazzling the age.
The Music Bureau all transmitted these arts,
passing them down through generations without end.
Thus, commonly they are called the Póhóu arts,
which is a corrupted pronunciation of Fúlóu.
Jiāozhǐ
The land of Jiāozhǐ
was quite fertile.
When people settled there,
they first learned to sow and cultivate.
Its soil is black earth,
and its qi is virile and potent.
Therefore, its fields are now called 'virile fields,'
and its people 'virile people.'
They have rulers,
also called 'Virile Kings';
they have ministers,
also called 'Virile Marquises.'
They divided their land into 'virile commanderies.'
Nányuè
The people of Nányuè were not ashamed of banditry and theft.
At that time, Commandant Tuó governed Pānyú,
and so raised troops to attack them.
A divine being happened to descend
to assist them.
For their household, he crafted a single crossbow;
with one shot,
it killed ten thousand Yuè troops;
with three shots,
thirty thousand.
Tuó, learning the reason,
withdrew his fortifications and halted his soldiers,
returning to camp below Wǔníng County.
He then sent his son Shǐ as a hostage,
requesting to establish friendly relations.
Chǐguō
In the south there was a man
who traveled all under heaven.
He was seventy feet tall,
and his waist circumference matched his height.
He wore vermilion robes with a white sash,
and a red snake coiled around his neck.
He neither drank nor ate,
but swallowed three thousand evil ghosts at dawn
and three hundred at dusk.
This man fed on ghosts,
using mist as his broth.
His name was Chǐguō,
also called Shíxié,
and also called Huángfù.
Dùnxùn
The country of Dùnxùn,
during the Liáng Wǔ dynasty,
presented local products as tribute.
Their country was on a sea island,
a land a thousand li square,
subject to Fúnán, three thousand li to the north.
Their custom was
bird burial after death.
When about to die,
relatives and guests would sing and dance, escorting them outside the city walls.
Birds like geese but red in color,
countless in number, would fly in.
The family would avoid them,
and the birds would peck
until the flesh was entirely consumed,
then depart.
They would then burn the bones and sink them into the sea.
Duòpódēng Country
The country of Duòpódēng was east of Línyì,
bordering Hēlíng to the south,
and Shùlí to the west.
They grew rice,
which ripened once every month.
They had writing,
inscribed on palm leaves.
For the dead, they would fill the mouth with a golden jar,
thread it through the four limbs,
then apply balsam resin, sandalwood, aloeswood, and borneol camphor,
pile up firewood, and cremate them.
The Āiláo barbarians:
their ancestor was a woman named Shāhú,
who lived on Láo Mountain.
While fishing in the water,
she felt as if touched by something,
became pregnant for ten months, and gave birth to ten sons.
The present southwestern barbarians are their descendants.
Hēlíng Country
Hēlíng was south of the Zhēnlà country,
on an island in the Southern Sea,
with Pólì to the east,
Duòpó to the west,
and the great sea to the north.
They erected wooden poles to form city walls,
built large houses with multi-storied pavilions,
and covered them with palm bark.
They used ivory for beds,
and made wine from willow catkins,
which could also intoxicate when drunk.
They ate by hand.
They were poisonous;
if an ordinary person shared their dwelling or lodging place,
it would cause sores to grow on their body.
If one had intercourse with them,
they would die.
If their swirling fluids
touched plants or trees, they would wither.
Customarily, they made wine from coconut trees,
sweet in taste,
which could also intoxicate when drunk.
Zhēnlà Country
The country of Zhēnlà was five hundred li south of Huān Prefecture.
Their custom was
to offer guests betel nut, borneol camphor, fragrant clamshell powder, and the like,
as hospitality and feasting gifts.
Their wine was considered lewd and filthy;
in private rooms, they drank it with their wives,
but avoided doing so in the presence of elders.
Also, when engaging in marital relations,
they did not wish others to see,
a custom shared with the Middle Kingdom.
The people of the country did not wear clothes;
if they saw someone wearing clothes,
they would all laugh at them.
Customarily, they had no salt or iron,
using bamboo crossbows to shoot insects and birds.
Liúchóu Country
Emperor Yáng ordered Zhū Kuān to subdue the Liúchóu country.
Upon returning,
he captured over a thousand men and women along with various local products,
which differed greatly from those of the Middle Kingdom.
They wove tree bark into cloth,
very fine and white,
with a width of three chi, two or three cun.
There was also fine patterned cloth,
about one chi wide.
He also obtained several dozen jin of golden bramble pomegranate wood,
its color like true gold,
dense and fine,
with patterns coiled and gathered like beautiful brocade,
very fragrant and exquisite.
It could be used for pillows and table surfaces,
surpassing even aloeswood and sandalwood.
That land had no iron.
When Zhū Kuān returned to Nánhǎi Commandery,
he placed iron shackles and locks
on many of the strong adult men from Liúchóu,
fearing they would escape or rebel along the way.
Upon reaching Jiāngdū,
before presenting them,
he had the shackles removed.
They all grasped the shackles in their hands,
kowtowing, reluctant to part with them,
valuing them more than the Middle Kingdom valued gold.
Their bodies were short and small,
resembling the Kūnlún people.
Mùkè
Guō Zhòngchǎn’s *Record of Xiāngzhōu* states:
Seventy lǐ west of Pínglè County,
there is Róng Mountain,
upon which dwell many Wood Guests.
Their form resembles that of small children;
their songs, weeping, and clothing
are no different from those of humans.
Yet they hide and appear unpredictably.
Their dwellings are extremely exquisite.
At times they go to market to trade and make utensils,
indistinguishable from people.
When exchanging goods with others, they also do not haggle over the price.
Present-day Zhāozhōu Pínglè County
Jiāopú Country
One thousand five hundred lǐ southwest of Yǒngchāng Commandery,
there is the Jiāopú Country.
Its people have tails.
When they wish to sit,
they first dig a hole in the ground
to rest their tails.
If by chance their tail is accidentally broken,
they die immediately.
Mùyǐn Prefecture,
a prefecture of Zhūyá.
The land has no springs;
the people do not dig wells,
but all rely on tree sap for their needs.
The Āsà tribe
hunts many insects and deer.
They cut the meat,
layer it,
and press it with stones to extract the juices.
They tax rice and grass seeds from Persia, Fúlín, and other countries, and ferment them within the meat juices.
After several days,
it transforms into wine,
which can intoxicate when drunk.
Xiàoyì Country,
its borders extend over three thousand lǐ.
It lies on a flat plain,
using wood to form a stockade,
over ten lǐ in circumference.
Within the stockade are more than two thousand households,
surrounded by over five hundred wooden stockades.
The climate is consistently warm;
in winter, plants do not wither.
It is suitable for sheep and horses,
but has no camels or cattle.
The customs are honest and straightforward;
they are fond of hosting guests and companions.
Their bodies are tall and large,
with high-bridged noses,
yellow hair and green eyes,
red beards and loose hair,
faces the color of blood.
Their only weapons are lances.
The land is suitable for the five grains;
it produces gold and iron;
they wear hemp cloth.
The entire populace practices sorcery;
they do not know the Buddhist Dharma,
and have over three hundred sorcerer shrines.
They have ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
They do not engage in trade;
they call themselves the Xiàoyì people.
Both men and women wear ornaments.
They prepare food once a day,
and eat it for a month,
often consuming leftover food.
Moreover, the entire country has no wells or rivers;
all their planting
depends on rain to grow.
They spread silk fabric on the ground
to collect rainwater for use.
Digging wells yields bitter water,
and seawater is salty.
The local custom is to wait for the sea tide to recede,
then gather fish from the flat ground to eat.
Pómílàn Country
The Pómílàn Country is 25,550 lǐ from the capital.
West of this country there is a mountain,
steep and perilous,
with many apes atop it.
The apes are extremely large,
and often ravage the fields and crops.
Each year there are two to three hundred thousand of them.
After the start of spring in the country,
they muster armored soldiers
to fight the apes.
Although tens of thousands are killed each year,
they cannot eradicate their nests.
Bōbálì Country
The Bōbálì Country lies in the southwestern sea.
They know almost nothing of the five grains,
eating only meat.
They often pierce the veins of cattle to draw blood,
mixing it with milk to drink raw.
They have no clothing,
only covering their lower bodies with sheepskins.
Their women are fair and comely;
the people themselves capture and sell them to foreign merchants,
fetching several times the price.
The land produces only ivory and āmòxiāng.
When Persian merchants wish to enter this country,
they gather in groups of several thousand,
wrap cloth around themselves,
and young and old together prick their blood to swear an oath,
only then trading for their goods.
Since ancient times, it has not been subject to foreign countries.
In war they use ivory shields,
wild ox horn lances,
and equipment such as armor, bows, and arrows.
They have two hundred thousand infantry.
The Dàshí frequently attack and raid them.
Kūnwú
Kūnwú has land salt,
extending over ten lǐ,
with no water,
naturally occurring,
vermilion salt.
When the moon is full, it is like accumulated snow,
sweet in flavor;
when the moon wanes, it is like thin frost,
bitter in flavor;
when the moon ends,
the salt also ends.
Moreover, in that country they pile up trenches
to form mounds,
resembling pagodas,
with three layers.
Dry corpses reside above,
wet corpses reside below.
Burying nearby is considered the utmost filial piety.
They gather in large felt tents,
hanging colored silks and garments inside,
weeping and transforming them.
Tattooed-Face Lǎozi
The Yuè people are accustomed to water;
they must tattoo their bodies to avoid the calamity of flood dragons.
Nowadays, in the southern regions there are tattooed-face Lǎozi,
likely a surviving custom of carving the forehead.
Wǔxī Mán,
when parents die,
they place the corpse outside the village,
burying it after three years.
They beat drums and sing along the road,
with relatives feasting, dancing, and performing,
for over a month.
They use all their property to make a coffin,
then beside a high mountain by a river,
half help to chisel a niche to bury it.
They lower the coffin with ropes from the mountain,
considering higher placement as the utmost filial piety.
Thereafter, they never again offer sacrifices.
When first bereaved,
they abstain from salt for three years.
Rain-Falling Children
During the Wèi period,
at the home of Prince Chōng of Héjiān,
eight or nine small children fell in the rain,
dropping into the courtyard,
about five or six cùn tall.
They said of themselves,
“Our home is southeast of the sea;
due to wind and rain,
we were blown here.”
Speaking with them,
they were quite knowledgeable,
all as recorded in historical accounts.
Dog Country
The governor of Língzhōu, Zhōu Yù, did not consume meat or blood,
and once told Liú Xún:
In recent years, while returning from the Qīnghù Sea to Mǐn,
I encountered fierce winds,
and drifted for five days and nights,
not knowing how many thousand miles I had traveled,
passing through six countries in total.
The first was the Dog Country.
On the same ship was a man from Xīnlúo,
who said it was the Dog Country.
Soon after,
we indeed saw people-like beings, naked,
holding dogs as they emerged,
and upon seeing the ship, they fled in alarm.
Next, we passed the Hairy People Country,
where the inhabitants were small in stature,
all with disheveled hair covering their faces,
and bodies covered in hair like monkeys.
Then we arrived at the Yěchā Country.
The ship struck a hidden rock and was damaged,
so we carried the passengers and goods ashore.
Waiting for the tide to recede,
we beached the ship to repair it.
Initially unaware we were in this country,
several men ventured deep into the forest to gather wild vegetables,
when suddenly they were chased by yěchā,
and one was captured.
The others fled in panic.
Looking back,
they saw several yěchā devouring the captured man together.
Those on the ship were terrified and at a loss.
Moments later,
over a hundred yěchā arrived,
all with red hair and naked bodies,
mouths agape and eyes glaring angrily.
Some carried wooden spears,
and there were females carrying their young.
The boatmen and merchants, over fifty in total,
then united, using bows, crossbows, spears, and swords to confront them.
Indeed, they shot down two yěchā,
who were then carried away, howling and screaming as they fled.
After they left,
we cut down trees to set up a stockade,
to guard against their return.
The yěchā feared crossbows
and did not come again.
After staying for two days,
the ship was fully repaired,
and we departed with the wind.
Next, we passed the Land of Giants,
where the people were all tall and wild.
Upon hearing the clamor from the ship,
they fled in alarm and did not reappear.
Then we passed the Liúqiú Country,
where the people were very small,
all uniformly dressed in linen and courteous.
They eagerly brought food
to exchange for nails and iron.
The man from Xīnlúo partially translated their language,
urging us to pass through quickly,
saying that if people from Huá drifted to this country,
they feared it would bring disaster.
Afterward, we sailed on
and passed the Land of Dwarves,
where the people were naked
and as small as five- or six-year-old children.
With the ship’s provisions exhausted,
the crew went together to search for their nests.
Soon after,
they indeed captured thirty or forty and brought them back,
cooking them for food.
Two days later,
we encountered an island and went to fetch water.
Suddenly, a herd of goats appeared;
upon seeing people, they merely raised their heads to look,
showing no fear or avoidance,
and were both fat and large.
Initially suspecting someone on the island tended them,
yet there were absolutely no human traces.
We captured them,
managing to catch about a hundred,
and ate them all.
In Nánmán,
the chieftains of the southern regions often select fine goose down,
layer it with cloth and silk,
and quilt it into blankets,
then stitch it crosswise.
Their warmth and softness are no less than that of silk wadding.
It is commonly said
that goose down is soft, warm, and cool in nature,
especially suitable for covering infants
to ward off convulsive diseases.
The Fùfù people:
When a man of the Fùfù people desires a girl from another household,
he leads young men carrying white clubs
to wait for her on the path to the market.
Once she passes,
they seize and bind her, taking her back.
After one or two months,
he and his wife go to confess the offense.
This custom is called “binding a wife.”
The people of Nánhǎi:
Both men and women of Nánhǎi have thick, black hair.
Each time they wash it,
they add ash to flowing water,
then wash their hair in the water,
and apply lard to their hair.
By the fifth or sixth month,
when the rice is ripe,
the people all shave their hair and sell it in the market.
After shaving,
they again apply lard.
By the fifth or sixth month of the following year,
it can be sold again.
Also, in Nánhǎi, butchering cattle is often done by women,
called “slaughtering wives” or “slaughtering mothers.”
They tie the ox to a large tree,
hold a knife, and enumerate its offenses:
“At such a time, I led you to plow, but you would not go forward;
at such a time, I rode you to cross water, but you did not move promptly.
How can you escape death now?”
Then they lift its neck with a whip
and slash it with a knife.
When a poor man’s wife in Nánhǎi is pregnant,
he goes to a wealthy household
to pledge the unborn child for sale.
This custom is called “pledging the womb for sale.”
Or, if one’s own child is not yet old enough to wear clothes,
but a neighbor’s child is somewhat suitable for sale,
one may borrow that child to sell,
marking a stick to record its height.
When one’s own child grows to match the stick’s length,
the borrowed child is then returned.
Selling sons and daughters is like discarding dirt;
neither father nor son feels sorrow.
Rìnán:
The “Tiānbǎo Records” state:
The Jiù Mountain in Rìnán
stretches continuously for who knows how many thousand miles.
It is inhabited by naked people,
descendants of the Báimín.
They tattoo their chests with floral patterns,
use a purple powder-like substance
to paint beneath their eyes,
and remove their two front teeth
as adornments of beauty.
The Jūmí Country
In the year of Emperor Shùnzōng's accession to the throne,
the state of Jūmí presented as tribute fire-repelling sparrows,
one female and one male,
water-treading pearls,
everlasting ice,
and day-changing grass.
The fire-repelling sparrows
were pure black,
about the size of swallows,
their calls clear and bright,
unlike ordinary birds.
Placed in raging flames,
the fire would scatter on its own.
The emperor praised their marvel,
and so placed them in a fire-crystal cage,
hanging it in his bedchamber.
At night, palace women would even burn them with wax torches,
yet they could never harm their feathers.
The water-treading pearls
were black like iron,
as large as chicken eggs.
Their surfaces were scaly and wrinkled,
with holes inside.
It was said that if one entered rivers or seas with them,
one could walk freely upon great waves.
The emperor initially did not believe this to be true,
so he ordered a skilled swimmer
to thread them with five-colored silk,
tying them to his left arm.
Since venomous dragons feared them,
he was sent into the dragon pool.
The man then walked upon the waves,
as if on level ground,
and also dove into the water,
remaining for a long time before emerging again,
his entire body completely dry.
The emperor found this extraordinary,
and thus bestowed imperial delicacies upon the envoy.
By the Chángqìng era,
palace consorts tried playing with them by the sea pool,
whereupon they transformed into strange dragons
and entered the pool.
Soon, clouds and mist suddenly arose,
and they could no longer be pursued.
The everlasting ice
was said to come from a great frozen mountain in their country,
where there was ice
that did not melt for a thousand years.
When brought to the capital,
it remained pure and cold as before;
even under the blazing sun of intense summer heat,
it never melted.
Chewing it,
it was no different from ice in the Central Plains.
The day-changing grass
resembled plantains,
growing several feet long,
with a single stem and a thousand leaves.
When planted, within a hundred paces it turned dark as night.
Initially stored in a treasure box,
its lid was sealed with foreign paintings.
When the emperor saw it, he angrily said:
"Turning one's back to light and facing darkness—
what value does this grass have?"
He ordered it burned along with the box before the envoy.
The envoy was initially displeased,
but upon withdrawing,
said to the Court of State Ceremonial:
"Our state considered day-changing a marvel,
yet now the emperor deems facing darkness wrong—
truly, this can be called enlightened virtue."
Nánzhào
In Nánzhào, on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month,
known as the Star-Returning Festival,
they would roam the Wind-Sheltering Terrace,
commanding the Qīngpíngguān to compose poems.
The Piàoxìn's poem said:
"Sheltered from wind at Shànchǎn Terrace,
gazing afar, I see Téngyuè.
Alas, past and present,
remain mist and moon as ever.
Since I dwell in Zhèndàn,
my guards are like Kuí and Qì.
In those past imperial fortunes,
through hardships, I revered loyal valor.
Unaware the year draws to close,
deeply moved by the Star-Returning Festival.
Yuán and Chǎng
share one heart,
descendants may pass this on."
The Qīngpíngguān Zhào Shūdá said:
"The imperial carriage avoids the star's return,
Bōluó, brave and fierce,
Rivers wide, ice hard to form,
land warm, plums bloom first.
Decrees reach the Lǐróu, harmonious,
tributes offered, Nòng Jiǎn come.
Wishing to offer my unworthy self,
for a thousand years serving the roaming terrace."
Lǎo Women
In the south, there are Lǎo women
who rise immediately after giving birth.
Their husbands lie in bed,
eating and drinking like nursing mothers.
If not carefully guarded,
the pregnant woman's ailments all arise.
Their wives, however, suffer no hardship,
cooking, gathering firewood, and carrying on as usual.
It is also said
that among the Yuè custom,
when a wife gives birth,
after three days,
she bathes in streams or rivers.
Returning,
she prepares congee to feed her husband,
who wraps himself in quilts, holding the newborn,
sitting on the bed,
called a "birthing father."
Such is their reversal.
Southern Monks
Southerners largely do not believe in Buddhism.
Although there are one or two Buddhist temples,
officials tax those who become monks,
to oversee and demand monastic lands and donated wealth.
Occasionally, there are one or two monks
who enjoy keeping wives and eating meat,
merely residing at home,
unable to perform even minor Buddhist rites.
Locals marry their daughters to monks,
calling them "teacher-husbands."
If someone falls ill,
they make paper round coins
and place them beside Buddha statues.
Or they invite monks to set out food offerings;
the next day,
they slaughter sheep or pigs to feast them,
calling it "ending the fast."
Also, in small southern commanderies,
there are often no black-robed clergy.
Whenever imperial virtuous decrees are proclaimed,
they must pretend to have monks or Daoists accompany the ceremony.
When Emperor Táng Zhāozōng ascended the throne,
Liǔ Tāo was the proclamation envoy to Róng and Guǎng.
When the pardon edict arrived,
it was sent to subordinate prefectures.
Yázhōu had never had monks,
so
they were temporarily appointed for the occasion.
During the proclamation,
one pretend monk refused to take his assigned position.
The prefect Wáng Hóngfū found it strange and asked him.
The monk said:
"My turn of duty is unfair;
assignments are mixed up.
Last year I already acted as King Wénxuān,
this year I'm assigned to be a monk again."
Those who saw this could not help but laugh uproariously.
Pānyú
In Guǎngzhōu's Pānyú County, there were often villagers who would lodge complaints, saying,
"Last night, my vegetable garden was lost,
and now I recognize it as being in a certain place.
I request the county magistrate to issue a judgment so I can retrieve it."
A visitor from the north was astonished by this claim
and thus questioned them.
The villagers explained,
"In the shallow waters of the sea, there are algae and duckweed-like plants
that, when blown by the wind,
mix with sand.
Their roots float,
and where the sand accumulates to a thickness of three to five feet,
it becomes suitable for cultivation,
either for irrigation or for gardens.
At night, thieves steal these gardens and move them over a hundred li away,
as if they were rafts or bamboo mats floating on the current.
Because of this, vegetable growers
are often found on the sea."
Also, during the Dragon Boat Festival in Pānyú,
one could hear a clamor in the streets,
with voices selling "love potions."
Surprised and amused, people would go to watch,
only to find old women carrying
exotic herbs from the mountains,
selling them to wealthy ladies
as potions to attract men.
It was believed that herbs gathered on this day were especially potent.
It was also said
that if one searched in magpie nests,
they might find two small stones,
called "magpie pillows."
Those obtained on this day were considered the best.
When women encountered these,
some would pull out gold hairpins or remove earrings to pay for them.
Women's Work in Lǐngnán
In Lǐngnán, regardless of whether a family was poor or wealthy,
girls were not taught needlework, spinning, or weaving as essential skills.
Instead, they focused on kitchen duties,
diligently handling knives and kitchen tools.
Those skilled at pickling, salting, or making fermented fish
were considered excellent women.
Is this perhaps the innate nature of those in remote regions?
Thus, among the common folk,
when competing for marriage proposals,
people would say to each other:
"My daughter cannot sew robes or mend jackets—
she clearly has no skill in that;
but when it comes to preparing water snakes or yellow eels,
she outdoes everyone else."
Taro Soup
The Bǎiyuè people are fond of eating frogs.
At any banquet or gathering,
this is considered a delicacy.
First, water is placed in a pot,
then small taro is added and cooked.
When the broth boils with bubbles like fish eyes,
the frogs are added.
Each frog clings to a piece of taro as it cooks,
hence the dish is called "hugging taro soup."
Alternatively, bamboo skewers are placed in the broth first,
followed by the frogs.
When served at the banquet,
the frogs are still holding the skewers,
eyes wide and mouths agape.
Guests at the table would joke, saying:
"They look like sellers of lamp wicks."
It was also said
that frogs with scabby skin were the best.
When thrown into boiling water,
they would leap out,
and their skin would shed automatically.
Once the skin was removed,
they could be prepared for the meal.
Once, an old man heard this and
strongly disapproved,
saying:
"You must never remove this 'brocade coat,'
as its flavor is exceptionally delicious."
Those who heard this could not help but laugh.
Honey-Squeak
The Liáo people of Lǐngnán enjoy making "honey-squeak,"
which consists of fetal mice whose eyes have not yet opened,
their bodies still pink and wriggling.
They are fed honey,
then pinned to the banquet table,
where they squirm and crawl.
Guests pick them up with chopsticks,
bite into them,
and they squeak,
hence the name "honey-squeak."
Nánzhōu
In the Shǔ kingdom of Wáng, there was a man named Liú Yǐn, who was skilled in writing.
He once recounted
how, as a youth, he succeeded to the position of military supervisor in Yì Province and sent a letter,
requesting
to be assigned to the south of Qiánwū,
a place called Nánzhōu.
The region was mountainous and treacherous,
with narrow paths impassable for riding.
Both nobles and commoners walked with canes,
and their baggage was all carried by porters.
Where porters could not reach,
even the county magistrate or his assistant had to carry their own loads.
As he approached Nánzhōu,
the prefect sent someone with a letter to greet him.
Upon arrival, one or two men came forward carrying baskets,
placed Liú Yǐn inside a basket,
and carried him off, swinging their arms as they walked.
Whether climbing mountains or entering valleys,
no matter how high or deep,
they covered about a hundred such places daily,
using their fingers and nails to cling and climb,
advancing inch by inch.
Inside the basket,
one had to sit with their back to the carrier,
as this was the local equivalent of a carriage or horse.
Upon nearing the prefecture,
the prefect also came out in a basket to greet him at the outskirts.
The prefectural seat was located among mulberry forests,
with only a few thatched huts.
The prefect and officials were all Han Chinese,
and they were very thoughtful and righteous.
The next day, the prefect said:
"You should pay a brief visit to the generals."
He then sent someone to guide him to the military compounds.
Each compound was about ten li apart,
also situated beneath the forest trees.
In a thatched cottage,
three to five high-ranking officers
welcomed him with utmost courtesy.
They then cooked a calf,
but first took the fine feces from the calf's colon,
placed it on a banquet plate,
mixed it with chopsticks,
and blended it into vinegar,
only then did they eat the calf meat.
The locals called this fine feces "holy fasting food."
Without this dish,
a banquet was considered incomplete.
When the meal was about halfway through,
they served steamed worm wraps.
These wraps were made by taking worms from the stems of bracken ferns,
similar to today's caterpillars,
wrapping them in lotus leaves, and steaming them.
Liú Yǐn forced himself to eat,
but the next day, he left much of it untouched.
The Tale of Lǐ Wá
The Lady of Qiānguó, Lǐ Wá,
was a courtesan of Cháng'ān.
Her integrity and conduct were extraordinary,
worthy of praise.
Therefore, the former Investigating Censor Bái Xíngjiǎn composed her biography.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a Governor of Chángzhōu, the Duke of Xíngyáng.
His name is omitted,
not recorded.
At that time, his reputation was very high,
and his household was exceedingly wealthy.
At the age of fifty,
he had a son,
who had just reached his capping ceremony.
He was handsome, bright, and eloquent,
truly outstanding among his peers,
deeply admired and respected by his contemporaries.
His father loved and prized him,
saying:
"This is the thousand-li steed of our family."
When he was to take the provincial examination for the xiùcái degree,
as he was about to depart,
his father lavishly prepared his clothing, ornaments, carriages, and horses,
and calculated the expenses for his lodging and provisions in the capital.
He said to him:
"I observe your talent;
you should achieve supremacy in a single attempt.
Now I have prepared two years' worth of supplies,
and moreover, I have enriched your allowance,
to help you fulfill your ambition."
The young man also regarded passing the highest examination as easily as pointing at his palm.
Setting out from Pílíng,
he arrived in Cháng'ān after over a month,
and resided in Bùzhèng Ward.
Once, returning from an excursion to the East Market,
he entered through the east gate of Píngkāng Ward,
intending to visit a friend in the southwest.
Arriving at Míngkē Lane,
he saw a residence,
whose gate and courtyard were not very spacious,
but the buildings within were imposing and deep,
with one door closed.
There was Wá, leaning against a maidservant with twin buns, standing there.
Her enchanting beauty was exquisite,
unmatched in her generation.
The young man suddenly saw her,
unconsciously reined in his horse for a long time,
lingering, unable to leave.
So he pretended to drop his whip on the ground,
waiting for his attendants,
ordered them to pick it up,
and repeatedly glanced at Wá.
Wá turned her gaze and stared intently,
their mutual affection was strong,
yet in the end, he dared not speak a word and left.
From then on, the young man felt as if he had lost something.
So he secretly inquired of his friend who was familiar with Cháng'ān's pleasures.
His friend said:
"This is the residence of the courtesan Lǐ."
He asked:
"Can Wá be sought?"
The friend replied:
"The Lǐ family is quite wealthy.
Those who previously associated with her
were mostly noble relatives and powerful clans.
What she received was very extensive;
without accumulating a million,
you cannot move her heart."
The young man said:
"If only I worry about not succeeding,
even a million,
why begrudge it!"
Another day,
he dressed in clean clothes,
and went with a grand retinue.
He knocked on the door,
and soon a maid opened it.
The young man said:
"Whose residence is this?"
The maid did not answer,
but ran inside, shouting loudly:
"It's the gentleman who dropped his whip the other day!"
Wá was greatly pleased and said:
"You go and detain him for now;
I will tidy my makeup, change clothes, and come out."
Hearing this,
the young man secretly rejoiced.
He was then led to the inner wall,
where he saw an old woman with white hair and a hunched back,
who was Wá's mother.
The young man knelt, bowed, and addressed her:
"I have heard there is a vacant courtyard here;
I wish to rent it to live in.
Is this true?"
The old woman said:
"I fear it is shallow, crude, cramped, and narrow,
unworthy of a gentleman's residence;
how dare I speak of rent?"
She invited the young man into the guest reception hall,
which was very splendid.
Sitting opposite him,
she then said:
"I have a young daughter,
with modest skills,
but she delights in meeting guests;
I wish to have her meet you."
So she ordered Wá to come out.
With bright eyes and fair wrists,
her every step was enchanting and alluring.
The young man immediately stood up in surprise,
not daring to look up at her.
After they exchanged bows,
they exchanged pleasantries about the weather.
In every gesture, she was beautiful and charming,
such as he had never seen before.
They sat down again,
brewed tea and poured wine;
the utensils were very clean.
After a long time, dusk fell,
and the drum sounded for the fourth watch.
The old woman inquired how far away he lived.
The young man deceived her, saying:
"Several lǐ outside Yánpíng Gate."
Hoping that its distance would cause her to ask him to stay.
The old woman said:
"The drum has already sounded;
you should return quickly,
and not violate the curfew."
The young man said:
"I have been fortunate to share laughter and joy,
unaware that the day has grown so late.
The road is long and vast,
and within the city, I have no relatives.
What shall I do?"
Wá said:
"If you do not blame our humble and crude place,
and are just about to reside here,
what harm is there in staying the night?"
The young man repeatedly glanced at the old woman.
The old woman said:
"Very well, very well."
The young man then summoned his servant,
bringing two rolls of silk,
asking to use them to prepare a night's meal.
Wá smiled and stopped him, saying:
"The etiquette between host and guest
is not like this.
Tonight's expenses,
I wish, from our poor household,
to offer you coarse fare.
The rest can wait for another time."
He firmly declined,
but she ultimately did not allow it.
Soon they moved to sit in the western hall.
The curtains, drapes, and couches
were dazzlingly brilliant;
the dressing cases, quilts, and pillows
were also all luxurious and beautiful.
Then they lit candles and served the meal,
with a great variety of delicacies.
After clearing the meal,
the old woman rose.
The young man and Wá's conversation grew intimate,
with witty banter and teasing,
leaving nothing untouched.
The young man said:
"The other day, I happened to pass by your gate,
and met you just inside the screen.
Afterwards, my heart was constantly and earnestly thinking of you,
even in sleep and while eating,
I never once ceased."
Wá replied:
"My heart is the same."
The young man said:
"My coming today
is not merely to seek lodging,
but to fulfill the wish of my life.
Only I do not know what fate has in store."
Before he finished speaking,
the old woman arrived,
inquired the reason,
and he told her everything.
The old woman laughed and said:
"Between men and women,
great desire exists.
If feelings are mutually agreeable,
even the command of parents
cannot control it.
My daughter is truly crude and unworthy;
how could she be fit to share a gentleman's pillow and mat!"
The young man then descended the steps,
bowed and thanked her, saying:
"I wish to become a servant."
The old woman then regarded him as her son-in-law,
and they drank until intoxicated before parting.
At dawn,
he moved all his belongings,
and took up residence in the Lǐ household.
From then on, the young man concealed his traces and kept to himself,
no longer in contact with relatives and friends.
He would daily gather with actors and entertainers of his kind,
indulging in playful banter, outings, and feasts.
When his purse was completely empty,
he sold his fine horse and his household servants.
After a little over a year,
his wealth, servants, and horses were all gone.
Lately, the old madam's attitude had gradually grown cold,
but Wá's affection grew even deeper.
One day,
Wá said to the young man:
"I have known you for a year,
but we still have no child to carry on the line.
I have often heard that the Bamboo Grove Deity
responds to prayers as swiftly as an echo.
Shall we go to make an offering and seek his blessing,
would that be all right?"
The young man, unaware of her scheme,
was overjoyed.
He then pawned his clothes at a shop
to prepare the sacrificial animals and wine,
and went with Wá to the temple to pray.
They stayed for two nights before returning.
Riding their donkey back,
when they reached the north gate of the ward,
Wá said to the young man:
"In this alley to the east,
is the house of my aunt.
Shall we rest there and pay her a visit,
would that be all right?"
The young man did as she said.
They had not gone a hundred paces ahead
when they indeed saw a carriage gate.
Peering inside,
it was very spacious.
A maidservant behind the carriage stopped them and said:
"We have arrived."
The young man dismounted.
Just then, someone came out and inquired:
"Who is it?"
They replied:
"It is Lǐ Wá."
The person then went in to announce them.
Soon an old woman arrived,
about forty-some years old,
who greeted the young man and said:
"Has my niece arrived?"
Wá got down from the carriage.
The old woman came forward to greet her and said:
"Why has it been so long since you visited?"
They looked at each other and laughed.
Wá led the young man to bow to her.
After the meeting,
they all entered together through the western halberd gate into a side courtyard.
Within was a mountain pavilion,
with bamboo and trees lush and verdant,
and ponds and pavilions of secluded beauty.
The young man said to Wá:
"Is this your aunt's private residence?"
She smiled without answering,
and replied with other topics.
Soon tea and fruits were served,
all very rare and exquisite.
After a meal's time,
a man came riding a large horse from Dàyuān,
sweating and galloping up, saying:
"The old madam has suddenly fallen gravely ill,
she hardly recognizes anyone.
You should return quickly."
Wá said to her aunt:
"My heart is in turmoil.
I will ride ahead,
and will send the carriage back,
then come with my husband."
The young man intended to follow her,
but her aunt whispered with a maidservant,
waved her hand at him,
and told the young man to wait outside the door,
saying:
"The old madam is about to die.
We should discuss the funeral arrangements,
to meet the urgent need.
How can you hastily follow her away?"
So he stayed,
and together they calculated the expenses for the funeral rites and offerings.
As evening fell,
the carriage had not returned.
The aunt said:
"Why is there no message?
You, sir, go quickly to check on them,
and I will follow shortly."
The young man then went,
arriving at the old residence,
but the gate was tightly locked and bolted,
sealed with mud.
Greatly alarmed,
he questioned the neighbors.
A neighbor said:
"Lǐ originally rented this place to live,
and the lease has expired.
The landlord took it back himself,
and the old madam moved away two days ago."
When asked where they had moved to,
he said:
"I do not know the place."
The young man was about to rush to Xuānyáng Ward
to question the aunt,
but it was already late,
and he calculated he could not make it in time.
So he took off his outer garments,
pawned them for a meal,
and rented a bed to sleep.
Filled with rage and anger,
from dusk till dawn,
he did not close his eyes.
At daybreak,
he rode a lame donkey and set off.
Upon arrival,
he repeatedly knocked on the gate,
but for a long time no one answered.
He called out loudly several times,
and a eunuch slowly emerged.
The young man hastily asked him:
"Is my aunt here?"
He replied:
"There is no such person."
The young man said:
"She was here last night.
Why are you hiding her?"
He asked whose residence this was,
and the man said:
"This is the residence of Cuī Shàngshū.
Yesterday, someone rented this courtyard,
saying they were waiting for a distant cousin to arrive,
and left before evening."
The young man, bewildered and frantic,
was at a loss what to do,
so he returned to his old lodgings in Bùzhèng Ward.
The innkeeper, pitying him, provided a meal.
The young man, resentful and aggrieved,
refused food for three days,
and fell gravely ill.
After more than ten days, he grew even worse.
The innkeeper, fearing he would not recover,
moved him to a funeral shop.
Lingering on for some time,
all the people in the shop
pitied him and took turns feeding him.
Later, he gradually recovered,
and could walk with a cane.
From then on, the funeral shop employed him daily,
having him hold the mourning curtains,
earning wages to support himself.
After several months,
he gradually regained his strength.
Whenever he heard the funeral dirges,
he would sigh, feeling he was worse off than the dead,
and would sob and shed tears,
unable to stop himself.
Returning, he would imitate them.
The young man was intelligent and quick-witted,
and before long,
he mastered the subtleties of the songs,
becoming unmatched even in Cháng'ān.
Earlier,
the two funeral shops that supplied funeral utensils
had been competing for superiority.
The eastern shop's hearses and carriages were all exceptionally fine,
almost unbeatable.
Only their funeral dirges were inferior.
The manager of the eastern shop, knowing the young man's superb skill,
collected twenty thousand coins to hire him.
His veteran colleagues
all compared their abilities,
secretly teaching the young man new tunes,
and harmonizing with him.
After several ten-day periods,
no one knew of this.
The managers of the two shops said to each other:
"Let us each display the funeral utensils we supply on Tiānmén Street,
to compare their quality.
The loser
shall pay a fine of fifty thousand coins,
to cover the cost of wine and food.
Is that acceptable?"
Both shops agreed,
and so they invited witnesses to draw up a contract,
signed with guarantees,
and then displayed their wares.
Men and women gathered in great crowds,
numbering tens of thousands.
Thereupon, the ward head reported to the thief-catcher,
and the thief-catcher informed the capital governor.
People from all directions
rushed to the scene,
leaving the lanes empty of residents.
From morning they displayed their wares,
until noon,
having presented in turn all the carriages, hearses, and ceremonial implements,
the western shop was completely outmatched,
and its master looked ashamed.
Then, a tiered couch was set up in the southern corner,
and a man with a long beard,
holding a bell, stepped forward.
Surrounded by several guards,
he raised his beard and lifted his eyebrows,
clenching his wrist and nodding his head as he ascended.
He then sang the lyrics of "White Horse."
Relying on his past victories,
he glanced left and right,
as if no one else were around.
The audience praised him in unison,
and he believed himself to be unrivaled at the time,
impossible to humble.
After a while,
the manager of the eastern troupe set up a connected couch in the northern corner.
A young man wearing a black headscarf,
accompanied by five or six attendants,
arrived holding a fan—
it was the young man.
He straightened his clothes,
moved with great deliberation,
and began to sing,
his expression as if he could hardly bear it.
He sang the chapter "Xièlù,"
his voice clear and soaring,
resonating through the forest.
Before the melody ended,
the listeners were already sobbing and covering their faces in tears.
The manager of the western troupe was ridiculed by the crowd,
and feeling increasingly ashamed,
he secretly placed the bet money in front of him,
then slipped away unnoticed.
The entire audience was stunned,
unable to comprehend what had happened.
Earlier, the emperor had issued an edict,
ordering provincial governors
to come to the capital once a year,
which was called "presenting accounts."
At that time,
it happened that the young man's father was in the capital,
and changing his official robes with his colleagues,
he secretly went to watch the performance.
There was an old servant,
who was the husband of the young man's wet nurse,
and upon seeing the young man's demeanor and speech,
he almost recognized him but did not dare,
and tears began to flow.
The father, startled, questioned him,
and the servant replied:
"The singer's appearance
bears a striking resemblance to your deceased son."
The father said:
"My son was killed by thieves because of his wealth.
How could he have ended up like this?"
After speaking,
he too wept.
Upon returning,
the servant hurriedly went out,
and inquired among the troupe members:
"Who was the singer earlier,
so remarkably skilled?"
They all said:
"He is the son of a certain family."
When asked for his name,
it had been changed,
and the servant was deeply shocked.
He slowly approached,
and drawing near, observed him closely.
The young man saw the servant,
his expression changed, and he tried to retreat,
intending to hide among the crowd.
The servant then grabbed his sleeve and said:
"Aren't you so-and-so?"
They held each other and wept,
and then the servant took him back.
Upon arriving home,
the father scolded him:
"With such conduct,
you have disgraced our family.
How can you show your face
and see me again?"
He then made him leave on foot,
and they went to the east of Xìngyuán at Qūjiāng,
where he stripped off his clothes.
He whipped him several hundred times with a horsewhip.
The young man, unable to endure the pain, fell unconscious,
and his father abandoned him and left.
His teacher ordered his close companions
to secretly follow him,
and upon returning, they reported to the group,
all expressing sorrow and lament.
They ordered two men to bring a reed mat and bury him.
When they arrived, they found his chest slightly warm,
and after lifting him for a long time,
his breath gradually returned.
So they carried him back together,
and using a reed tube, they fed him small sips of liquid,
and by the next morning, he had revived.
Over a month later,
he still could not move his limbs on his own,
and the places where he had been whipped were all festering,
emitting a foul odor.
His companions grew concerned,
and one night, they abandoned him by the roadside.
Passersby all pitied him,
often tossing him leftover food,
which allowed him to fill his stomach.
After a hundred days,
he was finally able to rise with the help of a cane.
He wore a cloth robe,
which was patched in a hundred places,
tattered like a hanging quail.
Holding a broken bowl, he wandered through the neighborhoods,
making a living by begging for food.
From autumn to winter,
he spent nights in dung-filled caves,
and during the day, he roamed the markets.
One day, when it was snowing heavily,
driven by cold and hunger,
he ventured out into the snow,
his cries for food filled with suffering,
and all who heard or saw him were deeply moved.
At that time, the snow was especially heavy,
and many households kept their outer doors closed.
When he reached the east gate of Ānyì,
he followed the lanes,
along the walls,
turning north at the seventh or eighth house,
where one door had its left leaf open—
it was Wá's residence.
Unaware of this,
he repeatedly cried out urgently:
"I am starving and freezing!"
His voice was mournful and piercing,
unbearable to hear.
Wá, hearing it from her chamber,
said to her maid:
"This must be the young man.
I recognize his voice."
She hurried out.
Seeing him emaciated, covered in sores,
barely human in appearance,
Wá was deeply moved.
She then said to him:
"Aren't you so-and-so?"
Overwhelmed with anguish, the young man collapsed,
unable to speak,
only nodding his head.
Wá stepped forward, embraced his neck,
and wrapping him in an embroidered jacket, led him back to the western wing.
