She cried out in a long, mournful wail:
"That you have come to this state is
my fault."
She fainted and then revived.
The old madam, greatly alarmed, rushed over
and said:
"What is this?"
Wá replied:
"It is the young man."
The madam immediately said:
"He should be driven away.
Why have you brought him here?"
Wá composed herself, turned her gaze away, and said:
"No,
he is from a respectable family.
In the past, he rode in a grand carriage,
carried gold and finery,
and came to my chamber,
but before long, he had squandered everything.
Moreover, we schemed together,
abandoned him, and drove him away—
such behavior is inhuman.
We caused him to lose his way,
making him unfit for human society.
The bond between father and son
is a natural instinct.
Yet we severed that affection,
leading to his near death and abandonment,
and now he is in such dire straits.
Everyone under heaven
knows it was because of me.
His relatives fill the court,
and once those in power thoroughly investigate the matter,
disaster will befall us.
Moreover, deceiving heaven and betraying others,
even the gods and spirits will not protect us—
we will bring calamity upon ourselves.
I have been your daughter
for twenty years now.
Calculating the wealth I have earned,
it amounts to no less than a thousand pieces of gold.
Now you are over sixty years old,
and I wish to calculate the cost of twenty years of food and clothing to buy my freedom,
so that I may go elsewhere with this young man.
The place we go will not be far,
and I will be able to care for you morning and night,
and that will be enough for me."
The madam saw that her resolve was unshakable,
and so she agreed.
After giving the madam the remaining money,
There were a hundred taels of gold.
In the northern corner, there were four or five households,
and they rented a small courtyard.
Then, she and the scholar bathed,
changed his clothes,
prepared soup and porridge to clear his intestines,
and then used butter and milk to nourish his organs.
After more than ten days,
they finally served him delicacies from land and sea.
His headscarf, shoes, and socks
were all made of rare and exquisite materials.
Within a few months,
his skin and flesh gradually became fuller.
By the end of the year,
he had fully recovered as before.
At another time,
Wá said to the scholar:
"Your body is already healthy,
and your spirit is strong.
With deep and quiet contemplation,
silently recalling the studies of the past,
can you review them?"
The scholar thought and said:
"I remember only about two or three out of ten."
Wá ordered a carriage to go out,
and the scholar rode along.
They arrived at a bookstore selling classical texts near the southern side gate of the Qítíng,
where she had the scholar select and purchase books,
spending a hundred taels of gold in total,
and brought them all back.
She then urged the scholar to cast aside all distractions and focus on his studies,
working day and night,
diligently and tirelessly.
Wá often sat beside him,
and only went to sleep late at night.
When she saw him growing tired,
she would encourage him to compose poetry and prose.
After two years, his studies greatly advanced,
and he had read extensively
all the literary works in the land.
The scholar said to Wá:
"Now I can take the imperial examinations."
Wá said:
"Not yet.
You must refine your skills thoroughly,
to prepare for all challenges."
After another year,
she said:
"Now you may go."
Thus, he passed the highest level of the imperial examination in one attempt,
and his reputation shook the examination halls.
Even senior scholars who read his essays
could not help but show respect and admiration,
wishing to befriend him,
but found it impossible.
Wá said:
"Not yet.
Nowadays, if a scholar merely passes an examination,
he thinks he can obtain a high position in the court,
and claim the finest reputation in the land.
But your past is tainted and humble,
unlike other scholars.
You must sharpen your tools further,
to achieve another victory,
so that you can stand among the many talents,
and compete with the best."
From then on, the scholar worked even harder,
and his reputation grew even greater.
That year, a grand examination was held,
and the emperor summoned talents from all directions.
The scholar took the "Direct and Extreme Admonition" policy examination,
and ranked first,
being appointed as an assistant in the Chéngdū prefectural government.
All officials below the three highest ranks
became his friends.
As he was about to take up his post,
Wá said to the scholar:
"Now that I have restored you to your original self,
I have not failed you.
I wish to spend my remaining years
returning to care for my elderly mother.
You should marry a woman from a noble family,
to perform the ancestral rites.
Marry within the respectable circles,
and do not disgrace yourself.
Strive to take care of yourself,
for I shall leave from now on."
The scholar wept and said:
"If you abandon me,
I will cut my own throat and die."
Wá firmly refused to stay,
but the scholar pleaded even more earnestly.
Wá said:
"I will accompany you across the river,
to Jiànmén,
and then you must let me return."
The scholar agreed.
After more than a month,
they reached Jiànmén.
Before they could depart, an official appointment arrived,
and the scholar's father was summoned from Chángzhōu,
appointed as the governor of Chéngdū,
and concurrently as the inspector of Jiànnán.
After twelve days,
his father arrived.
The scholar then presented his card,
and met his father at the postal station.
His father did not dare recognize him,
but upon seeing the official titles of his grandfather,
he was greatly astonished,
invited him up the steps,
and embracing him, wept bitterly for a long time.
He said:
"You and I shall be father and son as before."
He then inquired about the details,
and the scholar recounted everything from beginning to end.
His father was greatly amazed,
and asked where Wá was.
The scholar said:
"She accompanied me here,
and is to return now."
His father said:
"That cannot be."
The next day,
he ordered the carriage to go with the scholar first to Chéngdū,
leaving Wá at Jiànmén,
where he built a separate residence for her.
The following day,
he ordered a matchmaker to arrange the marriage between the two families,
prepared all six wedding rites to welcome her,
and thus they became a couple like those of Qín and Jìn.
After Wá completed the wedding rites,
during seasonal festivals and sacrifices,
she diligently fulfilled her duties as a wife,
managed the household strictly and orderly,
and was highly cherished and respected by her relatives,
Several years later,
the scholar's parents both passed away,
and she observed mourning with utmost filial piety.
A spiritual fungus grew by the mourning hut,
with one stalk bearing three blossoms,
and the local officials reported this to the emperor.
Moreover, dozens of white swallows
nested on the layered roof of their house.
The emperor found this extraordinary,
and bestowed additional honors and rewards.
After the mourning period ended,
he was repeatedly promoted to high and prestigious positions.
Within ten years,
he served as governor of several commanderies.
Wá was enfeoffed as the Lady of Qiānguó,
and they had four sons,
all of whom became high officials,
the lowest among them still serving as the governor of Tàiyuán.
Their brothers and in-laws all belonged to prominent families,
and the family flourished both internally and externally,
with none able to rival them.
Alas,
a courtesan of such background,
yet with such virtue and conduct,
even the ancient paragons of womanhood
could not surpass her.
How could one not sigh in admiration!
My paternal great-uncle once served as the prefect of Jìnzhōu,
then transferred to the Ministry of Revenue,
and became the commissioner of water and land transport,
holding three posts that succeeded the scholar's,
thus he was well acquainted with the details of this story.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
I and Lord Lǒngxī Gōng Zuǒ,
discussing the virtuous character of women,
thus recounted the story of the Lady of Qiānguó.
Gōng Zuǒ clapped his hands and listened attentively,
urging me to write a biography.
So I took up my brush,
and recorded it in detail to preserve it.
It was the autumn eighth month of the Yǐhài year,
written by Bái Xíngjiǎn of Tàiyuán.
The Biography of the Old Man of the Eastern City
The old man's surname is Jiǎ, his given name is Chāng,
a resident of Xuānyáng Ward in Cháng'ān.
He was born in the Guǐchǒu year of the Kāiyuán era (713 CE).
In the Gēngyín year of the Yuánhé era (810 CE),
he is ninety-eight years old,
his sight and hearing have not declined,
his speech is very calm and unhurried,
his mental energy is undiminished.
When he speaks of the affairs of the Tàipíng era,
they are vivid and worth hearing.
His father, Zhōng,
was nine chǐ tall,
his strength could drag an ox backward,
and he served as a palace guard due to his martial prowess.
In the fourth year of Jǐnglóng (710 CE),
holding a curtain pole,
he followed Emperor Xuánzōng into the Dàmíng Palace to exterminate the Wěi clan,
and escorted Emperor Ruìzōng to court to receive the feudal lords.
Thus he became a meritorious official of the Jǐngyún era,
serving as a personal guard with a long sword,
and was ordered to move his family east to Yúnlóng Gate.
When Chāng was seven years old,
he was exceptionally agile and nimble,
able to climb pillars and traverse beams.
He was skilled in conversation,
and understood the sounds of birds.
When Emperor Xuánzōng was still a prince,
he enjoyed the folk custom of cockfighting during the Qīngmíng Festival.
After ascending the throne,
he established
a cockfighting arena between the two palaces.
He sought out roosters from Cháng'ān,
with golden feathers and iron spurs,
thousands with high combs and raised tails,
and kept them in the cockfighting arena.
He selected five hundred young boys from the six armies,
to train, tame, and feed them.
The emperor's fondness for it
made the custom even more prevalent among the people.
The various royal families,
maternal relatives,
noble households,
and marquises
exhausted their treasuries and bankrupted themselves to purchase roosters,
to pay the price for the birds.
Men and women in the capital made cockfighting their occupation,
while the poor played with fake roosters.
When the emperor went on an excursion,
he saw Chāng playing with a wooden rooster by the roadside at Yúnlóng Gate.
He summoned him to become a boy in the cockfighting arena,
with clothing and food provided by the Right Lóngwǔ Army.
A child of three chǐ entering a flock of roosters,
was like playing with a group of youngsters.
The strong and the weak,
the brave and the timid,
their feeding times,
and signs of illness—
he could discern them all.
He would lift two roosters,
and they would fear and obey him,
following his commands like people.
The palace attendant in charge of the cockfighting arena, Wáng Chéng'ēn, spoke to the emperor,
who summoned Chāng for a test in the palace courtyard.
Everything met Emperor Xuánzōng's expectations.
That very day, he was made the leader of the five hundred boys,
and due to his loyalty, honesty, caution, and discretion,
the emperor greatly favored and loved him.
Gifts of gold and silk
arrived at his home daily.
In the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán (725 CE),
he took three hundred caged roosters to accompany the emperor to the eastern peak for the fēng sacrifice.
His father, Zhōng, died at the foot of Mount Tài,
and as a son, he received permission to escort the corpse back for burial in Yōngzhōu.
The county officials provided burial vessels.
The funeral carriage traveled by relay along the Luòyáng road.
In the third month of the fourteenth year (726 CE),
wearing his cockfighting attire,
he met Emperor Xuánzōng at the hot springs.
At that time, he was known throughout the land as the "Divine Cockfighting Child."
People of the time said of him:
"When raising a son, there's no need to teach him to read and write;
cockfighting and horse racing surpass studying books.
The Jiǎ family's child, only thirteen years old,
enjoys wealth and glory unmatched by any generation.
He can make roosters with golden spurs decide victory or defeat,
and follows the soft carriage in his white silk embroidered robe.
His father died a thousand lǐ outside Cháng'ān,
yet laborers were ordered to pull the funeral carriage along the road."
When Empress Zhāochéng was in the residence of the Prince of Xiāng,
she gave birth to the emperor on the fifth day of the eighth month.
After the restoration of the dynasty,
this day was established as the Qiānqiū Festival.
The people of the realm were granted oxen, wine, and three days of music,
which was called a 'pú' feast,
and this became customary.
Grand musical performances were held in the palace.
Some years, the pú feast was held in Luò,
and for the Yuánhuì and Qīngmíng festivals,
they were often held at Lí Mountain.
Every time this day arrived,
all kinds of music were performed,
and all the palace ladies attended.
Chāng wore a carved kingfisher-feather and golden-flower crown,
with brocade sleeves and embroidered jacket and trousers.
Holding a bell and a whisk,
he led
the flock of roosters,
standing in orderly ranks on the open square.
His gaze was like that of a deity,
his commands stirred the wind.
The roosters raised their feathers and shook their wings,
sharpened their beaks and spurs,
suppressed their anger and awaited victory,
advancing and retreating on schedule,
rising and falling with the flick of his whip,
never deviating from Chāng's commands.
Once victory or defeat was decided,
the strong went to the front,
the weak to the rear,
following Chāng in a goose formation,
returning to the cockfighting arena.
Wrestlers of ten thousand men,
sword-jugglers and pole-climbers,
ball-kickers and rope-walkers,
and those dancing atop poles—
all lost their spirit and looked dismayed,
hesitating and not daring to enter.
Were they not like those who teach monkeys to tame dragons?
In the twenty-third year (735 CE),
Emperor Xuánzōng arranged for him to marry the daughter of Pān Dàtóng, a member of the Líyuán troupe.
The groom's attire with jade pendants,
and the bride's embroidered jacket—
all came from the imperial storehouses.
Chāng's sons were named Zhìxìn and Zhìdé.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
his wife, Madame Pān, gained great favor with Consort Yáng due to her singing and dancing.
Husband and wife enjoyed imperial favor for forty years,
their grace and blessings never waning.
Was this not due to their skill in their arts
and caution in their hearts?
The emperor was born in the Yǒu year, under the sign of the rooster.
He had people wear court attire for cockfighting,
an omen of disorder in times of peace,
yet the emperor's mind remained unawakened.
In the fourteenth year (755 CE),
the Hú and Jié rebels captured Luò,
Tóng Pass could not be held,
and the imperial carriage fled to Chéngdū.
Chāng rushed to guard the imperial carriage,
leaving by night through the side gate.
His horse stumbled into a pit on the road,
injuring his foot so he could not proceed.
Leaning on a staff, he entered the Southern Mountains.
On every day he had formerly presented roosters,
he would weep loudly facing the southwest.
Ān Lùshān, when he had previously come to the capital,
had met Chāng outside Héng Gate.
During the rebellion in the two capitals,
he offered a thousand pieces of gold for Chāng in the markets of Cháng'ān and Luòyáng.
Chāng changed his name,
and took refuge in a Buddhist temple,
sweeping the grounds and striking the bell,
devoting his efforts to the Buddha.
After the Retired Emperor returned to Xīngqìng Palace,
and Emperor Sùzōng received the mandate in a separate hall,
Chāng returned to his old neighborhood.
His home had been plundered by soldiers,
and not a single item remained.
In plain clothes and looking haggard,
he could no longer enter the palace gates.
The next day,
he went out again to the road by the southern gate of Cháng'ān,
and saw his wife and children in Zhāoguó Ward.
Their faces were sallow and dark.
His son carried firewood on his back,
his wife carried old wadding.
Chāng gathered them and wept,
then parted from them on the road,
and went away for good.
He took up residence in a Buddhist temple in Cháng'ān,
studying the teachings of the great masters.
In the first year of Dàlì (766 CE),
he followed the virtuous monk Yùnpíng of Zīshèng Temple to live at Hǎichí in the East Market,
and erected a stone pillar inscribed with a dhāraṇī.
He could write well enough to record names,
and reading Buddhist sutras,
he could also comprehend their profound meanings and ultimate truths.
He used his good heart to transform the people of the marketplace.
He built monks' quarters and Buddhist halls,
and planted beautiful grasses and sweet trees.
By day, he piled earth around roots,
drew water to irrigate bamboo,
and by night, practiced correct meditation in the meditation room.
In the third year of Jiànzhōng (782 CE),
the monk Yùnpíng's life reached its end.
After performing the funeral rites,
Chāng enshrined the relic pagoda to the east of Zhènguó Temple outside the eastern gate of Cháng'ān.
With his own hands, he planted a hundred pine and cypress trees,
built a small hut,
and lived beneath the pagoda.
Morning and evening, he burned incense and swept the grounds,
serving his master as if he were still alive.
While Shùnzōng was still the Crown Prince,
he donated three hundred thousand coins
to establish for Jiǎ Chāng a memorial hall for the Great Master and a fasting house.
He also built outer quarters,
housing itinerant people,
and took their rent as income.
Jiǎ Chāng consequently ate only one bowl of porridge daily,
drank one liter of thin gruel,
slept on a grass mat,
wore padded clothes,
and anything beyond that he entirely dedicated to the Buddha.
His wife, Pān shì, later also disappeared without a trace.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
his eldest son, Zhìxìn,
enlisted in the army of Bīngzhōu,
and followed Grand Minister of Education Lǐ Suì to the capital for an audience.
He visited Jiǎ Chāng at Chángshòu Ward.
Jiǎ Chāng acted as if he had not given birth to him,
severing ties and sending him away.
His second son, Zhìdé, returned,
trading silk in the markets of Luòyáng,
traveling back and forth to Cháng'ān.
Yearly, he presented gold and silk to Jiǎ Chāng,
but all were refused.
So they both left,
and never came again.
During the Yuánhé era,
Chén Hóngzǔ of Yǐngchuān took a friend out through the Chūnmíng Gate,
and saw dense bamboo and cypress trees,
with the scent of incense wafting along the road.
He dismounted and visited Jiǎ Chāng beneath the pagoda,
listened to his words,
and forgot that the day was growing late.
Jiǎ Chāng lodged Hóngzǔ in the fasting house,
and spoke of the course of his own life,
all of which was coherent and orderly,
and then touched upon matters of royal governance.
Hóngzǔ asked about the order and chaos of the Kāiyuán era.
Jiǎ Chāng said:
"In my youth,
I sought favor from His Majesty by means of cockfighting,
and His Majesty kept me as an entertainer,
housing me in the outer palace.
How could I have been in a position to know the affairs of the court?
However, there are things I can tell you.
I saw the Vice-Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Dù Xiān
sent out to be Military Governor of Qìxī,
acting concurrently as Censor-in-chief,
beginning to wield the authority of the censorate to awe distant regions.
I saw Gēshū Hàn garrison Liángzhōu,
capture Shíbǎo Fort,
garrison Qīnghǎi City,
march beyond Báilóng,
cross the Conglīng Mountains,
and demarcate the Tiěguān Pass as the border,
overseeing all of Hézuǒ Circuit.
Only after seven appointments did he concurrently act as Censor-in-chief.
I saw Zhāng Yuè administer Yōuzhōu.
Each year when he entered the pass,
he would have long-shafted carts and freight wagons,
transporting the silk cloth from the corvée and tax quotas of Héjiān and Jìzhōu,
the carts linked axle to axle,
crowding into the pass gate.
They were delivered to the royal storehouses.
The fine silks from Jiānghuái,
the brocades from Bāshǔ,
were merely for the amusement and adornment of the inner palace.
On the Hézhōu-Dūnhuáng route,
military agricultural colonies were maintained yearly,
to supply the frontier garrisons with food.
The surplus grain was transported to Língzhōu,
shipped down the Huáng Hé,
and entered the Tàiyuán Granary,
to prepare for lean years in Guānzhōng.
The millet and wheat of Guānzhōng
were stored among the common people.
When the Son of Heaven made progresses to the Five Sacred Mountains,
with thousands of carriages and tens of thousands of riders in his retinue,
they did not consume the people's food.
During the seasonal festivals of summer and winter, I was able to return on leave,
and walking through the market streets,
I saw white robes and white cotton cloth for sale.
Walking through the neighboring shops and market lanes,
if someone was performing an exorcism for illness,
the ritual required one bolt of black cloth.
If they could not obtain it despite offering a high price,
they would finally use a turban of gauze as a substitute.
Recently, I, an old man, leaning on my staff, went out the door,
and looked along the streets and avenues.
Looking east, west, south, and north,
I saw fewer than a hundred people wearing white robes.
Could it be that everyone in the empire
is now bearing arms?
In the twelfth year of Kāiyuán,
an edict decreed that if a position for a Vice-Minister of the Three Departments was vacant,
priority should be given to those who had previously served as Prefects.
If a position for a Departmental Director was vacant,
priority should be given to those who had previously served as District Magistrates.
By the time I reached forty,
the officials and clerks of the Three Departments,
those with talent and reputation for administering justice,
the greater ones were sent out to govern commanderies,
the lesser ones to administer districts.
Since I have lived by the main road,
I have often seen commandery Governors resting their horses here,
and they all looked distressed,
unhappy that the court's screening had sent them to govern commanderies.
In selecting officials during Kāiyuán,
it was based on filial piety and fraternal duty, and ability to govern people, that is all.
I never heard that the Jìnshì, Hóngcí, or Bácuì examinations were how they obtained worthy men.
The general situation was like this."
Then he shed tears.
He spoke again, saying:
"The August Emperor had the northerners submitting from their felt tents,
the easterners from Jīlín,
the southerners from Diānchí,
the westerners from the Kūnyí tribes,
coming to assemble once every three years.
The ceremonial etiquette of their court audiences,
the grace and favor of the imperial presence bestowed upon them,
clothing them in brocades and silk wadding,
feeding them with wine and food,
allowing them to fulfill their duties and then depart—
in the capital, no foreign guests remained.
Now, northern barbarians mingle and dwell together with the capital's residents,
taking wives and bearing children.
Among the youth of Cháng'ān, there are those with barbarian inclinations.
Look at the styles of headdresses, boots, and clothing—
are they not different from before?
Is this not a portent of strange objects?"
Hóngzǔ remained silent, not daring to respond, and left.
The Tale of the Liǔ shì.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Hán Yì of Chānglí was renowned for his poetry,
but his disposition was rather carefree and unconventional,
and he was trapped in poverty.
There was a man named Lǐ Shēng,
who was a close friend of Hán Yì.
His family wealth amounted to a thousand pieces of gold,
and he was proud-spirited and loved talent.
His favored concubine was named Liǔ Shì,
a beauty unparalleled in her time,
who delighted in witty conversation and jesting.
She was also skilled at singing and reciting poetry.
Lǐ Shēng housed her in a separate residence,
which he used as a place for feasting and singing with Hán Yì,
and he lodged Hán Yì in a building next to it.
Hán Yì had long been famous,
and those who came to visit and inquire after him
were all outstanding talents of the time.
Liǔ Shì peeked at him from behind the door
and said to her attendant:
"How could Master Hán remain poor and lowly forever?"
She thus set her heart on him.
Lǐ Shēng had always held Hán Yì in high esteem
and was never stingy with him.
Later, when he learned of Liǔ Shì's feelings,
he prepared a feast and invited Hán Yì to drink.
When they were well into their cups,
Lǐ Shēng said:
"Madam Liǔ possesses extraordinary beauty,
and Scholar Hán's literary talent is exceptional.
I wish to offer Liǔ to share your pillow, Master Hán.
Is this acceptable?"
Hán Yì, startled and trembling, rose from his seat and said:
"You have shown me great kindness,
sharing your clothes and food with me for so long.
How could I possibly take away what you love?"
Lǐ Shēng insisted earnestly.
Liǔ Shì, seeing his sincerity,
then bowed twice
and took her place by the mat.
Lǐ Shēng seated Hán Yì in the guest's place,
filled their cups to the brim, and they were extremely joyful.
Lǐ Shēng further gave three hundred thousand in funds
to assist Hán Yì's expenses.
Hán Yì admired Liǔ Shì's beauty,
and Liǔ Shì admired Hán Yì's talent.
Both obtained what they desired,
and their joy can be imagined.
The following year,
the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, Yáng Dù, placed Hán Yì in the highest rank in the examinations.
After living in seclusion for about a year,
Liǔ Shì said to Hán Yì:
"Glorious reputation reaching one's parents is
what people of old valued.
How can you, for the sake of a lowly washerwoman,
delay the beauty of plucking orchids?
Moreover, the utensils and resources here
are sufficient to sustain me until your return."
Hán Yì then went to visit his family in Qīngchí.
A little over a year later,
when food ran short,
she sold her cosmetics and accessories to support herself.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
rebels overthrew the two capitals,
and men and women fled in panic.
Liǔ Shì, being exceptionally beautiful,
and fearing she would not escape harm,
cut her hair and disfigured her appearance,
taking refuge in the Fǎlíng Temple.
At that time, Hóu Xīyì was appointed Military Governor of Zīqīng from Pínglú,
and having long admired Hán Yì's reputation,
invited him to serve as his secretary.
After Emperor Xuān returned to power with divine martial prowess,
Hán Yì sent a messenger to travel discreetly
to search for Liǔ Shì.
He placed gold dust in a silk pouch
and inscribed on it:
"Willow of Zhāngtái,
Willow of Zhāngtái,
does your former verdant beauty still remain?
Even if your long branches hang as of old,
they must have been plucked by another's hand."
Liǔ Shì, holding the gold, sobbed,
and those around her felt sorrow and pity.
She replied:
"Willow branch,
in the fragrant season,
my regret is giving you in farewell year after year.
A single leaf, borne by the wind, suddenly announces autumn;
even if you come, how could you pluck me now?"
Not long after,
a foreign general named Shāzhā Lì,
having recently earned merit,
secretly learned of Liǔ Shì's beauty,
abducted her to his residence,
and favored her exclusively.
When Hóu Xīyì was appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and went to court for an audience,
Hán Yì was able to accompany him.
Upon reaching the capital,
he could no longer find where Liǔ Shì was staying
and sighed with longing incessantly.
By chance, at Lóngshǒu Ridge,
he saw a servant driving a carriage drawn by a dappled ox,
followed by two maidservants.
Hán Yì happened to follow it,
and from within the carriage came a voice asking:
"Could it be Vice Director Hán?
I am Liǔ Shì."
She had a maidservant whisper that she had been forced to submit to Shāzhā Lì.
Hindered by others in the carriage,
she asked him to please wait for her the next morning at the gate of Dàozhèng Ward.
At the appointed time, he went,
and she tied a jade box with a light silk cord,
filled it with fragrant ointment,
and handed it to him from the carriage,
saying:
"We must now part forever.
I hope you will keep this in sincere remembrance."
She then turned the carriage around
and waved her hand at him.
Her light sleeves fluttered,
the fragrant carriage rumbled away.
His gaze broke, his mind bewildered,
lost in the startled dust.
Hán Yì was overwhelmed with emotion.
It happened that the various generals of Zīqīng were gathering for music at a tavern,
and they sent someone to invite Hán Yì.
Hán Yì forced himself to respond,
but his expression and demeanor were downcast,
and his voice was mournful and choked.
There was a military officer named Xǔ Jùn,
who prided himself on his strength and courage,
stroked his sword and said:
"There must be a reason.
I wish to be of use."
Hán Yì had no choice
and told him everything.
Xǔ Jùn said:
"Please give me a few words in your handwriting,
and I will bring her to you immediately."
He then put on a barbarian-style robe,
strapped on two quivers,
and with one horseman,
went straight to Shāzhā Lì's residence.
Waiting until Shāzhā Lì had traveled over a *li* from his home,
he loosened his collar, took hold of the reins,
forced the gates and pushed open the doors,
hurried in and shouted:
"The General has been taken ill!
He has sent me to summon his lady!"
The servants and attendants shrank back in fear,
not daring to look up.
He then went up to the main hall,
showed Liǔ Shì Hán Yì's note,
helped her onto a saddle horse,
and they sped off so fast the dust flew and the traces broke.
In a flash, they arrived.
Xǔ Jùn stepped forward, holding his robe, and said:
"Fortunately, I have not failed in my mission."
All those present gasped in amazement.
Liǔ Shì and Hán Yì
held hands and wept,
and together they ended the drinking gathering.
At that time, Shāzhā Lì enjoyed exceptional favor and grace.
Hán Yì and Xǔ Jùn, fearing disaster,
went to see Hóu Xīyì.
Hóu Xīyì was greatly astonished and said:
"Such deeds as I have done in my life—
could Jùn really act like this?"
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"Acting Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue and Vice Director of the Ministry of Works, concurrently Censor Hán Yì, has long served among my staff,
and his meritorious service has been repeatedly demonstrated.
Some time ago, he left to take the provincial examinations.
His concubine Liǔ Shì, cut off by the violent rebels,
took refuge with a famous nun.
Now, under the enlightened rule and peaceful governance,
all regions, near and far, follow transformation.
General Shāzhā Lì, violent and lawless,
relying on his slight merit,
seized a woman of determination,
interfering with a government that practices non-action.
My subordinate general, concurrently Vice Censor-in-Chief Xǔ Jùn,
whose clan originates from Yōujì,
is bold-hearted and courageous in decision,
took back Liǔ Shì
and returned her to Hán Yì.
His righteous fervor came from his innermost heart,
and though it clearly shows the sincerity of his stirred feelings;
he did not report the matter beforehand,
and thus indeed lacked the discipline of obeying orders."
Soon an imperial edict was issued:
"Liǔ Shì should be returned to Hán Yì.
Shāzhā Lì is granted two million in cash."
Liǔ Shì returned to Hán Yì.
Hán Yì later was promoted repeatedly, eventually becoming a Secretary in the Secretariat.
However, Liǔ Shì was one who aspired to guard her virtue but could not fully achieve it;
Xǔ Jùn was one who admired righteous fervor but did not act with full understanding.
If Liǔ Shì had been chosen for her beauty,
then the sincerity of 'warding off the bear' and 'declining the carriage' could have been continued;
If Xǔ Jùn were to be recommended for his talent,
then achievements like those at Cáo Kē and Miǎnchí could be accomplished.
For deeds become known through their traces,
and merit is established by deeds.
It is regrettable that Yù Yīn met with misfortune,
his righteous courage merely stirred in vain,
and none of it aligned with the proper way.
Is this not a case of change that deviates from the norm?
Truly, it was due to the circumstances he encountered.
The Tale of Everlasting Regret
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the celestial signs were harmonious,
and all within the Four Seas was tranquil.
Emperor Xuánzōng had been on the throne for many years,
and had grown weary of the toil of governance,
so all affairs of state,
great and small,
he began to entrust to his chief ministers.
Gradually, he withdrew into his inner palace for excursions and feasts,
amusing himself with music and feminine beauty.
Previously,
Empress Yuánxiàn and Consort Wǔ Shū had both enjoyed his favor,
but they had passed away one after the other.
Although within the palace there were thousands of girls from good families,
none pleased his eye.
The Emperor's heart was unsettled and unhappy.
At that time, every year in the tenth month,
the imperial carriage would proceed to the Huáqīng Palace.
Ladies of the inner and outer courts,
resplendent in their finery, would follow in his train.
Bathing in the lingering warmth of the sun's rays,
they were granted the hot springs for their ablutions.
Amidst the spring breezes and divine waters,
they moved with graceful ease.
The Emperor's heart stirred with feeling,
as if dimly anticipating an encounter.
But looking around him, before and behind,
the painted faces seemed as common as dirt.
He issued an edict
to Gāo Lìshì,
commanding him to search secretly among the outer palaces.
Thus, he found the daughter of Yáng Xuányǎn of Hóngnóng at the residence of the Shòu Prince.
She had already reached the age of capping.
Her hair was lustrous and her skin fine-textured;
her figure was slender yet full, perfectly proportioned;
her demeanor was graceful and alluring,
like Lady Lǐ of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
A separate hot spring pool was prepared,
and an edict granted her permission to bathe and cleanse herself.
When she emerged from the water,
her body was delicate, her strength slight,
as if unable to bear the weight of silken gauze.
Yet her brilliance shone forth,
radiantly illuminating all around her.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
On the day of her formal presentation,
the "Rainbow and Feather Garments" melody was performed to welcome her.
On the night they pledged their love,
he bestowed upon her golden hairpins and a jeweled box inlaid with gold to secure their bond.
He further commanded her to wear the "步搖" headdress,
from which dangled golden ear pendants.
The following year,
she was formally installed as Guìfēi,
her ceremonial allowances being half those of the Empress.
From then on, she cultivated her beauty,
sharpened her wit,
and displayed a myriad of charming and graceful mannerisms
to match the Emperor's desires.
The Emperor doted on her all the more.
Whether inspecting the customs across the nine provinces,
or performing the fēng and shàn sacrifices upon the Five Sacred Mountains,
whether on snowy nights at Líshān
or spring mornings at Shàngyáng Palace,
she traveled in the same carriage as the Emperor,
rested in the same chamber,
feasted at his exclusive table,
and slept in his exclusive quarters.

Although there were the Three Ladies, the Nine Concubines, the Twenty-Seven Wives of the Palace, the Eighty-One Imperial Consorts, along with the talented ladies of the rear palace and the singing girls of the Music Bureau, none could make the Son of Heaven cast a glance their way.
From this time on, no other woman from the Six Palaces received the Emperor's favor.
It was not merely her exceptional beauty and captivating demeanor
that alone achieved this;
it was also because of her intelligence and keen understanding,
her skill in clever and artful flattery,
and her ability to anticipate his wishes and desires—
qualities that are truly beyond description.
Her uncles and brothers were all appointed to high and prestigious positions,
ennobled as marquises.
Her sisters were enfeoffed as Ladies of States,
their wealth rivaling that of the imperial house.
Their carriages, robes, and mansions
were on par with those of the Grand Princesses,
while the imperial favor and influence they enjoyed
even surpassed them.
They came and went through the palace gates without being questioned,
causing the senior officials of the capital to view them with fear and resentment.
Therefore, the popular songs of the time said:
"When a girl is born, do not grieve and lament;
when a boy is born, do not rejoice with delight."
And also:
"A son gains no marquisate, a daughter becomes a consort;
behold, a girl now becomes the pillar of the family."
Such was the envy she aroused in people's hearts.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
her elder brother, Yáng Guózhōng, usurped the position of Chief Minister,
and foolishly manipulated the reins of state.
When Ān Lùshān led his troops towards the capital,
he used the pretext of punishing the Yáng family.
The Tóng Pass fell,
and the imperial carriage, with its kingfisher-feather banners, fled south.
Departing along the road from Xiányáng,
they halted at Mǎwéi.
The Six Armies hesitated and wavered,
halting their spears and refusing to advance.
The attending officials and officers prostrated themselves before the Emperor's horse,
requesting the execution of the offender (Cuò) to appease the empire.
Yáng Guózhōng, bearing the yak-tail tassel and the basin of water (symbols of submission and request for punishment),
died by the roadside.
But the feelings of the attendants were not yet assuaged.
The Emperor asked them,
and those who dared to speak at that time
requested that the Guìfēi be sacrificed to quell the empire's wrath.
The Emperor knew it was unavoidable,
yet could not bear to see her die.
He turned his sleeve to cover his face,
and had her led away.
In that moment of panic and confusion,
she ultimately met her end beneath a length of silk cord.
Afterwards, Emperor Xuánzōng took refuge in Chéngdū,
while Emperor Sùzōng ascended the throne in Língwǔ.
The following year,
the great villain met his end,
and the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
Emperor Xuánzōng was honored as Tàishàng Huáng (Retired Emperor),
and went to be cared for in the Southern Palace,
later moving from the Southern Palace to the Western Inner Palace.
As time passed and circumstances changed,
joy ended and sorrow came.
Whenever it came to spring days,
or winter nights,
when the pond lotuses bloomed in summer,
or the palace locust trees shed their leaves in autumn,
and the disciples of the Líyuán Academy,
with their jade pipes, would produce a sound,
and he heard a single note of the "Rainbow and Feather Garments" melody,
then the Emperor's countenance would grow sorrowful,
and those around him would sigh and weep.
For three years, his heart remained fixed in one thought,
and his longing did not diminish.
He sought her in his dreams and soul,
but vaguely and without success.
It happened that a Daoist priest came from Shǔ,
who knew of the Emperor's longing for Consort Yáng.
He claimed to possess the arts of Lǐ Shàojūn.
Emperor Xuánzōng was overjoyed,
and commanded him to summon her spirit.
The magician then exhausted his arts to search for her,
but she did not come.
He could also let his spirit roam and command the ether,
ascending to the celestial realms,
descending into the underworld,
to seek her,
but still did not see her.
He then searched extensively throughout the four directions and the heights and depths,
east to the utmost edge of heaven's shore,
crossing over Pénglái and Yíngzhōu,
where he saw the highest immortal mountain.
Upon it were many towers and pavilions.
Below the western wing was a grotto entrance,
facing east.
Peering at its gate,
he saw an inscription reading "The Courtyard of the Jade Consort, Tàizhēn."
The magician took out his hairpin and knocked on the door.
A young maid with double hair buns came out to answer.
Before the magician could hastily speak,
the maid with double buns went back inside.
After a short while, a green-clad serving girl arrived,
and asked him whence he came.
The magician then declared himself an envoy of the Táng Son of Heaven,
and conveyed his mission.
The green-clad girl said:
"The Jade Consort is just now resting.
Please wait a little while."
At that time, the sea of clouds was deep and vast,
and within the grotto-heaven, the day was waning.
The jade doors were tightly shut,
and all was silent and still.
The magician held his breath and gathered his feet,
standing with hands clasped before the gate.
After a long time, the green-clad girl invited him in,
saying:
"The Jade Consort is coming out."
Presently, he saw a person
wearing a golden lotus crown,
draped in purple gauze,
adorned with red jade pendants,
and trailing phoenix slippers.
Seven or eight attendants accompanied her.
She bowed to the magician,
and inquired after the Emperor's well-being.
Next, she asked about events since the fourteenth year of Tiānbǎo.
When she finished speaking, she appeared sorrowful.
Pointing to the green-clad girl,
she had her fetch the golden hairpins and the jeweled box inlaid with gold.
She broke each in half,
and handed them to the envoy, saying:
"In gratitude to the Tàishàng Huáng,
I respectfully offer these objects,
to seek renewal of our former affection."
The magician received her words and the tokens,
and as he was about to depart, his expression showed insufficiency.
Táng Wáng Xiānkè was the nephew of Liú Zhèn, a court official during the Jiànzhōng era.
Initially,
after Xiānkè’s father passed away,
he and his mother returned to her maiden family.
Zhèn had a daughter named Wúshuāng,
who was a few years younger than Xiānkè.
Both were still children,
playing and frolicking together.
Zhèn’s wife often jokingly called Xiānkè “the young master Wáng.”
Several years passed like this,
and Zhèn took especially good care of his widowed elder sister and Xiānkè.
One day,
Xiānkè’s mother fell seriously ill.
Summoning Zhèn, she made an agreement with him:
“I have only one son,
and you can imagine how much I care for him.
My regret is that I will not live to see him married.
Wúshuāng is dignified, beautiful, and intelligent—
I have long cherished her.
In the future, do not let her marry into another family.
I entrust Xiānkè to you.
If you truly promise me this,
I can close my eyes without regret.”
Zhèn said,
“Sister, you should rest quietly and take care of yourself;
do not trouble yourself with other matters.”
But his sister never recovered.
Xiānkè escorted her coffin
back to Xiāngdèng for burial.
After the mourning period ended,
he reflected on his own circumstances:
lonely and solitary as he was,
he ought to seek marriage
to continue the family line.
Wúshuāng had grown up—
would his uncle, despite his high rank and official prominence, abandon their old agreement?
So he packed his belongings and went to the capital.
At that time, Zhèn served as Commissioner of Taxes and Tributes,
and his residence was magnificent,
filled with carriages and caps of officials.
After Xiānkè paid his respects,
he was placed in the study quarters,
mingling with the students.
The uncle-nephew relationship remained as before,
but he heard nothing about the marriage arrangement.
Once, through a crack in the window, he caught a glimpse of Wúshuāng—
radiant and beautiful,
like an immortal from heaven.
Xiānkè became frantic,
fearing that the marriage might not come to pass.
He then sold his belongings,
obtaining several million coins,
and lavished gifts on his uncle and aunt’s attendants,
down to the servants and stable hands.
He also hosted banquets,
gaining access to the inner quarters.
All his cousins treated him with respect.
On his aunt’s birthday,
he bought novel gifts to present—
exquisite carvings of rhinoceros horn and jade
for her hair ornaments.
His aunt was delighted.
Ten days later,
Xiānkè sent an old maidservant
to convey his marriage proposal to his aunt.
His aunt said,
“This is my wish as well;
we should discuss the matter soon.”
A few evenings later,
a maidservant came to tell Xiānkè:
“The mistress just spoke to the master about the marriage.
The master said,
‘I never agreed to it before.’
From the way he spoke,
it seems there may be a problem.”
Hearing this, Xiānkè’s heart sank.
He stayed awake until dawn,
afraid his uncle would reject him,
yet he dared not slacken in his duties.
One day,
Zhèn went to court at sunrise.
Suddenly, he galloped back home,
sweating and panting.
He only cried,
“Lock the gates! Lock the gates!”
The whole household was terrified,
not knowing what had happened.
After a long while, he said:
“The troops from Jīngyuán have rebelled.
Yáo Lìngyán has led soldiers into the Hányuán Hall.
The emperor has fled north through the garden gate,
and all officials are rushing to join him.
I was worried about my wife and daughter,
so I came back briefly to make arrangements.”
He urgently summoned Xiānkè:
“Take charge of household affairs for me,
and I will give Wúshuāng to you in marriage.”
Xiānkè received the order
with surprise and gratitude, bowing in thanks.
Zhèn then packed twenty loads of gold, silver, silks, and brocades,
saying to Xiānkè:
“Change your clothes,
escort these goods out through the Kāiyuǎn Gate,
and find a secluded inn to stay.
I, your aunt, and Wúshuāng
will leave through the Qǐxià Gate
and catch up with you by circling the city.”
Xiānkè followed his instructions.
By sunset,
he had waited long at the inn outside the city, but they did not arrive.
The city gates had been locked since afternoon.
He gazed south until his eyes grew weary.
Then he mounted his horse,
lit a torch, and circled the city
to the Qǐxià Gate—
it was also locked.
There were several gatekeepers,
holding white clubs,
some standing, some sitting.
Xiānkè dismounted and asked slowly:
“What has happened in the city?”
He also asked,
“Did anyone leave through this gate today?”
A gatekeeper replied:
“Grand Marshal Zhū has become emperor.
In the afternoon, a man wearing a double hat
led four or five women,
trying to leave through this gate.
Everyone in the street recognized him—
they said it was Commissioner Liú.
The gate officers did not dare let him out.
As evening approached, pursuing cavalry arrived
and drove them all north.”
Xiānkè cried out in anguish,
then returned to the inn.
Near the end of the third watch,
the city gates suddenly opened.
Torches lit up the night like day,
and soldiers armed with weapons
shouted that executioners were leaving the city
to search for officials outside.
Xiānkè abandoned his baggage and horse, fleeing in panic.
He returned to Xiāngyáng
and lived in a village for three years.
Later, learning that the capital had been recaptured,
order restored in Cháng’ān,
and peace returned to the land,
he went back to the capital
to inquire about his uncle.
On Xīnchāng South Street,
as he halted his horse in hesitation,
someone suddenly bowed before him.
Looking closely,
he recognized Sāihóng, an old servant from his family.
Sāihóng had originally been born into the Wáng household;
his uncle often found him useful,
so he had kept him.
They clasped hands and shed tears.
Xiānkè asked Sāihóng:
“Are my uncle and aunt well?”
Sāihóng said,
“They are both at the Xīnghuà residence.”
Overjoyed, Xiānkè said,
“I will cross the street to see them.”
Sāihóng said,
“I have been freed from servitude
and now have a small house as a tenant,
making a living by selling silk.
It is already late tonight—
why not stay at my place for the night,
and we can go together early tomorrow?”
He led Xiānkè to his home,
where food and drink were plentiful.
As darkness fell,
news arrived:
“Commissioner Liú accepted a false appointment from the rebels.
He and his wife were both executed,
and Wúshuāng has been taken into the palace.”
Xiānkè wailed in grief and injustice,
moving the neighbors to pity.
He said to Sāihóng:
“The world is vast,
yet I have no relatives to turn to—
I do not know where to go.”
He asked further:
“Which of the old household servants remain?”
Sāihóng said,
“Only the maid Cǎipíng, who served Wúshuāng.
She is now in the residence of General Wáng Suìzhōng of the Imperial Guards.”
Xiānkè said,
“There is surely no hope of seeing Wúshuāng again,
If I could see Cǎipíng,
even death would be enough."
Thus, he sent in his card and requested an audience.
Meeting Suìzhōng as a junior relative,
he recounted the whole story in detail,
expressing his willingness to pay a high price
to redeem Cǎipíng.
Suìzhōng deeply appreciated his sincerity,
moved by the affair, and agreed to it.
Xiānkè rented a house
and lived with Hóng and Cǎipíng.
Sāihóng often said, "Young master, you are growing older;
it is time to seek an official post.
Why do you remain depressed and unhappy,
how will you pass the time?"
Xiānkè, moved by his words,
earnestly pleaded his case to Suìzhōng.
Suìzhōng recommended Xiānkè to the Capital Prefect Lǐ Qíyùn.
Qíyùn appointed Xiānkè, based on his previous service, as the Magistrate of Fùpíng County,
in charge of the Chánglè Courier Station.
After several months,
news suddenly arrived that a palace eunuch was escorting thirty palace women to the imperial mausoleum
to prepare for cleaning duties,
and they would lodge at the Chánglè Courier Station.
Ten curtained carriages arrived and stopped.
Xiānkè said to Sāihóng:
"I have heard that the palace ladies selected for the inner court
are mostly daughters of officials and gentry.
I fear Wúshuāng might be among them.
Could you take a look for me,
is that possible?"
Hóng said:
"There are thousands of palace ladies,
how could it possibly be Wúshuāng?"
Xiānkè said:
"Just go;
human affairs are never certain."
Thus, he had Sāihóng pose as a station attendant,
brewing tea outside the curtain,
and gave him three thousand coins.
He instructed him:
"Guard the tea set firmly,
do not leave even for a moment.
If you suddenly see something,
report to me immediately."
Sāihóng assented and left.
The palace women were all behind the curtain,
so they could not be seen,
only the noise of nighttime chatter could be heard.
Late into the night,
when all activity had ceased,
Sāihóng washed the utensils and tended the fire,
not daring to sleep.
Suddenly, he heard a voice from behind the curtain say:
"Sāihóng, Sāihóng,
how did you know I was here?
Is the young master well?"
After speaking, she sobbed.
Sāihóng said:
"The young master is in charge of this station.
Today, suspecting that you might be here,
he sent me to inquire after you."
She said again:
"I cannot speak long.
After I leave tomorrow,
go to the northeast room's cabinet,
under the purple mattress, and retrieve a letter to deliver to the young master."
After speaking, she left.
Suddenly, there was a commotion behind the curtain,
saying:
"A palace woman has fallen ill;
the eunuch urgently demands medicine."
It was Wúshuāng.
Sāihóng hurriedly reported to Xiānkè,
who exclaimed in surprise:
"How can I get to see her?"
Sāihóng said:
"They are currently repairing the Wèi Bridge.
You could pretend to be an official overseeing the bridge repairs.
When the carriages cross the bridge,
stand close to them.
If Wúshuāng recognizes you,
she will surely open the curtain,
and you might catch a glimpse."
Xiānkè did as he said.
When the third carriage passed,
the curtain indeed opened,
and he caught a glimpse—
it was truly Wúshuāng.
Xiānkè was overwhelmed with sorrow, longing, and regret,
unable to contain his emotions.
Sāihóng retrieved the letter from under the mattress in the cabinet
and delivered it to Xiānkè.
There were five sheets of floral paper,
all in Wúshuāng's own handwriting,
the words mournful and poignant,
narrating everything in detail.
Xiānkè read it,
swallowing his bitterness as tears fell—
this was their eternal farewell.
The letter concluded:
"I have often heard the imperial envoy say
that in Fùpíng County, there is an old jailer named Gǔ,
a man of great heart in this world.
Can you seek him out now?"
Xiānkè then submitted a request to the prefecture,
asking to be relieved of his station duties
and return to his original post.
He then sought out Old Jailer Gǔ,
who lived in a village cottage.
Xiānkè paid him a visit
and met Mr. Gǔ.
Whatever Mr. Gǔ desired,
Xiānkè spared no effort to provide,
gifting him silks, jewels, and precious jades
beyond count.
For a full year, he did not broach the subject.
When his term of office ended,
he lived idly in the county.
Mr. Gǔ suddenly came to him,
saying to Xiānkè:
"I, Hóng, am a mere warrior,
and I am growing old.
What use am I?
Yet you, young master, have treated me with utmost sincerity.
I have observed your intentions—
you have a request of this old man.
I am a man of deep feeling,
and moved by your profound kindness,
I am willing to sacrifice myself to repay you."
Xiānkè wept and bowed,
confessing the truth to Mr. Gǔ.
Mr. Gǔ looked up to the sky,
slapping his forehead several times, saying:
"This matter is extremely difficult.
Nevertheless, I will try to fulfill it for you, young master,
but do not expect it to happen overnight."
Xiānkè bowed and said:
"If only I could see her while I live,
how could I dare set a limit on how long it takes?"
Half a year passed without news.
One day, there was a knock at the door—
it was Mr. Gǔ sending a letter.
The letter said:
"The messenger from Máo Mountain has returned;
come here at once."
Xiānkè galloped on horseback to see Mr. Gǔ,
who said not a word.
When he questioned the messenger again,
Mr. Gǔ merely replied:
"It is done;
have some tea first."
Late at night,
he said to Xiānkè:
"Is there a maidservant in your household who recognizes Wúshuāng?"
Xiānkè answered with Cǎipíng,
and immediately fetched her.
Mr. Gǔ examined her carefully,
smiling with pleasure, saying:
"Lend her to me for three to five days;
you may return home for now."
Several days later,
rumors suddenly spread:
"A high-ranking official has passed through,
disposing of the palace women at the mausoleum."
Xiānkè was deeply disturbed by this.
He sent Sāihóng to investigate the victim—
it was Wúshuāng.
Xiānkè wailed in grief,
then sighed:
"I had placed my hopes on Mr. Gǔ,
but now she is dead.
What can be done?"
He wept and sobbed,
unable to control himself.
That night, in the deep hours,
there came urgent knocking at the door.
Upon opening it,
it was Mr. Gǔ,
leading in a sedan chair.
He said to Xiānkè:
"This is Wúshuāng.
She is dead now,
but her heart is still faintly warm.
She will revive the day after tomorrow.
Administer some medicinal broth sparingly,
and be absolutely quiet and discreet."
After speaking,
Xiānkè carried her into the inner room
and kept watch alone.
By dawn,
warmth had spread throughout her body.
Upon seeing Xiānkè,
she cried out once and fainted again.
She was revived only after treatment lasting into the night.
Mr. Gǔ then said:
"Lend me Sāihóng for a moment
to dig a pit behind the house."
When the pit was somewhat deep,
He drew his sword and cut off the head of the messenger in the pit.
Xiānkè was terrified.
Gǔ Shēng said:
"Young master, do not be afraid.
Today I have repaid your kindness in full.
I have heard that the Taoist priests of Máo Shān possess a certain drug art,
and those who take the drug die instantly,
but revive after three days.
I had someone specially obtain one pill.
Yesterday, I ordered Cǎipíng to disguise herself as a palace envoy,
claiming that Wúshuāng was part of a rebellious faction,
and bestowed this drug upon her, ordering her to take her own life.
At the foot of the mausoleum,
under the pretext of being a relative,
I redeemed her body with a hundred bolts of silk.
All along the roads and postal stations,
I have bribed heavily,
ensuring that no information will leak.
The Máo Shān messenger and the bearers of the sedan,
have been dealt with in the wilderness.
For you, young master,
I will also take my own life.
You must no longer stay here.
Outside the door, there are ten sedan carriers,
five horses,
and two hundred bolts of silk.
At the fifth watch, take Wúshuāng and depart immediately,
change your names and wander to avoid disaster."
After speaking,
he raised his sword,
and though Xiānkè tried to save him,
his head had already fallen.
So he covered the body together with the others.
Before dawn, they set off,
traveled through Sìshǔ and down the gorges,
and settled in Zhǔgōng.
Hearing no news from the capital,
they took their family and returned to their estate in Xiāngdèng,
where Xiānkè and Wúshuāng grew old together,
with many children and grandchildren.
Ah!
In life, separations and reunions are many,
but rarely is there anything like this,
often said to be unparalleled in ancient or modern times.
Wúshuāng suffered confiscation in a time of turmoil,
yet Xiānkè's determination,
remained unshaken even in death.
Finally, through Gǔ Shēng's extraordinary method, he retrieved her,
though more than ten innocent people died.
After fleeing through hardships,
they returned to their hometown,
and lived as husband and wife for fifty years.
How extraordinary!
The Tale of Huò Xiǎoyù
During the Dàlì era,
there was a young man from Lǒngxī named Lǐ Yì,
who was twenty years old
and had passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
achieving high rank.
The following year,
he was selected for the bácuì examination
and awaited further testing at the Ministry of Personnel.
In the sixth month of summer,
he arrived in Cháng'ān
and took up residence in Xīnchāng Ward.
He came from a distinguished and noble family,
and from a young age possessed literary talent and intellect.
His beautiful phrases and excellent lines
were considered unmatched at the time,
and respected elders
unanimously praised and admired him.
He often prided himself on his romantic demeanor,
longing to find a perfect match.
He extensively sought out famous courtesans,
but for a long time, he had not found a suitable one.
In Cháng'ān, there was a matchmaker named Bào Shíyīniáng,
who was originally a maid in the household of Consort Xuē.
She had redeemed her contract and gained her freedom,
and it had been over ten years since then.
She was clever and resourceful,
skilled with words,
and had connections with wealthy families and noble relatives.
She had visited them all,
and in matters of matchmaking and strategy,
she was regarded as a leader.
She had often received generous gifts from Lǐ Yì, along with earnest requests,
and she felt quite indebted to him.
After several months,
while Lǐ Yì was leisurely staying in the southern pavilion of his residence,
around the hour of shēn to wèi,
he suddenly heard a very urgent knocking at the door.
It was said that Bào Shíyīniáng had arrived.
He straightened his clothes and went to greet her,
welcoming her and asking:
"Lady Bào,
what brings you here so suddenly today?"
Bào smiled and said:
"Has the young master had any good dreams lately?
There is a celestial being
who has descended to the mortal world.
She does not seek wealth or goods,
but only admires romance and talent.
Such a person
is a perfect match for you, Tenth Gentleman."
Upon hearing this, Lǐ Yì leaped up in excitement,
his spirit soaring and his body feeling light.
He took Bào's hand, bowing and thanking her repeatedly, saying:
"I would serve as her slave for a lifetime,
and even death would not daunt me."
He then asked for her name and residence.
Bào explained in detail:
"She is the youngest daughter of the late Prince Huò, and her given name is Xiǎoyù.
The prince loved her dearly.
Her mother is named Jìngchí,
and Jìngchí was the prince's favored concubine.
After the prince's passing,
his brothers, because she was born of a lowly concubine,
did not take her in,
so they divided the assets and gave her a share,
sending her to live outside the palace.
She changed her surname to Zhèng,
so people did not know she was a prince's daughter.
Her beauty is lush and radiant,
unlike anything I have ever seen in my life.
Her noble sentiments and graceful demeanor
surpass others in every way.
In music, poetry, and literature,
there is nothing she does not understand.
Recently, she sent me to find a good young man,
one whose character and style match hers.
I told her all about you, Tenth Gentleman,
and she already knew of your name, Lǐ Shíláng.
She was extremely pleased.
She lives in Shèngyè Ward, in the alley by the old temple,
in the house with the carriage gate.
I have already arranged a meeting with her.
Tomorrow at noon,
just go to the entrance of the alley and look for Guìzǐ,
and you will find it."
After Bào left,
Lǐ Yì immediately prepared for the journey.
He ordered his servant, Qiū Hóng,
to borrow a black horse with a golden bridle
from his cousin, Shàng Gōng, who served as a military advisor in the capital.
That evening,
Lǐ Yì washed his clothes and bathed,
groomed himself and dressed up,
filled with joy and excitement,
and stayed awake all night.
At dawn,
he put on his headscarf,
looked at himself in the mirror,
fearing only that things might not go well.
As he paced back and forth,
it reached midday.
He then ordered the carriage to depart quickly,
heading straight for Shèngyè Ward.
Upon arriving at the appointed place,
he indeed saw a maid standing and waiting.
She came forward and asked:
"Are you perhaps Lǐ Shíláng?"
He immediately dismounted,
and she had him lead the horse inside the courtyard,
quickly locking the gate.
He saw Bào coming out from inside,
smiling from afar and saying:
"What kind of young man is this, barging in so hastily?"
Before Lǐ Yì could finish his playful banter,
she led him through the inner gate.
In the courtyard, there were four cherry trees,
and to the northwest hung a parrot cage.
Seeing Lǐ Yì enter,
the parrot immediately said:
"Someone is coming in,
quickly lower the curtains."
Lǐ Yì was by nature reserved and calm,
but his heart was still filled with doubt and fear.
Suddenly hearing the bird speak,
he was startled and dared not proceed.
Hesitating for a moment,
Bào led Jìngchí down the steps to welcome him,
and they invited him to sit opposite them.
She appeared to be in her forties,
graceful and charming,
and her conversation and laughter were very captivating.
She then said to Lǐ Yì:
"I have long heard of your talent and romantic demeanor, Tenth Gentleman,
and now I see your elegant and refined appearance.
Truly, your reputation is well-deserved.
I have a daughter,
though she lacks proper instruction,
her appearance is not unattractive.
To be matched with a gentleman like you
would be quite suitable.
I have often heard Bào Shíyīniáng convey your intentions,
and now I would like to have her serve you forever."
Lǐ Yì thanked her and said:
"I am humble, dull, and foolish,
and never expected to receive such attention.
If you would accept me,
it would be an honor for life and death."
They then ordered wine and food,
and had Xiǎoyù come out from the eastern chamber of the hall.
Lǐ Yì immediately bowed to greet her.
He felt as if the entire room
was filled with jade trees and precious woods,
shining and reflecting each other,
and her gaze was dazzlingly brilliant.
She then sat beside her mother.
Her mother said to her:
"You often loved reciting the lines, 'When the wind moves the bamboo and the curtain opens,
I suspect it is an old friend coming.'
These are the very lines of Tenth Gentleman's poem.
You have been reciting and thinking about them all day—
how does it compare to meeting him in person?"
Xiǎoyù lowered her head and smiled softly,
whispering:
"Meeting in person is not as good as hearing the reputation,
but how could a talented man lack good looks?"
Lǐ Yì immediately stood up and bowed repeatedly, saying:
"The young lady values talent,
and this humble man values beauty.
Our mutual affections reflect each other,
combining talent and looks."
Mother and daughter looked at each other and smiled,
and then they raised their glasses for several rounds of wine.
Lǐ Yì stood up
and asked Xiǎoyù to sing.
At first, she refused,
but her mother insisted.
Her voice was clear and bright,
and the melody was exquisite and extraordinary.
As the wine ended and dusk approached,
Bào led Lǐ Yì to the western courtyard to rest.
The courtyard was quiet and the rooms spacious,
with luxurious curtains and drapes.
Bào ordered the maids, Guìzǐ and Huànshā,
to help Lǐ Yì remove his boots and untie his belt.
Soon, Xiǎoyù arrived,
her words gentle and warm,
her tone soft and charming.
As she removed her silk garments,
her demeanor was exceptionally alluring.
Under the lowered curtains and on the intimate pillow,
they enjoyed the utmost joy and love.
Lǐ Yì felt that even the encounters of Wūshān or Luòpǔ could not surpass this.
In the middle of the night,
Xiǎoyù suddenly looked at Lǐ Yì with tears in her eyes and said:
"I am from a courtesan family,
and I know I am not your equal.
Now, you love me for my beauty,
and I entrust myself to your kindness and virtue.
But I fear that once my beauty fades,
your affection will shift and change,
So that the dodder vine has nothing to cling to,
and the autumn fan is cast aside.
At the height of joy,
sorrow comes unbidden."
Shēng heard this,
and was deeply moved.
He then placed his arm as a pillow for her,
and gently said to Yù:
"All my lifelong wishes,
are fulfilled today.
Even if my bones are ground to powder,
I vow never to leave you.
Why do you speak such words, my lady?
Please bring plain silk,
that I may write our pledge upon it."
Yù then dried her tears,
and ordered her maid Yīngtáo
to lift the bed-curtains, hold the candle,
and bring Shēng the brush and inkstone.
In her leisure from music,
Yù was fond of poetry and books;
the boxes, brushes, and inkstones
were all old items from the Wáng family.
She then took an embroidered pouch,
and brought out three feet of plain silk with black-ruled lines from a Yuè lady, handing it to Shēng.
Shēng had always been talented and thoughtful;
taking up the brush, he completed the text,
invoking mountains and rivers as metaphors,
pointing to the sun and moon as witnesses of his sincerity.
Every sentence was earnest and sincere,
moving to hear.
When he finished writing,
she ordered it stored in a precious casket.
From then on, they were tenderly devoted to each other,
like kingfishers soaring among the clouds.
Thus they passed two years,
together day and night.
In the spring of the following year,
Shēng passed the imperial examination with distinction in literary composition and judgment,
and was appointed Registrar of Zhèng County.
By the fourth month,
when he was about to take up his post,
he went to pay respects to his family in the Eastern Capital.
Many relatives in Cháng'ān
held farewell banquets for him.
The spring scenery still lingered,
and the summer scenes were just beginning to flourish.
When the wine was finished and the guests had dispersed,
sorrow of parting filled their hearts.
Yù said to Shēng:
"With your talent, reputation, and fame,
many people admire you,
and wish to form marriage alliances;
surely there are many.
Moreover, you have strict parents at home,
and no principal wife in your chamber.
Now that you are leaving,
you will surely enter into a fine marriage.
The words of our pledge
will then be but empty talk.
Yet I have a small wish,
which I wish to state directly.
May it remain forever in your heart;
will you listen?"
Shēng, surprised and puzzled, said:
"What fault have I committed,
that you suddenly speak like this?
Please tell me what you wish to say;
I will certainly respect and comply."
Yù said:
"I am just eighteen,
and you are only twenty-two.
Until you reach the age for a proper marriage,
there are still eight years.
All the joy and love of my life,
I wish to fulfill within this period.
After that, you may splendidly choose a family of high standing,
to form a Qin-Jin alliance,
and it will still not be too late.
I will then renounce worldly affairs,
cut my hair and don black robes.
My long-cherished wish
will thus be satisfied."
Shēng felt both ashamed and moved;
tears flowed unbidden.
He then said to Yù:
"I swear by the bright sun,
that I will keep this vow in life and death.
To grow old together with you
still might not fulfill my sincere wish;
how would I dare to be unfaithful?
I earnestly beg you not to doubt,
but to remain here peacefully and wait.
By the eighth month,
I will certainly return to Huàzhōu,
and then send for you to welcome you,
so our reunion will not be far away."
A few days later,
Shēng bid farewell and went east.
Ten days after taking up his post,
he requested leave to go to the Eastern Capital to visit his family.
Before he reached home,
his mother had already discussed with him about his cousin, a young lady of the Lú family;
the marriage arrangement was already settled.
His mother was usually stern and resolute;
Shēng hesitated and did not dare to refuse or decline.
He then performed the ceremonial thanks,
and a near wedding date was set.
The Lú family was also a prominent clan;
when marrying a daughter to another family,
the betrothal gifts must amount to a million cash as agreed,
and if the sum fell short,
in principle it would not proceed.
Shēng's family was originally poor;
the matter required borrowing money.
So, using the pretext of leave,
he traveled far to visit relatives and friends,
journeying across the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
from autumn until summer.
Shēng himself felt he had betrayed their pledge,
and greatly delayed his promised return date.
He remained silent and did not let news reach her,
wishing to cut off her hopes.
He vaguely entrusted messages to relatives and friends,
not allowing any word to leak out.
Since Shēng had passed the promised date,
Yù repeatedly sought news of him.
Empty words and deceitful tales
varied from day to day.
She widely sought diviners and shamans,
and inquired everywhere through divination.
Carrying sorrow and nursing resentment,
for over a year,
she lay weak and ill in her empty chamber,
until she fell gravely ill.
Although Shēng's letters and messages had completely ceased,
Yù's longing and hope did not waver.
She bribed relatives and friends,
to get news through,
but as her search became urgent,
her funds were repeatedly exhausted.
She often secretly ordered her maids to stealthily sell clothing and playthings from her cases,
mostly entrusting them for sale at the shop of Hóu Jǐngxiān in the Western Market's consignment store.
Once she ordered her maid Huànshā
to take a purple jade hairpin
to Hóu Jǐngxiān's house to sell it.
On the way, she met an old jade craftsman from the palace workshops,
who saw what Huànshā was holding,
came forward and recognized it, saying:
"This hairpin was made by me.
In past years, the youngest daughter of Prince Huò,
when she was about to put up her hair,
ordered me to make this,
rewarding me with ten thousand cash.
I have never forgotten it.
Who are you?
How did you obtain it?"
Huànshā said:
"My young lady is precisely the daughter of Prince Huò.
Her family affairs have fallen into ruin,
and she has lost her status, belonging to another.
Her husband went east to the capital,
and there has been no news since.
Depressed and sorrowful, she fell ill,
and it is now nearly two years.
She ordered me to sell this,
to bribe people,
to seek news of him."
The jade craftsman sadly shed tears and said:
"Noble children,
losing their opportunities and falling into hardship,
can come to such a state.
My remaining years are nearing their end,
yet I witness such rise and fall,
and cannot help but feel sorrow."
He then took her to the residence of Princess Yánxiān,
and fully recounted the previous events.
The princess also felt sorrow and sighed for a long time,
and gave one hundred and twenty thousand cash.
At that time, the Lú girl whom Shēng was betrothed to was in Cháng'ān.
After Shēng had completed the betrothal payments,
he returned to Zhèng County.
In the twelfth month of that year,
he again requested leave to enter the city for the marriage,
secretly divining for a quiet residence,
not letting anyone know.
There was a Jīngdiàn graduate named Cuī Yǔnmíng,
Shēng's maternal cousin,
a man of very honest and kind nature.
In past years, he had often enjoyed gatherings with Shēng in the Zhèng household,
sharing cups and laughter,
without any estrangement.
Whenever he received news from Shēng,
he would faithfully inform Yù.
Yù often provided him with firewood, fodder, and clothing,
supporting Cuī,
and Cuī was quite grateful.
When Shēng arrived,
Cuī faithfully informed Yù of everything.
Yù, resentful and sighing, said:
"How could such a thing happen in this world?"
He invited all his relatives and friends,
summoning them from many directions.
Li Shēng, on his part, felt he had broken his promise by missing the appointed date,
and knowing that Yù's illness was grave and lingering,
he was ashamed and remorseful, forcing himself to sever ties,
and ultimately refused to go.
He would leave in the morning and return at dusk,
hoping to avoid her.
Yù wept day and night,
completely forgetting to eat or sleep,
longing for a single meeting,
yet finding no opportunity.
Her grief and indignation grew deeper,
and she lay weak and exhausted on her bed.
From then on, those in Cháng'ān who knew of this matter,
the refined and romantic gentlemen,
all sympathized with Yù's deep affection;
the chivalrous and heroic types,
were all angered by Li Shēng's heartless conduct.
It was already the third month,
and many people were out enjoying the spring scenery.
Li Shēng, along with five or six companions, went to Chóngjìng Temple to admire the peonies.
Strolling along the western corridor,
they took turns reciting poems.
Among them was a man named Wéi Xiàqīng from Jīngzhào,
a close friend of Li Shēng's,
who was also in the group.
He said to Li Shēng:
"The scenery is exceedingly beautiful,
the plants and trees are flourishing.
How pitiful is Lady Zhèng,
bearing her grievances alone in an empty room.
That you, sir, can ultimately abandon her,
truly marks you as a cruel man.
A true gentleman's heart
should not be like this.
You, sir, ought to reflect upon this."
Amidst these reproaches and admonishments,
suddenly there appeared a gallant gentleman,
wearing a light yellow ramie robe,
carrying a vermilion-colored
bow,
with a handsome and elegant demeanor,
and lightly luxurious clothing.
He was followed only by a young foreign servant with cropped hair.
Stealthily approaching to listen,
he soon stepped forward and bowed to Li Shēng, saying:
"Are you not Lǐ Shíláng?
My clan originates from Shāndōng,
and we are connected by marriage to the imperial relatives.
Although I lack literary talent,
my heart has always delighted in worthy men.
I have long admired your reputation and brilliance,
and have constantly yearned to meet you.
Today, I am fortunate to have this encounter,
allowing me to behold your noble countenance.
My humble residence
is not far from here.
I also have musicians and singers,
sufficient to delight the spirit.
There are eight or nine enchanting beauties,
and over ten fine horses—
all at your disposal as you wish.
I only hope you will pay a visit."
Li Shēng's companions,
hearing these words,
praised and admired the man all the more.
So Li Shēng rode alongside the gallant gentleman,
swiftly passing through several wards,
until they reached Shèngyè.
Knowing they were near Zhèng Yù's dwelling,
Li Shēng had no wish to pass by.
He then fabricated an excuse,
intending to turn his horse around.
The gallant gentleman said:
"My humble home is just a stone's throw away;
can you bear to abandon me thus?"
Then he grabbed the reins of Li Shēng's horse
and led it forward.
In the midst of this delay,
they had already reached the lane where Zhèng Yù lived.
Li Shēng, his spirit bewildered,
whipped his horse, wanting to turn back.
The gallant gentleman hastily ordered several servants
to seize and carry him forward.
They hurriedly pushed him through the carriage gate,
and immediately ordered it locked.
Then they announced:
"Lǐ Shíláng has arrived!"
The entire household was startled and overjoyed,
their voices audible outside.
The night before,
Yù had dreamed that a man in a yellow robe brought Li Shēng to her,
led him to the mat,
and had Yù remove his shoes.
Startled awake, she told her mother,
and then interpreted it herself, saying:
"'Shoe' (xié) signifies 'harmony' (xié);
it means husband and wife will reunite.
'To remove' (tuō) means 'to sever' (jiě).
Having reunited only to be severed,
surely means an eternal parting.
Judging from this omen,
we are destined to meet,
but after meeting,
I shall die."
At dawn,
she asked her mother to help her dress and do her hair.
Her mother, seeing her long illness,
thought her mind was confused and unsettled,
and did not quite believe her.
Nevertheless, with reluctant effort,
she forced herself to dress and arrange Yù's hair.
Just as her toilette was completed,
Li Shēng indeed arrived.
Yù had been gravely ill for a long time,
needing help even to turn over.
Suddenly hearing of Li Shēng's arrival,
she abruptly rose by herself,
changed clothes and came out,
as if inspired by a divine force.
Then she met Li Shēng.
With contained anger, she fixed her gaze upon him,
and spoke no more.
Her frail form and delicate beauty
seemed unable to bear the intensity of emotion.
From time to time, she covered her face with her sleeve,
then turned back to look at Li Shēng.
Moved by the sight and pained by the person,
all present sighed and wept.
After a short while,
dozens of platters of wine and food
arrived from outside.
Everyone looked on in astonishment.
Hastily asking the reason,
they learned it was all sent by the gallant gentleman.
So they laid out the feast,
and sat down together.
Yù then turned her body and face aside,
gazing sidelong at Li Shēng for a long time.
Finally, she raised a cup of wine, poured it on the ground, and said:
"I am a woman,
whose fate is as wretched as this;
you are a man,
whose heart is as faithless as this.
In the bloom of youth and tender years,
I shall die bearing this hatred.
My kind mother is still alive,
yet I cannot support her in her old age.
Fine silks, music, and song—
from now on are ended forever.
The suffering I shall carry to the Yellow Springs,
is all caused by you.
Master Lǐ, Master Lǐ,
now we part forever.
After I die,
I shall become a fierce ghost,
and make your wives and concubines
never know peace for the rest of their days!"
Then she took Li Shēng's arm with her left hand,
threw the cup to the ground,
and after several long, mournful cries, she died.
Her mother then placed the corpse in Li Shēng's arms,
telling him to call to her,
but she did not revive.
Li Shēng wore mourning garments for her,
weeping bitterly day and night.
On the evening before the burial,
Li Shēng suddenly saw Yù within the funeral curtains,
her appearance lovely and beautiful,
just as in life.
She wore a pomegranate-red skirt,
a purple vest,
and a red-green cape.
Leaning sideways against the curtain,
holding an embroidered sash in her hand,
she looked at Li Shēng and said:
"I am ashamed that you see me off,
and that affection still remains.
Even in the netherworld,
how could I not be moved and sigh?"
Having spoken,
she was seen no more.
The next day,
she was buried at Yùsù Plain in Cháng'ān.
Li Shēng went to the gravesite,
poured out his grief, and then returned.
Over a month later,
he performed the wedding rites with Miss Lú.
Saddened by memories and stirred by objects,
he remained depressed and joyless.
In the fifth month of summer,
he traveled with his wife Lú
back to Zhèng County.
About ten days after arriving in the county,
while Li Shēng was sleeping with Miss Lú,
suddenly there came a scolding sound from outside the bed curtains.
Startled, Li Shēng looked
and saw a man,
He appeared to be in his twenties,
with a gentle and handsome appearance.
Hiding behind the curtain,
he repeatedly beckoned to Lú Shì.
The young man, flustered and frightened, stood up,
circled the curtain several times,
but the figure vanished in an instant.
From then on, the young man harbored suspicion and resentment in his heart,
filled with endless doubts and jealousies.
Between husband and wife,
life became unbearable.
