Occasionally, close relatives
gently tried to persuade and comfort him,
and the young man’s feelings eased slightly.
Ten days later,
the young man returned from outside again,
and Lú Shì was playing the zither on the bed.
Suddenly, a patterned inlaid box was thrown in through the door,
about an inch square,
containing a light silk cloth,
tied into a love knot,
which fell into Lú Shì’s lap.
The young man opened it to look,
and saw two red beans,
one click beetle,
one fáshāzī,
and a small amount of lǘ□mèi.
At that moment, the young man roared in anger,
his voice like that of a jackal or tiger.
He grabbed the zither and struck his wife with it,
demanding that she tell the truth.
Lú Shì, however, could never explain herself.
After that, he often violently beat her,
subjecting her to all kinds of cruelty and abuse,
and eventually took the matter to court and divorced her.
After Lú Shì was sent away,
if the young man ever shared a bed
with a maidservant or concubine,
he would immediately become jealous,
and sometimes even killed them for it.
Once, while traveling in Guǎnglíng,
he obtained a famous courtesan named Yíng Shíyīniáng,
whose appearance was delicate and charming.
The young man was very fond of her.
Whenever they sat facing each other,
he would often say to Yíng:
"I once obtained a certain courtesan in a certain place,
who committed a certain offense,
and I killed her using a certain method."
He repeated this daily,
hoping to make her fear him,
so as to maintain strict discipline in the household.
When he went out, he would cover Yíng on the bed with a bathtub,
sealing it all around,
and upon returning, he would inspect it carefully
before opening it.
He also kept a short sword,
extremely sharp,
and once said to a maidservant:
"This is made of Géxī iron from Xìnzhōu,
and it only cuts off the heads of wrongdoers."
In general, whenever the young man saw a woman,
he would become suspicious and jealous.
Even after marrying three times,
his behavior remained the same as before.
The Tale of Yīngyīng
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar named Zhāng.
His nature was gentle and refined,
his appearance elegant and handsome,
and inwardly he possessed firmness and integrity;
nothing improper could sway him.
Sometimes when friends gathered for outings or banquets,
amidst the clamor and commotion,
others would all be boisterous and eager,
as if fearing they might miss out;
Zhāng merely complied amiably,
yet remained ultimately unperturbed.
Because of this, by the age of twenty-three,
he had never been intimate with a woman.
Those who knew him questioned him about it.
He excused himself, saying:
"The Rhapsody on the Lecher is not about one who loves beauty,
but about one with vile conduct.
I am truly one who appreciates beauty,
yet I have simply not encountered the right one.
How can I explain this?
Generally, when it comes to things of exceptional quality,
I have never failed to linger over them in my heart.
This shows that I am not one who forgets passion."
The questioner took note of this.
Not long after,
Zhāng traveled to Pú.
About ten miles east of Pú,
there was a monastery called Pǔjiù Temple,
where Zhāng took lodging.
It happened that a widowed lady of the Cuī family,
who was returning to Cháng'ān,
was passing through Pú
and also stopped at this temple.
Lady Cuī
was a daughter of the Zhèng family;
Zhāng's mother was also from the Zhèng family,
so tracing their kinship,
she was a maternal aunt from a different branch.
That year,
Hún Jiān died in Pú.
There was a eunuch, Dīng Wényǎ,
who was incompetent in military affairs.
The soldiers, taking advantage of the mourning period, became disorderly
and plundered the people of Pú extensively.
The Cuī family household
possessed considerable wealth
and many servants.
Traveling and lodging there, they were terrified
and did not know where to turn for protection.
Previously, Zhāng had been on good terms with some associates of the Pú garrison commander.
He requested officers to protect them,
and thus they escaped disaster.
After more than ten days,
the Surveillance Commissioner Dù Què, bearing the Emperor's command to assume overall military authority,
issued orders to the army,
and the troops thereby became pacified.
Lady Zhèng felt profoundly grateful for Zhāng's kindness.
She therefore prepared a feast and invited Zhāng,
hosting a banquet for him in the main hall.
Furthermore, she said to Zhāng:
"Your aunt, a lonely widow,
raising young children,
unfortunately encountered the great turmoil of the troops' rebellion.
Truly, she could not have preserved her own life,
nor the lives of her young son and daughter.
It is as if you gave them life.
How can this be compared to ordinary kindness?
Now I shall have them meet you with the courtesy due an elder brother,
hoping in this way to repay your kindness."
She summoned her son,
named Huānláng,
who was about ten years old,
with a very gentle and handsome appearance.
Next, she summoned her daughter:
"Come out and bow to your elder brother.
Your elder brother saved your life."
After a long delay, she declined, pleading illness.
Lady Zhèng angrily said:
"Elder Brother Zhāng protected your life.
If not for him,
you would have been captured.
Can you still cling to distant propriety?"
After a long while, she finally came.
She wore ordinary clothes, her face radiant,
without any added adornment.
Her hair hung down, meeting her dark eyebrows;
only a faint blush graced both cheeks.
Her beauty was extraordinary,
her brilliance stirring to behold.
Startled, Zhāng bowed to her in greeting.
She then sat beside Lady Zhèng.
Because she had been compelled by Lady Zhèng to appear,
her gaze was fixed and resentful,
as if her body could scarcely bear it.
When asked her age,
Lady Zhèng said:
"She was born in the seventh month of the year Jiǎzǐ of the present Emperor's reign,
and now it is the year Gēngchén of the Zhēnyuán era.
She is seventeen years old."
Zhāng tried gently to guide the conversation with words,
but she did not respond.
The banquet concluded without further exchange.
From then on, Zhāng was captivated by her.
He wished to express his feelings to her,
but found no way to do so.
Cuī had a maidservant named Hóngniáng.
Zhāng privately bowed to her several times,
and seizing an opportunity, finally confided his heartfelt feelings.
The maid was indeed startled and dismayed.
Blushing, she fled.
Zhāng regretted it.
The next day,
the maid came again.
Zhāng, ashamed, apologized to her,
and spoke no more of his request.
The maid then said to Zhāng:
"What you, young master, said,
I dare not speak of,
nor dare I reveal it.
However, the marital relations of the Cuī family
are well known to you, sir.
Why not, on account of your kindness, seek to marry her?"
Zhāng said:
"Since my childhood,
my nature has been such that I do not engage in casual liaisons.
Sometimes, even when among beauties in silken garments,
I have never cast a lingering glance.
I never imagined that
I would ultimately be ensnared like this.
Yesterday, during that single banquet,
I nearly lost my self-control.
These past few days,
I walk forgetting to stop,
eat forgetting to be full.
I fear I cannot last beyond a day or two.
If I were to seek marriage through a matchmaker,
going through the betrothal rituals and inquiries,
then within two or three months,
you would be looking for me in the shop of dried fish.
What do you advise me to do?"
The maid said:
"Cuī is chaste and cautious, guarding herself.
Even her elders cannot offend her with improper words.
The schemes of a servant like me
would certainly be hard for her to accept.
However, she is skilled at composing literature.
Often she ponders over verses,
lingering long in melancholy yearning.
You, sir, might try to confuse her with love poems expressing your feelings.
Otherwise, there is no way."
Zhāng was greatly pleased.
He immediately composed two spring-themed poems and gave them to her.
That evening,
Hóngniáng came again,
holding a colored letter paper which she gave to Zhāng, saying:
"This is by Cuī's command."
Its title was "Moonlit Night, the Fifteenth of the Month."
The verses read:
"Awaiting the moon beneath the western wing,
the breeze approaches, the door half-open.
Brushing the wall, flower shadows stir—
could it be my fair one comes?"
Zhāng also faintly understood its meaning.
That evening
was the fourteenth day of the second month.
East of Cuī's quarters was an apricot tree.
By climbing, one could cross over.
On the evening of the full moon,
Zhāng used a ladder to climb the tree and cross over,
reaching the western wing.
The door was indeed half-open.
Hóngniáng was asleep on the bed.
Zhāng startled her awake.
Hóngniáng exclaimed in alarm:
"How did you get here, young master?"
Zhāng then deceived her, saying:
"Cuī's letter summoned me.
Please inform her for me."
Shortly after,
Hóngniáng returned,
saying repeatedly:
"She's coming!
She's coming!"
Zhāng was both delighted and apprehensive,
certain that he would succeed.
When Cuī arrived,
she was in formal attire, her expression stern.
She sternly reproached Zhāng:
"Your kindness, elder brother,
saved my family.
It is profound.
Therefore, my kind mother entrusted her young son and daughter to you.
How could you, through an unworthy maid,
convey licentious and wanton words?
You began by righteously protecting others from disorder,
yet end by seeking to take advantage of disorder for your own gain.
This is replacing one disorder with another.
How far apart are they?
I wished to conceal your words,
To protect another's deceit,
is unrighteous;
to reveal it to my mother,
would betray another's kindness,
is inauspicious;
to entrust it to maids and servants,
I fear they would not convey my true sincerity.
Therefore, I rely on this short letter,
wishing to state my feelings myself,
yet still fearing you might find it difficult to accept,
so I use these humble and plain words,
hoping they will surely reach you.
This improper action,
can I not feel ashamed in my heart?
I only wish to restrain myself with propriety,
and not descend into disorder. 」
After speaking,
she turned and left.
Zhāng Shēng was lost in thought for a long time,
then climbed back over the wall and left,
and from then on, he despaired.
Several nights later,
Zhāng Shēng was sleeping alone by the window,
when suddenly someone woke him.
Startled, he rose,
and saw Hóngniáng carrying bedding and a pillow.
Patting Zhāng, she said:
「She has come!
She has come!
Why are you still sleeping? 」
Then she placed the pillow and double bedding and left.
Zhāng Shēng rubbed his eyes and sat upright for a long time,
still suspecting it was a dream,
yet he waited with proper decorum.
Soon, Hóngniáng escorted Cuī Shì to him,
who arrived looking shy and radiant,
her limbs too weak to move,
her former dignified composure,
no longer the same.
That night was the eighteenth of the month,
the slanting moon was bright,
its faint light illuminating half the bed.
Zhāng Shēng felt as if floating,
and suspected she might be an immortal,
not thinking she had come from the mortal world.
After a while,
the temple bell tolled,
dawn approached,
and Hóngniáng urged her to leave.
Cuī Shì wept softly and plaintively,
and Hóngniáng escorted her away,
without a word spoken the entire night.
At daybreak, Zhāng Shēng rose,
doubting himself:
「Was it all a dream? 」
When it grew light,
he saw her makeup on his arm,
her fragrance on his clothes,
the glimmer of tears,
still shining on the bedding.
After this, more than ten days passed,
with no further news.
Zhāng Shēng composed a thirty-verse poem titled "Meeting an Immortal,"
before finishing,
Hóngniáng happened to arrive.
So he gave it to her,
to present to Cuī Shì.
From then on, she allowed him again,
coming secretly at dawn,
leaving secretly at dusk,
staying together in what was previously called the Western Wing,
for almost a month.
Zhāng Shēng often inquired about Madame Zhèng's intentions,
and she said:
「I can do nothing about it,
so I intend to let it be. 」
Not long after,
Zhāng Shēng was about to go to Cháng'ān,
first explaining his feelings to her.
Cuī Shì showed no difficulty in her words,
yet her sorrowful expression was moving.
On the eve of his departure,
he could not see her again,
and Zhāng Shēng then went west.
Several months later,
he traveled again to Pú,
and stayed with Cuī Shì for several more months.
Cuī Shì was very skilled in calligraphy,
and good at writing,
but though he repeatedly asked for her writings,
he never saw them.
Often Zhāng Shēng tried to provoke her with his own writings,
but she seldom read them.
Generally, Cuī's outstanding qualities were:
her arts were exquisite,
yet she appeared unaware;
her speech was quick and eloquent,
yet she rarely engaged in conversation.
Her affection for Zhāng was deep,
yet she never expressed it in words.
At times, she was melancholy and reserved,
often as if unaware;
expressions of joy or anger,
were rarely seen.
Once, late at night, she played the qin,
a sorrowful and mournful tune,
Zhāng secretly listened,
but when he asked her to play again,
she never did.
Because of this, he became even more intrigued.
Soon, Zhāng Shēng had to leave for the civil examinations,
and was to go west again.
On the night before his departure,
he did not speak of his feelings,
but sighed sorrowfully beside Cuī Shì.
Cuī already knew secretly that they would part,
and with a respectful demeanor and gentle voice,
slowly said to Zhāng:
「You began with disorder,
and end with abandonment,
it is only fitting,
I dare not resent it.
If you had begun with disorder,
and ended with commitment,
that would have been your kindness;
then the vow of lifelong devotion,
would have had its fulfillment,
so why feel deeply sorrowful about this departure?
Yet since you are unhappy,
I have no way to comfort you.
You often said I am good at playing the qin,
but before, I was too shy,
and could not play for you.
Now that you are leaving,
I will fulfill your sincere wish. 」
So she ordered the qin to be brought,
and played the prelude to "Rainbow Skirt, Feathered Dress,"
but after a few notes,
the mournful melody became chaotic,
no longer recognizable as the tune.
Those around sighed with emotion,
and Cuī abruptly stopped.
Throwing down the qin,
she wept continuously,
hurried back to Madame Zhèng's quarters,
and never returned.
The next morning, Zhāng departed.
The following year,
he failed the literary examinations,
so Zhāng stayed in the capital,
and sent a letter to Cuī,
to express his feelings.
Cuī Shì's reply in the letter,
is roughly recorded here.
It said:
「Upon reading your letter,
I feel your affection is too deep,
the feelings between us,
bring both sorrow and joy.
You also sent a box of floral ornaments,
and five inches of lip balm,
gifts to adorn the head and lips.
Though I receive such special favor,
for whom should I adorn myself?
Seeing these things deepens my feelings,
only adding to my sighs of sorrow.
I hear you are staying in the capital for your career,
the path of advancement,
surely lies in comfort and ease.
But I regret that a secluded and humble person like me,
is forever cast aside,
such is my fate,
what more can I say?
Since last autumn,
I have often felt lost,
in the midst of noise and laughter,
I sometimes force myself to smile and speak,
but alone on quiet nights,
tears never cease.
Even in dreams,
I often feel choked with emotion.
Thoughts of separation,
linger and entwine,
as if they were ordinary;
before our secret meetings ended,
my soul was already shattered.
Though half the quilt still feels warm,
my thoughts of you are distant.
Since we parted yesterday,
a year has swiftly passed.
Cháng'ān, a place of pleasure,
stirs emotions and memories,
how fortunate you have not forgotten our humble past,
and remember me without weariness.
My humble feelings,
have no way to repay you.
As for the vow of lifelong commitment,
it remains unchanged.
In the past, as cousins,
we sometimes dined together,
Seduced by a maidservant's persuasion,
I thus offered my private devotion.
With a young maiden's heart,
I could not remain steadfast.
You, sir, played the zither to woo,
and I, lowly as I am, did not refuse like the woman who threw the shuttle.
When we shared the bed,
the righteousness was profound and the affection deep.
In my simple and foolish sentiment,
I believed it would be an eternal bond.
How could I have expected that after meeting you, sir,
you could not settle your feelings,
leading to the shame of my self-offering,
and I can no longer openly serve you with towel and cap.
With lifelong regret,
what words can express my sighs?
If a benevolent man would consider,
and condescend to fulfill this obscure wish;
even on the day of my death,
it would be as if I were still alive.
But if a man of principle disregards sentiment,
abandoning the small for the great,
considering the prior union as disgraceful conduct,
and regarding the pledged vow as something to be deceived.
Then even when my bones turn to dust and my form vanishes,
my sincere heart will not perish;
carried by the wind and dew,
it will still cling to your pure dust.
The sincerity of life and death,
is expressed here in full;
facing the paper, I sob,
unable to fully convey my feelings.
Take utmost care of yourself!
Take care, utmost care!
A jade ring,
which I played with in my childhood,
I send to adorn your lower garment.
Jade is chosen for its steadfastness and unchangeable luster,
the ring for its endless continuity.
Along with a skein of tangled silk,
and a patterned bamboo tea roller.
These few things are not precious enough to be valued,
but my intention is for you, sir, to be as true as jade,
and my humble wish to be as unbroken as the ring.
Tear stains are on the bamboo,
sorrowful thoughts entwine like silk,
expressing feelings through objects,
to forever consider it as a token of affection.
The heart is near but the body far,
with no chance to meet again.
The deep sorrow concentrated within,
unites our spirits across a thousand miles.
Take utmost care of yourself!
The spring wind is often harsh,
it is good to eat heartily.
Be cautious in speech and take care of yourself,
do not deeply dwell on one as lowly as me.
Zhāng Shēng showed her letter to those he knew,
and thus many people of the time heard of it.
His friend Yáng Jùyuán, who was fond of composing verses,
therefore wrote a quatrain titled "Poem for Lady Cuī":
"Even Pān Ān's jade-like elegance is not as pure,
in the courtyard, the huì grass melts with the first snow.
The romantic talented man is full of spring thoughts,
heartbroken by a single letter from Lady Xiāo."
Yuán Zhěn from Hénán,
also continued Zhāng Shēng's "Huìzhēn Poem" with thirty rhymes.
The poem says:
A faint moon shines through the window curtain,
fireflies' light crosses the azure sky.
The distant sky begins to fade into mist,
low trees gradually become hazy.
Dragon's breath passes through the courtyard bamboo,
phoenix songs brush the well-side paulownia.
Gauze drapes hang like thin mist,
jade pendants tinkle in the gentle breeze.
With vermilion banners follows the Golden Mother,
cloud-hearted, holding the Jade Boy.
Deep in the night, all is quiet,
morning meeting in drizzling rain.
Pearls gleam on patterned shoes,
flowers brighten the hidden embroidered dragon.
Jade hairpins parade like colorful phoenixes,
silk shawls cover the crimson rainbow.
She says she comes from Yáohuá's shore,
going to court the Jade Palace.
While wandering north of Luò City,
by chance, she turns east of the Sòng house.
Playful teasing meets slight refusal at first,
tender feelings already secretly connect.
Lowered hair like cicada shadows stirs,
turning steps, jade dust veils.
Turning her face, flowing like flowers and snow,
ascending the bed, embracing the brocade cluster.
Mandarin ducks dance neck to neck,
kingfishers share a joyful cage.
Eyebrows, shyly gathered,
lips, vermilion, warm and melting.
Fragrance clear as orchid stamens,
skin moist, jade flesh full.
Too weak to move the wrist with effort,
much charm in a bowing posture.
Sweat flows like pearls dotting,
hair disheveled, lush green.
Just rejoicing in the thousand-year meeting,
suddenly hearing the fifth watch end.
Lingering, sometimes with regret,
affectionate feelings hard to conclude.
Slow face bearing sorrowful demeanor,
sweet words vow pure heart.
Giving the ring to show fate's union,
keeping the knot to express shared heart.
Powdered tears flow on the night mirror,
dim lamp, distant dark insects.
Splendid light still lingering,
rising sun gradually brightening.
Riding the duck, returning to Luò,
playing the flute, also ascending Sōng.
Clothes fragrance still tinged with musk,
pillow greasy, still stained with rouge.
Dense grass by the pond,
floating, thinking of islet reeds.
Plain zither sings the resentful crane,
clear Han River watches returning geese.
Vast sea truly hard to cross,
high sky not easy to soar.
Wandering clouds have no fixed place,
Xiāo Shǐ is in the tower.
Zhāng's friends who heard of it,
were all astonished and found it strange,
yet Zhāng's resolve was also severed.
Zhěn was particularly close to Zhāng,
and thus inquired about his words.
Zhāng said:
"Generally, those destined by heaven to be exceptional beauties,
if they do not bring calamity upon themselves,
must bring calamity upon others.
If the Cuī maiden had encountered wealth and honor,
riding on favor and pride,
not as cloud,
not as rain,
but as flood dragon or hornless dragon,
I do not know what transformations she would have undergone.
In the past, Xīn of Yīn,
Yōu of Zhōu,
ruled over a million-state,
their power was very great.
Yet one woman ruined them,
dispersed their masses,
slaughtered their persons,
to this day laughed at by the world.
My virtue is insufficient to overcome such a demon,
therefore I endure my feelings."
Those seated at the time all sighed deeply.
Over a year later,
Cuī had already married someone else,
and Zhāng had also taken a wife.
Passing by her residence,
he then spoke to Cuī through her husband,
requesting to meet as her maternal cousin.
Her husband told her,
but Cuī ultimately did not come out.
Zhāng's sincere resentment and longing,
showed on his face.
Cuī, knowing this,
secretly composed a poem:
"Since growing thin, my radiant beauty fades,
a thousand turns, ten thousand times, too lazy to leave bed.
Not for others' sake that I am ashamed to rise,
but for you, haggard, yet ashamed to face you."
In the end, she did not see him.
Several days later,
as Zhāng Shēng was about to depart,
she again composed a poem to sever ties:
"Now cast aside, what more to say?
Back then, you were intimate yourself.
Take the feelings of old times,
and cherish the person before you now."
From then on, they never heard from each other again.
Many people of the time praised Zhāng as one who skillfully corrected his faults.
I often, in gatherings with friends,
frequently mention this idea,
so that those who know might not act,
and those who act might not be deluded.
In the ninth month of the Zhēnyuán year,
the official Lǐ Gōngchuí,
stayed at my residence in Jìng'ān Lane,
and spoke of this matter.
Gōngchuí was profoundly struck and exclaimed in wonder,
and thus composed the "Yīngyīng Song" to pass it on.
Cuī's childhood name was Yīngyīng,
Gōngchuí used it to title his piece.
Zhōu Qín Travel Record
In the Zhēnyuán era,
I sat for the imperial examination but failed,
and was returning to the area between Wǎn and Yè.
Upon reaching the south road of Yīquè, at the foot of Mínggāo Mountain,
I intended to lodge at the Dà'ān inn.
As dusk fell,
I lost my way and did not arrive.
After traveling more than ten li further,
I came upon a very smooth path.
The moon had just risen at night,
when suddenly I smelled an extraordinary fragrance like that of fine incense.
I hurried forward along the path,
unaware of tiring or the distance.
Seeing a bright light,
I thought it was a farmhouse.
Pressing ahead,
I reached a residence,
whose gate and courtyard resembled that of a wealthy family.
A yellow-clad gatekeeper said:
"What brings you here, sir?"
I replied:
"I am Niú Sēngrú,
who sat for the imperial examination but failed.
I was originally heading to the Dà'ān inn,
but mistakenly took the wrong path and came here.
I merely beg for a night's lodging,
nothing more."
A young maid with her hair in a small bun, dressed in blue, came out
and reproached the yellow-clad one:
"Who is it outside?"
The yellow-clad one said:
"A guest, a guest."
The yellow-clad one went in to announce,
and after a short while came out and said:
"Please come in, sir."
I asked whose great mansion this was.
The yellow-clad one said:
"Just enter,
no need to ask."
Passing through more than ten gates,
I reached a great hall,
veiled with beaded curtains.
There were several hundred gatekeepers in red and yellow garments
standing on the steps.
Those on the left and right said:
"Bow."
A voice from behind the curtain said:
"I am Empress Dowager Bó, mother of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
This is a temple.
You, sir, should not have come here.
What brings you to this humble place?"
I said:
"My home is in Wǎn-Yè.
On my way back, I lost my way.
Fearing death from wolves and tigers,
I dared to entrust my life here."
When I finished speaking,
the Empress Dowager ordered her attendants to roll up the curtain and rise from her seat, saying:
"I am but an old mother of the former Hàn dynasty,
and you are a renowned scholar of the Táng dynasty.
We are not ruler and subject.
I hope we can dispense with formalities.
Please come up to the hall to meet."
The Empress Dowager wore plain silk garments.
Her appearance was majestic and imposing,
and she did not seem very old.
She consoled me, saying:
"Has your journey been arduous?"
She then invited me to sit.
After the time it takes for a meal,
laughter was heard from within the hall.
The Empress Dowager said:
"The breeze and moonlight are exceptionally fine tonight.
By chance, two female companions have come to visit,
and moreover, we have encountered a distinguished guest.
We must certainly hold a gathering."
She called to her attendants to invite the two ladies to come out and meet the scholar.
After a long while,
two women arrived from within,
followed by several hundred attendants.
The one standing in front
had a slender waist and a long face,
with abundant hair and no makeup,
dressed in blue garments.
She appeared to be just over twenty.
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is Lady Qī, consort of Emperor Gāozǔ."
I bowed to her,
and Lady Qī also bowed.
The other one
had soft skin and a graceful figure,
with a serene and elegant demeanor,
her radiance shining far and near.
She wore many embroidered floral garments,
and was younger than the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is Wáng Qiáng, consort of Emperor Yuán."
I bowed to her as I had to Lady Qī,
and Wáng Qiáng returned the bow.
Each took their seats.
Once seated,
the Empress Dowager said to a purple-clad palace eunuch:
"Invite the ladies of the Yáng and Pān families to come."
After a long time,
multicolored clouds were seen descending from the sky,
and the sound of laughter and conversation gradually drew near.
The Empress Dowager said:
"The Yáng family has arrived."
Suddenly, the sounds of carriages and horses intermingled,
and silken garments gleamed brilliantly,
too dazzling to behold directly.
Two women descended from the clouds.
I stood up and stepped to the side.
I saw the first one,
with a slender waist and beautiful eyes,
her appearance exceedingly lovely,
dressed in yellow garments,
and wearing a jade crown.
She appeared to be around thirty.
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is the Tàizhēn Consort of the Táng dynasty."
I immediately prostrated myself in audience,
bowing according to the rites of a subject.
Tàizhēn said:
"I offended the late emperor.
The imperial court does not count me among the ranks of consorts.
To perform such rites
would be meaningless, would it not?
I dare not accept."
Instead, she returned the bow.
The other one
had full features and keen eyes,
a petite and pure white complexion,
with very small teeth,
and wore loose, broad garments.
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is Consort Pān Shū of Qí."
I bowed to her as I had to the Consort.
Then the Empress Dowager ordered food to be served.
After a short while, the food arrived.
It was fragrant and exquisite in countless ways,
all dishes whose names I did not know.
I merely wished to fill my stomach,
but could not eat my fill.
Soon, wine was also served.
The vessels and utensils were all like those of royalty.
The Empress Dowager said to Tàizhēn:
"Why have you not come to visit for so long?"
Tàizhēn replied respectfully:
"Sānláng
has frequently visited Huáqīng Palace,
and I, being in his retinue, could not come."
The Empress Dowager also said to Consort Pān:
"You also did not come.
Why is that?"
Consort Pān could not suppress a hidden smile,
and gave no proper reply.
Tàizhēn then looked at Consort Pān and answered for her:
"Consort Pān told Yùnú [me] that
she was vexed by Dōnghūn Hóu's wild and unrestrained behavior,
hunting all day long,
so she could not pay her respects in time."
The Empress Dowager asked me:
"Who is the Son of Heaven today?"
I replied:
"The present emperor is the eldest son of the late emperor."
Tàizhēn laughed and said:
"So Shěn Pó's son has become the Son of Heaven.
How extraordinary."
The Empress Dowager said:
"What kind of ruler is he?"
I replied:
"A minor official like me is not qualified to judge the sovereign's virtue."
The Empress Dowager said:
"No matter,
just speak."
I said:
"Among the people, he is said to be sagely and martial."
The Empress Dowager nodded three or four times in agreement.
The Empress Dowager ordered more wine and additional music.
The musicians were all young women.
After the wine had circulated several rounds,
the music also ceased.
The Empress Dowager requested Lady Qī to play the qin.
Lady Qī adjusted the jade rings on her fingers,
their light illuminating the seats.
She took up the qin and played,
its sound full of sorrow.
The Empress Dowager said:
"Scholar Niú has chanced upon this place,
and the various ladies have also happened to visit.
Now, we have no way to fully enjoy the pleasures of a lifetime.
Scholar Niú is, after all, a man of talent.
Why not each compose a poem to express our aspirations?
Would that not be excellent?"
So each was given paper and a brush,
and in a short while, the poems were completed.
The Empress Dowager's poem said:
"In the moonlit bedchamber and flowered palace, I once served my lord,
To this day, I still feel ashamed before Lady Guǎn.
The Hàn court was once a place of music and song,
But now, mist and grass have weathered many autumns and springs."
Wáng Qiáng's poem said:
"In the snow-covered yurt, spring is nowhere to be seen,
Though my Hàn clothes are old, the tear stains are fresh.
Now, I resent Máo Yánshòu the most,
For loving to paint people wrongly with his brush."
Lady Qī's poem said:
"Since leaving the Hàn palace, I have ceased the Chǔ dances,
Unable to apply makeup, I resent the king.
Without gold, how could I welcome the old merchant?
How could the Lǚ clan ever fear the wooden strength?"
Tàizhēn's poem said:
"Golden hairpins fell to the ground as I parted from my lord,
Crimson tears flowed like pearls, soaking the imperial bed.
After the clouds and rain dispersed at Mǎwéi,
The Lí Palace no longer dances to 'Rainbow Skirt.'"
Lady Pān's poem said:
"How many times have the autumn moon and spring breeze returned?
The rivers and mountains remain, but the palaces are no more.
Dōnghūn once made this a lotus land,
Now I only dream of wearing the golden-threaded robe."
They repeatedly invited me to compose a poem,
And I could not refuse,
So I complied and wrote:
"A fragrant breeze led me to the Great Luó Heaven,
On moonlit ground and cloud-covered steps, I bowed to the cave immortals.
Together we spoke of the sorrows of the mortal world,
Unaware of what year this night might be."
There was another woman skilled at playing the flute,
With short hair and elegant attire,
Her appearance was exceedingly beautiful,
And she was also very charming.
Lady Pān brought her along,
The Empress Dowager seated her beside her,
Occasionally ordering her to play the flute,
And often offering her wine as well.
The Empress Dowager looked at her and asked:
"Do you recognize her?
This is Shí's Lǜzhū.
Lady Pān raised her as a sister,
So Lady Pān brought her along."
The Empress Dowager then said:
"Could Lǜzhū possibly have no poem?"
Lǜzhū then thanked her and composed a poem:
"The people of today are not those of the past,
The flute's melody vainly resents Zhào Wáng Lún.
Crimson fades, jade shatters beneath the flowered tower,
The Jīngǔ Garden will see no spring for a thousand years."
After the poem,
When the wine arrived,
The Empress Dowager said:
"Scholar Niú has come from afar,
Who will accompany him tonight?"
Lady Qī rose first and declined:
"Rúyì has grown up,
It is certainly not possible,
And it should not be this way."
Lady Pān declined:
"Dōnghūn died for Yù'ér, and the state was lost,
Yù'ér should not betray him."
Lǜzhū declined:
"Commandant Shí was strict and harsh,
Even in death,
I cannot bring disorder."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Tàizhēn is now the honored consort of the Táng Emperor,
We cannot speak of other matters."
Then she turned to Wáng Qiáng and said:
"Zhāojūn first married Hūhán Chányú,
And later became the wife of Zhūléi's younger brother, the Chányú,
So she is accustomed to it,
And what can the Hú ghosts of the bitter cold lands do?
Zhāojūn, please do not refuse."
Zhāojūn did not reply,
But lowered her brows in shame and resentment.
Soon, each retired to rest,
And I was escorted by attendants to Zhāojūn's courtyard.
As dawn approached,
The servants announced it was time to rise,
Zhāojūn wept as she bid farewell.
Suddenly, word came from outside that the Empress Dowager summoned me,
So I went out to see her.
The Empress Dowager said:
"This is no place for you to linger long,
You should return quickly,
Now it is time to part,
I hope you do not forget the joy we shared."
She called for more wine,
After the wine was served again,
Lady Qī, Lady Pān, and Lǜzhū all shed tears,
And finally, I took my leave.
The Empress Dowager sent a red-robed attendant to escort me to Dà'ān,
Upon reaching the western road,
The escort suddenly vanished.
By then, it was already dawn,
I arrived at Dà'ān Village,
And asked the villagers,
The villagers said:
"About ten lǐ from here,
There is a temple to Empress Bó."
I turned back,
Gazed at the temple,
But it was ruined and desolate, impossible to enter,
Not at all like what I had seen before.
The fragrance on my clothes lingered for over ten days without fading,
And I never understood how it happened.
Record of Unseen Melodies
The former Presented Scholar Wáng Shū, styled Xuéyuán,
was originally from Lángyá.
In the spring of the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era, he passed the imperial examination.
He once resided among the famous mountains between Zōu and Lǔ to pursue his studies.
Shū himself recounted that
four years prior,
while traveling to the capital to take the examination with his registration documents,
he lodged for the night at an inn in Xíngyáng.
There he met a scholar from Péngchéng named Chéng Zìxū,
who, due to family matters, was unable to sit for the examination
and was returning to his hometown.
Encountering Shū,
they spoke of the hardships of their respective journeys.
Zìxū, styled Zhìběn,
also spoke of strange things he had witnessed in the human world.
That year,
on the eighth day of the eleventh month, Zìxū was returning eastward.
The next day,
he arrived at Wèinán County.
The sky was overcast and gloomy,
making it impossible to tell the time of day.
The county magistrate, Lí Wèi, detained him for several rounds of drinks.
Relying on the strength of his horse,
Zìxū ordered his servant and baggage
to go ahead and wait for him at the Chìshuǐ Inn,
while he himself lingered a while longer.
Exiting the eastern gate of the county town,
a bleak wind swept the ground,
and swirling snow filled the sky.
Before he had traveled many li,
it was nearly dark.
Zìxū's servant
had already been sent ahead,
and there were no other travelers on the road,
leaving no one to ask for directions.
By this point, he no longer knew where he was.
The road passed south of the Dōngyáng Post Station,
following the path to the Chìshuǐ Valley mouth.
About three or four li from the station,
there was a low-lying hamlet.
In the faint moonlight filtering through the trees,
he could barely make out a Buddhist temple.
Zìxū pushed open the gate
and hurried inside,
as the snow fell even more heavily.
Thinking that a Buddhist temple
must house resident monks,
and hoping to seek shelter there,
he urged his horse forward.
Inside, he could just discern several empty rooms running north to south,
silent and without lamplight.
After listening intently for a long while,
he faintly heard what seemed like the sound of someone breathing.
So he tied his horse to a pillar on the west side
and called out repeatedly, "Abbot, Venerable Monk,
show compassion and save me tonight."
Gradually, he heard a response:
"The old and sick monk Zhì Gāo is here.
My attendant has just gone to the village to beg for alms,
so there is no way to get a light.
With snow like this,
and it being so late at night,
what brings you here, traveler?
Where have you come from?
With no neighbors around for miles,
how can you find help?
If tonight you do not mind my illness and filth,
and are willing to stay here,
you can avoid exposure.
I can also share the straw bedding I have spread out;
you may rest your body here."
With no other options,
Zìxū was quite pleased to hear this.
He then asked, "Venerable Gāo, from what region do you hail?
Why do you dwell here?
And what is your lay surname?
Since I have received your kindness,
I should also learn of your background."
He replied:
"This humble monk's lay surname is Ān.
I was born west of the desert.
Originally, I exerted my strength
and followed fate to come to the Central Kingdom.
I have not been here long,
and the buildings and courtyards are overgrown and desolate.
For a scholar like yourself to descend upon this place,
I have nothing to offer for your reception.
I only hope you will not take offense."
Through this exchange,
Zìxū largely forgot his earlier fatigue.
He then said to Venerable Gāo:
"Now I understand the parable of seeking treasure and finding a phantom city;
the Tathāgata did not establish this metaphor in vain.
Today, Venerable Gāo is my guide.
Venerable Gāo's original school
certainly has teachings such as this for subduing the mind."
Suddenly, there was a sound as if several people were approaching in unison,
and then he heard someone say:
"What excellent snow!
Is the Master present?"
Before Venerable Gāo could respond,
he heard one person say:
"Senior Cáo should go first."
Another said:
"Senior Zhū Bā should go first."
Then he heard someone say:
"The path is wide enough;
Senior Cáo need not insist on yielding.
We can go together."
Zìxū, thinking there were many people,
felt increasingly emboldened in his heart.
After a short while,
it seemed they had all arrived by the seating area.
One among them asked:
"Master, do you have a guest staying here tonight?"
Venerable Gāo replied:
"A traveler just arrived seeking lodging."
Zìxū was dazed and confused,
unable to discern their forms clearly.
Only the foremost person,
silhouetted against the eaves and snow,
appeared vaguely to be wearing a black fur robe,
with patches of white on the back and sides.
That person first asked Zìxū:
"Traveler, why have you trudged through the snow
to come here in the dark of night?"
Zìxū then told him the whole truth.
That person then asked Zìxū his name,
and he replied:
"Presented Scholar Chéng Zìxū."
Zìxū then also spoke up, saying:
"In the darkness, I cannot properly greet your esteemed faces.
Lest in the future we have no record for our descendants,
please each state your official title and name."
Then he heard one person say:
"Former Patrol Officer of the Héyīn Transport Commission,
Probationary Left Xiaowei Guard Helmet and Armor Officer, Lú Yǐmǎ."
The next person said:
"Visitor from Táolín,
Deputy Light-Chariot General, Zhū Zhōngzhèng."
The next person said:
"Qùwén, surname Jìng."
The next person said:
"Ruìjīn, surname Xī."
By now, it seemed they were all seated around.
Initially, because Chéng-gōng was sitting for the examinations,
Yǐmǎ brought up the topic of discussing literature.
Yǐmǎ said:
"When I was a child,
I heard people reciting the Master's poem 'Gathering Snow to Form a Mountain.'
I still remember it now.
Tonight's scene
vividly brings it to mind.
Does the Master recall it?"
Venerable Gāo said:
"What were the words?
Try to recite them."
Yǐmǎ said:
"What I remember goes:
'Whose family sweeps the snow to fill the courtyard?
A thousand ravines and ten thousand peaks held in a single fist.
My heart, unawares, feels the cold invade my robes;
For how many years did I once dwell within this scene?'"
Zìxū was utterly bewildered, as if lost,
his mouth agape and eyes staring,
especially unable to comprehend.
Venerable Gāo then said:
"The Snowy Mountains are my homeland's mountains.
In years past, I happened to see children piling snow,
which stood like peaks and ridges of a mountain.
Gazing west toward my old country with melancholy,
I thus composed this poem.
Senior Cáo is truly brilliant—
how is it you remember
this humble monk's old, clumsy lines?
If not for Senior Cáo sincerely keeping them on your lips,
I would indeed have forgotten them."
Yǐmǎ said:
"The Master strides with ease in distant, wild lands,
freeing himself from the snares of worldly affairs.
Your lofty virtue
can be said to stand foremost among your peers.
As for minor figures like myself,
who rush about in the dust of your wake,
how
dare we glimpse such heights and distances?
This spring, Yǐmǎ came to the city on official business.
By nature, I am dull and obtuse.
The high cost of living in the capital
pressed upon me unbearably.
Constantly a traveler,
though I toiled day and night,
my expected income was meager,
my burdens were not light,
and I often feared punishment and censure.
Recently, I received from my bureau a transfer to a nominal post,
hoping through hardship to seek exemption.
Last night, I left Chánglè City and lodged below its walls..."
I lament my toils in the dusty world,
and deeply yearn for the life of a wild deer or mountain elk.
Thus I sent these to my companions,
composing two clumsy poems.
Facing all you esteemed authors,
I wish to recite them impromptu,
but dare not release them so hastily."
Zìxū said:
"What a fortunate night this is,
to hear such fine verses."
Yǐmǎ again modestly replied:
"Despite my crude and shallow skills,
especially with the literary master present here,
how dare I display my clumsy work?"
Zìxū earnestly urged:
"I wish to hear them,
I truly wish to hear them."
Yǐmǎ then recited his poem clearly:
"East of Cháng'ān, the road to Luòyáng,
wheels never cease, dust billows vast.
Striving for gain, racing ahead, whips eagerly applied,
all who meet are aged by the dust.
Day ends, the long river不计程,
alone I walk apart from the flock, unable to cry out.
Fortunately, there is the lush green grass by the riverbank,
come spring, it can still console this traveler's heart."
All present said:
"Exceedingly lofty work."
Yǐmǎ modestly replied:
"Clumsy and poor,
clumsy and poor."
Zhōngzhèng said to Gāo Gōng:
"I have heard that scholars from the northern deserts
often recite and chant your esteemed verses.
Now we are here in Yǐngchuān,
and having just attentively listened to what Registrar Lú recited,
it cleansed my dull ignorance,
refreshing my mind and spirit.
You must have many newly composed works.
The entire gathering thirsts to hear them chanted.
Could you not show us two or three pieces,
to nourish everyone's eager gaze?"
Gāo Gōng asked to wait for another day.
Zhōngzhèng said again:
"Seeing all these distinguished gentlemen gathered,
why begrudge the 'Rabbit Garden'?
Elegant discourse and lofty conversation
are indeed a splendid event of the time.
Now we are far from the market stalls,
the night is late yet spirits remain high.
Wine cups are certainly not to be sought,
roasted meats cannot be obtained.
The rites between host and guests are lacking,
leaving much shame and embarrassment.
We are just contemplating the mind and savoring thoughts,
yet you gentlemen have nothing to fill your bellies all night.
What good does our blushing do?"
Gāo Gōng said:
"I have heard that fine conversation can make one forget hunger and thirst.
Just like you, Bā Láng,
your strength aids the living,
your actions follow the proper tracks.
Attacking cities and rewarding troops—
these are your strengths.
But because the twelve links of dependent origination
all arise from craving;
in the vast sea of suffering,
afflictions follow birth.
Where can one perceive Bodhi?
Through which gate can one leave the burning house?"
Zhōngzhèng replied:
"In my foolish view,
the tracks of overturned carts follow one another;
revolving in evil paths of rebirth;
the retribution of cause and effect, earlier and later,
is a matter quite clear.
Guiding one to cultivate practice,
the principle returns to this."
Gāo Gōng laughed heartily,
then said:
"The Buddhist teachings esteem purity,
achieving the Way is then true enlightenment,
enlightenment is Buddhahood.
As in Bā Láng's discourse just now,
you have deeply grasped it."
Yǐmǎ laughed loudly.
Zìxū said again:
"Just now, General Zhū repeatedly requested the Venerable's new compositions.
In my humble opinion,
I truly wish to behold such treasures.
Does the Venerable, because I, Zìxū, am a distant guest,
and not within your Dharma, look down on me?
Moreover, the Venerable's capacity and insight are extraordinary,
your moral stature deep and lofty.
Surely your style, rhythm, talent, and thoughts
must stand unparalleled for a time;
exquisite, marvelous, fresh, and pure,
casting off vulgar mannerisms.
How can you ultimately keep secret the remaining thoughts from your coughs and spittle,
and not chant one or two pieces
to open our ears and eyes?"
Gāo Gōng said:
"I am deeply indebted to the Xiùcai for his earnest request.
The matter is difficult to firmly refuse.
Moreover, this old monk is ill, disabled, frail, and weak;
long having abandoned study and reading,
the way of composing verses
was never my strength.
Yet it is Zhū Bā who without cause picks at my shortcomings.
However, during my illness I happened to compose two pieces describing myself.
Can you, Master Shí, listen to them?"
He said:
"I wish to hear them."
His poem said:
"Holding coarse robes, hiding my name, no fixed trace,
crossing a thousand miles of flowing sands, my wasted countenance.
After transmitting the mind-ground of the Southern School,
this body should then grow old at Shuāngfēng.
Because of a weighty cause in Jambudvīpa,
I left the Western Lands and came to Xiánqín.
Since lacking strength, I ceased practicing the Way,
and merely became a wandering ascetic, unattached."
Again, the sound of praise was heard from all present.
After a while, unsettled,
Qùwén suddenly said from his seat:
"Long ago, Wáng Zǐyóu visited Dài Āndào in Shānyīn.
The snowy night was bright,
yet he turned back upon reaching the gate,
thus spreading the theory of 'why must one see Dài?'
At that time, all valued transcendent inspiration.
Now, Chéng Jūn can be said to meet friends through literature,
looking down upon Yuán Ān and Jiǎng Xǔ.
In my youth,
I possessed considerable brilliance and spirit.
My nature loved falcons and hawks.
During that time,
I hunted, roamed, galloped, and raced.
My former woods lie in the southeastern corner of Cháng'ān,
east of Yùsù Chuān's altars.
I have a poem on chanting snow, presented to Cáozhōufáng,
unable to resist the assault of poetic madness,
I have soiled your lofty discernment.
Thereupon I chanted the poem:
'I love this drifting, six-pointed lord,
light jade, fitting floss, dancing in the vast sky.
At that time, I was just pursuing the Qín Prime Minister,
leaping and prancing over plains and streams, delighting in the north wind.'
After presenting the poem,
Cáozhōufáng greatly appreciated this poem of mine,
but then posed a challenge, saying:
is that not lacking restraint?'
I then cited that ancients still called bamboo 'gentleman,'
later worthies considered this a famous argument,
using it as evidence.
Cáozhōufáng was tongue-tied,
not knowing how to reply.
However, Cáozhōufáng was never one who understood poetry.
Wū Dà once said to me:
'It is rare to find one with the same taste.'
These words are not false.
Now he has taken up a distant official post,
participating in military affairs of Dōngzhōu,
several thousand li away.
Miáo Shí—
his temper is fierce and domineering.
Relying on his many relatives,
he demands people serve him.
If Lǔ lacked gentlemen,
from whom would he take them?"
Ruìjīn said:
"How dare I accept that.
Haven't seen Miáo Shēng for several days?"
He said:
"About ten days.
So where is Miáo Zǐ now?"
Qùwén said:
"He shouldn't be far either.
Knowing our gathering here,
he ought to understand and come."
Not long after,
Miáo Shēng hurriedly arrived.
Qùwén pretended delight,
patting his back and saying:
"Just as I wished!"
Qùwén then introduced Miáo Shēng and Zìxū to each other with bows.
Zìxū first stated his name,
Miáo Shēng said:
"My surname is Miáo, name Jièlì."
The words exchanged between guest and host
were quite numerous and detailed.
Ruìjīn, sitting beside them, said:
"Now is the time for bitter chanting!
All you gentlemen are masters,
but old Xī's poetic ailment flares up again.
What to do, what to do?"
Zìxū said:
"Earlier, I received Xī Shēng's regard and friendship, which was not shallow.
Why do you still begrudge your precious gems,
Greatly disappointed?"
Ruìjīn retreated hesitantly and said:
"Dare I not provide a laugh for this grand gathering?"
Then he recited three recent poems:
"Dancing before the mirror, vying for the phoenix's splendor,
Approaching the arena, the falcon's fist is set.
Just thinking of the immortal staff days,
I crane my neck, gazing before the tower.
Nurturing combat, form like wood,
Welcoming spring, substance like clay.
If truly wind and rain exist,
Why fear dwelling in lowly traces?
To escape Tián Wén's difficulty,
I often cherish Jì Juān's kindness.
Wishing to know the wild demeanor of the fields,
At frosty dawn, it calls in the desolate village."
After Ruìjīn finished reciting,
loud sounds of praise were heard in the darkness.
Gāo Gōng said:
"Gentlemen, do not treat General Zhū as merely a warrior.
This gentleman is deeply versed in principles of names,
and also skilled in literary composition.
Yet he still says nothing,
secretly judging us in his heart—
this is perhaps not acceptable.
Moreover, Chéng Jūn is a guest from afar;
this one evening's gathering
is what the Buddhist gate calls a meeting born of many lifetimes' affinity,
like roosting birds sharing the same tree.
Should we not, because of this, leave behind a topic for conversation in future times?"
Zhōngzhèng rose and said:
"Master, these words of yours
are like planting thorns for Zhōngzhèng.
If the sentiments of the crowd are suspicious and obstructive,
how dare I not obey your command?
However, Lú reaching out to act—
bringing trouble upon himself—
what about that?"
Gāo Gōng said:
"Please listen quietly, gentlemen."
Zhōngzhèng's poem said:
"Bringing chaos to Lǔ, bearing a false reputation,
Traveling in Qín, moved by Níng Shēng.
Waiting, startled by the chancellor's panting,
Using it to recognize Gé Lú's cry.
Millet and grain flourish the farmers' prosperity,
Carriages and canopies lack the sentiment of the Way.
Recently, my physical strength declines,
My sole intent is to return to farming."
Gāo Gōng sighed and said:
"Zhū Bā's literary brilliance is such as this,
yet he has not left his scattered official rank.
Who then are those guiding the imperial carriage?
How unjust,
how unjust."
Yǐmǎ said:
"Brother Fúfēng,
by chance has some ties.
Our family's Qiūcí, with its dark patterns, is extremely exhausted;
fond of noise, disliking quiet,
fond of affairs, extravagant,
his interest lies in concluding matters,
courageous in leading the charge.
That he does not come to this gathering—
one can imagine the regret."
Qùwén said to Jièlì:
"The Wèi family brothers
do not live far away.
Neither going nor coming,
what use is there in still cherishing aspirations?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Friends assist each other,'
yet you still have distant thoughts.
We must send a note to summon them;
my humble opinion is quite in favor of this good deed."
Jièlì said:
"I originally intended to visit Wèi the Elder,
but just as the discussion of literature was at its peak,
I unconsciously delayed.
Respecting your command,
now I ask the gentlemen not to rise;
Jièlì will briefly go to the Wèi family and return immediately.
Otherwise,
I will bring the Wèi brothers along,
is that acceptable?"
All said:
"Agreed."
Jièlì then left.
Not long after,
Qùwén, before the crowd,
secretly criticized Jièlì, saying:
"This stupid fellow, in character,
what great claws or talons does he have?
I have heard he is quite honest and clean,
good at managing storehouses.
But what about the ugliness of the wax aunt,
how can it be concealed from public opinion?"
Little did he know that Jièlì and the Wèi family were coming hand in hand,
and upon reaching the door,
they caught a glimpse of his words.
Jièlì rolled up his sleeves in great anger and said:
"Heaven gave birth to Miáo Jièlì,
directly descended from Dòu Bóbǐ.
Received the surname from the distant Chu ancestor Fén Huáng Rú.
Divided into twenty clans,
sacrificial rites and shared offerings,
even recorded in the *Book of Rites*.
How can a single Jìng Qùwén,
remnant of Pánhù,
long and thin without distinction,
not counted among human relations,
only fit to tame and play with children,
fiercely guarding the wine banner,
flattering like a demon fox,
stealing fat to please the kitchen god—
how dare he speak of others' strengths and weaknesses?
If I do not display my modest skill,
Jìng Zǐ will say I have no literary talent at all,
making everyone look down on me in the future.
Now, before the master, I will recite a crude poem,
and let's see how it is?"
The poem said:
"Ashamed of the deep favor from the meat-eating lord,
At day's end, coiled like a dragon, lying on broidered quilts.
Moreover, learning from the wise to know white and black,
How can fine rank move my heart?"
Zìxū greatly admired it.
Qùwén said:
"You do not know the whole story,
and heavily add false accusations.
I am truly a descendant of Xiàng Xū from the Spring and Autumn period.
You take me for a Pánhù hybrid,
like comparing Chényáng to a side room—
to me, it is vastly different and exaggerated."
Zhōngzhèng deeply felt troubled that the exchange between the two families had not ceased,
and said:
"I wish to act as Yì Liáo to resolve the grievances of both.
Is that acceptable?
In the past, my Féng Chǒufù
indeed, along with Xiàng family's Fén Huáng,
repeatedly formed alliances during the Spring and Autumn period.
Now there is a distinguished guest present;
why do you two slander each other's ancestors?
If words suddenly reveal flaws,
it will make Chéng Gōng laugh until his teeth feel cold.
Moreover, let us focus on reciting poetry;
I firmly request the noise cease."
Then Jièlì led the Wèi brothers to meet Zìxū.
At first, they appeared somewhat pale.
The two came forward;
the elder was called Wèi Cánghù,
the younger Cánglì.
Zìxū also stated his name.
Cánghù then went around the seats and said:
"Elder brother, younger brother."
Jièlì then praised the Wèi brothers before the crowd:
"Hidden traces in the grassy wilds,
conduct renowned among famous clans;
above, they correlate with the constellations,
intimacy reaching deep into the liver and gall.
Moreover, the eight rivers of Qín
truly penetrate the heavenly prefecture;
thus, the twenty clans of the old forest
are mostly from Xiánjīng.
I heard my brother recently composed a poem on old endeavors,
praised as very beautiful at the time.
How may we hear it?"
Cánghù replied:
"Your younger brother mistakenly attends this banquet of guests,
where authors gather like clouds.
Wishing to speak,
I first increase my shame.
Now, having no alternative,
I soil the ears and eyes of you gentlemen.
The poem says:
'Niǎoshǔ is my home river,
King Zhōu once hunted for worthies here.
Once separated from the days of Zǐ and Mǎo,
One should see the sea turn to mulberry fields.'"
Jièlì praised it:
"Brother, in the future you will surely bear a great reputation.
If justice exists,
this literary piece will not perish."
Cánghù bowed and thanked him:
"Cánghù is suited to hidden retirement;
fortunate to accompany this group of talents.
Brother, your praise is excessive;
your younger brother mistakenly receives weighty words,
feeling as if bearing thorns."
All the seated guests laughed.
At that time, Zìxū was just listening to the fine works of the guests,
with no leisure to think of his own writing,
and only said:
"The gentlemen's pure talent, elegant and ornate,
all are like seeing the whole ox while wielding the blade."
Zhōngzhèng thought there was sarcasm,
and secretly slipped away.
Gāo Gōng sought him but could not find him.
He said:
"Zhū Bā left without saying goodbye,
why?"
Yǐ Mǎ replied:
"Zhū Bā's family has been enemies with the Pào clan for generations,
he left because he detests hearing talk of sharpening knives on whetstones."
Zì Xū apologized for his lack of insight.
At this time, Qù Wén alone engaged Zì Xū in discussion and debate,
saying to Zì Xū:
"In the actions and withdrawals, the expansions and contractions of ordinary people,
a gentleman still esteems their ability to act according to the occasion.
Wagging the tail to beg for food,
is why the fierce tiger perceives the subtle signs;
sometimes barking for a close friend,
one cannot abandon this principle
just because the master lacks virtue.
Though I, Qù Wén, am untalented,
I also have two poems expressing my aspirations to present to you."
The poems said:
"Serving my lord, sharing joy and sharing sorrow in righteousness,
why compare the chaff and bran, content and at rest?
It is not clinging to a stump, vainly waiting for a hare;
in the end, I shall chase the deer, emerging from the wooded hill."
"In youth, I once bore the use of a hungry eagle,
within my heart, I never had the mind of a pampered crane.
Sweeping away the autumn grass, I think of leaving my dwelling;
on the plain, fur and blood stir as I follow the hunt."
Zì Xū admired and was stirred without limit,
completely forgetting the suffering of the entire night.
Just as he was about to boast of his old compositions,
he suddenly heard a distant temple striking its bell.
Then the sounds of clapping shoulders and clamor ceased entirely.
Staring intently, he saw nothing at all,
only feeling the wind and snow piercing through the window,
and a foul stench assaulting his nose.
Only a rustling sound as if something was moving,
but when he shouted questions loudly,
there was absolutely no reply.
Zì Xū's mind was in a daze,
not daring to rashly step forward and grope about.
Retreating to look for the horse he had tied up,
it was indeed in the western corner of the house,
its saddle and blanket covered in snow,
the horse standing chewing on a post.
While he hesitated,
the dawn light had already begun to make things distinguishable.
Then, north of the house wall,
there was a camel,
belly pressed down, legs kneeling,
ears drooping, mouth chewing.
Zì Xū, sensing the strangeness of the past night,
proceeded to search all around.
Outside the room, under the northern porch,
he soon saw again a thin, emaciated black donkey,
with three places worn through along its spine,
white hair growing thickly, nearly covering them.
Raising his gaze to the northern arch of the house,
slightly as if something was quivering and stirring,
he then saw an old chicken crouching there.
Proceeding to the north of the collapsed seat in the Buddha hall where the statue was set,
there was an empty patch of ground several tens of paces wide from east to west.
Under the window, there were places with colored paintings;
the locals had once piled long stalks of wheat
in between them,
and he saw a large tabby cat sleeping on top.
A short distance away, there was also a broken gourd used for holding field irrigation water,
next to it was a tattered bamboo hat discarded by a shepherd boy.
Zì Xū then kicked it,
and indeed found two hedgehogs,
wriggling and moving.
Zì Xū looked all around in search,
quiet with no one in sight.
Unable to bear any longer the cold and exhaustion of the night,
he gathered the reins and shook off the snow,
mounted his horse, and left.
Circling around,
he exited north of the village,
on the left side of the road passed an old garden with a firewood fence,
and saw an ox trampling the snow and chewing grass.
Not more than a hundred paces beyond this,
the whole village carted manure here, fortunately piling it up.
As Zì Xū passed below,
a pack of dogs barked noisily.
Among them was one dog,
its fur all neatly shorn,
its appearance very strange,
glancing sidelong at Zì Xū.
Zì Xū urged his horse on for a long time,
then encountered an old man,
who pushed open a bramble gate,
having risen early to clear a path through the snow.
Zì Xū reined in his horse and inquired of him.
He replied:
"This is the estate of my old friend, Commandant Péng of the Right Army.
Where did you, young master, stay last night?
It seems from your baggage you were like someone who lost his way."
Zì Xū spoke of what he had seen the previous night.
The old man, leaning on his broom, said in surprise:
"Extremely strange,
extremely strange.
Last night's weather was windy and snowy.
The farm first had a sick camel;
fearing it would die,
they covered it north of the Buddha hall,
under the念佛社 (Buddha-recitation society) house.
A few days ago,
government porters from Héyīn passed by,
with one exhausted donkey
unable to go on.
I pitied its remaining life and could not abandon it,
so I exchanged a hu of grain to keep it here,
and did not tether it either.
That lean ox in the pen
is also kept by the farm.
Just now hearing this account,
I don't know why such strange things happened."
Zì Xū said:
"Last night I already lost my saddle and pack,
now I am starving and freezing severely.
Some matters cannot be hastily spoken of;
the gist is as such,
hard to relate in full detail."
Then he whipped his horse and galloped away.
Arriving at Chìshuǐ Inn,
he saw his servant boys,
who were just then surprised at their master's separation from them,
and had begun busily searching for him.
Zì Xū sighed with emotion,
as if he had lost his soul for several days.
The Tale of Xiè Xiǎo'é
Xiǎo'é's surname was Xiè,
she was from Yùzhāng,
the daughter of a merchant.
At the age of eight, she lost her mother,
and was married to Duàn Jūzhēn, a knight-errant from Lìyáng.
Jūzhēn was proud and righteous,
associating with heroes and outstanding men.
Xiǎo'é's father had amassed great wealth,
concealing his name among merchants,
and often traveled by boat with his son-in-law Duàn,
going back and forth on the rivers and lakes.
At that time, Xiǎo'é was fourteen years old,
just having come of age,
when her father and husband were both killed by robbers,
who plundered all the gold and silk.
Duàn's brothers,
Xiè's nephews and other relatives,
along with several dozen servants, were all thrown into the river.
Xiǎo'é was also wounded in the chest and had her leg broken,
drifting in the water,
until she was rescued by another boat.
After a night, she revived.
Thus, wandering and begging for food, she reached Shàngyuán County,
and took refuge in the chamber of the nun Jìngwù at Miàoguǒ Temple.
When her father first died,
Xiǎo'é dreamed that her father said to her:
"The one who killed me,
is 'monkey in a carriage',
'grass at the east gate'."
A few days later,
she again dreamed that her husband said:
"The one who killed me,
is 'walking through grain',
'one day husband'."
Xiǎo'é could not understand it herself,
so she often wrote these words,
widely seeking wise men to decipher them,
but for years she could not find the answer.
In the spring of the eighth year of Yuánhé,
I had just left my post as an assistant in Jiāngxī,
and was sailing east in a small boat,
stopping over at Jiànyè.
I climbed the tower of Wǎguān Temple,
where there was a monk named Qíwù,
who valued virtue and loved learning,
and was on good terms with me.
He thus told me:
"There is a widow named Xiǎo'é,
who often comes to the temple,
showing me a twelve-character riddle,
which I cannot decipher."
I then asked Reverend Qí to write it on paper,
and leaning against the railing, I traced the characters in the air,
concentrating and pondering silently.
Before the seated guests grew weary,
I had fully understood the text.
I had the temple boy quickly summon Xiǎo'é to come forward,
and inquired about the circumstances.
Xiǎo'é sobbed for a long time,
and then said:
"My father and husband,
were both killed by bandits.
Afterward, I once dreamed that my father told me:
'The one who killed me is "monkey in a carriage",
"grass at the east gate".'
And I dreamed that my husband told me:
'The one who killed me,
is "walking through grain",
"one day husband".'
For years, no one has been able to understand it."
I said:
"If that is the case,
I have carefully examined it.
The one who killed your father is Shēn Lán,
and the one who killed your husband is Shēn Chūn.
Now, 'monkey in a carriage':
the character for 'carriage' (車),
removing the top and bottom strokes,
becomes 'Shēn' (申).
Moreover, Shēn corresponds to the monkey in the zodiac,
hence 'monkey in a carriage'.
'Grass' (草) below 'gate' (門),
with 'east' (東) inside 'gate' (門),
forms the character 'Lán' (蘭).
As for 'walking through grain',
it means passing through fields,
which also represents 'Shēn' (申).
'One day husband':
adding one stroke above 'husband' (夫),
with 'sun' (日) below,
forms the character 'Chūn' (春).
The one who killed your father is Shēn Lán,
and the one who killed your husband is Shēn Chūn,
this is perfectly clear."
Xiǎo'é wept bitterly and bowed twice,
writing the four characters "Shēn Lán, Shēn Chūn" on her clothing,
vowing to seek out and kill the two bandits,
to avenge their wrongs.
Xiǎo'é then asked my surname and official background,
and left with tears streaming down.
Afterward, Xiǎo'é dressed in men's clothing,
working as a servant among the rivers and lakes.
After more than a year,
she reached Xúnyáng Commandery,
where she saw a paper notice on a bamboo door,
saying that a servant was needed.
Xiǎo'é then responded to the call and went to the door,
asking about the master,
and it turned out to be Shēn Lán.
Lán brought her home,
and Xiǎo'é, though filled with anger, appeared submissive.
Staying by Lán's side,
she became very dear to him.
Matters of gold and silk income and expenditure,
were all entrusted to Xiǎo'é.
After more than two years,
he still did not know that Xiǎo'é was a woman.
Previously, the gold, treasures, brocades, and embroideries of the Xiè family,
along with clothing and utensils,
had all been plundered to Lán's home.
Whenever Xiǎo'é handled these old objects,
she would secretly weep for a long time.
Lán and Chūn
were cousins,
at that time Chūn's family lived at Dúshùpǔ north of the great river,
and he and Lán had close and frequent dealings.
Lán and Chūn would often go away together for a month,
returning with much wealth and silk.
Each time they left Xiǎo'é with Lán's wife,
Lán,
and his wife to guard the household,
providing Xiǎo'é with ample wine, meat, and clothing.
One day,
Chūn brought a carp and wine to visit Lán,
and Xiǎo'é privately sighed:
"Master Lǐ's profound insight and mysterious discernment
all match the words of the dream.
This is Heaven enlightening his mind,
my goal is about to be achieved."
That evening,
Lán and Chūn gathered,
and all the bandits arrived,
drinking to their fill.
After the villains had all left,
Chūn was deeply drunk,
and lay down in the inner room,
while Lán also slept uncovered in the courtyard.
Xiǎo'é secretly locked Chūn inside,
drew her dagger,
and first cut off Lán's head,
then called for the neighbors to come together.
Chūn was captured inside,
Lán lay dead outside,
and the stolen goods were recovered,
amounting to tens of millions.
Initially,
Lán and Chūn had dozens of accomplices,
whose names Xiǎo'é had secretly memorized,
and they were all captured and executed.
At that time, the prefect of Xúnyáng, Lord Zhāng,
admired Xiǎo'é's integrity,
and actions,
and reported the matter in full,
requesting commendation for her,
so she was spared the death penalty.
This was in the summer of the twelfth year of Yuánhé.
After avenging her father and husband,
she returned to her hometown,
and saw her relatives.
The powerful families in the village competed to seek her hand in marriage,
but Xiǎo'é vowed not to marry,
so she cut her hair, put on coarse clothing,
and sought the Way at Niútóu Mountain,
taking as her teacher the great nun Jiǎng,
a Vinaya master.
Xiǎo'é's will was firm and her practice austere,
braving frost and rain to gather firewood,
never tiring in body or strength.
In the fourth month of the thirteenth year,
she finally received full ordination at Sìzhōu's Kāiyuán Temple,
taking Xiǎo'é as her Dharma name,
so as not to forget her origins.
That summer,
I was returning to Cháng'ān,
passing by the banks of the Sì River,
and visited Shànyì Temple,
paying respects to the great virtuous nun Lìngcāo.
I saw dozens of newly ordained nuns,
with clean-shaven heads and fresh robes,
dignified and graceful in demeanor,
standing in attendance on either side of the teacher.
One of the nuns asked the teacher:
"Is this official not the twenty-third son, Judge Lǐ of Hóngzhōu?"
The master said:
"Indeed."
She said:
"That I was able to avenge my family's wrongs,
and wash away the shame of injustice,
is all due to the judge's kindness."
She looked at me, weeping sorrowfully.
I did not recognize her,
and inquired about her story.
È replied:
"My name is Xiǎo'é,
formerly a widowed beggar woman.
The judge once helped me discern the names of the two bandits, Shēn Lán and Shēn Chūn,
do you not remember?"
I said:
"At first I did not recall,
but now I understand."
È then wept.
She fully recounted how she had recorded Shēn Lán and Shēn Chūn,
avenged her father and husband,
and fulfilled her aspiration,
After finishing,
she described the hardships she endured throughout her endeavor.
Xiǎo'é also said to me:
"To repay the judge's kindness,
there will come a day,
how could it be in vain?"
Alas!
I was able to discern the names of the two thieves,
and Xiǎo'é was able to complete the avenging of her father and husband's wrongs,
the ways of the divine are not obscure,
clearly evident.
Xiǎo'é, with her dignified appearance and profound words,
intelligent and upright,
burned her fingers and crippled her feet,
vowing to seek the true reality.
Since entering the monastic path,
her clothes held no silk or cotton,
her meals no salt or dairy;
aside from monastic discipline and Chan principles,
she spoke not a word.
Several days later,
she told me she was returning to Niútóu Mountain.
Boarding a small boat on the Huái River,
she wandered southward,
and we never met again.
The gentleman says:
Unyielding in her vow,
avenging her father and husband,
this is integrity;
mixing among servants and laborers,
unrecognized as a woman,
this is chastity.
In a woman's conduct,
only chastity and integrity,
can be maintained from beginning to end,
like Xiǎo'é,
sufficient to warn the hearts of those who defy the Way and disrupt norms under heaven,
sufficient to demonstrate the integrity of chaste husbands and filial wives under heaven.
I have detailed the previous events,
elucidated the hidden text,
which secretly aligns with the unseen,
and accords with human hearts.
To know of goodness and not record it,
is not the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
therefore I compose this biography to honor her virtue.
The Biography of Courtesan Yáng
Courtesan Yáng
was a woman of extraordinary beauty from the wards of Cháng'ān.
Her demeanor was most elegant,
and she took pride in her alluring appearance.
When dukes, princes, and great men hosted guests,
they vied to invite her to their banquets,
and even those who did not drink
would surely raise their cups to the brim and enjoy themselves fully for her sake.
The young men of Cháng'ān, once they visited her chamber,
would nearly reach the point of ruining their lives and squandering their fortunes without regret.
Thus, her fame topped the courtesan registers,
and she was greatly sought after in her time.
Commander Jiǎ of Lǐngnán,
was a son of nobility.
His wife was originally a woman from the imperial relatives' quarter,
and treated the commander with great ferocity.
They had an earlier agreement:
if he had disloyal intentions,
he would meet death under a sharp blade.
The commander, having been noble since youth,
was fond of licentiousness,
and inwardly suffered under his wife,
unable to act as he wished.
So he secretly offered a heavy bribe,
had her name removed from the courtesan register,
and took her to Nánhǎi,
housing her in another residence.
He would join her during his free time,
and return stealthily at night.
The courtesan was clever by nature,
and served the commander with particular diligence.
In daily life, she maintained herself with womanly duties,
and unless it was reasonable,
she did not act rashly.
Moreover, she treated the commander's attendants generously,
and was able to win their favor.
Thus, the commander doted on her even more.
It happened that after a year or so,
the commander fell ill,
and was near death.
He longed to see the courtesan once more,
but feared his wife.
The commander had always been close with the Imperial Army Supervisor,
so he secretly sent word to convey his wish,
asking him to devise a plan.
The Supervisor then deceived the wife, saying:
"The general is gravely ill,
and wishes to have someone skilled in nursing and preparing medicines to attend to him,
so that he may recover quickly.
I have a good maidservant,
who has long served in noble households,
and is adept at pleasing others.
I beg the lady to allow this maidservant to comfort the general's body,
what do you say?"
The wife said:
"The honored eunuch is a trustworthy man,
very well.
If it causes me no hardship,
then quickly summon the maidservant here."
The Supervisor then ordered the courtesan to pose as the maidservant to see the commander,
but before the plan could be carried out, the matter was exposed.
The commander's wife then gathered several dozen sturdy maids,
lined them with white clubs,
and had a cauldron of boiling oil lit in the courtyard, lying in wait.
When she arrived,
they would throw her into the boiling pot.
Hearing this, the commander was greatly terrified,
and urgently ordered to stop the courtesan from coming.
Moreover, he said:
"This was my own idea,
and nearly implicated her.
Now, fortunately, I am not yet dead,
I must ensure she escapes the tiger's jaws,
otherwise,
it will be too late."
So he gave her a great quantity of rare treasures,
ordered his servants to prepare a light boat,
and escorted the courtesan back north.
From then on, the commander's anguish deepened,
and within ten days, he passed away.
The courtesan had just reached Hóngzhōu,
when the news arrived.
The courtesan then returned all the commander's gifts,
set up a memorial tablet, and wept, saying:
"The general died because of me.
Since the general has died,
what use is my life?
How could I let the general die alone?"
She then removed the offerings and killed herself.
Now, a courtesan serves others with her beauty,
and without benefit, she does not engage.
Yet Yáng was able to repay the commander with her death,
this is righteousness;
refusing the commander's gifts,
this is integrity.
Although she was a courtesan,
is she not worthy of praise?
The Biography of Fēiyān
Wǔ Gōngyè of Línhuái,
during the Xiántōng era,
served as Registrar of Merits in the Hé’nán Prefecture.
His beloved concubine was named Fēiyān,
surnamed Bù,
whose appearance and demeanor were delicate and beautiful,
as if unable to bear the weight of fine silks;
she excelled in Qín music,
was fond of literary composition,
and was especially skilled at playing the óu (pottery percussion instrument),
its tones harmonizing with string and wind instruments.
Gōngyè doted on her greatly.
Their neighbor to the north was the residence of the Zhào family of Tiānshuǐ,
also a family of officials and nobility,
whose name cannot be explicitly stated.
Their son was named Xiàng,
handsome, upright, and cultured,
just around twenty years of age,
and at that time was observing mourning rites.
Suddenly one day,
through a crack in the southern wall,
he caught a glimpse of Fēiyān,
and his spirit and vitality were utterly lost,
he neglected food and forgot sleep.
He then richly bribed Gōngyè’s gatekeeper,
and confided his feelings to him.
The gatekeeper showed a troubled expression,
but was again swayed by the substantial profit,
and instructed his wife to wait for a moment when Fēiyān was alone,
and fully convey Xiàng’s intentions to her.
Fēiyān, hearing this,
only smiled faintly, gazed intently, and did not reply.
The gatekeeper’s wife relayed everything to Xiàng,
Xiàng’s heart became wild and agitated,
not knowing how to contain himself,
so he took Xuē Tāo stationery,
and inscribed a quatrain, saying:
"At one glimpse of a beauty that topples cities,
my worldly heart can only guess in vain.
Not following Xiāo Shǐ away,
I intend to learn from Ā Lán to come."
He sealed what he had written in secret,
and entreated the gatekeeper’s wife to deliver it to Fēiyān.
Yān, having finished reading it,
sighed for a long while,
and said to the old woman:
"I too have caught a glimpse of Gentleman Zhào,
most excellent in talent and appearance.
In this life, my fortune is thin,
I cannot be matched with him."
It was because she despised Wǔ’s crude and boorish nature,
that he was not a suitable match.
She then composed a reply in verse,
writing on golden phoenix stationery, saying:
"Green sorrow dims my paired moth-eyes, I cannot hold myself steady,
only because hidden regrets lie within the new poem.
Your heart should resemble the grievance in a zither’s heart,
to whom shall these tender spring feelings, wordless and deep, be directed?"
She sealed it and handed it to the gatekeeper’s wife,
instructing her to give it to Xiàng.
Xiàng opened the letter,
chanted and recited it several times,
clapped his hands joyfully and said:
"My affair is settled!"
He then took Shànxī jade-leaf paper,
and composed a poem to express his gratitude, saying:
"I treasure the fair one’s gift of lovely words,
on colored paper, fragrant brushwork, both deep in feeling.
Thinner than cicada wings, hard to convey regret,
dense as fly heads, yet not fully expressing the heart.
It seems like falling blossoms bewildering a jade-green grotto,
I only think of light rain sprinkling a secluded lapel.
A hundred times the news, a thousand times the dream,
I fashion them into a long song to send to the green zither."
After the poem was sent, ten days passed,
and the gatekeeper’s wife did not come again.
Xiàng worried and feared the affair was exposed,
or that Fēiyān had reconsidered.
On a spring evening,
sitting alone in the front courtyard,
he composed a poem, saying:
"Green dark, red hidden, rising twilight mist,
alone I harbor hidden regrets before the small courtyard.
In the deep, fine night, with whom to speak?
Stars separated by the Milky Way, the moon at half the sky."
The next day,
as he rose at dawn and was chanting,
the gatekeeper’s wife came to convey Fēiyān’s words, saying:
"Do not be surprised at ten days without word,
