it is because I have been slightly unwell."
Thereupon she handed Xiàng a linked-cicada brocade sachet,
along with a poem on green moss stationery, saying:
"Too weak for solemn adornment, I lean by the embroidered sill,
secretly inscribing cicada brocade, thoughts endless.
Lately I have gained a spring-sickness of sorrow,
willow frail, flowers drooping, timid of the dawn wind."
Xiàng tied the brocade sachet to his bosom,
carefully read the brief note,
and fearing Yān’s melancholy thoughts might increase her illness,
he cut black-lined paper for a reply, saying:
"Spring days draw long,
the human heart is quiet with sorrow,
ever since that glimpse,
my dream soul has long been enslaved.
Though like a feathered carriage and dusty robe,
meeting is difficult to achieve;
yet my cinnabar sincerity, bright as the sun,
vows to attend you devotedly.
Moreover, I hear that taking advantage of spring brings many feelings,
your fragrant steps are out of harmony.
Wasting your ice-and-snow beauty,
depressing the fine aura of orchid and iris,
the extreme of worry and repression,
makes me wish I could not soar and fly;
I hope for eased feelings,
do not let it reach pallor and emaciation.
Do not辜负 these short verses,
how could I disregard our later meeting?
My bewildered inch of heart,
how can writing fully express?
Along with this, I present my humble lines,
looking up to continue your glorious composition.
The poem says:
I hear your sorrow is for seeing spring,
I imagine you sealing the cicada brocade, green moth-eyes frowning.
Knocking my head to report to Lady Yān:
the foremost in romance is most damaging to a person."
Once the gatekeeper’s wife obtained the reply,
she went straight to Yān’s chamber.
Wǔ, being an official in the prefecture,
had numerous and busy public duties,
sometimes on night duty for several nights,
or not returning home all day.
At this time, it happened that he had gone to the prefectural offices,
Yān opened the letter,
and was able to leisurely examine and ponder it,
then after a long while sighed deeply and said:
"A gentleman’s will,
a maiden’s heart,
feelings in accord, souls communing,
make the distant seem as near."
Thereupon she closed the door and lowered the curtain,
and wrote a letter, saying:
"Your humble concubine is unfortunate,
orphaned while still wearing childish hair.
In between, deceived by matchmakers,
I was paired with a petty sort.
Whenever clear breeze and bright moon,
moving jade bridges,
to increase longing;
autumn curtains, winter lamps,
drifting golden markers to convey regret.
How could I have expected, young master,
that you would suddenly send such fine words?
Opening the glorious letter, my thoughts take flight,
chanting the beautiful lines, my gaze is cut off.
What I regret is that the waves of Luòchuān separate us,
Jiǎ Wǔ’s wall is high,
joined clouds cannot reach the Qín terrace,
presenting dreams is still distant from the Chǔ peaks.
Yet I still hope Heaven will grant my sincere plea,
spirits will lend subtle opportunity,
for one audience with your pure light,
even nine deaths I would not regret.
Along with this, I inscribe a short piece,
to convey my hidden feelings.
The poem says:
"Painted eaves’ spring swallows should roost together,
Luò riverbank’s paired mandarin ducks, would they fly alone?
Ever regretting those Táoyuán maidens, companions all,
casually among flowers seeing their lord depart."
Having sealed it,
she summoned the gatekeeper’s wife,
and instructed her to deliver it to Xiàng.
Xiàng, reading the letter and poem,
and seeing that Yān’s feelings were somewhat urgent,
was overjoyed and unable to contain himself,
but simply burned incense in a quiet room,
and prayed devoutly while awaiting news.
One day, as evening approached,
the gatekeeper’s wife came with hurried steps,
smiling and bowing, saying:
"Does Gentleman Zhào wish to see an immortal?"
Xiàng was startled,
and questioned her repeatedly.
She conveyed Yān’s words, saying:
"Tonight the Registrar is on duty at the prefecture,
it can be called a fine time.
My humble home’s rear courtyard,
is the wall before the young master’s residence.
If you do not disdain this favor,
I specially hope for your gracious coming.
My heart holds ten thousand layers,
all await our meeting and conversation."
Once it grew dark,
Xiàng then climbed a ladder and ascended,
Yān had already ordered a double couch placed below.
Once he descended,
he saw Yān adorned in fine attire and full dress,
Standing beneath the blossoms.
After bowing in greeting,
both were so overcome with joy they could not speak,
and so hand in hand they entered the hall through the back door.
Then, turning their backs to the lamp and loosening the curtains,
they gave full expression to their tender affection.
When the morning bell first tolled,
she again escorted Xiàng to the foot of the wall.
Yān held Xiàng’s hand and wept, saying:
“Today’s meeting
is due to a bond from a former life.
Do not think that I, lacking the resolve of jade’s purity or pine’s steadfastness,
am so wanton and unrestrained.
It is simply because of your graceful demeanor
that I could not restrain myself.
I hope you will deeply understand this.”
Xiàng said:
“Embracing a beauty rare in this world,
and seeing a heart that surpasses others,
I have already sworn to the hidden powers,
to forever cherish our joyful intimacy.”
After speaking,
Xiàng climbed over the wall and returned home.
The next day,
he entrusted the old gatekeeper woman to present Yān with a poem, which said:
“Though the Ten Caverns and Three Purities are paths blocked,
with a sincere heart one may still approach the Jasper Terrace.
The fragrant breeze of auspicious incense leads thoughts deep into the night;
I know it is the immortal carriage from the Stamen Palace that has come.”
Yān read the poem and smiled faintly,
then in turn presented Xiàng with a poem, saying:
“In longing, I fear only not recognizing each other;
upon meeting, I still worry about parting from you.
I wish to transform into a crane beneath the pine,
a pair flying away into the marching clouds.”
She sealed it and gave it to the old gatekeeper woman,
also instructing her to tell Xiàng:
“It is only because I have some small talent for verse
that things are thus; otherwise,
what great literary face would you, sir, be making?”
Within less than ten days,
they often managed to meet once in the rear courtyard.
They expressed their subtle, intimate thoughts,
and poured out their long-held hearts’ desires,
believing that neither ghosts nor spirits knew of it,
and that heaven and man were aiding them.
Sometimes, inspired by the scenery before their eyes,
they would convey their feelings through song and verse.
Their comings and goings were frequent,
and cannot all be recorded.
A full year passed like this.
Not long after,
Yān several times beat her maidservant for minor faults.
The servant secretly harbored resentment,
and seizing an opportunity, told Gōngyè everything.
Gōngyè said:
“Be careful what you say;
I will watch and investigate.”
Later, on his scheduled duty day,
he falsely submitted a request for leave.
When evening came,
he went on duty as usual,
but then secretly hid near the neighborhood gate.
Once the street drums had sounded,
he crept home on his belly.
Following the wall to the rear courtyard,
he saw Yān leaning against the door, softly chanting,
while Xiàng was leaning on the wall, gazing sidelong at her.
Gōngyè, unable to contain his fury,
rushed forward intending to seize him.
Xiàng, sensing this, leapt away.
Gōngyè grabbed at him,
and caught hold of half his short jacket.
He then entered the room,
called Yān, and interrogated her.
Yān’s face changed color and her voice trembled,
but she did not tell him the truth.
Gōngyè grew even angrier.
He bound her to a large pillar,
and whipped her until the blood flowed.
She only said:
“In life we were able to be close;
what regret is there even in death!”
Late in the night,
Gōngyè, weary, dozed off.
Yān called her favorite maidservant, saying:
“Bring me a cup of water.”
When the water arrived,
she drank it all and died.
Gōngyè awoke,
and was about to whip her again,
but she was already dead.
He then untied her, lifted her, and placed her in the inner chamber,
calling out to her repeatedly,
announcing that Yān had died suddenly from a violent illness.
Several days later,
she was buried at Běimáng,
but all in the neighborhood lanes knew she had met a violent death.
Xiàng consequently changed his clothes and name,
and fled far away to the region of Jiāngzhè.
Among the talented scholars of Luòyáng were two, named Cuī and Lǐ,
who often associated with Military Adjutant Wǔ.
Cuī composed a poem whose final couplet read:
“Just like the flower-passing man when the drinking party ends,
leaving the most luxuriant branch abandoned on the empty bed.”
That night,
he dreamt that Yān thanked him, saying:
“Though my looks did not match the peach and plum,
my withering and falling surpassed theirs.
Holding your excellent verses,
my shame and admiration are boundless.”
Lǐ’s poem ended with the couplet:
“If her lovely spirit and fragrant soul still exist,
she should still feel ashamed to see the woman who threw herself from the tower.”
That night,
he dreamt that Yān pointed a halberd at him,
and, shaking her hand, said:
“A gentleman has a hundred lines of conduct;
have you, sir, fulfilled them all?
Why must you, relying on a few words, so bitterly slander and disparage me?
I shall make you bend underground to bear witness to this.”
Several days later,
Lǐ died,
which people of the time found strange.
The Tale of the Numinous Response
Twenty li east of Jīngzhōu,
there lies the old Xuē Jǔ City.
At the corner of the city is the Shànnǚ Qiū,
spanning several li in breadth and length,
with reeds and rushes forming lush green clusters,
and ancient trees standing sparse and tall.
Its waters are deep and emerald green,
with no one able to fathom their depth.
Aquatic spirits and strange creatures
are often seen there.
The local people built a shrine beside it,
called the "Shrine of the Ninth Maiden."
Every year, during floods or droughts, prayers and exorcisms
were offered there with requests.
Furthermore, over two hundred li west of the prefecture,
north of Cháonà Town,
there is another pool spirit named after the place,
called the "Cháonà Spirit."
In terms of spiritual efficacy and responsiveness,
it surpasses even the Shànnǚ Spirit.
In the fifth year of the Qiánfú era,
while Military Governor Zhōu Bǎo was stationed there,
from the beginning of mid-summer,
clouds and vapors frequently appeared,
taking shapes like strange peaks,
like beautiful women,
like rats or tigers,
rising from the two pools.
They stirred fierce winds,
shook with thunder and lightning,
tore off roofs and uprooted trees,
lasting for several moments before ceasing.
They injured people and damaged crops,
causing great harm.
Bǎo blamed himself and strove to improve,
believing his governance was insufficient,
thus incurring the wrath of the dark spirits.
On the fifth day of the sixth month,
while taking a break from official duties in his residence,
he felt drowsy and wished to sleep,
so he removed his headscarf and lay down on his pillow.
Before he had fully fallen asleep,
he saw a warrior wearing a helmet and armor,
holding an axe and standing at the foot of the steps,
saying:
"There is a female guest at the gate,
wishing to request an audience.
I have come first to seek your permission."
Bǎo asked:
"Who are you?"
The warrior replied:
"I am your gatekeeper,
who has served you for many years."
As Bǎo was about to question him further,
he saw two maidservants ascending the steps.
They knelt before him and said:
"The Ninth Maiden has come specially from her suburban villa to seek an audience.
She has sent us first to convey her message to you, esteemed sir."
Bǎo said:
"The Ninth Maiden is not a relative or close acquaintance of mine.
How dare I rashly meet her?"
Before he finished speaking,
auspicious clouds and a light drizzle appeared,
and a strange fragrance filled the air.
Suddenly, a woman appeared,
around seventeen or eighteen years old,
dressed in plain, light-colored robes,
with a graceful and delicate appearance.
She descended from the air
and stood in the courtyard corridor.
Her demeanor was elegant and refined,
possessing a beauty unmatched in the world.
She was accompanied by over ten attendants,
all dressed in bright, clean garments,
resembling the retinue of a princess.
Moving gracefully and hovering about,
she gradually approached his resting place.
Bǎo intended to step aside briefly
to await her intentions.
A servant stepped forward and said:
"Our noble mistress, recognizing your high principles,
believes she can entrust you with a sincere request.
Thus, she wishes to lay bare her grievances
before you, esteemed sir.
Would you, esteemed sir, bear to not rescue her in her dire straits?"
Bǎo then invited her to ascend the steps to meet him.
The etiquette between host and guest
was solemn and respectful.
She sat on the couch,
surrounded by auspicious mists,
with a purple aura filling the courtyard.
She composed herself and lowered her head,
appearing sorrowful and distressed.
Bǎo ordered wine and food to be served,
treating her with great courtesy.
Suddenly, she straightened her sleeves, rose from her seat,
and hesitantly said:
"I have resided in the suburban gardens
for many years,
enjoying your generous hospitality and virtue,
and have received deep kindness from you.
Though I endure lonely nights on a cold bed,
I am content to remain so for life.
As a lonely widow with a place to rely on,
my burdens have only grown heavier.
However, the paths of the visible and invisible worlds differ,
and our actions and whereabouts are at odds.
Now, compelled by emotion and propriety,
how can I remain silent?
If you can understand my hidden feelings,
I dare to reveal them to you."
Bǎo said:
"I wish to hear your story.
I hope to learn of your lineage.
If I can be of assistance,
how could I use the difference between the visible and invisible worlds as an excuse?
A noble person sacrifices himself to achieve benevolence,
upholding righteousness and determination;
braving boiling water and scorching fire,
to redress injustices—
this is my aspiration."
She replied:
"My family originally hailed from Màoxiàn in Kuàijī,
and settled by a deep pool in the Eastern Sea.
Our ancestral graves and mulberry trees
have been there for over a hundred generations.
Later, we encountered an era of misfortune,
and disaster befell our household.
Five hundred members of our clan suffered the calamity of being burned by the Yǔ family.
Our lineage was nearly extinguished.
Unable to bear sharing the same sky with our enemies,
we fled to secluded cliffs,
but our deep grievances remained unavenged.
During the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty,
Emperor Wǔ, driven by curiosity,
summoned people to communicate with the Dragon Palace,
to enter the Withered Mulberry Island,
and to use the rare delicacy of roasted swallows
to befriend the seventh daughter of the Lord of Dòngtíng, the Treasure Keeper,
in order to seek rare treasures.
Soon, we heard that our family enemy, Yǔ Píluó,
from Báishuǐláng in Màoxiàn,
resigned from his official post and relinquished his seal,
intending to accept the emperor's command and undertake the mission,
harboring sinister intentions.
By this means, he sought to enter the Dragon Palace,
under the pretext of seeking treasures,
to destroy our clan's descendants.
Fortunately, the astute Jié Gōng,
discerning that he was motivated by personal vendetta,
sought to inflict harm on the innocent,
feared that his actions would bring disgrace
and dishonor to the emperor's command.
He advised Emperor Wǔ,
who then halted the plan.
Instead, he sent Ōuyuè Luózǐchūn from Luòlí County in Hépǔ Commandery to go in his place.
My ancestors,
ashamed to share the same sky with their enemies,
and fearing future calamities,
led their clan
to conceal their traces and vanish from sight,
changing their surname and name,
and sought refuge in Ān Village, Zhēnníng County, Xīnpíng.
Clearing away brambles and digging caves,
they built dwellings there.
Our ancestors' humble abode
became almost like a distant, foreign land.
Now, after three generations of settling there,
my ancestor first became the Língyìng Jūn (Spirit-Responsive Lord),
and was later enfeoffed as Yìngshèng Hóu (Responding-to-Holiness Marquis).
Later, due to his widespread aid as a dark spirit,
and his merits and virtues benefiting the people,
he was further enfeoffed as Pǔjì Wáng (Universal Aid King).
His awe-inspiring virtue touched the people,
and he was highly regarded by the world.
I am the king's ninth daughter.
When I came of age, I was married to the youngest son of the Stone Dragon of Xiàngjùn.
My husband, inheriting a violent nature,
was in the prime of his youth,
unrestrained by laws,
and unchecked by his strict father.
He governed with cruelty,
showing no regard for ritual or propriety.
Before a year had passed,
he indeed incurred heaven's punishment,
causing the ruin of his clan and the end of his line,
erasing his name and traces.
Only I alone
barely escaped with my life.
My parents pressured me to remarry,
but I ultimately defied their orders.
Princes and marquises sent proposals,
with carriages arriving one after another.
My resolve was firm,
and I even considered disfiguring myself.
My parents, angered by my stubbornness,
banished me to a separate estate in this region,
cutting off all communication.
It has been thirty-six years now.
Though I have not yet been reconciled with my parents' kind faces...
It has been a long time since I performed the duties of warming the bed in winter and cooling it in summer for my parents, and
living in seclusion away from the crowd
has been quite satisfying.
In recent years, the young dragon of Cháonà,
because his younger brother was unmarried,
secretly sent betrothal gifts,
with sweet words and generous offerings,
but I sternly refused and he came again.
To destroy my nature and ruin my form
is nearly impossible.
Cháonà then established friendly relations with my father,
wishing to accomplish this matter,
and thus had his younger brother temporarily move to the west of the royal domain,
intending to offer him as a hostage to our king,
to secure the marriage alliance.
My father, knowing that I could not be swayed,
ordered Cháonà to send troops to press me.
I also led over fifty of my household servants,
armed them with weapons,
and engaged in battle on the outskirts of the plains.
Outnumbered and outmatched,
we fought three battles and were defeated three times.
My troops were weary and exhausted,
with no support to rely on.
I intended to gather the remaining forces,
and make a last stand with my back to the city,
but feared that the waters of Jìnyáng were swift,
and the fires of Táichéng were fierce.
Once the city fell,
I would be humiliated by the stubborn youth.
Even if I perished and descended to the springs below,
I would have no face to meet the son of the Shí family.
Thus, the *Book of Songs* says:
‘That cypress boat,
floats mid-river.
With hair in two tufts,
he is truly my mate.
Until death, I swear to have no other.
O mother, O Heaven!
Why will you not understand me!’
These are the words of the widow of the heir of Wèi, swearing an oath.
It also says:
‘Who says the rat has no teeth?
How then does it pierce my wall?
Who says you have no wife?
Why then do you hasten my lawsuit?
Though you hasten my lawsuit,
I will not follow you.’
This is from Shào Bó hearing lawsuits,
when the customs of decline and disorder waned,
The teachings of chastity and faithfulness flourished,
Thus, violent men
could not violate chaste women.
Now, your teachings
can penetrate both the manifest and the obscure,
Setting an example for past and present.
The teachings of chastity and faithfulness
are certainly not inferior to those of Jī Shì.

He walked among the curtains and screens,
as if there were someone attending to his toiletries.
He called out and ordered a candle to be lit,
but there was no response.
He then raised his voice and shouted at them.
Only then did they speak, saying:
"The realms of the living and the dead are separate;
I hope you will not press me with the light of a lamp."
Zhōu Bǎo secretly realized this was unusual,
so he held his breath and quieted his voice,
slowly saying to them:
"Could it be that you are the Ninth Maiden?"
The reply came:
"I am an attendant of the Ninth Maiden.
Yesterday, thanks to you, we borrowed troops,
saving us from peril.
However, because matters of the hidden and visible realms differ,
we were unable to command them.
If you can honor our initial agreement,
I hope you will reconsider it."
Soon, the gauze window gradually brightened,
and when he fixed his gaze to look,
there was nothing to be seen, all quiet.
Bǎo pondered this for a long time,
before finally understanding its meaning.
He then summoned his officials,
ordering them to check the military register,
selecting the names of those who had died,
obtaining five hundred cavalrymen,
and fifteen hundred infantrymen.
From among them, he selected Yāyá Mèng Yuǎn,
appointing him as the temporary commander of the expeditionary camp.
A dispatch was sent to the deity of Shànnǚ Qiū.
On the eleventh day of that month,
he withdrew the soldiers garrisoning the temple.
As they appeared before the hall,
during their maneuvers,
one armored soldier fell to the ground,
his mouth moving and eyes blinking,
but when questioned, he gave no response,
nor did he seem like someone who had died suddenly.
He was placed in the corridor,
and only at dawn did he regain consciousness.
Bǎo then sent someone to question him,
and he replied:
"At first, I saw a person,
dressed in a blue robe,
coming from the east,
who greeted me with great courtesy.
He said to me:
'Our noble mistress has received immense kindness from the Prime Minister,
saving her from fire and drowning,
yet she has not fully expressed her sincerity.
Relying on your intelligence and discernment,
she wishes to convey her hidden feelings once more,
and hopes you will not decline.'
I urgently refused with other words,
but he then took me by the sleeve,
and I fell into a daze and collapsed.
I only felt myself following closely behind the blue-robed figure,
and soon arrived at the temple,
where I was hurried along with quick steps,
until I reached the curtains.
There, the noble mistress said to me:
'Yesterday, thanks to the Prime Minister's compassion for my isolation and peril,
he sent you to garrison our humble domain.
Traveling back and forth on the roads,
you must have been weary.
I have recently received the Prime Minister's loan of troops once more,
which deeply satisfies my sincere wishes.
I see that the soldiers and horses are elite and strong,
and their armor and weapons are sharp and effective.
However, the temporary commander Mèng Yuǎn,
is of light talent and low rank,
and utterly lacks strategy and foresight.
On the ninth day of this month,
more than three thousand roaming troops
came to raid our outskirts.
I then ordered Mèng Yuǎn to lead the newly arrived officers and soldiers
to intercept them on the plains,
but the ambush was not set up secretly,
and they were instead defeated by the enemy forces.
I greatly desire a general skilled in strategy,
so I am sending you back quickly,
to convey my true feelings.'
After speaking,
I bowed and took my leave,
feeling dazed as if drunk,
and knew nothing more."
Bǎo verified his account,
finding it consistent with his dream.
Intending to investigate the previous matter,
he dispatched Zhìshèng Guān envoy Zhèng Chéngfú to replace Mèng Yuǎn.
On the evening of the third day of that month,
in the rear polo field of the yamen,
he poured wine and burned incense,
sending a dispatch requesting the Ninth Maiden deity to take charge.
By the sixteenth day,
a report came from Zhìshèng Guān, stating:
"On the night of the thirteenth day of this month,
from the third watch onward,
the Guān envoy died suddenly."
Bǎo was shocked and sighed,
sending someone to rush and see.
Upon arrival, it was indeed confirmed he had died,
only his heart and back were not cold.
Even in the hot month, the corpse was kept,
yet it did not decay.
His family found this very strange.
Suddenly, one night,
a gloomy wind blew fiercely,
whipping up sand and stones,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees,
flattening all the crops,
and only stopping at dawn.
Clouds and mist spread in all directions,
not clearing for several nights.
By dusk,
there was a sudden clap of thunder,
splitting the sky like a crack.
Chéngfú suddenly groaned and sighed several times,
and his family opened the coffin to look,
and after a long while, he revived.
That evening,
relatives and neighbors all gathered,
mingling grief and joy.
After two nights, he was as before,
and his family questioned him about the reason.
He then said:
"At first, I saw a person,
wearing a purple sash,
riding a black horse,
with more than ten attendants,
who dismounted at the gate,
and summoned me to meet.
After exchanging courtesies and pleasantries,
he handed me a dispatch, saying:
'Our noble mistress had a dream of blowing dust,
knowing that you possess talent to command the age,
wishing to follow the precedent of Nányáng,
and thinking to annihilate the enemy of the state.
She has sent me, her humble servant, with these ceremonial gifts,
to briefly show respect to you, sir.
And she hopes to restore the state's fortunes once more,
and hopes you will not find her three visits burdensome.'
I had no time for other words,
only saying I did not dare.
During the exchange of toasts,
I already saw the betrothal gifts laid out below the steps,
with saddled horses, weapons, armor, brocades, colored garments, playthings, quivers, and the like,
all arranged in the courtyard.
Unable to decline,
I bowed twice and accepted them.
I was then urged to mount the carriage,
and the horse I rode was exceptionally majestic and strong,
its decorations fresh and clean,
and the attendants were orderly and solemn.
In an instant, we traveled over a hundred lǐ,
and about three hundred armored cavalry arrived,
to escort and guard us.
It had the air of a great general's entourage,
and I too felt quite pleased with myself.
In a moment,
I saw a great city in the distance,
its battlements lofty and towering,
its moats deep and broad,
and I was bewildered, not knowing where I was.
Soon, outside the suburbs,
tents and music were prepared,
and a feast was set.
After the banquet, we entered the city,
with onlookers packed like walls,
and minor officials calling out announcements,
crisscrossing among them.
The gates we passed through,
I could not count their number.
When we reached a certain place,
it seemed like a government office.
Attendants asked me to dismount and change clothes,
then hasten to see the noble mistress.
The noble mistress sent someone to convey a message,
requesting to meet with the etiquette of host and guest.
I thought to myself that since I had received official documents, weapons, armor, and military equipment,
I was already a subject,
so I firmly declined,
and entered in full military attire to see her.
The noble mistress sent someone again to relay a message,
asking me to remove my quiver,
saying that between host and guest,
the formalities could be reduced.
I then set aside my weapons and hastened in,
seeing the noble mistress seated in the hall.
I paid my respects,
following the etiquette between ruler and subject.
After bowing,
she repeatedly called me to ascend the steps.
I bowed again,
and ascended from the western steps.
I saw attendants with red makeup and dark eyebrows,
their hair coiled like dragons and phoenixes, standing in attendance.
There were several dozen groups;
those playing stringed instruments and holding pipes,
dressed in exotic attire and performing duties,
numbered several dozen more;
those with golden belts and purple robes,
dragging sashes and gathering hairpins while hurrying to the corners,
were not limited to just one person;
those in light furs with broad sashes,
white jade girding their waists,
standing densely arrayed beneath the steps,
were numerous indeed.
Next, five or six female guests were summoned,
each with a dozen or so attendants,
shoulder to shoulder and step by step,
they advanced in a continuous line.
I too lowered my gaze and bowed deeply,
not daring to perform a full prostration.
Once seated,
several senior officers,
were all commanded to take their seats,
wine was raised,
and music was presented.
When the wine reached the noble princess,
she straightened her sleeves and lifted her cup,
about to rise and speak,
to recount the intent behind the earlier summons.
Suddenly, beacon fires rose on all sides,
shouts and clamor erupted, saying:
'The rebel Cháonà's infantry and cavalry, numbering tens of thousands,
at dawn today,
breached the fortress,
and have already entered our territory.
Advancing along multiple routes simultaneously,
smoke and flames are unceasing,
we request troops to be dispatched for relief.'
Those seated in attendance looked at each other, their faces pale,
the women had no time to bid farewell,
and scattered in disarray.
The officers descended the steps to bow and give thanks,
standing still to await orders.
The noble princess approached the balcony and said to me:
'I received an extraordinary plea from the minister,
pitying his solitude and helplessness,
I dispatched troops,
to rescue him from peril.
However, with chariots and armor inadequate,
strategy and tactics must be considered.
Now, not rejecting our humble means,
the reason I have appointed you, General,
is precisely for this crisis.
I hope you will not decline due to our remote and secluded location,
and lend a little assistance to our shortcomings.'
Then she bestowed upon me two warhorses,
a suit of golden armor,
banners, flags, and ceremonial axes,
precious treasures and utensils,
filling the courtyard and dazzling the eyes,
too numerous to count.
Two maids,
were given military tallies,
the rewards were exceedingly generous.
I bowed, received them, and departed,
summoning the generals,
directing the troops,
inside and outside, responses echoed.
That night, we left the city,
successive scouts reported,
all saying,
the enemy's momentum was growing fierce.
I was well acquainted with the mountains, rivers, and geography,
the terrain's strengths and weaknesses,
so I led the army out by night.
A hundred li from the city,
I deployed at key positions,
clearly announced rewards and punishments,
issued orders to the three armies,
and set three ambushes to await them.
As dawn approached,
the deployment was complete.
The enemy, complacent from previous successes,
advanced rather recklessly,
still thinking they faced Mèng Yuǎn's command.
I personally led light cavalry,
ascended a height to observe,
and saw dust and smoke converging from all sides,
their battle formations orderly and strict.
I first sent light troops to provoke battle,
feigning weakness to lure them.
Engaging with short weapons,
we fought while retreating.
The sounds of metal and drums,
seemed to split heaven and crack earth.
I led the troops in a feigned retreat,
they also pressed forward with full force,
with one roar of drums and shouts,
the ambush troops all rose,
fighting across a thousand li,
attacking from all sides.
Their army was utterly defeated,
the dead lay like hemp,
with each engagement they fled again,
the cunning youth of Cháonà,
escaped the blade and fled,
the soldiers following in flight,
numbered no more than a dozen.
I selected thirty swift horsemen to pursue,
and indeed captured him alive under my banner.
Thus, blood and flesh stained the grass and trees,
fat and grease moistened the plains,
the stench of filth cleared the air,
spears and armor piled up like mountains.
The enemy commander was sent swiftly by light chariot to the noble princess,
who ascended the Píngshuò Tower to receive him.
All the officers and people of the state,
gathered together,
led before the tower,
he was questioned with propriety,
he only pleaded guilty,
and said nothing else.
Then he was ordered taken to the market for execution by waist-cutting.
At the moment of execution,
a messenger arrived post-haste,
from the king's place,
bearing an urgent decree,
ordering a swift pardon for him.
It said:
'Cháonà's crime,
is my crime,
you may pardon him,
to lessen my fault.'
The noble princess, overjoyed that her parents had again communicated,
unable to contain her happiness,
said to the generals:
'Cháonà's reckless action,
was by my father's command;
now ordering his pardon,
is also my father's command.
In the past, I disobeyed the command,
which was to preserve my chastity;
now if I disobey again,
it would be inauspicious.'
So she ordered his bonds removed,
and had him escorted back by a single horseman,
before reaching Cháonà,
he died of shame on the road.
For my merit in defeating the enemy,
I was greatly favored and rewarded,
soon being ceremonially appointed as General Who Pacifies Troubles,
granted a fief of thirteen thousand households in Shuòfāng.
Additionally bestowed with a mansion,
carriages, horses, precious vessels,
clothing, maids, and servants,
gardens, estates, and residences,
banners, flags, and armor.
Next, the various generals,
were rewarded according to their merits.
The next day, a grand feast was held,
those seated numbered no more than five or six,
the six or seven women from before all came to attend,
their graceful demeanor and enchanting appearance,
were even more captivating.
We drank deeply throughout the night,
very joyfully.
When the wine reached the noble princess,
she raised her cup and said:
'My misfortune,
to have lived in empty chambers since youth,
heaven endowed me with solitary chastity.
Not obeying my strict father's command,
I have secluded myself here for thirty-six years.
Disheveled and disheartened,
yet not finding death.
The neighboring youth's coercion,
nearly brought me to ruin.
Were it not for the minister's extraordinary kindness,
and the general's mighty valor,
then I, a silent woman of the state of Xī,
would have become Cháonà's prisoner.
I shall forever speak of this grace,
never forgetting it all my days.'
Then she took a seven-treasure cup to pour wine,
and had someone present it to General Zhèng.
I therefore rose from my seat,
bowed twice and drank.
From then on, I felt a strong desire to return home,
pleading earnestly and reasonably,
I was granted a month's leave,
and after the feast, I departed.
The next day,
after bidding farewell and giving thanks,
leading my thirty-some subordinates, I returned along the coming path,
the places I passed through,
hearing chickens and dogs,
filled me with deep sorrow.
In a moment, I reached home,
saw my family gathered weeping,
the spirit tablet solemnly displayed.
One of my subordinates,
urged me to quickly enter the coffin's seam,
I wished to step forward,
and was incited by those around him.
Suddenly, he heard a clap of thunder,
and woke up with a start.”
From then on, Chéngfú no longer managed his family property,
but entrusted all future matters to his wife and children.
Indeed, after one month,
he passed away without illness.
When he was about to die suddenly,
he told his close relatives:
“I was originally skilled in strategy and served in the military,
devoting myself to the army.
Although I never achieved any remarkable feats,
I did accomplish some modest deeds.
After encountering trouble and being implicated,
I was banished here.
My lifelong aspirations and ambitions
have been suppressed and unfulfilled.
A true man should eventually stir up great winds
and topple massive waves,
topple,
crush Mount Tài like an egg,
and divert the Eastern Sea to drown fireflies.
I will unleash my hawk-and-hound heart
to avenge injustices for others.
I will soon receive my mission,
and part ways with you all.
It will not be long now.”
On the thirteenth day of that month,
someone set out from Xuējǔ City
at dawn, traveling over ten lǐ,
when the sky was just beginning to brighten.
Suddenly, he saw dust rising from carriages ahead,
with splendid banners and flags,
and several hundred armored cavalry.
In their midst was a man
with an imposing and majestic aura.
Drawing closer to look,
it was Zhèng Chéngfú.
This person was astonished for a while,
then stood by the roadside.
He saw them sweep by like wind and clouds,
arriving at Shànnǚqiū.
In an instant,
they vanished without a trace.
Xiàhóu Dǎn
During the Liáng dynasty, Xiàhóu Dǎn served as a high-ranking official.
Though his family was poor, he loved to keep musicians.
The female musicians had no fine clothes or ornaments,
so when guests arrived,
he would have them play music from behind a curtain.
People at the time said the curtain was Xiàhóu’s musicians’ clothing.
Wáng Sù
Wáng Sù, styled Gōngyì, served as Shàngshū Lìng in the Later Wèi dynasty.
He was from Lángyá.
Sù was the son of Huàn, the Governor of Yōngzhōu in the Qí dynasty.
He was erudite and knowledgeable in many fields,
with exceptional literary talent and eloquence,
and served as Secretary of the Qí dynasty.
In the eighteenth year of the Tàihé era,
he returned north to the Later Wèi.
At that time, Emperor Gāozǔ was newly constructing the capital at Luòyì,
and for all the institutions being established,
Sù, with his broad knowledge of past affairs,
provided great assistance.
Emperor Gāozǔ held him in high regard,
often calling him “Wáng Shēng.”
While Sù was in Jiāngnán,
he married a daughter of the Xiè family.
After arriving in the capital,
he also married a princess.
Later, the Xiè woman became a Buddhist nun
and came to seek out Sù.
Seeing that Sù had married the princess,
Xiè composed a five-character poem to present to him.
The poem read:
“Once a silkworm on the mulberry leaf,
now silk upon the loom.
Having spun and gone with the victor,
I still recall the time of entanglement.”
The princess replied to Xiè on behalf of Sù:
“The needle is for threading,
its eye always holds silk.
Having obtained silk to sew anew,
how can it take in the old thread?”
Sù was deeply regretful and resentful,
so he built the Zhèngjué Temple for her to reside in.
Lǐ Yánshí
Lǐ Yánshí, Grand Tutor of the Later Wèi dynasty,
was the maternal uncle of Emperor Zhuāng.
During the Yǒng’ān era,
he was appointed Governor of Qīngzhōu.
When he was about to depart to take up his post,
the Emperor said to Shí:
“The custom of ‘embracing bricks’
is known throughout the ages as difficult to govern.
Uncle, you must apply yourself diligently
to fulfill the court’s trust.”
Shí replied:
“My years approach the evening of life,
my vitality is like the morning dew;
the human world grows distant,
as I draw near the pine-covered hills.
I have long sought to retire in leisure,
yet Your Majesty, mindful of our kinship,
has favored this old minister,
sending me on a night journey without companions,
to tailor brocade across ten thousand lǐ.
I respectfully accept Your Majesty’s clear command,
and dare not fail in my duty.”
At that time, the Attendant Gentleman Huángmén Yáng Kuān was by the Emperor’s side.
Not understanding the meaning of “embracing bricks,”
he privately asked the Secretary Wēn Zǐshēng.
Zǐshēng said:
“I heard that His Majesty’s elder brother, Prince Péngchéng, served as Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and learned from his guests who accompanied him to Qīngzhōu
that the people of the Qí region
have shallow and fickle customs.
They engage in empty talk and lofty discussions,
focusing solely on glory and profit.
When a new governor is about to enter the region,
the common people all embrace bricks and kowtow
to show their goodwill.
But when he is replaced and returns home,
they pelt him with bricks,
showing how quickly their loyalty reverses, faster than turning a hand.
Thus, a ballad in the capital says:
‘In the prison, there are no detainees,
prisoners;
in the houses, there are no people from Qīngzhōu.
Even if the family’s circumstances are poor,
the heart holds no sorrow.’
The meaning of ‘embracing bricks’
originates from this.”
Xún Jì of Yǐngchuān
was a refined and famous scholar,
with profound insight and exceptional discernment,
standing out in his time.
Cuī Shùrén of Qīnghé once said of the scholar-officials of Qí:
“The people of Qí
outwardly pretend to be virtuous,
but inwardly harbor vulgar stinginess.
They treat others as lightly as feathers,
and value profit as keenly as awls and knives.
They love chasing empty fame
and flattering those in power to build their reputations.
Wherever power and influence lie,
they rush to align themselves.
If there is nothing to gain,
they abandon it immediately.”
This speaks to their extreme fickleness and shallowness.
Lǐ Yìchēn,
a native of Lǒngxī,
resided in Wèi.
He was appointed as a surveillance commissioner from the position of registrar of Xiányáng.
He was orphaned and impoverished in his youth.
In the early establishment of the Táng dynasty,
he had no means of livelihood.
He lived together with his second cousin Yìchēn and third cousin Shàngdé,
serving their paternal aunt
with the same attentiveness as towards their own parents.
During the Wǔdé era,
they all became jìnshì.
They shared a single donkey
and traveled to the capital.
When they reached Tóngguān,
heavy rain fell,
and they sought lodging at an inn.
The innkeeper, despising their poverty,
excused himself by saying there were too many guests
and refused to take them in.
With nowhere to go, advancing or retreating,
they lingered by the gate.
A merchant from Xiányáng saw them and invited them in.
Many fellow lodgers murmured in disapproval.
The merchant said:
"These three are traveling scholars.
Now they have nowhere to stay.
How can we watch them in such distress?"
He then invited them to share his sleeping quarters.
After several days, the weather cleared,
and the roads became passable.
Yìchēn and the others discussed selling the donkey to buy a feast.
The merchant secretly learned of this,
firmly stopped them,
and instead provided them with travel provisions.
After Yìchēn passed the imperial examination,
he served in various positions in Xiányáng.
He summoned the merchant
and treated him as an equal.
The merchant did not recognize him at first,
but merely felt apprehensive and withdrew respectfully.
Yìchēn explained the reason,
and only then did the merchant realize,
whereupon Yìchēn invited him into the main hall.
Later, Yìchēn served as a surveillance commissioner.
Liú Lóng
Liú Lóng, later named Yìjié,
in the early Wǔdé era,
presented a plan to Emperor Gāozǔ, saying:
"Now our righteous army numbers tens of thousands,
all stationed in the capital.
Firewood is expensive, while cloth and silk are cheap.
If we gather trees from the streets and imperial gardens for firewood,
and exchange it for silk,
we could obtain several hundred thousand bolts annually.
Moreover, within the treasury stores of silk,
each bolt has excess material on the rollers.
If we cut off these surplus portions,
to cover miscellaneous expenses,
we would easily gain tens of thousands of segments."
Emperor Gāozǔ adopted both suggestions.
Péi Xuánzhì
During the Wǔdé era,
there was a monk named Xìnyì,
who practiced meditation
and followed the Three Stages school,
establishing an inexhaustible treasury at Huàdù Temple.
treasury.
After the Zhēnguàn era,
donations of money, silk, gold, and jade
accumulated beyond measure.
This monk was often put in charge of managing it.
It was divided into three portions:
one portion for maintaining and repairing temples throughout the land,
one portion for relieving the suffering of the hungry and destitute,
and one portion for unrestricted offerings.
Men and women crowded to perform rituals and confess sins,
vying to make donations without order.
Some even brought carts loaded with coins and silk,
left them as donations, and departed,
without leaving their names.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
there was a man named Péi Xuánzhì,
who was diligent and devoted in his monastic discipline.
He entered the temple to perform cleaning duties.
After more than a decade,
the temple community,
considering his conduct flawless,
entrusted him with guarding this treasury.
Later, he secretly stole gold,
taking amounts
that were nearly impossible to count,
yet the temple community remained unaware.
When the monks sent him on an errand,
he never returned.
Astonished and suspicious of the reason,
they inspected his living quarters,
where they found a poem inscribed:
"Placing a sheep under a wolf's jaw,
setting bones before a dog.
Unless one is an arhat,
how could one avoid stealing?"
His whereabouts thereafter were unknown.
The Ministry of Revenue Official
During the Zhēnguàn era,
the Imperial Medical Service petitioned for dùruò herbs,
and an imperial order was sent to the Ministry of Revenue.
A ministry official, citing Xiè Tiǎo's poem which says:
"Gather dùruò in Fāngzhōu,"
assigned Fāngzhōu to tribute the herbs.
A clerical officer in that prefecture commented:
"Fāngzhōu does not produce dùruò.
This must be a mistake from reading Xiè Tiǎo's poem.
For a ministry official to make such a judgment,
is he not afraid the Twenty-Eight Mansions will laugh at him?"
Emperor Tàizōng heard this and laughed heartily,
then transferred the official to serve as a judicial officer in Yōngzhōu.
Yú Shìnán
Emperor Tàizōng intended to send cherries to the Duke of Xī,
but using the term 'present' seemed too respectful,
while 'bestow' seemed too condescending.
He asked Yú Shìnán for advice.
Shìnán replied:
"In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Liáng sent gifts to the Prince of Bālíng of Qí, calling it 'a provision.'"
The emperor followed this example.
Yùchí Jìngdé
Yùchí Jìngdé was skilled at disarming opponents of their lances.
Prince Qí, Yuánjí, was also adept with the lance.
Emperor Gāozǔ tested them in front of Xiándé Hall.
He said to Jìngdé:
"I have heard you are skilled at disarming lances.
Let Yuánjí hold a lance with its blade removed."
Jìngdé said:
"Even with the blade attached,
he could not harm me."
Thus, the blade was attached.
In a brief moment,
Jìngdé disarmed him three times.
Yuánjí was greatly ashamed.
Yú Shìjī
Yú Shìnán's elder brother Shìjī and Xǔ Jìngzōng's father Shànxīn
were both killed by Yǔwén Huàjí.
Fēng Déyí, then a secretary in the Central Secretariat,
witnessed the entire event.
He later remarked to others:
"When Shìjī was executed,
Shìnán prostrated himself, begging to die in his place;
when Shànxīn died,
Jìngzōng danced and pranced, pleading for his own life."
Lái Héng,
younger brother of the Grand Councilor Lái Jì,
the brothers successively held high administrative power,
which contemporaries considered an honor.
Héng's father, Lái Hù'ér,
was a fierce general of the Suí dynasty.
At that time, Yú Shìnán's son, lacking talent or skill,
served as the Director of the Palace Buildings.
Xǔ Jìngzōng heard of this
and sighed:
"How upside-down the service of affairs has become,
that it reaches such a state!
Lái Hù'ér's son becomes a chancellor,
while Yú Shìnán's son works as a carpenter."
Ōuyáng Xún
When Empress Wéndé passed away,
all officials attended the mourning.
Ōuyáng Xún, the Director of the Palace Timing, had an exceptionally ugly and strange appearance,
and many pointed at him.
The Secretariat Drafter Xǔ Jìngzōng saw him and laughed loudly,
for which he was impeached by the censor,
and demoted to Military Aide of Hóngzhōu.
Xǔ Jìngzōng
Emperor Tàizōng campaigned against Liáo,
constructing flying ladders to approach their city walls.
There was a volunteer who became the leader of the ladder crew.
Arrows and stones from within the city fell like rain,
yet he strove to be the first to ascend.
Duke Yīng, Lǐ Shìjì, pointed at him and said to the Secretariat Drafter Xǔ Jìngzōng:
"Is this man not exceedingly robust?"
Jìngzōng replied:
"Not robust,
it's just that he does not yet understand careful consideration."
When the Emperor heard this,
he intended to punish him.
Yuán Wànqǐng served as the administrative clerk for the Liáodōng circuit.
He drafted a proclamation,
ridiculing Gāolì,
stating, "They do not know to guard the strategic point of the Yālù River."
Mòlízhī replied:
"I have respectfully received your instruction."
He then moved troops to guard it.
Wànqǐng was consequently banished to Lǐngnán.
Guō Wùjìng
Guō Wùjìng, the assistant magistrate of Nánpí in Cāngzhōu, was by nature muddle-headed.
Once, staying at an inn with the Registrar Liú Sīzhuāng,
he said to Zhuāng:
"Accompanying the imperial carriage is terribly difficult.
I, Jìng, once accompanied the carriage,
and lost my family members for three days,
finally finding them under the tent of an attendant official."
Zhuāng asked:
"Was your wife among them?"
Jìng said:
"If she weren't among them,
what else would I be talking about?"
He also said to Zhuāng:
"There are many thieves nowadays.
Last night after the second watch,
as I, Jìng, was coming from outside,
a thief
suddenly walked out from inside my room."
Zhuāng asked:
"What was stolen?"
Jìng said:
"Nothing."
Zhuāng said:
"If nothing was stolen,
how do you know he was a thief?"
Jìng said:
"I just saw him scurrying away in a panic,
and couldn't help but suspect him."
Táng Lín
Táng Lín was by nature tolerant and benevolent,
often forgiving.
Once, intending to attend a funeral,
he ordered a servant boy to go back and fetch a white robe.
The boy mistakenly brought another garment,
and, fearing punishment, dared not present it.
Lín noticed this
and said to him:
"Today my energy flow is adverse,
it is not suitable for grieving and weeping.
The fetching of the white robe can stop for now."
Another time, he ordered medicine to be brewed, but it was not done properly.
Secretly realizing the reason,
he then said:
"Today is dark and gloomy,
it is not suitable to take medicine.
You may discard it."
He never exposed their faults.
Sū Guī and Lǐ Qiáo's Sons
Emperor Zhōngzōng once summoned the sons of the chancellors Sū Guī and Lǐ Qiáo for an audience.
Both sons were still in their childhood years.
The Emperor welcomed and patted them in front of him,
bestowing generous gifts.
He then spoke to the two boys, saying:
"You should recall the books you have studied.
You may speak of something you could present to me."
Sū Tǐng (Sū Guī's son) responded:
"Wood follows the marking line to become straight;
the sovereign follows remonstrance to become sage."
Lǐ Qiáo's son, whose name is lost,
also stepped forward and said:
"He cut the shins of those who waded in the morning;
he cut out the heart of the worthy man."
The Emperor said:
"Sū Guī has a son.
Lǐ Qiáo has no son."
Lóu Shīdé
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
the chancellor Lóu Shīdé was gentle, respectful, and cautious.
He never had the slightest conflict with anyone.
When his younger brother was appointed prefect of Dàizhōu,
Shīdé admonished him:
"I am very worried that you will contend with others."
His brother said:
"If someone spits on my face,
I will simply wipe it off and leave."
Shīdé said:
"That is not enough.
When someone spits on your face,
it is because they are angry.
Wiping it off
goes against their feelings.
Why not wait for it to dry by itself?"
His methods of self-preservation and avoiding harm
were all of this kind.
Also, Wǔ Zétiān's prohibition against slaughter was quite strict,
and officials suffered from only having vegetables.
Shīdé, serving as the Censor-in-chief,
was on a mission and arrived at Shǎn.
The cook presented meat.
Shīdé asked:
"An imperial decree forbids slaughter.
Why is this here?"
The cook said:
"A wolf killed the sheep."
Shīdé said:
"What a sensible wolf!"
And then ate it.
When fish slices were presented,
he again asked why this was here.
The cook again said:
"A wolf killed the fish."
Shīdé then loudly scolded him:
"You dimwit!
Why not say it was an otter?"
The cook immediately said it was an otter.
Shīdé also recommended him for promotion.
Lǐ Huì
Lǐ Huì served as the Chief Administrator of Yōngzhōu.
His private residence had a tower
overlooking a wine shop.
The shopkeeper once waited for Huì and said:
"I am a person of lowly status.
Although etiquette may not require it,
my family has elders and children.
I do not wish for outsiders to peer in.
My home is pressed close to Your Excellency's tower,
making coming and going inconvenient.
I beg to take my leave from here."
Huì demolished his tower that very day.
Sòng Zhīwèn,
during Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
sought to become a North Gate Academician,
but was not granted permission.
He composed the "Poem of the Bright River" to express his intent.
The poem reads:
"The bright river can be gazed upon but not approached;
I wish to board a raft and inquire of the ford.
Moreover, taking the Weaving Maid's loom stone,
I would still visit the fortune-teller in Chéngdū."
When Zétiān saw his poem,
she said to Cuī Róng:
"It is not that I do not know Zhīwèn has talent and refinement,
but it is because he has a mouth affliction."
This was because Zhīwèn suffered from a tooth disease,
causing his mouth to often smell foul.
Zhīwèn felt ashamed and resentful for the rest of his life.
Lù Yuánfāng
Lù Yuánfāng served as Vice Minister of the Chancellery and Secretariat,
holding the position of chancellor.
When Wǔ Zétiān intended to make promotions or appointments,
she would always consult him first.
Yuánfāng would secretly recommend candidates,
not revealing the favor he bestowed,
so no one knew of it.
The memorials and documents he had previously submitted
were sealed in a case,
and his family members never saw them.
On his deathbed,
he ordered them burned.
He said:
"I have performed many hidden virtues for others.
The subsequent blessings for my descendants will certainly not decline.
My lifespan was originally destined to be long,
but because I headed the selection bureau,
evaluating and classifying officials,
I injured my spirit and mind."
Having spoken, he passed away.
Chén Xīmǐn
Sīxíng Sīchéng Chén Xīmǐn, due to his lack of talent in holding office,
caused all affairs to stagnate.
The clerks of the Sīxíng office
nicknamed him "Master of the Brush,"
meaning that when he held the brush,
it would not descend for half a day,
hence the name "Master of the Brush."
He was also called "Press Confucius,"
meaning he made so many deletions and revisions
that the paper became full of holes,
hence the name "Press Hole."
Lǐ Xiáng
Lǐ Xiáng, courtesy name Shěnjǐ,
was from Zhàojùn.
His grandfather was Jīhéng,
and his father was Yǐng,
both generations passing down Confucian traditions.
Lǐ Xiáng possessed talent, literary flair, and courage,
but was unrestrained and unconventional.
He began his career as the Wèi of Yántíng.
While in Yántíng,
during an evaluation,
he was pushed aside by the Lùshì Cānjūn.
Lǐ Xiáng said to the Cìshǐ:
"The Lùshì relies on the authority of the Jiūcáo,
occupying a critical position,
and arbitrarily praises or criticizes others.
If I were to hold the brush,
I could also craft such words."
The Cìshǐ said:
"Please try to comment on the Lùshì's evaluation report."
He then handed him the brush.
Lǐ Xiáng immediately wrote the Lùshì's evaluation as follows:
"Timid in deciding major cases,
fond of nitpicking,
petty delays.
Hides his own lack of clarity,
claims others are always muddled.
Two disputes before the steps,
only cease after a fight.
Prisoners in the jail,
won't leave without a pardon."
This became the most talked-about joke in the land.
Fáng Guāngtíng
Fáng Guāngtíng served as a Shàngshū Láng.
His old friend Xuē Zhāo was exiled,
and sought refuge with Guāngtíng,
who hid him.
After the matter was exposed,
Yùshǐ Lù Yíyì pressed him urgently.
Guāngtíng grew fearful,
and went to see the current chief minister.
The chief minister said:
"You are a court official,
why did you hide this man?"
He replied:
"Guāngtíng has an old friendship with Xuē Zhāo.
He came to me in desperate straits,
and his offense was not a major one.
Could I have refused to take him in?
If I had captured and sent him to the authorities,
how would those in the court
have treated Guāngtíng thereafter?"
The chief minister admired his righteousness,
and had him appointed as Cìshǐ of Cízhōu,
with no further repercussions.
Guāngtíng once attended the funeral of a relative or friend.
Exiting Dǐngmén,
as evening approached and he was hungry,
he encountered a vendor selling cakes,
and ate with several companions.
He never carried money,
and had nothing to pay with.
The vendor pressed him,
so Guāngtíng told him to come to his place for payment,
but the vendor refused.
Guāngtíng said:
"I'll give you my official title—
I am a Yòutái Yùshǐ.
You can follow me to collect payment."
People of the time appreciated his free-spiritedness.
Cuī Sījīng,
during Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
someone accused his cousin Cuī Xuān of plotting rebellion.
The case was handed to Yùshǐ Zhāng Xíngjí for investigation.
The accuser had first lured and hidden Cuī Xuān's concubine,
then claimed the concubine was about to expose the plot,
so Xuān killed her
and threw the body into the Luò River.
Xíngjí investigated
but found no evidence.
Wǔ Zétiān was angry,
ordering a reinvestigation,
but Xíngjí reported the same as before.
Wǔ Zétiān said:
"Cuī Xuān's rebellion is clear,
yet you are lenient and indulgent.
If I order Jùnchén to investigate,
you will regret it."
Xíngjí said:
"I am not as skilled in handling cases as Jùnchén,
but Your Majesty entrusted me,
requiring solid evidence.
If I follow orders and wrongly exterminate a clan,
is that what a judge should uphold?
I must believe Your Majesty is testing me."
Wǔ Zétiān said sternly:
"If Cuī Xuān indeed killed the concubine,
his rebellion would naturally be clear.
If the concubine is not found,
how can he clear himself?"
Xíngjí, afraid,
pressured Cuī Xuān's family to search for the concubine.
Sījīng then placed money and silk
on both sides of Zhōngqiáo,
offering rewards for information on the hidden concubine,
but for several days heard nothing.
Moreover, whenever his family secretly discussed matters,
the accuser would immediately know.
Sījīng suspected a conspirator within the household,
so he pretended to tell Xuān's wife:
"We need three hundred bolts of silk
to hire an assassin to kill the accuser."
Then, at dawn, he lay in wait before the tribunal.
In Xuān's household, there was a resident guest surnamed Shū,
from Wùzhōu,
whose conduct had been impeccable,
serving Xuān's family,
and trusted by Xuān like a family member.
Shortly after,
he saw this man go to the tribunal to bribe the gatekeeper,
to communicate with the accuser.
The accuser then claimed:
"The Cuī family hired someone to assassinate me,
I request this be reported."
The tribunal was alarmed.
Sījīng had always respected this guest,
never suspecting him.
He secretly followed him,
and upon reaching Tiānjīn Bridge,
realizing he had no reason to go to the tribunal,
scolded him:
"You treacherous villain!
If the Cuī family is ruined,
they will surely implicate you as a conspirator.
How will you clear yourself then?
If you can produce the Cuī family's concubine,
I will give you five hundred jiān of silk,
enough to build a lifelong fortune back home.
Otherwise,
I will certainly kill you."
The man repented and apologized,
then led Sījīng to the accuser's house,
where they found and rescued the concubine.
Thus, Xuān was exonerated.
Cuī Shí
Táng dynasty Cuī Shí
passed the imperial examination as a Jìnshì in his youth.
Within less than ten years,
he oversaw the imperial examinations,
and was promoted to the Ministry of War.
His father, Cuī Yī,
had also served in the Ministry of Rites,
and now father and son served together in the same ministry as Shìláng.
Later, he became chief minister three times,
at the age of only thirty-six.
When Cuī first assumed power,
he was just twenty-seven,
dignified and elegant in demeanor,
with clear and beautiful literary talent.
Once, he went out of Duānmén at dusk,
descended Tiānjīn Bridge,
and recited on horseback:
"Spring outing to Shànglín Park,
flowers fill Luòyáng City."
Zhāng Yuè, then Shìláng of the Ministry of Works,
gazed at him from afar and sighed:
"These lines can be emulated,
this position can be attained,
but his youth cannot be matched."
Lǚ Tàiyī
Lǚ Tàiyī served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Revenue.
The Bureau of Revenue was adjacent to the Bureau of Appointments.
At that time, the Bureau of Appointments sent an official document
ordering the Bureau of Revenue to erect thorny hedges along its walls
to prevent unauthorized communication with the Bureau of Evaluation.
Tàiyī replied:
"Considering that Bureau of Appointments,
the office overseeing evaluations,
should be concise, clear, and efficient,
why must it plant hedges and thorns?"
The ministry admired his sharp wit.
Xǔ Jièyán
Xǔ Jièyán served as the governor of Lángyé.
A prisoner hanged himself in the jail,
so he had the jail warden from the previous year flogged.
The jail warden said:
"I was merely in charge of maintaining the jail.
If the walls were not sturdy,
the prison cells were damaged,
and thieves escaped from within,
I could still be pardoned due to the long duration of my maintenance duties.
How much more so when the prisoner hanged himself to death?
What crime did the jail warden commit?"
Jièyán angrily replied:
"You are a petty official;
your actions naturally warrant a beating.
What more do you have to complain about?"
Dù Fēng
Dù Fēng, the magistrate of Lìchéng County in Qízhōu,
in the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
when the emperor traveled east to perform the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
Fēng was in charge of provisions.
He had thirty coffins made
and placed them in the traveling palace.
The officials considered this inappropriate,
but Fēng said:
"The imperial procession is passing through now,
and the entire imperial harem is accompanying it.
If someone suddenly dies,
how could we obtain coffins?
If we do not prepare in advance,
will we not regret it later?"
When the provisioning commissioner entered the traveling palace,
he saw coffins displayed under the tents,
gleaming brightly.
Startled, he rushed out
and said to the prefect:
"The sage emperor is performing the fēng sacrifice on the sacred mountain
to pray for blessings and longevity.
Who made these coffins?
And what are they intended for?
How extremely inauspicious!"
He was about to report this to the emperor
when the prefect ordered Fēng to be found.
Fēng hid under his wife's bed,
pretending to have been sentenced to death.
His family wept for him.
Fortunately, his brother-in-law, Zhāng Tuán, who served as a censor,
intervened on his behalf,
and the matter was resolved.
Fēng's son, Zhōng,
at the time served as an assistant in Yǎnzhōu.
The military governor ordered him to manage the fodder for the stables.
Zhōng said:
"There are too many imperial horses;
if we cook the grain on the day it is needed,
I fear it will not be sufficient.
It would be better to prepare in advance."
So he cooked over two thousand dàn of millet and beans in a cauldron,
stored them in a cellar,
and sealed it while they were still hot.
When it was time to provide the provisions and they were retrieved,
they had all spoiled and turned foul.
He fled,
still fearing he would not escape punishment.
He ordered his attendant to buy half a shēng of bànxià,
cooked it with mutton, and ate it,
hoping to die.
However, the poison failed to harm him, and he grew even fatter.
People at the time said,
"Such a father could only have such a son."
A Commoner of Xiūwǔ County
In the second month of the twenty-ninth year of the Kāiyuán era,
a man from Xiūwǔ County married off his daughter.
The groom's family came to fetch the bride,
and the carriage followed.
The bride's father, fearing that villagers would block the carriage,
borrowed a fine horse
and had her ride it,
while her younger brother followed on a donkey,
riding a hundred paces behind the carriage.
Suddenly, two men emerged from the grass.
One seized the horse,
while the other drove it from behind, making it gallop away.
The younger brother could not catch up,
so he reported it to his father.
The father and relatives searched for her,
but could not find her all night.
About thirty lǐ from the bride's home,
there was a village school.
At that time, evening classes were held,
and many students stayed overnight.
Early in the morning, when they opened the door,
they saw a woman outside,
naked, with her tongue cut out,
and blood dripping from her private parts.
The students asked her,
but when she opened her mouth, blood flowed,
and she could not speak.
The students reported it to their teacher.
The teacher came out to look,
gathered the students, and said:
"I have heard the Master say,
'In mountains and forests dwell kuí and wǎngliǎng;
in waters dwell dragons and wǎngxiàng;
in the earth dwell fényáng.'
Our dwelling is near Tàiháng Mountain,
a place where monsters are born.
Could this be a mountain spirit or wild demon?
Why not attack it?"
So they threw bricks and stones at her.
Since her tongue was cut out,
she could not speak.
The students struck her,
and she eventually died.
When daylight came,
they realized she was not a demon.
Soon after, the bride's family came searching
and found her.
They seized the teacher and his students and took them to the county office.
The deputy magistrate, Lú Fēng, interrogated them,
and they had indeed killed her.
He then reported it to the commandery.
The teacher and students were flogged,
and three of them died,
but the robbers were never caught.
Lǐ Yuánxiāo
Lǐ Yuánxiāo served as the prefect of Yízhōu.
He was angry with his assistant, Què Chéngmíng,
and ordered him to be stripped and flogged outside the screen.
Chéngmíng was a cunning man.
After exiting the screen,
he happened to meet the erudite Liú Cóngjìn, who arrived late
and was about to enter the office.
Chéngmíng, seeing that Cóngjìn was a scholar,
seized him and began stripping him,
deceiving him by saying:
"The prefect is angry that you are late to the office.
He ordered me to take men and fetch you,
and to have you stripped and brought in immediately."
Cóngjìn believed him,
so he removed his clothes.
Chéngmíng signaled to the clerks and guards,
who seized Cóngjìn and brought him in,
while Chéngmíng escaped.
Yuánxiāo saw the stripped man brought in
but did not realize it was Cóngjìn.
So he had him flogged several dozen times.
Cóngjìn stood up and apologized, saying:
"I have received the grace of your flogging,
but may I ask what crime I have committed?"
Yuánxiāo said:
"You have been tricked by Chéngmíng."
Cóngjìn had nothing more to say
and went inside.
Wáng Jū
When Xuánzōng was still a prince,
he often roamed between the Wéi and Dù districts south of the city.
Once, while chasing a cunning hare,
he became so engrossed in the pleasure that he forgot to return.
With a dozen or so of his companions,
they grew very hungry and weary,
so they rested under a large tree in a village.
It happened that a scholar
invited the emperor to his home.
His family was very poor,
having only a village wife and a donkey.
The emperor had not sat long
when the scholar slaughtered the donkey and cooked millet,
preparing a feast
with abundant wine and meat.
The emperor looked on and found it very strange.
When he spoke with him,
he found him open and extraordinary.
He asked his surname,
and it was Wáng Jū.
From then on, whenever the emperor roamed the Wéi and Dù districts,
he would always visit Jū’s home.
Jū’s discussions and opinions
aligned with the emperor’s thoughts,
and the emperor grew increasingly fond of him.
When the Wéi clan monopolized power,
the emperor was deeply worried
and secretly confided only in Jū.
Jū said:
"When there is chaos, kill them.
Why show them any favor?"
The emperor then adopted Jū’s strategy
and quelled the internal turmoil.
He repeatedly appointed Jū as Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and indeed, Jū was honored with posthumous sacrifices.
Lǐ Shìzhī
Lǐ Shìzhī entered official service
without serving as a clerk or registrar,
and directly became an Assistant Governor;
without serving in the two capital regions,
he became the Governor of the Capital;
without serving as a Censor or Vice Censor-in-Chief,
he became the Grand Master of Remonstrance;
without serving in the two departments or as a Secretary,
he became a Chancellor;
without serving as a Prefect,
he became a Military Commissioner.
Bái Lǚzhōng
Bái Lǚzhōng was widely versed in literature and history
and lived in seclusion in Liángchéng.
Wáng Zhìyīn and Yáng Yáng both recommended him.
Soon, he requested to return to his hometown,
and was granted the title of Grand Master of Court Discussion.
A fellow villager said to Lǚzhōng:
"Your family is poor,
yet you never received a single peck of rice
or a bolt of silk.
Although you obtained the fifth rank,
it is merely an empty title.
What practical benefit does it bring?"
Lǚzhōng cheerfully replied:
"In past years, when the Khitan invaded,
every household was conscripted for door-to-door labor.
I was specifically exempted by the county authorities
because I had read a few books,
and to this day, I feel ashamed.
Although I do not receive a salary or rewards,
I am still a fifth-rank household.
I can lie high for the rest of my life,
exempt from corvée labor.
This is not easy to obtain."
The Night-Shining Curtain
When Yáo Chóng served as Chancellor,
he once had an audience in the informal hall.
He lifted his left foot,
but it was not very nimble.
The emperor said:
"Do you have a foot ailment?"
Chóng replied:
"I have an ailment of the heart and belly,
not a foot ailment."
He then stepped forward and reported several hundred words of accusations against Zhāng Yuè.
The emperor angrily said:
"Return to the Secretariat,
and announce that you shall investigate the matter together with the Vice Censor-in-Chief."
But Yuè was unaware of this.
It happened that an official reported the time as three quarters past noon,
and Yuè rode his horse home first.
Chóng urgently summoned Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Línfǔ
and handed him the previous edict.
Línfǔ said to Chóng:
"Yuè is very cunning.
We must surely corner him,
and assign him to a harsh post."
Chóng said:
"The Chancellor has committed an offense,
but we should not press him too hard."
Línfǔ added:
"If you cannot bear to do so,
then Yuè will surely come to no harm."
Línfǔ only handed the edict to a junior censor,
and on the way, he reported that his horse had stumbled.
About a month before Chóng’s accusation,
there was a tutor in Yuè’s household
who had an affair with Yuè’s most favored maidservant.
When the illicit affair was discovered and captured,
it was reported to Yuè.
Yuè was very angry
and intended to thoroughly investigate the case with the Capital Governor.
The tutor said loudly:
"Being unable to resist beauty
is also human nature.
In times of urgency, might you need someone?
Why are you so stingy with a maidservant?"
Yuè found his words remarkable and released him,
and even gave him the maidservant to take away.
The tutor left and was not heard from for several months.
There was no news of him.
Suddenly one day,
he came directly to visit Yuè,
his face full of worry.
He said:
"I have long felt grateful for your kindness
and wished to repay it.
Now I hear that you have been framed by Chancellor Yáo,
and the external investigation is about to be completed.
You are unaware of it,
and danger is imminent.
I wish to obtain something you treasure in your life
to devise a plan with the Ninth Princess,
and I may be able to have you released immediately."
Yuè then pointed out all the treasures he owned one by one,
but the tutor said of each:
"This is not enough to resolve your crisis."
After pondering for a long time,
he suddenly said:
"Recently, someone from Jīlín Commandery sent me a night-shining curtain."
The tutor said:
"My task is accomplished."
He then asked Yuè to write a few lines by hand,
pleading with sincere words,
and hurriedly rushed out.
By nightfall,
he finally reached the residence of the Ninth Princess.
The tutor fully explained Yuè’s situation
and also presented the night-shining curtain as a gift.
He said to the princess:
"Does His Majesty not recall the time in the Eastern Palace,
when he thought of ensuring a beginning and an end,
and showed favor to Chancellor Zhāng?
Why does he now instead believe slander?"
The next morning,
the princess went to court for an audience
and fully reported the matter.
The emperor was moved,
and urgently ordered Gāo Lìshì to go to the Censorate and announce:
"The previously investigated matter
shall all be dismissed."
The tutor was never seen again.
Bān Jǐngqiàn
During the Kāiyuán era,
when the court selected and appointed officials,
it always promoted the most capable and suitable.
Since culture and institutions flourished,
outstanding talents, whether entering or leaving the capital,
all regarded local appointments as minor.
Even for powerful provinces and major prefectures,
if appointed from redundant officials in the central court,
it was considered a demotion at the time.
Bān Jǐngqiàn went from the Investigation Commissioner of Yángzhōu
to become the Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review in the capital,
passing through Dàliáng on the way.
Ní Ruòshuǐ was the prefect there,
and he held a grand farewell feast in the western suburbs.
After the banquet,
Jǐngqiàn boarded his boat,
and Ruòshuǐ watched the dust from his departure,
saying to his subordinates:
"Bān’s journey this time,
how is it any different from ascending to immortality?
To serve as his attendant,
I would gladly do so."
He remained silent for a long while
before finally turning his carriage back.
Later, he composed a poem and sent it to the Chancellor’s office,
to express his sincerity,
and the poem was praised and admired at the time.
Xuē Lìngzhī
In the second year of the Shénlóng era (706 CE),
in Mǐn,
a man from Chángxī named Xuē Lìngzhī passed the imperial examination.
During the Kāiyuán era (713–741 CE),
he served as a tutor in the Eastern Palace.
At that time, the officials in the palace lived in idleness and obscurity,
so he lamented his situation through poetry,
writing on the wall:
"The morning sun rises round and bright,
shining upon this scholar's plate.
What is there upon the plate?
Only alfalfa climbing the railings.
The rice is coarse, hard to scoop with a spoon;
the soup is thin, chopsticks find little to hold.
One can barely manage morning and evening—
how to endure the year's cold?"
The Emperor, while visiting the Eastern Palace,
saw this.
He took a brush and added:
"The woodpecker's beak is long,
the phoenix's feathers are short.
If you dislike the cold of pines and cassia,
then go chase the warmth of mulberry and elm."
Because of this, Lìngzhī pleaded illness and returned east.
When Emperor Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict summoning him,
but Lìngzhī had already died.
Yǔwén Róng
Emperor Xuánzōng appointed Yǔwén Róng as the Commissioner for Land Survey.
Róng acted arbitrarily and arrogantly;
those who did not fully align with him
were inevitably slandered and falsely accused.
He secretly reported that Lú Cóngyuàn had extensively acquired fields and gardens,
owning several hundred qǐng of land.
The Emperor had always held Cóngyuàn in high regard
and had several times considered him for the position of chancellor;
moreover, his clan was prestigious, his official career illustrious, and his marital connections prominent,
reaching a peak of influence at the time.
Therefore, the Emperor also hesitated to speak gravely of his fault,
merely referring to Cóngyuàn as "the old man with many fields."
Cóngyuàn had grown up in Xiàngzhōu in his youth
and sat for the míngjīng examination.
He often followed the five categories of recommendation,
achieved the third rank in the decree examination,
and was appointed as the sheriff of Xià County.
From his earlier míngjīng status to becoming Vice Minister of Personnel,
took only ten years.
From Vice Director of Personnel to Vice Minister,
took only seven months.
Gēshū Hàn
During the Tiānbǎo era (742–756 CE),
Gēshū Hàn was the military governor of Ānxī,
controlling a territory of several thousand lǐ,
and his authority and commands were highly renowned.
Therefore, the people of the western frontier sang of him:
"The Big Dipper's seven stars are high,
Gēshū Hàn carries his sword at night.
The Tibetans are all slaughtered,
and we build
two layers of moats."
At that time, he dispatched the capital liaison officer
and military commander Zhāng Zhuó to the capital to report on affairs.
Encountering Yáng Guózhōng's monopolization of power and corruption,
Zhuó lingered and did not return,
instead offering bribes to establish connections.
When Hàn later arrived at the capital
to report at court,
Zhuó, learning of Hàn's arrival,
feared
and sought Yáng Guózhōng's promotion and appointment.
Guózhōng then appointed Zhuó as concurrent Censor-in-Chief,
and acting military governor of Jiànnán Xīchuān.
After the imperial decree was issued,
Zhuó went to Hàn's residence to bid farewell.
Hàn ordered his subordinates to seize him in the courtyard,
enumerated his offenses,
had him beaten with a staff and killed,
and only then reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor instead bestowed Zhuó's corpse
and further ordered Hàn to administer another hundred blows to the corpse.
Cuī Yǐnfǔ
Among the Líyuán entertainers was a young foreigner skilled at playing the flute,
who received particular favor.
He once offended Cuī Yǐnfǔ, the magistrate of Luòyáng,
and then fled into the palace grounds.
Emperor Xuánzōng, at an unusual time,
using some other matter as a pretext,
summoned Yǐnfǔ for an audience.
The young foreigner was at his side.
Pointing at him, the Emperor said:
"I ask you for this person—
may I have him?"
Yǐnfǔ replied:
"Your Majesty's words
demean your servant and elevate an entertainer.
I request to resign from my post."
He bowed twice and departed.
Emperor Xuánzōng hastily said:
"I was only joking with you."
He then ordered the young man dragged out,
and outside the gate,
he was immediately beaten to death with a staff.
Soon after, the Emperor ordered his release,
but he was already dead.
He then bestowed upon Yǐnfǔ one hundred bolts of silk.
Xiāo Sōng
Emperor Xuánzōng once held Sū Tǐng in high regard
and wished to rely on him as chancellor.
The courtesy and attention he showed him,
and his consultations, were exceptional among all officials.
The day before he intended to appoint him chancellor,
the Emperor, wanting secrecy
and not wishing those around him to know,
waited until late at night.
He then ordered the drafting of the edict
and inquired of his attending officials:
"Who is on duty in the outer court?"
He then had him summoned by candlelight.
The one who arrived was the Secretariat Drafter Xiāo Sōng.
The Emperor immediately gave Sōng Tǐng's name
and ordered him to draft the appointment document.
When it was completed,
the wording read:
"A treasure of the state."
The Emperor pondered it three or four times
and said to Sōng:
"Tǐng
is the son of Guī.
I do not wish to mention his father's name;
please revise it."
The Emperor also ordered the screen from his bedchamber removed and given to Sōng.
Sōng, ashamed and fearful, broke into a sweat,
and for a long time could not put brush to paper.
The Emperor, thinking Sōng was deliberating at length,
must be crafting something precise and meticulous,
unconsciously leaned forward on his mat to watch.
He merely changed it to:
"A jewel of the state."
Nothing else was altered.
After Sōng withdrew,
the Emperor threw the draft on the ground and said:
"He is merely impressive in appearance!"
Those nearby could not help but laugh.
Hearing this,
the Emperor quickly rose and covered his mouth,
saying:
"Although Sōng's talents are not outstanding,
in terms of a minister's dignity,
none can compare.
My earlier words were only in jest."
His silent understanding and divine discernment
were often of this kind.
Chén Huáiqīng
was a man of Lǐngnán.
He kept over a hundred ducks.
Later, while cleaning manure from the duck pen,
