he noticed a sparkling light in the manure.
He tried washing it in a basin of water,
and obtained ten liǎng of gold.
He then observed where they fed
and at the foot of the hill behind his house,
found placer gold in the soil.
He extracted several thousand jīn.
People at the time did not know of it,
and Huáiqīng thus became immensely wealthy,
rising to the post of prefect of Wúzhōu.
Zōu Fèngchì
To the east of the southern gate of Huáidé Ward in the Western Capital,
there was a wealthy merchant named Zōu Fèngchì.
His shoulders were high and his back was hunched,
resembling a camel,
so people of the time called him "Zōu the Camel."
His family was immensely wealthy,
with gold and treasures beyond count.
He often associated with high-ranking court officials,
and his inns, shops, gardens, and residences
were spread all across the land.
Goods from all directions were gathered by him,
and even the ancient Yī Bái
could not surpass him.
The male and female servants in his household
wore brocade clothes and ate jade-like delicacies;
the utensils and objects they used
were all astonishing for their time.
Once, on the occasion of his daughter's wedding,
he invited various court officials to attend the ceremonial feast,
with several thousand guests.
At night, the prepared tents
were extremely luxurious.
When the bride was about to emerge,
surrounded by maidservants,
adorned in fine silks, pearls, and jade,
with dangling hairpins and trailing shoes,
the most dazzling among them
numbered in the hundreds.
Everyone was stunned,
unable to tell who the bride was.
He once also sought an audience with Emperor Gāozōng,
requesting to purchase all the trees in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
offering a bolt of silk per tree.
He himself said:
"Even if the mountain trees are exhausted,
my silk will not run out."
Although the matter did not proceed,
it was widely recounted throughout the land.
Later, he committed an offense and was exiled to Guāzhōu,
but was pardoned and returned.
After his death,
his descendants fell into poverty.
There was also a man named Wáng Yuánbǎo,
who in his old age enjoyed jesting and banter,
moving about in the neighborhoods and markets,
and was well-known among people.
Because the coin inscription had the characters "yuán bǎo,"
people thus called coins "Old Wáng,"
which became very popular at the time.
Another account says
that Emperor Xuánzōng once summoned Wáng Yuánbǎo,
asking how much private wealth he had.
He replied:
"I beg to take a bolt of silk
and tie it to a tree on Your Majesty's Southern Mountain.
When the Southern Mountain trees are exhausted,
my silk will still not be depleted."
Also, when Emperor Xuánzōng was in the Hányuán Hall,
gazing at the Southern Mountain,
he saw a white dragon stretching across the mountain ridge.
He asked his attendants,
but all said they did not see it.
He urgently summoned Wáng Yuánbǎo to ask him,
and Yuánbǎo said:
"I see a white object
stretching across the mountain top,
but cannot discern its shape."
The noble ministers nearby inquired:
"Why is it that we do not see it?"
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"I have heard that extreme wealth can rival nobility.
I am the noblest in the land,
Yuánbǎo is the wealthiest in the land,
hence we can see it."
Gāo Lìshì
After Gāo Lìshì was exiled to Wūzhōu,
in the mountains
and valleys, there was much shepherd's purse,
but people did not eat it.
Moved by this,
he composed a poem to express his feelings.
"In the two capitals, it is sold by the jīn,
but in Wǔxī, no one gathers it.
Though barbarian and civilized lands differ,
its scent and taste never change."
Later, when he was pardoned,
and returning to Wǔxī,
on the way he met a Yǔlín army soldier from the Kāiyuán era,
who had been exiled to Lǐngnán for an offense.
Stopping the carriage to inquire about old times,
he then learned that the Retired Emperor had already passed away.
Gāo Lìshì gazed northward, wailing and weeping,
then vomited blood and died.
Wáng Wéi
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
when the rebel forces captured the two capitals,
they extensively plundered civil and military court officials,
as well as eunuchs, palace ladies,
musicians, and cavalry.
Each time they captured several hundred people,
they guarded them strictly with weapons
and sent them to Luò
yáng.
Some fled into the mountains and valleys,
but were eventually hunted down, captured, and coerced,
and given official caps and belts.
Ān Lùshān was particularly intent on the musicians,
searching for them quite urgently.
Within ten days,
he captured several hundred members of the Líyuán troupe.
The rebels then held a grand gathering at the Níngbì Pond,
feasting several dozen pseudo-officials.
They lavishly displayed treasures from the imperial treasury,
arraying them all around.
When the music began,
the former Líyuán members could not help but sigh,
facing each other with tears falling.
The rebels all bared their blades and drew full bows to threaten them,
yet their sorrow could not be restrained.
There was a musician named Léi Hǎiqīng
who threw his instrument to the ground
and wept bitterly facing west.
The rebel faction then bound Hǎiqīng at the Xìmǎ Hall,
dismembered him to make an example,
and those who heard of it were all pained and sorrowful.
Wáng Wéi was at that time detained by the rebels in the Pútí Buddhist Temple;
hearing of this,
he composed a poem:
"Ten thousand households grieve, wild smoke rises from the fields,
when will the hundred officials again face the court?
Autumn locust leaves fall in the empty palace,
at Níngbì Pond's edge, pipes and strings play."
Shǐ Sīmíng
After Ān Lùshān's defeat,
Shǐ Sīmíng continued the rebellion.
When he reached the Eastern Capital,
encountering ripe cherries,
and his son being in Héběi,
he wanted to send some to him,
so he composed a poem to accompany the gift.
The poem said:
"A basket of cherries,
half already red,
half already yellow.
One half to Huái Wáng,
one half to Zhōuzhì."
After finishing the poem,
his attendants praised it,
all saying:
"Your Lordship's poem is excellent,
but if you could say 'one half to Zhōuzhì,
one half to Huái Wáng,'
it would rhyme slightly better with the character 'yellow.'"
Sīmíng angrily said:
"How could my son be placed below Zhōuzhì?"
Sīmíng advanced swiftly to Yǒngníng County,
where he was killed by his son Cháoyì.
Sīmíng said:
"You kill me too early;
Lùshān at least reached the Eastern Capital,
but why are you in such haste?"
Sīmíng's son was pseudo-enfeoffed as Huái Wáng,
and Zhōuzhì was his tutor.
Dòugǔ
At the beginning of the Zhìdé era,
during the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
there was a great famine in Hédōng.
Over fifteen lǐ of wasteland produced dòugǔ,
which, swept away one evening, grew again,
yielding about five or six thousand dàn.
The grains were very round, fine, and excellent,
and people relied on them to survive.
Rùnzhōu Tower
In the southern corner of Rùnzhōu,
there is a tower named the Wànsuì Tower.
It was commonly said that if smoke emerged from the tower,
the regional inspector would die,
or if not die, then be demoted.
Before the Kāiyuán era,
Rùnzhōu was considered ominous,
[missing text].
Dǒng Wǎn served as the surveillance commissioner of Jiāngdōng,
and once resided in this prefecture.
At that time, smoke emerged during the daytime,
causing the regional inspectors to worry and fear, in great distress,
even to the point of anxiety unto death.
During the Qiányuán era,
suddenly smoke again emerged during the daytime,
forming a circle about a foot in diameter,
rising straight up several zhang.
An official secretly observed it,
approached to look at the smoke,
and found it came from a crack in the corner of the tower.
Drawing closer to inspect,
it turned out to be mosquitoes.
Below the tower was a well,
which had no water,
dark and deep.
Small insects like mosquitoes,
black and tiny.
Every evening when it cleared,
they emerged from the cracks, forming clusters and rising upward.
Viewed from afar, they resembled smoke;
when one tried to grasp them with a hand,
they were merely mosquitoes and gnats.
From then on, it was known to be not an omen,
and the regional inspectors no longer worried.
Qiū Wéi
Qiū Wéi retired from office and returned to his hometown,
and was specially granted half of his official salary.
After his mother passed away,
the local authorities were uncertain about continuing the stipend,
so they inquired with the surveillance commissioner Hán Huàng.
Huàng believed that granting an official retirement salary
originally did not involve administrative duties,
and it was specially ordered to provide the salary
to kindly support elderly officials.
It should not be altered due to mourning,
so he ordered it to be continued as before.
Only during the spring and autumn seasons,
the allowances for sheep and wine were not provided.
Although there was no written regulation for this,
it was praised as a fair compromise.
Péi Jí
After Zhū Cǐ rebelled,
Péi Jí and several other scholars,
pretending to be slaves,
sought to exit the city.
Jí’s appearance was unimpressive,
and he presented himself as Gāncǎo.
The gate guard said:
"These fellows
are certainly not slaves.
As for Gāncǎo,
we have no suspicions about him."
Lǐ Bàozhēn
Lǐ Bàozhēn was stationed in Lùzhōu,
and military supplies were lacking,
with no plan on what to do.
There was an elderly monk,
greatly trusted and respected by the local people.
Bàozhēn thus requested of him:
"May we borrow the monk’s way
to aid the military,
is it possible?"
The monk said:
"Nothing is impossible."
Bàozhēn said:
"Just say that a day is chosen for self-immolation at the polo ground,
and we plan to dig a tunnel connecting to the official residence.
Once the fire starts,
we will secretly assist
your escape."
The monk gladly agreed,
and thus made a public announcement.
Bàozhēn ordered firewood and oil to be piled up at the polo ground.
Then a seven-day Buddhist ceremony was held,
with incense and lamps day and night,
chanting and various rituals mixed together.
Bàozhēn also led the monk into the tunnel,
to make him unsuspecting.
The monk then ascended the altar, holding an incense burner,
preaching to the crowd.
Bàozhēn led the supervising army, officials, and officers,
prostrating below him.
They donated their salaries as alms,
piling them beside him.
Thus, men and women crowded together.
Donations amounted to hundreds of millions.
After seven full days,
they sent him into the pile of firewood,
poured oil to ignite the flames,
struck bells and chanted Buddha’s name.
Bàozhēn had already secretly sent people to fill the tunnel,
and in a moment,
both the monk and the firewood turned to ash.
A few days later,
they recorded the obtained wealth,
and transported it into the military supply treasury.
They separately sought several dozen so-called relics,
built a pagoda to store them.
Yáng Zhìjiān
Yán Zhēnqīng served as the regional inspector of Fǔzhōu.
Among the locals was Yáng Zhìjiān, who loved learning but lived in poverty,
unknown to his fellow villagers.
His wife, due to insufficient financial support,
demanded a divorce document to seek separation.
Zhìjiān sent her off with a poem:
"In earlier years, determined, I followed a teacher early;
Today, instead, my temples are streaked with gray.
Downcast, I know my pursuit of success came late;
Wasting time, I willingly say my advancement is delayed.
Golden hairpins may freely adorn new hair;
The phoenix mirror lets another paint your brows.
From now on, we are but fellow travelers on the road;
Meeting again will be like parting at the mountain’s descent."
His wife took the poem,
went to the prefectural office with a petition,
seeking to remarry.
Zhēnqīng ruled on the petition:
"Yáng Zhìjiān early on adhered to Confucian teachings,
and quite renowned for poetry.
Though his heart aspired to high rank,
his person has not yet received an inch of salary.
His foolish wife, seeing he had not met success,
did not stay even briefly.
Not emulating Jì Quē’s wife,
who supported her husband’s good endeavors;
solely imitating Zhū Mǎichéng’s wife,
who despised her good man.
She disgraces the village,
damages morals and customs.
If there is no punishment,
who will curb such frivolous arrogance?
The wife shall be caned twenty strokes,
then allowed to remarry freely.
As for Scholar Yáng Zhìjiān,
provide him with grain and silk,
and additionally appoint him to the army."
People from all around heard of this,
and all were pleased and convinced.
From then on, among women in Jiāngbiǎo,
none dared abandon their husbands.
Zhào Cún
In Féngyì's Dōngkū Valley,
there was a recluse named Zhào Cún,
who in the fourteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
was over ninety years old.
He took refined elixirs,
and his body was extremely light and vigorous.
He himself said:
"My father, named Jūnchéng,
also enjoyed a long life.
He once served Duke Yǎn, Lù Xiàngxiān,
and spoke of Duke Yǎn's magnanimity,
which was certainly beyond ordinary measure.
Duke Yǎn deeply believed in Buddhist scriptures.
His younger brother, Jǐngróng, privately criticized him, saying:
'My elder brother is obsessed with this teaching—
what good does it do?'
Xiàngxiān replied:
'If there truly is no path or bridge in the afterlife,
after a hundred years,
I will naturally be with you all.
But if by chance there are rewards and punishments,
then my share of merit will surpass yours.'"
When he served as the Grand Administrator of Féngyì,
many of his military aides were scions of prominent families.
Because Xiàngxiān was benevolent and tolerant,
they made a playful wager among the staff.
One said:
"I can twirl my official tablet in front of the hall,
strain my eyes wide,
bow casually to the Administrator,
shout a greeting, and walk out—
is that acceptable?"
The others all said:
"If you truly do this,
we will gladly forfeit a feast of wine and food."
That person then did it,
but Xiàngxiān looked at him as if he saw nothing.
Another military aide said:
"What you did was too easy.
I can go before the Administrator's hall,
smear my face with ink,
wear a green robe,
perform a divine dance,
and stroll slowly out."
The colleagues all said:
"No,
if you dare to do this,
we will pool five thousand coins from our salaries
as the forfeit."
The second military aide then did it,
and Xiàngxiān again acted as if he saw nothing.
They all paid their wagers,
treating it as a joke.
A third military aide said:
"What you did was extremely easy.
I can go before the Administrator's hall,
dress as a woman doing her makeup,
and imitate a new bride bowing four times to her parents-in-law—
what then?"
The others said:
"That is unacceptable.
If the benevolent one becomes angry,
you will surely be scolded and humiliated.
But if you dare to do it,
we are willing to contribute ten thousand coins from our salaries
as the forfeit."
The third military aide
then applied powder and makeup,
wore a high chignon with hairpins,
put on women's clothing,
hurried in,
and bowed deeply four times.
Xiàngxiān still did not find it strange.
Jǐngróng was furious and said:
"My elder brother is a regional inspector of the three commanderies,
yet now he has become the laughingstock of the world."
Xiàngxiān calmly said to Jǐngróng:
"It is their military aides who are the laughingstock—
how could I be laughed at?"
Earlier, Fáng Guǎn had once served as the Sheriff of Féngyì.
Xiàngxiān's clerk, Dǎng Fēn,
encountered him on a broad street,
and was slow to dismount from his horse.
Guǎn dragged Fēn down
and struck his back dozens of times.
Fēn complained to Xiàngxiān,
who asked:
"Where are you from?"
Fēn said:
"Féngyì."
He asked again:
"What official is Fáng Guǎn?"
Fēn said:
"The Sheriff of Féngyì."
Xiàngxiān said:
"The Sheriff of Féngyì punishing a commoner of Féngyì—
why are you reporting this to me?"
Guǎn then went to see Xiàngxiān,
explained the incident,
and requested to resign from his post.
Xiàngxiān said:
"Regarding Dǎng Fēn's offense,
you could have beaten him,
or not beaten him;
as an official, you beat him—
that's done.
You may resign,
or not resign."
Several years later,
Guǎn became the Magistrate of Húchéng in Hóngnóng,
and was temporarily assigned to Mǐnxiāng.
It happened that Xiàngxiān was summoned from Jiāngdōng to the capital,
and stopped at Mǐnxiāng.
At noon, he met Guǎn,
and kept him until dusk.
Guǎn did not dare to speak.
Suddenly, Xiàngxiān said to Guǎn:
"Bring your bedding—
we can spend the night
talking."
Guǎn complied,
but in the end, not a single word was exchanged.
Upon arriving at the capital,
he recommended Guǎn as a Censor.
Jǐngróng again said:
"In recent years, when Fáng Guǎn was in Féngyì,
you paid him no attention.
Now, after four or five years apart,
you meet by chance on the road,
exchange not a single word,
yet upon reaching the capital, you recommend him as a Censor—
why?"
Xiàngxiān replied:
"You do not understand.
Fáng Guǎn, as a person,
lacks nothing in all matters,
except that he does not speak.
Now he has stopped speaking,
so I am employing him for that."
Among the officials, many greatly admired his magnanimity.
Yán Zhèn
Yán Zhèn governed Shānnán,
when a man came begging for three hundred thousand coins,
his demeanor was excessively arrogant.
Zhèn summoned his son, Gōngbì, and others to ask their opinion.
Gōngbì said:
"This is truly unacceptable.
If he dares to act so presumptuously,
he must be deranged.
You, sir, need not oblige him."
Zhèn angrily said:
"You will surely bring ruin to our family.
You should only encourage me to do good deeds—
how can you urge me to be stingy with money and silk?
Moreover, this man, without discrimination,
came to me begging for three hundred thousand coins—
he is truly no ordinary person."
He ordered his attendants to give him the full amount.
Thereafter, scholars from the Three Rivers regions
submitted to him eagerly, fearing to be left behind,
and none made rash or excessive demands.
Lú Qǐ
When Lú Qǐ was chancellor,
he ordered Lǐ Kuí to go to the Tibetan region.
Kuí addressed Emperor Dézōng, saying:
"I do not fear the distance,
but I fear dying on the road
and failing to fulfill Your Majesty's command."
The emperor was moved with pity for him
and said to Lú:
"Is Lǐ Kuí not too old?"
Qǐ replied:
"An envoy for peace with the western tribes
must be thoroughly familiar with court affairs;
no one but Kuí will do.
Moreover, if Kuí is sent,
then among the officials, those younger than Kuí
will not dare decline distant missions."
After Kuí arrived in the Tibetan region,
the Tibetan chieftain asked:
"I have heard that the Táng house has a foremost man, Lǐ Kuí.
Is it you, sir?"
Kuí replied:
"No.
That Lǐ Kuí—
how would he be willing to come here?"
Fearing he might be detained,
he deceived him with this.
Kuí's family background
was foremost,
his literary talent was foremost,
and his official rank was foremost.
When Kuí retired and returned to the Eastern Capital,
Minister of Education Dù Yòu, having left his post in Huáihǎi,
went to Luòyáng and visited him.
Speaking of this "foremost" reputation,
Kuí said:
"As for family status,
a family has its origins;
I inherited its abundance.
Official rank was merely a matter of circumstance.
Now my body is withered and frail,
and I will soon depart this world.
All is emptiness—
what 'foremost' is there?"
Wéi Gāo
When Wéi Gāo was in Xīchuān,
whenever a soldier or officer was to marry,
he would give fine brocade robes to the groom's family
and silver-embroidered robes to the bride's family,
along with ten thousand cash each.
For deaths and funerals, he did likewise;
for training, he did likewise.
Those who submitted internally were enriched,
those who traveled from afar were welcomed.
He levied the utmost in taxes,
so he always had surplus resources.
Thus, the military government flourished while the common people were heavily burdened.
In his later years, he presented monthly tributes,
which ultimately led to the rebellion of Liú Pì.
The world ridiculed him for this.
Lù Chàng
Lǐ Bái once wrote the song "The Difficulty of the Shǔ Road," saying:
"The Shǔ road is difficult,
more difficult than climbing to the blue sky."
Bái wrote this to criticize Yán Wǔ.
Later, Lù Chàng wrote "The Ease of the Shǔ Road," saying:
"The Shǔ road is easy,
easier than treading level ground."
Chàng wrote this to flatter Wéi Gāo.
Initially, Chàng gained Gāo's favor,
so he composed "The Ease of the Shǔ Road" and presented it to him.
Gāo was greatly pleased
and rewarded him with eight hundred bolts of silk.
After Wéi passed away,
the court wanted to hold him accountable for past actions.
Reviewing the weapons he had previously presented,
they found the characters "Dìng Qín" engraved on them.
Those who were not on good terms with him
sought to fabricate a charge.
Chàng submitted a memorial explaining:
"When I was in Shǔ,
I saw the making of the presented weapons.
'Dìng Qín' was the artisan's name."
Thus, he was exonerated.
Mǎ Chàng
Mǎ Suì's son, Chàng,
presented large apricots from his estate to Dòu Wénchǎng,
who offered them to Emperor Dézōng.
Dézōng had never seen such apricots
and was rather suspicious.
He ordered a palace envoy to seal the apricot tree.
Chàng, in fear, offered his residence,
which was converted into the Fèngchéng Garden.
The buildings and timber were all dismantled and taken into the palace.
Wú Còu
Emperor Dézōng summoned Wú Còu unexpectedly and appointed him as the Governor of the Capital.
He was ordered to assume office immediately.
Còu hurried there,
and by the time the guests arrived at his office,
a banquet was already laid out.
Someone asked:
"How was this so fast?"
An official replied:
"The two markets daily have banquet supplies;
one just lifts the pots and takes them.
Thus, a feast for three to five hundred people
can often be prepared instantly."
Yuán Cān
When Yuán Cān defeated Yuán Tiào,
he captured several dozen of his false nobles and ministers.
The prefectures and counties prepared large stocks of shackles,
intending to send them alive to the capital.
Cān said:
"These are wicked commoners;
why trouble people over them?"
He then had them flogged on the buttocks and sent away.
Lǐ Miǎn
When the former chancellor Lǐ Miǎn served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
a subordinate's father suffered from a gu illness.
The man made a wooden effigy,
inscribed Miǎn's name and title on it,
and buried it in his father's grave mound.
Someone discovered this and reported it to Miǎn.
Miǎn said:
"To avert disaster for his father—
this is also pitiable.
Let him be."
Some said:
"Lǐ Miǎn lost the defense of Liángchéng;
he should also be demoted."
A discussion said:
"Not so.
When Lǐ Xīliè rebelled and ran amok,
his momentum was unstoppable;
Heaven was merely amplifying his crimes to bring down punishment.
Moreover, Miǎn was not skilled in adapting to change,
and reinforcements did not arrive.
At that time,
the Guānfǔ region was already in turmoil,
and people's hearts were shaken.
With the ability of a civil official,
facing a tiger-wolf's path,
he led his entire army south in retreat—
could anyone without judgment have done so?"
Yú Gōngyì
After Lǐ Shèng pacified the rebellion of Zhū Cǐ,
Emperor Dézōng read the victory bulletin announcing the recapture of the city, which said:
"I have already cleansed the palace grounds
and reverently paid homage at the ancestral tombs.
The bells and stands remain unmoved,
and the temple's appearance is as before."
The emperor wept aloud, overcome with emotion,
and all the attendants and palace ladies sobbed.
The bulletin was composed by Yú Gōngyì.
Commentators held that among court victory bulletins,
none matched this one.
Later, Gōngyì was resented by Lù Zhì,
who falsely accused him of improper conduct at home.
He was given a copy of the "Classic of Filial Piety,"
and thus ended his life in hardship.
Xíng Jūnyá
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
Xíng Jūnyá served as the military governor of Lǒngyòu Líntáo.
The presented scholars Liú Shīlǎo and Xǔ Yáozuǒ went to pay him a visit.
As the two guests were seated,
a man of very unusual appearance,
with a large head and short legs,
entered wearing hemp clothes.
Without waiting for the guest officer to announce him,
he went straight in to see Jūnyá.
Cupping his hands at his forehead, he said:
"Presented scholar Zhāng Fén dares not bow."
Jūnyá, having served in the military for many years,
was not at all surprised by this.
He then bowed and invited Fén to sit,
paying no attention to Yáozuǒ
and Shīlǎo.
Shortly after, an official came by with a case,
concerning a deficiency in funds and goods from the banquet management office.
Jūnyá examined the account books,
finding over fifty thousand cash missing,
which had been concealed and leaked by the responsible officials.
Jūnyá was furious,
and was just ordering an investigation into where the funds had gone.
Fén then brushed his sleeves and stood up, saying:
"I shall take my leave."
Jūnyá apologized, saying:
"I happen to have official business,
which I must briefly settle,
and dispatch.
I have not
offended you in any way,
why do you suddenly announce your departure?"
Fén replied:
"When I was in the capital,
I often heard that west of the capital there was a Xíng Jūnyá who propped up the heavens with his head and the earth with his feet.
Today, in front of me,
you are arguing with a banquet official over thirty or fifty thousand cash.
Is this man worthy of such contention?"
Jūnyá found this very strange,
so he released the banquet official
and became close with Fén.
Fén said to Jūnyá:
"When I was in the capital taking the examinations,
I often spent two thousand strings of cash each year,
all from social interactions.
From Wéi Èrshísān of Jiànnán,
to Zhāng
Shísān of Xúzhōu,
in a single day,
guests came in several ranks.
For those as high as secretaries and counselors,
fine food and drink were required.
For those as middle-ranking as supplementary officials,
chicken and pork had to be cooked,
either raw or sliced."
Then, pointing at Shīlǎo and Yáozuǒ, he said:
"For presented scholars like these gentlemen,
who have come from afar to visit,
you serve only coarse food.
Why not treat them better?"
Yáozuǒ was startled.
Hesitantly,
the two guests took their leave and departed.
Jūnyá gave each of them five bolts of silk.
He had the inner hall cleaned and prepared for Zhāng Fén,
who stayed for over a month,
and was given five hundred bolts of silk.
Fén then went to Wǔgōng,
where Yáozuǒ was lying ill in his lodgings.
Fén did not even bow to him.
Two years later, Yáozuǒ passed the imperial examination,
but refused to take up an official post.
He later suffered from ailments of the waist and legs.
When Wǔ Yuánhéng was stationed in the west,
in Chuān,
he took pity on Yáozuǒ's frail condition
and recommended him to serve as a pacification inspector,
also acting as magistrate of Guǎngdū County.
After one year, he passed away.
Zhāng Zào
During the Zhēnyuán era,
the Ministry of Revenue wanted to cut down the pagoda trees along the roads of the two capitals for firewood,
and replace them with small trees.
They first sent an official order to Huàyīn.
Huàyīn County Captain Zhāng Zào wrote a judgment on the order, saying:
"Where Duke Shào rested,
the trees were not cut down;
where the former emperor once traveled,
how can we dare to fell them?"
The plan was then abandoned.
Lǚ Yuányīng
Lǚ Yuányīng served as the Tuánliàn of È-Yuè.
One night, he climbed the city wall,
but the parapet was already locked.
The guard said:
"Military law forbids opening the gate at night."
Yuányīng told him:
"The Vice Censor-in-Chief is climbing the wall himself."
The guard replied:
"In the dark, it is impossible to distinguish right from wrong.
Even the Vice Censor-in-Chief may not pass."
Yuányīng then returned.
The next morning,
he promoted the guard to a high position.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ was a scholar who admired antiquity,
and was famous in his time.
In the late Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
an edict was issued requiring monks and nuns to be tested on a certain number of pages of scriptures.
Those who failed
were ordered to return to secular life.
Zhāngwǔ was then serving as Deputy Governor of Chéngdū.
A mountain monk came to visit him, saying:
"I have practiced meditation for years,
and have never recited scriptures.
Now I am being forced to take the test,
and my previous efforts will be wasted.
I hope you, elder, will consider my situation."
Zhāngwǔ gave him a poem, which said:
"The Southern School has always allowed expedient means,
so where in the heart is there still a need for scriptures?
Go well to the clouds and waters by the bìchú,
for on which mountain are the pines and cypresses not green?"
The examiner then exempted him.
Yuán Zhěn
Yuán Zhěn served as a censor
and was sent on a mission to Dōngchuān.
In Xiāngchéng, he wrote a poem titled "For Magistrate Huáng,"
the preface of which reads:
"In previous years, I once drank in Xiè County,
and I was often the toastmaster.
Once, in the hall of Deputy Magistrate Dòu,
a man arrived late
and repeatedly violated the drinking rules,
so he was forced to drink over a dozen cups in succession.
Unable to bear the exhaustion,
he fled the banquet.
After sobering up, I asked about him
and learned he was Deputy Magistrate Huáng of the former Yúqīng.
After that, I never encountered such a situation again.
In the third month of the fourth year of Yuánhé,
I was sent on a mission to Dōngchuān.
On the sixteenth day,
I arrived at Póuchéng.
Looking at the post station, there was a large pond
with magnificent towers and pavilions.
After a while,
Magistrate Huáng came to welcome me.
Observing his appearance,
I vaguely recognized him.
Asking about his previous position,
I realized he was the same Deputy Magistrate Huáng who had fled the banquet.
When I recounted the past events,
Huáng was puzzled at first but then understood.
He then offered me a jug of wine
and invited me aboard his boat.
At the time, I was on the road where Zhūgě had once campaigned,
and I was overwhelmed by feelings of the present and memories of the past.
So I composed the poem 'For Magistrate Huáng,' which goes:
In former years, we once drank to our heart's content.
Magistrate Huáng was exhausted by the flying cups.
He fled the banquet back then,
but today he greets me before my horse.
Vaguely, I forget names and titles,
but gradually, I recognize a lifetime's acquaintance.
Old friends are all far away,
but in a foreign land, my eyes are briefly clear.
He invites me to sit side by side on the couch,
and together we pole the boat along.
Thoughts of wine are scattered by the wind,
frost edges sweep level with the ground.
Unable to bear deep or shallow toasts,
I am still moved by the sentiments of past and present.
Winding along the Qīpán Road,
sloping up to the city walls several zhang high.
Flowers seem to smile like the woman of Bāo,
the plank walkway recalls Lord Wǔ's campaign.
One kind lies buried in secluded stones,
old and idle, a name for a thousand years."
In □
When Chancellor Niú Sēngrú was sitting for the imperial examinations,
he knew that Yú □ was exceptionally talented,
so he specially went to Xiāngyáng to seek his acquaintance.
After staying for several days,
he was received twice,
but was treated as an ordinary visitor.
Niú angrily left.
After he had gone,
Yú suddenly summoned his guest officer and asked:
"Has the scholar Niú left in the past few days?"
The officer replied:
"He has already left."
"What did you give him as a gift?"
He said:
"Five hundred coins."
"Did he accept them?"
He said:
"He threw them in the courtyard and left."
Yú was greatly regretful,
and said to his aides:
"My affairs are numerous,
and there must have been oversights."
He immediately ordered a junior officer,
to take five hundred bolts of silk,
and a letter,
to pursue him.
He said:
"If he has not left the boundary,
bring him back immediately;
if he has already left the boundary,
then give him the letter."
The junior officer caught up with him outside the boundary,
Niú did not open the letter,
but bowed and returned.
Xuē Shàngyǎn
When Yú □ was powerful in Xiāngyáng,
the court sent the senior eunuch Xuē Shàngyǎn to oversee his army.
When Shàngyǎn arrived,
□ initially did not treat him well,
but Shàngyǎn remained calm.
After ten days,
he requested to go on an outing,
and when he returned to his residence in the evening,
the tents, carpets, and various utensils
had all been renewed;
moreover, fifty oxcarts were lined up,
filled with colorful silks.
Shàngyǎn nodded,
but said nothing.
□ sighed and said:
"What kind of omen is this?"
Gāo Chěng
Gāo Chěng served as a Secretariat Drafter for nine years,
yet his home had no drafts of imperial edicts.
Someone asked:
"Previous generations all had collections of edicts,
why did you burn them?"
He replied:
"The words of the sovereign should not be kept in private homes."
Lǚ Yuányīng
When Lǚ Yuányīng was the留守 of the Eastern Capital,
he often played chess with a recluse.
During a game,
official documents piled up,
and Yuányīng was just then holding a brush to review them.
His chess partner thought that Lǚ would certainly not pay attention to the game,
so he secretly moved a piece to secure his own victory.
Lǚ had already noticed it,
but the chess partner was unaware.
The next day,
Lǚ asked the chess-playing recluse to go elsewhere,
and no one inside or outside could understand why.
The chess player also felt uneasy,
so Lǚ gave him bolts of silk as a parting gift.
About ten years later,
Lǚ fell seriously ill and was nearing his end.
With his children and nephews gathered before him,
Lǚ said:
"In your associations and friendships,
you must choose carefully.
When I was the留守 of the Eastern Capital,
there was a chess player, and so on,
I dismissed him for another matter.
Moving one chess piece
is not worth minding,
but the intention behind it is fearsome.
If I had spoken of it immediately,
I feared he would be worried and frightened;
if I never spoke of it,
I was afraid you might be careless in your understanding."
After speaking,
he passed away with a sigh.
Wáng È
Master Hóng said:
"The southeast of Yǒngníng Ward in Cháng'ān is the golden cup land,
and the west of Ānyì Ward is the jade cup land."
Later, Yǒngníng became the residence of Wáng È,
and Ānyì became the residence of the Prince of Běipíng, Mǎ Suì.
Later, both Wáng and Mǎ's properties were taken into official possession.
Wáng's residence was successively bestowed upon Hán Hóng and others,
Shǐ Xiànchéng, Lǐ Zàiyì, etc.
This is what is called the golden cup breaking and then being mended;
Mǎ Suì's became the Fèngchéng Garden,
which is the jade cup breaking and remaining incomplete.
Another account says,
Lǐ Jífǔ's residence in Ānyì,
and Niú Sēngrú's residence in Xīnchāng,
Master Hóng called Lǐ's residence the jade cup,
once broken, it cannot be made whole again.
The golden bowl may be damaged,
but it can perhaps be remade.
Niú's residence was originally the home of the Director of the Palace Buildings, Kāng Lóng.
Lóng himself discerned the lay of the hills and terrain,
believing that his residence would produce a chancellor.
Later, whenever the annual appointment of chancellors was made,
Lóng would crane his neck to watch.
The residence was eventually obtained by Sēngrú.
Lǐ's residence later came into the possession of Liáng Xīn.
The Jiangxi Post Station Official
In Jiāngxī, there was a post station official who prided himself on his competence.
He reported to the prefect,
that the station was in order,
and requested an inspection.
So the prefect went.
The first room was the wine storeroom,
with all kinds of fermented beverages fully matured.
Outside, there was a painted deity.
The prefect asked:
"Who is this?"
He said:
"Dù Kāng."
The prefect said:
"Your efforts are more than sufficient."
Another room was called the tea storeroom,
with all kinds of teas fully stored.
Again, there was a deity.
Asked who it was,
he said:
"Lù Hóngjiàn."
The prefect was even more pleased.
Another room was called the pickle storeroom,
with all kinds of vegetables fully prepared.
Again, there was a deity.
Asked which deity it was,
he said:
"Cài Bójiē."
The prefect laughed heartily and said:
"You are mistaken."
Wáng Zhòngshū
When Wáng Zhòngshū was a court official,
he was friendly with Mǎ Féng.
He often reproached Féng, saying:
"Your poverty is unbearable,
why not seek epitaph commissions for relief?"
Féng replied:
"I just saw someone galloping on horseback to call a doctor,
I can wait."
Zhōu Yuàn
During the Yuánhé era,
several officials in the ministry were drinking freely in the department,
talking about their lifelong preferences and aversions.
Some said they loved paintings and board games,
others feared reckless actions and flattery.
Zhōu Yuàn, an official in the Ministry of Works, alone said:
"I love the observation commissioner of Xuānzhōu.
I fear tigers."
Zhāng Jiàn
From the time Zhāng Jiàn began his official career until he became the Director of the Palace Library,
he often held diplomatic posts,
went to the frontier three times,
and died at Chìlǐng.
The Lotus Water Clock
The Yuè monk Sēngchè obtained the lotus water clock on Lúshān,
and passed it on to Wéi Dān, the surveillance commissioner of Jiāngxī.
Originally, Huìyuǎn, because in the mountains they did not know the water clock,
took copper sheets to make a device,
shaped like a lotus flower.
Placed on the water in a basin,
water leaked through a hole in the bottom,
and when half full it would sink,
sinking twelve times each day and night,
serving as a rhythm for religious practice.
Even with the varying lengths of winter and summer days,
or when clouds obscured the moon or it was dark,
there was no discrepancy.
Táng Qú
Jìnshì Táng Qú was learned in literature,
but grew old without achieving success.
He was skilled at weeping;
every time he uttered a sound,
the tone was mournful and poignant.
Whenever he encountered human affairs that were pitiable,
Qú would weep for them,
and those who heard would shed tears.
Once while traveling in Tàiyuán,
he encountered a military feast,
and after drinking became merry, he wept.
The entire gathering was displeased,
and the host ended the banquet because of it.
Face Powder Money
The surveillance commissioner of Húnán had a provision called "the wife's face powder money,"
which began with the wife of Yán Gǎoqīng.
The prefect of Liǔzhōu also had this money,
which was provided by a military officer for the prefect's wife.
Is this not absurd!
Wéi Zhíyí
In the early Yuánhé era,
Wéi Zhíyí was demoted to registrar of Yázhōu.
Prefect Lǐ Jiǎ, pitying him as a traveler far from home,
thus issued an official document stating:
"The aforementioned official has long served in the ministerial courts,
and is quite familiar with public affairs.
We are fortunate to hope for his assistance in governance.
Do not hesitate to detain a worthy man;
it is necessary to request that he act as military yátuī."
Lǐ Guāngyán
Lǐ Guāngyán had achieved great merit for his time,
and his position and reputation were prominent and illustrious.
He had a daughter who was not yet betrothed,
and his staff advisors thought he would certainly select an excellent son-in-law.
Taking a casual opportunity,
one greatly praised a certain Xiùcai named Zhèng,
for his literary learning and family background,
his graceful demeanor and refinement,
hoping that Guāngyán would give his daughter to him in marriage.
On another day he mentioned it again,
and Guāngyán then declined to the staff advisor, saying:
"I, Guāngyán, am but a military man.
Having encountered many difficulties,
I happened to establish some slight merit.
How could I presumptuously seek a famous clan,
and invite gossip?
I have already selected an excellent son-in-law myself,
which you gentlemen do not yet know."
He then summoned a minor clerk from the reception office,
pointed at him and said:
"This is the match for my daughter."
He immediately promoted him to a close position,
and moreover divided his wealth to support him.
When the staff heard of it,
they all considered it appropriate.
Consider that Guāngyán lived in an era of flourishing civil governance,
and feared the disaster of 'the bow being stored away' after its use.
His actions aimed at avoiding harm from afar,
and the principle lay in avoiding suspicion.
How would he dare to form ties with powerful clans,
thus certainly undermining his original intent?
Compared to those who must marry from the Guó or Gāo clans,
or seek marriage with Wáng or Xiè families,
is he not far superior?
Lǐ Yì
In the early Chángqìng era,
Zhào Zōngrú served as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
presiding over the suburban and temple rituals.
He had been removed from the position of chancellor for over thirty years,
and was seventy-six years old,
yet public opinion considered him vigorous and healthy.
The regular attendant Lǐ Yì laughed and said:
"Zhào is a jìnshì whom I, as an examination official in the Eastern Prefecture, sent forward."
Wú Wǔlíng
During the Chángqìng era,
Lǐ Bó was appointed surveillance commissioner of Guìguǎn,
and recommended the famous Confucian scholar Wú Wǔlíng as his deputy.
According to precedent,
when the deputy assumes office,
he should present his quiver and bow case and formally express thanks.
A few days later,
a banquet was held at the polo field.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Wú then heard that women were gathering in the viewing stands to watch,
and felt deeply ashamed by this.
Wú, being proud and spirited,
wished to retaliate for this humiliation.
He then went up,
sat cross-legged on the platform,
lifted his clothes, exposed himself, and urinated.
Bó, being intoxicated,
saw this and became greatly enraged,
ordering the guards to send him to the yá office for beheading.
At that time, there was a yá officer named Shuǐ
Lán,
who knew this could not be done.
He therefore used proper protocol to stop and rescue him,
sending many people to guard him.
Bó was extremely drunk,
was helped back to his quarters to sleep,
and woke up late in the night.
Hearing his family gathered and weeping very sorrowfully,
he was startled and asked the reason.
They then said:
"Yesterday we heard noise and clamor from the pavilion feast,
and also heard the order to the yá office to behead the deputy commissioner.
Not knowing the details of the matter,
we feared disaster would befall us,
hence our grief."
Bó was greatly alarmed,
and urgently sent a messenger to inquire.
Shuǐ Lán reported in full:
"Although I received the strict order yesterday,
I did not dare to carry it out.
Now the deputy commissioner is still sleeping in the yá compound,
unharmed."
Bó at dawn
went early to the yá compound,
humbly apologized and admitted his fault.
Host and guest, superior and subordinate,
all blamed themselves,
and their mutual respect increased.
At that time there was no army supervisor,
so he then recommended Shuǐ Lán for the prefect of Yízhōu as a reward.
Although Wǔlíng had literary talent,
he was fierce, stubborn, provocative, and contentious,
and was feared by others.
He had also once served as a regional inspector within Róngzhōu,
prefect,
and his corruption crimes were numerous and flagrant.
An imperial edict
ordered the staff officers of Guǎngzhōu to interrogate him.
The investigating officer was young,
and also proud of his own examination success.
He showed absolutely no leniency,
pressing the case with great urgency.
Wǔlíng could not bear his indignation,
and therefore inscribed a poem on the roadside Buddhist hall, which said:
"The sparrow comes pursuing the high typhoon,
Looking down on the hawk and harrier, its spirit proud.
It claims it can grow wings for a thousand miles,
Yet at dusk it returns again to the weeds."
Wéi Qiándù
Wéi Qiándù served as palace censor,
with duties in the Eastern Capital.
Niú Sēngrú, because he topped the decree examination list,
first,
was appointed captain of Yīquē.
When attending at the censorate for an audience,
Qiándù did not know the basis of Sēngrú's official appointment.
He asked what background he had for entering officialdom.
Sēngrú replied:
"Jìnshì."
He asked again:
"How did you manage to enter the capital region?"
Sēngrú replied:
"I passed the decree examination consecutively,
and shamefully topped the list."
Sēngrú was quite surprised in his heart,
and upon returning told Hán Yù about it.
Yù said:
"You, sir, are truly a young scholar,
so Censor Wéi certainly would not know.
I passed the examinations over ten years ago,
and my reputation for wildness
has already filled the world,
yet Censor Wéi still does not know of me.
Why should you find it strange?"
Zhào Zōngrú
Zhào Zōngrú, while serving as Acting Left Vice Director and concurrently as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
oversaw the Court which had a lion dance performance.
It was equipped with the colors representing the five directions,
and was not performed except for court assemblies or diplomatic banquets.
At this time, a eunuch in charge of the music of the Imperial Music Bureau
sent an official document requesting it.
Zōngrú did not dare to refuse,
and reported the matter by memorial to the Chief Ministers.
The Chief Ministers considered that this matter fell under the jurisdiction of the relevant office,
and that it was inappropriate for him to have reported it to them.
Zōngrú was endlessly worried and fearful.
The Chief Ministers reprimanded him for being timid and incapable of handling affairs,
had him transferred to a sinecure post,
and appointed him as Junior Mentor to the Crown Prince.
Xí Kuí
Regarding the edict for Hán Yù's initial demotion,
Drafter Xí Kuí composed the text, which said:
"He achieved the imperial examination degree early,
and also gained some reputation."
After Xí had passed away,
many of his friends said:
"Xí had no worthy sons or younger brothers;
how could he have suffered from yin-toxin cold damage and yet avoided eating unclean things?"
Hán said:
"Xí avoided eating unclean things too late."
People asked:
"Why?"
He said:
"His wording was inappropriate.
How could there be a reproachful statement saying merely
'also gained some reputation'?"
Liú Yǔxī
When Niú Sēngrú was preparing for the examinations,
he was often looked down upon by his peers.
He once submitted his writings to Reminder Liú Yǔxī.
Facing his guests, Liú unrolled the scroll,
swiftly wielding his brush to alter and delete the text.
Moreover, he said:
"Our esteemed senior is sure to achieve his aim."
Although Niú bowed in thanks for the polishing,
he remained resentful.
After more than thirty years had passed,
Liú was transferred to Rǔzhōu,
while Sēngrú was governing Hànnán.
Niú made a detour and halted his procession there.
After staying for two nights, during a wine-induced revelry,
he directly expressed his meaning through a poem.
Liú, understanding the poem's intent,
finally realized it referred to his alteration of Niú's manuscript years before.
He therefore admonished his sons, Xiánzuǒ and Chéngyōng, saying:
"I intended to fulfill the aim of helping others mature,
but never expected to do wrong.
Moreover, Minister Niú of Hànnán
possesses lofty insight and broad capacity,
with few who can compare.
In the past, Zhǔfǔ Yǎn's household
was exterminated by Sūn Hóng;
Jī Shūyè met his death due to Zhòng Huì's words.
Therefore, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi warned his son, saying:
'In my great fits of anger,
and my minor faults,
be careful not to imitate them.'
As you pursue advancement,
maintaining moderation is the best course."
Sēngrú's poem said:
"For forty springs a Lang official in the Vermilion Office,
Among famed seniors past and present, no one else compares.
Let's not discuss the world's affairs of rise and fall,
But just behold the person present before the wine cup.
Pearls and jade should turn to coughs and spittle,
Mountains and rivers still seem to reveal their vital spirit.
Do not resent my relying on wine to speak lightly;
I shall yet present my writings to follow in your dust."
Yǔxī's poem said:
"In former years I once served as a minister of the Hàn court,
In late age, only this old, ailing body remains.
When first I saw Xiàngrú completing his rhapsody,
Later, for the Chancellor, I became a gate-sweeper.
Recalling past events, I sigh long and deep,
But rejoice, blessed by your radiant presence, frequent in talk and laughter.
I still have the old cap and sword from those times;
Awaiting you for three days, I'll brush off the dust."
Niú chanted and harmonized with the poem,
and his previous resentment somewhat dissipated.
He said:
"The matter of 'three days',
how dare I presume to accept it?!
Thereupon, they moved the feast and reveled the whole night,
before finally setting their procession in order to depart.
Téng Mài
Téng Ní devoted himself earnestly to poetry.
Traveling afar to Jízhōu,
he called upon his clansman, Mài.
Mài thought, "In our family, scholars are rare;
this younger brother is truly a thousand-li steed."
He often recited his lines:
"White hair cannot tolerate a Prime Minister,
Yet, like an idle guest, covers the whole head."
Also, from his "Inscription on an Egret Screen":
"Reflected in water, it holds deep meaning;
Seeing people, it shows no fearful heart."
Mài further said:
"Emperor Wén of Wèi admired Chén Sī's learning;
Pān Yuè praised Zhèngshū's writings.
It honors gathering the fragrance of one house;
why consider a clansman as distant?"
After Ní had taken the autumn examinations,
he took up his satchel to announce his travels,
and left a poem as a farewell.
Lord Téng, upon receiving it,
said with sorrow:
"In this life, I surely will not meet this young man again."
When he saw him off at the pavilion of Dàgāo,
the parting held unusual emotion.
Ní, when autumn deepened,
passed away at an inn in Shāngyú.
All who heard of it were wounded by grief.
Ní's poem said:
"In early autumn, on the river, bidding farewell to banners and flags,
For homeland and family, tears are about to fall.
A thousand li away, I know not where to set my foot;
The road ahead is just the time to listen to gibbons' cries.
In vain I strove with letters, my body ages emptily;
To return to woodcutting and fishing, the plan is now too late.
Wings broken and scattered, I cannot fly;
The crimson sky has no path to reach the Jasper Pool."
Lǐ Zōngmǐn
Lǐ Déyù was in Wéiyáng,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn was in Húzhōu,
appointed as a Guest Official with a sinecure.
Déyù was greatly afraid,
and sent a special envoy,
bearing generous gifts and goodwill.
Zōngmǐn did not accept them,
but took the route through Jiāngxī instead.
Not long after,
Déyù entered the position of Chancellor,
and passed through Luò.
Zōngmǐn was anxious and fearful,
and sought through various means someone well-connected to deliver a letter,
pleading
for a single meeting,
hoping to resolve the conflict.
The reply letter said:
"Resentment? There is none.
But a meeting would be without cause."
Initially, Déyù and Zōngmǐn had been on good terms early on,
both in the capital and the provinces,
mutually supporting each other's influence.
But as their positions rose,
they gradually began to undermine each other.
When Zōngmǐn was in power,
and Déyù was Minister of War,
Déyù, having gained a strategic advantage,
was certain to be greatly employed.
Zōngmǐn obstructed him through various means.
When Duke Bīn, Dù Cóng, entered the court,
he was a member of Zōngmǐn's faction,
and at the time was the Governor of the Capital District.
One day,
he visited Zōngmǐn,
and found him deep in thought.
Dù said:
"What are you pondering so deeply?"
He replied:
"Guess what I am thinking."
Dù said:
"Could it be about 'the Great Rong'?"
He said:
"It is indeed.
But how can we remedy this?"
Dù said:
"I have a plan,
but I fear Your Excellency will certainly not use it."
He said:
"Please tell me."
Dù said:
"The Great Rong has literary talent,
but did not advance through the imperial examinations.
If we let him oversee the examinations,
he would surely be pleased."
Zōngmǐn fell silent,
and after a long while said:
"Consider a lesser option."
Dù said:
"There is another office
that could also appease his discontent."
Zōngmǐn said:
"What office?"
Dù said:
"The Censor-in-Chief."
Zōngmǐn said:
"That would work."
Duke Bīn repeatedly made an agreement with him,
then hurried to visit and said:
"Just now, Chancellor Zōng had an intention,
which he ordered me to convey."
He then spoke of the appointment as Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Déyù was surprised and delighted,
and tears suddenly fell in pairs.
He said:
"This is a high-ranking official position;
how dare I, a humble man, accept such a recommendation?"
He repeatedly expressed his gratitude.
Dù returned to report,
and Zōngmǐn again discussed it with Yáng Yúqīng.
In the end, it was sabotaged,
leading to future calamities.
Féng Sù,
during Emperor Wénzōng's reign,
served both in the capital and the provinces,
and enjoyed an excellent reputation.
He came close to becoming Chancellor several times.
He was also skilled at currying favor with the powerful eunuchs of the Northern Bureau,
and won the favor of them all.
One evening,
a Palace Commandant sealed a box
and sent it to him.
Opening it,
he found two black
hats inside,
along with perfumed facial ointments and the like.
At that time, officials currying favor with powerful eunuchs
who were about to receive a high appointment
would always receive such items as a token.
Féng was overjoyed,
and first presented them to Chancellor Yáng Sìfù,
as he had often served in his secretariat.
Féng also had a fondness for splendid, fresh, and clean attire,
and from evening until dawn,
would wear multiple layers of fine clothing.
He selected several swift horses,
with saddles and trappings gleaming on the ground,
unmatched by any.
Féng, believing he had received the token,
thought it improper to attend court in his usual order,
and wanting to fully indulge in satisfaction,
changed his appearance and attire before entering.
When he reached the waiting area,
an official announced there was an edict,
but he pretended not to know.
When the time came,
there was indeed an edict.
The herald held the silk proclamation—
it must be for the Chancellorship.
As it was about to be announced,
the herald faced the hall,
bowed deeply holding the decree,
and loudly called out the name of the high official being appointed.
Then he shouted loudly:
"Xiāo Fǎng!"
Féng collapsed in shock,
was helped back to his residence,
fell ill, and died.
It turned out that when the draft appointment was being prepared that evening,
and was about to be sent to the Academy of Scholars,
Emperor Wénzōng said to his close ministers:
"Féng Sù's character
does not seem calm and steady;
Xiāo Fǎng, currently overseeing the Salt and Iron Monopoly,
in my observation,
possesses the demeanor of a senior minister."
Thus, he replaced him.
Lǐ Huí
In the early years of the Tàihé era,
Lǐ Huí served as a staff officer in the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
overseeing the examinations.
He did not recommend Wèi Mó,
and Mó deeply resented him for this.
During the Huìchāng era,
Huí was serving as Vice Minister of Justice,
while Mó was the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Once, Mó was waiting for an audience at the palace gate
along with several other officials who had the privilege of direct audience.
Mó said:
"Years ago, when I was a candidate from the prefecture,
I had the honor of not being recommended by you, sir.
What brings us together here today?"
Huí immediately replied:
"Even now, I would still not recommend you."
Mó's expression changed at this,
and his resentment grew even stronger.
Later, when Huí was demoted to serve as Prefect of Jiànzhōu,
Mó attained a high ministerial post.
When Huí submitted official documents,
Mó refused to accept any of them.
Subsequently, Huí became angry with a minor official under his jurisdiction
and had him caned and dismissed from his post.
In Jiànzhōu, such minor officials
could shield people from corvée labor,
and those seeking to be registered under their protection
would spend no less than several hundred thousand cash.
This official was not distressed by the caning,
but only hated being dismissed and barred from service.
He therefore fled to the capital
to appeal his grievance to the current chief ministers,
but none of the ministers would hear his case.
At noon one day,
he was resting under the shade of a pagoda tree,
looking haggard and worn.
A bystander, noticing he seemed troubled,
quietly inquired,
and the man recounted his whole story.
Thereupon, the bystander advised him, saying:
"...The Prefect of Jiànyáng (Lǐ Huí) has long been at odds with the Vice Director of the Secretariat (Wèi Mó).
Why don't you,
go to him?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
they saw Wèi Mó's mounted attendants coming down from the Secretariat.
The man always carried his written petition with him,
so he did as advised,
and bowed toward the approaching dust.
The attendants in the vanguard asked him,
and he replied:
"A commoner from Jiànzhōu appealing a grievance."
When Wèi heard this,
he reversed his horse-tail whisk,
and tapped his saddle, ordering a halt.
Upon reading the petition,
it listed over twenty accusations.
The first item stated
that he had taken children of the same clan into his residence.
Wèi Mó then used this to vigorously forge a major case against him.
At that time, Lǐ Huí had already been transferred to the post of Prefect of Dèngzhōu.
While traveling and passing through Jiǔjiāng,
he encountered an imperial censor sent to investigate the case,
and was forced to return to Jiànyáng.
He was ultimately convicted and demoted to Military Advisor of Fǔzhōu,
and died in that place of exile.
Zhōu Fù
When Yuán Zhěn was in Èzhōu,
Zhōu Fù served as his aide.
Zhěn once composed a poem
and ordered the staff in his bureau to compose matching verses.
Fù then put on his official cap, held his tablet, went to see Zhěn, and said:
"I merely associated with eminent men,
and mistakenly obtained a degree.
In truth, I am incapable of both poetry and prose."
Zhěn praised him, saying:
"To be so honest and sincere
is worthier than being skilled in poetry."
Yáng Xīgǔ
was a member of the prominent Yáng clan of Jìngtài.
They formed cliques and alliances,
often pledging to die for one another.
Their power and influence were overwhelming,
and their strength was unshakable.
They were comparable to the Cuī clan from the same locality,
but were more sincere and honorable.
Xīgǔ's nature was pedantic and eccentric.
When he first sat for the Jìnshì examinations,
he submitted his writings to a Vice Minister.
The Vice Minister praised them.
Xīgǔ then rose and replied:
"These writings
are not my composition."
The surprised Vice Minister questioned him further,
and he said:
"These were composed for me by my younger brother, Yuánbō."
The Vice Minister was greatly astonished and said:
"Nowadays, among those seeking fame,
more than half use ghostwriters.
If they tuck a scroll in their sleeve
and present it to a senior,
there is none who does not privately boast,
thinking no one is their equal.
Your intent,
is enough to rectify this decadent trend."
He was also fanatically devoted to Buddhism.
He often kept monks in his residence,
displayed Buddha statues,
mixed with banners and canopies,
creating what is called a 'place of practice'.
Every day at dawn,
he would enter this space,
prostrate himself on the ground,
and have a monk stand on his back
while reciting the *Diamond Sutra* three times.
He was also extremely fastidious about cleanliness.
When the internal urge to relieve himself arose,
he would first remove all his clothes,
and only then go wearing high clogs.
Liǔ Yǔxī
Liǔ Yǔxī,
demoted from Vice Director of the Bureau of State Farms to Military Advisor of Lǎngzhōu,
remained there for a full ten years
before being recalled to the capital.
It was spring,
and he composed a poem titled "For the Gentlemen Viewing Flowers":
"Purple paths, red dust brush against one's face;
All who return speak of viewing flowers.
In the Xuándū Temple, a thousand peach trees stand—
All planted after Liǔ Láng went away."
The poem spread throughout the capital that very day.
Someone envious of his fame
reported it to the chief minister,
falsely accusing him of harboring resentment.
On another day when he had an audience,
the chief minister sat with him,
offering him generous consolation.
But as soon as he took his leave,
the minister said:
"Your recent new poem—
it unfortunately caused you trouble.
What can be done?"
Not many days later,
he was sent out as Prefect
of Liánzhōu.
Liǔ Yǔxī himself recounted:
"In the spring of the 21st year of the Zhēnyuán era,
when I was Vice Director of the Bureau of State Farms,
this temple had no flowers.
That year, I was sent out to govern Liánzhōu.
Reaching Jīngnán,
I was further demoted to Military Advisor of Lǎngzhōu.
After residing there ten years,
an edict summoned me to the capital.
Everyone was saying
that a Daoist priest had personally planted celestial peach trees,
and the whole temple was ablaze like red clouds.
Thus I wrote the former poem,
merely to record the event of the time.
Soon after,
I was sent out to govern again,
this time to Liánzhōu for fourteen years,
before I finally became Director of the Bureau of Receptions.
Revisiting the Xuándū Temple,
it was utterly desolate, without a single tree left,
only hare's-foot clover and wild oats
swaying
in the spring breeze.
Therefore, I composed another twenty-eight-character poem,
to await future visits.
This was in the third month of the second year of the Tàihé era."
The poem reads:
"A hundred acres in the courtyard, half are moss;
Peach blossoms all gone, rape flowers now bloom.
Where is the priest who planted the peach trees now?
The Liǔ Láng of before has come again alone."
Cuī Zhènshǐ
During the Huìchāng era,
the imperial army campaigned against Zhāoyì,
but for a long time had not achieved success.
The enemy's roving troops
often scattered and emerged from the mountain foothills,
plundering Xíng, Luò, Huái, and Mèng.
They also dispatched several thousand light troops,
disguised as a flock of sheep,
scattered across the mountain valleys,
to lure the imperial army.
The imperial soldiers saw them from afar,
and so divided up to ambush and capture them.
Consequently, they were not in formation,
and moreover were unprepared,
whereupon close-quarters combat ensued,
trampling and chaos multiplied,
over a distance of several tens of *lǐ*,
and the imperial army suffered a great defeat.
That month,
the Eastern Capital and its borders,
along with the various prefectures,
hearing of this, were greatly shaken,
and all increased their preparations and tightened security.
The commanders-in-chief Wáng Zǎi and Shí Xióng, among others,
all fortified their positions and defended themselves.
Emperor Wǔzōng sat in court displeased,
and summoned his chief minister Lǐ Déyù and others, saying to them:
"Wáng Zǎi and Shí Xióng,
do not fight the rebels for Us,
and though We have repeatedly dispatched palace commissioners to urge them on,
We still hear of their hesitation and vacillation.
How can We allow the rebel faction to simply reach the Eastern Capital?
You, Sir, today may return late for Our sake,
and separately devise and arrange matters for the army at the front, then report back."
At the time, the chancellors Chén Yíxíng and Zhèng Sù
stood silently with clasped hands, listening to the command.
Déyù returned to the Secretariat,
and immediately summoned the Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Huí,
fully explaining the Emperor's intent.
He said:
"The Vice Censor-in-Chief must make a trip,
to reprimand the military commanders,
so that success may be seen early.
Be careful not to disobey."
Huí accepted the command at that very moment,
and so submitted his name for the Emperor's information.
It was said:
"We now wish to appoint Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Huí as the Urge-the-Army Commissioner."
The Emperor said:
"Approved."
That very day,
Lǐ set out from the Yíntái,
with fifty officials from the lodging bureaus guiding and accompanying him,
until he reached Hézhōng,
where he advanced at a leisurely pace,
waiting for Wáng Zǎi and others to arrive at the Hézhōng border to welcome him,
before proceeding.
The two commanders arrived east of Yìchéng,
standing armed on the left side of the road,
in the manner of outer prefecture colonels welcoming a superior.
Huí halted his horse,
and received their formal greetings and inquiries about his well-being.
The two commanders then advanced a few steps further,
bowed deeply and delivered their address,
but Huí flicked his whip,
paying them little heed.
Once the formalities were completed,
the two commanders moved to the side,
bowing their heads and awaiting orders.
Huí, from atop his horse, said sternly:
"Where is the duty clerk for today?"
The assembled officials spurred their horses forward to receive orders.
Huí said:
"Demand from them a written pledge with a deadline for defeating the rebels."
The two commanders bowed deeply, sweating,
and requested sixty days to defeat the rebels.
Should they exceed the deadline,
they requested that military law be applied to them.
Thereupon, the two commanders were greatly frightened,
and leading their personal troops, they beat the drums,
and the soldiers advanced together.
In all, after fifty-eight days,
they attacked and captured Lùchéng,
and presented the severed head of Liú Zhěn.
The task accomplished,
Huí returned to report.
Sixty days later,
he was promoted from Vice Censor-in-Chief to Vice Director of the Secretariat and Participator in Determining Governmental Matters.
Lǐ Qúnyù
After Lǐ Qúnyù had relinquished his post at the Tiānlù Pavilion,
and was returning to Cényáng,
he passed by the temple of the Two Consorts,
and inscribed two poems, which said:
"North of Little Lone Islet, by the cloud-fringed shore,
The two maidens, bright-adorned, still stand serene.
The wild temple faces the river, spring's stillness profound;
Ancient tablets, wordless, amid lush, tangled grass.
The east wind near the tomb blows fragrant angelica;
The setting sun deep in the mountains, the cuckoo weeps.
Still as if frowning, gazing toward the imperial tour—
The Jiǔyí peaks, like dark brows, beyond the Xiāng River."
And also:
"Before the Huánglíng Temple, sedge grass in spring,
The maiden of Huánglíng in bright crimson skirt anew.
A light boat, small oars, she goes off singing her song—
Far waters, long mountains, enough to kill with sorrow."
Later he inscribed another:
"Before the Huánglíng Temple, spring has emptied out;
The cuckoo drips blood, wailing in the pine-swept wind.
I know not where their pure spirits have now fallen—
I suspect they wander in the clouds of autumn hues."
Lǐ himself felt that the second
poem,
moving from 'spring emptied' to 'autumn hues,'
was hesitant and wished to revise it,
when two young ladies appeared, saying:
"We are Éhuáng and Nǚyīng.
Two years from now,
we shall join you, Sir, in a journey of clouds and rain."
Lǐ then noted what they had said,
and in a moment their figures vanished.
He then paid respects to their divine images and departed.
Crossing again the lakes and mountains,
he reached Xúnyáng.
The prefect Duàn Chéngshì, long a friend of Lǐ's through poetry and wine,
was told the whole story.
Duàn therefore teased him, saying:
"I did not know you were Emperor Yú Shùn's Marquis of Pìyáng."
Two years after Qúnyù inscribed the poems,
he passed away in Hóngzhōu.
Duàn then wrote a poem mourning him, which said:
"Thirty years amid wine and verse,
Reckless and abrupt, the world's noisy din.
In enlightened times, not dying like Mí Héng,
Having scorned all nobles, you return to the Nine Springs."
And also:
"Adding talk of Huánglíng affairs,
Now hastened by the bright day's call.
Old, without children's burdens,
Who will weep for you at the spring terrace?"
Wēn Tíngyún
Wēn Tíngyún enjoyed great fame for his lyrics and rhapsodies.
Initially, when he was about to be recommended from his hometown,
he traveled as a guest between the Jiāng and Huái regions,
and Yángzǐ's deputy Yáo Xù bestowed generous gifts upon him.
Tíngyún was young then,
and the money and silk he obtained
were mostly spent in the pleasure quarters.
Xù was greatly angered,
caned him and drove him out,
and because of this, Tíngyún ultimately failed the examinations.
His elder sister,
the wife of Zhào Yǐ,
each time Tíngyún failed the exams,
would gnash her teeth at Xù.
One day,
there was a guest in the hall,
and Madame Wēn happened to ask the guest's name.
The attendants replied that it was Xù.
Madame Wēn then came out into the main hall,
stepped forward, seized Xù's sleeve, and wailed loudly.
Xù was utterly astonished,
and moreover, her grip on his sleeve was firm,
and he could not free himself,
not knowing what to do.
After some time,
Madame Wēn finally said:
"My younger brother, in his youth, feasted and roamed—
a common human sentiment.
Why did you cane him?
To this day he has achieved no success;
is this not due to you?"
She wailed loudly again,
and only after a long time did she release him.
Xù returned home, indignant and shocked,
and in the end fell ill because of this and died.
Miáo Dān
Miáo Dān passed the imperial examination and became a jìnshì,
living idly in Luòyáng for years,
unable to endure his poverty.
Someone suggested that to divine his future prospects,
he could use sound-based divination.
Dān immediately ordered his sons and nephews to sweep and clean the main hall,
set up a table and burn incense,
fasten his belt and hold his official tablet,
sitting upright to await a single word.
His residence was remote and secluded,
and for a long time, he heard nothing.
As the day grew late,
a vendor selling dried fish arrived,
and Dān focused his mind intently to listen carefully.
His household servant called out repeatedly,
and the vendor carried the fish inside.
In truth, he had not a single coin,
and only after a long while did he come out.
The vendor, delayed by his exit,
was already angry,
and upon seeing that someone had slightly cut his fish,
the vendor looked at it,
and cursed:
"Beggar boy,
you'll starve to death in the end,
why do you delay me like this?"
Earlier, Dān had once returned from traveling outside,
and on the way fell seriously ill,
unable to climb or ascend.
Suddenly, he saw someone returning with a coffin cart,
and because the price was cheap,
he hired it and rested inside.
Upon reaching the east gate of Luòyáng,
the gatekeeper did not know there was someone inside,
and questioned where it came from.
Dān thought he was surprised at him,
and slowly replied:
"A scholar fell ill on the road,
unable to afford other things,
please do not find it strange."
The gatekeeper said:
"I have guarded this gate for thirty years,
and have never seen a coffin that can speak."
Later, Dān ended up as the governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Péi Xūn
Péi Xūn's appearance was short and small,
and his nature was especially straightforward and unrestrained.
Once drinking with his father, Péi Chí,
during a gathering,
Chí ordered a flying cup toast,
each time addressing the person,
they had to describe themselves.
Chí passed the cup to Xūn and said:
"A short man talks too much,
a broken cart needs many wedges.
Péi Xūn, a thousand points."
Xūn drank and returned the cup, saying:
"The bat does not see itself,
yet laughs at the swallow on the beam.
Eleventh Young Master, ten points."
Chí was the eleventh son,
and in anger, he beat Xūn.
Cí'ēn Temple was connected to Qǔjiāng
and various scenic spots in the capital,
and each year, the names of those who newly passed the examinations
were all listed here.
Xūn often went sightseeing with relatives and acquaintances,
and seeing his father's name and those of other families on the plaques,
most were already deceased,
he said to others:
"These are all records of ghosts."
Dèng Chǎng,
was a student of Fēng Jiào.
Initially, when he took the examinations,
due to his humble and poor background, he did not pass.
Niú Wèi and his brothers,
sons of Niú Sēngrú,
had influence,
and were also wealthy.
They said to Chǎng:
"We have a younger sister who is not yet married,
would you be willing to marry her?
We will exert our efforts for you,
how could it be just one examination success?"
At that time, Chǎng was already married to a woman from the Lǐ family,
whose father had served in Fújiàn,
rising to the rank of Píngshì,
and had two daughters who were both skilled in calligraphy.
The examination papers Chǎng submitted
were mostly written by these two daughters.
Chǎng considered himself poor and lowly,
and certainly
unable to achieve rapid advancement,
so he selfishly coveted their offer,
and agreed.
After
passing the examination,
he married into the Niú family.
Not long after,
Chǎng took his Niú family wife and returned home.
As they approached home,
Chǎng deceived his Niú family wife, saying:
"It has been a long time since I returned home,
please allow me to go ahead and wait for you,
is that acceptable?"
The Niú family wife agreed.
Upon arriving home,
he did not dare reveal the matter.
The next day,
the Niú family wife's servants drove her luggage straight in,
and immediately brought out the curtains, miscellaneous items, and things she usually enjoyed,
arranging them in the courtyard.
The Lǐ wife was shocked and said:
"What is this for?"
The servant said:
"Our lady is about to arrive,
and ordered us to display these."
The Lǐ wife said:
"I am the wife,
who is this 'lady'?"
She then clutched her chest, wailed loudly, and collapsed to the ground.
When the Niú family wife arrived,
she realized she had been betrayed,
and requested to see the Lǐ wife, saying:
"My father is a chancellor,
and my brothers all serve in the ministry,
even if I were disliked, could I not find a place to marry?
Is my misfortune
only yours, madam?
Now, I wish to share this with you, madam.
Even if you resent Dèng Láng,
can you bear not to consider your two daughters?"
At that time, the Lǐ wife was about to take the matter to the authorities,
but her two daughters held her sleeves and stopped her.
Later, Chǎng served as Assistant Director of the Imperial Library, assigned to the eastern capital,
and was extremely stingy.
When Huáng Cháo entered Luòyáng,
he fled to Héyáng to avoid the chaos,
where the military governor Luó Yuángǎo invited him to serve as deputy.
Later, when Huáng Cháo's rebels came again,
he fled with Yuángǎo,
but all the gold and silk he had hidden underground
were taken by a group of bandits.
Cuī Xuàn,
son of Cuī Yuánlüè.
The death of Lú Shèn,
a military advisor in the capital,
was caused by Xuàn,
and public opinion at the time considered it an injustice.
Xuàn's son, Cuī Hàng,
during the Qiánfú era,
also became chancellor.
During Huáng Cháo's rebellion,
his entire clan was slaughtered,
and public opinion considered it retribution for Lú Shèn's death.
Initially, although Cuī Xuān was a remonstrance official,
his marriage leave
was a private matter;
although Lú Shèn held a government post,
it was a public matter.
They argued over the use of a courier station hall.
After Shèn was imprisoned,
he wrote a letter to the chancellor,
comparing himself to Mèngzǐ
and likening Xuān to Qián Fèng.
Xuān had extensive factional connections,
and everyone did their utmost for him.
Shèn came from a humble background,
and moreover, Xuàn was also Xuān's student,
and as chancellor at the time,
he submitted a false accusation.
Xuān was demoted from Left Rectifier of Omissions to magistrate of Yángzhái,
and as Shèn traveled to Chánglè Slope,
he was ordered to commit suicide.
A palace envoy happened to return,
encountered Xuān,
took out a throat from a bag and said:
"Rectifier,
this is Lú Shèn's throat."
Xuān was deeply displeased.
When the capital fell,
the Cuī family's sons also had their clan slaughtered.
Alas!
They say the Way of Heaven is lofty,
how clear it is!
Wáng Duó
When the late Chancellor, Duke of Jìnguó, Wáng Duó, was serving as a Vice Director,
Lǐ Pián was in charge of the Ministry of Revenue.
Every year, rice was transported from the Jiānghuái region to the capital,
with the cost of water and land transport
amounting to seven hundred cash per dǒu.
The price of rice in the capital
was forty cash per dǒu.
A proposal was made to stop transporting rice from Jiānghuái,
and instead collect seven hundred cash per dǒu.
Duó said:
"This is not a good plan.
If we purchase rice in the capital,
it will inevitably deplete the capital's food supply;
if we transport rice to replenish Guānzhōng,
from Jiānghuái to the capital,
it will also benefit countless poor people along the way."
At that time, the system of purchasing rice had already been implemented,
and in the end,
no one dared to oppose the proposal.
When the government in the capital purchased rice,
the price of rice indeed rose sharply.
Within less than ten days,
the Ministry of Revenue requested to abolish the system,
because
no people came to sell rice.
Then those with insight
admired Duó's ability to foresee events.
Duó eventually rose to high office because of this.
Lǐ Pín
Lǐ Pín and Wáng Duó passed the imperial examination in the same year.
Later, both gained official positions,
but Pín often feared that Duó would become chancellor first,
leaving him behind.
By the time Lù Yán was sent out to govern a province,
Pín's influence had further declined.
Duó was gentle and easy to control,
which endeared him to the eunuchs.
When Wéi Bǎohéng was about to be appointed to a high position,
he could not precede his patron.
He was going to appoint Duó,
and Pín secretly learned of this.
Carrying a pot of homemade wine, he visited Duó and said:
"You are about to be promoted to an important post.
I fear I may not be able to cling to your coattails.
I wish to serve you in advance, even in a small way.
May I?"
He then ordered wine and drank.
Duó's wife, née Lǐ, suspected it was poisoned,
and sent a maidservant
to relay a message to Duó:
"You may risk your own life,
but please think of your wife and children."
Pín exclaimed in surprise:
"Do you think this wine of mine is poison?"
He immediately called for a large cup,
filled it himself,
drank it, and left.
Wéi Bǎohéng
Wéi Bǎohéng wanted to appoint Péi Xiū as a Vice Director in a ministry.
At that time, Lǐ Zhāng was the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Wéi first sent Lú Wàng to convey his intention,
to sound out whether it was possible.
Lǐ said:
"The Chancellor should just make the appointment;
there is no need to consult me first."
Lú thought that if the current chancellor's authority
were thwarted by Lǐ,
it would damage his dignity.
Therefore, he advised Wéi not to make the appointment.
The Robed Daoist
In the Táng dynasty, a scholar, after leaving court, went to visit a friend.
Seeing a robed Daoist seated there,
he left displeased.
Another day,
he said to his friend:
"Why do you favor such a coarse-robed fellow?
I don't understand his words,
and moreover, I find his odor offensive."
His friend replied:
"The odor of coarse robes
is hardly worse than that of bronze and milk.
The stench of bronze and milk
stands shoulder to shoulder with you,
and follows in your footsteps.
You live among them,
yet feel no shame,
and instead mock me for associating with a virtuous man of the mountains and wilderness?
Eminent men of the Southern Dynasties
considered the croaking of frogs and the scent of wild herbs superior to music.
I regard coarse robes
as far better than today's red and purple official robes."
Lù Qún and Lú Hóngzhèng
The Secretariat Drafter Lù Qún and the Supervising Secretary Lú Hóngzhèng
had different temperaments but were close friends.
Lù was thin, austere, and plain,
never speaking of the marketplace or court;
Lú was tall, robust, and prosperous,
never speaking of mountains or rivers.
Lù spent his days planning to recline in leisure;
when there were draft edicts,
he would review them at his residence;
Lú never requested leave,
and when there were visiting guests,
he would receive them at his office.
Though their preferences differed,
they were deeply fond of each other.
One day, there was heavy snow in the capital.
Lù was on leave,
while Lú was about to go to court late.
Passing by the Xīnchāng residence,
