he saw Lù at the thatched pavilion by the southern wall,
gazing at the mountain snow.
Wearing a deerskin hat and a crane-feather cloak,
he had built a fire and ordered wine,
enjoying the fine scenery.
Hearing of Lú's arrival,
he said with great delight:
"Just what I wished for!"
He immediately ordered him to be welcomed in.
Lú, resplendent in his golden and purple robes,
was dignified and imposing;
Lù sat in Daoist attire,
his mood solitary and pure.
Lù said:
"Lú the Sixth,
Lú the Sixth,
you never come to see me.
Why is that?"
Lú replied:
"My term is almost up,
and I still have to provide for my family.
I go to the Chancellor's residence daily
to seek
an appointment outside the capital."
Lù said with a sorrowful expression:
"To press against the gates of power—
why must it come to this?
Moreover, fate is predetermined;
you only weary yourself in vain.
My homemade wine is quite mellow;
will you stay for a drink?"
Lú said:
"There is urgent business at the ministry
waiting for my decision."
Lù then called to his servant:
"Lú the Sixth wishes to leave.
Bring the medicinal porridge prepared early this morning in two bowls;
I will share it with Lú the Sixth."
Lú said loudly:
"No, I cannot."
Lù asked:
"Why not?"
Lú replied:
"This morning's rice was cold,
and since I have a long journey ahead,
I have already eaten roasted meat at home."
When people of the time heard of this,
they thought that Lù's refined elegance
and Lú's outstanding vigor
each expressed their true natures.
Bì Xián
Bì Xián’s family was originally humble and poor.
At the beginning of the Xiántōng era,
his maternal uncle was still serving as a Wǔbó in Tàihú County.
Xián felt deeply ashamed of this,
and often had people persuade his uncle to resign from his post,
so that he could arrange an official position for him.
After repeated attempts,
the uncle ultimately refused to comply.
Xián then specially appointed a candidate named Yáng Zài as the magistrate of Tàihú,
inviting him to the ministerial residence,
and entrusted him with the task of removing his uncle from his lowly position
and sending him to the capital.
When Magistrate Yáng took office,
he fully conveyed Xián’s intentions.
The Wǔbó said:
"I am a lowly man;
how could I have a nephew who is a chancellor?"
Yáng insisted and urged him,
to which he replied:
"Every year in autumn and summer,
I consistently receive sixty thousand coins in customary fees.
If nothing goes wrong,
I will have ample means for life.
I wonder what official position the chancellor intends to appoint me to?"
Yáng then reported this in full to Xián,
and Xián also agreed with his reasoning,
ultimately not forcing his will.
The false chancellor of the Shǔ state, Yǔ Chuànsù, and his cousin Níngjì
once served as magistrates of Tángxīng County in Shǔ Prefecture.
Among the clerks was a man named Yáng Huì, who had modest talent and usefulness,
and the Yǔ brothers were mindful of him.
When they successively held power in Shǔ,
they wanted to appoint Yáng Huì as a Mǎzhǎng to repay him.
Huì said:
"My service as a clerk
is known far and wide.
To presumptuously take an official post
would hardly silence people’s talk.
How could I exchange the support of several thousand households
for the empty title of Mǎzhǎng?"
Although he was later given an honorary title,
he was only appointed as a Jiànjiào official,
and ultimately did not give up his county duties.
Lǐ Shīwàng
was a member of the imperial clan.
Confident in his own abilities,
he aspired to take on a regional governorship as his responsibility.
While traveling through Qióng and Shǔ,
he became thoroughly acquainted with the bravery and timidity of the southern barbarians,
and thus submitted a memorial,
requesting that several prefectures be carved out from Xīchuān
to establish the Dìngbiān Army Jiedushi in Línqióng.
The imperial decree approved this,
and Shīwàng was promoted from Deputy Magistrate of Fèngxiáng
to assume this post.
At that time, senior generals of Xīchuān resented his division of their jurisdiction
and secretly communicated with Nánzhào.
Thus, the barbarian armies, guided by local magnates near the border,
invaded and harassed the Shǔ region.
The military officer Dòu Pāng
was unable to stop them.
Shīwàng was also dismissed because of this.
Gāo Pián
When Grand Marshal Gāo Pián, Prince of Bóhǎi, was stationed in Shǔ,
while inspecting the border,
he arrived at Zīzhōng Commandery
and lodged at the prefect’s office.
Opposite the commandery, on the mountaintop, was the Kāiyuán Buddhist Temple.
That evening at dusk,
the monks performed rituals and chants,
with conch shells and Buddhist hymns alternating.
Bóhǎi
ordered the military patrols to arrest and shackle them all.
The next morning,
he had them flogged on the back and expelled.
Summoning his officers and officials, he said to them:
"The monks’ rituals and chanting
are not in themselves offenses.
But in this temple,
ten years from now,
dozens of bald men will rise in rebellion.
I am thus taking this action to suppress it in advance."
Later, local men shaved their heads, took up weapons, and called themselves the "Great Bald Ones" and "Lesser Bald Ones,"
occupying this temple as their stronghold.
Wéi Zhòu
Chancellor Wéi Zhòu was skilled at managing his livelihood.
East of Jiānglíng Prefecture, he had a country estate
with fine fields and excellent lands,
renowned as the most fertile;
he accumulated rice like a hill,
all of it surplus grain.
At the beginning of the Xiántōng era,
he was appointed Jiedushi of Lǐngnán.
Emperor Yìzōng, considering Pānyú a land of pearls and jade,
admonished him with the story of the Greed Spring.
Zhòu calmly memorialized:
"At my Jiānglíng estate, the stored grain
still amounts to seven thousand stacks.
Thus, I truly have nothing to covet."
The Emperor said:
"This is what is called a 'Man of Ample Grain.'"
The Son of the Wáng Family
After Huáng Cháo’s retreat from the capital,
repairs were made to the damaged and ruined areas.
At that time, a son of the Wáng family from Dìng Prefecture,
commonly known as Wáng Jiǔhú,
resided in the upper capital.
Extremely wealthy,
he contributed three hundred thousand strings of coins
to assist in repairing the Zhūquè Gate.
When Emperor Xīzōng decreed the reconstruction of Ānguó Temple was completed,
he personally descended in his carriage
to hold a grand vegetarian feast.
He then struck the new bell ten times,
donating ten thousand strings of coins.
He ordered the various high ministers
to each strike it as they wished.
The Emperor said:
"Whoever can donate one thousand strings of cash
may strike the bell once."
After the feast,
Wáng Jiǔhú, half-drunk, entered
and went straight up to the bell tower,
striking it one hundred times in a row.
He then had one hundred thousand strings of coins transported from the West Market into the temple.
Liú Tuì,
a native of Tónglú,
early on advanced through literary talent as a Jìnshì.
His father once admonished him, saying:
"Pursue your examinations and advancement as you will;
whether you end in poverty or success,
I place no expectations on you.
After I die,
be sure not to offer sacrifices to me."
He then boarded a small boat,
finding amusement in fishing,
and ultimately no one knew where he went.
Tuì later rose to high office,
and was appointed to govern Shāngyú.
His thoughts of offering seasonal sacrifices
thus ceased.
On his deathbed,
he also admonished his son
in accordance with his late father’s command.
The Shǔ Minister of Rites, Cuàn,
was his son,
and often spoke of this to his colleagues.
A gentleman remarked:
"Families upholding the teachings of propriety emphasize mourning and sacrifices.
What kind of man was this predecessor of the Liú family?
As for Tuì, a man of broad learning,
perhaps he had his reasons,
though the times did not understand them."
Pí Rìxiū
During the Xiántōng era,
the Jìnshì Pí Rìxiū submitted two memorials.
The first
proposed that Mèngzǐ be made an examination subject.
It read in part:
"Your servant has heard that the Way of the Sages
does not go beyond the Classics.
What descends from the Classics
does not go beyond the Histories.
What descends from the Histories
does not go beyond the Philosophers.
Among the Philosophers, the one whose Way does not differ
is Mèngzǐ.
To abandon this and follow the other philosophers
is to inevitably reject the Classics and Histories,
and such men are enemies of the Sages."
The text is lengthy and not fully recorded here.
He requested that the books of Zhuāngzǐ and Lièzǐ be abolished,
that Mèngzǐ be made primary,
and that those capable of comprehending his meaning
be selected in the examinations in the same manner as those proficient in the Classics.
The second memorial
proposed that Hán Yù be honored with sacrifice in the Imperial Academy.
It read in part:
"Your servant has heard that the Way of the Sages
lies in nothing more than seeking usefulness.
Usefulness
during one's lifetime
can be known for a time;
usefulness after death
can be known for ten thousand generations."
It further stated:
"Mèngzǐ and Xún Qīng
assisted and supported the Way of Confucius,
which continued down to Wénzhōngzǐ.
The Way of Wénzhōngzǐ was vast,
and the one who could succeed to its excellence,
was surely Hán Yù!"
Pí Rìxiū, styled Xíměi,
was a native of Jìnglíng in Xiāngyáng.
From youth he devoted himself to literature
and lived in seclusion at Lùmén Mountain,
calling himself the Drunken Chanting Scholar.
When he first arrived at the examination grounds,
the Vice Minister of Rites, Zhèng Yú, thinking his appearance unimpressive,
teased him, saying:
"Your talent and learning are considerable,
but what about that one day?"
He replied:
"Your Excellency should not discard two days because of one day."
Meaning that one should not reject a man's words because of the man,
and all the examination candidates admired and submitted to him.
He rose to the post of Erudite of the National Academy
and resided in Sūzhōu.
He was a literary friend of Lù Guīméng,
and authored the *Wén Sǒu*,
in ten volumes,
and the *Pízi*, in three volumes,
which were widely circulated.
He served as an administrative assistant to Qián Liú.
Prefect Guō
In Jiānglíng, there was a man named Guō Qīláng.
His family's assets were extremely abundant,
making him the wealthiest among the rich of Chǔ City.
Between the Jiāng, Huái, Hé, and Shuò regions,
all merchants relied on his goods for buying and selling in their travels.
In the early years of the Qiánfú era,
a merchant was in the capital,
and for a long time there was no news of him.
Master Guō went personally to inquire after him.
Having met him,
he recovered all that was owed,
amounting to only fifty or sixty thousand strings of cash.
The young man became addicted to the pleasures of courtesans,
obsessed with drinking and gambling.
After three or four years,
more than half was spent.
At that time, in the late Táng,
court administration was corrupt,
so the young man paid several million to the gate of those selling official titles,
and as a commoner easily obtained the post of Prefect of Héngzhōu.
He then decided to return to his hometown.
At that time, Zhǔgōng had recently suffered from the banditry of Wáng Xiānzhī.
The neighborhoods and people
were different from former days.
Returning to his old residence,
he found no buildings at all.
Inquiring after his family,
it took several days to learn.
His younger siblings had perished in the military turmoil.
Only his mother and one or two maidservants remained,
living in a few thatched huts,
their coffers completely empty,
making a living day and night by sewing and needlework.
Among the young man's luggage,
there were still two or three thousand strings of cash.
Relying on this, they managed to recover somewhat.
He then hired a boat to take his mother to his post.
Passing Chángshā,
they entered the Xiāng River,
and moored at the northern river of Yǒngzhōu.
On the bank was a Buddhist temple named Dōushuài.
That evening they lodged there,
tying the mooring rope under a large cedar tree.
At midnight,
suddenly a great storm arose,
waves churned, the bank collapsed,
the tree fell and pressed upon the boat,
the boat could not bear it and sank.
The young man and a boatman
pulled his mother
ashore,
barely escaping with their lives.
All the other maidservants and servants, along with their belongings,
were swept away by the raging waves.
At dawn,
they sought refuge in the monks' quarters.
His mother, shocked, fell ill
and died after several days.
In panic and distress,
he rushed to Línglíng
to report to the Prefect.
The Prefect arranged the burial for him,
and daily provided him with gifts.
Having observed the mourning period,
he then took up residence in Yǒng Prefecture.
Alone and poor,
with no relatives or acquaintances,
day and night he suffered from cold and hunger.
Having traveled the rivers and lakes since youth,
he was quite familiar with matters of wind and water,
so he took up steering poles on passing boats,
to seek food and clothing.
The people of Yǒngzhōu
called him "Pole-Grasping Prefect Guō."
From then on, his appearance differed from the past,
no different from the group of boatmen.
Lǐ Déquán
In the capital, there was a man named Lǐ Guāng,
of unknown origin.
He served Tián Lìngzī with flattery and sycophancy,
and Lìngzī favored him,
making him a commander of the Left Army.
One day, he was memorialized and appointed Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng,
but the day after the edict was issued,
he died without illness.
Lǐ Guāng had a son named Déquán,
over twenty years old.
Lìngzī then appointed him to an important post.
When Emperor Xī fled to Shǔ,
he followed Lìngzī in escorting the imperial carriage,
and stopped in Chéngdū.
At that time, Lìngzī and Chén Jìngxuǎn monopolized state power,
and everyone feared their authority.
Lǐ Déquán, being close to them,
was revered and served by all, near and far.
Crafty and powerful men seeking fame and profit
often bribed Déquán,
using him as a connection.
Within a few years,
he amassed bribes worth tens of millions,
and his official rank rose to Pillar of State with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon,
concurrently Vice Director of the Right.
Later, when Jìngxuǎn fell,
and he was pursued by officials,
he escaped and fled to Fùzhōu,
his clothes in tatters,
begging for food along the roads.
There was a man named Lǐ Ān,
who had often served as a stable hand in Fùzhōu,
and was acquainted with his father.
Suddenly seeing Déquán,
and pitying his ragged state,
he invited him to his private home.
Ān had no sons,
so he acknowledged him as a nephew.
Before half a year had passed,
Ān was about to die.
Déquán then changed his name to Yànsī,
and requested to succeed Lǐ Ān in service,
simply coveting his food and clothing,
that is all.
Soon he obtained a position as a horse keeper for the prefect,
and those who recognized him
all looked at him and said:
"Look, it's Horse-Tending Vice Director Lǐ."
Kǒng Wěi
After Kǒng Wěi, the Duke of the State of Lǔ, became Chancellor,
he said to his nephews and nieces:
"When I recently served as Vice Minister of War,
I, along with Wáng Jìngōng Duó,
served as Academicians of the Hóngwén Institute,
overseeing the institute's affairs.
After taking office,
while inspecting the halls,
Jìngōng said:
'In the past, when I served as Vice Minister of War,
I, along with Chancellor Dù Bīngōng Cóng,
served as Direct Academicians of the Hóngwén Institute,
overseeing the institute's affairs.
In late spring,
he invited me to admire peonies in this very hall.
He said:
"This hall, compared to when Wú Yì was in charge,
was occupied by him,
requiring only a single room.
Now it is so magnificent,
but you are unaware
that it will soon be reduced to ashes."
Upon hearing these words,
I engraved them in my heart.
He also said to me:
"In the future, you, my lord, may also occupy
this seat,
and perhaps it will be tolerable.
But for those who come after you,
they will suffer the consequences."
Looking at it from my perspective today,
Bīngōng's words
have largely come true.
'" At that time, Emperor Zhāozōng had just ascended the throne,
and Kǒng Wěi became Chancellor.
The affairs of the court,
its institutions,
were utterly ruined,
so Wěi was moved by the past words and lamented the times.
Lǐ Kèzhù
Lǐ Kèzhù served as the Chief Minister of the Dàlǐ Temple.
Emperor Zhāozōng was in Huàzhōu.
Cuī Luán, the magistrate of Zhèng County,
had a commoner accuse him of manipulating the price of silk and satin,
The prefect Hán Jiàn ordered it to be calculated as embezzlement,
and submitted it to the three
judicial departments for sentencing.
The Censorate and the Ministry of Justice
submitted a memorial,
stating that the crime warranted execution by hanging.
The Dàlǐ Temple did not submit a memorial for several months.
Jiàn asked Minister Lǐ:
"Is Magistrate Cuī a relative of yours?
Why haven't you submitted a memorial?"
Kèzhù replied:
"To assist in your governance."
Hán said:
"Magistrate Cuī committed embezzlement;
how can you say it is my fault?"
Lǐ said:
"I have heard that you have manipulated prices,
and the amount is nearly ten thousand."
Hán said:
"I am the military governor of Huàzhōu,
and the people of Huà are my people."
Lǐ said:
"The people of Huà are the Son of Heaven's people,
not your people.
If that is the case,
then the people of Zhèng County
are Magistrate Cuī's people."
Jiàn was convinced by his argument,
so he spared Magistrate Cuī from punishment,
and demoted him to the position of Deputy Magistrate of Yǐngyáng.
The Capital Scholar
Recently, several scholars in the capital gathered for a banquet,
and they discussed how a person's courage or timidity
must stem from their boldness.
If one's boldness is strong,
they will naturally have nothing to fear,
and can be called a true man.
Among the attendees, one scholar boasted:
"When it comes to boldness,
I truly possess it."
The others laughed and said:
"We must test it,
only then can we believe you."
Someone said:
"I have a relative's residence,
which was once extremely haunted,
and is now locked and empty.
If you can stay alone in this residence
for one night without fear,
we will treat you to a feast."
The man said:
"As you command."
The next day, he went there.
It was not actually a haunted house,
but merely temporarily vacant.
So they prepared wine, fruits, lamps, and candles for him,
and escorted him to the residence.
The others said:
"What else do you need, sir?"
He replied:
"I have a sword,
which can serve for self-defense.
Please do not worry."
The others then left the residence,
locked the door, and returned.
This man was actually quite timid.
As night approached,
he tied the donkey he had ridden to another room,
and his servants were not allowed to accompany him.
He then went to the pavilion to stay,
not daring to sleep at all.
He only extinguished the lamp, held his sword, and sat,
trembling with fear.
By the third watch,
the moon rose,
casting slanting light through the window cracks.
He saw something on the clothes rack that looked like a bird flapping its wings,
fluttering and moving.
The man, trembling, forced himself to stand up,
swung his sword once,
and it fell against the wall with a thud,
making a clattering sound.
After that, it was silent,
with no further noise.
Overwhelmed with fear,
he dared not investigate further,
but simply sat holding his sword.
By the fifth
watch,
suddenly something
climbed the steps and pushed the door.
The door did not open,
so it stuck its head out through the dog hole,
panting heavily.
The man was terrified,
swung his sword forward to slash,
but accidentally fell over,
dropping his sword.
He dared not look for the sword,
fearing the thing would come in.
He crouched and hid under the bed,
not daring to move further.
Suddenly, he became drowsy
and fell asleep until dawn.
The servants had already unlocked the gate,
and when they reached the pavilion,
they saw only the dog hole,
splattered with blood in a mess.
Everyone cried out in shock,
and the scholar finally came to his senses.
He opened the door, still trembling.
He recounted in detail the battle with the creature the previous night,
and everyone was astonished.
They searched under the wall,
and found only a straw hat,
half-broken on the ground—
the "bird" he had slashed at during the night.
It was merely an old, tattered hat
blown by the wind,
resembling a bird flapping its wings.
The sword was beside the dog hole.
Everyone then searched around the hall for traces of blood,
and found that the donkey he had ridden
had its mouth slashed,
with its lips and teeth broken.
It turned out that at dawn, when it was untied,
it stuck its head into the dog hole,
and was struck by the sword.
Everyone laughed uncontrollably,
supported him as they returned,
and the scholar was so frightened
that it took him ten days to recover.
Mèng Yǐ
In Xúzhōu's Xiāo County,
there was a farmer named Mèng Yǐ who excelled at trapping foxes and raccoon dogs.
He never missed a single one.
Once, taking advantage of a free moment,
he carried his spear and walked through the wilderness.
It happened that the sun was about to set,
when he saw, several hundred paces to the left of the road,
a desolate grave mound standing tall,
with a narrow path through the grass,
as if there were traces of someone.
So he entered it,
and probed the dark places with his spear.
It seemed as if someone grabbed and pulled it,
and it wouldn't budge.
He asked, "Are you a ghost or a human?
A monster or a spirit?
Why do you seize my spear and not let go?"
From the darkness came a reply:
"I am a human."
He then ordered him to come out.
The man fully and honestly told him:
"My surname is Lǐ.
Yesterday, I was a thief,
and was imprisoned in the military prison of Yǎnzhōu's military inspector.
My body was bound with all five types of shackles,
and where I was beaten,
wounds and bruises covered my entire body.
So I watched for a chance to climb over the prison wall,
and fled for my life here.
My life or death is entirely up to you."
Mèng took pity on him and was about to take him home,
placing him inside a double wall,
and later, after an amnesty was issued, he came out.
Mèng was known for being skilled at hunting;
among flying and running creatures,
none could escape him.
Yet one day, from within a desolate grave mound,
he retrieved a prison escapee and took him home.
Those who heard of it all laughed heartily at him.
The Wrestler of Zhènwǔ
During the Guāngqǐ era,
Wáng Biàn, the military commissioner of the four armies of the Left Shéncè Army, went out to garrison Zhènwǔ.
He held a banquet,
and after the music and performances were finished,
he ordered wrestling matches.
There was a man, extremely burly and tall,
who had come from a neighboring prefecture to compete in strength,
and over a dozen men in the army, in terms of physique and arm strength,
were all unable to defeat him.
The commander also admired his strength.
So he selected three men,
to face him one after another,
and the burly man defeated them all.
The commander and the seated guests
praised him for a long time.
At that time, there was a scholar sitting at the banquet,
who suddenly stood up and said to the commander:
"I can take this man down."
The commander was quite startled by his words,
but since his request was firm,
he allowed it.
The scholar descended the steps,
first went into the kitchen,
and after a short while came out,
then tucked in his clothes,
and advanced with his left fist clenched.
The burly man smiled and said:
"This one finger will surely knock him over."
As they gradually closed in,
the scholar quickly extended his left hand and showed it to him,
and the burly man fell down in a daze,
causing the entire gathering to laugh heartily.
The scholar walked slowly out,
washed his hands, and returned to his seat.
The commander questioned him:
"What technique was that?"
He replied:
"In recent years, while traveling as a guest,
I once met this man at a roadside inn.
As soon as he approached the dining table,
he staggered and fell.
A companion of his said:
'He's afraid of jiàng;
seeing it makes him fall immediately.'
I heard this and remembered it.
Just now I went to the kitchen,
asked for a little jiàng,
and held it in my hand.
When this man saw it,
he indeed fell over on his own,
merely adding to the banquet's amusement."
There was a military judge named Biān Xiù,
who witnessed this incident.
Zhào Chóng
Zhào Chóng was dignified, pure, and upright,
and no miscellaneous guests came to his door,
as he admired the style of Wáng Méng and Liú Zhēncháng.
His character was lofty and stern,
and he did not write literary compositions,
earning the nickname "Stele Without Inscription."
Whenever it came to transferring officials,
by old custom each would recommend one person to replace themselves,
but Chóng never recommended anyone.
He said:
"In the court, there is no one who can replace me."
Because of this, the world thought less of him.
Hán Wò,
in the first year of Tiānfù, entered the Hànlín Academy.
That winter,
the imperial carriage journeyed to Fèngxiáng,
and Wò had the merit of accompanying the emperor.
At the beginning of the restoration,
the emperor personally promised to appoint Wò as chancellor.
Wò memorialized:
"Your Majesty's fortune coincides with a restoration;
you must employ men of great virtue
to steady customs and morals.
My examination supervisor, the Right Deputy Director Zhào Chóng,
can meet Your Majesty's selection.
I beg to withdraw the appointment intended for me and confer it upon Chóng;
it would be a great blessing for the empire."
The emperor greatly praised and sighed at this.
The next day,
an edict was issued appointing Chóng,
along with the Vice Minister of War Wáng Zàn, as chancellors.
At that time, Liáng Tàizǔ was in the capital,
and having long heard that Chóng was frivolous,
and also having grievances with Zàn,
he rushed in to request an audience,
and before the emperor,
fully detailed the strengths and weaknesses of the two gentlemen.
The emperor said:
"Zhào Chóng was recommended by Hán Wò."
At that time, Wò was at the emperor's side,
and the Prince of Liáng rebuked him.
Wò memorialized:
"I dare not argue with a high minister."
The emperor said:
"Hán Wò, withdraw."
Soon after, he was demoted and sent to Mǐn.
Hence, Wò's poem says:
"With hands afflicted by wind, too lazy to unfold an eight-line letter,
With eyes ailing, I cease to watch the nine-move board.
Through the window, sunlight flies like wild horses,
Before my desk, bamboo tubes grow like reed pipes.
In planning my life, clumsy as adding legs to a snake,
In serving the state in peril, I once stroked the tiger's whiskers.
In this whole world, could there be none who silently understand?
I wonder who now would test the flutes of Qí."
Xuē Chāngxù
When King Qí, Lǐ Màozhēn, dominated Qín and Lǒng,
the secretary of Jīngzhōu, Xuē Chāngxù, was a pedantic and eccentric man.
This was his innate nature.
When it came to writing elegant prose and wielding the brush,
he was simply incapable.
Even meeting his wife had its appointed times.
He would always observe proper decorum:
first ordering a maidservant to relay messages back and forth,
going through several rounds of such exchanges,
and only when it was deemed permissible
would he then take a candle and go to her chamber.
Once there, after some lofty, empty conversation
and partaking of tea and fruit, he would withdraw.
If he wished to visit the curtained bedchamber,
the ritual was the same.
He once said:
"Because the matter of continuing the family line is of great importance,
I wish to divine an auspicious occasion for it."
He would always wait for an invitation and permission.
Later, when he followed the military governor of Jīngzhōu to lead troops at Tiānshuǐ,
and they faced off against the Shǔ forces at Qīngní Ridge,
the Qí army was hard-pressed by supply transport difficulties,
and upon hearing that the Liáng forces had crossed the border,
they secretly withdrew their troops overnight,
greatly fearing a surprise attack by the Shǔ army.
As the Jīngzhōu commander was about to depart,
he suddenly remembered while mounting his saddle and said:
"Pass on a message to the secretary:
tell him to mount up quickly."
After repeated urgings,
Xuē was found hiding under a thatched hut.
He said:
"Tell the Grand Tutor
to please go ahead first.
This morning is an inauspicious day for me."
The military commander was furious.
He had men haul him onto the saddle,
whipped his horse to drive it forward,
while Xuē still covered his face with something.
He said:
"It is proper etiquette on an inauspicious day not to see guests."
This was truly a human oddity.
Everyone in Qín and Lǒng knew of him.
Grand Tutor Jiāng
In Shǔ, there was a man known as Grand Tutor Jiāng.
His given name is lost.
He was from Xǔtián.
In his youth, he was captured by the Yellow Turbans,
losing both his parents.
He followed the First Ruler on campaigns,
repeatedly achieving meritorious deeds.
Later, he successively commanded several military districts,
rising to the highest official rank.
There was an old stableman named Jiāng
who had tended to fodder for decades.
Every time Jiāng entered the stables,
if he saw even a minor fault by the old man,
he would certainly flog him.
This went on for years.
Counting the total,
it neared several hundred lashes.
Eventually, the old man could no longer endure the whippings.
He tearfully pleaded with the lady of the house,
begging to be released to return to his hometown.
The lady asked:
"Where are you from?"
He replied:
"From Xǔtián."
"And what family do you have left?"
He replied:
"When I was captured,
I had a wife and a son.
To this day, I do not know their whereabouts."
She further asked his son's childhood name,
as well as his wife's surname, given name, and birth order,
along with close relatives in the household.
He told her everything.
When Jiāng returned home,
his wife relayed the full story,
that Old Jiāng wished to take leave and return home,
and through questioning had learned the names of his lost son and relatives.
Jiāng was greatly astonished.
Suspecting this was his father,
he sent someone to inquire in detail:
"What distinctive mark does your son have on his body?"
The old man said:
"My son has a black mole on the sole of his foot.
I don't remember anything else."
Jiāng broke into loud weeping.
He secretly had the old man escorted beyond Jiànmén Pass.
Then he memorialized to the First Ruler:
"My father has recently come from east of the pass."
He then brought him into his residence with gold, silk, carriages, and horses.
Father and son were reunited as before.
To atone for the fault of having beaten his father,
Jiāng provided alms to tens of thousands of monks
and never again whipped any of his attendants for the rest of his life.
Kǎng Yìchéng
During the Chángxīng era of the Later Táng,
the Imperial Guard Commander Kǎng Yìchéng
often assigned soldiers to private duties,
with one serving as a courtyard attendant at his residence.
He too had occasionally given him minor floggings.
Suddenly one day,
taking pity on the man's age, he asked his surname.
The man said his surname was Kǎng.
Upon further questioning about his hometown, clan, and offspring,
he realized it was his father.
They then embraced and wept.
Those who heard of it were all astonished.
Gāo Jìchāng
When Later Táng Zhuāngzōng crossed the river,
Gāo Jìchāng of Jīngzhǔ said to his retainer Liáng Zhèn:
"I served Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng
and barely escaped with my life.
Since the Lóngdé era,
I have sought only to live in peace.
Now I am going to have an audience with the emperor.
I must also test him.
If he plans to manage all four directions,
he will certainly not detain me.
If he transfers me to another military district,
that could be a blessing for my descendants.
This trip is decided."
After returning from the imperial court,
he said to Liáng Zhèn:
"The new ruler fought a hundred battles
before gaining Hénán.
To his meritorious officials, he boasts, showing a handwritten copy of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
He also raised a finger and said:
'I won the empire on the tip of my finger.'
Thus, the achievement belongs to him alone;
what place is there for his ministers and aides?
Moreover, he goes on hunting excursions for ten days without returning.
How can the sentiments of the court and the country endure this?
I can rest easy without worry."
He then built the western walled city,
preparing defenses against the enemy.
Within three years,
Zhuāngzōng lost the throne.
Such foresight of a hero,
accurate to the very moment,
truly deserved to be passed on to his descendants.
The Wife of Minister Shěn
There was a Minister of Works named Shěn whose given name is lost.
He once served as a personal aide to a military governor of Qín.
His wife was fierce and indiscreet,
and also jealous.
Shěn often felt as if he were in a prison.
Later, taking advantage of a period of leisure and retirement,
he took his wife and children,
and settled them in Fèngzhōu.
He himself went to Dōngchuān to travel and seek his fortune,
intending to permanently sever ties with his incompatible spouse.
Huá Hóng was governing Dōngshǔ,
and he and Shěn had been friends since their humble days.
He addressed Shěn as "elder brother."
When Shěn arrived, Huá went to the outskirts to welcome him,
grasped his hand and recounted their long separation,
and treated him like a true elder brother.
He then specially built a mansion for him,
with servants, horses, gold, silk, utensils, and curios—
lacking nothing.
He sent over a dozen female attendants and servants,
firmly forbidding them to return north.
Shěn also hinted slightly at his domestic troubles,
and had no intention of returning home.
After about a year,
a letter arrived from home,
saying his wife had left Fèngzhōu
and come to Dōngshǔ herself.
Shěn was terrified upon hearing this,
and immediately informed his host,
who sent people to turn her back.
His wife sent a letter,
solemnly pledging and vowing,
saying:
"From now on, I will certainly change my former nature,
and wish to grow old together with you."
She arrived within a few days.
When she first arrived,
she was quite gentle and mild;
but after ten days or so,
her former behavior resumed.
All the female attendants, maids, and servants were whipped and scattered like stars,
and her husband's head and face
were all scratched and bruised.
Huá Hóng heard of this,
summoned Shěn, and said to him:
"I wish to kill her for you, elder brother.
What do you think?"
Shěn said it was not permissible.
Ten days later, she acted out again.
Shěn then entered the government office,
his spirit utterly dejected.
Huá, knowing the situation,
secretly dispatched two men with swords,
dragged her out from behind the curtains,
and slew her at the foot of the steps.
They discarded the corpse in the Tóng River,
and then reported to Shěn.
When Shěn heard this,
he was overcome with shock and terror,
to the point of losing his senses.
The corpse remained in the rapids, not drifting away.
They then had someone poke it with a bamboo pole,
and it then followed the current.
The next day,
it was again in the same rapids as before.
This happened three times.
Huá had them tie a stone to it and sink it.
Shěn also, within less than ten days,
was lost,
his soul departed.
Was it not
that the incompatible spouse became a foe?
How tragic!
Did Shěn have some past enmity with her?
Yáng Qú
and Wáng Zàn,
were famous scholars of the central court.
There was a certain Yáng Qú from Hóngnóng
who once traveled beyond the mountain ranges.
Seeing the landscapes of Yángshuò and Lìpǔ,
he constantly cherished them in his heart,
and spoke of them incessantly.
Qú had frequented Zàn's household,
and as they interacted more casually,
he unconsciously expressed it in words, saying:
"Has the Vice Minister ever seen the landscapes of Yángshuò and Lìpǔ?"
Zàn replied:
"Unless one has beaten someone until their lips split and teeth fall out,
how could one get to see them?"
He then laughed heartily.
This saying meant that the lands beyond the ranges
were places one only went to if banished.
Yuán Jìqiān
Yuán Jìqiān, a Junior Director of the Imperial Armory of the Jìn, often recounted:
"I once resided in Qīngshè,
borrowing a
mansion to live in.
I heard it was haunted by many malign apparitions.
At dusk, I dared not step beyond the courtyard gate,
and the whole household was frightened,
unable to sleep peacefully.
Suddenly, one evening,
we heard a roaring sound,
as if someone was calling from inside a jar.
The sound was deep and muffled.
The entire family, master and servants alike, were terrified,
certain it was the most fearsome of the hauntings.
We then peeked through a crack in the window,
and saw a creature, bluish-black in color,
moving about in the courtyard.
That night the moonlight was dim.
After watching it for a long time,
it seemed like a dog's body,
but its head could not be raised.
We then struck its head with a staff.
Suddenly, with a loud crash,
the family dog yelped in surprise and ran off.
It turned out that day, people from the manor had come to deliver taxes,
and had cooked porridge right there.
The cauldron was still there with some leftovers.
So the dog had stuck its head into the empty vessel,
and couldn't get it out.
The whole family then burst into laughter,
and finally slept peacefully."
Emperor □
At the end of the Kāiyùn era of the Jìn dynasty,
the Khitan ruler Yēlǜ Déguāng was returning to his own country from Biàn,
when he died in Luánchéng of Zhào.
His people cut open his abdomen,
removed all the internal organs,
filled it with about a *dan* of salt,
and transported it back.
People of the time called it the "Emperor □."
